Causes of methemoglobinemia Drugs Local anesthetics : benzocaine, lidocaine, prilocaine Dapsone ; sulfonamides (incl. sulfamethoxazole) Nitrates and nitrites : nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, amyl, butyl and isobutyl nitrite Phenazopyridine ; phenacetin Chloroquine, primaquine Cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, flutamide Chemicals and food Aniline dyes (shoe dyes, marking inks) Naphthalene (mothballs); chlorobenzene; nitrophenol; paraquat; silver nitrate; TNT Nitrate-rich well water ; food high in nitrates or adulterated with nitrites Nitrous gases (arc welding); fire Inherited and infants Hemoglobin M; N

2 History Ask about Why it matters The episode Onset, duration, time of day, previous episodes A first episode always gets admitted. Recurrent episodes point to vasospasm or chronic disease. Triggers: cold air or water, emotional stress, altitude, exertion Cold or stress suggests Raynaud's . Altitude or exertion in someone with cardiopulmonary disease suggests desaturation. Chest pain, dyspnea, confusion Tissue hypoxia and ischemia, the patient who needs treatment now. Background Congenital heart disease, heart or lung disease The commonest setting for cyanosis. Ask what their usual saturation is. Hypercoagulable state PE or arterial thrombosis. Family history of cyanosis or blood disease Hereditary methemoglobinemia, hemoglobin M, G6PD deficiency. Exposures: the toxic causes Don't miss Every drug, including OTC, supplements and herbals Ask specifically about topical anesthetic sprays (benzocaine before endoscopy), dapsone, nitrates, sulfonamides and phenazopyridine . Home and work chemicals Aniline and azo dyes, phenacetin, nitrates, mothballs, well water. Dyes, metals, pigments on the skin Pseudocyanosis, which is a colour without hypoxia. Infants and children Poor feeding, sweating with feeds, lethargy, poor weight gain, breathing trouble Congenital heart disease. Episodic spells of cyanosis, fast breathing and agitation “Tet spells” in tetralogy of Fallot: less blood reaches the lungs and more is shunted right to left.

3 Physical Exam Spotting cyanosis is unreliable . Observers disagree, and room light, temperature and skin pigmentation all change what you see. Look where it's easiest to see. Check Look for → think Where is the blue? Lips, perioral skin, tongue, oral mucosa, conjunctivae Central cyanosis. Nail beds, fingers and toes Peripheral cyanosis. Check the pulses and capillary refill. Sharply demarcated white-then-blue digits, sometimes the ear or tongue Raynaud's. Face, neck and arms swollen, plethoric, with distended veins SVC syndrome. Vitals and airway Airway, work of breathing Upper airway obstruction, respiratory insufficiency. BP, HR, temperature Shock states. Temperature is usually normal. SpO 2 with peripheral pulses and refill A low reading with poor perfusion may just be poor circulation. A reading stuck near 85% suggests methemoglobin. Newborn RR > 60, apneic pauses, deep breathing, sweating with feeds Nonspecific: lung, heart, infection, metabolic, GI or CNS. Pauses may be CNS immaturity. Think congenital heart disease . Head to toe Mental status Hypoxic or toxic injury. Fundi Dilated, tortuous veins and papilledema in cyanotic congenital heart disease. Neck JVD (pulmonary edema, right heart strain). Lungs Crackles, wheeze, poor air entry. Heart Rate and rhythm, gallops, murmurs (especially in a newborn), central pulse strength. Abdomen Hepatosplenomegaly (polycythemia vera, right heart failure), a pulsatile mass or bruit (an aneurysm that embolizes). Extremities Pulses, refill, signs of chronic vascular disease (hair loss, a cold limb). Clubbing means chronic hypoxemia: cyanotic heart disease, endocarditis, COPD, CF, cirrhosis, Crohn's. Nail-bed hemorrhages or end-organ damage suggest a thrombotic or embolic process.

4 Investigations Test When · what it tells you Bedside The blood itself Chocolate brown , even in room air, suggests methemoglobin. Put a drop on white filter paper and expose it to 100% O 2 : normal blood turns bright red, methemoglobin doesn't change . Pulse oximetry Trap Methemoglobin absorbs both wavelengths (660 and 940 nm), so the probe reads about 85% whatever the real PaO 2 . Blood ABG (ideally on room air) The real SaO 2 and PaO 2 . A normal PaO 2 with cyanosis points to an abnormal hemoglobin. CO-oximetry Order it specifically for suspected methemoglobin or CO . It reports sulfhemoglobin as methemoglobin . Non-invasive pulse CO-oximetry gets less accurate below SaO 2 95% and above a methemoglobin of 14%. CBC and smear Polycythemia, erythrocytosis, anemia; red cell shape and fragments. D-dimer When PE is a possible cause. Imaging and cardiac Chest x-ray Consolidation, effusion, edema, pneumothorax. An abnormal heart or mediastinal shadow suggests congenital heart disease. ECG, on every new presentation Dysrhythmia, ischemia. Right axis deviation or RVH suggests cor pulmonale or pulmonary hypertension. Echo Septal defects in infants; valve disease at any age. CT pulmonary angiogram (or Doppler, rarely V/Q) Suspected PE. Ankle–brachial index Peripheral cyanosis that doesn't improve: arterial disease or occlusion.

5 Decision Rules Central cyanosis: ABCs, ABG, then oxygen A Improves on O 2 (PaO 2 ≥ 100 mmHg): get a CXR Normal heart shadow, so a lung cause. An infiltrate needs antibiotics and support. Pulmonary edema from CHF needs an ECG, an echo and diuresis. With no infiltrate, consider PE , hypoventilation, polycythemia or AV fistulae, and get a CTPA. If it's positive, anticoagulate and admit to the ICU. If it's negative, check the Hct: above 65%, phlebotomy plus IV fluids ; below 65%, IV fluids and admit. Abnormal heart shadow, so think cardiogenic. Get an ECG, echo and cardiac enzymes, support with inotropes, chronotropes or pressors, and look for the cause of the cardiogenic shock. Consult cardiology and admit. Patients with chronic cyanotic heart disease may not need the ICU, or even admission; ask their cardiologist. B No improvement (PaO 2 ≤ 100 or SaO 2 ≤ 70): get a CXR plus CO-oximetry, and methemoglobin, CO and cyanide levels In respiratory distress , look for tension pneumothorax (needle or tube), upper airway obstruction (open it, intubate, surgical airway if needed), bronchospasm (beta-agonists, steroids) and PE. Not in distress , think of a shunt or an abnormal Hb: chronic methemoglobinemia, G6PD deficiency, sulfhemoglobin, chronic cyanotic heart disease. Peripheral cyanosis: ABCs, SpO 2 , then oxygen A Improves on O 2 : think of a low-output state Hypovolemia needs fluids and a search for the cause. Sepsis needs fluids, antibiotics, pressors and source control. Cardiogenic shock needs an echo plus inotropes, chronotropes or pressors. B No improvement: think of vascular occlusion, and warm the limb It improves with warming : vasospasm from cold exposure. Refer to rheumatology and consider nifedipine. It doesn't : peripheral vascular disease, or an arterial embolus or thrombosis. Measure ABIs and call vascular surgery. In critical limb ischemia, consider IV heparin with them, and look for an embolic source (endocarditis, an AAA). The oxygen test What the response to high-flow O 2 tells you ↑ Improves : a diffusion problem. – Doesn't improve : a shunt or V/Q mismatch (consolidation, right-to-left cardiac shunt) or an abnormal hemoglobin . ! Not in distress and still blue on 100% O 2 : think cardiac shunt, methemoglobin or sulfhemoglobin. Methemoglobinemia: who gets methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes, plus O 2 Symptomatic hypoxia : dysrhythmia, angina, respiratory distress, seizures, coma, or Methemoglobin > 30% First decontaminate skin exposures

1 Differentials The things that kill are shock (usually septic), respiratory failure and CNS infection . Non-infectious causes exist but rarely present with fever as the main complaint. Infectious causes Critical Treat empirically, now Systemic Sepsis or septic shock , meningococcemia Neuro Meningitis , cavernous sinus thrombosis Resp Bacterial pneumonia with respiratory failure GI Peritonitis Emergent Find and treat in the ED Resp Bacterial pneumonia; peritonsillar or retropharyngeal abscess, epiglottitis (airway) Cardiac Endocarditis, pericarditis GI Appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, intra-abdominal abscess GU Pyelonephritis, PID Pelvic inflammatory disease: ascending infection of the uterus, tubes and ovaries. , TOA Tubo-ovarian abscess: a walled-off collection that complicates PID. Neuro Encephalitis, brain abscess Skin Cellulitis, soft-tissue abscess, infected pressure ulcer Non-emergent Common, usually outpatient Resp Otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis, bronchitis, influenza, TB GI Colitis, enteritis GU Cystitis, epididymitis, prostatitis Non-infectious causes Critical MI; PE or pulmonary infarction Intracranial hemorrhage; stroke NMS Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: fever, rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability after an antipsychotic. ; thyroid storm; acute adrenal insufficiency Transfusion reaction; pulmonary edema Emergent CHF; dehydration; recent seizure Sickle cell disease; transplant rejection Pancreatitis; DVT Non-emergent Drug fever ; malignancy Gout; sarcoidosis; Crohn disease Post-myocardiotomy syndrome Who is in front of you changes the list Patient What's usually going on Young, otherwise healthy Self-limited viral illness or a focal bacterial infection. Mortality is under 1%. Hunt for the rare killer: meningitis, meningococcemia, systemic MRSA, septic or toxic shock, peritonitis . Over 65, chronic disease, immunosuppressed Mostly bacterial : respiratory, urinary, skin and soft tissue (> 80%) . Also consider meningitis, cholecystitis, appendicitis and diverticulitis, which present atypically. Older adults have 5–10× the UTI risk and 15–20× the appendicitis risk, and even influenza can kill them. Fever or hyperthermia? Mechanism → what fixes it Fever Pyrogens (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, interferon) make the hypothalamus produce PGE 2 , which raises the set point . Antipyretics work because COX inhibitors block PGE 2 . Normal is 36.0–37.8 °C , and ≥ 38.3 °C is agreed by nearly everyone to be fever (the CDC uses > 37.8,

2 History Characterize the fever, find the source, then work out how vulnerable the host is. In older patients, family and caregivers often give the most useful history. Ask about Why it matters The fever itself Onset, duration, how high Sets the severity and the pace of the workup. Timing and pattern Some patterns point to a specific disease (e.g. periodic fevers in malaria ). Chills, then sweats Chills come while the set point is rising , so a reading taken early can still be normal. Recheck. Sweating means the set point is falling back. Antipyretics taken, and when Can hide the fever at triage. Where is the source? Cough, sputum, shortness of breath Pneumonia. Older patients often have neither cough nor dyspnea. Dysuria, frequency, flank pain UTI or pyelonephritis. Often completely absent in older adults . Severe sore throat, muffled voice A “hot potato” voice suggests epiglottitis or a deep neck abscess , which threatens the airway. Headache, neck stiffness, confusion Meningitis or encephalitis. Abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea An abdominal source. Lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia PID or TOA, so do a pelvic exam . Skin redness, wounds, boils; hot joints Cellulitis or a soft-tissue abscess; joint inflammation. Who is the host? Age > 65, diabetes, renal failure, chronic disease High risk, with a low threshold to admit. Cancer with recent chemo or radiation Suspect neutropenia or another immunocompromised state. Prosthetic valve, line, port or other device Endocarditis or device infection. Can be critical to the diagnosis. Recent surgery, admission or treatment Nosocomial organisms. Baseline mental and physical function Ask someone who knows them. A subtle change may be the only sign. Exposures and drugs Travel, recent or remote Exotic infections (e.g. malaria). MRSA risk Skin infections in household or close contacts; military, prison, contact sports. Full medication list Drug fever. A new antipsychotic raises NMS. Beta blockers blunt the heart rate response. Older adults: the atypical presentation Red flag Confusion, falls, trouble walking, new incontinence, not eating, lethargy, weakness May be the only sign of pneumonia or UTI. 75% of functional decline in nursing-home residents is infection.

3 Physical Exam Vitals first, then a head-to-toe hunt for the source . Let the patient's symptoms point you, but in the old and the immunosuppressed check everywhere, because the exam can be quiet. Check Look for → think Vitals Temperature: how you take it Rectal (or a bladder probe if there's a Foley) is the most accurate in the ED. Axillary and tympanic are unreliable. Oral readings are skewed by hot or cold drinks, smoking and hyperventilation. Rectal runs about 0.7–1.0 °C above oral . Temperature: no fever? The old, the very young and the chronically ill may not mount one. Temperatures fluctuate, so recheck . Heart rate Expect about +10/min for every 0.55 °C (1 °F) . A relative bradycardia suggests a beta blocker, factitious or drug fever, typhoid, brucellosis or leptospirosis. A frank bradycardia suggests rheumatic fever, Lyme disease, viral myocarditis or endocarditis. Respiratory rate Expect about +2–4/min per °C . More than that means a respiratory infection or the acidosis of shock . Blood pressure, mental status Hypotension and marked tachypnea predict a severe, complicated course. Head to toe Ears, sinuses, throat, teeth Otitis, sinusitis, pharyngitis, dental infection, peritonsillar or retropharyngeal abscess . Watch for the muffled voice. Fundi Rarely positive: disseminated candidiasis, miliary TB, endocarditis, toxoplasmosis, leukemia. Neck Lymph nodes, masses, a goitre or thyroid mass. Nuchal rigidity is useful if present, but it is often absent in the very young or debilitated even with meningitis. Cervical arthritis and Parkinson disease cause stiffness at baseline. Lungs Localized crackles or rhonchi, a rub, dullness. COPD, CHF and poor effort hide pneumonia in older adults. Heart A pericardial rub (pericarditis) or a new murmur (endocarditis). Abdomen Can be deceptively benign in older adults, people with diabetes and anyone on steroids or immunosuppressants. Rectal, when indicated Enteritis, perirectal abscess, prostatitis. Genitals and pelvis Bartholin abscess, urethral or vaginal discharge, epididymitis or orchitis. Pelvic exam for PID or TOA. Skin and extremities Rash, petechiae , hot joints, cellulitis or abscess. Bone tenderness without trauma (long bones, spine) suggests osteomyelitis or tumour. In the bedridden, look for pressure ulcers . What the skin can tell you Petechiae: pinpoint, flat and non-blanching. This leg is from ITP, but early meningococcal rash can look just like it, so the story and the vitals decide. James Heilma

4 Investigations Let the history and exam choose the tests. The two that matter most, especially in older adults, are the urinalysis and the chest x-ray . Test When · what it tells you First line Urinalysis Highly accurate for UTI, especially in men , though not foolproof. Chest x-ray Pneumonia. Harder to read with COPD, CHF, dehydration or chronic lung disease. ABG or VBG Picks out the critically ill (acidosis) who need treatment now. Tests that mislead WBC count Trap Neither sensitive nor specific. It can be high without serious infection and normal in life-threatening infection . Don't let it rule anything in or out. ESR and other inflammatory markers Patchy sensitivity and poor specificity. Cultures Blood and urine cultures For older or chronically ill patients with acute fever and no obvious source, and for any unexplained severe febrile illness. The results don't change what you do in the ED. Outpatient blood cultures Almost never. A patient sick enough to need blood cultures needs admission and empiric antibiotics. Abscess culture, Gram stain Culture skin and soft-tissue abscesses when the patient is at risk of MRSA. Indwelling line or port Culture it, and it may need to come out. Targeted Lumbar puncture Altered mental status, headache, meningismus, or neurologic symptoms that an infection outside the CNS doesn't explain. CT head before the LP Focal neurologic findings , or a suspected embolic source such as endocarditis, to exclude a mass or abscess. Never delay antibiotics for the CT or the LP in suspected meningitis. CT abdomen Appendicitis, diverticulitis, cholecystitis, obstruction, perforation, abscess. Plain abdominal films are rarely useful. Ultrasound Cholecystitis. Thyroid function tests When thyroid storm is suspected. Still no source Think broader: autoimmune (ANA, RF, ESR), malignancy, TB (PPD), and CT of the abdomen and pelvis.

5 Decision Rules The approach as a flowchart Febrile adult Unstable? Altered mental status · respiratory distress · hemodynamic instability Yes Resuscitate Quick history and exam, then airway and O 2 , monitor, IV fluids . Consider rapid cooling and broad-spectrum antibiotics, antivirals, antifungals . Once stable, do the full history and exam ↓ No Complete history and head-to-toe exam Meanwhile IV fluids, antipyretics, antiemetics and analgesia as needed Positive findings? Yes Targeted Order the specific tests , then treat or refer No Consider UA, CBC, CXR Positive results? Yes Targeted Back to the specific tests, then treat or refer No Reassess the clinical status Improved Watchful waiting and symptomatic treatment Unchanged Assign the likeliest category and work it up: Infectious Autoimmune: ANA, RF, ESR Malignancy Miscellaneous Consider the extra tests → Worsened Extra tests: LP, CT abdomen and pelvis, PPD, blood and urine cultures. Then resuscitate and give empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, antivirals and antifungals. Rosen's Figures 9.1 (unstable) and 9.2 (stable), redrawn as one chart. SIRS criteria How Rosen defines sepsis: SIRS plus an infection T Temperature > 38 °C or < 36 °C HR Heart rate > 90/min RR Respiratory rate > 20/min , or PaCO 2 < 32 mmHg WBC > 12,000 or < 4,000/µL , or > 10% bands Two or more = SIRS. Rosen notes that its reliability is increasingly questioned. A SIRS-positive patient can have a mild, self-limited infection or the start of severe sepsis, so it doesn't decide the disposition for you. Severe sepsis or septic shock needs IV fluids and prompt antibiotics. Beyond Rosen Sepsis-3 (2016) replaced the SIRS definition. Sepsis is now life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection , meaning an acute rise of ≥ 2 SOFA points. Septic shock means needing vasopressors to keep the MAP ≥ 65 with a lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids. qSOFA is two or more of RR ≥ 22 , altered mentation (GCS < 15) and SBP ≤ 100 . It predicts death and prolonged ICU stay in suspected infection, but it is not part of the definition. The 2021 Surviving Sepsis guideline recommends against using qSOFA alone as a screening tool in place of SIRS, NEWS or MEWS, because it is more specific but less sensitive. It also sets antibiotic timing: within 1 h for possible septic shock or probable sepsis. For possible sepsis without shock, do a rapid workup and give them within 3 h if infection is still likely. Singer M et al

6 Cases Two published cases, one decision at a time. Answer before you read on: the explanation opens only after you pick. Case 1 · a real case Fever, a spreading rash and a BP of 78 A young adult, the unstable side of the flowchart, and the rash in the pictures above The story A 26-year-old man is transferred from another ED for a higher level of care. He has never had a meningococcal vaccine and has an alcohol use disorder. A week ago he developed fever, chills and muscle aches. Since then he has had neck stiffness, nausea and vomiting , and a rash that is spreading fast . He also mentions a recent COVID-19 exposure. Temp 38.0°C BP 78/53 HR 185 Skin: a violet, net-like rash of purpura and petechiae covers both arms and legs, the abdomen and the chest. What do you do first? CT head, then a lumbar puncture, then antibiotics once the CSF confirms meningitis Draw blood cultures and wait for the Gram stain to pick the antibiotic Resuscitate (airway and O 2 , monitor, IV fluids) and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics now Give acetaminophen and recheck his vitals in an hour Resuscitate and give antibiotics now. A BP of 78/53 and a HR of 185 put him on the unstable side of the flowchart : resuscitation and broad-spectrum antimicrobials come before the workup is finished. Fever, a spreading non-blanching rash and shock is meningococcal septicemia until proven otherwise . CT and LP can come later, but they never delay the antibiotics. Blood cultures are fine if they take minutes, not if they take an hour. Beyond Rosen NICE: antibiotics within 1 hour of arrival. The first bloods Hematology & chemistry On admission Test Result Flag Reference White cell count 2.06 ×10 3 /µL L 3.98–9.57 Hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL L 13.0–17.0 Platelets 55 ×10 3 /µL L 150–400 PT 25.9 s H 11.9–15.0 PTT 52.5 s H 23.0–35.4 INR 2.3 H 0.9–1.2 Fibrinogen 159 mg/dL L 204–488 D-dimer > 20 µg/mL FEU H ≤ 0.50 Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL H 0.72–1.25 Using the SIRS criteria, how many can you confirm right now? None: 38.0 °C isn't a fever, so this isn't SIRS One: the heart rate Three: the temperature, heart rate and white count Two: the heart rate and the white count Two. SIRS needs a temperature above 38 °C, so 38.0 doesn't count. A HR of 185 (> 90) counts, and so does a WBC of 2.06, because below 4 counts as well as above 12. His RR wasn't reported. Two criteria plus an infection is sepsis by Rosen's definition . Notice that his white count was low , not high. A normal or low WBC never reassures you. Read the

1 Differentials Syncope causes up to 3% of ED visits , and nearly half are admitted or observed. Patients 65 and older make up 80% of those admissions. Recurrence is as high as 50%. Presyncope carries a similar mortality and is worked up the same way. Critical Rosen's must-consider list Life-threatening dysrhythmia ; MI Critical aortic stenosis ; HCM ; tamponade Massive PE Thoracic dissection ; AAA SAH ; stroke Severe hypovolemia or hemorrhage; ruptured ectopic Sepsis; toxic-metabolic derangement Emergent Cardiac and other Tachy: VT, VF, SVT, WPW, torsades Brady: sinus node disease, 2nd and 3rd degree AV block, pacemaker or ICD malfunction Channelopathies: long QT, Brugada Outflow: mitral, aortic or pulmonic stenosis; atrial myxoma; pulmonary hypertension; congenital heart disease Cardiomyopathy Hypoglycemia, hypoxemia (CO), seizure, drugs Usually benign Vasovagal : emotion, pain, instrumentation Situational : micturition, defecation, cough, swallowing, vomiting, Valsalva, weightlifting, after exercise Carotid sinus : necktie, shaving, turning the head Orthostatic : dehydration, drugs, autonomic failure Hyperventilation; psychogenic; breath-holding spells (children) Mimic How to tell Seizure May have an aura; postictal confusion ; tongue biting, incontinence. Brief myoclonic jerks happen in syncope too. Hypoglycemia Gradual onset, incomplete recovery without treatment; diabetes or insulin; sweaty, confused. Drop attack Not syncope : no loss of consciousness. Older adults; sudden loss of tone, ataxia, vertigo. Vertebrobasilar TIA, subclavian steal Brought on by a change in posture or neck movement, or by using the affected arm. Look for vertigo, dysarthria, dysphagia and unequal arm pulses . Narcolepsy and cataplexy, psychogenic Known history; a variable pattern; a diagnosis of exclusion.

2 History The history and exam alone give the diagnosis in about 45% of patients. Get the story from witnesses too, plus the paramedics' first vitals and rhythm strip. Ask about before, during and after. Ask about Points toward Before Setting and trigger: emotion, pain, needles, micturition, defecation, cough, eating Reflex (vasovagal or situational) . Standing up, after exercise, in the heat Orthostatic . During exertion Red flag Outflow obstruction (AS, HCM) or an exercise-induced dysrhythmia. About 30% of athletes who die during exercise had syncope beforehand. Sitting or lying down ; palpitations Red flag Fairly specific for a cardiac cause. Turning the head, shaving, a tight collar Carotid sinus hypersensitivity. Prodrome: lightheaded, sweaty, nauseated, vision greying Reflex or orthostatic. No prodrome raises the risk. Aura Seizure. During How fast it came on and how long it lasted Abrupt onset, or more than a few seconds of unconsciousness, suggests a serious (often cardiac) cause, though the data are soft. Jerking movements Can occur in any syncope. Prolonged convulsions suggest seizure. Injury from the fall Treat it, but don't let it distract you from why they fell . After Rapid, complete recovery Dysrhythmia, reflex. Incomplete recovery , with ongoing pain or dyspnea MI, PE, dissection, AAA, SAH (the symptom persists). Postictal confusion, tongue biting, incontinence Seizure. Associated symptoms Chest pain, dyspnea Ischemia, dissection (tearing, with back pain), PE . Abdominal or back pain AAA ; in a woman of reproductive age, ruptured ectopic . Sudden severe headache SAH (the sentinel event may resolve). Bleeding: melena, heavy periods; vomiting, diarrhea Anemia or volume loss, i.e. orthostatic. Perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm Hyperventilation. Background Heart failure ; CAD, structural heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, diabetes, hypertension CHF is the key predictor of short- and long-term death. These raise the risk; age, CHF and CAD predict mortality. Family history of sudden death before 50 Inherited channelopathy or cardiomyopathy. Pacemaker or ICD Device malfunction. Possible pregnancy Ectopic; the patient often doesn't know she's pregnant. Medications (see the next row) The commonest fixable cause in older adults, through polypharmacy and interactions. High-yield drugs QT-prolongers (amiodarone, sotalol, flecainide, procainamide, and many others), beta blockers , other antihypertensives and vasodilators (CCBs, nitrates, ACEi or

3 Physical Exam Focus on the cardiovascular and neurologic systems, and look for anything that explains a low-flow state. Check Finding → think Pulse rate and rhythm Tachycardia, bradycardia, other dysrhythmias. Blood pressure; orthostatic vitals when the story fits Shock. Orthostasis from hypovolemia or drugs. Orthostatic vitals help only when standing reproduces the symptoms with a significant HR rise or BP drop; they are unreliable as a measure of volume. Respiratory rate Tachypnea suggests hypoxia, PE or hyperventilation. Temperature Sepsis, causing volume depletion. Skin Pallor, sweating: poor perfusion. Head Trauma. Papilledema means raised ICP. Ketones on the breath mean ketoacidosis. Neck Carotid bruit (cerebrovascular disease); JVD (right heart failure, tamponade, PE ). Lungs Crackles, wheeze: infection or left heart failure. Heart Systolic murmur : aortic stenosis or HCM . A rub suggests pericarditis or tamponade. Abdomen A pulsatile mass means AAA. Rectal exam (if anemia or GI bleed suspected) Gross blood or melena . Pelvis Bleeding or adnexal tenderness: ectopic , anemia. Both arms' pulses and BP Unequal: subclavian steal or thoracic dissection . Neurologic exam Altered mental status or focal findings: seizure, stroke, other primary neurologic disease. Carotid sinus massage Safe, and occasionally revealing, when the history suggests carotid sinus hypersensitivity.

4 Investigations Test When · what it shows The one test for nearly everyone 12-lead ECG Yield 2–9% (lower under 40 with no heart disease), but cheap and non-invasive. Skip it only for young, healthy patients with a clear vasovagal story . Look for: Dysrhythmia, heart block, pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave) Long QTc Brugada : RBBB pattern with ST elevation in V1–V3 Ischemia, LVH or hypertrophy RV strain (PE) Diffuse ST elevation or electrical alternans (pericarditis, tamponade) Cardiac monitor in the ED Catches transient dysrhythmias. Only when the history and exam point there CBC; rectal exam Anemia or a GI bleed. Glucose, electrolytes Hypoglycemia, metabolic causes. β-hCG Any woman who could be pregnant: ectopic . Troponin; D-dimer; BNP MI; PE; CHF. Add a CXR or lung ultrasound when CHF is suspected. Toxicology screen, ABG, prolactin Drugs; acid–base, hypoxemia, CO; seizure. CT head Only with a headache (especially sudden), neurologic findings , trauma, or a new or focal seizure. Primary neurologic causes of syncope are rare. Echo; CTPA or CT aortogram; abdominal US or CT; pelvic US Outflow obstruction or tamponade; PE or dissection; AAA; ectopic. Usually inpatient or outpatient Holter or event monitor Reliable, healthy patients with a suspected benign dysrhythmia (e.g. episodic SVT or AF). Telemetry, echo, stress test, EP study, coronary imaging Known heart disease, or a serious dysrhythmia suspected. Tilt table; EEG; carotid ultrasound Chronic orthostasis in older adults and children; a suspected seizure; stroke or TIA. Even after a history, exam and ECG, up to 50% have no firm diagnosis . That is why the next section is about risk , not diagnosis.

5 Decision Rules The approach (Rosen's algorithm) 1 Young, no comorbidities, a typical story, no alternative? This is neurally mediated . An exam for anemia or another benign contributor is all they need. 2 Everyone else: ECG Abnormal : a dysrhythmia needs prolonged monitoring; ischemia needs a cardiac workup. Consider that workup even with a normal ECG in at-risk patients. 3 Normal ECG: orthostatic changes? Present : check the hemogram for anemia or hemorrhage, and look for volume depletion or a drug. Absent , so follow the clues. A reflex story: neurally mediated (carotid massage if it fits). Venous return: β-hCG and echo or US (pregnancy, tamponade). Outflow: CTA and echo (PE, dissection, stenosis, HCM). Focal neuro signs: CT head (stroke, TIA, SAH). Metabolic: chemistry (hypoglycemia, adrenal insufficiency). Seizure-like: EEG. Admit Rosen's hard indications Hx Chest pain , unexplained shortness of breath , history of CHF , or significant valvular disease ECG Ventricular dysrhythmia , ischemia , a significantly prolonged QT , or a new bundle branch block Consider monitoring for age > 65, known cardiovascular or congenital heart disease, family history of sudden death, serious comorbidity (e.g. diabetes), or exertional syncope. Markers of short-term risk Rosen's list, drawn from the published rules Patient Age > 65; male CHF ; cardiovascular or structural heart disease; serious dysrhythmia Family history of sudden death before 50 Event and findings No prodrome ; exertional ; supine Dyspnea SBP < 90 Abnormal ECG Hct < 30% (Hb < 90 g/L) Rosen's caution: no prediction rule has performed acceptably in rigorous validation, or shown itself better than an emergency physician's gestalt. Don't apply any of them strictly or alone. The San Francisco Syncope Rule's “CHESS” items (CHF, Hct < 30%, abnormal ECG, shortness of breath, SBP < 90) are all on this list. Canadian Syncope Risk Score Beyond Rosen Adults after the ED workup, when no serious cause has been found. Tap what applies. Clinical evaluation Predisposition to vasovagal symptoms : triggered by a warm crowded place, prolonged standing, fear, emotion or pain −1 History of heart disease : coronary or valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, CHF, non-sinus rhythm (on ECG, a documented atrial or ventricular arrhythmia, or a device) +1 Any SBP < 90 or > 180 , from triage to disposition +2 Investigations Troponin > 99th percentile +2 Abnormal QRS axis (< −30° or > 100°) +1 QRS > 130 ms +1 QTc > 480 ms +2 Diagnosis in t

1 Differentials Step 1: is this a true loss of power? Most weak patients have a systemic problem that starves nerve and muscle of substrate. Their neurologic exam is non-focal. Systemic (non-neurologic) The most common group by far Volume: dehydration Composition: glucose, Na, K, Ca; uremia, high CO 2 , bilirubin, ketoacids Red cells: anemia or polycythemia Pump: myocardial ischemia Vascular tone: vasodilatory shock of any cause Demand: infection, endocrinopathy, toxin Mitochondria: severe sepsis, toxins Global CNS depression: sedatives, stimulant withdrawal Trap A systemic illness can look focal , especially in a limb already weakened by an old stroke. Real focal findings (lateralized weakness, numbness, an unsteady gait, a cranial nerve deficit) still earn a careful neurologic workup. Step 2: if it's neuromuscular, find the level. These patients usually have an asymmetric finding on the neurologic exam. Critical Cortex / subcortical Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke Brainstem Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke Cord Ischemia; compression by disc, abscess or hematoma Nerve Guillain–Barré syndrome NMJ Myasthenic or cholinergic crisis , botulism, tick paralysis, organophosphates Muscle Rhabdomyolysis Emergent Cortex / subcortical Tumour, abscess, demyelination Brainstem Demyelination Cord Transverse myelitis; compression by disc or spondylosis Nerve Compressive plexopathy (hematoma, aneurysm); paraneoplastic, vasculitis, uremia Muscle Inflammatory myositis Non-emergent Peripheral neuropathies Diabetes and other endocrinopathies Alcohol and other toxins; vitamin deficiency Entrapment or external compression; trauma Connective tissue disease; paraneoplastic Rosen's five chapter questions, each a classic pattern, are in the quiz at the end .

2 History First pin down what “weak” means to the patient. Then ask about time course, distribution, the company the weakness keeps, and exposures. Ask about Why it matters What they mean Tired and unwell, or can't move a part? Malaise and fatigue point to the systemic list. A real loss of power is neuromuscular. Time course Sudden Ischemia or hemorrhage until imaging says otherwise. Gradual over days to weeks Demyelination (MS, ADEM) or tumour. Over days, an ascending GBS or a progressive NMJ process (botulism). Fluctuating, worse later in the day NMJ disorder , e.g. myasthenia gravis. Episodic attacks Periodic paralysis (a potassium channelopathy). Distribution Stairs, rising from a chair, lifting arms overhead Proximal weakness, which points to muscle (myositis, rhabdo) or occasionally NMJ. Clumsy hands, tripping, trouble with fine movements Distal weakness, which points to peripheral neuropathy. Face, eyelids, double vision, swallowing, speech Brainstem, NMJ (botulism, myasthenia) or several cranial neuropathies. Red-flag company Red flag Severe headache With a hemiparesis: hemorrhage or mass . Midline back pain With leg weakness: cord compression (disc, abscess, hematoma). Bladder or bowel trouble A cord or cauda equina lesion , unless something else explains it. Short of breath, can't lie flat, weak cough Respiratory muscle failure (GBS, crisis), or CHF on the systemic side. Vertigo, nausea, diplopia, dysarthria Brainstem or posterior circulation. Systemic review Orthopnea, chest pain; blood loss; urinary symptoms; fever CHF or ischemia; anemia; UTI (especially with new incontinence in an older adult); infection. Drugs and exposures Anticoagulants Hematoma: epidural (cord) or retroperitoneal (plexus) . Statins Rhabdomyolysis. Acetylcholin­esterase inhibitors A myasthenic patient getting worse may be in cholinergic crisis . Amino­glycosides, quinolones, beta blockers Can worsen NMJ disease . Sedatives; stimulant withdrawal; alcohol Global CNS depression. Alcohol also causes neuropathy and compression palsies after lying still for hours. Pesticides, ticks, suspect food or wounds Organophosphates, tick paralysis, botulism.

3 Physical Exam Vitals and a general exam come first, because abnormal vitals send you to the systemic list. Then do a neurologic exam built to answer one question: where is the lesion? Lesion Tone and reflexes Other clues UMN : cortex, internal capsule, brainstem or cord tracts Spastic (arms in extension, legs in flexion), hyperreflexic ; pronator drift, Hoffmann, upgoing toe May be absent in the first hours. One sign is enough to place it in the CNS. LMN : anterior horn, root or nerve Flaccid, reduced reflexes Fasciculations, cramps; a dermatome or nerve-territory sensory loss NMJ Reflexes preserved No sensory loss; fatigable; ocular and bulbar muscles first; autonomic signs if presynaptic Muscle Reflexes preserved Proximal, often tender, no sensory loss Check Look for → think General Vitals Tachycardia, tachypnea, fever, hypothermia or hypotension means a systemic cause , and treat it now. Hypotension with quadriparesis suggests neurogenic shock . Skin, mucosa, heart, lungs Pallor, dehydration, CHF, infection: is substrate getting to the muscle? Skin, for the rarer clues Beyond Rosen A tick hiding in the scalp (tick paralysis); a rash over the knuckles (dermatomyositis). See the pictures below. Breathing Shallow, rapid breaths, accessory muscles, weak neck flexion or pooling secretions suggest respiratory muscle fatigue and aspiration risk . Face and cranial nerves Facial symmetry Look closely for a flattened nasolabial fold before calling it “no face involvement”. Forehead Forehead involved too, with the whole half of the face weak: a CN VII lesion (nerve or pontine nucleus). Eyes, pupils, palate Ptosis (CN III or sympathetic), CN VI palsy, nystagmus; poor soft palate rise. Dilated, sluggish pupils with a dry mouth point to a presynaptic NMJ problem (botulism, Lambert–Eaton, organophosphates). Cortical signs Neglect, a visual field cut or aphasia place it in the cortex. Face, arm and leg equally weak suggests the internal capsule. Limbs, sensation, sphincters Myotomes and nerve territories One root or one nerve: radiculopathy, plexopathy or neuropathy. Pinprick level A spinal level means a cord lesion. It can be as high as T2 with normal arms. Pain and temperature loss on the opposite side suggests Brown–Séquard. Pinprick lost over the arms, light touch kept Central cord syndrome : the crossing pain fibres are hit, while light touch and the posterior columns are spared. Reflex pattern in quadriparesis LMN signs at the cord level and UMN signs below it.

4 Investigations Labs mostly rule out the systemic causes . Imaging is chosen by where you think the lesion is. Test When · what it tells you Everyone with generalized weakness ECG, troponin Myocardial ischemia, which can present as weakness, especially in older adults and people with diabetes. The ECG also shows hyperkalemia (below). Glucose, electrolytes (Na, K, Ca), renal function Metabolic causes; K is the key value in periodic paralysis . Hemoglobin Anemia or polycythemia. Lactate, urinalysis Hypoperfusion and sepsis; a urinary source. Neuromuscular CK Raised in inflammatory myositis and rhabdomyolysis . This and K are the two labs that help on the neuromuscular side. Pulmonary function: vital capacity, inspiratory force Any suspected GBS or bulbar or respiratory weakness. Repeat them to catch a decline. Imaging Brain imaging Sudden focal weakness , to find occlusion or hemorrhage. Spine imaging, immediately Any weakness that localizes to the cord (UMN signs below a level, sensory level, sphincters), and suspected cauda equina . Image urgently with quadriparesis and hypotension. No ED imaging needed Lesions from the roots down (radiculopathy, plexopathy, neuropathy) don't always need it, unless you suspect cauda equina (or a compressing hematoma). Hyperkalemia on the ECG: a man on hemodialysis came in profoundly weak after a weekend fishing trip. His potassium was 9.6 . There are no P waves to be found, the QRS complexes are very wide, and the T waves in V3 to V5 are tall and peaked. Michael Rosengarten, ECGpedia , CC BY-SA 3.0. Beyond Rosen Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: IV calcium first. Calcium protects the heart's membranes but doesn't lower the potassium. Insulin with glucose and nebulized salbutamol shift potassium into the cells. Only dialysis, potassium binders and loop diuretics take it out of the body. Keep the patient on a monitor even if the first ECG looks normal. Lindner G et al., Eur J Emerg Med 2020;27:329–37 (a KDIGO conference summary).

5 Decision Rules Localize by pattern: the flowchart Weak patient Weak all over, with no focal loss of power? A non-focal neurologic exam Yes Systemic Work down the systemic list : circulation first (heart, red cells, oxygen, vascular tone), then plasma volume and composition, then metabolism (endocrine, toxin, sepsis). No One limb only? Yes Root, plexus or nerve Reduced reflexes with a root or nerve-territory sensory loss: radiculopathy, plexopathy or neuropathy. UMN signs: a motor-strip lesion or Brown–Séquard. No sensory loss, normal reflexes: NMJ. Older or diabetic with a “weak” arm but full power: myocardial ischemia . No Arm and/or leg on one side? Look hard at the face first: a flat nasolabial fold counts Yes Brain or cord Face on the same side: opposite cortex, corona radiata or internal capsule Face on the other side ± other CN signs: brainstem No face: medial cortex, a discrete corticospinal lesion, or Brown–Séquard Sudden means stroke or bleed until imaging says otherwise; gradual, demyelination or tumour. No Both sides? Yes Cord, cauda equina, nerve or muscle Legs: anterior cord, cauda equina, GBS Arms or hands: central cord All four: cervical cord, GBS (legs weaker than arms) Proximal only: myositis, rhabdo, occasionally NMJ Distal only: neuropathy (GBS if acute); check the saddle All four limbs: rule out the systemic causes first. No Face only Which muscles are weak? CN VII only The upper and lower face on one side, with everything else normal: Bell's palsy , mastoiditis or parotitis With long-tract signs Ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria or dysphagia plus cerebellar, field, sensory or UMN signs: the brainstem No long-tract signs NMJ (acute and progressive: botulism; chronic and fluctuating: myasthenia) or a cranial polyneuropathy (a GBS variant, the meninges, the skull base) Rosen's Figure 10.1, redrawn as one chart, with detail added from the chapter text. Beyond Rosen Bell's palsy, the isolated CN VII branch: steroids for everyone without a contraindication. Antivirals alone don't help. Adding them to steroids is suggested only for a severe or complete palsy. The best timing is unclear, but in one trial the benefit was seen only when steroids started within 48 hours . If the eye won't close, protect it with lubricating drops and ointment. No improvement, or getting worse: refer to a specialist and image to rule out a tumour. de Almeida JR et al., CMAJ 2014;186:917–22 (the Canadian guideline). Airway and breathing in neuromuscular weakness Who to

6 Cases Two published cases, one decision at a time. Both men were suddenly weak in all four limbs after a fall. Answer before you read on: the explanation opens only after you pick. Case 1 · a real case Can't move his arms or legs, a week after a fall Quadriparesis, the cervical cord on everyone's mind, and the systemic list first The story A 79-year-old man has found it harder and harder to move over the last 24 hours, and now he can't move his arms or legs at all . He has had diarrhea for two weeks , and he fell a week ago. He has had a thrombotic stroke before, and he has right bundle branch block and chronic kidney disease . He takes irbesartan and spironolactone for his blood pressure. Nothing is new, and he takes no NSAIDs. SpO₂ 90% RA Other vitals Normal Exam: alert and fully oriented. Power is 0/5 proximally , 1/5 in the fingers and 2/5 in the toes. All four limbs are flaccid and the reflexes are absent. His speech is slurred, he can't swallow his saliva well, his neck is weak, and there's a mild right facial droop. Sensation, eye movements and pupils are normal. The team is worried about a central cord injury from the fall, or a stroke. What do you check first? An MRI of the cervical spine A CT head and a stroke call An ECG, and his potassium, glucose and other electrolytes A lumbar puncture for GBS The ECG and the electrolytes. Weakness in all four limbs makes you think of the cervical cord, but Rosen says to assess these patients first for the medical causes of global weakness . His history points straight at potassium: an ARB plus spironolactone , CKD, and two weeks of diarrhea. The exam fits too. There is no sensory loss at all and no sensory level, which a cord injury bad enough to paralyze him would almost always cause. And the facial droop doesn't rule a systemic cause out: Rosen warns that systemic illness can look focal, especially in someone who has had a stroke. While you wait He is drooling, his voice is slurred, his neck is weak, and his saturation is 90% on air. Whatever the cause turns out to be, what is the danger right now? A pressure injury from lying still Aspiration and respiratory failure, because the weakness has reached his throat and breathing muscles A DVT from being immobile Nothing urgent: he is alert and talking His airway and his breathing. Rosen: neck and pharyngeal weakness signals a risk of aspiration, and weakness of the diaphragm or the hypopharynx, or tiring respiratory muscles, is a reason to intubate. Being al

Wk 1 · Thyroid & parathyroid physiology 2.2 · Hyper/hypoparathyroidism & calcium disorders If You Remember Nothing Else Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin) . Hypercalcemia > 2.55 · admit > 3.0 · IV calcium if < 1.9 with symptoms. High calcium → check PTH. High or "normal" = primary hyperPTH (or FHH). Suppressed = malignancy (PTHrP), vitamin D, granulomas. Primary hyperPTH + malignancy = > 90%. FHH vs primary hyperPTH = urine. FeCa < 0.01 = FHH (don't operate) · > 0.02 = primary hyperPTH. Low calcium → check phosphate. High PO₄ = PTH problem (low PTH = hypoparathyroidism, high PTH = PHP). Low PO₄ = vitamin D problem. Treat high: saline → furosemide (only once hydrated) → zoledronate, calcitonin as a bridge. Treat low: IV calcium gluconate, fix magnesium; chronic = calcitriol + calcium, aim low-normal. The loop Low Ca⁺⁺ → PTH → bone, kidney and (via calcitriol) gut → Ca rises → PTH off. Slide from the Week 1 lecture. PTH Calcitriol Switched on by Low Ca (CaSR on chief cells) PTH → renal 1α-hydroxylase Bone ↑ resorption Resorption when Ca is needed Kidney Ca ↑ reabsorption (DCT) ↑ reabsorption Kidney PO₄ ↓ reabsorption (wastes it) ↑ reabsorption Gut Only via calcitriol ↑ Ca and PO₄ absorption Net Ca ↑, PO₄ ↓ Ca ↑, PO₄ ↑ Parathyroids: usually 4, behind the thyroid; chief cells make PTH (full activity in amino acids 1–34). The PTH receptor is shared with PTHrP , which is how tumours cause hypercalcemia. 99% of body calcium is in bone; only the ionized fraction is active. Step 2 of 7 · Week 3 Sex Development & CAH Where normal differentiation breaks, the two big DSD groups, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia from the steroid pathway to the salt-wasting crisis. Wk 3 · Disorders of Sex Development & CAH Wk 3 · Female tract development If You Remember Nothing Else First two tests: karyotype + pelvic/abdominal ultrasound (uterus? gonads? big adrenals?). Use neutral words: gonads, phallus, labioscrotal folds. 46,XX overvirilized = CAH by a mile. 46,XY undervirilized = most often 5α-reductase deficiency (AR, high T:DHT) or partial androgen insensitivity (X-linked). Complete AIS looks female and is found at puberty. 21-hydroxylase (~95% of CAH): ↓ cortisol, ↓ aldosterone (75% salt-wasters), ↑ androgens. Low cortisol → high ACTH → hyperplasia. Diagnose with a high 17-OHP. Salt-wasting crisis at 1–3 weeks (low Na, high K, acidosis, hypoglycemia). Boys look normal at birth, so the newborn screen catches them. Treat for life: hydrocortisone 10–15 mg/m²/day divided + fludrocortisone (± salt) + stress dosing. Don't rush sex assignment ; assignment ≠ surgery. Step 2 of 10 · Week 1 Diabetes Diagnosis & T1DM Care Who has diabetes, which type, and how a child with type 1 is run day to day. Drugs, insulin pharmacology and DKA were Review 2. 1.1 · Pathophysiology T1DM & T2DM 1.2 · T1DM in children 1.4 · Approach to endocrine disease 1.5 · T2DM diagnosis If You Remember Nothing Else Any one of: fasting glucose ≥ 7.0, A1c ≥ 6.5% (adults; not for suspected T1DM), 2-h OGTT or random ≥ 11.1 mmol/L. Symptoms (thirst, polyuria, weight loss) → one abnormal value is enough. No symptoms → repeat on another day. Acute illness or steroids can raise glucose: confirm once recovered. A high reading reflects the dose before it. High lunch glucose → raise the breakfast rapid-acting dose. Hypoglycemia: can they swallow? Oral glucose if yes, glucagon if no, recheck in 15 min. The numbers that diagnose Test Prediabetes Diabetes Fasting glucose 6.1–6.9 (IFG) ≥ 7.0 2-h 75 g OGTT 7.8–11.0 (IGT) ≥ 11.1 A1c 6.0–6.4% ≥ 6.5% Random glucose — ≥ 11.1 with symptoms Why these cut-offs? They're where retinopathy risk starts to climb steeply. Type 1 or type 2 in an adult? Usually inferred from the course and the response to treatment. A normal TSH rules out primary thyroid disease, except when you suspect pituitary/hypothalamic disease: then order TSH + FT4 . Thyrotoxicosis = too much hormone from anywhere. Hyperthyroidism = the gland is making it. Radioiodine uptake splits them: high → reduce production; low (thyroiditis, exogenous) → support only. Graves: methimazole first (remission possible). Making the hormone NIS pumps iodide in, pendrin moves it into the colloid, TPO iodinates and couples tyrosines on thyroglobulin. TSH turns up all three. Slide from the lecture. Thyroid hormone raises metabolic rate, heat, heart rate and β-receptor numbers, which is why thyrotoxicosis looks adrenergic. Step 2 of 7 · Week 4 Vaginal Discharge What normal looks like across the cycle, the four bedside tests, and the four causes: BV, candida, trichomonas and atrophic vaginitis. 4.5 · Vaginal discharge If You Remember Nothing Else Estrogen → glycogen → lactobacilli → pH under 4.5. Little estrogen (before puberty, after menopause) means a higher pH, thin mucosa and more infections. Clear, stretchy "egg-white" mucus at ovulation is normal . Colour is a clue, not a diagnosis. Use pH, whiff and the wet mount. In family practice a vaginal swab is often all you'll do, and that's fine once you've looked at the vulva, vagina and cervix . BV: fishy, thin, coats the walls, pH > 4.5, whiff positive, clue cells . Not an STI. Oral metronidazole, no alcohol. Candida: itch, cottage cheese, splash dysuria, satellite lesions, pH normal , pseudohyphae. Fluconazole once or a topical azole. Trich: profuse yellow, malodorous, pH > 4.5 but whiff negative , motile trichomonads, NAAT is the gold standard. Is an STI: oral metronidazole (never the gel) and treat partners. Atrophic: postmenopausal dyspareunia and postcoital bleeding, parabasal cells → local estrogen . Watery discharge? Look at the cervix : it can be cancer. Step 2 of 8 · Week 5 · 5.1 Post-menopausal Bleeding Any bleeding after menopause is endometrial cancer until you've shown it isn't. The pathway, the four biopsy reports, hyperplasia and the two endometrial cancers. 5.1 · Post-menopausal bleeding If You Remember Nothing Else PMB = any bleeding after 12 months without a period. It is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise . Usually it isn't, but the onus is on you to exclude it. Work-up: stable? → history → speculum + bimanual → TVUS + endometrial biopsy. A normal Pap doesn't clear her: it samples the cervix, not the endometrium. Endometrium < 5 mm is normal , on HRT or not. But recurrent bleeding with a thin lining still gets a biopsy : skipping it misses cancer 4% of the time. Commonest cause: atrophy (a diagnosis of exclusion). Most serious: hyperplasia or carcinoma. "Insufficient tissue" is no result: repeat the biopsy. Hyperplasia turns on atypia. Without → progestin (megestrol, LNG-IUD), re-biopsy at ~3 months. With → hysterectomy + BSO , because 30–40% already have cancer. Type 1 endometrioid (90%): estrogen-driven, hyperplasia first, better outcome. Type 2 serous (10%): estrogen-independent, atrophic lining, older women, worse outcome. The work-up The work-up, reused from the lecture page (drawn there from the module's prose). The 5 mm cutoff holds whether or not she is on HRT. Before any of it: is she stable? Test What it gives you The catch Speculum exam The cause in the office: endometrial mass at the os, ulcerated cervical mass None. Always do it TVUS Endometrial thickness: < 5 mm normal On HRT, > 50% measure > 5 mm; < 4% of those have pathology Endometrial biopsy 99.6%

Every later decision in the pregnancy is measured against these. 5.12 · Care in the first trimester If You Remember Nothing Else Serum β-hCG: < 5 negative, > 25 positive. A sac is usually visible at about 1500 transvaginally , about 5000 transabdominally . It's intrauterine only when you see a gestational sac and a yolk sac . Date by the first ultrasound, not the LMP. Crown–rump length up to 14 weeks; any scan before 23 weeks beats the LMP; an IVF transfer date beats everything . Once set, the due date never moves : a later mismatch is a growth question. GTPAL counts pregnancies, not babies (twins = one), except L, which counts living children . T ≥ 37 weeks, P 20 to 36+6, A < 20. Fundus at the symphysis at 12 weeks, the umbilicus at 20 ; from 20 weeks, fundal height in cm ≈ weeks. Everyone: CBC, group & screen, rubella, hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis, GC/chlamydia, urine culture, and an offer of eFTS at 11–14 weeks . HSV is not routine ; TSH only with known thyroid disease. Preterm births and losses are what make a pregnancy higher-risk, and plain G/P hides them. 4 Order the baseline bloods. Step 2 of 10 · Week 6 Preterm Labour & PPROM Who's at risk, how to tell threatened from true preterm labour, the four tools and their cut-offs, and what to do when the waters break early. 6.1 · Approach to preterm labour If You Remember Nothing Else Term starts at 37+0. Threatened preterm labour = symptoms, cervix may or may not change. Preterm labour = contractions plus cervical change . One exam can't tell them apart without a baseline: re-examine . Biggest risk factor: a previous spontaneous preterm birth. Also multiples, a short cervix, cone biopsy (more than LEEP), cervicitis or BV, smoking, both age extremes. Most cases are idiopathic . Hydrate and check the urine first. Dehydration and UTI are common causes of an irritable uterus. Four tools: tocolysis buys 48 h (indomethacin < 32 wk, nifedipine > 32) · betamethasone < 34 wk · MgSO 4 < 34 wk once birth is imminent · penicillin if GBS is positive or unknown. PPROM (waters break before 37 wk): confirm with pooling, nitrazine, ferning . Give steroids + latency antibiotics . Deliver instead for chorioamnionitis, abruption or fetal distress. entries.t: DKA vs. HHS: Who Gets What
entries.x: DKA vs. HHS: Who Gets What DKA HHS Typical patient Younger, T1DM (absolute insulin deficiency) Older, T2DM (relative insulin deficiency) Onset Acute — hours, not days Over several days Why no ketosis in HHS? — Enough insulin remains to suppress lipolysis/ketone formation , just not enough to prevent hyperglycemia Age isn't a perfect discriminator — people with T1DM are living longer, so DKA can occur in older patients too. Shared precipitants Dehydrating illness (gastroenteritis, flu) Physically stressful illness: sepsis, MI, stroke, surgery, thyrotoxicosis, trauma Inability to access medications (rationing insulin, missed doses — often financial) Medications: steroids (worsen insulin resistance), SGLT2 inhibitors, cocaine DKA-specific: insulin withheld intentionally (e.g. for weight control)

DKA: Presentation & Labs History: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain; can progress to lethargy, obtundation, coma if untreated Feared complication: cerebral edema/seizures — more common in children Exam: appears (often very) ill; ↓BP, ↑HR; dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor (dehydration); breath may smell of acetone; Kussmaul breathing (hyperventilation compensating for the acidosis) Lab Finding Glucose High (often >15 mmol/L) — but doesn't have to be Serum & urine ketones Elevated (acetone, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate) Anion gap Elevated [Na − (Cl + HCO3)] — tracked to confirm the acidosis is resolving with treatment Bicarbonate & pH Low (acidotic) — bicarb is being consumed buffering the acid; pH might be ~7.01 vs. normal 7.4 Plasma osmolality Mildly high (from the elevated glucose and sodium) Creatinine May be high (dehydration)

HHS: Presentation & Labs History: polyuria, polydipsia; lethargy progressing to obtundation (coma is rare); no abdominal pain or vomiting (a key difference from DKA) Exam: appears ill; ↓BP; dry mucous membranes, low skin turgor; no hyperventilation, no acetone breath Lab Finding Glucose High, sometimes very high Creatinine Elevated (dehydration) Sodium May be low, from the high glucose Potassium More likely normal (no acidosis) — can be high if renal failure from dehydration is also present Anion gap, pH, bicarbonate Normal or only slightly abnormal Serum osmolality Very high

Comparing DKA & HHS At the bedside, the split comes down to two questions — is there acidosis, and are there ketones: Two questions separate them; the treatment pathway then converges. DKA HHS pH ≤ 7.3 > 7.3 Plasma glucose > 15 mmol/L > 30 mmol/L Serum bicarbonate < 18 mEq/L > 15 mEq/L Plasma/urine ketones Positive Negative or trace Anion gap > 12 < 12 Serum osmolarity Variable > 320 mOsm/kg (high) Water deficit ~6 L ~9 L

Sodium & Potassium Pearls Sodium: it's usually falsely low High glucose pulls water into the vascular space, diluting sodium — so the measured (lab-reported) sodium can look low even when a patient's true sodium/water balance is fine or even high. Always correct sodium for the glucose before interpreting it. Potassium: normal-looking serum level ≠ normal total-body potassium Patients can be significantly whole-body depleted of potassium even when the initial serum K looks normal (or even high) — this is most pronounced in DKA. Insulin normally drives K into cells ; without it, K shifts out of cells (extracellularly), masking the true deficit on a serum draw. Once you start treating with insulin, that shift reverses — K moves back into cells and the serum level can fall sharply . Low K can cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias, so it must be monitored closely and replaced via IV as needed.

Treatment of DKA & HHS The approach is essentially the same for both: ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) Fluids: normal saline — often many litres, given the degree of dehydration IV insulin: always in DKA, almost always in HHS Monitor every 1–2 hours: level of consciousness; sodium/potassium/pH; glucose (hourly while on the insulin drip, usually point-of-care); volume status/heart failure risk (especially in the elderly). Once BG falls to ~12–14 mmol/L, add dextrose to the IV fluid (D5W with NS) — this lets the insulin infusion continue (needed to fully resolve the acidosis/normalize the anion gap) without causing hypoglycemia.

Preventing DKA & HHS T1DM sick-day rules T2DM sick-day rules Continue at least some insulin even when not eating (usually a lower basal dose) Frequent monitoring when ill Frequent BG and urine ketone checks when ill Stop dehydrating medications during GI upset (SGLT2 inhibitors, diuretics, metformin) Illness itself can raise blood glucose — taking insulin during sick days is safe (and usually necessary), even with reduced oral intake. Not every case is preventable (a sudden vomiting illness can still land someone in the ER) — but common, addressable themes behind DKA/HHS include: withholding insulin to control weight, withholding medications due to financial constraints , uncertainty about what to do on sick days, new steroid prescriptions, and major body stresses (infection, MI, stroke). Always ask why.

Chronic Complications: The Framework Patients are usually well aware of these risks already — complications shouldn't be used as a scare tactic for "compliance," and even excellent DM management doesn't guarantee they won't happen. Many organ systems can be affected — eyes, kidneys, heart, brain, nerves, feet — but they sort cleanly into three buckets: Category Includes Microvascular Retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy Macrovascular Myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral vascular disease Other Cataracts, glaucoma

Retinopathy Three clinically meaningful stages: Stage Significance Background Not vision-threatening; can improve or worsen over time with BG control Pre-proliferative Not likely vision-threatening yet, but may advance Proliferative Can threaten vision — must be treated Normal → background → pre-proliferative → proliferative retinopathy. Background: small dot hemorrhages; microaneurysms (small dots around vessels) Pre-proliferative: retinal infarcts (cotton wool spots); lipid exudates (serum leaking into the retina); macular edema (can change vision) Proliferative: new fragile blood vessels; risk of bleeding into the vitreous — must be treated

Nephropathy The kidney is a highly vascular structure, so it's a natural target: Capillary basement membrane thickening → matrix accumulation → fibrosis. Capillary basement membrane thickens → matrix accumulates in the glomerulus → fibrosis → loss of glomerular filtration surface → decreased renal function.

Neuropathy Driven in part by microvascular disease in the small vessels that supply the nerves themselves (the vasa nervorum ) — poor circulation causes microinfarcts, and nerves demyelinate with axons swelling and degenerating. The vasa nervorum — the blood supply the nerve itself depends on. Type Detail Peripheral sensorimotor Most common. Glove-and-stocking distribution (hands are rarely affected in their entirety) Autonomic e.g. gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction Cranial CN III palsy is most common; also Bell's palsy Amyotrophy — Sensorimotor neuropathy & Charcot's foot Most commonly presents as numb, tingling, itchy feet — often progressive over years and severe enough to disturb sleep. Loss of protective sensation puts the foot at risk for ulcers, infection, amputation, and Charcot's foot . Charcot's arthropathy: unsensed repeated injury → joint destruction → the "rocker-bottom" deformity. Poor blood supply to nerves → impaired sensation → injuries go unnoticed Poor blood supply to skin → wounds heal poorly → easier to get infected Charcot's arthropathy: inability to sense injury → significant foot deformity, including the rocker-bottom deformity
Macrovascular & Other Complications Macrovascular Other Myocardial infarction Cataracts Stroke Glaucoma Peripheral vascular disease (toe/foot/leg amputation)

Why Do Complications Happen? There's no single cause — understanding the mechanisms matters because it opens multiple avenues for prevention (and drug development). Direct glucose toxicity to blood vessels and nerves Oxidative stress and free radical generation Increased intracellular sorbitol → cells swell osmotically → cell injury ↑ VEGF → abnormal angiogenesis Hypertension — direct vascular damage Hyperlipidemia — contributes to atherosclerotic plaques Protein glycation — glucose incorporated into protein structure impairs normal function Inflammation (especially in T2DM) & a hypercoagulable state — both promote thrombotic events
The Framing Question Does my patient have an endocrine problem? Every endocrine gland problem breaks down the same way — think about structure , then think about function . It can sometimes be both.

Structure vs. Function Adrenal disease as the worked example — but this same fork applies to any endocrine gland: Diagnostic approach to a suspected endocrine problem. The structural–functional fork applies to any gland; adrenal disease is shown as the worked example. Both classifications may apply to the same patient. Eponyms worth knowing cold Eponym Means Cushing Disease ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma Addison Disease Adrenal cortex destruction → primary adrenal failure Conn Syndrome Aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma Note the distinction: Cushing Disease is a specific pituitary cause, while Cushing Syndrome is the umbrella term for any cause of cortisol excess.

Structural Problems: Masses Two questions for any mass: benign or malignant? and, if benign, where is it, and what does it press on? A pituitary mass makes this concrete — the local effects depend entirely on which direction it grows: Direction of growth Structure affected Clinical finding Superior (optic chiasm) Optic chiasm Assess visual fields — classic finding is bitemporal hemianopsia or bitemporal superior quadrantopsia Lateral (cavernous sinus) CN III (oculomotor) Assess EOMs. Complete palsy: dilated non-reactive pupil, eye "down and out," ptosis CN IV (trochlear) Difficulty moving the affected eye down while adducted CN VI (abducens) Difficulty with lateral movement of the affected eye CN V1 / V2 (trigeminal) Altered sensation of forehead/cheek on the affected side Inferior (sphenoid sinus) Sphenoid sinus CSF rhinorrhea

entries.t: Functional Problems: The HPA Axis as a Model
entries.x: Functional Problems: The HPA Axis as a Model Every functional endocrine problem is a feedback loop. Take the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis: Systemic stress (cold, hypoglycemia, fear, etc.) Hypothalamus → CRH Anterior pituitary → ACTH Adrenal cortex → Cortisol Cortisol then negative-feedbacks both the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary to shut the axis back down. What does cortisol actually do? System Effect Glucose ↑ hepatic glucose production, gluconeogenesis, glycogen synthesis; inhibits glucose uptake/use in peripheral tissue Cardiovascular Mineralocorticoid effects (K⁺ out / Na⁺ in) — maintains BP Fat ↑ lipolysis, central fat deposition Bone Inhibits osteoblasts, activates osteoclasts, ↓ GI calcium absorption Muscle Skeletal muscle catabolism Connective tissue / skin Inhibits fibroblasts, ↓ collagen synthesis Immune function Anti-inflammatory (↓ IFN, IL-12, TNF)

entries.t: Stimulation & Suppression Tests: A Reality Check
entries.x: Stimulation & Suppression Tests: A Reality Check Dynamic testing isn't always needed — diagnosis often comes from history, exam, imaging, and a "static" hormone level alone. There are many suppression/stimulation tests, and many ways to get them wrong. Deciding which test to order — and running it accurately and safely — isn't expected of a generalist, with two exceptions : Test Used to screen for 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test Cushing syndrome (hormone excess → try to suppress it) 250 µg ACTH stimulation test Acute/subacute adrenal failure (hormone deficiency → try to stimulate it) General rule: suspect a deficiency → stimulation test. Suspect excess → suppression test.

entries.t: Where Does This All End Up? Treatment 101
entries.x: Where Does This All End Up? Treatment 101 The same structure/function fork decides treatment too — a useful shortcut for any endocrine problem, not just the diagnosis: Treatment approach by problem type. The same structural–functional classification that drives diagnosis also determines the treatment category.

Learning Objectives Describe the important pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM). Describe the important pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).

Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus T1DM is immune-mediated destruction of the insulin-producing β-cells in the islets of Langerhans. Histology shows CD3 + T-cell infiltration destroying insulin-producing cells while neighbouring glucagon-producing α-cells are spared. CD3-mediated destruction of insulin-producing β-cells (brown) vs. spared glucagon-producing α-cells (pink). Atkinson et al. Lancet 2014;383:69–82 Genetic susceptibility Polymorphisms in multiple genes — both within and outside the MHC — are associated with T1DM. It's a polygenic disease, not the result of one gene. Family history Risk of developing T1DM Monozygotic twin has T1DM 50% Non-monozygotic sibling has T1DM 5% No family history 0.4% Redondo et al. BMJ 1999;318:698 · Kaprio et al. Diabetologia 1992;35:1060–7 Role of autoantibodies Autoantibodies are identified in up to 85% of patients with T1DM. Four have been well characterized: Insulin / proinsulin Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) Insulinoma-associated protein 2 (IA-2) Zinc transporter (ZnT8) The more antibodies present, the higher and faster the risk of progressing to clinical T1DM: More autoantibodies (0→4) → faster progression to clinical T1DM. Orban et al. Diabetes Care 2009;32:2269–74 Stages of development T1DM doesn't appear overnight — functional β-cell mass declines through three proposed stages before clinical disease is diagnosed: Stage β-cell autoimmunity Glycemia Symptoms Stage 1 Present Normoglycemia Presymptomatic Stage 2 Present Dysglycemia Presymptomatic Stage 3 Present Dysglycemia Symptomatic (clinical T1DM) Insel et al. Diabetes Care 2015;38:1964–74

Diagnosis of Diabetes & Prediabetes The same glycemic thresholds are used to diagnose both types of diabetes: Test Prediabetes Diabetes FPG (mmol/L) 6.1–6.9 (IFG) ≥ 7.0 2-hr PG, 75g OGTT (mmol/L) 7.8–11.0 (IGT) ≥ 11.1 A1C 6.0–6.4% ≥ 6.5% (adults; not for suspected T1DM) Random PG (mmol/L) — ≥ 11.1 Fasting = no caloric intake for ≥ 8 hours. Random = any time of day, regardless of time since last meal. Punthakee et al. Can J Diabetes 2018;42(Suppl 1):S1–S325

Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus T2DM pathophysiology sits on a spectrum — from predominantly insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency , to a predominantly insulin secretory defect with insulin resistance (Punthakee et al. Can J Diabetes 2018;42(Suppl 1):S1–S325). A growing pandemic T2DM and obesity have risen in parallel worldwide, and both are projected to keep climbing: Year People with T2DM People with obesity 1980 108 million 0.85 billion 2020 463 million 2.00 billion 2045 (projected) 700 million 2.45 billion Saeedi P, et al. Diabetes Res Clin Pract. 2019;157:107843 The "Ominous Octet" T2DM used to be taught as a problem of just three organs (muscle, liver, pancreas). DeFronzo's "Ominous Octet" reframes it as eight organs/tissues all converging on hyperglycemia — and each one is a distinct drug target. DeFronzo's Ominous Octet. De Fronzo R. Diabetes 2009;58:773–95 (Banting Lecture) 1 · Pancreas (β-cell) Decreased insulin secretion. ~80% of β-cell function is already lost by the time a patient reaches the prediabetes range. 2 · Pancreas (α-cell) Increased glucagon secretion. Multifactorial, partly driven by reduced GLP-1; the liver is also more sensitive to glucagon in diabetes, so the same glucagon level drives more gluconeogenesis. 3 · Liver Increased hepatic glucose production. Basal HGP is significantly higher in T2DM and correlates strongly with fasting plasma glucose (r = 0.85). 4 · Intestine Decreased incretin effect. GLP-1 falls; GIP actually rises, but the insulin response to GIP is blunted — acquired GIP resistance rather than a simple deficiency. 5 · Fat cells Increased lipolysis. Adipocytes resist insulin's antilipolytic effect, raising free fatty acids (FFAs), which stimulate gluconeogenesis and suppress insulin secretion. Once adipocyte storage capacity is exceeded, fat spills into muscle, liver, and β-cells — worsening resistance and secretion respectively. 6 · Kidney Increased glucose reabsorption. SGLT2 expression rises with hyperglycemia, reabsorbing more filtered glucose and further potentiating the hyperglycemia. 7 · Muscle Decreased glucose uptake. Insulin-stimulated glucose disposal (both whole-body and at the tissue level) is markedly blunted compared to controls. 8 · Brain Neurotransmitter/appetite dysfunction. GLP-1 normally acts on the hypothalamus and mesolimbic reward system to increase satiety; this signal is blunted in T2DM — the mechanism GLP-1 receptor agonists exploit for weight loss. De Fronzo R. Diabetes 2009;58:77

Learning Objectives Summarize the implications of pre-pregnancy DM (types 1 and 2) vs. gestational diabetes (GDM) for mother and baby. List the Diabetes Canada criteria for diagnosing GDM and for optimal BG control in GDM and pre-pregnancy DM. Compare the risks of GDM with the risks of pre-pregnancy DM.

Pre-Pregnancy DM: Malformation Risk High blood glucose can affect organogenesis , which is essentially complete by ~8 weeks — often before a woman knows she's pregnant. That's the whole case for preconception control, not just control once pregnant. Major structural defects cluster in weeks 3–8 — before most women know they've conceived. mothertobaby.org Malformation risk spans neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida), cardiac defects (transposition of the great vessels, coarctation, ASD, pulmonary stenosis), and GI/GU/skeletal anomalies (duodenal atresia, renal agenesis, caudal regression syndrome). Congenital malformation risk overall is 1.7–9.4% (vs. 2–4% baseline). Absolute anomaly risk climbs steeply with periconceptional A1c. Guerin et al. (2007), Diabetes Canada Target preconception A1c is ≤ 7.0% (some push for < 6.5%) — optimal control is associated with a 70% reduction in congenital anomalies.

Pre-Pregnancy DM: Through the Pregnancy Stage Insulin Needs 1st trimester May fall — higher hypoglycemia risk 2nd trimester Rise slowly (rising placental hormones → insulin resistance) 3rd trimester Rise a great deal more, regardless of intake Postpartum Drop remarkably — breastfeeding can lower BG further Pre-eclampsia: double the risk vs. non-diabetic pregnancy (10% vs. 5%); can progress to eclampsia. Retinopathy can worsen with poor control; usually settles postpartum. Screen before, during, and within a year after pregnancy. Nephropathy: ARBs and ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy; usually settles postpartum. Infants are more prone to macrosomia and postpartum hypoglycemia — but are not at risk of being born with diabetes themselves.

Gestational Diabetes (GDM) GDM is a transient DM diagnosed at 24–28 weeks , driven by the insulin resistance of weight gain and placental hormones. It resolves after delivery but marks increased risk for "true" diabetes later — up to 60% of women, depending on follow-up length and other factors. Because the hyperglycemia sets in well after organogenesis, GDM carries no increased malformation risk . The risks instead come from a sustained high glucose load: macrosomia (> 4 kg, risking birth trauma and asphyxia), higher C-section rate, stillbirth, and postpartum hypoglycemia/hypocalcemia/hyperbilirubinemia. Insulin demand keeps climbing through pregnancy; in GDM, production can't keep pace — the widening gap is the hyperglycemia. kidsatriskfordiabetes.com

Screening, Treatment & BG Goals Two-step screening for gestational diabetes (Diabetes Canada; universal screening preferred). All glucose values are plasma, in mmol/L. A single value at or above threshold on the OGTT is sufficient for diagnosis. Treatment: low simple-carb diet in 3 meals + 3 snacks, post-meal walks, home BG monitoring. If BG stays high: insulin or metformin first-line; glyburide crosses the placenta (neonatal hypoglycemia risk) and is more of a fallback. BG goals — same across GDM, T1DM, and T2DM: fasting < 5.3 mmol/L, 1hr post-meal < 7.8 mmol/L (T1/T2 also target A1c < 6.5%, balanced against hypoglycemia risk). All GDM treatment stops after delivery, but a 75g OGTT at 6 weeks–6 months postpartum rules out ongoing diabetes.

entries.t: GDM vs. Pre-Pregnancy DM, Side by Side
entries.x: GDM vs. Pre-Pregnancy DM, Side by Side GDM Pre-Pregnancy T1/T2 DM Congenital malformation risk No Yes, depending on A1c at conception Preconceptual folic acid No Yes A1c monitoring Don't check Preconception, then monthly Insulin needs during / after pregnancy Rise / fall, meds can stop Rise (can be very high by term) / fall, doses lowered Maternal HTN & obstetric intervention risk Increased Increased Infant risk of DM at birth No No Infant risk of low BG at birth Yes Yes

Case: Catching It Early 35-Year-Old, First Pregnancy via Fertility Treatment PCOS; mother has T2DM. 25 weeks; weight 100 kg, BP 135/95. 50g screen 8.5 mmol/L → 75g OGTT: fasting 6.5 / 1hr 10.9 / 2hr 10.6 mmol/L, all elevated — GDM diagnosed . Diet and post-meal walking controlled lunch/supper, but fasting and post-breakfast stayed high → started on aspart 4 units pre-breakfast + detemir 6 units at bedtime. By 37 weeks, doses had climbed to aspart 40/10/10 units and detemir 60 units — tracking the expected third-trimester rise. Baby estimated at the 97th percentile → induced at 38 weeks. Delivered vaginally at 4.5 kg; 2 days in NICU for low BG and jaundice, then breastfed well. At 6 months postpartum: 40 lb lost, active, and a normal 75g OGTT — diabetes avoided.

Key Takeaway Watch for the woman diagnosed with "GDM" who actually has undiagnosed type 2 (or early type 1) DM. Diagnosis still happens at 24–28 weeks either way — but if it's really pre-existing diabetes, the BGs won't normalize after delivery, and medication needs during pregnancy tend to run unusually high for "just GDM."
