entries.t: Start Here: It Is the Same Wall Every Time
entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: Start Here: It Is the Same Wall Every Time The lecture moves organ by organ, which makes it look like six unrelated things to memorise. It is not. Every hollow organ in this tract is built to the same three-layer plan, and the names change more than the structure does. Drawn for these notes, not from the deck — the lecture presents each organ separately. The vagina ends in adventitia rather than serosa because most of it sits below the peritoneal reflection — there is no peritoneum there to give it a serosa. The plan in real tissue. That intricate branching lumen is the tube’s mucosa thrown into plicae — nothing else in the body looks like this, so it identifies a fallopian tube on sight.

entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: The Tract, Organ by Organ Click any structure for its epithelium, the feature that identifies it down the scope, and what goes wrong with it. The gynecologic tract — what lines what Click any structure → Select a structure to see what lines it, how you recognise it, and why it matters. Skin, then mucosa Vulva Labia majora — true skin: keratinized stratified squamous with hair follicles and eccrine, apocrine and sebaceous glands. Labia minora — non-keratinized stratified squamous, usually no adnexae . That single difference is how you tell them apart on a slide. Bartholin’s glands sit posterolateral to the introitus: mucinous acini, ducts lined by transitional epithelium, becoming squamous at the orifice. Skene’s glands are the paired periurethral mucus-secreting glands. Pathology: lichen sclerosus (inflammatory, and a risk factor), leukoplakia, and squamous cell carcinoma . Mucosa · muscularis · adventitia Vagina Non-keratinizing stratified squamous, no keratin layer at the surface and no glands. Non-keratinizing stratified squamous , and importantly no glands — vaginal lubrication is transudate plus cervical mucus, not vaginal secretion. The epithelium is estrogen-dependent: estrogen loads it with glycogen, which lactobacilli ferment to lactate and keep the pH acidic. After menopause estrogen falls, the epithelium thins and glycogen drops — atrophic vaginitis, and a rise in pH. The junction organ Cervix The lowermost part of the uterus, connecting uterus to vagina. It has two different epithelia , which is the whole point of it: Ectocervix (facing the vagina) — non-keratinizing stratified squamous . Endocervix (the canal) — mucus-secreting columnar glandular . Between them, the transformation zone . The transformation zone is the most common site of cervical neoplasia — covered in its own section below. Mucosa of the uterus Endometrium Glands plus stroma , in two layers. The functionalis is the outer layer that responds to hormones and is shed each month. The basalis is the deep layer that is never shed and regenerates the functionalis afterwards. Its appearance changes completely across the cycle — that is the second half of this lecture. If the basalis is destroyed (over-aggressive curettage, infection), the functionalis cannot regrow — intrauterine adhesions and amenorrhoea, or Asherman syndrome. Muscular wall Myometrium Thick interlacing bundles of smooth muscle — the bulk of the uterus, and what generates labour contractions. Covered on the outside b

entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: The Transformation Zone If you take one thing from the cervix, take this. Two epithelia meet at the cervix, and where they meet, one is actively converting into the other. The cervix face on. The transformation zone is the ring between the two epithelia — glandular endocervix inside, squamous ectocervix outside. The transformation zone in section, with the matching histology beneath each region. Left to right: endocervical columnar epithelium sitting on reserve cells → those reserve cells proliferating into immature metaplastic squamous epithelium → the squamocolumnar junction → mature stratified squamous ectocervix on its basal layer. From Kumar, Abbas, Fausto, Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease , 2005, as used in the lecture. Why This One Strip of Tissue Causes Almost All Cervical Cancer Metaplasia means actively dividing immature cells . HPV infects dividing basal-type cells, and integration into a dividing cell is what allows persistent infection to progress to dysplasia. Mature squamous epithelium and mature glandular epithelium are both far less vulnerable — the vulnerable population exists only in the transformation zone, and only while metaplasia is going on. That is the entire rationale for cervical screening: the Pap test scrapes the transformation zone , and a sample without endocervical or metaplastic cells may not have reached it. If cytology is abnormal, biopsy follows for tissue diagnosis.

entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: The Endometrium Through the Cycle Three appearances, and each one is a direct readout of which hormone is dominant. If you can name the hormone, you can predict the picture. The cycle as one picture — gonadotropins, follicle, steroid levels and the endometrium, on a common time axis. Everything below is the bottom strip of this figure seen down the microscope. 1 · Proliferative, low power. Numerous small, round, evenly spaced glands — these are straight tubes cut across. 2 · Secretory, low power. Thicker, and the glands are now tortuous and gaping — the “sawtooth” outline, with secretion in the lumens. 3 · Menstrual. The architecture has gone: collapsed crumbling stroma, broken glands, and blood everywhere. Proliferative, high power. Pseudostratified, crowded, darkly staining nuclei with mitotic figures in both gland and stroma. Mitoses are the finding. Secretory, high power. Nuclei pushed to the base by secretory vacuoles , secretion in the lumen, and no mitoses . If you see… It is… Straight tubular glands + mitoses Proliferative — estrogen-driven Coiled sawtooth glands + secretions, no mitoses Secretory — progesterone-driven, so ovulation has happened Collapsed stroma, broken glands, blood Menstrual Why the Biopsy Is Taken Endometrial sampling answers a small number of specific questions: infertility (is the endometrium secretory, i.e. did she ovulate?), abnormal uterine bleeding , and any post-menopausal bleeding , where the job is to rule out malignancy. It is also indicated when endometrial cells appear on a Pap smear in a woman over 45 — those cells have no business being there. The link back to physiology: a secretory endometrium is proof of ovulation, because only the corpus luteum makes enough progesterone to produce it. Persistent proliferative endometrium in a woman who should be cycling means unopposed estrogen — the setup for hyperplasia.

entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: The Ovary Through the Cycle The follicle is a structure that grows, ruptures, converts into an endocrine gland, and then scars. Each stage has a name and a look. The whole cycle laid out around one ovary, read clockwise: primordial → primary → secondary → mature (Graafian) → ovulation → corpus luteum → corpus albicans . In life these stages are not synchronised like this — the drawing compresses a whole cycle into a single section. From Byer, Shainberg & Galliano, Dimensions of Human Sexuality , 5e, as used in the lecture. Developing follicle in the cortex — oocyte, granulosa layers around it, theca outside that. Corpus luteum, low power. Large and conspicuously folded — the collapsed wall of the ruptured follicle. Ovarian cell of origin Benign Borderline Malignant Surface epithelial Serous cystadenofibroma Serous borderline tumour High-grade serous carcinoma Germ cell Teratoma (usually benign) · dysgerminoma (malignant) Sex cord–stromal Fibroma · granulosa cell tumour The classification is not arbitrary trivia — it follows the three cell populations in the section above. A granulosa cell tumour comes from the cell that makes estradiol, and behaves accordingly (precocious puberty, post-menopausal bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia).

entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: Week 1: The Journey Everything in week 1 happens while the embryo is in transit. It is dividing the whole way down the tube, but not growing — each division halves the cell size, so the whole ball stays the size of the original oocyte until it reaches the uterus. Week 1, drawn along the route. Read right to left: ovulated oocyte → fertilization → cleavage down the tube → morula → blastocyst , arriving in the uterine cavity. Cells divide but the embryo does not grow — blastomeres just get smaller, so the ball stays oocyte-sized until it implants. Step What actually happens Fertilization One of 200–300 million sperm reaches the oocyte in the ampulla . The acrosomal cap releases enzymes to get through the corona radiata and zona pellucida ; contact with the oocyte membrane triggers the zonal reaction , the block to polyspermy . Pronuclei fuse → diploid zygote, 44 + XX or XY . Cleavage Mitoses producing blastomeres : 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32. At 16–32 cells it is a morula . Blastulation Day 4: a cavity appears and it becomes a blastocyst , sorted into embryoblast (inner) and trophoblast (outer). Hatching Day 5: enzymes dissolve the zona pellucida . Nothing can implant through it, so it must go. Decidual reaction The secretory endometrium from Part 1 is the landing site — progesterone from the corpus luteum has already filled those coiled glands with glycogen. If implantation happens the secretions feed the embryo; if not, it is shed as menses. Clinical: Ectopic Implantation Implantation anywhere other than the uterine cavity. It is a surgical emergency because those sites cannot accommodate a growing pregnancy and rupture with major haemorrhage. Site Share Tubal — ampulla ~70% , isthmus ~12%, fimbrial ~11%, interstitial ~2% ~95% Ovarian ~3% Abdominal ~1% Cervical rare Note it is the ampulla in both the normal and the abnormal story: it is where fertilization happens, so it is where a delayed embryo implants. Anything that slows tubal transport — prior PID with scarring, prior ectopic, tubal surgery, smoking — raises the risk. Percentages from Bouyer et al., Hum Reprod 2002;17:3224–30 (1,800 consecutive cases). The lecture slide gives 96–98% tubal, 4% ovarian, 1% cervical and 1% abdominal, which sums to more than 100% — the figures above are the population-based numbers.

entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: Week 2: The Rule of Twos This is the most memorable week, because everything in it splits in half. Learn the three pairs and week 2 is done. Coronal section, week 2. The amniotic cavity (blue) forms within the epiblast; the yolk sac (yellow/orange) is enclosed by the hypoblast. The bilaminar disc is the thin double floor between them — epiblast on top, hypoblast below. Everything around it is support tissue. Drawn for these notes — the deck states the rule of twos in prose. The invading syncytiotrophoblast is the layer that makes hCG. The rest of week 2 is placenta construction. Extraembryonic mesoderm covers the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast and the outer surfaces of the yolk sac and amnion; a cavity opens within it — the chorionic cavity (extraembryonic coelom). Chorionic villi — built from cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast and extraembryonic mesoderm together — invade maternal tissue, fetal vessels grow into them, and the uteroplacental circulation begins . Clinical: hCG The syncytiotrophoblast secretes human chorionic gonadotropin . Its job is to keep the corpus luteum alive so progesterone keeps flowing — without it the corpus luteum regresses on schedule and the endometrium is shed with the pregnancy in it. The placenta takes over steroid production at around 7–9 weeks (the luteal–placental shift), after which the corpus luteum is no longer needed. hCG shares the α subunit of LH, FSH and TSH and acts on the LH receptor — the link straight back to the HPG axis lecture . It is detectable throughout pregnancy, which makes it the pregnancy test. Precision point: the slide says low hCG indicates ectopic pregnancy. More accurately, it is the trend that matters — a rise of <35–50% over 48 hours , or a plateau, suggests a non-viable pregnancy (ectopic or failing intrauterine). An hCG above the discriminatory zone (roughly 1,500–3,500 IU/L depending on the centre) with no intrauterine gestational sac on transvaginal ultrasound is the finding that points to ectopic. A single value is almost never diagnostic.

entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: Week 3: Gastrulation Two layers become three. This is the week that sets the entire body plan, and it is the week teratogens do the most damage. The primitive streak appears at the caudal end and sets the longitudinal axis — and therefore left and right; the pit at its cranial end is the primitive node , and the head forms there. Gastrulation in section. Epiblast cells dive in at the streak: the first wave replaces the hypoblast to become definitive endoderm ; the second spreads between the layers as intraembryonic mesoderm ; whatever epiblast is left on top becomes definitive ectoderm . Every germ layer comes from epiblast — fate follows where the cell migrated. The result, in coronal section. Mesoderm has subdivided into midline notochord , paraxial (somites → bone, muscle, dermis), intermediate (kidneys, gonads) and lateral plate (body and gut wall, and the cavity that becomes the intraembryonic coelom ). The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural tube — which is where week 4 picks up. What each germ layer becomes Ectoderm Mesoderm Endoderm Epidermis and appendages (hair, nails, sweat glands, tooth enamel, mammary glands) Anterior pituitary Sensory epithelia of eye, ear, nose Heart and pericardium, entire circulatory system Connective tissue, cartilage, bone, skeletal muscle Kidneys , gonads , genital ducts Spleen, adrenal cortex , pleura Epithelial lining of the GI and respiratory tracts Lining of bladder and most of the urethra Parenchyma of thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, tonsil, liver , pancreas Neural tube (ectoderm) → CNS, PNS, ANS. Neural crest (ectoderm) → meninges, ganglia, melanocytes, adrenal medulla . Two pairs are worth pinning down because they get confused: adrenal cortex is mesoderm but adrenal medulla is neural crest ; and for the gut, endoderm supplies the epithelial lining while mesoderm supplies the muscle and connective tissue of the wall.

entries.t: Week 4: Closing the Tube, Folding the Body
entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: Week 4: Closing the Tube, Folding the Body Drawn for these notes — the deck shows only a dorsal sketch and describes the stages in prose. Until the neuropores close, the neural canal is open to amniotic fluid — which is why an open defect leaks alpha-fetoprotein into amniotic fluid and maternal serum. The canal becomes the ventricular system and central canal ; the walls become brain and spinal cord . The slides give day 24 (cranial) and day 26 (caudal). The commonly cited textbook values are day 25 and day 27 ; either way the point is that both close in the fourth week, roughly two days apart. Folding, and the body plan In week 4 the flat trilaminar disc folds in the median and horizontal planes, driven by differential growth — the rim of the disc grows fast while the yolk sac does not. A flat disc becomes a C-shaped, three-dimensional body . Three consequences worth knowing: The yolk sac is pinched down to the vitelline duct , and the gut tube forms. The intraembryonic coelom is divided into the three body cavities: pericardial , pleural and peritoneal . The connecting stalk becomes the umbilical cord . Head fold and tail fold curl the flat disc into a C. The yolk sac narrows to the vitelline duct , the gut tube forms, and the connecting stalk becomes the umbilical cord . Organogenesis is under way. The heart is the first organ to function — a heartbeat is detectable by week 4. The lungs are the last , and are not fully functional until birth.

entries.t: What Can Go Wrong, and When
entries.p: Histology of the Gynecologic Tract & Early Embryogenesis
entries.x: What Can Go Wrong, and When A teratogen is any agent that interferes with development of the embryo or fetus. Whether an exposure matters depends almost entirely on when it happens. Drawn for these notes; the deck’s own timeline marks the three periods but not the organ windows. Bar positions are schematic, not exact gestational boundaries. The practical rule: an exposure before the missed period is usually all-or-none; an exposure in the first trimester is the one to take seriously. Teratogen What it does Alcohol No safe amount, no safe time. Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder; FAS is the severe end — cognitive, behavioural and physical. ~10.5 per 10,000 in Canada. Entirely preventable. Rubella Congenital rubella syndrome: sensorineural deafness, cataracts, PDA . Up to 90% if infected in the first 11 weeks, ~60% at 11–16, ~6% at 17–30, nil after 30. Viruses are teratogenic; bacteria generally are not. Antiepileptics Valproate and carbamazepine → spina bifida . Valproate interferes with folate metabolism; also cleft lip and renal defects. Tetracyclines Stained teeth, enamel hypoplasia. Nicotine Miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth, growth restriction, low birth weight, SIDS. Cannabis ~2.3× stillbirth; later developmental and hyperactivity disorders. ACOG advises against it throughout. Radiation High acute doses → microcephaly, intellectual disability, growth restriction, leukaemia. Diagnostic imaging is a different order of magnitude — no demonstrated risk below 50 mGy (5 rad) , teratogenic threshold before 16 weeks ~ 100–200 mGy . Radioiodine is the real hazard after ~week 10. Maternal factors Malnutrition → low birth weight. Obesity → more NTDs. Age >35 → chromosomal abnormalities, hypertension, gestational diabetes; >40 → miscarriage, preterm, ectopic. Paternal age → autism, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, childhood leukaemia. The One Intervention That Works Best Folic acid, started before conception. The neural tube closes on days 25–27 — roughly when a missed period is first noticed. Supplementation begun after a positive pregnancy test is already late. That single timing fact is why folate is recommended to anyone who could become pregnant, not to people who already know they are. Most of these conditions are multifactorial — genes plus environment together. Neural tube defects, cleft lip ± palate, congenital heart disease and type 1 diabetes are the standard examples.

Learning Objectives Identify the hormones and proteins in the feedback loop of the HPG axis. Label the factors that work in positive and negative feedback in this cycle. Where a section goes past the slides it is marked, with sources at the bottom.

entries.t: The Whole Axis in One Picture
entries.x: The Whole Axis in One Picture Learn this diagram first. Every later section is a zoom-in on one arrow of it. Drawn for these notes as a clean overview — the lecture’s own version of this diagram is in the pulse-generator section below. Two feedback rails, not one: steroids reach both upper storeys, inhibin reaches only the pituitary and only suppresses FSH. That asymmetry is the reason FSH and LH can move in opposite directions in the same patient — an isolated high FSH with a normal LH says the germ-cell compartment has failed while steroid output is holding. Why Three Storeys Each relay adds a place to apply control — the hypothalamus is where nutrition, stress, sleep and exercise get a vote. It also explains why you measure LH and FSH: they sit above the gonad, so they say which storey is broken. Low steroid with high gonadotropins = the gonad failed (primary hypogonadism). Low steroid with low or normal gonadotropins = the fault is upstream (secondary/central).

The Hypothalamus: Where Everything Sits The hypothalamus sits at the base of the forebrain, below the thalamus and above the pituitary. It is not one structure but a cluster of nuclei — discrete balls of cell bodies, each with its own job — laid out along a rostral–caudal axis from the preoptic area at the front to the mammillary bodies at the back. It also runs energy expenditure, body weight, fluid balance, blood pressure, temperature and sleep, which is why reproduction fails first when anything else goes wrong: it is all wired into the same box. The nuclei themselves — preoptic area at the front, arcuate at the base right against the median eminence . Plant, Front Neuroendocrinol 2012;33:160–68, via the lecture. Now work through them one at a time Click any structure → Select a structure in the diagram to read what it does and why it matters for the HPG axis. Rostral · nucleus Preoptic area Where most GnRH cell bodies live in primates. It also contains the AVPV , the kisspeptin population that carries the positive feedback arm — the one that produces the LH surge. The origin of the entire axis. Rostral–middle · nucleus Paraventricular nucleus (PVN) The only nucleus with both neuron types in bulk: magnocellular (oxytocin, vasopressin → posterior pituitary) and parvicellular ( CRH , TRH → portal system). Where stress touches reproduction — PVN CRH suppresses GnRH. Middle · nucleus Dorsomedial nucleus (DMH) Relays between the suprachiasmatic nucleus and the PVN, integrating arousal, feeding, circadian output and stress. Not a direct HPG player — a landmark on the map. Middle · nucleus Supraoptic nucleus (SON) Sits above the optic tract — hence the name. Almost entirely magnocellular : axons run the whole way down the stalk and release oxytocin and vasopressin into the systemic circulation. The cleanest magnocellular example — the neuron is the endocrine cell. Middle · nucleus Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) The master circadian clock, directly above the optic chiasm, entrained by light through the retinohypothalamic tract. Gates the timing of the LH surge — the pulses are clock-anchored. Middle · nucleus Ventromedial nucleus (VMH) The satiety centre — lesions here produce hyperphagia and obesity. Sits immediately above the arcuate: energy balance and reproduction share the neighbourhood. Middle · the important one Arcuate nucleus The infundibular nucleus in humans. It sits at the very base, against the median eminence, so its neurons dump peptide straight i

entries.t: Two Kinds of Neuron, Two Ways Out
entries.x: Two Kinds of Neuron, Two Ways Out Hypothalamic endocrine function is carried by exactly two neuron types. The difference is simply how far the axon goes , and everything else follows from that. Both routes on one picture. Neurons ending in the median eminence release peptide into the first capillary bed; the portal veins carry it down the stalk to a second capillary bed among the endocrine cells of the anterior lobe. The neurons that run all the way through to the posterior lobe release their hormone there, straight into the systemic circulation. © 2004 Pearson Education, via the lecture. Parvicellular Magnocellular Also called Hypophysiotrophic Neurohypophyseal Cell bodies Arcuate, preoptic, periventricular, PVN Supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei Axon ends In the median eminence — goes no further In the posterior pituitary , having crossed the ME and run down the stalk Releases into The portal circulation, locally The general circulation, directly Products GnRH , CRH, TRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine Oxytocin, vasopressin Net effect Tells another cell to make a hormone The peptide is the hormone The hypophysial portal system A portal system passes blood through two capillary beds in series. Here: superior hypophyseal artery → primary plexus in the median eminence, where parvicellular endings release GnRH → long portal veins down the stalk → secondary plexus in the anterior pituitary, where GnRH binds GnRH-R on gonadotropes and LH and FSH enter the same capillaries. Why a Private Circuit Concentration: nanogram quantities dumped systemically would be diluted into nothing — which is why serum GnRH is not a clinical test and you measure the pituitary hormones instead. Fidelity: a pulse only carries information if it arrives as a pulse; the systemic circulation would smear it flat. Specificity: nothing else in the body ever sees a GnRH level high enough to matter.

GnRH: The Molecule GnRH is a decapeptide . It is made by endocrine and non-endocrine cells and acts in endocrine, paracrine, autocrine and juxtacrine modes. Mammalian GnRH is GnRH-I (pGlu–His–Trp–Ser– Tyr –Gly– Leu – Arg –Pro–Gly), the key regulator of gonadotropin release. A second form, GnRH-II , originally found in chicken hypothalamus and also present in humans, differs at positions 5, 7 and 8 (Tyr→His, Leu→Trp, Arg→Tyr) and has largely non-pituitary roles. The receptor GnRH-R is a GPCR signalling through G q/11 → PLC → IP 3 /DAG → Ca 2+ and PKC . The mammalian type I receptor is the only known GPCR with no C-terminal tail , so it resists fast arrestin-driven internalisation — which is why the axis tolerates hourly pulses without desensitising, yet still shuts down under continuous occupancy through receptor downregulation. Both halves are exploited by the drugs below. (Receptor structure not on the slides.) GnRH signalling is not confined to the hypothalamus and pituitary : receptors are also found in ovary, granulosa luteal cells, uterus, placenta, breast, prostate and choriocarcinoma cell lines.

entries.t: Pulsatility: The Signal Is the Rhythm
entries.x: Pulsatility: The Signal Is the Rhythm The single most important idea in the lecture. GnRH neurons spontaneously depolarise in a coordinated fashion and secrete into the median eminence in pulses , driving pulsatile LH and FSH release. Cultured GnRH neurons do the same in a dish, so the pulse-generating capacity is intrinsic . The pituitary reads how often GnRH arrives, not how much — change the frequency and you change which gonadotropin gets made. GnRH pulse frequency and what the pituitary makes Pick a regimen → Slow 1 pulse every 3 h Moderate 1 pulse every 90 min Fast 1 pulse every hour Continuous constant infusion LH balanced FSH balanced Slow pulses favour FSH A slow GnRH pulse frequency preferentially drives FSH-β gene transcription. In ovariectomised rhesus monkeys with the hypothalamus lesioned and GnRH replaced artificially, dropping the rate from one pulse per hour to one every three hours made LH fall variably but made FSH rise every time . Where you see it: the luteal–follicular transition . As the corpus luteum dies, progesterone falls, GnRH pulses speed back up from their slow luteal rate — but the window of slow pulsing is what lets FSH climb and recruit the next cohort of follicles. The physiological middle Around one pulse every 60–120 minutes is the normal working range across most of the cycle, with LH and FSH both released and each GnRH pulse producing a matching LH pulse. FSH pulses are harder to see than LH pulses even here — FSH has a longer half-life and a component of constitutive secretion, so its trace is smoother. Fast pulses favour LH Rapid pulse rates preferentially drive the α and LH-β subunit genes. In GnRH-deficient men given progressively faster pulses — 120 minutes down to 15 — mean LH rose while FSH did not change . Where you see it: the late follicular phase running into the LH surge. Persistently fast pulsing raises the LH:FSH ratio — the pattern classically described in PCOS , where high LH relative to FSH drives thecal androgen without matching follicular maturation. Continuous GnRH switches the axis OFF This is the counter-intuitive one. Give GnRH constantly and gonadotropin output collapses: the gonadotrope desensitises and GnRH receptors are downregulated . Knobil’s hypothalamic-clamp experiments showed it directly — pulsatile GnRH restored gonadotropin secretion in lesioned monkeys, while continuous GnRH produced only a transient response before shutting down. This is not a curiosity. It is the entire mechanism o

entries.t: Kisspeptin: How Steroids Actually Reach the Pulse Generator
entries.x: Kisspeptin: How Steroids Actually Reach the Pulse Generator The slides flag this and leave it hanging: estradiol and progesterone control GnRH release, but they do not act on the GnRH neuron . The reason is concrete — GnRH neurons do not express ERα , the receptor subtype required for steroid feedback control of gonadotropin secretion. So the signal has to be relayed, and the relay is kisspeptin , whose neurons are ERα-positive. Drawn for these notes — the deck names kisspeptin as the strongest regulator but does not separate the two populations. The relay that makes steroid feedback possible. Two kisspeptin populations, opposite signs, same target. This is also how the same hormone — estradiol — can be inhibitory for most of the cycle and abruptly stimulatory at mid-cycle: it is not the hormone that changes, it is which population is dominant and for how long the level has been held up. The human proof: loss-of-function mutations in KISS1R /GPR54 — and in TAC3 / TACR3 , neurokinin B and its receptor — cause normosmic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Remove the relay and the axis never starts. About three-quarters of kisspeptin cells in the human infundibular nucleus co-express neurokinin B and dynorphin (the KNDy neurons): neurokinin B pushes the pulse on, dynorphin shuts it off. (KNDy detail from Endotext.) Nutrition, body fat, stress, exercise and photoperiod all converge on Kiss1 expression — the route by which a marathon runner or an underweight patient loses their cycle: leptin falls → arcuate kisspeptin falls → GnRH pulses stop.

entries.t: GnRH Analogues: Turning the Physiology Into a Drug
entries.x: GnRH Analogues: Turning the Physiology Into a Drug Both agonists and antagonists are used to terminate GnRH-receptor-mediated signalling . They reach the same destination by opposite routes, and that difference is the whole clinical decision. Drawn for these notes — the deck describes the flare in prose only. Same endpoint, different path. The agonist has to stimulate the receptor before it can exhaust it, so testosterone rises for the first week. The antagonist simply blocks, so it falls from the first dose. GnRH agonist GnRH antagonist Agents Leuprolide (Lupron), nafarelin (Synarel), goserelin (Zoladex) Degarelix (Firmagon), ganirelix (Antagon), cetrorelix (Cetrotide), abarelix (Plenaxis) At the receptor Occupies it continuously — stimulates first, then desensitises and downregulates Binds competitively and reversibly , blocking LH and FSH release Onset Delayed — weeks, with an initial flare Immediate , no surge Net effect Men: LH falls → testicular testosterone suppressed. Women: LH/FSH fall → ovarian estradiol suppressed. Where this is used Prostate cancer → antagonist. No surge, so no tumour flare (bone pain, cord compression, obstruction) and no need for antiandrogen cover. Degarelix is approved in Europe and the USA. IVF → antagonist. Prevents a premature LH surge during FSH stimulation — cetrorelix , ganirelix . Agonist where a few weeks of flare is tolerable and depot dosing wins: endometriosis, fibroids, central precocious puberty. Hence the exam trap: a man on leuprolide for metastatic prostate cancer with worsening bone pain at day 5 is having the flare, not treatment failure.

entries.t: LH and FSH: Structure and Signalling
entries.x: LH and FSH: Structure and Signalling Both are named for what they do in the ovary — a historical accident, since they do just as much in the testis. Feature Detail Structure Glycoproteins of two subunits. The α subunit is shared with TSH and hCG; the β subunit is unique and determines biological activity Receptor GPCR → adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP → PKA LH targets Theca (ovary) and Leydig (testis) — stimulates cholesterol side-chain cleavage FSH targets Granulosa (ovary) and Sertoli (testis) — in the testis also stimulates androgen-binding protein Release Pulsatile, following the GnRH pulses Why the Shared α Subunit Matters hCG shares that α subunit and has a β close to LH-β, so hCG activates the LH receptor — hence hCG as the ovulation trigger in IVF, and hCG cross-reacting at the TSH receptor in molar pregnancy or hyperemesis. It is also why pregnancy tests measure β -hCG: the α subunit alone would pick up LH, FSH and TSH. The two-cell, two-gonadotropin rule Neither gonadal cell can make estradiol alone — each is missing an enzyme the other has. Drawn for these notes; the deck gives this as a list of bullet points. The two-cell, two-gonadotropin model. The enzymatic division of labour is deliberate: it means estrogen output is controlled by two independent gonadotropins at two separate points, so the follicle cannot make estradiol without FSH having selected it. Inhibin, activin, and why FSH is regulated differently In response to FSH, granulosa and Sertoli cells secrete inhibin , a glycoprotein that feeds back on the FSH-producing pituitary cells and reduces their responsiveness to GnRH — a loop that touches FSH and leaves LH alone. Peptide Source Effect on FSH Inhibin B Granulosa cells (early follicular phase); Sertoli cells in the male ↓ Suppresses — blocks activin at its receptor Inhibin A Dominant follicle and corpus luteum ↓ Suppresses Activin Gonad and the gonadotrope itself ↑ Stimulates FSH synthesis and release directly Follistatin Pituitary, paracrine ↓ Suppresses indirectly — binds and sequesters activin Why FSH Is Held More Tightly FSH has a second feedback system LH does not have : activin–inhibin–follistatin reports from the germ-cell compartment rather than the steroid-producing one. That is why the two dissociate, usefully: High FSH, normal LH — germ-cell failure (falling ovarian reserve, low inhibin B); steroid output still holds. High LH:FSH — the PCOS pattern, from persistently fast pulsing. Both high, steroid low — primary gonadal failu

entries.t: Steroids: One Precursor, Four Rings, Two Conversions That Matter
entries.x: Steroids: One Precursor, Four Rings, Two Conversions That Matter Steroids are terpenoid lipids : four fused rings in a 6–6–6–5 arrangement. Every steroid differs from the others only by the functional groups hung on those rings and their oxidation state — which is why a single enzyme can change a hormone’s identity completely. All of them start as cholesterol . The whole steroid tree. For this lecture follow only three things: the entry point top-left (cholesterol → pregnenolone by side-chain cleavage — the rate-limiting step, and the pink colour code means mitochondria ); the androgen block in blue; and the two arrows out of it — aromatase into the pink estrogen triangle, and 5α-reductase down to dihydrotestosterone. The mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid arms belong to the adrenal lecture. The rate-limiting step Cholesterol → pregnenolone, inside the mitochondrion. StAR shuttles cholesterol from the outer to the inner mitochondrial membrane — that transport is the real bottleneck — and CYP11A1 (P450scc) then cleaves the side chain. This is the step LH stimulates, which is why an LH pulse raises testosterone within minutes rather than hours. The two conversions that matter Aromatase (CYP19A1) 5α-reductase (SRD5A2) Reaction Androgen → estrogen (androstenedione→estrone, testosterone→estradiol). Aromatises the A ring — an irreversible commitment to the estrogen class Testosterone → DHT , a far more potent androgen that cannot be aromatised Where Granulosa cells (FSH-induced), adipose, placenta, brain, bone, Sertoli cells. After menopause, adipose aromatisation to estrone is the main estrogen source Skin, hair follicle, prostate , external genitalia Drug Anastrozole, letrozole — ER-positive breast cancer, postmenopausal Finasteride, dutasteride — BPH, androgenetic alopecia Testosterone sits at a fork: through aromatase it becomes estradiol (in men, closing the epiphyses and maintaining bone density); through 5α-reductase it becomes DHT (external genitalia, prostate, male-pattern hair). Because DHT cannot be aromatised, blocking 5α-reductase shifts testosterone toward the estrogen arm — the mechanism of finasteride-related gynaecomastia, and why the two drug classes are never interchangeable. Release and transport Steroids cannot be vesicle-packaged and stored. Progesterone and estradiol are not stored in the follicle or corpus luteum : they are secreted as fast as they are made, then bound to plasma proteins. Steroid Carried by Needs conversion first? Estra

How Steroids Actually Signal Two routes, and the genomic one has two sub-routes. The distinction that matters is timescale . The two pathways from the lecture, both genomic . The ligand crosses the membrane unaided, binds its cytoplasmic receptor, and the complex enters the nucleus. (1) Direct — the receptor dimer binds a hormone response element on the DNA itself. (2) Indirect — the receptor never touches DNA, and instead tethers to other transcription factors and rides them to their genes. Either way the output is new mRNA and new protein , over hours to days. Wierman, 2007, via the lecture. There is a third route the slide does not draw: a non-genomic one, through membrane receptors such as GPER1 (GPR30) , working via kinase cascades and Ca 2+ flux with no new transcription at all. That is what accounts for steroid effects appearing in seconds to minutes — too fast for transcription to explain. (Added; not on the slides.)

Learning Objectives Describe the clinical presentations of, and explain the management of, osteomalacia . Describe the clinical presentations of, and explain the management of, Paget's disease . Describe the clinical presentations of, and explain the management of, osteogenesis imperfecta .

What Osteomalacia Is A defect in bone matrix mineralization. The osteoid is laid down normally; it simply does not get mineralized. Same disease, two names depending on when it strikes: Age Name What you see Childhood — growth plates still open Rickets Deformity at the growing ends of bone — classically bowing of the long bones , because unmineralized bone bends under weight Adulthood — growth plates closed Osteomalacia No growth deformity; weak bones that fracture, plus pain and muscle weakness Rickets. The bowing is the hallmark — unmineralized bone deforming under load. On the radiograph the metaphyses are widened, cupped and frayed, because that is where growth and mineralization should be happening. Glisson, 1651. "A disease common to children" — described nearly four centuries ago, and still with us wherever sunlight, diet or absorption fail. The mineralization defect produces weak bones that fracture — and it is often mistaken for osteoporosis . Malabsorption syndromes are a common cause — celiac disease in particular. Proximal muscle weakness (myopathy) can be severe and contributes to falls. A patient who is falling and fracturing has two problems from one deficiency. Why Confusing It With Osteoporosis Matters Both present as fragility fractures in someone with thin-looking bones on imaging, and osteomalacic bone can look osteopenic on a radiograph. But they are different problems: osteoporosis is too little bone , osteomalacia is bone that is not mineralized . The blood work separates them, and it is not subtle. In osteoporosis, calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase are all normal — that is why the work-up there is aimed at excluding secondary causes. In osteomalacia they are frankly abnormal. The consequence of getting it backwards is real: an antiresorptive given to someone with uncorrected vitamin D deficiency and hypocalcemia treats the wrong mechanism and can drive the calcium lower still. Correcting vitamin D and calcium comes first, always.

entries.t: Vitamin D: Why It Sits at the Centre
entries.x: Vitamin D: Why It Sits at the Centre Vitamin D is essential for calcium absorption , and adequate calcium absorption is what prevents secondary hyperparathyroidism and limits bone resorption . Take the vitamin D away and the sequence runs itself: less calcium absorbed → PTH rises to defend the serum calcium → PTH leaches calcium out of bone . The skeleton pays for the gut's failure. Etiology — four routes to a deficiency Category Mechanism 1. Decreased availability of vitamin D Insufficient sunlight exposure · nutritional deficiency · malabsorption · hydroxylation defects · nephrotic syndrome 2. Liver disease The site of 25-hydroxylation — the first activation step 3. Chronic renal failure The site of 1α-hydroxylation — the second, rate-limiting activation step 4. Anticonvulsant therapy Induces hepatic enzymes that accelerate vitamin D catabolism Note that categories 2 and 3 map onto the two hydroxylation steps of vitamin D activation — liver first, kidney second. Knowing where each organ sits in the pathway is enough to reconstruct this list. See vitamin D and calcium homeostasis for the pathway itself, and 2.2 for what PTH does with the result. Why Older Patients Are the Ones Who Get Caught Four separate things go wrong at once, and none of them individually would be enough: Formation and processing of vitamin D may be impaired · exposure to sunlight may be limited · dietary sources provide little vitamin D · and adherence to supplementation may be inconsistent . Skin synthesis falls, the person goes outside less, the diet was never a real source, and the tablet that would fix it does not reliably get taken. How much is actually in things Source Vitamin D content Sunlight The main source — and the one that fails first Multivitamin pill 200–1000 IU Calcium tablet containing vitamin D 120–1000 IU Fortified milk Fluctuates — 37–50 IU/100 mL, or 111–150 IU per cup Dedicated supplements 400 or 1000 IU per tablet The practical point is the size of the numbers. A cup of fortified milk supplies roughly a tenth of a 1000 IU tablet, so diet alone will not correct a real deficiency — which is exactly why sunlight is listed as the main source and why supplementation is the intervention.

Investigations and Treatment Modality Finding Laboratory ↓ calcium and ↓ phosphate · ↑ alkaline phosphatase · ↓ urinary calcium Radiology Pseudofractures — healed microfractures. Bone may also simply look osteopenic Bone biopsy The gold standard , but usually not necessary Alkaline phosphatase is the marker of bone turnover here, and it is raised for a specific reason: osteoblasts are working hard, producing matrix that never gets mineralized. High ALP means active bone formation — it will come up again in Paget's, for a related reason. Urinary calcium is low because there is barely any calcium being absorbed to excrete, and PTH is retaining what little there is. Pseudofractures (Looser–Milkman zones) of the pelvis and left femoral neck. They are transverse lucent bands running perpendicular to the cortex, typically bilateral and symmetrical — ribbons of unmineralized osteoid, not true breaks. Courtesy of CJ Menkes, MD, as shown in the lecture. Treatment It depends on the underlying cause — correcting a celiac enteropathy is as much part of the treatment as the supplement. Then replace what is missing: vitamin D , plus phosphate and calcium supplements if those are low. Baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D Regimen < 30 nmol/L 50,000 IU ergocalciferol for 12 weeks , then 800–2000 IU daily 30–75 nmol/L 800–2000 IU daily Repeat the level in 3 months in either case The Lecture's Own Case A 23-year-old woman with celiac disease presents with falls, muscle weakness , and the femoral neck film above. The diagnosis is pseudofractures due to vitamin D deficiency — and every element of the stem points there: celiac disease is the classic malabsorptive cause, proximal myopathy explains the falls, and the lucency is a Looser zone. The distractors are the two diseases it gets confused with. Atypical fracture from bisphosphonate use is subtrochanteric, in someone who has been on the drug for years — not a 23-year-old. Femoral neck fracture due to osteoporosis would be a true fracture, and osteoporosis at 23 with normal-looking labs is not the story. The age and the celiac history are the whole question.

Paget's Disease A metabolic disease characterized by excessive bone destruction and repair — a localized disorder of bone remodelling. The sequence has two steps, and both matter: Increased osteoclastic activity leads to increased bone resorption. Osteoblastic activity increases in response , producing new bone — but new bone that is structurally abnormal and fragile . That is the central idea: the problem is not that too little bone is made. Often more bone is made. It is the wrong bone — laid down too fast and in a disorganized pattern, so it is bigger, denser on film, and weaker in life. It is relatively common: 5% of the population , rising to 10% of those over 80 . Normal trabecular bone on the left, pagetic bone on the right. The pagetic trabeculae are thicker and there is more of them — and the architecture is chaotic. More bone, worse bone. Clinical features Feature Detail Usually asymptomatic Found on routine X-rays or an elevated alkaline phosphatase . This is how most cases present Severe bone pain Pelvis, femur, tibia Skeletal deformities Bowed tibia , kyphosis, frequent fractures Skull involvement Headaches, increased hat size , deafness Increased warmth over the bone Due to increased vascularity — a physical sign you can elicit at the bedside Skull involvement, clinically. The vault expands — which is what "increased hat size" actually means as a history question. The same thing on film. An enlarged skull with a patchy, fluffy "cotton wool" appearance from the disruption of normal bone architecture. Courtesy of Nicky Kelepouris, MD. Normal tibia on the left, pagetic tibia on the right: expanded, with a thickened cortex and coarse trabeculae, and denser than normal . Compare this with osteoporosis or osteomalacia, where bone looks less dense — Paget's is the metabolic bone disease that makes bone look like there is more of it.

Investigations Finding Alkaline phosphatase Very high — the osteoblasts are working furiously Calcium Normal , or increased in the case of immobility Phosphate Normal Urinary hydroxyproline Increased — a marker of bone turnover, released as collagen is broken down Bone scan For the extent of disease — which bones are involved, and how many Radiographs The initial lesion may be destructive and radiolucent ; involved bones are expanded and denser than normal , with multiple fissure fractures Why the bone scan is the extent test. The clinically obvious lesion is the clavicle; the scan shows the pelvis and femur are involved too. Paget's is localized but frequently multifocal , and you cannot know how much disease there is from the part the patient noticed. Three Diseases, Three Lab Patterns Calcium Phosphate Alkaline phosphatase Osteomalacia ↓ ↓ ↑ Paget's disease Normal (↑ if immobile) Normal ↑↑ very high Osteoporosis Normal Normal Normal Alkaline phosphatase is raised in the first two and normal in the third, so ALP is the test that says "this is not osteoporosis." Calcium and phosphate then split the other two: low in osteomalacia, normal in Paget's. An isolated raised ALP with a normal calcium, in a well patient, is the classic accidental route into a diagnosis of Paget's — provided the liver has been excluded as the source first.

Complications Complication Mechanism 1. Fractures The new bone is structurally abnormal and fragile 2. Hypercalcemia Only in the case of immobility — resorption continues while formation stalls 3. Cranial nerve compression — deafness Expanding skull bone narrows the foramina the nerves run through 4. Spinal cord compression Expanded vertebrae encroaching on the canal 5. Osteosarcoma — 1–3% Signalled by marked bone pain, a new lytic lesion, and a rising alkaline phosphatase 6. High-output congestive heart failure Due to increased vascularity — pagetic bone is a low-resistance shunt, and enough of it raises cardiac output until the heart cannot sustain it 7. Osteoarthritis Deformed bone alters joint mechanics at the joints it abuts Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone — soft tissue swelling and destruction of the anterior femoral cortex, in a femur whose trabecular thickening shows the underlying Paget's. Rare at 1–3%, but it is why new pain and a rising ALP in known Paget's is never dismissed. Courtesy of Jonathan Kruskal, MD.

Treatment and Who to Treat Symptomatic: analgesia for the pain. Bisphosphonates — zoledronate. These target the overactive osteoclast that starts the whole cycle. Calcitonin as an alternative. Indications for treating an asymptomatic patient In asymptomatic individuals with evidence of active disease — an elevated ALP, or scintigraphy showing active lesions — treatment should be considered when there is: Evidence of disease in the skull, long bones, spine, or bone abutting a joint. A surgical procedure planned in a pagetic site. Paget's disease and congestive heart failure. Why Those Three, Specifically Each maps onto a complication you are trying to prevent rather than treat. Skull, spine and bone abutting a joint are exactly the sites where expansion causes something irreversible — deafness, cord compression, secondary osteoarthritis. Congestive heart failure is the high-output state, and reducing turnover reduces the vascularity driving it. Surgery in a pagetic site is the one that is easy to forget and the most immediately dangerous: pagetic bone is highly vascular , so operating on it risks serious haemorrhage. Treating beforehand reduces the vascularity and makes the operation safer. The Lecture's Own Question Paget's of the left femur, ALP three times the upper limit of normal . Best treatment: zoledronate — a potent IV bisphosphonate, and first-line for active Paget's. The distractors are worth separating. Alendronate is a bisphosphonate too and does work, but the IV agent is the preferred first-line here and gives a more durable remission. Denosumab is an antiresorptive used in osteoporosis, not a Paget's drug. And teriparatide is the one to actively avoid : it is an anabolic that stimulates bone formation, and it is contraindicated in Paget's disease and in unexplained elevations of alkaline phosphatase , precisely because of the baseline osteosarcoma risk this disease already carries.

Osteogenesis Imperfecta Among the more common of the rare bone disorders. Incidence 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births . Mostly involves mutations in type 1 collagen — COL1A1 and COL1A2 account for 85–90% of cases . 16 subtypes identified, and the number is growing. Clinical features The recognisable set: fragility fractures, short stature, bowing deformities of the long bones, basilar skull deformities and blue sclerae . Forlino and Marini, Lancet 2016;387:10028. And beyond the skeleton: hearing loss · dentinogenesis imperfecta · aortic root dilatation and valvular insufficiency · wormian bones · pectus excavatum or carinatum. Why the Sclerae Are Blue, and Why the Aorta Is Involved Both answers are the same answer: type 1 collagen is not a bone protein, it is a connective tissue protein. Bone is where the consequences are loudest, but it is not the only place the defect exists. The sclera is largely type 1 collagen. Make it thinner and more translucent and the choroid's pigment shows through from behind — the blue is not a pigment, it is a see-through sclera. Collagen is also present in the lining of blood vessels, which is why aortic root dilatation and valvular insufficiency belong on the list — and why an echocardiogram is part of routine surveillance rather than an afterthought. The same logic covers the teeth (dentine is collagen-based) and the hearing loss (the ossicles and their attachments). Clinical characteristics by subtype — the point being how much they vary. Blue sclerae occur in 91% of type I but only 18.6% of type IV , and average fracture counts differ several-fold between subtypes. "Osteogenesis imperfecta" names a spectrum, not one disease. Patel et al., Clin Genet 2015;87:133–140.

Management and Prognosis Lifelong monitoring The surveillance list follows directly from the list of affected tissues: What How often Growth and head circumference Ongoing Hearing test, bone mineral density, ECG and echocardiogram Every two years Neurologic examination and cranial assessment As indicated by symptoms or behavioural changes — the concern is basilar invagination Skeletal radiographs Every 1–2 years Spirometry Yearly — chest wall deformity and scoliosis restrict lung volumes Management of the bone disease IV bisphosphonates are the mainstay of treatment. Optimal duration has not been studied. Indications to treat: long bone deformities · vertebral compression fractures · more than 3 fractures per year . Prognosis Highly variable. Type 1 has a normal life span . Type 2 is lethal in the perinatal period . The subtype is the prognosis. The Lecture's Own Question A 17-year-old woman with OI type 1 , 5 long-bone fractures in the last year without trauma and without atypical fractures, regular periods, normal vitamin D. The answer is zoledronate — she meets the treatment indication (> 3 fractures per year) and IV bisphosphonates are the mainstay . The stem does real work ruling things out: normal vitamin D excludes osteomalacia as the reason she is fracturing, regular periods exclude hypogonadism as a secondary cause, and no atypical fractures means she is not already suffering from an antiresorptive. On the distractors: teriparatide is an anabolic contraindicated in young adults with open epiphyses because of osteosarcoma risk — the same contraindication family as Paget's above, and directly relevant at 17. Raloxifene is a SERM used for postmenopausal osteoporosis and has no role here. Denosumab is not the established mainstay in OI, and stopping it triggers rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures — a poor choice in someone facing decades of treatment.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Learning Objective Explain the epidemiology of osteoporosis, including the treatment care gap. The assessment and treatment sections below go beyond that single objective, following the structure of the lecture notes. See the source line at the bottom for which parts came from the slides and which from the Canadian guideline.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Definition: Three Doors In Osteoporosis is not one number. Any one of these establishes the diagnosis: Route Criterion The catch Clinical Presence of a fragility fracture Excludes fractures of the skull, hands, feet and ankles, and any fracture with significant trauma. A hip fracture from a standing-height fall counts; a skull fracture does not. Densitometric BMD T-score < −2.5 A number, not a symptom — and most people who fracture are not below this line. Risk-based > 20% 10-year fracture risk Applies in the absence of both a fragility fracture and a T-score < −2.5 — the third door for people the first two miss. Why Three Definitions Rather Than One Each catches a different failure of the others. A T-score alone misses the majority of people who actually fracture, because bone quality and fall risk are not measured by densitometry. A fracture alone is a diagnosis made too late. The risk-based door exists to identify the person who has not yet fractured and whose density is not yet dire, but whose combined risk factors already put them where treatment helps.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Epidemiology: Bigger Than You Think Annual incidence in Canadian women — osteoporotic fractures against the diseases that get far more attention: Osteoporotic fractures outnumber heart attacks and breast cancer combined, by a wide margin. Stroke, also shown on the original slide, sits between the two right-hand bars. Canadian hip-fracture data from Leslie et al., Osteoporos Int 2010; non-hip extrapolated from Burge et al., J Bone Miner Res 2007; CIHI 2009; Canadian Cancer Society 2009.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: The Treatment Gap Here is the comparison the whole lecture is built around: A fracture is to osteoporosis what a heart attack is to cardiovascular disease — a sentinel event that should trigger secondary prevention. One of these is treated like that; the other is not. Bessette et al., Osteoporos Int 2008; Austin et al., CMAJ 2008. The gap has been widening . Treatment rates were higher a decade ago; as bisphosphonates fell out of favour — driven largely by fear of the rare harms covered below — prescribing declined without the risk of fracture declining with it. What undertreatment costs Outcome Figure Lifetime risk of hip fracture, age > 50 12.1% 1 year after hip fracture — unable to carry out more than one IADL 80% 1 year after hip fracture — unable to walk independently 40% 1 year after hip fracture — death 29% 5-year mortality after hip fracture 23.5% 5-year mortality after vertebral fracture 15.7% Note the 1-year and 5-year hip figures are not a contradiction — they come from different cohorts and different eras. The point they share is that hip fracture mortality is measured in tens of percent, not fractions of one.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Clinical Presentation It is a silent disease. Most patients have no symptoms until they fracture — which is exactly why case-finding depends on risk factors and densitometry rather than on how the patient feels. Vertebral fractures are graded by the loss of vertebral body height. Moderate and severe grades are the ones that feed prediction models — and many are found incidentally, never having caused a recognised episode of back pain. Accumulated vertebral fractures produce the kyphotic spine — the visible end-stage of a disease that was silent throughout. Physical signs worth looking for Sign Threshold Prospective height loss (measured over time) > 2 cm Historical height loss (versus recalled peak height) > 6 cm Rib-to-pelvis distance < 2 finger-breadths Occiput-to-wall distance > 5 cm All four are surrogates for the same thing — vertebral height that has already been lost. Falls risk assessment belongs in the same examination.

entries.t: Assessment: T-Score, Z-Score and Who to Scan
entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Assessment: T-Score, Z-Score and Who to Scan T vs Z — Different Comparators, Different Jobs T-score compares the patient's bone density to a healthy young adult at peak bone mass. That is the comparison the diagnostic threshold of −2.5 is built on, because the question it answers is "how much bone have you lost from your best?" Z-score compares them to people of their own age and sex . Losing bone with age is expected, so a normal Z-score is unremarkable — but a markedly low Z-score means the patient is losing bone faster than their peers, which points at a secondary cause rather than ordinary ageing. That is the score that should prompt you to go looking. Who gets a BMD scan Age Indication ≥ 70 Screen — no risk factors required 65–69 With 1 risk factor 50–64 With a prior fracture or ≥ 2 risk factors The risk factors: previous fragility fracture after age 40 · glucocorticoids (> 3 months in the last year at prednisone > 5 mg/day) · ≥ 2 falls in the last year · parent who fractured a hip · BMI < 20 kg/m 2 · a condition causing secondary osteoporosis · current smoking · alcohol ≥ 3 drinks/day . Blood work A short, targeted panel — aimed at excluding secondary causes and at making sure the treatment you are about to give is safe: Test Why Calcium, corrected for albumin Screens for hyperparathyroidism and malignancy — and hypocalcemia must be corrected before starting an antiresorptive. See corrected calcium . CBC Anemia or cytopenias point toward myeloma and other marrow disease Creatinine Renal function constrains drug choice — bisphosphonates are contraindicated at low clearance Alkaline phosphatase Raised in Paget's disease, osteomalacia, and bone metastases TSH Thyrotoxicosis causes bone loss — see subclinical hyperthyroidism , which is explicitly associated with it 25-OH vitamin D Deficiency must be corrected alongside any pharmacotherapy Fracture risk tools FRAX CAROC Status Preferred in the 2023 Canadian guideline Acceptable alternative Inputs More clinical risk factors, including glucocorticoids, smoking, alcohol, rheumatoid arthritis, parental hip fracture; BMD optional but better with it Age, sex, femoral neck T-score, with adjustment for fragility fracture and glucocorticoid use Output 10-year probability of major osteoporotic fracture and of hip fracture 10-year risk category — low, moderate, high Trade-off More granular, captures more of the risk that BMD alone misses Simpler, faster, fewer inputs Either way, the number that matters downstream is

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Treatment 1: Lifestyle Comes First This applies to everyone, treated or not. Recommendation Exercise Balance, functional training and progressive resistance training, more than twice weekly — to reduce falls and maintain physical function and bone strength. Weight-bearing is the operative principle. Falls prevention A formal falls-risk assessment. Most fractures require a fall; removing the fall removes the fracture. Calcium Meet the RDA from food where possible — women > 50 and men > 70: 1200 mg/day ; men 50–70: 1000 mg/day . If dietary intake is adequate, supplementation is not recommended to prevent fractures. Vitamin D RDA 600 IU/day (51–70) and 800 IU/day (> 70). Because that is hard to reach from diet, a minimum 400 IU daily supplement is suggested alongside vitamin D-rich foods. The Nuance People Get Wrong Calcium and vitamin D are not a treatment for osteoporosis — they are the nutritional floor that the actual drugs are built on. Supplementing calcium in someone already meeting the RDA through diet does not prevent fractures, and the trials that established every drug below gave their participants a minimum of roughly 400 IU of vitamin D and up to 1000 mg of calcium. That is the context in which those drugs work, not a substitute for them.

entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: Treatment 2: Choosing a Drug The drug classes, mechanisms and adverse-effect profiles are covered in detail in Drugs Affecting Vitamin D & Calcium Homeostasis . What matters here is the sequence : Pharmacotherapy pathway, 2023 Osteoporosis Canada guideline. A bisphosphonate is the default; the two side branches are the specific situations that override it. Note that anabolic therapy is never the endpoint — it must be followed by an antiresorptive. The classes, in one line each Class Agents Role Antiresorptive stop bone being broken down Bisphosphonates — alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid First line for almost everyone Denosumab (RANKL antibody) When bisphosphonates can't be used — but commits the patient to uninterrupted therapy Raloxifene (SERM) Second line; vertebral fracture reduction Hormone therapy Menopausal symptom control with a bone benefit, rather than a primary osteoporosis drug Anabolic build new bone Teriparatide , romosozumab First for severe or multiple vertebral fractures — then hand off to an antiresorptive

entries.t: The Two Harms That Created the Gap
entries.p: Osteoporosis: Epidemiology, Assessment & the Treatment Gap
entries.x: The Two Harms That Created the Gap These are the adverse effects that made prescribing fall — worth knowing precisely, because the fear of them is out of proportion to their frequency. Osteonecrosis of the jaw Atypical femoral fracture Caused by Bisphosphonates and denosumab Bisphosphonates and denosumab Where Jaw — typically after dental extraction or with poor dental health Subtrochanteric — below the lesser trochanter, in the femoral shaft Warning sign Exposed bone, non-healing dental socket New thigh or groin pain, often prodromal and often bilateral Frequency Rare — and the reason the drug holiday exists, since risk rises with cumulative duration Keeping the Risk in Proportion Both harms are real, both are rare, and both scale with how long treatment continues — which is precisely why the guideline builds in a defined treatment period and a drug holiday rather than treating indefinitely. Set against them: a 29% one-year mortality after hip fracture, and a 12.1% lifetime hip fracture risk over the age of 50. The treatment gap exists because the rare, nameable, drug-attributable harm feels more salient than the common, diffuse, disease-attributable one. Recognising that asymmetry is the actual clinical skill this lecture is teaching.

Learning Objectives Describe the clinical presentation of primary hyperparathyroidism and primary hypoparathyroidism. Explain the differential diagnosis of hypercalcemia and the etiologies of hyperparathyroidism. Explain the differential diagnosis of hypocalcemia and the etiologies of hypoparathyroidism. Describe the acute and chronic treatment of hypercalcemia and hypocalcemia, accounting for the underlying etiology.

Calcium Homeostasis: The Numbers The full loop — parathyroid, bone, kidney, gut and vitamin D — is covered in Drugs Affecting Vitamin D & Calcium Homeostasis : falling plasma Ca ++ triggers PTH, which pulls calcium from bone, reclaims it in the kidney, and (via vitamin D, made from sunlight or diet ) absorbs more from the gut; rising calcium then shuts PTH off. What that lecture skips is the numbers. Serum calcium exists in three forms, and only one of them is biologically active: Composition of total serum calcium. Only the ionized fraction is free and biologically active; the rest is bound to albumin or complexed to anions. This is why a total-calcium result misleads when albumin is abnormal — the bound fraction moves with the albumin while the active fraction may not have changed at all.

Corrected Calcium A lab reports total calcium — ionized plus protein-bound plus complexed. Since roughly 40% rides on albumin, a low albumin drags the total down while the active ionized fraction is unchanged; a high albumin does the reverse. Correcting avoids calling a hypoalbuminemic patient hypocalcemic, or missing real hypercalcemia. The Formula Corrected Ca (mmol/L) = Measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − Albumin [g/L]) A change in albumin of 1 g/L shifts measured calcium by 0.02 mmol/L, in the opposite direction — so the formula adds back what albumin took away (or subtracts what it artificially added). Worked example: Measured Ca 2.6 mmol/L, albumin 20 g/L. Corrected Ca = 2.6 + 0.02 × (40 − 20) = 2.6 + 0.4 = 3.0 mmol/L — a value that looked borderline is actually significant hypercalcemia once the low albumin is accounted for. When the true value matters and albumin is markedly abnormal, an ionized calcium measured directly is more reliable than any correction formula.

Hypercalcemia: Definition & Presentation Hypercalcemia = corrected total calcium > 2.55 mmol/L (or an elevated ionized calcium). Symptoms depend on both the absolute value and the rate of rise — a slowly-developed hypercalcemia can be markedly elevated and still nearly asymptomatic, while a rapid rise to a similar level can be florid. Mild hypercalcemia is commonly asymptomatic and picked up incidentally. The classic mnemonic is "stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones" — each with a mechanism worth knowing, not just memorizing: System Findings Why Renal ("stones") Nephrolithiasis, polyuria (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), acute/chronic renal insufficiency Excess filtered calcium supersaturates urine with calcium salts; calcium also activates the calcium-sensing receptor A G-protein-coupled receptor that lets tissues directly sense extracellular calcium — expressed in the parathyroid and, importantly, along the kidney tubule in the collecting duct and thick ascending limb, which blunts the response to ADH and impairs the countercurrent gradient — the kidney literally can't concentrate urine as well. Skeletal ("bones") Bone pain/tenderness, cystic bone lesions, skeletal demineralization, spontaneous fractures Direct consequence of the resorption driving the hypercalcemia in the first place — PTH or PTH-like signaling pulling calcium out of bone faster than it's replaced. GI ("groans") Abdominal pain, pancreatitis (acute/chronic), constipation, vomiting, anorexia Calcium reduces smooth muscle excitability (constipation); high intraductal/intracellular calcium can trigger premature intra-pancreatic trypsinogen activation, precipitating pancreatitis. Cardiovascular Short QT interval, arrhythmias, hypertension Extracellular calcium speeds the plateau (phase 2) of the cardiac action potential — shortens the ST segment specifically, which shortens the QT. Neuro/psychiatric ("psychiatric overtones") Confusion, personality change, depression, apathy High extracellular calcium raises the threshold for neuronal depolarization, generally reducing excitability — the opposite direction from hypocalcemia's tetany.

Etiology: PTH-Mediated vs. PTH-Independent The cleanest way to organize the differential is by whether PTH is driving it — and a single PTH level splits the whole list in two: PTH splits the differential in two; together, primary hyperPTH and malignancy cover >90% of cases. PTH-mediated PTH-independent Primary hyperparathyroidism Hypercalcemia of malignancy Tertiary hyperparathyroidism (chronic renal failure) Vitamin D intoxication / chronic granulomatous disease Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) Medications; hyperthyroidism, acromegaly, pheochromocytoma, adrenal insufficiency, immobilization, parenteral nutrition, milk-alkali syndrome Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy account for >90% of cases. Malignant hypercalcemia works two ways: bony metastases releasing calcium locally (e.g. breast), or a humoral factor secreted systemically — PTHrP (lung, kidney, adult T-cell leukemia; acts on the PTH receptor), lymphokines (myeloma), prostaglandins, or vitamin D-like steroids (lymphoma). Minor causes (<10%): exogenous vitamin D; granulomatous disease (sarcoid, TB — activated macrophages make their own 1α-hydroxylase, producing calcitriol outside PTH control); immobilization with high bone turnover (Paget's, thyrotoxicosis); FHH (inactivating calcium-sensing receptor mutation); milk-alkali syndrome; and thiazides (reduced renal calcium excretion, usually transient). Within primary hyperparathyroidism specifically: parathyroid adenoma (80%) , parathyroid hyperplasia, parathyroid carcinoma (rare), and familial syndromes (familial isolated hyperparathyroidism, hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome, MEN syndromes).

entries.t: Telling Primary HyperPTH and FHH Apart
entries.x: Telling Primary HyperPTH and FHH Apart Case — 65F, Osteoporosis Work-Up Back pain, radius/ulna fracture at 52, ulna fracture at 61, hysterectomy at 35. Thyroid and renal function normal. Initial Ca 2.95 mmol/L, albumin 45 g/L. Repeat Ca 2.73 mmol/L, phosphate 0.69 mmol/L, PTH 14 pmol/L (ref. 1.6–6.9), 25-OH vitamin D 70 nmol/L. Correcting for her high-normal albumin: 2.73 + 0.02 × (40 − 45) = 2.63 mmol/L — still hypercalcemic, and a reminder the correction runs both directions. Elevated PTH, low-normal phosphate (PTH wastes phosphate), sufficient vitamin D: textbook primary hyperparathyroidism . Both primary hyperPTH and FHH present with hypercalcemia and a PTH that's elevated or inappropriately normal — the fractional excretion of calcium (FeCa), from a 24-hour urine collection, is what separates them: Fractional Excretion of Calcium FeCa = (Urine Ca × Serum Cr / 1000) / (Serum Ca × Urine Cr) — from a 24-hour urine collection. It answers one question: given how high the calcium is, is the kidney letting a normal amount spill into urine, or is it hanging onto calcium it shouldn't? In FHH the mutated receptor needs a higher calcium before it registers as high, so the kidney keeps reabsorbing as though calcium were normal and little reaches the urine. In primary hyperparathyroidism the sensing is intact, so more calcium escapes despite PTH's reabsorptive pull. Distinguishing FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism by renal calcium handling. Both present with hypercalcemia and a PTH that is elevated or inappropriately normal, so the calcium and PTH values alone cannot separate them. a About 20% of FHH cases fall in the 0.01–0.02 overlap zone. Interpret only once the patient has been off thiazide diuretics for 3 months, with a normal magnesium and 25-OH vitamin D > 50 nmol/L — each of these independently lowers urinary calcium and mimics the FHH pattern.

Treatment of Acute Hypercalcemia Inpatient admission is generally required if corrected Ca > 3 mmol/L. 1 Volume repletion — normal saline, 4–6 L deficit. Hypercalcemia itself causes volume depletion (the nephrogenic-DI-like polyuria above), which further impairs renal calcium clearance — rehydrating alone starts to help. 2 Forced diuresis — 4–10 L NS plus furosemide plus K⁺, only once well hydrated. Loop diuretics block the Na-K-2Cl transporter in the thick ascending limb, which (among other things) disrupts the lumen-positive gradient that normally drives passive calcium reabsorption there — more calcium is forced into urine. Never given before volume is repleted, or it just worsens the depletion. 3 IV bisphosphonate (zoledronate). Shuts down osteoclast-mediated bone resorption — the definitive fix for most causes, but takes 2–4 days to take full effect. 4 Calcitonin. Works within hours (inhibits osteoclasts and increases renal calcium excretion directly) but tachyphylaxis sets in within 48 hours — useful as a bridge while the slower bisphosphonate takes effect, not as monotherapy. 5 Prednisone 40–60 mg/day, then taper — for myeloma or vitamin D intoxication specifically. Glucocorticoids suppress the extra-renal 1α-hydroxylase activity that granulomatous tissue and some lymphomas use to overproduce calcitriol, and have direct cytotoxic/anti-cytokine effects in myeloma — this is a cause-specific step, not a general one.

Treatment of Primary Hyperparathyroidism Presentation Approach Mild, asymptomatic, age > 50 No treatment (monitor) or medical therapy — bisphosphonates, denosumab, estrogen, or cinacalcet (a calcimimetic that increases the CaSR's sensitivity to calcium, directly opposing the FHH mechanism above) Symptomatic, or meets a surgical indication below Parathyroidectomy General measures regardless of severity: adequate hydration, and avoid thiazides and lithium — both raise calcium further (thiazides reduce renal excretion as above; lithium alters the calcium-sensing receptor's set-point similarly to FHH, raising PTH). Indications for surgery: serum calcium > 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit of normal · BMD T-score < −2.5 at the lumbar spine, femoral neck, total hip, or 1/3 radius · vertebral fracture · creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min · 24-hour urine calcium > 10 mmol/day with increased stone risk · nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis present · age < 50.

Hypocalcemia: Etiology by Lab Pattern Hypocalcemia results from failure to secrete PTH, failure to respond to PTH, vitamin D deficiency, failure to respond to vitamin D, or (rarely) acute complexation of calcium. In practice, phosphate is what splits these into recognizable buckets, because PTH and vitamin D pull phosphate in opposite directions: Phosphate splits PTH-axis problems from vitamin D problems; PTH then splits deficiency from resistance. Why Phosphate Splits This Way PTH wastes phosphate at the kidney (inhibiting proximal tubule reabsorption). Remove PTH (hypoparathyroidism) or make the kidney deaf to it (pseudohypoparathyroidism) and phosphate reabsorption goes unchecked — it climbs as calcium falls. Vitamin D deficiency is the mirror image: calcitriol absorbs both , so both fall, and the compensatory secondary PTH rise wastes what phosphate is left. Same low calcium, opposite phosphate. Vitamin D deficiency is more common than either PTH disorder — causes include malabsorption (it's fat-soluble), renal or liver failure (both metabolic steps live there — see the vitamin D lecture ), certain drugs (phenytoin accelerates hepatic vitamin D catabolism), rare dietary deficiency, and inadequate sun exposure (classically causing rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults). Minor/other causes: hypoalbuminemia (falsely low total calcium — see corrected calcium above), hypomagnesemia (alcohol use, malabsorption), pancreatitis (calcium is saponified by fatty acids released from peripancreatic fat necrosis), tumor lysis/rhabdomyolysis/sepsis, and massive transfusion (citrate anticoagulant in banked blood chelates calcium).

Pseudohypoparathyroidism Type 1a is true PTH resistance — the kidney has normal or high PTH but doesn't respond, so calcium stays low and phosphate stays high, just like hypoparathyroidism, except PTH itself is elevated (appropriately trying to compensate, unsuccessfully). It carries a recognizable phenotype called Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy : round facies, short stature, and short 4th/5th metacarpal and metatarsal bones. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism has the identical Albright's phenotype but no PTH insensitivity — calcium and phosphate are normal. The two are genetically related, and the distinction comes down to a single, high-yield genetics concept: Why the Same Mutation Gives Two Different Diseases Both come from an inactivating GNAS mutation — the gene encoding G s α, the protein PTH's receptor signals through. GNAS is genomically imprinted Only one parent's copy of certain genes is active in certain tissues — the other is epigenetically silenced, whether or not it is mutated in the renal tubule: only the maternal copy works there. Maternal mutation → the kidney's only working copy is gone → PTH resistance → PHP 1a . Paternal mutation → the kidney is unaffected → normal calcium, but the Albright's phenotype still appears in non-imprinted tissues → pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism . Because G s α is shared machinery, PHP 1a often shows resistance to TSH and gonadotropins too.

Diagnosing Primary Hypoparathyroidism Diagnosis: persistent hypocalcemia with a low or inappropriately-normal PTH (it should be climbing in response to low calcium — a "normal" PTH here is actually a failure to respond appropriately). After neck surgery, hypocalcemia must persist 6 months before it's labeled permanent hypoparathyroidism — many cases from parathyroid gland stunning/devascularization recover within that window. Cause Share Post-surgical (thyroid/parathyroid/neck surgery) ~75% — the leading cause overall Non-surgical: autoimmune, infiltrative, post-radiation, functional (magnesium insufficiency or excess), metastatic, genetic ~25% combined

Symptoms of Hypocalcemia Low ionized calcium lowers the threshold for neuronal and muscle membrane depolarization — the opposite direction from hypercalcemia — which is why the clinical picture is one of hyperexcitability rather than lethargy. Timing Findings Acute, severe Tetany — perioral paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, laryngeal spasm, seizures, palpitations Acute, mild Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs (below) Chronic Emotional instability, anxiety, "brain fog," paresthesias, cataracts, dry skin, brittle nails Overtreatment Movement disorders, nephrolithiasis (from iatrogenic hypercalciuria) Two bedside signs worth knowing precisely, since they're easy to blur together: Chvostek's sign: tap the facial nerve just anterior to the ear, over the parotid gland.
