More precisely: it is estradiol whose feedback flips. For most of the cycle estradiol suppresses LH. But once it is high enough, for long enough — which only a mature dominant follicle can produce — the same hormone stimulates it. The result is a roughly 10-fold rise in LH and a smaller rise in FSH. That is why the surge only happens once per cycle, and only when a follicle is ready: the follicle itself sets it off by making the estradiol. It is a timing signal the ovary sends to the brain saying "this egg is ready." Two More Fixes to Your Notes "It ovulates, then turns into corpus luteum, and produces estrogen." The corpus luteum does make some

entries.t: Menstruation: Normal, and What Goes Wrong
entries.p: Physiology of Puberty & the Menstrual Cycle
entries.x: Menstruation: Normal, and What Goes Wrong If an embryo fails to implant , the corpus luteum degenerates into a corpus albicans, estradiol and progesterone fall, and the functional layer of the endometrium sloughs along with the unfertilized ovum and menstrual blood. The basal layer stays intact , so the functional layer can regenerate next cycle. What is normal Parameter Normal Cycle length 21–35 days — only 15% of women actually have a 28-day cycle Duration of menses 3–10 days (mean 5.2) Blood loss Up to 80 mL per cycle Menarche Mean age 12.7 Left: cycle length clusters around 28 days, but with a wide normal spread. Right: cycles are most irregular in the first years after menarche and in the years before menopause — the axis not yet mature, and the axis running out of follicles. Cunningham et al., Williams Obstetrics , via the lecture. Where Cycle-Length Variation Comes From The luteal phase is fixed — the interval from ovulation to menstruation stays constant at about 14 days, because the corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan. The follicular phase varies , and that variation is primarily genetic. So a 35-day cycle is a 21-day follicular phase plus a 14-day luteal phase; a 24-day cycle is a 10-day follicular phase plus the same 14. Practically: ovulation happens about 14 days before the next period , not 14 days after the last one. Taking a menstrual history Ask about Why First day of the last menstrual period Dating, and the possibility of pregnancy Age at menarche Early or delayed puberty; years since the axis matured Cycle length and regularity 21–35 days is normal; irregular cycles suggest anovulation Duration and heaviness — products used, how often changed, clots, flooding, night-time changes Heavy menstrual bleeding is quantified by its impact, not by measuring blood Bleeding between periods or after intercourse Suggests a structural or cervical cause rather than a hormonal one Pain — timing, severity, time off school or work Primary versus secondary dysmenorrhea Premenstrual symptoms PMS / PMDD — see below Contraception and sexual history Hormonal contraception changes every other answer on this list The deck lists these as an objective without giving the list on a slide; this is a standard menstrual history, added so the objective is covered. Dysmenorrhea: why periods hurt 1 The endometrium sloughs and releases prostaglandins. At the start of menses, prostaglandins from the shedding lining drive strong uterine contractions. 2 Intrauterine pressure

entries.p: Physiology of Puberty & the Menstrual Cycle
entries.x: Premenstrual Symptoms: PMS and PMDD PMS PMDD What it is Recurrent, moderate to severe affective, physical and behavioural symptoms The severe, disabling end — affects relationships and ability to work Timing Develop in the luteal phase and resolve within a few days of menstruation How common 30–40% of women 3–8% Affective and behavioural symptoms Physical symptoms Irritability, mood swings, anger · depression and anxiety · social withdrawal · poor concentration · crying spells · changes in sexual desire · altered sleep Breast tenderness · bloating, gas, abdominal pain · swelling of hands and feet · headache · fatigue · food cravings · acne Timing Is the Diagnosis What makes it PMS or PMDD is not which symptoms occur but when : luteal phase on, resolving shortly after menses begins, with a symptom-free stretch after menstruation. That symptom-free week is what separates premenstrual disorders from depression or anxiety that simply gets worse before a period. It is why diagnosis relies on the patient charting symptoms prospectively across at least two cycles, rather than recalling them. Cause is largely unknown. The leading idea is an enhanced responsiveness to normal fluctuations of estrogen and progesterone — the hormone levels are normal; the brain's reaction to them is not. Serotonin and GABA signalling are both implicated in the altered central neurotransmission. Treatment: suppress ovulation (the combined oral contraceptive — no cycle, no luteal phase), SSRIs , and light therapy. PMDD may respond to the same.

entries.t: Menopause: The End of the Line
entries.p: Physiology of Puberty & the Menstrual Cycle
entries.x: Menopause: The End of the Line The follicles run out, and FSH climbs. Ovarian reserve falls to about 25,000 by age 38, then the rate of loss accelerates; by about 51 fewer than 1,000 remain. Estradiol and progesterone fall with them, and FSH rises steeply — nothing is left to feed back. Feature Detail Definition 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea , and/or FSH consistently above 30 Average age The slide text says 53 for North American women; the deck's own figure above marks 51 as the average final menstrual period, which matches most published figures Timing is predetermined Set by the number of follicles at birth — and genetic: women tend to go through menopause around the same age as their mothers Mechanism Ovarian follicles depleted → estradiol and progesterone decline → FSH rises as the pituitary is "screaming" at the ovaries Menopause is the textbook primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism: the gonad has failed, so the trophic hormone is high. Contrast the pituitary case in 3.2 , where the testosterone was just as low but the gonadotrophins were not raised — secondary hypogonadism. Same low sex steroid; the FSH tells you which end of the axis failed. Why this framework matters The HPO axis is a complex interplay of stimulation and inhibition by circulating hormones — but understanding the basic framework is what lets you treat the common disorders ( dysmenorrhea, heavy bleeding, oligomenorrhea ) and provide effective contraception , which works by exploiting exactly the negative feedback described above.

Learning Objectives List the causes of incomplete virilization in an individual with a 46,XY karyotype. List the causes of virilization in an individual with a 46,XX karyotype. Understand the presentation of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). Understand the management of CAH. Describe the appropriate clinical and laboratory assessment of an infant with ambiguous genitalia. Consider how you would communicate your findings of a DSD to the parents. Understand the factors to consider when assigning sex to a newborn with a DSD. Dr. Stein's two-part module (Part A: virilization; Part B: CAH). It builds directly on 3.7 (how the tract normally develops) and on the adrenal steroid pathway in 3.1 .

entries.t: What a DSD Is, and Isn't
entries.x: What a DSD Is, and Isn't This is about biological sex: the anatomy. It is not about gender identity, gender expression or sexual orientation; those are in 3.8 . The scene: a baby is born, and the first thing the parents ask is "boy or girl?" Here the genitals don't obviously say. Definition The phenotype is atypical enough to cause uncertainty about which sex to assign at birth What doesn't match One or more of: karyotype · gonadal histology · internal genitalia · external genitalia How common Genital differences needing genetic or endocrine work-up: about 1 in 4,500 births Not always at birth A DSD can instead show up as abnormal puberty later Who's involved Multidisciplinary : endocrinology, genetics, surgery/urology, gynecology, neonatology, social work, psychology and mental health support for the parents

First, How It Normally Works Every DSD is a break somewhere on this diagram. Learn it and the differential writes itself. Step Does SRY (on the Y) Turns the gonad into a testis Sertoli cells → AMH Müllerian ducts regress (no uterus); stabilizes the Wolffian ducts Leydig cells → testosterone Builds the male internal genitalia (Wolffian ducts) 5α-reductase: T → DHT DHT builds the male external genitalia No SRY Ovaries and the female tract, but normal ovaries still need a normal 46,XX . It isn't just "no Y"

entries.t: Examining the Newborn, and the Words to Use
entries.x: Examining the Newborn, and the Words to Use If it looks more female, describe If it looks more male, describe Labia majora and minora · any labial fusion · 1 or 2 urogenital openings · clitoral size Scrotum: median raphe and rugation · where the urethral opening is (tip, or along the shaft = hypospadias) · phallus length and width · palpable testes? It's a spectrum. The Prader stages run from normal female through I–V to normal male: more labial fusion, a bigger phallus, and the urethral opening moving toward the tip. Until you know the diagnosis, use neutral words: Say Not Gonads Testes / ovaries Phallus (and measure it : "2 cm") Penis / clitoris; micropenis / clitoromegaly Labioscrotal folds Labia / scrotum Urogenital opening Urethra / vagina This is also how you talk to the parents: describe what you see without committing to a sex you may have to take back.

The Case: Baby A.H. Born by spontaneous vaginal delivery at 40 weeks (mother had diet-controlled gestational diabetes); birth weight 3,052 g; Apgars 9 and 10. Initially identified as male. At 4 days old, someone raises a concern about the genitalia: 3 cm phallus Hyperpigmented, fused, rugated labioscrotal folds A single urogenital opening at the base of the phallus No gonads palpable What next? The first question is: an overvirilized girl or an undervirilized boy ? Karyotype : 46,XX or 46,XY? Pelvic/abdominal ultrasound : quick and easy. Is there a uterus (Müllerian structures)? Where are the gonads? What do the adrenals look like? Other labs based on the differential. Baby A.H.'s answer is in Part 2 . (The case slides use clinical photographs, which are left out here; the findings are listed above.) Drawn for these notes from Part A's differential slides, which list the causes by karyotype but don't lay out the tests as a decision. The karyotype splits the differential. For 46,XX, 17-OHP answers the CAH question. For 46,XY, the testosterone level and the T:DHT ratio sort the rest. The ultrasound point in each box (uterus or not) follows from whether AMH was made.

The Groups 46,XY DSD: testes, but the outside is incompletely virilized . 46,XX DSD: ovaries, but the outside is virilized . These two are the common ones. Ovotesticular DSD and mixed gonadal dysgenesis (45,X/46,XY) are less common and not the focus now. From the lecture.

46,XY DSD: The Undervirilized Male Three places to break : the testis doesn't form, the hormones aren't made, or the hormones aren't sensed. The two highlighted in orange are the most common . Level Causes Testis doesn't develop Complete or partial gonadal dysgenesis ; testicular regression (e.g. lost blood supply) Androgen not made Leydig cell hypoplasia ( LH deficiency or LH-receptor defect) · testosterone biosynthesis enzyme defects · 5α-reductase deficiency · AMH problems Androgen not sensed Androgen insensitivity : T and DHT are made, but the receptor doesn't work 5α-reductase deficiency Testosterone can't be turned into DHT. The diagram shows why only part of the body is affected: testosterone builds the internal ducts, DHT builds the prostate and the outside. Karyotype 46,XY Inheritance Autosomal recessive Internal Normal male ; testes in the abdomen, inguinal canal or labioscrotal folds External Ambiguous Puberty Incomplete virilization: sparse facial and pubic hair, no temporal recession or acne Diagnosis High testosterone : DHT ratio (after hCG stimulation) Androgen insensitivity: partial vs complete Partial androgen insensitivity: a partly working androgen receptor. X-linked recessive; diagnosed by DNA analysis of the receptor gene. Partial (PAIS) Complete (CAIS) Receptor Partly works Doesn't work at all At birth Ambiguous , micropenis, or near-normal male Looks like a typical girl Gonads Testes Testes Puberty Incomplete virilization, gynecomastia, azoospermia Diagnosed here , when periods don't come Genetics 46,XY, X-linked recessive Why Testosterone vs DHT Matters So Much Testosterone and DHT act on the same androgen receptor, but different tissues depend on different ones . Testosterone itself builds the Wolffian ducts (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles), and later muscle and voice. DHT , a stronger androgen made locally by 5α-reductase, builds the external genitalia and prostate , and later drives facial and body hair, acne and male-pattern balding. That explains both patterns. In 5α-reductase deficiency the inside is male but the outside is ambiguous; at puberty the testosterone surge virilizes partly, but DHT-dependent features (beard, acne, temporal recession) stay sparse. In androgen insensitivity neither hormone works, so in the complete form the outside is fully female. AMH still works, though, so there's no uterus , which is why these girls have no periods. Mechanism added to link the lecture's slides.

46,XX DSD: The Overvirilized Female Too much androgen reaching a female fetus. From the fetus itself: CAH (by far the most common) , or an androgen-secreting tumour of the ovary or adrenal. Or from the mother, across the placenta : a virilizing tumour or androgenic drugs. From the lecture.

What CAH Is A family of autosomal recessive defects in adrenal steroid synthesis , about 1 in 10,000 births . 21-hydroxylase deficiency is about 95% ; 11β-hydroxylase 5%; 3β-HSD 1%. Focus on 21-hydroxylase. From the lecture.

entries.t: The Steroid Pathway: Follow the Block
entries.x: The Steroid Pathway: Follow the Block 21-hydroxylase blocked (red). Nothing can get down to the mineralocorticoid or cortisol columns, so everything piles up above the block, including 17-OH progesterone , and spills sideways into the androgen column. Block at 21-hydroxylase → can't make aldosterone or cortisol . Precursors ( 17-OHP ) back up and are shunted to androgens → testosterone and DHT → virilization . Low cortisol → no negative feedback → ACTH keeps rising → ACTH keeps driving the gland → the adrenal cortex grows: hyperplasia . It gets big even though it isn't working properly. The same pathway runs through the adrenal lecture , where CAH appears as a cause of primary adrenal insufficiency, and through 3.4 , where it's a cause of peripheral precocious puberty. The "hyperplasia" you can see. Normal adrenal (left) vs CAH (right). In older children and adults the adrenals are hard to see on ultrasound, but in newborns they are easy to see , and a big CAH adrenal stands out. That's one reason the ultrasound is a first test. From the lecture.

21-Hydroxylase Deficiency: A Spectrum Caused by mutations in the CYP21A2 gene (the "21-B gene") on chromosome 6 . How much enzyme is left decides the picture. Classic salt-wasting Classic simple virilizing Non-classic (late onset) Share 75% of 21-OHD About 25% — Mutations 2 severe 1 of the 2 relatively mild Mild Enzyme left < 1% 1–5% More Cortisol Deficient Deficient Adequate Aldosterone Deficient : salt wasting Enough for salt and water balance (renin may be high) Normal Androgen excess Yes Yes Mild Presents At birth or in a salt-wasting crisis Virilization Not at birth. Before puberty: premature pubarche. After: hirsutism, acne, oligomenorrhea (a PMOS look-alike), infertility Non-classic CAH is one of the conditions you must exclude before diagnosing PMOS, with a 17-OHP level. See 3.10 .

Diagnosis High 17-OHP is the diagnostic test (it sits just above the block). In a salt-losing crisis: low Na, high K, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia. Finding Because ↑↑ 17-OHP Backs up behind the 21-hydroxylase block ↓ Na, ↑ K, metabolic acidosis No aldosterone: the kidney wastes salt and holds K + and H + Hypoglycemia No cortisol Baby A.H.: The Answer Karyotype 46,XX , so a genetic girl: an overvirilized female. 17-OHP = 400 (normal < 10). That's dramatically high and confirms 21-hydroxylase-deficient CAH . The hyperpigmented folds fit too: high ACTH also stimulates pigment.

11β-Hydroxylase Deficiency: The Hypertensive One Block one step lower. Androgens still pile up, so there's still virilization. But the precursors that build up now include deoxycorticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol. Why This One Raises Blood Pressure 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) is a potent mineralocorticoid in its own right. When it accumulates it holds on to salt and water just as aldosterone would. So instead of a salt-wasting, hypotensive crisis, these babies are hypertensive . Much rarer than 21-hydroxylase deficiency (about 5% of CAH).

entries.t: How CAH Presents, and Why Boys Get Missed
entries.x: How CAH Presents, and Why Boys Get Missed Girls: virilized genitals (clitoral hypertrophy, variable labial fusion; at worst a single urogenital opening), so they're usually spotted at birth . Boys: just a bigger penis and a darker scrotum, easy to miss. The salt-losing crisis comes at 1–3 weeks , not at birth. Unrecognized, it causes neonatal death . From the lecture. Why the Newborn Screen Matters Most for Boys A girl with salt-wasting CAH usually gets picked up at birth because her genitals look different. A boy looks normal and goes home, then crashes into an adrenal crisis at 1–3 weeks. CAH is now part of newborn screening in Canada , which measures 17-OHP on the heel-prick sample, so boys are found before the crisis.

Long-Term Management Piece Details Glucocorticoid, for life Hydrocortisone 10–15 mg/m²/day, split into 2–3 doses (the lecture bases it on a normal cortisol secretion of about 12.5 ± 3 mg/m²/day). Once growth is finished, prednisone or dexamethasone in older adolescents Mineralocorticoid (salt-wasters) Fludrocortisone (Florinef) 0.05–0.2 mg once daily . Infants may need extra oral salt Prevent adrenal crisis Stress dosing : increase the glucocorticoid during illness or other stress to prevent a salt-losing crisis Genital surgery Discussed with some families, depending on the degree of virilization Education and surveillance Ongoing Why hydrocortisone in children: it is plain cortisol, and the least growth-suppressing option. The longer-acting prednisone and dexamethasone are held until growth is finished. Stress dosing is the same principle as in any adrenal insufficiency; see 3.1 .

entries.t: Assessing a Newborn With Ambiguous Genitalia
entries.x: Assessing a Newborn With Ambiguous Genitalia History: family history of ambiguous genitalia or virilization, and of unexplained neonatal crises or deaths (think CAH); the pregnancy: maternal health, medications , whether the mother herself virilized. Exam: general exam, dysmorphic features and other midline defects, palpate for gonads , and describe and draw the genitalia (labioscrotal folds, phallus length, number, position and size of openings). From the lecture.

Assigning Sex Controversial, and the evidence is weak. Outcome data come from adults whose sex was assigned 20–30 years ago with the technology and surgery of the time, but it's the best we have. Diagnosis What happened 46,XX CAH About 90% assigned female in infancy identify as female. The evidence supports raising even markedly virilized 46,XX CAH infants as female 46,XY complete androgen insensitivity 100% assigned female identify as female 46,XY 5α-reductase deficiency About 60% of those assigned female, who virilize at puberty , identify as male; 100% of those assigned male identify as male 46,XY partial AIS, androgen synthesis defects, gonadal dysgenesis About 25% have gender dissatisfaction , whether assigned male or female The consensus (ESPE / Lawson Wilkins Pediatric Endocrine Society) Sex assignment does not have to mean surgery. You can assign sex at birth without operating. Evidence for the different treatments is lacking , so individual and family considerations are essential. Only surgeons experienced in genital reconstruction, who know the long-term outcomes, should be involved early. At birth 1 Refer to a tertiary centre : endocrinology, neonatology, genetics, gynecology, urology, social work and psychology. 2 Delay assigning the sex of rearing until all the investigations are complete. 3 Ask the family not to name the baby and not to register the birth yet. 4 A team discussion with the family decides the best path for this child. Factors in the decision The underlying diagnosis Genital appearance and the surgical options either way The need for lifelong hormone replacement The potential for fertility The family's views , and sometimes cultural practices Talking to the Parents Not knowing their baby's sex is extremely unsettling and stressful for a family. Describe what you see in neutral words , explain that a team will find out what's going on, and be honest that it takes time. Build in psychology and social work support from the start. Waiting on the name and registration isn't bureaucracy: it keeps the family from committing to a sex before the facts are in.

Learning Objectives Review the diagnostic criteria for gender incongruence and gender dysphoria. Develop an approach to the care of a pediatric transgender or gender-nonconforming individual. Develop an approach to a patient looking for support in social and medical transition, adult and pediatric. Review the guidelines for starting gender-affirming hormone therapy. Compare the risks of other health issues in the transgender population with those of the general population. Plan a gender-inclusive environment in your clinic. Two recorded talks from a symposium: Dr. Van Uum (adult endocrinology, the diagnosis and hormone treatment of adults) and Dr. Stein (pediatric endocrinology, London's Pediatric Gender Pathway Service). The inclusive-language section at the start of 3.6 is the same idea applied to the anatomy lab.

Definitions Four separate ideas. Knowing someone's sex tells you nothing about their gender identity, and neither tells you their sexual orientation. Not a binary. Beyond cis and trans men and women there are non-binary, genderfluid, two-spirit, agender and other identities. The slide is a guide, not a complete list; use the words the patient uses. Term Plain meaning Sex Biological status: chromosomes, gonads, internal and external genitalia (male, female, or a DSD; see 3.9 ) Gender Psychological status: attitudes, feelings and behaviours associated with being male, female, or elsewhere on the spectrum Gender identity How a person perceives and presents themselves. Cisgender = matches the sex assigned at birth; transgender = differs from it; plus the whole spectrum between Sexual orientation Who someone is attracted to (heterosexual, gay, lesbian, bisexual, pansexual). A separate question from identity Gender dysphoria Distress about a mismatch between identity and assigned sex, often with anxiety, depression and mood problems, and made worse by social stigma, isolation and rejection

Making the Diagnosis Parents often ask: how do you know this isn't a phase? The answer is the guidelines plus, above all, listening to the young person's story over time . WPATH (World Professional Association for Transgender Health) Standards of Care, version 8 (2022) : the main guideline used by Canadian pediatric centres and worldwide. Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline (2017) : North American, and it overlaps heavily with WPATH. ICD-11 gender incongruence (the criteria WPATH uses). The last bar, play, toys and playmates, applies to younger children. What you're really looking for, in three words: Insistence They are clear this is their true gender identity Persistence It has been going on for a long time, even if they only told people recently Consistence It stays the same as you follow them in clinic: male, female, non-binary, or consistently fluid The slide quotes WPATH's board: gender diversity is a common and culturally diverse human phenomenon that should not be judged as inherently pathological or negative . The diagnosis exists to open the door to care, not to label the identity as a disease.

entries.t: Asking About It: the Initial Assessment
entries.x: Asking About It: the Initial Assessment Gender identity questions belong in every adolescent HEADSS history. Simple, open questions work best. Four areas, with ready-made questions: identity ("Some young people feel they were born in the wrong body. Have you ever felt like that?"), persistence ("How long? How did puberty affect you?"), gender-nonconforming behaviour (toys, clothes, swimwear, favourite characters or avatars), and sources of distress ("What do you think about your body?"). Lopez et al., 2016, from the lecture.

entries.t: How Common, and Why Mental Health Comes First
entries.x: How Common, and Why Mental Health Comes First About 1 in 300 Canadians aged 15+ are transgender or non-binary (2021 Census, published 2022), and two-thirds are under 35 . Probably an underestimate: under-15s aren't counted and it's a general census form. School surveys: 1.2–4.1% of adolescents. The most important slide in the lecture. Suicidality 2–3× higher; 47% of Ontario trans youth have thought about suicide and 19% have attempted. A supportive family: about 4% ; a non-supportive one: about 60% . With hormones, surgery and a team that includes mental health, outcomes match the general population . What This Means for You as the Doctor Anxiety, mood disorders and suicidality are common. The single biggest thing that moves the risk isn't a drug: it's whether the young person is listened to and supported , at home and in your clinic. Screening for suicidality, connecting families to support, and not making the young person fight to be believed are all treatment.

entries.t: Who Can Start, and What Happens First
entries.x: Who Can Start, and What Happens First WPATH criteria for adults: (1) persistent, well-documented gender dysphoria; (2) capacity to decide and consent; (3) age of majority (youth follow their own pathway); (4) other medical or mental health issues reasonably well controlled . Those issues don't exclude anyone. The pre-treatment checklist. Note item 2: hormones reduce fertility , so reproductive options come up before the first dose (sometimes with a referral to reproductive endocrinology). If you're the family doctor: document the dysphoria when it first comes up. Six months or a year of notes makes the referral much stronger. A psychosocial assessment by a qualified professional confirms the diagnosis and readiness. In some countries it must be a mental health professional; in Canada it can be a family doctor or other trained clinician. The endocrinologist's role: start treatment safely, advise on doses and side effects, and handle problems. Usually not the one who makes the diagnosis, and not able to follow everyone long term, so patients are set on the right path and handed back to primary care. Patients may need a written letter confirming they are on supervised hormone therapy, for travel, documents and other situations.

Two Goals, Two Regimens Adult hormone therapy does two things (Endocrine Society 2017): Suppress the body's own sex hormones, reducing the secondary sex characteristics of the assigned sex. Replace them with hormones that match the gender identity, using the same principles as treating hypogonadism. Trans women (feminizing) Trans men (masculinizing) Replace with Estradiol : oral or transdermal patch; rarely injection Testosterone : injection (enanthate or cypionate) or transdermal gel/patch Suppress with An anti-androgen : spironolactone (androgen-receptor blocker; the usual choice in North America), cyproterone acetate (more common in Europe), or a GnRH agonist (shuts down LH/FSH, so testosterone falls) Usually not needed: testosterone at male levels suppresses the ovaries Dr. Van Uum is explicit: you don't need to know the doses .

What Changes, and When Feminizing: most changes start at 3–6 months and peak at 2–3 years (fat redistribution, breast growth, smaller testes). Voice: no change. Estrogen can't undo what testosterone did to the larynx. Masculinizing: changes start at 1–6 months , but the full effect can take up to 4–5 years (facial and body hair). Voice deepens on testosterone. Periods stop within 1–6 months. Why the table matters: patients need realistic expectations of what will change, how much, and how long it takes. The lecturers suggest giving it in writing.

Monitoring Trans women (on estrogen) Trans men (on testosterone) How often Every 3 months in the first year , then 1–2 times a year Hormone levels Testosterone suppressed to < 50 ng/dL (female range); estradiol no higher than the peak physiologic range, 100–200 pg/mL Testosterone in the normal male range (400–700 ng/dL). Injections: measure midway between doses (weekly shot: day 3–4; every 2 weeks: day 6–8). Gel: any time after the first week The drug-specific lab Potassium (and electrolytes) on spironolactone Hematocrit / hemoglobin : testosterone causes erythrocytosis Bone Consider bone density, especially if hormones are stopped or taken irregularly , or after gonadectomy Cancer screening Screen the organs that are there : mammography if there is breast tissue, prostate screening if there is a prostate, Pap tests if there is a cervix From the Endocrine Society monitoring tables shown in the lecture (Tables 14 and 15). The estradiol target is given in pg/mL; in the recording it is roughly converted to pmol/L. For reference, 100–200 pg/mL is about 370–730 pmol/L.

Reading a Testosterone Level Total testosterone has three parts. Only the albumin-bound and free parts can reach the cells: the bioavailable testosterone. Fraction Bound how Active? SHBG-bound Tightly, to sex hormone-binding globulin No Albumin-bound Loosely; lets go easily in the tissues Yes Free Not bound (a small fraction) Yes Bioavailable T = albumin-bound + free. Free androgen index = testosterone ÷ SHBG. Routine monitoring uses total testosterone, because bioavailable T costs more and varies more. Check bioavailable T when the total doesn't match the clinical picture. Obesity and insulin resistance lower SHBG , so total T looks low while bioavailable T is normal.

Testosterone: Injection, Gel or Pill? In practice, injections or transdermal gel are used, both in trans men and in testosterone replacement generally. From the lecture. Injection Transdermal gel/patch Oral capsules How often Every 1–2 weeks (sometimes 4) Daily 2–3 times a day Catch Level rises then falls: a "roller coaster" Skin irritation; transfer to others; lost with sweating (e.g. applying it, then going to the gym) Needs fatty food to be absorbed; levels spike and crash within hours Monitoring Halfway between injections Any time Practically impossible Adherence Documented (given by a clinician) Self-reported Self-reported

Risks of Hormone Therapy Likely increased risk. Estrogen: VTE , gallstones, raised liver enzymes, weight gain, high triglycerides. Testosterone: polycythemia , weight gain, acne, balding, sleep apnea. Possible, or no clear, increase. Breast and reproductive cancers: no increase shown (hypothesized but not proven). Diabetes: unclear. VTE risk is higher with oral estrogen than transdermal. Risk level Estrogen (feminizing) Testosterone (masculinizing) Likely increased Venous thromboembolism , gallstones, raised liver enzymes, weight gain, hypertriglyceridemia Polycythemia , weight gain, acne, androgenic alopecia, sleep apnea Likely, if other risk factors Cardiovascular disease — Possible Hypertension, hyperprolactinemia or prolactinoma (rare) Raised liver enzymes, hyperlipidemia Possible, if other risk factors Type 2 diabetes Psychiatric destabilization, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes No increase / inconclusive Breast cancer Bone loss, breast, cervical, ovarian and uterine cancer Two Things to Do Before Starting Before estrogen, ask about VTE: a personal or family history of clots changes the plan. Before and on testosterone, follow the hematocrit: testosterone drives red cell production, and it mustn't climb too high. Both are the "likely increased" risks at the top of the table.

Surgery Surgery can be genital ("bottom") or chest ("top") . WPATH asks for one or two referrals, depending on the surgery, from qualified professionals who share responsibility for the decision. In Ontario, two health care providers must support the referral , and unlike some US settings they don't have to be psychiatrists. From the lecture.

Three Steps, Three Decisions Fully reversible → partially reversible → irreversible. Each is its own decision, fitted to that person's goals. Some young people need only step 1 to feel settled; others go through all three. Nothing hormonal happens until puberty has started. From the lecture. 0 Before puberty (e.g. an 8-year-old): no medical treatment. Mental health support for the child and guidance for the family on how to support them as they grow. 1 Puberty blockers (fully reversible): from Tanner stage 2 . Pause puberty and buy time. 2 Gender-affirming hormones (partly reversible): testosterone or estrogen, usually from around 16 , sometimes earlier. 3 Surgery (irreversible): top surgery from 16, after 1 year on hormones . Genital surgery is not done in children .

Step 1: Puberty Blockers The pause button. A GnRH agonist ( Lupron , leuprolide) turns off LH and FSH, so the gonads go quiet. Criteria: Long-lasting gender nonconformity or dysphoria (insistence, persistence, consistence). Dysphoria worsened at the onset of puberty . Other psychological, medical or social problems addressed : supported, not necessarily cured. Reached Tanner stage 2. Informed consent. Blockers slow or stop Why it helps Pubertal development · linear growth · androgen-dependent hair · voice deepening · breast or testicular/penile growth · menstruation · libido · "teenage behaviour" Time to keep exploring identity without the distress of breasts, erections or periods that don't fit. Mood and depressive symptoms improve Why More GnRH Means Less Puberty The pituitary only responds to GnRH that comes in pulses . A long-acting agonist gives a constant signal, which down-regulates the pituitary's GnRH receptors, so LH and FSH fall. Stop it and pulsing resumes : puberty carries on normally, which is why this step is fully reversible. It is the same drug and logic used for central precocious puberty in 3.4 . Fertility preservation: before any hormones Must be discussed before any hormonal intervention , including blockers. Hard for a 14-year-old to picture what their adult self will want, but necessary. Egg preservation is expensive and not covered by provincial health plans; it can be traumatizing; and it requires being off hormones with normal gonadal function (1–2 normal periods). Refer to a fertility clinic if they want more information or want to proceed.

Step 2: Gender-Affirming Hormones Eligibility: confirmed persistence; the patient can consent (parental support is preferred but not required ); usually around 16 , earlier if there are compelling reasons (in London, patients as young as 14 commonly start). The decision should make sense to the young person, the family and the team. From the lecture. Testosterone. Permanent: hair, deeper voice , clitoral enlargement, extra height (if still growing). Reversible: muscle, libido, stopping periods. Risks: balding (permanent), acne, erythrocytosis , liver and heart effects. Estrogen. Permanent: breast development , better bone mineral content. Reversible: softer skin, less muscle, fat redistribution, less body hair. Risks: breast cancer, lower adult height, clots , gallstones, triglycerides, prolactinoma. The yellow box on both slides is the key point: most side effects come from supraphysiologic levels, whether from dosing errors or from taking more than prescribed. The goal is levels in the normal range for the affirmed sex, checked regularly. Both hormones improve bone mineral content . The breast cancer risk on estrogen is listed here as increased; the adult risk table above calls it unproven. The two talks use different sources.

Step 3: Surgery Genital surgery: not until the legal age of majority and at least a year living in the affirmed role, so it is not part of pediatric care. Top surgery can happen in adolescence: age 16 , 1 year of hormone therapy , and patience , because the wait lists are long. From the lecture.

> Female Reproductive The reproductive block: family planning, fertility, the drugs used in gynecology, and the common gynecologic presentations. The anatomy, embryology and hormone axes behind it all are in Endocrinology Week 3 . Week 4 Family Planning, Gynecology & Prenatal Screening Abortion, infertility, contraception and gynecologic drugs; discharge, STIs, cervical screening and early pregnancy; bleeding, the vulva and pelvic pain; and prenatal genetic screening → Week 5 Menopause, the Pelvic Mass, the Breast & Pregnancy Post-menopausal bleeding, the pelvic mass, menopause, D&C and hysterectomy; breast pathology and common breast problems; early pregnancy — care providers, teratogens, first-trimester ultrasound and bleeding; then first-trimester and antenatal care, sexual health, the anatomy scan and hypertension in pregnancy → Week 6 Preterm Birth, Bleeding & Labour Preterm labour and PPROM, the small fetus, and antepartum hemorrhage; then labour itself — the normal process and fetal monitoring, induction, forceps and vacuum, caesarean and TOLAC, postpartum hemorrhage, and hemorrhagic shock; then the first weeks after birth — neonatal care, postpartum care and lactation → Later weeks will be added as they're covered. POM2 — a work in progress.

Learning Objectives Define the normal amount of bleeding in a menstrual cycle. List the components of PALM-COEIN. Identify main causes of anovulation. Analyze findings on pelvic examination using an understanding of causes of AUB. Identify the structural causes of AUB on pathology. Describe the clinical presentations of cervical cancer or endometrial cancer with regards to AUB. List investigations used in the diagnosis of AUB. Select appropriate medical treatments for AUB. Dr. Shannon Arntfield's 40-minute module. She explicitly hands off objectives 5 and 6 to other lecturers — the structural causes on pathology are Dr. Weir's 4.12 , and the postmenopausal bleeding side of endometrial cancer sits in a separate Week 2 repro lecture. The normal menstrual cycle underneath all of this is 3.3 , and the HPO axis is 2.6 . She also flags what this talk deliberately skips: pediatric bleeding (except precocious puberty and sexual abuse, covered in Peds) and PCOS (covered in Endo).

Normal vs Abnormal Everything other than a normal period. The list of medical terms exists so you recognize them — the last line is the actual instruction: "Developing an approach rather than memorizing definitions ." Dr. Arntfield's slide. The deck sends you to Week 1 for the normal parameters rather than restating them, so here they are, since objective 1 asks for a number: Parameter Normal Outside normal Frequency Every 24–38 days <24 d = frequent · >38 d = oligomenorrhea · none = amenorrhea Duration ≤8 days (typically 2–7) >8 d = prolonged Volume 5–80 mL per cycle >80 mL = heavy menstrual bleeding , or any volume heavy enough to interfere with quality of life Regularity Predictable cycle to cycle Irregular timing, or bleeding between cycles Added From Outside the Deck The 24–38 day / ≤8 day / 5–80 mL figures are the FIGO parameters and are not on these slides — they come from the FIGO terminology system as reproduced in the NIH StatPearls chapter on abnormal uterine bleeding, checked against the same 24–38 day definition used in the Alberta primary-care AUB pathway. In practice nobody measures 80 mL; the clinically useful version is "heavy enough to interfere with her life," which is why the history questions below are about pad changes and clots rather than millilitres.

Approach: Divide by Age The first fork. Reproductive age is this lecture; the greyed-out groups have their own lectures. The two sub-bullets — adolescence and perimenopause — are the reason Part 5 exists. Dr. Arntfield's slide. Age changes the differential enough that it earns the top of the algorithm. The pre-pubertal patient raises precocious puberty and sexual abuse ; the postmenopausal patient is a cancer work-up until proven otherwise. In between, the differential is the one below — but weighted differently at 15 than at 45.

PALM-COEIN The FIGO system. Left column = structural (you can see it). Right column = non-structural (you cannot). Her alternative mnemonic. Use whichever sticks — but note it catches two things PALM-COEIN hides: Baby and Infection . Letter Cause What it is P Polyp Endometrial or endocervical outgrowth A Adenomyosis Endometrium grown into the myometrium — a bulky, boggy, tender uterus L Leiomyoma Fibroid. Subclassified by location — submucosal ones bleed most M Malignancy & hyperplasia Endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma, cervical cancer, CIN C Coagulopathy von Willebrand disease, thrombocytopenia, liver disease, leukemia O Ovulatory dysfunction Anovulation — the biggest single bucket. Expanded below E Endometrial A primary endometrial/local haemostatic problem with a structurally normal uterus I Iatrogenic Hormonal contraception, anticoagulants — you have to ask N Not yet classified Everything unfitted, e.g. AV malformation Her Own Caveat Dr. Arntfield says she would personally collapse O vulatory dysfunction and E ndometrial into one idea , because in practice they get investigated identically — bloodwork plus consideration of an endometrial biopsy. She also points out that iatrogenic is where the patient's contraception and blood thinners belong, and jokes that with her collapsing "the COEIN may be more of a COIN than a COEIN." Take that as permission to hold the mnemonic loosely. Don't Lose the Two Non-PALM-COEIN Causes PALM-COEIN is explicitly a system for non-gravid women, and infection has no letter. So you must add them back manually: pregnancy (the most common cause of amenorrhea, and a frequent cause of unscheduled bleeding) and infection — an erosive cervicitis or a bad herpes outbreak can produce spotting. Both appear in her ABC's list, which is arguably why she offers it. Infection is covered in 4.6 ; early pregnancy bleeding is 4.9 .

Anovulation: the Main Underlying Cause Her framing: AUB is the umbrella, anovulation is the biggest thing underneath it — so ask the next question, what causes anovulation? The answer is the HPO axis, one level at a time. The eight common causes in one picture. Note how many are not ovarian at all — body weight, exercise and stress all act at the hypothalamus. Slide figure credited to Verywell. The whole framework. Top of the axis = hormonal (history + labs). Bottom = anatomic (exam + imaging). That split is what tells you which tests to order. Her annotated version — the three annotations are the teaching content , not the loop diagram. Read them in order down the axis. 1 Hypothalamus — is GnRH still pulsatile? A coordinated cycle requires pulsatile GnRH release. Anything that flattens the pulse stops the cycle: physical or emotional stress , body mass (the female athlete triad Low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction and low bone mineral density in athletes. The classic cause of hypothalamic amenorrhea in a young, highly active patient. , anorexia, malnutrition) and chronic disease . 2 Pituitary — what else does it make? Beyond LH/FSH: TSH and prolactin . Either one abnormal will disrupt the cycle, which is why they are on the standard bloodwork panel. A prolactinoma is a specific, findable cause. 3 Ovary — did it form, and is it still working? Did it form: chromosomal causes such as Turner syndrome 45,X. Gonadal dysgenesis means the ovaries never develop functionally, so there is primary ovarian insufficiency. . Was it injured: radiation or chemotherapy for a childhood cancer. Also premature ovarian insufficiency and declining reserve in perimenopause. 4 Uterus and outflow tract — anatomic. And here, she repeats it for the third time: remember pregnancy. It is the most common reason for amenorrhea and must be excluded in anyone who could conceivably be pregnant.

Why the Differential Comes First The Argument She Makes Hardest "Doing a battery of tests, not necessarily knowing what you're looking for, can get you too far down a rabbit hole" — her example being an incidental finding with no clinical relevance . If you hold the differential in your head first, you target the exam and the investigations, and you interpret what you find. This is the whole logic of objective 4, and it is why the PALM-COEIN box is pasted in the corner of every one of her exam and workup slides. Two history points she singles out: Ask about contraception by name. "Most women, when asked do you take any medications , will not include their contraceptive choice." A Mirena is her example — the patient does not think of it as a medication at all. Iatrogenic bleeding is common and free to diagnose if you ask. Ask about pregnancy risk in private. A 13- or 14-year-old may not disclose sexual activity, or a history of trauma or abuse, with a parent in the room. She frames getting the patient alone in a safe environment as part of the history, not an optional courtesy.

Physical Examination Note the corner box: this slide is the structural (PALM) half of the exam. Of inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation, gynecology uses only the first two . Dr. Arntfield's slide. Manoeuvre What you are looking for Maps to Inspection — vulva, vagina, cervix Skin and colour change, atrophy, fissures · abnormal discharge · lesions or irregular vascularity on the cervix Malignancy, infection, atrophy Bimanual palpation — two fingers in the vagina, one hand above the symphysis, lifting the uterus and ovaries into the abdominal hand Size , mobility and descent (prolapse) of the pelvic organs Leiomyoma, adenomyosis, pregnancy, malignancy Fixation A pelvis that feels fixed rather than mobile Malignancy — cervical, and some ovarian How to Read an Enlarged Uterus Enlargement alone does not distinguish the causes — pregnancy , a bulky adenomyotic uterus , and fibroids all enlarge it, and so can cancer. What separates malignancy out on exam is fixation : benign enlargement stays mobile, while an infiltrating tumour tethers the pelvic structures. That is the exam finding to actually chase. Bring your instruments in with you. Many gynecologic investigations are part of the exam — swabs, the Pap, and targeted biopsies. If you worked out the differential beforehand, you know what to have on the tray, and you do not have to bring the patient back. Left to right as she narrates them. Herpes — an erosive infection producing spotting, not heavy bleeding, and tender. Cervix — normal at the edges, atypical centrally with abnormal vascularity ; that appearance earns a targeted biopsy , not just a Pap. Two fibroid views — a single subserosal fibroid hanging off the uterus (palpable bimanually or rectovaginally), then a multi-fibroid uterus where some nodules sit outside and some are embedded in the wall. Dr. Arntfield's slide. For the hormonal / endocrine (COEIN) half of the exam she moves to general appearance, which her slide illustrates with clinical photographs rather than text: Body habitus and BMI — signs of the female athlete triad, anorexia or bulimia; or the high body mass associated with PCOS and with endometrial cancer risk. Bruising and petechiae — evidence of a coagulopathy. Cushingoid appearance — a recognizable pattern worth pausing on. Signs of thyroid disease , galactorrhea (prolactin), and hirsutism and acne (androgens, PCOS).

The Workup The same split again, made operational. Structural questions get imaging and tissue; non-structural questions get bloodwork. Dr. Arntfield's slide. Question Test Why that one Is there a structural lesion? Pelvic ultrasound The go-to in gynecology, preferred over CT — no radiation, and genuinely better than CT for visualizing pelvic structures including the ovaries Infection or cervical disease? Pap ± swabs (gonorrhea, chlamydia) Taken during the exam you are already doing Is the tissue abnormal? Targeted biopsy — vulva, cervix or endometrium "Targeted" is the operative word: biopsy the lesion you saw Coagulopathy? CBC, INR, PTT Anemia from the bleeding itself, plus the coagulation profile Ovulatory / HPO dysfunction? FSH, LH, estradiol, TSH, prolactin Walks the axis from pituitary down PCOS or Cushing's? 17-OH progesterone, androgen profile Only if the history and exam point there Pregnant? β-hCG Her fourth mention. Also a safety step — see below Order Matters, Not Just Content Her point about sequencing: you do not want to biopsy the inside of a uterus that contains a pregnancy . So β-hCG is not just a diagnostic test, it is a gate you pass before instrumenting the uterus. The usual real-world order is bloodwork → ultrasound → Pap and biopsy , with the exam-based tests folded into whichever visit makes sense. Left — the office endometrial biopsy done today: a thin plastic pipelle passed through the cervix, sampling the lining by aspiration. The cells go into formalin and off to pathology. Warn her about the cramping — it is significant and it happens with no anaesthetic. Right — dilation and curettage , how this was done in the OR 30–40 years ago. Dr. Arntfield's slide.

The Ladder Treatment is fast to teach because it is cause specific — deliver the baby, treat the endocrinopathy, remove the mass. But since anovulation is the commonest cause, it usually collapses to regulating the bleeding . Dr. Arntfield's slide. Tier Agents What it achieves Non-hormonal Iron · NSAIDs (ibuprofen) · tranexamic acid (Cyklokapron) Reduces the amount of flow. Does not touch regularity. Baseline therapy for a mild pattern Hormonal — combined OCP in any route: oral, transdermal patch, vaginal ring First-line for mild-to-moderate bleeding. Reduces both intensity and irregularity Hormonal — progestin only Depo-Provera · Mirena · Visanne (dienogest) No estrogen — the option when estrogen is contraindicated. All three often induce amenorrhea GnRH agonist Lupron Shuts the axis down at the hypothalamus. Excellent for acute haemorrhage ; heavy menopausal side-effect profile, so not for long-term use Minimally invasive / surgical UAE, endometrial ablation · VH, LAVH, TAH Named on the slide but explicitly outside this lecture's scope Counsel Her About Amenorrhea First Depo, Mirena and Visanne each have a high likelihood of stopping her periods altogether . Dr. Arntfield is emphatic that you must clarify this in advance, because most women read "no periods" as pathological or dangerous — and they have reasonable grounds for thinking so. So ask what her goal is: if she does not want periods, that points you toward these agents; if a monthly period matters to her, it points you away from them. The same question decides between the options, not just whether to warn her. The concept slide, and the best single summary of how to actually choose. Dr. Arntfield's slide. The mechanism, in her words: "If estrogen is the fertilizer, progesterone is the lawnmower ." Any progestin thins the endometrium over time, giving shorter, lighter cycles — or none at all. You are exploiting non-contraceptive benefit. Contraceptives almost always have one, and cycle control is the one being used here. Anti-androgenic options for PCOS: Diane-35 (cyproterone acetate) and Yaz ( drospirenone A progestin with anti-androgenic and anti-mineralocorticoid activity, used where the cosmetic androgenic features of PCOS matter. ) carry an anti-androgen in place of a standard progestin — well suited to PCOS with hirsutism and acne . Choice is driven by patient preference, cost, side effects and ease. The OCP's oral route is often preferred — but it needs daily remembering, so ask her whether

What the Two Groups Share Group them in your head: adolescents and perimenopausal women both have an HPO axis that is not reliably ovulating , so both have higher rates of irregular, unpredictable, heavy bleeding than the mid-reproductive-age group. Where they differ is the thing you must not miss. Adolescence. The differential on the left, the severity-graded treatment on the right. Perimenopause. Same anovulation, but malignancy rates are climbing — and the case at the bottom is why you take the bleeding history seriously. Adolescence The immature HPO axis takes about 2 years to mature. Many girls will take that long to develop regular cycles — so anovulation here is often physiological. But "it will get better" is not the same as "don't treat." She makes this point from a call shift days before recording: a 14-year-old in the department needing intensive treatment for genuinely heavy cycles. Treatment is graded — mild: iron + reassurance · moderate: low-dose OCP first line · severe/acute: serial hemoglobin, coagulation studies, IV estrogen. This is the life stage an eating disorder develops or entrenches , and a very common time to be heavily athletically involved — so the female athlete triad belongs on the differential. Menarche may be the first time an inherited coagulopathy is unmasked. Absent an injury, the onset of periods can be the presenting event for an undiagnosed blood dyscrasia — most commonly von Willebrand disease . Keep it in mind for the adolescent bleeding very heavily from the start . Pregnancy risk exists and may be hard to elicit with a parent present. See the history note in Part 2. Monday's Small Group Covered the Opposite Complaint — Amenorrhea The Week 4 Child Health small group on pediatric gynecology is a team-based session with no lecture : its guide states plainly that "pre-reading is assigned ahead of time; the material will not be reviewed in session." Its required reading is Gray SH, "Menstrual Disorders", Pediatrics in Review 2013;34(1):6–18 . So nothing below was said out loud in class — it is what the session assumed you already knew , which makes it worth having in one place. The session's own objectives You should be able to… List the prerequisites for normal menstruation in an adolescent Define primary and secondary amenorrhea Outline an approach to investigation based on primary vs secondary , delayed vs normal pubertal development , and presence or absence of hyperandrogenism Name the most likely etiology from the

Learning Objectives Review pregnancy termination options in Canada. Compare options based on gestational age and describe the risks of abortion. Compare the risks of termination with the risks of pregnancy. Outline counselling about fertility and contraception. Dr. Stephanie Black, generalist OB/GYN at LHSC, who provides this care herself. Contraception in detail is 4.3 ; the drugs are 4.4 .

The Words The obstetrical cut-offs: 20 weeks / 500 g separates an abortion from a stillbirth. Any sign of life at birth is a live birth , whatever the gestational age. Term Means Abortion Termination of a pregnancy by removal or expulsion of a fetus or embryo from the uterus Spontaneous abortion Miscarriage Therapeutic abortion Any induced abortion, whatever the reason "Abortion" in a chart may mean a miscarriage. Read which one is meant.

How Common It Is Who has abortions. 81% unmarried, but 60% already have at least one child , and half are under 25. About 35% of women will have had one by age 45. The three "no"s at the bottom are the evidence base for the myths section : no effect on fertility, no harm to mental health, no link to breast cancer . Number Meaning 204 per 1,000 live births Rate of termination (CDC 2021), roughly unchanged over 20 years 11.6 per 1,000 women International rate. 48% are still unsafe , and 97% of those are in developing countries ~97,000 Abortions reported in Canada in 2022 (the most recent data) Half of pregnancies Unintended: no contraception, contraceptive failure, ambivalence, or sexual assault

entries.t: The Law: How Canada Got Here
entries.x: The Law: How Canada Got Here Year What happened 1969 Abortion permitted only in a hospital, if a committee of doctors decided the pregnancy endangered the woman's health or life. Strict criteria, long delays 1982 Charter of Rights and Freedoms : any law contravening it can be struck down 1988 R v Morgentaler : the Supreme Court strikes the abortion law down as unconstitutional, violating section 7 (life, liberty and security of the person) 1989 After a boyfriend obtained an injunction against Chantal Daigle , the Supreme Court rules that a father or male partner has no veto 1990 Bill C-43 (two years' jail for providers where health was not at risk) passes the Commons but dies on a tie vote in the Senate 1995 Rulings force Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to allow private clinics, but coverage outside hospitals stays inconsistent Nov 2014 New Brunswick drops the rules that an abortion must be done by an OB/GYN and certified in writing by two physicians Jun 2015 Abortion added to the inter-provincial billing agreement , so care is portable like every other procedure Jul 2015 Mifepristone approved by Health Canada (not actually available until 2017) Jan 2017 Abortion services available on Prince Edward Island for the first time Today No federal law at all. Abortion is legal, treated like any other procedure, governed by provincial and medical regulation Two things to take from the timeline. Most abortions in Canada are provided by family physicians in standalone clinics , not by specialists in hospitals. And the barriers that were lifted recently — two-doctor certification, paying out of pocket in another province — were lifted within the last decade .

entries.t: Access: It Depends Where You Live
entries.x: Access: It Depends Where You Live From 12 weeks in Nunavut and PEI to nearly 25 in BC. The eastern provinces mostly stop at 16 weeks . London is the referral centre for eastern Canada; provinces west of here send patients to BC. CIHI 2022: 97,211 abortions; 76,884 outside hospitals vs 20,327 in them. Note that CIHI's method table (below) totals 96,982 rather than 97,211 — the two tables count slightly different sets, so the percentages and the total come from different tables. Access is guaranteed by the Canada Health Act , but availability and the gestational limit vary across a very big country. In Ontario, OHIP covers abortion in both hospitals and clinics. Surgical abortion is provided up to about 24 weeks; induction abortion beyond 25 weeks exists at only one centre and is extremely limited. Beyond that, patients may be referred to cooperating clinics in the United States. Where the limits differ between the lecture's table and the spoken Ontario figure (23+6 vs 24+6), they reflect moving targets that change as services change.

When, and With What Complications Method, 2022: surgical 60.5% , medical 39.5% . The medical share has climbed steadily since mifepristone arrived in 2017. 98% have no complication. The rest, in order: hemorrhage, infection, retained products , or a combination. Anything else is very rare. Two-thirds of abortions happen in the first trimester (30.4% at or before 8 weeks and 35.6% between 9 and 12 weeks, in the 2017 hospital data), and the numbers fall steadily with advancing gestation. Why people present late. The big segments are no symptoms of pregnancy , denial and denial-like processes , chaotic lives and late diagnosis of a fetal anomaly . "Took this long to decide" is one of the smallest slices, which is the opposite of the common assumption. From the lecture.

Before Any Abortion The checklist. Confirm an intrauterine pregnancy and the gestational age (usually ultrasound; with a good history, early medication abortion can be provided "no-touch" and virtually). History, Rh status (for WinRho), informed consent , and counselling about the procedure and contraception. No referral is needed — most clinics are self-referral. From the lecture.

Choosing Medical or Surgical The trade-off in one table. Medical : no procedure, no anaesthetic, done at home with control and privacy, but it takes days to weeks, needs follow-up, and the bleeding feels heavy. Surgical : invasive and provider-performed, but a predictable timeframe, >99% success , no required follow-up and lighter bleeding. Medical can often be started the same day . From the lecture.

Mifepristone and Misoprostol Five years from application to availability , then heavy restrictions (a 6-hour course, physician dispensing) that have since been lifted . The course is still available for anyone who wants it. Progesterone blockade → decidual necrosis + contractions + cervical ripening → detachment and expulsion. Drug What it is What it does Mifepristone (RU-486) Anti-progestin , a derivative of norethindrone Binds the progesterone receptor without activating it. Progesterone is required to maintain an early pregnancy, so blocking it causes decidual necrosis and bleeding . Also softens the cervix and increases sensitivity to prostaglandins , raising the frequency and amplitude of contractions (peak at 36–48 h ) and lowering the threshold for uterine contractility. Some effect within 15 minutes Misoprostol Prostaglandin E 1 analogue Cervical ripening : less collagen, more soluble collagen, more matrix metalloproteinases, collagen degradation. Uterine contraction : inhibits adenylyl cyclase → less cAMP → more calcium → increased uterine tone Methotrexate (older option) Antimetabolite blocking dihydrofolate reductase Blocks DNA synthesis, acting on the cytotrophoblast rather than the embryo , so implantation stops. Used up to 49 days . Teratogenic (cranial malformations, palsies, growth delay, limb deformities), so follow-up is essential Two jobs, two mechanisms. Left, the cervix is softened by breaking down collagen. Right, the muscle is contracted through less cAMP and more intracellular calcium. Given after mifepristone, which has already sensitized the uterus to prostaglandins, it is far more effective. From the lecture. Methotrexate, the older regimen. It blocks dihydrofolate reductase and so DNA synthesis, acting on the cytotrophoblast rather than the embryo to stop implantation. Used up to 49 days , and kept for when mifepristone isn't available or is contraindicated. Because it is teratogenic , follow-up to confirm success is essential. From the lecture. The "Abortion Reversal" Claim Some providers claim that high-dose progesterone after mifepristone can reverse it. It can't. The patient is still making just as much progesterone as before; the problem is that the receptor is blocked . Mifepristone is all-or-nothing at the receptor: flooding the system with progesterone does not undo it. Changing one's mind after taking it is, in any case, very uncommon given the counselling beforehand.

The Protocol and the Follow-Up Mifegymiso: mifepristone first, then misoprostol 800 µg 24–48 h later (usually buccal: fewer GI effects than oral, better tolerated than vaginal). 90% abort within 24 h of the misoprostol. Confirming it worked. ↓ 50% by day 3 , or ↓ 80% by 7–14 days = success. A plateau means failure and needs surgery. Some patients follow up with ultrasound instead, at 2 weeks (earlier scans often show a thick endometrium the uterus will clear on its own). Mifepristone + misoprostol Methotrexate + misoprostol Up to 70 days (10 weeks) 49 days (7 weeks) Regimen Mifepristone 200 mg buccal/oral, then misoprostol 800 µg 24–48 h later Day 1: MTX 50 mg/m² IM . Day 5–7: misoprostol 600 µg vaginally; if no bleeding in 24 h, another 800 µg. Day 8: quantitative β-hCG; repeat a week later with an office visit Success 95–98% Lower; used when mifepristone isn't available or is contraindicated If it fails >50% complete with a second 800 µg dose ; <5% (about 3%) need surgical evacuation Surgical evacuation, and it must happen: MTX is teratogenic A slide typo to know: the dosing slide writes mifepristone as "200 mcg". The dose is 200 mg . The misoprostol dose, 800 µg, is correct. Advantages Disadvantages Non-invasive · patient autonomy and control · private, at home · inexpensive (covered by OHIP; about $350 without coverage) · technically simple, can be provided from an office and a pharmacy · same-day start · an option when the uterine cavity can't be accessed surgically Both patient and physician must commit to follow-up (up to 10% need at least one reminder) · longer treatment interval · GI side effects: diarrhea, stomach pain, nausea · 10% have delayed evacuation over days to weeks · heavy bleeding and cramps when the pregnancy passes (codeine-containing analgesia is usually prescribed) · up to 5% (typically ~3%) fail

Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) An office procedure, essentially the same as an endometrial biopsy: a cannula plus a hand-held aspirator, no electric suction and no OR . The cannulas and the aspirator. Up to 10 weeks gestation. Paracervical block with 1% lidocaine at a minimum; other sedation offered if available. Most patients, especially nulliparas , need some cervical dilatation. Transilluminate the tissue to confirm chorionic villi and a gestational sac , or do a post-procedure ultrasound to confirm an empty uterus. Failure rate 0.25%. Good for: office setting, immediate, private, local anaesthetic only, cost-effective. Not for: contraindications to local anaesthesia, a patient who can't cooperate with the exam, or very young or distressed patients who may need sedation.

Dilatation & Curettage (Suction D&C) Vacuum or suction aspiration up to and including 14+0 weeks , using a rigid cannula on an electric suction machine. It can be done under local with a cervical block, but conscious or moderate sedation is usually offered, and general anaesthetic in some hospital settings. Cervical preparation. Chemical: misoprostol orally, buccally or vaginally 1–12 h before. Osmotic: laminaria (a seaweed) or synthetic Dilapan , placed in the internal os 24 h before, which slowly absorb fluid and open the cervix (the photo shows one expanding over 24 h). Hegar dilators , sized in millimetres. Rule of thumb: dilate to about the number of weeks' gestation (a 12-week pregnancy → about 12 mm). 1 Bimanual exam : confirms size and expected gestation, and tells you whether the uterus is anteverted or retroverted so instruments go the right way and don't perforate. 2 Speculum, prep and paracervical block (lidocaine, sometimes with vasopressin and/or epinephrine to reduce blood loss). Pre-operative antibiotics are given for a therapeutic abortion. 3 Mechanical dilatation only if needed. If cervical prep was adequate, skipping it means less discomfort and less infection , because fewer instruments pass through the vagina into the uterus. 4 Suction curettage to remove all products. Sharp curettage is unnecessary in the vast majority of cases and carries a higher complication rate, including Asherman syndrome. Complications (all inside that <2% overall rate). Cervical shock: a vasovagal reaction during the block, lasting minutes. Uterine perforation: during dilatation or suction; finish the case under ultrasound or laparoscopic guidance , with the choice guided by the instrument size, the site (fundus vs laterally near the uterine arteries) and the patient's stability. From the lecture. Complication Recognize it by Do Hemorrhage More likely with uterine atony , a low implantation or a larger gestational age A repeat curettage may be needed to confirm everything is out Hematometra (post-abortal syndrome) Blood collecting in the cavity: excruciating pain, an enlarging uterus, little or no bleeding , often urinary retention Re-evacuate immediately Advantages of D&C over medical abortion: less risk than general anaesthesia (it can be done with conscious sedation), faster recovery, much less bleeding afterwards, quicker discharge without required follow-up, high patient acceptance and cost-effectiveness.

Second Trimester Surgical: D&E Medical: induction of labour How Pre-operative cervical ripening (osmotic, mechanical and/or medical), ± fetal intracardiac injection of digoxin or KCl , then decompression and removal of the uterine contents, usually under general anaesthetic. Beyond 18 weeks , serial applications of dilators Misoprostol induction, generally after intracardiac KCl or digoxin Up to Generally 25 weeks Used beyond that, and for genetic terminations Advantages Fewest complications of the second-trimester methods; much shorter from start to finish; fewer retained products Allows the pregnancy to be delivered whole for autopsy or genetic examination , and allows memory-making for families Risks General anaesthetic, uterine perforation, hemorrhage, infection (multiple instrumentations), incomplete procedure — all rising with gestational age Length (24 h or more), bleeding, and retained placenta : 5–10% need an urgent D&C or D&E anyway The lecture's own point: the greatest obstacle to safe D&E in Canada is the shrinking number of skilled practitioners . That is starting to turn around, helped by a second-trimester providers group formed during the pandemic so that clinicians know who offers what.

Compared With Continuing the Pregnancy Legal abortion is the safest outcome on the table : 0.567 deaths per 100,000, against 1.19 for miscarriage, 7.06 for live birth and 31.9 for ectopic pregnancy. Continuing a pregnancy is more than 12× more dangerous than ending it. Grimes, 2006, from the lecture.

Contraception Afterwards Ovulation can return as early as 2 weeks after a first-trimester abortion, so contraception should start immediately if wanted. Every method is appropriate : having an abortion is not a contraindication to anything. Review all of them. Timing: a pill, patch, ring or Depo-Provera can start the same day as a surgical abortion, or on the day of the day-3 bloodwork after a medical one. An IUD or implant can go in during the surgical procedure (painless under sedation), or at the two-week visit once a medical abortion is confirmed complete. Expulsion is slightly higher when an IUD is placed immediately ( 3.8% ), but still under 5%. If a method failed, offer a different one — and work out why it failed: cost, trouble swallowing or remembering pills, fear of needles, a partner who won't use condoms, or a medical reason to avoid estrogen (previous DVT, migraine with aura, smoking over half a pack a day over age 35). IUDs have their own limits, such as a uterine malformation or the cost of insertion and removal. If the procedure is done by a surgeon under general anaesthetic and the patient has completed childbearing , a tubal ligation can be offered at the same time.

Fertility and Emotions Afterwards Asherman syndrome. Left, the HSG : black filling defects inside the triangular cavity are adhesions. Right, hysteroscopy : the cavity isn't open and smooth, it's stuck together. The most common emotional reaction is relief , sometimes with transient guilt, sadness or a sense of loss. Overall, patients are content with their decision. A safe abortion carries no greater risk to fertility than a D&C for miscarriage. Asherman syndrome : adhesions form in the endometrial cavity, sometimes causing secondary amenorrhea . Risk factors are uterine curettage (about 8% of cases), repeat curettage (most often for retained products or retained placenta postpartum), and infection. The slide puts the risk at up to 30% with a third consecutive procedure . Trauma is the major cause of intrauterine adhesions; the role of infection is controversial and hard to separate out, because infected products usually mean retained products, which mean another procedure. After a single, uncomplicated first- or second-trimester procedure, the risk is very low .

The Myths, Answered The list patients will bring you. The answers are below. From the lecture. Myth The answer Abortion causes breast cancer No evidence. The only biologically plausible thread is that breastfeeding slightly lowers breast cancer risk, so not carrying a pregnancy to term means not breastfeeding — which is no different from never being pregnant, or choosing not to breastfeed It's used as birth control The decision is almost never taken lightly . Patients needing repeat abortions are often experiencing reproductive coercion , financial hardship, isolation, abuse or trafficking, or have medical contraindications to contraception (or believe the myths about it) It's illegal in Canada No. There is no federal law. (US law is a separate, shifting picture; very few patients cross the border for care here) It causes infertility No , as above Only single women have abortions 80% are unmarried, so 1 in 5 are in a committed relationship , and 60% already have children Women from religious backgrounds don't Abortion doesn't discriminate by culture, religion, ethnicity, income, relationship status or parity Products of conception are used in makeup, vaccines or unethical research Not accurate. Where tissue is used in research, it is with ethics approval and the patient's explicit, informed permission

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Learning Objectives Outline a clinical approach to both acute and chronic pelvic pain. Recognize common causes of acute and chronic pelvic pain. List a differential diagnosis for both acute and chronic pelvic pain. Outline appropriate investigations for pelvic pain. Identify treatment options for common causes of pelvic pain. Dr. Stephanie Black's 39-minute module — the first half of one deck that covers acute then chronic pelvic pain; the chronic half is 4.14 . Declared conflict: Bayer advisory board for intrauterine contraception (Mirena/Kyleena), neither of which features here. How she intends it to be used: the deck is built as clinical cases, and she explicitly prompts you to pause at each case and build a differential and an investigation plan before revealing the answer — alone or with colleagues. The case answers are given below each case on this page, so cover them if you want to work through it her way. She also teaches 4.13 .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: History and Physical Come First One bullet, deliberately. It is critical for developing the differential , and therefore for narrowing the investigations and the treatment plan. Note the third bullet. The gynecologist's role is often to rule gynecologic causes out . Patients present anywhere — primary care, walk-in, gynecology office, or the ER. Worth actually reading through once. Her instruction is to take a moment and familiarize yourself with it — and her warning is that because this is the repro block, the lecture will lead you down the gynecologic column, but you must not forget the other five when you are the one examining the patient. Figure from UpToDate on Dr. Black's slide; reproduced with permission from Howard FM, "Acute Abdominal Pain," in Primary Care for Women , Lippincott Williams & Wilkins. History of the Pain — OPQRST The standard pain history, applied here. Dr. Black's slide. Element What to ask Why it discriminates Onset What was she doing? Sudden or gradual? Her key example: woken from sleep by sudden pelvic pain vs pain starting during physical activity gives very different differentials — the second raises torsion and ruptured cyst Duration How long, and is it constant? Separates acute from chronic (see 4.14 ) Quality Sharp, stabbing, colicky, burning Colicky suggests a hollow viscus; sharp and stabbing suggests an acute vascular or rupture event Location + Radiation Where, and does it go anywhere? Shoulder tip → diaphragmatic irritation → blood in the peritoneum. Back → torsion or renal Aggravating / alleviating Rest, eating, movement, heat Worse on eating points GI; positional change points to hemoperitoneum Associated symptoms GI (constipation, diarrhea, gas) · GU (dysuria) · systemic (fever) · vaginal discharge · vaginal bleeding Each one recruits a different column of the table above Physical Exam Dr. Black's slide. Vital signs first — her reasoning: clinical instability sends you down the life-threatening path , so this is a triage step, not a formality. Overall appearance from the end of the bed — does she look genuinely sick and unwell, or fairly healthy despite the pain? A cheap and surprisingly discriminating observation. Abdomen: inspection, auscultation, palpation. Pelvic: inspection of the external genitalia, speculum inspection, and bimanual palpation — two fingers in the vagina, one hand on the abdomen, palpating the uterosacral ligament insertions , the uterus , and the adnexal regions . Don't stop at the pain histor

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Case 1: Katie, 25 Answer: ectopic pregnancy, likely ruptured. Dr. Black's slide. Reading This Case Five findings, each of which independently raises the diagnosis. β-hCG 2345 — she is pregnant, and condoms are a method with real typical-use failure. Sudden RLQ pain + vaginal bleeding — the classic pair. Hb 82 — she is bleeding internally ; you cannot see it. Shoulder pain — blood in the peritoneum irritating the diaphragm (see below). Tenesmus — blood pooling in the pouch of Douglas irritating the rectum. Lightheaded — hypovolemia. Put together: not just an ectopic, but a ruptured one, and she is unstable. 98% are tubal. And read the IUD footnote carefully — it is a classic exam distinction, unpacked below. The classic triad: pelvic pain + amenorrhea + vaginal bleeding. Confirmed with β-hCG + TVUS . The IUD Point, Stated Precisely Her slide footnote is worth quoting almost exactly, because the sloppy version is wrong: IUDs do NOT increase the incidence of ectopic pregnancy. What they increase is the likelihood that a pregnancy is ectopic if a pregnancy occurs with an IUD in situ. The mechanism is straightforward once stated: the IUD is very effective at preventing intrauterine implantation, so it removes intrauterine pregnancies from the denominator far more than extrauterine ones — the proportion shifts without the absolute risk rising. Practically: an IUD user with a positive pregnancy test needs an ectopic excluded urgently. Risk factors to know: pelvic infection · previous ectopic · smoking · adhesions · multiple sexual partners · IUD in situ (as qualified above). Other sites beyond the tube: ovarian, cervical, cornual, abdominal, and caesarean-section scar . And the reason this matters: ectopic pregnancy accounts for 4–10% of first-trimester deaths in pregnancy. On TVUS: an empty uterus (UT), the left ovary (L OV), and an adnexal structure separate from both — the ectopic. At laparoscopy: the distended, blood-filled tube, with free blood in the pelvis. Two distinct pain mechanisms, and both are examinable. The pelvic pain itself is visceral pain from stretching of the hollow fallopian tube — which is why it is poorly localized and colicky before rupture. The shoulder-tip pain is referred , from blood of a ruptured ectopic irritating the diaphragm : the diaphragm's phrenic innervation (C3–C5) shares dermatomes with the shoulder, so the brain misattributes the signal. Dr. Black's slide. The methotrexate criteria are the highest-yield list on this page.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
entries.x: Case 2: Sara, 17 Answer: PID. Note the discriminators from Case 1 — β-hCG negative , WBC 22 , systemic infective symptoms, and foul-smelling discharge . Dr. Black's slide.
