Medications — specifically HRT, the birth control pill, tamoxifen Gynecologic events — pregnancy, birth, miscarriage Strenuous or vigorous exercise Other systemic or local findings · skin abnormalities On examination, do the clinical breast exam as above and extend it into a musculoskeletal exam — tenderness over the ribs or sternum , and pain on moving the arm suggesting the shoulder or pectoral muscles . The Question That Sorts Everything: Cyclical or Not? Cyclical — two thirds of cases. A hormonal response in which the ducts and stroma become reactive . It starts in the luteal phase and ends with menstruation . Non-cyclical — now you are thinking mastitis or another infection , medication-induced pain, Cooper's ligament stretch in a large pendulous breast, or extramammary causes in the chest wall, ribs or sternum that the patient simply describes as breast pain. Treating cyclical pain Measure Evidence as he presents it Low-fat, high-complex-carbohydrate diet A New York study found prolactin levels fell on this diet; a later Canadian randomised study found women with chronic breast pain did substantially better on it than on a normal diet Stopping smoking Smoking worsens breast pain. Cleveland Clinic work showed nicotine and cigarette smoke raise epinephrine in breast tissue , driving the cyclical pain Support bras and compresses First-line conservative measures Acetaminophen Simple analgesia Stopping offending medications OCP, HRT, tamoxifen — the drugs that alter hormone levels Cutting coffee An old wives' tale. Reducing caffeine has not actually been shown to improve breast pain

Mastitis — the Management Step Antibiotics first Cephalexin is the usual first choice — good against skin organisms, and Staph aureus is the commonest organism in mastitis Keep feeding Lactating women should continue breastfeeding and fully empty the breast — it makes the infection resolve faster If antibiotics don't work Ultrasound , then consider ultrasound-guided aspiration , and consider IV antibiotics Incision and drainage Last choice — not the go-to If redness or a mass persists Biopsy and mammogram. If things look fine, repeat imaging later The Breast Is the Exception to the Abscess Rule Anywhere else on the body — abdomen, arm — incision and drainage is the standard management of an abscess . In the breast it is not. The order is antibiotics → IV antibiotics → ultrasound-guided aspiration → I&D last . And the reason persistent redness earns a biopsy rather than another antibiotic course: inflammatory carcinoma is defined by looking exactly like diffuse acute mastitis (see 5.6 ). A "mastitis" that will not clear is the presentation you must not explain away. Investigating breast pain: under 35 with a normal exam, no further testing — it is most likely hormonal or musculoskeletal. Suspicious findings send you down the breast lump pathway . Pain without a lump can still be referred to the Breast Assessment Centre, but will be triaged less urgently than an obvious lump. And remember: the older the woman, the more likely breast pain reflects important pathology.

Physiologic vs Pathologic Discharge The Terminology Trap Physiologic discharge is galactorrhea — driven by a chemical or hormonal imbalance, not related to pregnancy or lactation . It can be a variety of colours , constant or intermittent, usually bilateral , and usually from several ducts ; it is expressed with nipple compression. Pathologic discharge means it comes from a lesion within the breast. He is emphatic that this does not mean something dangerous is going on — the commonest cause is a benign papilloma. "Pathologic" describes the source , not the seriousness. Causes of galactorrhea Nipple stimulation Including clothing that constantly rubs the nipples Pituitary disease Chiefly hyperprolactinemia (see 3.5 ) Drugs Agents that suppress dopamine , such as methyldopa Chest wall injury or thoracic surgery Damage to intercostal nerves produces a neural feedback response that raises prolactin Other medical conditions Chronic kidney disease · hypothyroidism · cirrhosis · stress Note the overlap he points out himself: kidney, thyroid and liver appear in both the gynecomastia workup and the galactorrhea workup. Learn them once. Features that say the discharge is from a lesion Unilateral · from a single duct · spontaneous · bloody or serous · associated with a mass · patient over 50 Investigating it Inspect the nipple — Paget's disease is a skin disease of the nipple that can also produce discharge ( 5.6 ). Then periareolar ultrasound and mammography , which are the mainstays, plus biopsy techniques as needed. Galactography (ductography) exists but he notes it is not much used in London . Cause Papilloma — essentially a wart within the duct The most common cause of pathologic nipple discharge. Benign Duct ectasia · fibrocystic change Also benign Malignancy — ductal carcinoma, inflammatory breast cancer Only 5–10% of nipple discharge

Epidemiology Lifetime risk of a woman developing breast cancer: 1 in 8. His one "remember this" number — the one on the billboards Breast cancer makes up about 25% of all female cancers Five-year disease-free survival: 88% — it was 81% when he inherited the slides, and about 58% in the 1960s Lifetime overall survival: 66% Read the pairs of bars. Lung has more cases and far more deaths. Colorectal has fewer cases but almost twice the deaths of breast. Breast has a big case burden and a comparatively good survival — and since under half of lung cancers are in women, breast dominates the female cancer picture.

The Ontario Breast Screening Program He cannot praise it enough as a family doctor, and the reason is structural rather than clinical. Provincially funded, age 50–74 , for women deemed normal risk Self-referral — the patient books herself from her 50th birthday CAR-accredited mammography facilities with a consistent reading radiologist Two-view screening mammogram Automatically books assessment and follow-up investigations; linked to the Breast Assessment Programs Why Self-Referral Is the Feature That Matters Because the patient enters and moves through the system without needing you . An abnormal screen goes straight to the Breast Assessment Centre for further imaging, and on to biopsy if needed, without referrals bouncing back and forth . His point: if he is away on vacation for two weeks, nothing gets delayed and nothing slips through the cracks. Screening myth Reality #1: "Mammograms are painful" Only 7–10% of women put it in the very uncomfortable or excruciating category. Most describe it as uncomfortable — "a really tight squeeze" #2: "The radiation causes cancer" It may increase risk — by about one cancer per million screens . A very low dose next to, say, an abdominal CT

entries.t: Who Gets Screened, and How Often
entries.x: Who Gets Screened, and How Often Risk Screening Usual risk Age 50–74, biennial mammogram High risk Screen annually What makes someone high risk One first-degree relative under 50 with breast cancer Two first-degree relatives with breast cancer at any age One first-degree relative, or a personal history, of ovarian cancer Family history of male breast cancer Pathologic diagnosis of atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia, radial scar, phyllodes tumour or LCIS Breast density greater than 75% Every entry on that pathology row comes straight out of 5.6 — the biopsy report is what moves a woman from biennial to annual screening.

entries.t: The Benefit, and What It Costs
entries.x: The Benefit, and What It Costs Benefit 25% reduction in mortality for 50–74 year olds Population-based projection — you need to screen about 70% of the population to realise it Per 1000 women screened, age 50–69 Per one death prevented 282 false positives Number needed to screen ~721 37 unnecessary biopsies 204 false positives and 26 unnecessary biopsies The Cochrane Framing — Why the Age Window Is 50 to 74 Assuming screening reduces breast cancer mortality by 15% and that overdiagnosis and overtreatment run at 30% , then for every 2000 women invited for screening throughout 10 years : one will avoid dying of breast cancer , 10 healthy women will be treated unnecessarily for a cancer that would never have been diagnosed, and more than 200 women will experience important psychological distress , including anxiety and uncertainty, for years, because of false-positive findings. Drop the start age to 40 and you get more false positives and a higher number needed to screen. Extend the end age to 75–80 and you would need to screen fewer women per death prevented — but you would increasingly be diagnosing cancers in elderly women who would not have died of them. 50 to 74 is where that trade-off is judged acceptable. His conclusion, and it is worth keeping: "mammography is not benign." It generates lumpectomies, mastectomies, biopsies, extra imaging and time off work. Accuracy note: the lecture audio states overdiagnosis as "3%", which is a mis-transcription — the source (Gøtzsche & Jørgensen, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;6:CD001877, which the deck cites) says 30% , and the rest of the quoted numbers only make sense with 30%. Verified against the Cochrane review, 25 Sept 2026.

Risk Factors His framing: the most important risk factors are things you can't do anything about. Factor Gender The biggest one — about 99% of breast cancers are in women Age Risk climbs steeply — see the table below Family history Two first-degree relatives: RR 4–5 · one first-degree relative: RR 2–3 · one second-degree relative: RR 1.2–1.5 Age-specific ten-year probability. A 20-year-old has a 1 in 1,479 chance of diagnosis in the next decade; a 50-year-old 1 in 42; a 70-year-old 1 in 25. The bottom row is the number to carry: lifetime 1 in 8 diagnosed, 1 in 39 dying . American Cancer Society, 2019 — a US table, and he notes it holds closely for Canada. Read the Second Column, Not Just the First The gap between being diagnosed and dying is the real story in that table. At every age the probability of diagnosis is several times the probability of death, and lifetime it is 1 in 8 versus 1 in 39 . That ratio is what "becoming a good prognosis tumour" looks like in numbers. Minor risk factors — RR 1.1 to 1.3 Lack of exercise · BMI > 30 · more than 2 drinks per day · early menarche and late menopause · no children and no breastfeeding · birth control pill for more than 5 years · HRT with estrogen and progesterone The Birth Control Pill Entry Needs Counselling, Not Just Quoting This is the one he says you will have to discuss with patients. When the studies are dissected, the association sits with the older triphasic formulations and the progestin they used. The modern pills , including the Tri-Cyclen Lo available in Canada, do not contain that progestin . Even then it is a small increase in relative risk — probably not a worrisome risk factor for a woman on a modern pill . Contraceptive counselling is 4.3 .

Genetic Risk and Testing 5% of all breast cancers have an identifiable gene mutation Most of those genes govern either DNA repair or regulation of cell growth — BRCA1 and BRCA2 Other syndromes matter too, notably Li-Fraumeni (p53) Lifetime risk for female BRCA carriers: 55–85% breast , 15–65% ovarian Send for genetic testing if… Patient under 35 Patient under 50 with two first- or second-degree relatives , at least one of whom is under 50 , or one with bilateral breast cancer , or one with serous ovarian cancer Three or more family members with breast or ovarian cancer at any age Male breast cancer Breast cancer in an Ashkenazi Jewish patient BRCA-negative patient under 35 with family members with sarcoma, brain tumours, leukemia or adrenocortical carcinoma — looking for Li-Fraumeni Two Counselling Points That Are Easy to Get Backwards 1. Test the affected relative, not the worried one. If you are the family member of someone you think carries a BRCA mutation, it should be that person who gets tested — a result from the affected patient is far more informative. 2. Timing is deliberate. Gene testing in an affected patient is done after life insurance has been obtained, childbearing is complete, and social relationships are stable. The genetic counsellors are explicit about getting those in order first — a diagnosis of a serious genetic condition has consequences beyond medicine. He also asked a genetic counsellor why the criteria exclude so many women . The answer: when one in eight women gets breast cancer, you will have an aunt or a cousin with it by chance alone. A family history has to be unusually strong or unusually early to mean something genetic. Management for a BRCA carrier Effect Prophylactic mastectomy 90% reduction ± Oophorectomy 50% reduction Intensive screening Annual MRI and mammogram — more sensitive than mammogram or ultrasound in these patients, but high false-positive rates leading to biopsy Chemoprevention Tamoxifen — roughly 50% reduction

entries.t: The Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care
entries.x: The Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care Population Recommendation Strength Women 40–49 Recommend NOT screening with mammography; the decision is conditional on the value the woman places on the benefits and harms Conditional; low-certainty evidence Women 50–74 Recommend screening with mammography every 2 to 3 years ; again conditional on her values. Ontario uses every 2 years Conditional; very-low-certainty evidence Not at increased risk Recommend NOT using MRI, tomosynthesis or ultrasound to screen Strong; no evidence Clinical breast exam Recommend NOT performing CBE to screen Conditional; no evidence Breast self-examination Recommend NOT advising women to practise it Conditional; low-certainty evidence

What a Diagnosis Actually Does Domain Cosmesis The breast can be a real part of a woman's identity. Mastectomy — prophylactic or therapeutic — affects appearance, confidence and security. Special bras and reconstructive surgery are available, and unlike cosmetic augmentation, reconstruction after mastectomy or a large lumpectomy is covered Genetic risk A BRCA2 carrier's children each have a 50% chance of inheriting it. Nothing is done while they are teenagers, so the parent carries the question of whether and when to tell them Insurability You want insurance before a diagnosis is on your chart — which he points out applies to you, securing disability and life insurance now Early menopause Prophylactic bilateral oophorectomy forces menopause, sometimes in a woman's mid to late thirties , affecting libido and relationships (see 5.3 ) Mental health Often healthy young or middle-aged women hit with a bad diagnosis out of nowhere. Profound effects — but also a genuine culture of resilience , with walks, runs and peer networks where patients find people who have been through it Support LHSC and the breast assessment program have social workers, psychologists and health specialists attached to the clinics. Family physicians do a lot of the counselling and navigation

Summary Breast complaints are common Most breast lumps are not cancers The older the woman, the more likely any breast complaint is serious The older the woman, the greater the risk of breast cancer If at normal risk, screen every two years from 50 to 74 ; if at high risk, screen yearly

Learning Objectives Describe the risks and complications of dilation and curettage. Dr. Stephanie Black, generalist Ob/Gyn, LHSC. A 12-minute module — one of two short procedural pieces that sit under the larger objective of developing a differential diagnosis for women presenting with first-trimester bleeding . A good deal of the surrounding context is in 4.1 and 4.9 .

What the Procedure Is Definition Vacuum aspiration of a pregnancy ≤ 14 weeks and 0 days gestation How Aspiration of uterine contents with a rigid plastic cannula attached to an electric suction machine Anesthesia Local, with a paracervical block , with or without conscious sedation — or a general anesthetic , depending on the resources at your centre Indications First-trimester pregnancy loss — incomplete, inevitable or missed abortion · therapeutic abortion What It Is Not For The module's own knowledge check asks which conditions a D&C can treat. Ectopic pregnancy is not one of them — the pregnancy is not in the uterus, so evacuating the uterus achieves nothing (see 4.9 ). Nor is endometritis , which is treated with antibiotics. And beyond 14+0 weeks the procedure is a D&E , not a D&C.

Cervical Preparation Peri-procedural cervical dilatation is usually required — but not for an incomplete or inevitable abortion, where the cervix is already open . Method Agent Timing Chemical Misoprostol — oral, buccal (inside the cheek) or vaginal 1–12 hours before the procedure Osmotic / mechanical Laminaria (a dried kelp / seaweed stick) or synthetic Dilapan , placed directly into the internal os ~24 hours before the procedure Osmotic dilators, and how they work. Top left is laminaria — literally dried seaweed from the kelp on the right, formed into a small stick. The bottom strip is Dilapan photographed at 0, 2, 4, 8 and 24 hours . Both slowly absorb fluid from the cervix and vagina, widening over time , which opens the cervix gradually and makes the procedure safer .

The Procedure, Step by Step Step Detail — and why 1. Bimanual examination Confirms gestational age and uterine size , and whether the uterus is anteverted or retroverted — which is how you reduce the risk of perforation 2. Paracervical block Often lidocaine , sometimes with vasopressin to reduce blood loss, sometimes with bicarbonate to reduce the sting of the local 3. Mechanical dilatation Not always needed if chemical or osmotic preparation was adequate. Avoiding it reduces discomfort and infection rates , because every instrument pass carries vaginal flora into a sterile cavity 4. Suction curettage Plastic suction curette attached to the electric suction machine. Sharp curettage with a metal curette is unnecessary in most cases Hegar dilators — a graduated set, each end a different diameter in millimetres. The rule is simple: the dilatation required equals the number of weeks of gestation . Eight weeks → dilate to 8 mm , which is the size needed to remove the products of conception. The suction curette , attached to tubing and an electric suction machine. Sharp metal curettage gives more tactile feedback that the uterus is empty — but at the cost of higher rates of Asherman's syndrome , so suction alone is preferred wherever possible.

Complications Complication What it is Management Cervical shock A vasovagal reaction as the paracervical block is placed. Lasts seconds to minutes . Only seen in a patient who is awake — not under general anesthetic Self-limited ; supportive care Uterine perforation 1 in 300 to 1 in 1000 , depending on the operator's expertise. A hole in the uterus, most commonly at the fundus . Can occur during dilatation or during suction Complete the procedure under ultrasound or laparoscopic guidance . A fundal perforation away from other organs usually needs only observation Visceral injury Rare. Bowel, bladder or major vessel — especially with suction or sharp curettage through a perforation May require major surgery, possibly laparotomy , to repair Infection As for any surgical procedure Antibiotic prophylaxis for therapeutic abortion , but not for D&C for missed abortion or pregnancy loss. Practice varies Cervical trauma Lacerations from the tenaculum (the instrument holding the cervix still for counter-traction) or from mechanical dilators Generally minor — repaired with absorbable suture Hemorrhage More likely with larger gestational age or abnormal placentation (partial molar or molar pregnancy). May indicate uterine atony or a low implantation site Repeat curettage may be necessary. Note general anesthesia is itself a risk factor , because it relaxes the uterus Hematometra (post-abortal syndrome) Rare but serious. Blood accumulates in the uterine cavity after the procedure. Presents with acute pain, sometimes urinary retention, and no vaginal bleeding Immediate re-evacuation of the uterus Retained products of conception < 1%. Usually small pieces of placenta or membrane. Presents with signs of infection and/or increased or prolonged bleeding Secondary D&C , or medical management with misoprostol to make the uterus contract and expel them Asherman's syndrome Uncommon, but the one that matters to a patient who still wants fertility. Adhesions form within the endometrial cavity, sometimes causing secondary amenorrhea and infertility Risk factors: sharp uterine curettage (8%) and repeat curettage — most often for retained products or retained placenta postpartum. Risk rises up to 30% by a third consecutive procedure within 24 hours . The role of infection is controversial Pain With No Bleeding Is the Red Flag Every other post-procedure complication announces itself with bleeding . Hematometra is the one that presents the opposite way — severe cramping pain, possibl

Learning Objectives Describe basic placental implantation and development. Develop a differential diagnosis for a woman presenting with first trimester bleeding, and summarize the causes. Spontaneous abortion: define spontaneous and recurrent abortion; differentiate the types; state 2 microscopic findings. Ectopic gestation: define it; list the risk factors; identify the most common location; describe 1 gross and 2 microscopic findings in tubal ectopic pregnancy. Gestational trophoblastic disease: list three types; compare complete and partial mole by clinical presentation, genetics and pathology; identify the gross and microscopic findings in choriocarcinoma; state the commonest site of metastasis. How to Use This Page Alongside 4.9 Dr. Emily Goebel's module is 60 minutes with no recorded lecture — it is a case-based text module with images and knowledge checks. Its spontaneous abortion and ectopic sections cover ground you already have clinically in 4.9 . Rather than repeat it, this page keeps those two sections to what the pathologist adds — what the tissue looks like and what proves the diagnosis — and links back for management. Placental development and gestational trophoblastic disease are new , and are covered in full. Dr. Emily Goebel, Pathologist, LHSC and Assistant Professor, Schulich. Images acknowledged to Dr. Michele Weir and Dr. Joanna Walsh .

How the Placenta Forms The placenta supports the fetus by supplying nutrients, eliminating waste and enabling gas exchange via the maternal blood supply. It is composed of chorionic villi and trophoblasts . The three trophoblasts Where they are Cytotrophoblast On the chorionic villi Syncytiotrophoblast Intermediate trophoblast At the placental implantation site Stage What happens Pre-implantation Development begins with implantation of the blastocyst , which has two cell types: the inner cell mass forms the fetus and fetal membranes, and the outer trophoblast cells form the placenta Implantation — Day 6 Trophoblasts interact with the endometrial decidual epithelium to enable invasion and implantation into the uterus Implantation — Day 8 Trophoblasts differentiate into the outer multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast and inner mononucleated cytotrophoblast Post-implantation Syncytiotrophoblasts erode maternal tissue to access maternal blood through the uterine spiral arteries . Cytotrophoblasts form primary chorionic villi , then secondary and tertiary villi, which carry embryonic vessels in their central cores . Anchoring villi attach to the decidua basalis ; branching villi grow outward to provide surface area for metabolite exchange The One Fact That Ties This to Everything Else Syncytiotrophoblasts produce hCG — the hormone measured in both serum and urine pregnancy testing. That single line connects this module to all of Thursday: it is why hCG appears at implantation ( 5.10 ), why trophoblastic proliferation in a mole drives hCG sky-high , and why serial hCG is how a mole and a choriocarcinoma are followed . Learn the cell, and the hormone follows.

entries.t: The Differential for Bleeding in a Reproductive-Age Woman
entries.x: The Differential for Bleeding in a Reproductive-Age Woman Tai, 25, nulliparous Abnormal vaginal bleeding and cramping. Was on the birth control pill, stopped a year ago because it made her gain weight. Sexually active with her boyfriend, condoms "most of the time" . Last menstrual period 2 months ago. Vitals stable. Abdomen soft with mild suprapubic tenderness. Pelvic exam: closed cervix, slightly enlarged uterus . Two mnemonics nested inside each other. The alphabet runs A to N for all causes of abnormal bleeding; "A" for anatomic expands into PALE — polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, endometritis; and "B" for baby is the pregnancy group — spontaneous abortion, ectopic gestation, gestational trophoblastic disease. The same framework appears in 4.10 and 4.12 ; age is what changes which branches are live. Where to Start, and With What In a young, reproductive-age woman, pregnancy complications are the number one cause to consider and must be ruled out before anything else. Of the whole investigation list the module offers — CBC, chest x-ray, Pap, cervical swab, clotting screen, endometrial sample, estrogen/progesterone, FSH/LH — the two that matter are serum β-hCG and pelvic ultrasound . For Tai: β-hCG positive; ultrasound shows a gestational sac in the endometrial cavity but no fetal heartbeat .

Spontaneous Abortion — Definitions and Types Spontaneous abortion: loss of a gestation prior to fetal extrauterine viability ( < 20 weeks ). It accounts for 15% of known pregnancies — underestimated, because very early losses go unrecognised. Three columns decide the type: is there bleeding , is the cervical os open or closed , and have products of conception passed . Incomplete may need a D&C for retained products. Recurrent = 3 or more , and earns a work-up plus referral to medical genetics . Clinical features: abnormal bleeding · prior secondary amenorrhea, or light period · abdominal cramping · passage of blood clot and/or tissue. Fetal causes Maternal causes Chromosomal and/or congenital abnormalities — the #1 cause Poor implantation (structural) Infection (TORCH) Chronic disease · endocrine abnormality · infection · inflammation In most cases the cause is unknown . The commonest cause of first-trimester bleeding overall is spontaneous abortion. What the Pathologist Needs to See — and Why It Matters Clinically Tai passes tissue five days later. Histologic examination of uterine contents — whether passed spontaneously or retrieved at D&C — can show fetal tissue , placenta (chorionic villi and trophoblasts) , placental implantation site , and gestational endometrium (endometrial glands and decidualised stroma). You must see products of conception — any of chorionic villi, trophoblasts, implantation site or fetal tissue — to prove an intrauterine gestation. This is the whole point. Decidualised endometrium tells you she was pregnant somewhere ; it does not tell you the pregnancy was in the uterus . Absent products of conception, an ectopic has not been excluded — which is exactly the situation the next section walks into. Note too that fetal parts may not be identifiable in very early losses, depending on gestational age.

Ectopic Gestation Fatima, 35 Brought to the emergency room with severe, worsening abdominal pain — finding it hard to talk through it. She and her husband have been trying to conceive for two years . Irregular periods, none for a few months. On careful pelvic examination, a tender adnexal mass . β-hCG positive but lower than expected for the predicted gestational age. Ultrasound: right tubal mass with a thin wall, empty uterus . The Triad Pain · amenorrhea · adnexal mass. In a reproductive-age woman, that combination is ectopic gestation until proven otherwise . Definition Implantation of products of conception at a site other than the endometrium Frequency 1–2% of all gestations Sites Fallopian tube — most common, 90% · ovary · cervix · abdomen Risk factors Pelvic inflammatory disease — the commonest cause · intrapelvic adhesions (previous appendicitis or pelvic surgery) · endometriosis · IUD in place · previous ectopic pregnancy Clinical The triad, plus shock from rupture and haemorrhage in some. hCG levels are normal, declining or are negative The chain from untreated chlamydia through PID to tubal damage is on 4.6 . What the specimen shows Gross Microscopic Enlarged and dilated fallopian tube. Cut surface shows haemorrhagic contents — haematosalpinx . The wall may be thinned or ruptured , and products of conception (fetus, granular placental tissue) may be visible Products of conception at an ectopic site: chorionic villi, trophoblasts (implantation site) and fetal parts Chorionic villi and implantation site — inside a fallopian tube. This is the diagnosis: products of conception in the wrong place . The same tissue that would prove an intrauterine gestation, found in the tube, proves an ectopic one. Image courtesy of Dr. Michele Weir, via the module. What Her Endometrium Looks Like — a Module Knowledge Check The module asks which of three endometrial appearances Fatima would have: decidualised endometrium , stromal plasma cells (endometritis) , or proliferative endometrium . Decidualised endometrium. Her body is pregnant and the endometrium has responded to progesterone, even though the pregnancy itself is in the tube. That is precisely why decidua without products of conception is a red flag rather than a reassurance.

The Three Types Gestational trophoblastic disease is abnormal trophoblast proliferation. Benign — hydatidiform mole Malignant Complete mole (commonest) · Partial mole Choriocarcinoma The genetics is the whole distinction. Complete mole: an empty ovum fertilised by one sperm that duplicates (90%) or by two sperm (10%) — diploid, entirely paternal , so no fetal tissue . Partial mole: a normal ovum fertilised by two sperm (or one that duplicates) — triploid, two paternal sets plus one maternal , so fetal tissue can be present . Everything in the comparison table below follows from that one difference.

Complete vs Partial Mole The table the objectives ask for , reproduced from Dr. Goebel's notes. The key rows are transcribed below for searching. Complete mole Partial mole Epidemiology 1/1000 pregnancies in USA · 1/500 in Asia — Clinical presentation Vaginal bleeding · uterus large for dates · hyperemesis · hypertension / pre-eclampsia · hyperthyroidism Vaginal bleeding · uterus small for dates · the associated symptoms of complete mole are rare Serum hCG Markedly elevated Low to normal Ultrasound "Snowstorm" pattern, no fetus formation Focal cystic change with fetus formation Gross Abundant swollen, large hydropic villi · no fetal tissue Lower volume of tissue · hydropic change involving only some villi · gestational sac or fetal tissue may be present Microscopic Diffuse hydropic change of most villi · trophoblastic proliferation Two villous populations — hydropic and small normal or fibrotic · less trophoblastic proliferation · irregularly shaped villi with stromal inclusions Genetics Diploid 46,XX or 46,XY — paternal chromosomes only Triploid 69,XXX or 69,XXY — two paternal and one maternal set Pathogenesis Fertilisation of an empty ovum by 1 sperm which duplicates (90%) or 2 sperm (10%) Fertilisation of an ovum by 2 sperm (diandric) most commonly, or by 1 sperm which duplicates Diagnosis Identified earlier (8–12 weeks) thanks to routine ultrasound. Definitive on examination of products of conception Often under-recognised clinically. Definitive on products of conception examined by a pathologist Outcome 80% cured by complete curettage · 15% invade the uterine wall or persist · 2–3% become choriocarcinoma Most cured by curettage · 5–10% invade or persist · rarely progresses to choriocarcinoma Both are followed with serial hCG until it declines to baseline . And a standing instruction from the notes: always send all tissue sampled or passed to pathology for histologic examination. Discrepancy in the source: the interactive module gives the partial-mole karyotype as "69 XXY or XXY", a duplication typo; the notes PDF gives 69,XXX or 69,XXY , which is used here. Why the Complete Mole Is the Sick One Every distinguishing feature traces back to how much trophoblast there is . A complete mole is all abnormal trophoblast and no fetus , so it proliferates unchecked — giving markedly elevated hCG , a uterus large for dates , and the systemic consequences of an enormous hCG load: hyperemesis , early pre-eclampsia , and hyperthyroidism (hCG is structurally similar

entries.t: Case — and What the Tissue Shows
entries.x: Case — and What the Tissue Shows Kim, 21, university student Vomiting for a week , vaginal bleeding for two days . Sexually active, no birth control . Cycles usually regular 5/28, but last menstrual period 9 weeks ago . β-hCG markedly elevated. Pelvic ultrasound shows a snowstorm pattern. Question Answer Most likely diagnosis Complete hydatidiform mole Next step in management Dilation and curettage (see 5.4 ) Recommendations Serial serum β-hCG until it reaches baseline · effective contraception (e.g. the oral contraceptive pill) · she should not try to conceive for at least a year , because of the risk of choriocarcinoma "Grape-like." All of the tissue is abnormal — swollen, large hydropic chorionic villi , and no fetal tissue at all . Image courtesy of Dr. Michele Weir, via the module. Two features, both required. Diffuse villous oedema in most villi, and abundant trophoblastic proliferation — the hallmark of a complete mole. No fetal tissue present. Why a Year, and Why Contraception Specifically The follow-up is the serial hCG — a rising or plateauing level after evacuation is how persistent disease or choriocarcinoma is detected. A new pregnancy would raise hCG too, and make that signal uninterpretable. So effective contraception is not incidental advice; it is what protects the surveillance test.

Gestational Choriocarcinoma A malignant trophoblastic tumour arising from any gestational event. Clinical Abnormal vaginal bleeding · persistent, markedly elevated hCG Prior gestation Hydatidiform mole 50% (more commonly complete ) · spontaneous abortion 25% · normal pregnancy 25% Timing Most follow a recent gestation, but it may occur after a long latency of years Gross Red haemorrhagic mass in the uterus , varying from tiny to large. Metastases are haemorrhagic ; most common site is lung Microscopic No villi · malignant trophoblast · haemorrhage and necrosis Diagnosis Often presumptive on clinical findings ; confirmed by identification of malignant trophoblast in a pathology sample Outcome >90% have lung metastases at diagnosis. Less frequently brain and liver. 80% five-year survival with chemotherapy overall. Death is related to liver or brain metastases and their haemorrhagic complications "No Villi" Is the Diagnostic Line A mole is abnormal villi . A choriocarcinoma has no villi at all — just malignant trophoblast, haemorrhage and necrosis. That single absence separates benign gestational trophoblastic disease from the malignant one down the microscope. And note the prognosis paradox worth remembering: over 90% already have lung metastases when diagnosed, yet 80% survive five years. Choriocarcinoma is exquisitely chemosensitive — widespread metastatic disease that is nonetheless usually curable, which is unusual enough in oncology to be examinable.

Summary Several causes of abnormal bleeding exist in reproductive-age women; pregnancy-related complications must be ruled out first . The commonest cause of first-trimester bleeding is spontaneous abortion Spontaneous abortion is categorised by bleeding, cervical os and passage of products ; causes are unknown, fetal or maternal You must see products of conception to prove intrauterine gestation Ectopic gestation is implantation outside the endometrium; most common site is the fallopian tube ; PID is the commonest risk factor ; the triad is pain, amenorrhea, adnexal mass GTD is abnormal trophoblast proliferation: hydatidiform mole (partial and complete) and choriocarcinoma Hydatidiform moles are a risk factor for choriocarcinoma Choriocarcinoma is haemorrhagic and most commonly metastasises to the lungs

entries.p: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
entries.x: Learning Objectives Describe how to diagnose pregnancy and set an estimated date of birth (EDB). Define GTPAL. List symptoms of pregnancy in the first 12 weeks. Describe the size and growth of the uterus over the first 12 weeks. List the tests required for a continuing pregnancy. Dr. Jordan Schmidt, 30 minutes in three recorded parts (14 + 5 + 11 min). The thread through all three: establish the pregnancy, the due date and the baseline early, because every later decision in the pregnancy is measured against them.

entries.p: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
entries.x: Diagnosing Pregnancy Situation How pregnancy usually announces itself Regular cycles, trying to conceive Missed menses (amenorrhea) — typically the first sign. Classic early symptoms: nausea/vomiting, urinary frequency, breast tenderness, and later in the trimester abdominal distension and bloating Irregular cycles, or not trying Symptoms matter more , because months without a period may be normal for her. Some present only once they feel fetal movement Altered bleeding Irregular spotting or a lighter-than-usual “period” can be early implantation bleeding — especially at the extremes of age and in women on the pill. Heavier early-pregnancy bleeding is easily mistaken for menses and delays the diagnosis Confirming it Urine hCG (over the counter, often done before she sees anyone) → serum hCG when you need certainty → ultrasound for a viable intrauterine pregnancy. Maternal, then external, perception of fetal activity also confirms it — sometimes months in. Serum β-hCG (IU/L) What it means < 5 Negative 5–25 Grey zone — a very early pregnancy, or within the lab's error > 25 Typically diagnostic of pregnancy ~1500 An intrauterine gestation is usually visible on transvaginal ultrasound ~5000 Usually visible on transabdominal ultrasound — lower in a very thin woman, higher with a high BMI What “confirmed intrauterine pregnancy” looks like. The gestational sac (blue) is the fluid space that lets the pregnancy grow without being compressed by the myometrium. The yolk sac (green) feeds the embryo until the placenta takes over. The embryo (yellow) is the developing fetus. A sac alone is not enough — you need at least a yolk sac to call it pregnancy tissue, which matters whenever an ectopic is on the table. Where This Picks Up Thursday's Lecture Dr. Schmidt gives the classic 1500 threshold. The first-trimester ultrasound lecture argues the discriminatory zone should be raised to 2000–3000 , because a normal pregnancy is sometimes not yet visible at 1500 — see 5.10 . Treat 1500 as “usually visible”, not “must be visible”.

entries.p: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
entries.x: Dating the Pregnancy Set the due date as early as possible . It is what every later decision hangs on — above all counselling at the peri-viable 23–24 weeks and managing post-dates at 41–42 weeks . Human gestation is ~280 days = 40 completed weeks from the last normal menstrual period (LNMP). Method How Rank IVF embryo transfer date Conception time is known exactly Overrides everything , including later ultrasound First-trimester ultrasound Crown–rump length (CRL) up to 14 weeks. If several early scans, use the first with CRL ≥ 10 mm (~7 weeks) The standard for everyone else — any ultrasound before 23 weeks is used instead of the LNMP (SOGC Guideline #303, 2014) Second-trimester ultrasound After 14 weeks CRL is unreliable (flexion and orientation vary), so use a composite: head circumference, biparietal diameter, abdominal circumference, femur length Used if no earlier scan Naegele's rule LNMP + 7 days − 3 months + 1 year . In practice a pregnancy wheel or online/app calculator A rough estimate only Naegele's worked example: LNMP 10 January 2026 → +7 days = 17 January → −3 months = 17 October → +1 year = EDB 17 October 2026 (exactly 280 days). CRL at two ages. Left: at ~7 weeks the embryo is an amorphous “peanut”. The slide's caption reads “10.8 cm”; it means 10.8 mm , which is right for 7 weeks 3 days. Right: by 9–12 weeks the head and rump are distinct, so the measurement is more precise. This scan reads CRL 6.51 cm = 12 weeks 6 days . If it were her first scan, 12+6 would become her dating. Why the Guideline Stopped “Keeping the LMP If It Fits” The old habit was to keep the LNMP date if it fell within the first scan's range of error. SOGC #303 looked at the dating evidence and found the early ultrasound is simply the most accurate estimate — even when it differs by only a day or two . So the first-trimester scan sets the date. After that the EDB is fixed . A later scan measuring “ahead” or “behind” means the fetus is larger or smaller than expected — a growth question, not a new due date. The one caveat he gives: every test has error, including a mis-transcribed report, so if a scan clearly contradicts everything else, clinical judgement can set it aside.

entries.p: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
entries.x: GTPAL Letter Counts Watch for G — Gravida Total pregnancies , including the current one — T — Term Pregnancies delivered at ≥ 37 weeks Twins at term = one T P — Preterm Pregnancies delivered at 20 to 36+6 weeks A stillbirth still counts here or in T A — Abortions Pregnancies ending before 20 weeks — spontaneous miscarriage, induced abortion, ectopic (medical or surgical) Any loss < 20 weeks, whatever the cause L — Living Currently living children she gave birth to Counts children, not pregnancies. Adopted children don't count P — Para (in the G/P shorthand) Pregnancies delivered at > 20 weeks Hides term vs preterm, multiples, stillbirths and neonatal deaths The lecture's three examples (all currently pregnant) GTPAL G/P 38-week live birth, 32-week stillbirth G3 T1 P1 A0 L1 G3 P2 10-week miscarriage, 36-week liveborn twins , 41-week singleton G4 T1 P1 A1 L3 G4 P2 Three deliveries at 39–40 weeks, one neonatal death at 10 days G4 T3 P0 A0 L2 G4 P3 G/P is quick and favoured in family medicine and uncomplicated histories (“G7 P6”); GTPAL is preferred because it shows the preterm births and losses that make a pregnancy higher-risk.

entries.t: The First 12 Weeks: Symptoms and Uterine Growth
entries.p: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
entries.x: The First 12 Weeks: Symptoms and Uterine Growth Symptoms are variable — some women have none, others blame them on something they ate — so they help but never confirm a pregnancy on their own. First trimester Why Later trimesters (if found late) Amenorrhea or irregular spotting hCG keeps the corpus luteum going, so the hormone drop that triggers menses never comes Amenorrhea finally noticed — especially with prior irregular cycles Nausea/vomiting , food aversions Rapidly rising hCG Nausea/vomiting Frequent urination Rising blood volume and GFR, pressure from the uterus, smooth-muscle relaxation Worse frequency, even incontinence Breast tenderness · fatigue · mood swings Hormonal stimulation; metabolic demand Abdominal bloating · fetal movements · heartburn It is urinary frequency , not urinary retention , that goes with early pregnancy — the module's own check turns on that word. Weeks Uterus Where the fundus is Non-pregnant About her closed fist Entirely in the pelvis 12 A small grapefruit At the pelvic brim / pubic symphysis 14–20 A small/medium cantaloupe; now an abdominal organ Rising, with lower abdominal distension 20 — At the umbilicus. From here, SFH in cm ≈ gestational age in weeks 20–26 Fundus tips forward towards the abdominal wall Organ displacement increases 28 to term A watermelon by term Upper abdomen: rectus diastasis possible; diaphragm pushed up, so breathlessness is common — though oxygenation itself is unchanged

entries.p: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
entries.x: First-Trimester Investigations A confirmatory hCG isn't always needed, but is useful with irregular cycles or a history of recurrent miscarriage or ectopic. Once the pregnancy is confirmed, order the baseline: Recommended for every pregnancy Why CBC Hemoglobin, MCV (a low MCV prompts hemoglobinopathy screening) and platelets Group & screen Blood type, Rh status , and any red-cell antibodies (see 5.14 ) Rubella Immunity. If non-immune, vaccinate postpartum — it is a live vaccine Hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis (VDRL) Treatments exist that reduce harm to her and the baby Gonorrhea / chlamydia Vaginal swab or urine Urine culture Asymptomatic bacteriuria — smooth-muscle relaxation means poorer bladder emptying and more infection For selected women When TSH Known hypo- or hyperthyroidism — the dose often needs adjusting Hepatitis C, HSV, other STIs High-risk population or known exposure. HSV is not routine : antibodies alone don't predict transmission; test for an active genital lesion near delivery Hemoglobinopathy screen Mediterranean, Southeast Asian or African ancestry (sickle cell), or a low MCV/Hb NIPT or CVS A known carrier of a testable condition (balanced translocation, muscular dystrophy…) eFTS — Offered to Everyone, at 11–14 Weeks The enhanced first trimester screen combines a nuchal translucency ultrasound with four serum analytes , adjusted for maternal age, ethnicity and gestation, to estimate the risk of trisomy 21 and other chromosomal problems. It is offered regardless of age or risk factors , because any pregnancy can be affected. Declining it still leaves later options. The screening menu in full is in 4.16 . Why the Thyroid Dose Changes The lecture's reasoning is that hCG resembles TSH (the audio says “thyroid hormone”, but the structural match is with TSH). hCG weakly stimulates the thyroid, so TSH can dip in the first trimester, and levothyroxine requirements usually rise 25–50% in pregnancy. That is why a woman with known thyroid disease gets a TSH early.

Learning Objectives Identify the timing of visibility and diagnosis of a normal pregnancy on ultrasound. Assist in assigning gestational age based on ultrasound. Describe a normal curve of β-hCG levels for a single intrauterine pregnancy. Describe the discriminatory zone as it relates to pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) and ectopic pregnancy. Describe the rate of decline of β-hCG in failing pregnancies. Dr. Angelos Vilos, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology — Assistant Professor, Fellowship Program Director in Reproductive Endocrinology and Infertility, and Medical Director of the Early Pregnancy Assessment Unit . Two recorded parts (9 and 13 min).

entries.t: When to Scan, and Why Not to Trust Dates
entries.x: When to Scan, and Why Not to Trust Dates Indications for first-trimester ultrasound To date a pregnancy — ideally between 7 and 12 weeks Threatened abortion — to document fetal viability Incomplete abortion — to identify retained products of conception Suspected multiple gestation — to determine chorionicity and amnionicity reliably Work-up for suspected ectopic, molar pregnancy or pelvic mass , including clinical signs of bleeding or pain Prior to pregnancy termination Quality criteria: transvaginal assessment of uterus and adnexa; may include transabdominal evaluation for free fluid or a mass high in the pelvis; performed by providers meeting minimum training and certification standards , with adequate equipment and oversight. Why the LMP Is Weaker Than It Looks Dating from the last menstrual period assumes all of the following : a regular 28-day cycle , ovulation at the midpoint , fertilisation on the middle day , correct recall of the LMP, and being off oral contraceptives for several months beforehand. Even when recall is perfect, ovulation, fertilisation and implantation cannot be certain without assisted reproduction. Why: waves of follicular development occur in normal cycles, sperm survive 5–7 days in the reproductive tract, and the ovulation-to-implantation interval can vary by as much as 11 days . The payoff is concrete: first- and second-trimester ultrasound dating has reduced inductions for post-term pregnancy .

entries.t: Gestational Sac and Mean Sac Diameter
entries.x: Gestational Sac and Mean Sac Diameter When present During the first 3–5 menstrual weeks What it is The chorionic cavity ; its echogenic rim is implanting chorionic villi and associated decidual tissue Smallest visible 2–3 mm on a high-frequency transvaginal transducer — about 32–33 days Growth Approximately 1 mm per day How to measure Mean of three orthogonal "inner to inner" diameters. Place the cursor on the sac, not the surrounding echogenic region Accuracy ±4–11 days. Rough rule: GA ≈ 30 days + MSD in mm When it stops being reliable >14 mm , or once an embryo can be identified . It also has greater inter-observer variability than CRL

Yolk Sac, Then Crown–Rump Length The yolk sac is the confirmation step. First structure inside the gestational sac, and proof of an intrauterine pregnancy . Can be seen when MSD reaches 5–6 mm (~5 weeks); should be seen when MSD reaches 8 mm (~5+5 weeks). Peaks at 6 mm by 10 weeks , then disappears. Not used for dating. How to measure it, and how it goes wrong. The longest straight line from the outer margin of the cephalic end to the rump, neck neutral . The reference chart grades planes from good down to unacceptable — the failures are an oblique section, poorly placed callipers, and a head that is bent or extended rather than neutral. The handover rule. Once an embryo is clearly seen, CRL is the most accurate estimate of gestational age — accurate to 3–8 days — and the mean sac diameter should no longer be used . Smallest margin of error between 7 and 60 mm. Best above 10 mm (~7 weeks) — and when several scans exist, use the earliest one with a CRL over 10 mm . Earlier is more accurate, because biological variation in size accumulates with gestation. Structure When it appears Size Gestational sac ~32 days 2–3 mm Yolk sac 5 to 5+5 weeks MSD 5–6 mm (can) → 8 mm (should) Crown–rump length 5+5 weeks 1–2 mm Fetal heart rate 6+0 weeks CRL ~3 mm Transvaginal vs Transabdominal — the Answer Has Changed Original studies found transvaginal superior for estimating gestational age. More recent studies find transabdominal non-inferior , provided a CRL is used and it is measured after 6 weeks . The explanation is simply better transabdominal technology today . And at the far end of the first trimester: CRL and biparietal diameter have equivalent accuracy between 12 and 14 weeks . CRL stays reliable to 84 mm (14 weeks) , after which BPD takes over .

What β-hCG Is and Does Secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast. Turns positive as implantation begins — 21–22 days post LMP, or 8 days post ovulation . The table is worth a glance for scale: from 5–50 mIU/mL at 3 weeks to a peak in the hundreds of thousands by 9–12 weeks. Four jobs, and the shape of the curve. Maintains the corpus luteum and its progesterone (which enables implantation), builds placenta and umbilical cord , suppresses myometrial contractions , and promotes fetal organ growth and angiogenesis . Note the enormous spread between the high and low curves at any given week — that spread is the reason a single value means so little.

How Fast Should It Rise? Teaching Study What it actually showed Historical — Doubling every 2 days. Deviation was taken to mean an abnormally developing fetus, threatened miscarriage or ectopic 1990 Cohort, n = 20 Viable IUP needed a rise of at least 66% in 2 days — the lower limit of the 85% CI , meaning 8% of viable pregnancies rose even slower 2004 Cohort, n = 287 The rise can be as low as 53% over 2 days and still be viable — the 99% CI . Fewer than 1% are slower , and it can go as low as 35% over 2 days Four things shift the level: maternal age, BMI, smoking and fetal sex — and all four are also associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes . Total hCG is directly proportional to placental weight at birth , which is the mechanistic thread tying those together. When a "Normal" Rise Is Not Normal Two studies make the point that a reassuring rise does not exclude an ectopic : 340 women presenting with pain or bleeding under 12 weeks and an inconclusive scan (PUL). 63 had a rise ≥66% over 2 days — i.e. "normal". Ten of those 63 (16%) turned out to have an ectopic. 200 women with diagnosed ectopic pregnancies. 60% had rising hCG at diagnosis , and 21% were rising above 53% over 2 days — a "normal" rate, in a known ectopic.

The Discriminatory Zone — Raised Pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) is a positive hCG without ultrasound evidence of a pregnancy. It is increasingly common because pregnancies are diagnosed much earlier than they once were — and because the hCG levels of early viable IUP, non-viable IUP and ectopic overlap considerably . This Contradicts the Number on 4.9 — Deliberately 4.9 teaches the discriminatory zone as 1500 transvaginal , from Dr. Sovran's handout and Dr. Kirby's session. Dr. Vilos's position is that this threshold should be raised. The original levels of 1000–2000 mIU did not account for slow-rising or low-normal hCG in viable intrauterine pregnancies , and so produced inappropriate diagnoses of pregnancy failure or ectopic pregnancy . Using 2000–3000 mIU instead keeps slower-growing normal pregnancies in the differential. The stated goal: fewer wrong diagnoses, and less unnecessary misoprostol, methotrexate, D&C and laparoscopy. Both numbers are examinable depending on who is asking. 1500 is the classic teaching; 2000–3000 is this lecture's correction. Know that the disagreement exists and why. Read the ratios, not just the multiples. Even at hCG ≥2000 with an empty uterus, the single most likely diagnosis is still a non-viable intrauterine pregnancy — twice as likely as ectopic. At 2000–3000 the chance of a viable IUP is 2% ; above 3000 it is 0.5% . Stable patient, hCG 2000–3000, no clear evidence of ectopic → repeat hCG ± ultrasound in a few days. Why: 1 It is more likely a non-viable IUP than an ectopic — roughly 2× 2 There is a 0.5–2% chance it is a viable IUP 3 If hCG continues past ~3000–3500 with no IUP , ectopic becomes more likely 4 If hCG falls 15–50% over 24 hours , it was likely a non-viable IUP 5 Risk of rupture across all PUL under close surveillance is as low as 0.03% , and in diagnosed ectopic as low as 1.7% hCG Does Not Predict Rupture There is no level at which you can say a tube is about to rupture, and no level at which you can say it will not. That is why the management question is about haemodynamic stability and symptoms , not about a number — and it is consistent with the Week 4 case where a falling hCG ended in rupture anyway ( 4.9 ).

entries.t: The Rate of Decline in Failing Pregnancies
entries.x: The Rate of Decline in Failing Pregnancies From 710 patients with non-viable intrauterine pregnancies managed without medical or surgical intervention. The decline is quadratic and depends on the absolute level — the higher the starting hCG, the faster it must fall. Starting hCG Minimum expected decline over 48 hours ≥ 5000 mIU/mL 35% 500 mIU/mL 24% 50 mIU/mL 12% A Falling hCG Does Not Mean It Was Not an Ectopic In a study of 200 diagnosed, untreated ectopic pregnancies with falling hCG , the decline matched the pattern of a spontaneous abortion in 8% of cases . So the rate of decline does not fully differentiate a resolving ectopic from a failing intrauterine pregnancy. Two consequences. A pregnancy is only considered resolved once hCG falls below 5 IU/L. And if the decline does not follow the predictable curve , re-evaluate for incomplete abortion or a non-resolving ectopic. Despite declining levels, a resolving ectopic may still rupture. Note the definitional point: a declining hCG without ultrasound evidence of an intrauterine pregnancy is a non-viable pregnancy by definition. The rate of decline in spontaneous abortion is 12–32% over 2 days , depending on the absolute value.

Conclusions All women should be offered a first-trimester dating ultrasound, ideally 7–12 weeks Done correctly it is more reliable than LMP and reduces inductions for post-dates Gestational sac by 32 days ; MSD usable to 14 mm or until a CRL is available; accuracy 4–11 days Yolk sac 5 to 5+5 weeks · CRL by 5+5 weeks · fetal heart by 6+0 weeks Once a CRL is detected it replaces MSD ; most reliable at ≥10 mm or 7 weeks ; accuracy 3–8 days CRL and BPD are equally accurate between 12 and 14 weeks hCG begins to rise 21 days post LMP or 8 days post ovulation Normal rise is ≥53% over 2 days (99% CI), or a doubling time of 1.4–2.1 days Non-viable IUP and ectopic can rise at the same rate as a viable IUP The discriminatory range should be raised from 1500 to 2000–3000 for stable PUL patients Decline in spontaneous abortion is 12–32% over 2 days depending on the absolute value

The Forty-Week Map | Week 5 | Female Reproductive | POM2 ← Week 5 POM2 · Weeks 4–5 · Pregnancy The Forty-Week Map What the fetus is doing, and every test, vaccine and check you order along the way, on one ruler. Weeks are counted the obstetric way, from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP). 280 days LMP → due date 5–10 weeks of peak teratogen risk 23–24 weeks: the peri-viable line The fetus Screening & diagnosis Bloodwork & swabs Vaccines & prevention Watching the mother A single moment Only if indicated Tap any bar or diamond for the details. On a phone, swipe the chart sideways. First trimester 12 +0 wk Drag to any week Happening at 12 weeks Built from the POM2 lectures: 4.16 Genetic Screening, 5.9 Teratogenesis, 5.10 First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound, 5.11 Pathology of First Trimester Bleeding, 5.12 Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester, 5.14 Topics of Antenatal Care, 5.15 Second Trimester Ultrasound and 5.16 Hypertension in Pregnancy, plus the course's own quiz questions for GBS, gestational diabetes and fetal movement. Teratology counts weeks from fertilization, two weeks behind the obstetric count, so the embryonic weeks 3–8 appear here as weeks 5–10. The anatomy scan window is 18–22 weeks in 5.15 and 18–20 in 4.16.

Learning Objectives The module gives no formal objectives; the lecture covers: Defining hypertension and classifying the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP). Their maternal, fetal and placental complications. How pregnancy changes blood pressure, and how hypertension changes pregnancy. Management — antihypertensives, magnesium sulphate, and the drugs to avoid. Dr. Jordan Schmidt, 26 minutes, one recorded lecture. Worldwide, HDP remain one of the leading causes of maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality .

Defining Hypertension Systolic Diastolic How Hypertension ≥ 140 ≥ 90 Two readings ≥ 15 minutes apart , seated and calm, cuff on the arm at heart level Severe hypertension ≥ 160 ≥ 110 With a very high BP, especially if she has symptoms, don't wait the 15 minutes to start treating. ≥ or >, and What “Preeclampsia” Requires Now The slides write “>140 / >90”. The international definition is ≥ 140 and/or ≥ 90 , so a reading of exactly 140/90 counts. The lecture teaches preeclampsia as hypertension + proteinuria , the classic definition. Current guidance (ISSHP 2021) is broader: new hypertension at ≥ 20 weeks with proteinuria, or other maternal organ dysfunction (neurological, pulmonary edema, low platelets or hemolysis, AKI, raised transaminases), or uteroplacental dysfunction (abruption, fetal growth restriction, abnormal Doppler, fetal death). Proteinuria is no longer mandatory. That lines up with the lecture's own “adverse conditions” list below.

The Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Classifying hypertension in pregnancy. Drawn for these notes — the lecture gives these as definitions in prose. “Adverse condition” follows the lecture's organ-system list below; eclampsia can, rarely, arrive with little preceding preeclampsia, more often with chronic hypertension or kidney disease. Category What defines it Why it matters Chronic (pre-existing) Before pregnancy or diagnosed before 20 weeks High BP while the placenta implants means more placental dysfunction . The earlier the onset, the higher the risk of preeclampsia ; diabetes or kidney disease raise it further Gestational After 20 weeks , normal BPs documented before, no adverse conditions An isolated BP problem, classically at 35–38 weeks. Onset nearer 20 weeks behaves more like chronic hypertension Preeclampsia Hypertension + proteinuria (± adverse conditions) Classically late in gestation, more common in first pregnancies — but any pregnancy, any parity Eclampsia Seizures , usually from poorly controlled preeclampsia Prodrome: new or worsening proteinuria, headache, neurological irritability (clonus, photosensitivity) HELLP Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets An atypical form — hypertension is not required

entries.t: Why 20 Weeks — BP Across a Normal Pregnancy
entries.x: Why 20 Weeks — BP Across a Normal Pregnancy The Dip That Makes the Rule Pregnancy drops systemic vascular resistance and expands vascular capacity to hold the rising blood volume. Resistance falls faster than plasma and red-cell volume can fill it, so BP falls from about 8–12 weeks and comes back to pre-pregnancy levels around 20–24 weeks (by 28 at the latest). So a high BP before 20 weeks is appearing despite the normal dip. It was almost certainly there before she was pregnant, and is filed as chronic . (The module's knowledge check: gestational hypertension is the one diagnosed at 30 weeks .) In preeclampsia the normal relaxation fails : the vessels don't dilate, and there is an exaggerated vasoconstrictor response to vasoactive substances in end organs. The trigger is unknown but clearly comes from the placenta , since delivering the placenta is the only cure . After delivery a transient postpartum worsening can occur, presumably as the last of the placental factor is released, which is why magnesium runs on after birth. Severe BP or preeclampsia unusually early? Think of Link Molar pregnancy Extremely high hCG and abnormal placentation → early-onset preeclampsia . The mole genetics are in 5.11 Thyroid storm Can be precipitated by very high hCG Theca lutein cysts From fertility treatment or any ovarian hyperstimulation The module's risk-factor check: molar pregnancy predisposes to preeclampsia. Smoking slightly lowers the risk of preeclampsia, while raising growth restriction and placental insufficiency. Hypothyroidism doesn't affect BP; hyperthyroidism can.

Complications Complications are maternal, fetal or placental (they overlap). How likely they are depends on pre-existing vs pregnancy-related disease, severity and comorbidities , and they are usually what decides when to deliver . The primary maternal worry is stroke : bring severe BP below 160/110 urgently , and investigate any neurological symptom for an intracranial event. System Adverse conditions — watch closely Severe complications — usually means deliver CNS Headache, visual disturbance Eclampsia · PRES Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome: acute, usually reversible brain edema, mostly in the posterior (parieto-occipital) regions, driven by severe hypertension and endothelial dysfunction. · TIA/stroke · GCS < 13 · retinal detachment, cortical blindness Cardiorespiratory Chest pain, dyspnea, O 2 sat < 97% Uncontrolled severe HTN · MI · sat < 90% · pulmonary edema · inotropic support Hematologic ↑ WBC, ↑ INR/PTT, ↓ platelets Platelets < 50 · transfusion needed Renal ↑ creatinine, ↑ uric acid Acute kidney injury · dialysis Hepatic Nausea/vomiting, RUQ pain , ↑ LFTs, low albumin Hepatic dysfunction ( INR > 2 ) · hepatic hematoma or rupture Feto-placental IUGR · oligohydramnios · absent/reversed end-diastolic flow Abruption with compromise · reversed ductus venosus flow · fetal death

Management Treatment depends on the category, severity, gestational age, comorbidities, and fetal and maternal status . The key idea: in chronic or gestational hypertension, the BP is the disease , so control it to protect the placenta and prevent progression. In preeclampsia, eclampsia and HELLP, the BP is a symptom . Treating it reduces maternal and fetal harm, but it doesn't treat the disease. Only delivery does. Setting Drug Dose (as given in the lecture) Oral — mild, stable Labetalol 100–400 mg PO bid–tid, max 1200 mg/day Nifedipine XL 20–60 mg PO od–bid, “max 60 mg/day” — see the note Methyldopa 250–500 mg PO bid–qid, max 2 g/day Severe Labetalol IV 20 mg IV, then 20–80 mg q30 min to max 300 mg (or 1–2 mg/min infusion), then oral Nifedipine (short-acting) 5–10 mg q30 min Hydralazine IV 5 mg IV, then 5–10 mg q30 min (or 0.5–10 mg/h infusion), max 20 mg Seizure prophylaxis Magnesium sulphate 4 g IV over 20 min , then 1–2 g/h until delivery and typically 12–48 h postpartum . It raises the seizure threshold; start it once the decision to deliver is made in severe preeclampsia Note on nifedipine XL: the slide's range (up to 60 mg twice daily) and its stated 60 mg/day maximum contradict each other. Check a current drug reference or the SOGC guideline for the ceiling before relying on either number. Avoid Why ACE inhibitors / ARBs Directly toxic to fetal kidneys , mainly in the second and third trimesters → oligohydramnios and fetal renal failure . There is growing evidence of first-trimester teratogenicity too. Switch before conception if possible (common in diabetic women, for kidney protection); otherwise switch urgently Diuretics Not unsafe, but ineffective : they cut intravascular volume while pregnancy physiology is expanding it A Correction to the Module's Own Feedback The knowledge-check answer calls methyldopa both an “alpha blocker” and a “diuretic”. It is neither. Methyldopa is a centrally acting α 2 -agonist. Hydrochlorothiazide is the diuretic in that question, and labetalol is the combined α/β-blocker. The answer itself is right: the drug that is contraindicated in pregnancy is the ACE inhibitor .

Learning Objectives Define the different methods of hysterectomy. Dr. Stephanie Black, generalist Ob/Gyn, LHSC — a 10-minute module sitting under the larger objective of developing a clinical approach to the post-menopausal woman presenting with bleeding ( 5.1 ).

The Vocabulary First Term What is removed Total hysterectomy Uterus and cervix Subtotal hysterectomy Uterus only — the cervix is retained + Salpingectomy … and the fallopian tubes + Salpingo-oophorectomy … and the fallopian tubes and ovaries "Partial hysterectomy" (lay term) Not a surgical term. Usually means removal of the uterus ± cervix ± tubes, with the ovaries retained The Conversation This Vocabulary Is Really About A hysterectomy alone does not cause surgical menopause. Only removing the ovaries does. So when a patient says she wants a "partial hysterectomy", what she is almost always asking is: can I keep my ovaries? Answering the question she asked, rather than correcting her terminology, is the point — and the consequences of getting it wrong for a woman under 40 are laid out in 5.3 under iatrogenic POI. When a hysterectomy is being considered for bleeding control, medical options should be tried first ; hysterectomy is reserved for failed medical management and special circumstances. The medical ladder is in 4.10 .

The Five Approaches The ideal hysterectomy is done in a minimally invasive fashion. Four of the five approaches below qualify; one does not. Approach Minimally invasive? Limitations What it adds Vaginal The gold standard Yes — no abdominal incisions at all. Short stay, same-day discharge Prior pelvic surgery / extensive scarring · large uterus (hard to manoeuvre out through the vagina) · narrow introitus or pelvis · tubes and ovaries not readily accessible from below · poor uterine descent or mobility , often in women who are nulliparous or have never been sexually active — LAVH Laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy Yes. Requires abdominal entry with laparoscopic instruments; part of the work is done vaginally. Same-day discharge possible Same as vaginal — very large uterus, poor uterine descent, narrow introitus or pelvis , because you still have to work within the vagina Assess the pelvis for scarring · create a bladder flap (dissect bladder off uterus and cervix) · helps with removal of tubes and ovaries · a "second look" for hemostasis through the existing ports once the vagina is closed TLH Total (or subtotal) laparoscopic hysterectomy Yes. Requires abdominal entry. Same-day discharge possible Large uterus · laparoscopic suturing takes skill and more operative time than any vaginal approach Excellent when the vagina or pelvis won't allow work from below , or with poor uterine descent . Allows difficult dissection of a scarred bladder off the cervix, and removal of tubes and ovaries Robotic Yes. Requires abdominal entry. Same-day discharge possible Extremely large uterus · laparoscopic suturing still takes skill and time Articulating instruments that get around corners, so a larger uterus is more manageable than laparoscopically . An excellent option for patients with morbid obesity , who carry increased morbidity from a large incision Abdominal Via laparotomy No. 2–3 day hospital stay Pfannenstiel (side-to-side) or midline vertical incision Reserved for more complex cancers , patient factors that rule out a minimally invasive approach, a very large uterus , or complications during an attempted minimally invasive approach The Hierarchy Is the Answer to the Module's Quiz Dr. Black states the rule twice, once for TLH and once for robotic: these are used in place of an abdominal hysterectomy, and should generally not replace a vaginal hysterectomy or LAVH. So the order is vaginal → LAVH → TLH / robotic → abdominal , and you move down it only when ana
