entries.x: > Week 5 Monday is the other end of the reproductive lifespan: bleeding after menopause and the endometrial pathology behind it, the pelvic mass under the microscope, the clinical management of menopause itself, and the two operations that keep coming up — D&C and hysterectomy. Tuesday is the breast, twice over — the pathology underneath and the three complaints that actually walk into a family practice. Thursday is early pregnancy from four directions — who provides the care, what harms a fetus, what the ultrasound and β-hCG actually show, and what the tissue looks like. Friday turns to antenatal care, hypertension in pregnancy and sexual health. The hormone physiology underneath Monday is in 3.3 and 2.6 ; the bleeding and pain framework it builds on is 4.10 and 4.12 . Monday Sept 28 The other end of the reproductive lifespan — bleeding after menopause, the pelvic mass, menopause itself, and the two operations that keep coming up. 5.1 Post-menopausal Bleeding The 12-month definition, the TVUS-and-biopsy pathway with its 5 mm cutoff, four biopsy reports and what each one means, atrophy, hyperplasia with and without atypia, and endometrial carcinoma from Lynch syndrome to staging → 5.2 Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass Every ovarian cell type and the tumour it makes: epithelial benign to borderline to malignant, the tubal origin of high-grade serous carcinoma, teratomas and germ cell markers, fibroma and granulosa cell tumour, and the metastases that masquerade as a primary → 5.3 Clinical Approach to Menopause Menopause, perimenopause and premature ovarian insufficiency; KNDy neurons and vasomotor symptoms; genitourinary syndrome of menopause and its treatment ladder; menopausal hormone therapy, its window and its contraindications; the non-hormonal options; and a three-part case → 5.4 Dilation & Curettage Vacuum aspiration to 14 weeks, cervical preparation with misoprostol or osmotic dilators, the procedure step by step, and the complications — perforation, hemorrhage, hematometra, retained products and Asherman's syndrome → 5.5 Hysterectomy Approaches Total vs subtotal, what "partial hysterectomy" actually means, and the five approaches ranked — vaginal, LAVH, laparoscopic, robotic and abdominal — with the limitations that push you down the list → Tuesday Sept 29 The breast, twice over — the pathology underneath, then the three complaints that actually walk into a family practice. 5.6 Pathology of the Breast One diagram that maps every lesion to th

Learning Objectives Define menopause and perimenopause. Explain the physiology of perimenopause and menopause. List common symptoms of menopause. Outline specific nutritional and exercise recommendations for women in menopause. Recommend non-hormonal strategies to minimize changes and risks associated with menopause. Explain how to use MHT in menopause. List benefits and risks of MHT that are evidence-based. Dr. Stephanie Moltner, MD FRCSC MSCP. The module is in two halves — physiology, then treatment — and closes with a three-part case you are explicitly asked to answer before revealing anything.

Definitions Term Definition Menopause Amenorrhea for 12 consecutive months. Average age in Canada 51–52 Early menopause Onset between 40 and 45 Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) Onset before 40 Perimenopause "Around menopause" — the transition when symptoms begin. She still has menses , but their frequency changes. Can start many years before the last menstrual period

Vasomotor Symptoms Feature Detail How common 80% of patients. About 20% report 20–30 episodes a day The hot flash itself An unwanted sensation of heat starting in the chest and rising to the face , lasting 3–4 minutes on average Impact Mood, cognition, quality of life. Severe hot flashes are linked to cardiovascular disease and bone health Other menopausal symptoms Sleep disturbance, joint aches, mood change, urogenital and sexual concerns, memory and concentration difficulty, hair and skin changes Where Hot Flashes Come From — Two Theories 1. KNDy neurons. New evidence shows KNDy neurons Hypothalamic neurons co-expressing kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin. They sit next to the thermoregulatory centre and are normally restrained by estrogen; without it they hypertrophy and fire excessively. in the hypothalamus become dysregulated and hyperactivated in the absence of estrogen . 2. Serotonin. A fall in serotonin upregulates the 5-HT 2A receptor, which shifts the thermoregulatory set point . Both theories are worth holding, because both have drugs attached : the KNDy pathway gives you NK3 receptor antagonists , the serotonin pathway gives you SSRIs/SNRIs . See the non-hormonal section below.

Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause GSM is the set of symptoms and signs resulting from estrogen deficiency of the genitourinary tract . It spans three territories, and patients may have any combination: Genital Sexual Urinary Dryness Lack of lubrication Urgency Burning Dyspareunia Dysuria Irritation Decreased libido Recurrent UTI Signs on examination Hypovascularity — paleness of vulva, prepuce, clitoris Reduction in labia majora / minora volume Loss of pubic hair Introital stenosis Fragile / thinning vestibule Vaginal signs: loss of secretions, decreased caliber, loss of elasticity, pale epithelium pH > 5.0 , because the flora has changed Why the pH Rises — and Why That Matters Clinically Estrogen thickens the vaginal epithelium and loads it with glycogen , which lactobacilli The dominant healthy vaginal bacteria. They ferment epithelial glycogen to lactic acid, which keeps the vaginal pH below about 4.5. ferment to lactic acid . No estrogen → no glycogen → no lactobacilli → pH climbs above 5 . That same mechanism explains atrophic vaginitis in 4.5 and the recurrent UTIs above — and it is why the treatment that actually fixes GSM is estrogen , not a moisturizer.

Perimenopause The symptoms are the same as menopause — but menses have not stopped , and that is what makes perimenopause harder to treat. Cycles may become longer or shorter, heavier or lighter before ceasing; the usual sequence is that they shorten, then lengthen, then stop . STRAW+10, the standard staging system for reproductive aging. Read it left to right as a timeline anchored on the final menstrual period . Note the two postmenopause columns: FSH rises (the brain pushes harder) while estrogen stays low (the ovaries have retired). The principal criteria are menstrual — endocrine measures are only supportive , which is why you do not diagnose menopause with a blood test. The Module's Own Knowledge Check Which hormones are decreased in the post-menopausal state? → Estradiol and progesterone. Ovarian function declines, so the ovarian hormones fall; the loss of feedback inhibition then raises FSH and LH . Getting the direction right on all four is the point. The axis itself is in 2.6 .

Premature Ovarian Insufficiency The ASRM work-up. Diagnosis needs FSH over 25 together with irregular periods . Then work through genetic, thyroid and autoimmune screening as the patient's picture directs; if all are negative it is idiopathic POI . ASRM 2024 guideline , via the lecture. Iatrogenic POI is the category students forget: a woman whose ovaries are removed before 40 — for example, risk-reducing surgery for a BRCA1 mutation — has POI, with all the same long-term consequences. Why early menopause matters Evidence from the Nurses' Health Study and a 2016 systematic review for menopause occurring before 45 : Outcome Increase Coronary heart disease events 50% Stroke 23% Cardiovascular mortality 19% All-cause mortality 12% Beyond the numbers: higher risk of cognitive decline , reduced quality of life from hot flashes, vaginal dryness, sexual dysfunction, mood and sleep disturbance, and poorer bone health . The Encouraging Half of That Finding In the long-term Nurses' Health Study analysis, women who started hormone replacement before age 50 had lower all-cause mortality than those who did not. Which reframes the whole conversation: in early menopause, MHT is not a lifestyle choice about hot flashes — it is replacing a hormone she should still have , for the years she should still have had it.

Treating GSM Treatment progresses from lifestyle and simple over-the-counter measures to targeted hormonal therapy , depending on severity and on what the patient wants. Step What and why 1. Lifestyle Vulvar hygiene — avoid irritants and triggers (scented products, douching, depilatory creams). Cut down caffeine , a known bladder irritant. Regular sexual activity , coitus or masturbation, genuinely helps by maintaining blood flow and tissue elasticity 2. Lubricants Reduce friction during intercourse . Water-based products are generally the most helpful 3. Moisturizers Polycarbophil or hyaluronic acid — they bind water and mimic a natural biofilm . Used regularly , not just before sex 4. Pelvic physiotherapy Very effective, especially for dyspareunia 5. Second line Estrogen is the mainstay — estradiol cream, tablet or vaginal ring, all inserted directly into the vagina. DHEA is inserted vaginally and converted to testosterone and estrogen within the mucosa . Ospemifene is an oral SERM Selective estrogen receptor modulator — agonist in some tissues, antagonist in others, depending on receptor isoform and local co-factors. See 4.4. with tissue-selective agonist effect on vaginal epithelium The actual Canadian products. Note the pattern in the dosage column: nearly all vaginal estrogens are loaded daily for about two weeks, then dropped to twice weekly . The ring is the once-every-three-months option. Ospemifene is the only oral agent here — everything else is local.

entries.t: Nutritional and Lifestyle Changes for Vasomotor Symptoms
entries.x: Nutritional and Lifestyle Changes for Vasomotor Symptoms Intervention Evidence Cognitive behavioural therapy and clinical hypnosis Shown to make a real difference Weight loss May help Yoga and exercise Excellent for overall health, but not shown to directly improve hot flashes Cooling techniques, avoiding triggers Useful Nutrition targets Sodium < 1300 mg · vitamin D 800 IU · calcium 1200 mg daily Natural health products Heavily promoted; no clear benefit shown . Possible exception: s-equol products — still not currently recommended

Menopausal Hormone Therapy Gold standard for VMS Estrogen — roughly a 75% reduction in vasomotor symptoms If she has a uterus You must add progesterone. Unopposed estrogen raises the risk of endometrial cancer (see 5.1 ) Estrogen routes Pill , transdermal patch , or gel Progesterone routes Oral tablets , or an IUD — Mirena or Kyleena, approved for 5 years of endometrial protection (Mirena has data supporting up to 8 years for contraception) Combined options Available as a single pill or patch , which makes treatment more convenient When it can be started safely No contraindications , under 60 , and within 10 years of menopause onset — the group with the greatest benefit and least risk Systemic MHT products in Canada. The useful structure is the left column: estrogens (oral, patch, gel) then progestogens (oral, intrauterine) . Notice Mirena and Kyleena appear here as the progestogen of an MHT regimen — the same device you met as a LARC in 4.3 , doing a different job. Combination preparations — one pill or patch instead of two. Two entries are worth naming: TSEC (conjugated estrogens + bazedoxifene ) uses a SERM instead of a progestogen for endometrial protection, and tibolone is a synthetic steroid with estrogenic, progestogenic and androgenic activity. The contraindications — note how short the progestogen column is. Almost everything that blocks MHT blocks the estrogen component. Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding tops both columns, which links straight back to 5.1 : work the bleeding up first . Why MHT Has Fewer Contraindications Than the Pill Students often import the combined-oral-contraceptive rules wholesale and refuse MHT to patients who could safely have it. The reason the lists differ is dose : the estrogen in a COC is 200–300 times more potent than the estrogen in menopausal hormone therapy. Contraceptive doses are designed to suppress an axis ; MHT doses are designed to replace a deficiency . Compare the COC contraindications in 4.3 .

Non-Hormonal Options for Vasomotor Symptoms Class Effect / note Antidepressants (SNRIs, SSRIs) 27–61% reduction. Usually tried first Gabapentinoids 45–71% reduction. Also first-line in practice Clonidine Listed as a reasonable option in the SOGC guideline, but not listed by the current Menopause Society guideline Oxybutynin For urinary incontinence . Adverse effects: dry mouth, GI upset, constipation, blurred vision Neurokinin receptor antagonists Fezolinetant (most recently approved in Canada) and elinzanetant Antidepressants and gabapentinoids tend to be used first, with careful attention to their side-effect profiles. Actual starting doses. Worth noticing that these are lower than the psychiatric doses of the same drugs — you are treating vasomotor symptoms, not depression. Mechanism of the newest drug class. Falling estradiol disinhibits the KNDy neuron , which drives efferent heat-dissipation pathways — the hot flash. NK3 receptor antagonists block neurokinin B at that neuron and calm it down, producing a significant reduction in vasomotor symptoms without giving estrogen. This is why the physiology at the top of the page was worth learning.

Assessing the Menopausal Patient Part of the visit What to cover Background Medical conditions, surgical history, allergies, medications HPI — menstruation Last menstrual period , cycle regularity, heavy or intermenstrual bleeding HPI — symptoms Hot flashes, sleep, mood, GSM , libido If considering MHT Always screen for contraindications — history of blood clots, breast cancer Physical Vulvar exam if she has GSM symptoms , to rule out a skin condition (see 4.11 ) Screening Is cervical screening due? ( 4.8 ) Endometrial biopsy Consider for abnormal bleeding — especially over 40, or heavy/intermenstrual bleeding. Also for anyone on MHT who is still bleeding beyond six months

The Case — Ms. Thomas How to Use This Section The module's instruction, verbatim: think about or write down your answers before revealing them — this will help you develop clinical thinking skills much more than simply reading the answers. Each answer below is a separate short video in the module; the substance is reproduced here. Visit 1 — 49 years old, annual check-up Healthy. 15 lb weight gain over the past year. Last menses 8 months ago. Mild hot flashes. What topics might you discuss at this appointment? She is in the right age range with symptoms of perimenopause . Reasonable ground to cover: Conservative management of hot flashes — cooling strategies such as loose clothing, fans, air conditioning Avoiding exacerbating factors — caffeine, alcohol, smoking Review what perimenopause is and what happens symptomatically during menopause The rising risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer and osteoporosis during menopause, and how to mitigate it: Canada's Food Guide dietary recommendations, regular aerobic exercise , maintaining a healthy weight Vitamin D and calcium supplementation Visit 2 — six months later, now 50 Worsening hot flashes that impair her ability to function as a kindergarten teacher. She wants to try HRT but is scared, because her cousin had endometrial cancer . Is she a candidate? What would you say about the cancer? Yes — she is a candidate. Nothing in her history is a contraindication, and a family history of an estrogen-dependent cancer is not a contraindication to HRT. To address the fear: Concurrent progestogen counteracts the proliferative effect of estrogen on the endometrium She would be given the lowest dose needed to control symptoms, and the plan re-evaluated at regular intervals to limit duration She must contact her physician for any vaginal bleeding , as that could signal endometrial disease There are good diagnostic options for assessing the endometrium , and HRT-related endometrial pathology is often caught early and treated Visit 3 — six months later again Hot flashes improved on HRT. But she now has a sharp, tearing sensation with intercourse and significant vaginal dryness . Describe your approach. Complete history focused on the nature of the pain , including a detailed social and relationship history — sexual dysfunction in women is almost always multifactorial Pelvic examination for vulvovaginal atrophy and for other vulvar conditions prevalent after menopause, particularly lichen sclerosus If it is vulvovaginal atrop

Learning Objective Contrast differences in provision of care between types of providers. A 14-minute conversation between Dr. Rachel Schaefer (CCFP), Sarah Redfearn (registered midwife, LHSC and Strathroy) and Dr. Laura Sovran (FRCSC). Abbreviations used throughout: OB obstetrician · OBGYN obstetrics and gynecology · MFM maternal–fetal medicine · SLE lupus · BPP biophysical profile · NST non-stress test.

entries.t: The Three Providers Side by Side
entries.x: The Three Providers Side by Side Family Medicine OB Midwife Obstetrician Training Family medicine plus 6–12 months extra obstetrical training 4-year direct-entry degree with substantial onsite clinical practice. 7 programs in Canada 5-year OBGYN residency. MFM = that plus a 2-year fellowship (sometimes 3) Who they care for Their own patients who become pregnant, plus referrals — most often from other family physicians Specialists in low-risk pregnancy and birth Complicated pregnancies; consultants to the other two Scope All routine antenatal, intrapartum and postpartum care for low-risk pregnancies Entire pregnancy, labour, birth and postpartum to 6 weeks . Scope varies by location and training All forms of delivery , including operative vaginal delivery and caesarean section Oxytocin in labour All family medicine providers manage it, for augmentation or induction Within scope in Ontario — but what that looks like varies hospital to hospital Yes Operative delivery Many perform vacuum-assisted vaginal deliveries . In some rural settings they also do caesarean sections — uncommon in more populated areas No Yes, all forms Epidural — Within the midwife's purview to manage. Sometimes with nursing support, sometimes a transfer of care — local policy recently changed so midwives manage it — Care of the baby From birth onwards, for years , if the baby joins their practice. Many see parent and baby to 6 weeks Parent and infant to 6 weeks None. "We hand off the baby as soon as it takes its first breath" Postpartum contact Continues routine care Three visits in the first week — within 24 h of delivery, then roughly every other day until the baby is gaining weight . Home visits routinely offered In low-risk cases, often only the 6-week visit Lactation Supports it as part of primary care Significant additional training ; very high breastfeeding success rates No lactation training. Can encourage, but only advise from personal experience Appointment length Standard primary-care visits 30 to 90 minutes or more , in clinic, at home or in hospital Standard consultation Consent model Informed consent Informed choice — which sometimes leads clients to choose outside the usual recommendations Informed consent Birth setting Hospital Home, birthing centre, clinic or hospital — the client chooses Hospital The Family Doctor's Distinctive Advantage Continuity, and an understanding of the whole patient. A family medicine OB brings their entire primary-care knowledge base into antena

When to Consult an Obstetrician Dr. Sovran is explicit that this is not an exhaustive list — it is meant to give a sense of the threshold. Phase Reasons to consult Antepartum Medically complicated patient — diabetes, essential hypertension, prior preeclampsia, elevated BMI, SLE and other medical conditions · fetal anomalies (to MFM) · atypical or abnormal antepartum fetal surveillance (e.g. abnormal BPP) · need for a planned caesarean section Intrapartum Fetal anomalies (MFM) · atypical or abnormal fetal surveillance · labour dystocia , failure to descend , assessment and rotation of fetal position · consideration of operative vaginal delivery or caesarean section · preeclampsia or eclampsia Postpartum Significant postpartum haemorrhage · third- or fourth-degree tear · preeclampsia developing postpartum Not every consult is a handover. Sometimes the obstetrical team will provide co-care through the pregnancy and delivery rather than a complete transfer — though preeclampsia usually does become a transfer of care . Preconception Counselling Is Underused MFM is involved in counselling medically complex patients to optimise health before conception — and Dr. Sovran's own view is that it is probably a very underutilised service . There is a lot of preventive medicine available. The difficulty is simply that pregnancy happens when it happens , not at the medically optimal moment.

The Maternal Health Team We must work together as a team Communication is key — updating the board, or telling an obstetrician there is a potential concern, is what keeps everyone on the same page The goal is patient-centred, supportive care , which will always lead to the best outcomes We all have our own strengths and skill sets , and recognising and respecting that matters Asking for help is not a failure Asking Happens at Every Level — Including Between Consultants At LHSC there are two obstetricians and gynecologists on call every night , and Dr. Sovran notes it is not uncommon for them to ask each other for help . It happens with nursing staff too — shoulder dystocia or postpartum haemorrhage needs extra hands, immediately. The point of the module is that the integrated team is the unit of care, and all three providers share the same goal .

entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Learning Objectives Compare and contrast benign versus malignant pelvic masses. Classify ovarian neoplasms based on histologic differentiation and clinical behaviour, and list common examples of each type. List benign and malignant masses in the ovary. List the patterns of spread for a malignant ovarian tumour. Explain why ovarian cancer has a high mortality rate. List the most common tumours that metastasize to ovary, and understand how they may present clinically and pathologically. List common germ cell serum markers, which tumours produce them, and explain why such markers are clinically useful. Explain the classic presentation of ovarian cancer and its outcomes. Dr. Chris Armstrong, Department of Pathology, LHSC — three recorded parts (30 + 20 + 16 min). His framing throughout: don't memorize every neoplastic condition of every cell type; learn the organizing scheme and the common things.

entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Normal Ovary First Normal ovary, gross and low power. The cut surface on the left shows a ruptured corpus luteum — she ovulated recently. The histology shows primordial and secondary follicles in a supporting stroma. Four cell populations, four tumour families. Theca and granulosa → sex cord–stromal tumours. The oocyte → germ cell tumours. The stroma → fibroma/thecoma. Where the epithelial tumours come from — the classic model. There is no epithelium inside the ovary, only on its surface. Ovulation ruptures that surface; involution traps epithelium in the stroma as inclusions. Those inclusions were long held to be the origin of epithelial neoplasia. Hold this thought — it gets revised below. The map for the whole lecture. Three compartments, each with benign, borderline and malignant members. Neoplasia is unregulated cell growth — and since every cell type in the ovary can undergo it, every compartment generates tumours. Everything below is just filling in this diagram. Who gets what Adults Epithelial tumours, by far the most common Young patients Germ cell tumours — and among those, teratomas are the most common Most ovarian neoplasms Are not malignant Malignancy More likely in the older / post-menopausal age group Not Everything That Makes a Mass Is a Neoplasm An endometrioma or a cystic corpus luteum can expand into a mass with the same clinical presentation — but they are not neoplastic. This lecture is about neoplasia; 4.15 and 4.13 cover the non-neoplastic masses.

entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: How a Pelvic Mass Presents Symptom Mechanism Pain Cystic tumours rupture or torse , causing pain and inflammation Distension Mass effect from a large tumour — or ascites , which some of these tumours produce Compression Big masses press on bowel and bladder → change in bowel or bladder habits Systemic Weight loss, fever, anorexia — usually a marker of metastatic disease Endocrine Sex cord tumours can be hormonally active. Estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia, peri- or post-menopausal bleeding. Androgens → hirsutism, virilization Asymptomatic Many are — and that is precisely why some ovarian cancers present late

entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Case 1 — 45F, Increasing Abdominal Girth 45-year-old woman with a large ovarian mass Increasing abdominal girth, vague pain, not feeling great. Investigations eventually find a large ovarian mass ; she goes to surgery and it arrives in the lab as a large, multiloculated cystic mass filled with glistening, gooey material. Impressive, but benign. Gross: thin-walled cysts, a "soap bubble" arrangement, no solid or fleshy areas, a smooth ovarian surface. Histology: a simple lining , nuclei all aligned along the base , no stratification, not mitotically active, mucin vacuoles in the cytoplasm. That's a mucinous cystadenoma . What the Pathologist Is Actually Looking At A cystic lesion is defined by what it's lined by . So the two questions are always (1) what cell type lines it, and (2) how is that epithelium behaving — orderly single layer, or crowded, stratified, tufting and detaching? Growth rate shows up architecturally, because cells growing too fast push their neighbours off the basement membrane. The epithelial subtypes. Serous — squared-off cuboidal cells, little cytoplasm, not very cohesive. Mucinous — columnar, with mucin vacuoles. Endometrioid mimics endometrial glands; clear cell is clear because of cytoplasmic glycogen (and tends to be malignant ); transitional is what gives rise to the benign Brenner tumour . Serous and mucinous are the two to actually know. Nomenclature — three words stuck together Dr. Armstrong's own description: pathologists don't have a great deal of imagination, we just stick a few descriptors together. The formula is cell subtype + architecture + behaviour : Name Decodes as Serous cystadenoma Serous lining · cystic · benign Serous cystadenofibroma Serous lining · cystic and fibrous · benign Serous borderline tumour Serous lining · pre-cancerous Serous adenocarcinoma Serous lining · gland-forming · invasive Why "Borderline" and Not "Dysplasia" Elsewhere in the female tract the pre-cancerous step is called dysplasia (vulva) or intraepithelial neoplasia (cervix — see 4.8 ). In the ovary the word borderline became entrenched instead. Same biology: it has acquired mutations but hasn't figured out how to invade yet. You will also see it called "atypically proliferating".

entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Case 2 — 52F, Borderline Tumour 52-year-old woman with an ovarian mass Pain and mass effect, an ovarian mass on imaging, surgical resection. Grossly it is again cystic — but this time the cyst lining is not smooth . Papillary excrescences. Soft, friable, exophytic projections lining the cyst. Soft, fleshy and exuberant is a concerning gross sign — it is architectural complexity you can see without a microscope. The four features of borderline, all visible here. Stratification (nuclei no longer along the base) · tufting · detached cell clusters · papillary architecture — with mild cytologic atypia and no stromal invasion . Borderline epithelial tumour Definition Architecturally complex, cytologically atypical, no frank invasion (a little micro-invasion is still called borderline) Treatment Surgical excision Prognosis Very good if all disease is removed — it has not learned to invade Complications Complication Detail Implants Extraovarian deposits of the same non-invasive neoplasia on peritoneal surfaces — mesenteric fat, omentum. Behave like multifocal disease rather than true metastasis. Only the serous subtype does this Invasive implants When implants acquire the mutations to invade. Bad — essentially peritoneal carcinoma, and treated as such Adhesions From the implants themselves Recurrence Implants or residual unresected disease. Slow-growing — may come back years later Progression To frankly invasive low-grade serous carcinoma Why Implants Are Only a Serous Phenomenon The peritoneum is lined by cells similar to the ovarian surface epithelium and the tube . So a serous neoplastic stimulus can plausibly arise multifocally across that whole lining — the ovary and the peritoneum are the same tissue answering the same signal. A mucinous, endometrioid or clear cell deposit in the omentum has no such explanation: that is cancer , and you should look for it.

entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Malignant Epithelial Tumours The line is crossed here. Grossly: still cystic, but now with much more solid, fleshy tissue . Microscopically: still serous morphology, but the cells are now invading the stroma (arrow). That makes it serous adenocarcinoma — the number one form of "ovarian cancer" . Low-grade serous carcinoma High-grade serous carcinoma Arises from A background of borderline tumour De novo — skips the borderline phase entirely Driver — Often p53 -mediated Origin Ovary Probably the tubal epithelium , not the ovary Tempo Slow , over years — slow-growing is not the same as benign Fast , and the form that kills Typical patient — Post-menopausal — younger if familial (BRCA1/2, breast–ovarian family history) The theory of origin has moved. Studies of clonality and of pre-cancerous lesions in the tube — STIC Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma: pre-invasive malignant change confined to the epithelium of the fallopian tube, most often at the fimbrial end. Now regarded as the precursor of most high-grade serous carcinoma. — showed that most so-called high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma is really tubal carcinoma that seeded the ovary . The right-hand panel is the older inclusion-cyst model, which still applies to the low-grade pathway. This Changed Practice, Not Just Nomenclature Not long ago, a tumour involving ovary and tube was called ovarian cancer by definition . The current term is tubo-ovarian . It's also why women with a BRCA mutation undergo prophylactic removal of the tubes and ovaries — and why opportunistic salpingectomy has become routine at hysterectomy (see 5.5 ). One Rule Worth Carrying: Bilaterality Epithelial tumours are often bilateral — with the exception of mucinous . So a bilateral borderline or malignant mucinous tumour should make you suspicious that you are not looking at a primary at all. That thread is picked up in Part 3. Spread, treatment and outcome Why ovarian cancer behaves the way it does. The ovary and tube hang free in the abdominopelvic cavity, so besides local invasion and nodal spread, tumour can simply seed itself across the peritoneum — diaphragm, liver and bowel serosa, and above all the omentum (right). Ovarian carcinoma treatment Primary treatment is surgical Uterus, ovaries and tubes · omentum · peritoneal biopsies · ± lymph nodes Debulking Remove as much tumour as possible, because of the propensity for peritoneal disease Staging Even with no visible disease, sample suspicious peritoneum — has it reached t

entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Mature Cystic Teratoma Mid-20s, abdominal pain, unilateral ovarian mass Imaging and exam show a unilateral ovarian mass. At resection it is partly cystic, partly solid, and contains greasy sebaceous material and hair . Hair and sebum in an ovarian cyst. Commonly called a dermoid cyst clinically; the proper name is mature cystic teratoma . Why "mature". A mix of fully differentiated adult tissues from all three germ layers — skin with keratin and sebaceous glands, respiratory epithelium (sometimes in a C-shape like primitive trachea), salivary-type glands, fat, cartilage, pigmented retinal epithelium, even teeth . As long as it is purely mature, it is entirely benign . The malignant counterpart. Grossly much more soft, fleshy tissue . Microscopically, immature tissue — usually primitive neuroepithelium . The more immature tissue, the higher the grade. The Other, Rarer Way a Teratoma Goes Bad A mature component can develop an adult-type malignancy : the squamous element becoming a squamous cell carcinoma , or the glandular element an adenocarcinoma . Rare, but it explains why "mature teratoma" isn't a promise for life.

entries.t: Malignant Germ Cell Tumours & Serum Markers
entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Malignant Germ Cell Tumours & Serum Markers Germ cells can become a whole human being, so under the wrong conditions they can differentiate along essentially any lineage — hence a long list of malignant germ cell tumours. The most common is dysgerminoma , the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma. They are uncommon overall , arise in the younger age group , and are often mixed (teratomas, by contrast, tend to be pure in the ovary). One branch point explains the whole family. No differentiation → dysgerminoma. Differentiation → embryonal carcinoma, which then goes either extraembryonic (yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma) or embryonic (teratoma). The markers in the next figure map straight onto this tree. Three classic associations worth memorizing. Dysgerminoma → LDH . Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumour → α-fetoprotein . Choriocarcinoma → β-hCG — which makes sense, since it is differentiating towards placenta . The overlap in the weaker columns is why markers aid diagnosis rather than make it. How Markers Actually Change Your Management Young woman, unilateral ovarian mass on ultrasound. α-fetoprotein sky high → higher probability of a malignant germ cell tumour → she goes straight to gynecology . No marker elevation and a simple cyst → you're thinking endometrioma or cystadenoma, and the urgency is different. Markers are also used for post-operative monitoring . And for the epithelial side: CA-125 , which may be elevated in serous carcinoma. Useful when working a patient up for the first time — it is not a screening test.

entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Sex Cord–Stromal Tumours Fibroma — the common incidental one 57-year-old woman, hysterectomy for leiomyomas Surgery for a benign reason, and — oh, by the way — a small, firm ovarian mass that needs working up. It may be sent for frozen section intraoperatively. Well circumscribed, firm, rubbery, homogeneous, no haemorrhage. Microscopically just bland spindled fibrous stroma — more collagen than normal ovarian stroma, so it takes up more pink. Usually unilateral. Benign, and common. (Add a cystic epithelial component and the name becomes cystadenofibroma , which classifies with the epithelial group.) Granulosa cell tumour — the hormonal one 63-year-old woman presenting with vaginal bleeding Not a mass complaint — post-menopausal bleeding . Endometrial biopsy shows atypical hyperplasia , so she needs a hysterectomy. Imaging also shows an adnexal mass . Hysterectomy and BSO are performed. The uterus first. In a 63-year-old the lining should be atrophic ; instead it is thick and shaggy . Histologically the glands are too many, too crowded, atypical, and fusing — and gland fusion in an endometrial sample is not a good sign . This is endometrial adenocarcinoma . Note this is exactly the 30–40% scenario from 5.1 : atypical hyperplasia on biopsy, carcinoma in the specimen. Now the ovarian mass. Fleshy with cystic and haemorrhagic areas, no real necrosis. Those haemorrhagic cysts sit in tissue with little fibrous support — which is why about 10% present with rupture and haemoperitoneum rather than with a mass. Where have we seen these cells before? The microfollicular pattern with Call–Exner bodies Small rosette-like spaces surrounded by granulosa tumour cells, recapitulating the follicle. A characteristic feature of adult granulosa cell tumour. recapitulates the follicle, and the nuclei have grooves . It is a tumour of the granulosa cells shown in the very first figure on this page. Granulosa cell tumour Behaviour Malignant, but slow-growing and indolent Recurrence Late — peritoneal recurrence even 10 years after resection is not unheard of Hormones Often estrogen-producing — so it can present with endometrial hyperplasia or peri-/post-menopausal bleeding rather than a mass Rupture ~10% present with symptoms of ruptured haemorrhagic cysts, possibly haemoperitoneum Slow-Growing Means Late Recurrence — Both Directions A rapidly growing high-grade tumour recurs early and aggressively . An indolent one recurs late . That is why granulosa cell tumour, which is uncommon

entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Case — 60F, Bilateral Ovarian Masses 60-year-old woman, abdominal discomfort and distension Ascites and bilateral, multinodular ovarian masses. At resection they are soft and fleshy with areas of cystic degeneration. Adenocarcinoma, and specifically mucinous. Nuclei are hyperchromatic, pleomorphic , mitotically active; cells bud off and invade . The cytoplasmic mucin vacuoles look like the goblet cells of intestinal-type epithelium — which is the clue. The Frozen-Section Moment Told at frozen section that an ovarian tumour "has a mucinous look to it" , the surgeon knows to go and look at the appendix — because a mucinous tumour metastatic to the ovary mimics an ovarian primary. This is the practical payoff of "beware the bilateral mucinous tumour". And there it is. The appendix is expanded by a mucocele-like lesion , its lumen filled with mucinous material, lined by the same mucin-producing atypical glandular epithelium. Appendiceal adenocarcinoma metastatic to the ovary , presenting as bilateral ovarian masses. Pseudomyxoma peritonei — "jelly belly". Neoplastic cells reach the surface of appendix or ovary, proliferate in the abdominopelvic cavity and keep secreting mucin until it fills the abdomen. A complication of advanced mucinous adenocarcinoma of GI origin mimicking an ovarian mass. Krukenberg tumour The pitfall. Grossly this is a bilateral, solid, rubbery, homogeneous, fibrotic ovary — which looks exactly like a fibroma . The difference is only visible down the microscope: diffuse infiltration of that stroma by signet ring cells . Freezing artefact makes those inconspicuous cells even easier to miss at frozen section. The primary. A gastric ulcer with rolled, rounded edges , and on cross-section diffuse infiltration of the stomach wall — diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma. The ovarian mass may be the initial presentation . Tumours that like to go to the ovary Note GI tract — appendix, stomach, colorectal The big one Biliary tract and pancreas Breast Especially lobular carcinoma — same single-cell infiltrative pattern, so it can also look Krukenberg-like Endometrium Still a metastasis, even though both organs are gynecologic Endometrium vs Ovary — a Genuinely Hard Call Endometrioid adenocarcinoma can be primary to the ovary . So when tumour is in both places, the pathologist must decide: ovarian primary spread to endometrium? endometrial primary spread to ovary? or two synchronous primaries?
