entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Summary Group What to carry away Types Epithelial, sex cord–stromal, germ cell. Epithelial → adults. Germ cell → young. Epithelial Serous most common subtype, mucinous also common. Benign / borderline / malignant, split on invasion . Carcinoma often presents late . Treated with surgical resection ± staging ± chemotherapy Germ cell Mature teratoma is the most common benign one; dysgerminoma the most common malignant one. Serum markers help guide management Sex cord–stromal Fibroma by far the most common — firm rubbery nodule, often incidental. Granulosa cell tumour the most common malignant one — estrogenic, slow-growing, late recurrence Metastatic GI, pancreatobiliary, breast, endometrium. Beware the bilateral mucinous tumour — check that appendix. Classic patterns: bilateral, multinodular, Krukenberg (signet ring), pseudomyxoma

entries.t: Every Ovarian Tumour on One Map
entries.p: Approach to & Pathology of a Pelvic Mass
entries.x: Every Ovarian Tumour on One Map Ovarian neoplasm Name it by the cell it came from · most are benign · cancer is likelier after menopause Surface epithelium Epithelial Adults · by far the most common Benign Serous cystadenoma Mucinous cystadenoma — huge, multiloculated Brenner tumour (transitional) Borderline Serous or mucinous: atypia + complex architecture, no stromal invasion Serous only → peritoneal implants Malignant High-grade serous — the killer: de novo , p53, starts in the tube (STIC) Low-grade serous — slow, grows out of a borderline tumour Mucinous · endometrioid · clear cell Clues CA-125 (serous) · often bilateral — except mucinous Oocyte Germ cell Young women Benign Mature cystic teratoma (“dermoid”) — all three germ layers: hair, sebum, teeth Borderline None — an epithelial category Malignant Dysgerminoma (ovarian seminoma) → LDH Yolk sac tumour → AFP Choriocarcinoma → β-hCG Embryonal carcinoma → weak AFP + β-hCG Immature teratoma — primitive neuroepithelium, graded Clues Serum markers — a sky-high AFP in a young woman goes straight to gynecology Granulosa, theca & stroma Sex cord–stromal Can be hormonally active Benign Fibroma — most common; firm, white, often incidental Thecoma Borderline None — an epithelial category Malignant Granulosa cell tumour — estrogen; Call–Exner bodies; slow, can recur 10 years later Sertoli–Leydig cell tumour — androgens Clues Estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia, post-menopausal bleeding. Androgens → hirsutism, virilization Somewhere else Metastatic Masquerades as a primary Malignant · where it came from Stomach → Krukenberg: bilateral, solid, fibroma-like, signet ring cells Appendix → bilateral mucinous tumour ± pseudomyxoma peritonei Colorectal · biliary / pancreas · breast (lobular) · endometrium Clues Bilateral · multinodular · diffusely infiltrative — go looking for a primary Every tumour in this lecture, sorted the way Dr. Armstrong builds the topic: first by the cell it came from, then by whether it has invaded. Drawn for these notes — it pulls all three parts together; his own three-compartment map is at the start of Part 1.

Learning Objectives Define post-menopausal bleeding. Outline a diagnostic pathway for a patient with PMB — vitals, history, physical exam, investigations, and when to refer to gynecology. Identify the causes of PMB, both the common ones and the life-threatening ones. Given four different pathology report scenarios in a patient with PMB, create a management plan. Define and outline potential treatments for vaginal atrophy. Define endometrial hyperplasia, state the biological significance of atypical vs non-atypical hyperplasia, and list common risk factors and treatment options. Define endometrial carcinoma, listing 2 major types and common risk factors. Contrast the clinical presentations of endometrial and cervical cancer. Outline staging, modes of spread and treatment for endometrial carcinoma. List reasons for increasing rates of endometrial cancer in Canada. A combined clinicopathologic module — Dr. Joanna Walsh (pathology), Dr. Jenna Rawlins (gynecology) and Dr. Ji Hyun Jang (gynecologic oncology). The point of combining them is that the same pathology report means different things in different clinical contexts, which is exactly what the four-biopsy case thread below is built to show.

Definition & Incidence PMB is any bleeding in a post-menopausal woman after the absence of menstrual flow for 12 months. That's it — a single episode of spotting counts. From a Scandinavian daily-diary study Finding 271 post-menopausal women kept a daily bleeding record for 1 year 11% had PMB Estimated incidence in the first 12 months after menopause 409 / 1000 person-years Estimated incidence > 3 years post-menopause 42 / 1000 person-years Astrup K. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand 2004;83(2):203. Why the Two Numbers Matter Bleeding is ten times more common in the first year after the last period than it is three years out. The further from menopause a woman is when she bleeds, the more unusual it is — and the harder you should look.

The Diagnostic Pathway Same skeleton as any bleeding patient: is she stable? → history → exam → investigations. Step What you do Vitals For any patient with bleeding, first determine is the patient stable? History General history as for any patient, plus a full gynecologic and obstetric history Physical General, including abdominal and pelvic exam Investigations Clinical, radiologic and pathologic — the three columns below Work-up of post-menopausal bleeding. Drawn for these notes — the module states this pathway in prose. The 5 mm cutoff applies whether or not she is on HRT; see the caveat in the table below. Clinical Test What it gives you Speculum exam Always a good idea in the office. May reveal an endometrial mass poking through the cervical os , or another cause such as an ulcerated cervical mass Endometrial biopsy 99.6% sensitivity for endometrial cancer. Poor detection of polyps and focal lesions — it is done blind. Required for: endometrium > 5 mm · recurrent bleeding with endometrium < 5 mm · post-menopausal bleeding Hysteroscopy Direct visualization and biopsy. Useful for focal lesions found radiologically (e.g. polyps), and when office biopsy isn't possible. Carries standard surgical risks Dilation & curettage Useful when office sampling isn't available, hysteroscopy is contraindicated, or hysteroscopy isn't available. In 50% of cases, < 60% of the endometrium is sampled — see 5.4 Radiology Test Numbers that matter Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) < 5 mm is the standard cutoff for a normal endometrium in a woman not on HRT . On HRT, < 5 mm is still considered normal — but > 50% will measure > 5 mm , and < 4% of those have endometrial pathology. Investigate if bleeding is persistent Saline infusion sonohysterogram (SIS) Indicated for a thickened endometrium > 5 mm . Sensitivity for focal lesions 93–100% , false positive rate 6–15% . Cannot discriminate benign from malignant endometrial lesions Pathology Microscopic slides of tissue retrieved from the endometrial cavity — by blind biopsy, hysteroscopy or D&C — to make the diagnosis that guides management. Which is where the rest of this page goes. A Negative Pap Does Not Clear a Patient with PMB The Pap test samples the cervix . PMB is usually coming from the endometrium . A normal Pap tells you nothing about the endometrial cavity, so yes, further investigation is still needed . (This is the module's own knowledge check.)

entries.t: Referral — and the Incidental Thickened Endometrium
entries.x: Referral — and the Incidental Thickened Endometrium Scenario What to do PMB plus risk factors for endometrial cancer Refer to gynecology Symptomatic or recurrent bleeding with focal pathology on biopsy (e.g. a polyp) Refer PMB with endometrium > 5 mm or a "vascular pedicle" Refer No bleeding , endometrial thickening found incidentally Do not routinely sample. Decide case-by-case on endometrial cancer risk factors Patient on tamoxifen , no bleeding Do not perform routine ultrasound looking for thickening Asymptomatic polyp on ultrasound Triage for intervention by polyp size, age and other risk factors Why Tamoxifen Gets a Special Rule Tamoxifen is a partial agonist in the endometrium (see 4.4 ), so it thickens the endometrium in almost everyone who takes it. Screening ultrasounds in asymptomatic users therefore generate a flood of false positives and unnecessary biopsies. Bleeding, not thickness, is the trigger in this group.

Causes of PMB The whole AUB differential, with the PMB-relevant ones circled. This is the same list you meet in 4.12 and 4.10 — age simply changes which branches are live. Note that atrophy and hyperplasia get added on the right; they are not a meaningful part of the differential in a 25-year-old. The most common causes of PMB Note Atrophy (genitourinary syndrome of menopause, "GSM") Most common. A diagnosis of exclusion Exogenous hormones HRT is a common cause — see below Endometrial adenocarcinoma Must be ruled out in every patient with PMB Endometrial hyperplasia The precursor lesion — atypia decides management Endometrial polyp Focal, so blind biopsy misses it

Four Biopsies, One History Four endometrial biopsies, all from the same clinical scenario: a 60-year-old woman with PMB . The amount of tissue on the slide depends on the procedure (blind, D&C, hysteroscopy) and on the state of the endometrium — and, as the reports below show, more tissue is not automatically worse news. Report Diagnosis What you tell her #1 Benign endocervical epithelial fragments. Insufficient endometrial tissue for assessment The biopsy needs to be repeated — by you or by a gynecologist. A non-diagnostic sample is not a negative result #2 Scant fragments of atrophic endometrium Benign. You can offer treatment for atrophy, but she must come back if bleeding persists or recurs #3 Atypical hyperplasia She may need a hysterectomy — refer to gynecology #4 Endometrioid adenocarcinoma She needs a hysterectomy — refer to gynecology The Trap in Report #1 "Insufficient tissue" looks like a benign result and reads like one to a tired clinician. It is actually no result at all — the cavity was never assessed. In a woman with PMB that is an unfinished work-up , not a reassurance.

Atrophy Endometrial, vaginal and vulvar atrophy is common after menopause, and the bleeding can come from exposed small blood vessels at any of those sites . It follows from hypoestrogenism , which causes microerosion, inflammation and spotting . Atrophy is a pathologic diagnosis of exclusion — it has to fit with everything else you found. Clinical features of vulvar / vaginal atrophy Treatment (usually by the family physician) Loss of labial fullness Nothing , if symptoms aren't troublesome Pallor of urethral and vaginal epithelium HRT Narrow introitus Local estrogen therapy — vaginal cream, vaginal pill or vaginal ring Minimal vaginal moisture Loss of urethral meatal turgor (collagenous support is lost) The full treatment ladder for genitourinary syndrome of menopause — lifestyle, lubricants, moisturizers, pelvic physiotherapy, then local estrogen, DHEA or ospemifene — is in 5.3 .

Endometrial Hyperplasia An abnormal proliferation — an "overgrowth" — of the endometrial epithelium. The gland:stroma ratio increases and the glands look too crowded down the microscope. Its risk factors are the same as those for type 1 endometrial adenocarcinoma , and nearly all of them reduce to prolonged unopposed estrogen : Endogenous vs exogenous unopposed estrogen. Obesity is endogenous because peripheral adipose aromatase The enzyme that converts androgens (androstenedione, testosterone) into estrogens. In adipose tissue it keeps producing estrone after the ovaries have stopped — unopposed by any progesterone. keeps converting androgens to estrone long after the ovaries stop. The bottom row — infertility, nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause — are associations , and they all describe more lifetime ovulatory cycles or more unopposed estrogen time . A note on HRT Fact Number Women experiencing PMB during the first six cycles of HRT 63% Women experiencing PMB in continued cycles 37% Endometrial hyperplasia in pure estrogen users after 12 months 10% … after 24 months up to 50% PEPI trial, J Am Med Assoc 1996;275:370–375; Van Gorp T, Maturitas 2002;42(2):93–104. A woman with a uterus cannot be on unopposed systemic estrogen. The frequency and intensity of bleeding depend on the regimen and the specific hormones; cyclic/sequential estrogen and progestin may carry some risk of hyperplasia or cancer with prolonged use. Clinical significance — it all turns on atypia Architecture barely moves the risk; nuclear atypia transforms it. 1% → 3% across architecture without atypia, but 8% → 29% once atypia is present — which is why the old four-way classification has collapsed into two diagnostic categories. The footnote is the real teaching point: 30–40% of complex atypical hyperplasia already harbours adenocarcinoma that the biopsy simply missed. Hyperplasia without atypia Atypical hyperplasia Risk Low chance of progression to malignancy High risk of concurrent or subsequent malignancy Management Medical. Progesterone — e.g. megestrol (Megace) or a levonorgestrel IUD Surgical. Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy , abdominal, laparoscopic or vaginal Follow-up Repeat biopsy, usually at 3 months Extensive evaluation to rule out concurrent cancer, then meticulous follow-up Also Eliminate the initial cause — remove exogenous estrogen, lifestyle change, weight loss High-dose progesterone only if surgery is contraindicated

Endometrial Carcinoma Endometrial vs Endometrioid — Not the Same Word Endometrial carcinoma is an epithelial tumour of the endometrium . Because endometrial epithelial cells form glands, it is an adenocarcinoma . Endometrioid describes what it looks like — the tumour cells still resemble normal endometrial glandular lining, just more crowded, more atypical, and invading stroma and usually myometrium. It is the commonest type, but not the only one: serous and clear cell carcinoma look quite different down the microscope. The #1 gynecologic tract malignancy . The 4th most common malignancy overall for women. Often curable — but it can kill. Clinical presentation Feature Detail Vaginal bleeding 90% of women with endometrial cancer present with it Stage at presentation 72% present with Stage 1 — tumour confined to the uterine corpus Other symptoms Cramping, pressure — not well delineated in the literature Pelvic exam May be completely normal , or may reveal an enlarged uterus ACOG. Obstet Gynecol 2005;106:413–7. Why Endometrial Cancer Has a Better Stage Profile Than Ovarian It announces itself early . The endometrium sits inside a cavity that drains out through the cervix, so a small tumour bleeds and the patient notices. Compare 5.2 : the ovary sits free in the abdominal cavity with nothing to bleed into and no early warning symptom — which is exactly why high-grade serous carcinoma presents at an advanced stage while 72% of endometrial cancers present at Stage 1 . The two major types Two diseases wearing one name. Type 1 is the estrogen story — same risk factors as hyperplasia, hyperplasia as its precursor, better outcome. Type 2 has nothing to do with estrogen , arises in an atrophic endometrium in older women, and does worse. A thin endometrium does not exclude type 2. Lynch Syndrome An inherited syndrome caused by defects in mismatch repair genes , which let cells with DNA damage proceed unchecked through the cell cycle. Most commonly associated with colorectal carcinoma — but women with Lynch syndrome carry a 40–70% lifetime risk of endometrioid endometrial adenocarcinoma , and it is often the sentinel cancer in these women. In Ontario, all endometrial carcinomas are tested for mismatch repair deficiency (further molecular testing may follow). If a deficiency is found in the tumour, genetic counselling ± further testing is recommended. Modes of spread An opened uterus with the cavity filled by polypoid tumour. Direct invasion into myometrium or cervix is

Key Points Structural causes must be excluded in any woman with PMB. Most common = atrophy . Most serious = carcinoma or hyperplasia Endometrial carcinoma must be excluded in a woman with PMB Appropriate investigations are TVUS and endometrial biopsy — and don't forget the speculum exam Risk factors for hyperplasia and type 1 (endometrioid) adenocarcinoma are the same: unopposed estrogen Hyperplasia matters because it is a precursor to carcinoma . Without atypia → medical. With atypia → surgical

Learning Objectives Review indications and results of appropriate ultrasound in pregnancy. Dr. Harrison Banner, maternal-fetal medicine, 15 minutes. The second trimester is 14+0 to 27+6 weeks . First-trimester dating and genetic screening are covered in 5.12 and 4.16 ; third-trimester growth and well-being scans are not part of this module.

One Scan, Five Jobs The anatomy scan (or “morphology study”) is a screening test offered to all . The module's knowledge check makes the point with four very different women: five prior losses, a stillbirth with a heart defect, a high-risk screen with a normal amniocentesis, and a healthy 21-year-old. Every one of them should have it. Job What it means 1. Dating and growth Dates the pregnancy if there was no first-trimester scan ; otherwise it is the baseline for monitoring growth later 2. Number of fetuses Confirms singleton or multiples; each fetus gets its own anatomy survey; chorionicity if not already known 3. Placental location Anterior or posterior — and its relationship to the cervix 4. Anatomy screen Rules out major congenital anomalies 5. Soft markers Findings that raise the risk of aneuploidy

Dating, Growth and Multiples The measurements behind “growth”. Four standard measurements go into a formula: biparietal diameter and head circumference (left), abdominal circumference , and femur length (right). The result is plotted against week-by-week charts to see whether the fetus is on track, ahead or behind. Dr. Banner is explicit that you don't need to know how the formula works. Two heads, two anatomy surveys. A multiple pregnancy means a full survey for each fetus. Chorionicity (the type of twins) can be assigned here, but it is easier and more accurate in the first trimester . At 18–22 weeks it is mostly for people presenting late. Why a late first scan is only a fallback for dating: after 14 weeks the fetus flexes and turns, so a single length is unreliable and a composite estimate has a wider range. The first-trimester crown–rump length remains the gold standard ( 5.12 ).

The Placenta Which wall? Here the placenta lies on the anterior wall. The red and blue is colour Doppler, showing flow in the umbilical cord . The scan also checks where the cord inserts, into the placenta and into the baby. How close to the cervix? A transvaginal view (not part of the standard scan, added when the placenta looks low). The placenta runs over the internal os , beside the fetal head: a placenta previa . Placental location is the finding that matters most for later bleeding in pregnancy, and the one most often tested.

Screening the Anatomy 2–3% of all pregnancies have a birth defect , from skin tags and extra digits to major heart defects. Not all can be seen antenatally, but more are found each year. Each organ system is checked against a standard list of views, every time. Three of the standard views. The cerebellar view of the brain (cerebellum, vermis, posterior fossa, thalamus); the facial profile (nasal bone, nose, chin); and the distal spine , the image used to rule out spina bifida. The four-chamber view : both ventricles and both atria in one cross-section of the thorax. The heart is also recorded as cine loops (short video clips) sweeping upward from this view, because it is a moving structure. Why find an anomaly before birth (the module's check: all of these) Counsel the parents about what to expect Direct further investigation — focused ultrasound, other imaging, genetic testing, antenatally or after birth Plan where and how to deliver — the level of care the baby will need Allow the option of termination for severe or life-limiting anomalies

Soft Markers Soft markers are not birth defects. They are findings seen more often in fetuses with trisomy 21 or 18 . A soft marker raises the risk above whatever earlier screening gave. It does not diagnose anything. It means further screening or testing is offered . Three examples. Left: a thickened nuchal fold , measured at the back of the neck, associated with trisomy 21 . Middle: an echogenic intracardiac focus , a spot in the heart as bright as bone, a small increase in trisomy 21 risk. Right: a choroid plexus cyst , a dark space where CSF is made, a slight increase in trisomy 18 risk. How to Say It to a Patient “More babies with Down syndrome have this finding than babies without it — it does not mean your baby has Down syndrome .” How much it matters depends on her prior risk from first-trimester screening. That is why the same marker can lead to reassurance in one woman and an offer of NIPT or amniocentesis in another. The full list of soft markers and the testing options are in 4.16 .

Learning Objectives Describe how you will approach issues involving sexuality as a family physician. Describe ways to inquire about sexual function and practices. List ways your office can be made into a safe space for these discussions. Contrast sexual function and response for heterosexual cis-men and cis-women. Define various sexual preferences. Dr. Krista Cameron, reproductive endocrinology and infertility (REI), 25 minutes. A text-based module with no recorded lecture ; the content is the module itself plus its 42-slide deck.

Why Ask at All How common What they raise Women 50–98% report at least one concern Interest in sex (or lack of it) · difficulty with orgasm · inadequate lubrication · dyspareunia · body image · unmet needs · wanting information · physical and sexual abuse, coercion Men ~40% report at least one concern Most commonly erectile dysfunction or premature ejaculation It climbs with every decade. Overall ED prevalence in men aged 40–70 was 52% in this cohort. Mild ED stays flat at ~18%; the growth is in moderate and severe . The module's point: because it changes with age, re-ask — a man who had no concerns at 45 may have new ones at 60. Step One Is About You Before you walk into the room, be honest about your own implicit biases . Everyone has them. The aim is to be aware of them so they don't come into the encounter.

The Sexual Response Cycle Model Stages Note Masters & Johnson , Human Sexual Response , 1966 Excitement → plateau → orgasm → resolution First direct laboratory study: > 10,000 episodes in 382 women and 312 men ; before it, research was animal studies. The phase boundaries were arbitrary and vary widely between people Kaplan , 1979 Desire (drive) → excitement → orgasm Cut the stages to three and added desire as the first Basson's circular model (shown below) A cycle, not a line Desire can be responsive — triggered by arousal — rather than always present first The model the module calls “most widely used”. The deck places this after the Kaplan slide, but the figure is Rosemary Basson's circular model (2001, reprinted in CMAJ 2005). Read it as a loop. Someone can start from multiple motivations (intimacy, well-being) rather than desire. Deliberate attention to stimuli is filtered through biological and psychological factors into subjective arousal , and then arousal triggers desire . Initial desire is marked variable : it may or may not be there at the start. The factors the module lists: psychological, biological, the stimulus, the arousal, the desire, the motivation. The one clinical difference to know: the refractory period. Both sexes pass through excitement, plateau and orgasm. Men then have a refractory period , which lengthens with age , before another orgasm is possible. Women have none , so line A can return to orgasm from plateau: multiple orgasms . In Masters & Johnson's original figure, B is arousal that plateaus without orgasm and C is a single rapid peak and fast resolution. Phase Women Men Excitement Clitoral and labial engorgement · inner two-thirds of the vagina expands · vaginal walls thicken · uterus elevates · breasts enlarge, nipple erection Penile erection · testes enlarge and elevate, scrotum contracts · nipple erection Plateau Vasocongestion of the lower third of the vagina · inner vagina fully expanded · uterus fully elevated · clitoris withdraws under the hood · labia minora darken Coronal ridge widens · glans turns purplish · testes rise further · a few drops of Cowper's gland secretion Orgasm Rhythmic contractions of vaginal walls, anal sphincter and uterus at 0.8-second intervals Internal bladder sphincter closes; vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate contract (emission); external sphincter relaxes and bulbocavernosus contracts (propulsion) — also at 0.8 s Resolution Everything returns to pre-arousal size · no refractory per

Taking a Sexual History The main difference from any other history: the patient, and often the doctor, is embarrassed . Patients, especially men, may feel ashamed to need help with something they think they should handle privately. The job is the same as any history: put them at ease, find the real problem, get the background and make a plan together. Technique What it looks like Listen for the side-door “I think I need a check-up.” “By the way, I have a discharge down below.” — often tacked onto a visit for something else Clarify vague words “A sore down below” could be anything from a bruise to the module's example of a rectal prolapse (its clinical photograph is left off this page) Confidentiality, early Assure it at the start. If you treat one partner of a couple, their disclosures stay private Their terminology Some patients won't know “intercourse” but will know “sex” Open questions and silence Let them tell it, and leave room to finish Repetition “Had an STI?” — no. “A sexually transmitted infection?” — no. “Ever been treated for gonorrhea?” — “Oh yes, once.” Ask the important questions from more than one angle Setting and body language Greeting, comfortable seating, privacy. Watch hands and arms, pectoral flush , posture. Postural echo (sitting in mirror image) signals rapport Time and composure 45–60 minutes is ideal and rarely possible, so book a longer follow-up. Don't show embarrassment, even about things outside your own experience; stay nonjudgmental

The 5 Ps Ask permission to talk about sexual health, and do it proactively , so the patient doesn't have to raise it. There is no standard, validated comprehensive sexual-health assessment tool ; the CDC's 5 Ps is the common framework. Open with: Are you sexually active now? Have you ever been? What is your gender, how do you identify, and what pronouns do you use? P Sample questions Partners How do your partners identify? How many in the past month, six months, lifetime? How satisfied are you with your (and your partner's) sexual functioning? Any change in desire or frequency? Practices Vaginal, oral, anal sex? Toy use? Protection / Past STIs Any sex-related infections? HIV risk factors (transfusion, needlestick, IV drug use, STIs, partners' risk)? Ever tested for HIV — would you like to be? How do you protect yourself? Pregnancy plans Are you trying to become a parent? What contraception do you use? Pleasure (optional) Devices or substances used? Pain with intercourse? Lubrication? Difficulty with orgasm, erection or ejaculation? Anything you'd like to change? When a diagnosis may affect someone's sex life, give permission to be curious : “Many people are concerned about how this condition might affect their sex life. What is your experience?” Their answer decides how much you then explain.

entries.t: Making Your Office a Safe Space
entries.x: Making Your Office a Safe Space Do Why Self-assess your comfort with different patient groups and your implicit biases You can't hide discomfort you haven't noticed Train staff in culturally sensitive terminology ; use gender-inclusive forms ; display diverse images The patient reads the room before you arrive Use the two-step method — ask gender identity and sex assigned at birth as separate questions — and use self-identified pronouns Signals that the practice values every patient's experience Put gender identity, pronouns and sexual preference on the intake form You walk in already knowing how they want to be addressed Be trauma-informed Adverse childhood experiences such as sexual abuse can make these conversations hard; the module links trauma-informed care resources (AAFP, AAP, CDC, National Council, SAMHSA) The deck's checklist. The one students trip on: ask “How many partners have you had in the past year?” rather than “Are you monogamous?” . The second assumes the answer. Say “partner” until you know more. Seven terms to keep straight. Sex is assigned at birth from biology. Gender identity is one's own sense of gender, which may match that sex ( cisgender ) or not ( transgender ). Gender expression is how one signals it; gender perception is how others read it. Sexual orientation is separate: who one is attracted to.

Sexual Orientation Sexual orientation is who you are romantically and sexually attracted to . Term Attracted to Heterosexual (straight) Only or almost only the “other” gender Homosexual (gay, lesbian, queer) Only or almost only the same gender Bisexual Both men and women — not necessarily equally or at the same time Pansexual (omnisexual) People of any gender Asexual No gender, sexually. Not the same as abstinence or celibacy , which is a choice not to have sex You will meet terms you don't know. Stay humble and ask. Patients won't fault you for not knowing, as long as you ask with empathy and then use their term.

Learning Objectives Explain the basics of teratogenesis. Give examples of teratogens. How This Module Works Dr. Janine Hutson's module is 15 minutes and has no recorded lecture — the lesson is delivered through an external platform, and the event page states plainly: "Please see attached slides which include all of the content in this lesson." So the deck is the lecture, and everything below comes from it.

What a Teratogen Is Definition A substance that may produce physical or functional defects in the human embryo or fetus after exposure in pregnancy Major anomaly Affects an infant's life expectancy, health status, physical or social functioning Minor anomaly Little or no impact on health or on short- or long-term function Why it matters 9 out of 10 pregnant women will take at least one medication

Timing Is the Whole Concept The single figure to know. Read it left to right. Weeks 1–2 — the period of dividing zygote, implantation and bilaminar embryo — is usually not susceptible . Weeks 3–8, the embryonic period, is organogenesis and carries the greatest sensitivity (the red bars). From week 9 onward the fetal period brings mostly functional defects and minor anomalies (the blue bars). Note how the CNS bar starts earliest and runs longest , and how palate and external genitalia stay sensitive well into the fetal period . Why Weeks 1–2 Are "All or Nothing" Before organogenesis begins, the conceptus is a ball of undifferentiated cells. An insult either kills enough cells that the pregnancy is lost , or the remaining cells replace what was damaged and development continues normally . There is no partially-formed organ to malform, because no organ has started forming. That is why the chart marks it "usually not susceptible" rather than "safe" — the risk is loss , not malformation.

The Four Categories, With Examples Category Examples What they cause Physical Radiation · hyperthermia Hyperthermia: spontaneous abortion, neural tube defects, cardiovascular defects, abdominal wall defects Infectious TORCH — plus syphilis, Zika, parvovirus — Maternal conditions Diabetes Neural tube, CNS, spine, cardiovascular and limb defects Chemical Medications · vitamins, minerals and herbal products · recreational drugs · toxins — Two Things Students Skip in That Table Vitamins, minerals and herbal products are in the chemical category. "Natural" is not a safety claim — it is a category of exposure that gets missed because patients do not think of it as medication and so do not report it. Diabetes is a teratogen. Not a risk factor in the vague sense — poorly controlled maternal diabetes produces a specific and recognisable spectrum of defects, which is precisely why glycaemic control before conception is a preventive intervention. The pre-conception genetics counterpart is 4.16 .

The FDA Drug Risk Classification A to X, and the logic runs along two axes at once: how much evidence exists and what that evidence shows . C is the large, awkward middle — no controlled studies in animals or humans, which is where a great many drugs sit. D is not a prohibition : risk exists, but benefits may outweigh it. X is the only categorical no. Read C as "We Don't Know," Not "Probably Fine" The gap between B and C is not a gap in safety — it is a gap in study . A category C drug has simply not been tested in the relevant way. The practical consequence is that "category C" is the start of a conversation about risk and benefit, not the end of one, and it is why the resources at the bottom of this page exist.

Case 30-year-old woman, previous renal transplant, on mycophenolate The numbers attached to that exposure: ~25% of those exposed will result in a malformation. ~50% spontaneous abortion. Why This Case and Not a Simpler One Because it is the hard version. She needs the immunosuppression — stopping mycophenolate risks the graft, and losing the graft is not a better outcome for a pregnancy. The teaching point is not "avoid teratogens"; it is that someone has to have this conversation before she conceives , when switching to an alternative agent is still possible. Once she is pregnant on mycophenolate, the 25% and 50% are already in play.

Counselling, in Three Phases Phase What you do Pre-conception Optimise disease management · optimise other considerations, e.g. 1 mg folic acid daily for antiepileptics · minimise the dose and the number of therapeutics · consider switching to an alternative medication · counsel appropriately as to potential teratogenesis Antenatal Potential dose increases Post-partum Potential dose adjustments · breastfeeding considerations · restarting medications · switching back to previous therapeutics The Antenatal Row Is Counterintuitive — Doses Often Go Up The instinct in pregnancy is to reduce drug exposure. But pregnancy changes pharmacokinetics substantially — plasma volume expands, renal clearance rises, and protein binding shifts — so a dose that was therapeutic before conception may become subtherapeutic . For conditions where loss of control is itself dangerous to the fetus (epilepsy being the obvious one), the dose is increased rather than cut . Then it is adjusted back down postpartum. The physiology behind this is Thursday's afternoon session on Physiological Changes in Pregnancy .

Where to Look Things Up Resource FRAME Clinic — Fetal Risk After Maternal Exposure Western Medicine & Dentistry and Children's Hospital, LHSC. The local referral for exactly the case above Reprotox Free app — quick access to information on drugs in pregnancy LactMed (NIH) Free app — drugs and breastfeeding

Learning Objectives Define labour dystocia; list the 4 Ps that impact labour; describe which components are modifiable and how. Describe the process of an induction of labour; list its reasons; describe a preinduction assessment; explain two ways of cervical ripening; explain the use of oxytocin in labour dystocia. List options and indications for operative vaginal birth; list indications for and complications of C-section. Describe inclusion and exclusion criteria for TOLAC; list the benefits of a successful VBAC and the complications of TOLAC. Define postpartum hemorrhage; describe its etiology (4 Ts); list its complications; describe the approach to an acute PPH; become familiar with the medications used to prevent and treat it. Dr. Laura Sovran, general obstetrics & gynecology. Four recordings with four decks, 75 minutes in total, though Elentra lists 36. It picks up where 6.4 leaves off. Dr. Sovran is explicit: “if it's not in the objectives, it will not be examined.” The details she labels FYI are marked that way below.

Labour Dystocia Abnormally slow progress through labour. It is the most common reason given for a caesarean . On the ward you'll hear it as: Term What stalls Example Failure to progress Cervical dilatation (first stage) Reaches 7 cm, then no change at all over 2, 4, 6, even 8 hours Failure to descend Descent of the head (second stage) Fully dilated, but the head never comes down into the pelvis What “abnormal” looks like on Friedman's graph. The solid curves are the normal multipara (fastest) and nullipara . The dashed ones are the deviations: a prolonged latent phase , a prolonged (protracted) active phase , a secondary arrest of dilatation (progress, then none), and uterine inertia with a prolonged second stage . At the other extreme is a precipitate labour. Slide from the Normal Labour deck. Not to Be Confused With: Shoulder Dystocia The head is delivered but the anterior shoulder is stuck behind the pubic bone . It is an obstetric emergency : without immediate maneuvers to free the shoulder, the baby can die. The longer it takes, the worse the injuries: fractures, brachial plexus injury, neurological injury, fetal death . The maneuvers are clerkship material.

The 4 Ps When an abnormal labour pattern is identified, assess each P and fix what can be fixed . P What it is Modifiable? How Power Contractions, plus maternal expulsive effort when pushing Yes Contractions: (1) artificial rupture of membranes (ARM), then (2) IV oxytocin in metered doses. Pushing: oxytocin if not already on; coach and encourage ; adequate analgesia . Passage The bony pelvis No Can't be altered without breaking bone. The coccyx sometimes fractures on its own during birth (never deliberately). Symphysiotomy , cutting the pubic symphysis to open the pelvis “like a book”, is a textbook last resort for severe shoulder dystocia. Passenger Fetal presentation, position and size Partly Presentation: external cephalic version for breech (or transverse), turning the baby through the abdomen, usually before labour. Position: manual or forceps rotation to occiput anterior. Size: can't be changed; induction may be considered if the baby is suspected to be large and it's appropriate. If the baby won't fit, that's CPD Cephalopelvic disproportion: the fetal head is too large for the maternal pelvis. It can only be diagnosed by a trial of labour, and it means a caesarean. → caesarean . Psyche Support in labour, emotional well-being Yes Continuous support from a partner, nurse, midwife or physician improves maternal and fetal outcomes and raises the chance of a spontaneous vaginal birth. Add pain control as she wishes , which doesn't mean an epidural for everyone. Why Pain Slows Labour Severe pain is a high-epinephrine state . The uterus may contract less effectively, and a woman in extreme pain can't push well. Support and analgesia address both, so psyche is a modifiable P, not a soft extra. The four pelvic shapes , shown as the inlet, the whole pelvis and a fetal head in position. The gynecoid pelvis is the widest and most forgiving . The android (the classically “male”, heart-shaped inlet) and platypelloid (flat) are the unfavourable ones. The anthropoid (long front-to-back) is usually adequate. Whatever the shape, it is permanent. Slide from the deck; the Normal Labour deck's contradictory ranking is flagged in 6.4 .

entries.t: Who Can Be Induced, and Why
entries.x: Who Can Be Induced, and Why Contraindications to induction are the contraindications to labour ( 6.4 ): placenta previa, vasa previa, cord presentation; abnormal lie (transverse); a prior classical caesarean or uterine surgery entering the cavity (e.g. a myomectomy); active genital herpes; and invasive cervical cancer . Indication: any condition that puts the mother or fetus at more risk by continuing the pregnancy. Examples, not an exhaustive list: Group Indications Timing Post-dates : beyond 42 weeks the risk of intrauterine fetal death rises, so induce before 42 Maternal Preeclampsia / gestational hypertension ( 5.16 ); diabetes (gestational or pre-existing); cardiac disease; significant cardiac, respiratory, renal or hematologic conditions; intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy Fetal Fetal growth restriction ( 6.2 ); oligohydramnios ; alloimmunization with fetal anemia (e.g. Rh, 5.14 ); fetal demise ; twins Membranes / placenta Prelabour rupture of membranes (including PPROM); placental abruption “Social” Increasingly, the ARRIVE indication below The ARRIVE trial ARRIVE is one of the indications at LHSC. It randomized low-risk nulliparous women to induction at 39+0 to 39+4 weeks or to waiting. Dr. Sovran calls the 39th week the sweet spot between maternal and fetal risk. Elective induction at 37–38 weeks brings more newborn transition problems. Spontaneous birth at those weeks is fine; it's inducing without a reason that isn't. It isn't offered to everyone yet because the system couldn't cope: everyone from 39 to 42 weeks would need inducing at once. Outcome (Grobman et al., NEJM 2018) Induction Waiting Result Caesarean 18.6% 22.2% Lower (RR 0.84, 0.76–0.93) Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy 9.1% 14.1% Lower (RR 0.64, 0.56–0.74) Perinatal death or severe neonatal complications 4.3% 5.4% Not significantly different (RR 0.80, 0.64–1.00) Perinatal deaths 2 3 Far too few to show a difference Flagged: the slide credits ARRIVE with “reduced stillbirth”. The trial did not show that. There were 2 versus 3 perinatal deaths, and the perinatal composite missed significance. The lower caesarean and hypertensive-disorder rates are real. Checked against the trial's registered results (NCT01990612) and the NEJM abstract, 2026-09-30.

The Preinduction Assessment Check Why Dates / gestational age So a presumed 39 weeks isn't really 37 Fetal position Vertex is the norm. Breech inductions happen rarely, and only with experienced providers. A transverse lie can't be induced. Estimated fetal weight , if one exists A third-trimester EFW isn't routine; if there is one, is the baby very big or small? Cervical exam Dilatation, effacement, position, consistency, station: does the cervix need ripening? Consent Explain the indication and how the induction will go A favourable (ripe) cervix means a shorter induction and a higher chance of vaginal birth . Dr. Sovran's analogy is a peach: an unripe, hard peach is almost impossible to tear open; a ripe one pulls apart around the pit. Success is also more likely with multiparity, ruptured membranes, lower BMI, greater height, a smaller baby , and no placental-insufficiency comorbidity such as preeclampsia. The Bishop score is the cervical assessment most used in North America to predict a successful induction. It scores five features: position, consistency, effacement, dilatation and station . < 6 = unripe / unfavourable → cervical preparation. > 6 = favourable. Slide from the deck.

entries.t: Two Stages: Ripen, Then Start Labour
entries.x: Two Stages: Ripen, Then Start Labour Stage 1 — ripen the cervix Goal: soften, efface and dilate the cervix to about 2 cm , enough to break the waters. Chemical: prostaglandins Mechanical: Foley catheter Options Cervidil , an insert behind the cervix “like a shoestring” that can be pulled out · Prostin gel , squirted into the vagina, can't be removed · misoprostol tablets, vaginal or oral A balloon catheter through the cervix (a double-balloon version exists but costs more and isn't used at LHSC) Can it start labour? Yes — less control over whether she goes into labour Rarely . It releases some natural prostaglandins, but the pattern is more predictable . End point A ripe cervix When the balloon falls out , she's usually about 2 cm The Foley balloon sits just above the internal os and presses the cervix open from inside. Slide from the deck. Stage 2 — start the contractions Artificial rupture of membranes (a small hook through the dilated cervix). Oxytocin, natural or synthetic, works better once the waters are broken , and sometimes ARM alone is enough. If contractions don't follow: IV oxytocin , titrated slowly up to strong contractions every 2–3 minutes . What matters is contractions that change the cervix , since that is the definition of labour. Why Oxytocin Means Continuous Monitoring During a contraction there is little or no blood flow to the placenta . The fetus reoxygenates between contractions. Too many contractions (tachysystole) shorten those rests and cause fetal heart rate abnormalities . So on oxytocin both the FHR and the number of contractions are monitored continuously ( 6.4 ). If you can't trace the contractions, for example with a high BMI, place an intrauterine pressure catheter . Augmentation For failure to progress in a labour that has already started 1. ARM (if the waters are intact) 2. Oxytocin infusion , titrated to a good contraction pattern and cervical change. It also strengthens contractions for pushing (power). 3. IUPC if the contractions can't be traced

Operative Vaginal Delivery If the baby can't be pushed out, there are only two other ways: assist it out of the vagina (forceps or vacuum) or caesarean . Both count as “operative births”. An operative vaginal delivery expedites the second stage : the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low. Forceps and vacuum. The vacuums shown are the hand-held Kiwi (A) and a softer cup (B). Forceps can do four things: traction, rotation, flexion, extension. A vacuum essentially only pulls. Slides from the deck. Indications Fetal Atypical or abnormal fetal heart tracing — the #1 reason · malposition (occiput transverse or posterior), which can be rotated Maternal Medical reasons to avoid Valsalva (cerebrovascular disease, cardiac conditions) · maternal exhaustion / ineffective pushing Labour Prolonged second stage Contraindications Absolute Non-vertex (face or brow) · unengaged head · incomplete dilatation · clinical CPD · fetal bleeding or bone-demineralization disorder (risk of intracranial bleeding and fractures) · any contraindication to vaginal birth Relative Unfavourable attitude of the head · rotation > 45° from OA or OP: contraindicated for vacuum, not for forceps · mid-pelvic station · prematurity FYI, not examinable: the 15 prerequisites. These are consent; no fetal contraindication; analgesia; an empty bladder ; ruptured membranes; vertex, fully engaged , fully dilated ; adequate contractions; no CPD; the exact position of the head known ; a skilled operator; backup staff; a backup plan (caesarean); and the risks weighed against the alternative. The one thing she says to know for the exam: a vacuum is not for rotation. Vacuum Forceps Can Traction ; can correct deflexion. Not rotation. Traction, rotation , flexion, extension Stop if (FYI) No progress after 3 contractions , 3 pop-offs , or > 20 min without imminent delivery Can't apply the blades correctly · no descent with traction · 20 min without imminent delivery Mother Lacerations, hematoma More soft-tissue lacerations than vacuum Baby Scalp lacerations and bruising, cephalohematoma , subgaleal hemorrhage , skull fracture, intracranial and retinal hemorrhage, jaundice , Erb's palsy , 6th and 7th nerve palsies Facial lacerations (~1%), cephalohematoma (~1%), intracranial hemorrhage (~0.1%), retinal hemorrhage, skull fracture; facial nerve palsy and eye trauma more than vacuum The mother still has to push . The instrument only assists. Used inappropriately or by an inexperienced operator, both put the baby

Caesarean Section The four most common indications Together, 70% of caesareans 1. Dystocia Failure to progress or descend 2. Atypical or abnormal fetal heart rate — 3. Previous caesarean Elective repeat 4. Malpresentation Breech or transverse Other indications: abnormal placentation ( placenta previa, vasa previa, accreta spectrum , 6.3 ) · mechanical obstruction (a fibroid or mass in the lower segment or cervix) · maternal infection (active HSV at delivery; HIV) · multiple gestation · cervical cancer · fetal congenital anomalies. Breech (types in 6.4 ) is more likely with uterine anomalies, pelvic tumours, placenta previa , hydrocephalus or anencephaly, oligohydramnios , a lax uterus ( multiparity, polyhydramnios, multiple fetuses ), and a previous breech. Cord prolapse Overt cord prolapse: a loop of cord comes ahead of the presenting part . In the vagina it feels like a pulsating rope . Slide from the deck. Type Cord is Overt Palpable or visible ahead of the presenting part Occult Beside the presenting part, compressed with each contraction Cord presentation Below the presenting part before the membranes rupture 0.17–0.4% of births. Lowest in vertex, highest in transverse. Risk factors: malpresentation (transverse, unstable lie, footling breech), polyhydramnios , prematurity, grand multiparity, pelvic masses, CPD or an unengaged head , multiple gestation, PPROM ( 6.1 ), male sex. A Surgical Emergency Whoever finds it gets on the bed and pushes the presenting part up off the cord , and keeps it there. The patient goes straight to the OR for an emergency caesarean . That person stays under the drapes, hand in place, until the baby is delivered through the incision. Incisions Skin Use Vertical midline Perhaps faster, less blood loss. Crash caesareans, previous midline scar, obesity, bleeding disorders. Pfannenstiel (low transverse) The standard. More cosmetic, less dehiscence , less pain. The uterine incision is the one that matters for the future. Almost all are low transverse (A, circled) , which keeps a trial of labour possible next time. A classical (H) , T-extension (C) or fundal (G) incision cuts the contractile upper segment. That is an absolute no to labour in any future pregnancy. How far an extension goes is decided and documented by the surgeon. Slide from the deck. Risks of a caesarean Risk Numbers from the deck Infection Endometritis 4–5% (35–40% without antibiotics); wound infection 2.5–16% Hemorrhage Average loss 800–1000 mL ; PPH is > 1000 m

Trial of Labour After Caesarean (TOLAC) After a caesarean, the next pregnancy is a choice: a trial of labour (TOLAC) or an elective repeat caesarean . A successful TOLAC is a VBAC (vaginal birth after caesarean). Overall success is 60–80% . Offer TOLAC when all of these hold Don't, if any of these 1–2 prior low segment (transverse) caesareans An adequate (not contracted) pelvis Urgent laparotomy available within 30 min : OR, anesthesia and staff on site. That may mean delivering outside her community. No contraindication to labour > 18 months since the previous caesarean She consents , accepting the risks Previous classical or inverted-T scar Previous hysterotomy or myomectomy entering the cavity Previous uterine rupture Any contraindication to labour She declines and requests an elective repeat caesarean Success more likely Success less likely Previous VBAC or previous vaginal birth Favourable cervix; spontaneous labour A non-recurring reason for the first caesarean (e.g. breech) Age < 40 Previous caesarean for dystocia Needing induction (cervical ripening) or augmentation Gestation > 40 weeks ; birth weight > 4000 g BMI > 30 ; hypertension Why try? A successful VBAC means a shorter stay, less VTE, less pain, less blood loss and transfusion, fewer neonatal breathing problems, less operative injury, less infection, and less previa, accreta and hysterectomy in future pregnancies . The risk: uterine rupture Deck Scar separation (dehiscence) — the old scar splits, not fully ruptured 1/200 = 0.5% True rupture — full-thickness separation of the myometrium, fetal parts extruded; catastrophic 1/1000 = 0.1% Rupture after a classical or T incision 4–9% — why they never labour Flagged: the deck's 0.1% for true rupture is low. The recording itself gives 0.2–1.5% after one low transverse scar. The largest prospective study, Landon et al. ( NEJM 2004, 17,898 trials of labour), found symptomatic rupture in 0.7% . Checked 2026-09-30. For the exam, the deck's figures are what was taught. For counselling, “under 1%” is closer. Risk rises with: scar type and number, a short interval between deliveries, induction or augmentation , macrosomia, multiparity, dystocia. Rupture of an unscarred uterus Very rare Causes Trauma (car crash), prolonged labour, uterotonics (oxytocin) Risk factors High parity, uterine anomaly, advanced maternal age, dystocia, macrosomia, multiples, short interpregnancy interval Signs of uterine rupture 1. Atypical or abnormal fetal heart rate — the first

Definition and Scale PPH is > 500 mL after a vaginal birth > 1000 mL at caesarean Any amount that causes cardiovascular instability Early vs late Within 24 h vs 24 h to 12 weeks An obstetric emergency and one of the top 5 causes of maternal death , in low- and high-resource settings alike Canada: 5.6 per 100 deliveries , closer to 10% when blood loss is measured by weight . Estimates are poor, so weigh the soaked pads and towels. Rising , with uterine atony the main driver 60% of women who have a PPH had identifiable risk factors before delivery , so assess risk antenatally and in labour

The 4 Ts T Mechanism Risk factors Tone (atony) — the #1 cause The uterus doesn't contract down on the placental-bed vessels Overdistension: polyhydramnios, multiples, macrosomia · Exhaustion: precipitous or prolonged labour, high parity, prolonged oxytocin, general anesthesia, anemia · Infection: prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis · Dysfunction: fibroids, placenta previa Tissue Something left inside stops the uterus contracting Retained membranes; incomplete placenta ( succenturiate lobe , morbidly adherent placenta , i.e. the accreta spectrum); blood clots Trauma Something is torn Lacerations of cervix, vagina, perineum (precipitous or operative delivery, episiotomy extension, malposition) · hematoma · extension at caesarean (malposition, a deeply engaged head, prolonged second stage) · uterine rupture (previous surgery) · uterine inversion (nullipara with a fundal placenta; excessive cord traction ) Thrombin The blood can't clot Pre-existing: von Willebrand disease, hemophilia A, ITP · Acquired in pregnancy: DIC , preeclampsia / HELLP , fetal demise, severe infection, abruption , amniotic fluid embolism · Iatrogenic: therapeutic anticoagulation Why Previa Is Under “Tone” The uterus stops bleeding mainly by contracting: the muscle fibres clamp the spiral arteries shut. The lower uterine segment has far fewer muscle fibres . When a placenta that implanted there comes off, there's little muscle to squeeze the vessels. Women with a previa are at high risk of PPH and transfusion because of where the placenta was ( 6.3 ). The deck writes the pre-existing platelet disorder as “idiopathic thrombotic purpura”. ITP stands for immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura.

Complications Complication Note Maternal death — Iron-deficiency anemia — Sheehan's syndrome Ischemic necrosis of the pituitary after severe postpartum hemorrhage and hypotension. The pituitary is enlarged in pregnancy and vulnerable; failure to lactate is often the first sign, followed by other hypopituitary features. Pituitary infarction → classically failure to lactate (pituitary failure is covered in 3.2 ) Blood-product exposure And its consequences Coagulopathy / DIC Consumptive, as in 6.3 Organ damage From hypotension and shock ( 6.6 )

Prevention Is Key Find and treat anemia in pregnancy early , and follow up the response. A non-anemic woman has more reserve to lose. Identify risk factors before delivery: go through the antenatal history. Active management of the third stage : a prophylactic uterotonic after every birth, vaginal or caesarean ( 6.4 ). In Canada that is oxytocin or carbetocin (a long-acting oxytocin analogue). Misoprostol is used in low-resource settings because it is stable at room temperature. Recognize and treat PPH early. Prophylactic and first-line uterotonics (SOGC Guideline No. 431, 2022). FYI, no doses on the exam. The point is to know that oxytocin and carbetocin are the prophylaxis, and that oxytocin is also first-line treatment . Misoprostol and TXA can be added for high-risk women. Slide from the deck.

Managing an Acute PPH “ORDER”: O xygenate, R estore circulating volume, D rugs, E valuate the response, R emedy the cause. All at once , with many hands. Call nurses, anesthesia and more help early. The PPH sequence. Drawn for these notes from the deck's six numbered steps. The branch point is the uterus under your hand. Boggy means tone, so give drugs. Firm yet still bleeding means look for a tear or retained tissue. Thrombin runs through all of it: that is why coags are drawn at the start and why DIC is treated on escalation. The Foley does two jobs. It keeps the bladder empty, because a full bladder stops the uterus contracting. On a urometer it also shows whether the resuscitation is working. Beyond drugs What it is Tamponade Uterine packing, or a Bakri balloon inflated inside the uterus to compress the bed Compression sutures At laparotomy, sutures that squeeze the uterus closed Ligation / embolization Tie off the uterine or internal iliac arteries , or have interventional radiology embolize the uterine arteries Hysterectomy The last resort PPH by stage (SOGC No. 431). Each stage adds blood loss, a lower blood pressure and a faster pulse. Stage 1 gets a first-line uterotonic, stage 2 a second-line one plus a search for other causes, and stage 3 the full resuscitation protocol. The stage 3 signs are those of hypovolemic shock . BP and HR may be variable, and a young woman compensates for a long time ( 6.6 ). Slide from the deck. Agent (familiarity only) What it is Watch out for Oxytocin (Syntocinon) Oxytocin-receptor agonist: prophylaxis and first-line treatment Large rapid IV doses: tachycardia, hypotension, ST depression; water retention Carbetocin (Duratocin) Long-acting oxytocin analogue — prophylaxis — Ergonovine (ergometrine) Second-line; an ergot alkaloid acting on adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors Hypertension (so not in preeclampsia); HIV protease inhibitors and NNRTIs; macrolides Carboprost (Hemabate, PGF 2α ) Second-line prostaglandin, IM or intramyometrial Asthma (bronchospasm); diarrhea Misoprostol (Cytotec) Prostaglandin E1 analogue: uterine contraction; room-temperature stable Fever, shivering Tranexamic acid (TXA) Antifibrinolytic : helps clots hold —

Learning Objectives Compare and contrast causes of antepartum hemorrhage. Define placental abruption, placenta previa and vasa previa. Describe sites from which bleeding may arise during pregnancy. List investigations and treatment for a woman presenting with hypotension and vaginal bleeding in pregnancy. Outline risk factors for placental abruption. List complications of placenta previa. Label the sites/origin of bleeding for each pathology. Describe how hemorrhage leads to coagulopathy. Dr. Jordan Schmidt, obstetrics (Dr. Harrison Banner is also listed on the module). One 22-minute recording; Elentra lists 23. This covers the second and third trimesters ; first-trimester bleeding is in 4.9 and 5.10 . How to resuscitate a woman in shock is 6.6 .

Where the Blood Comes From Source Causes Non-obstetric, common Hemorrhoids , vulvar/vaginal varicosities ; bladder infection, renal stones (hematuria can be mistaken for vaginal bleeding) Non-obstetric, rare Cervical, vaginal or perineal masses ; lacerations . Treated as they would be outside pregnancy. Placental / uterine Placental abruption , placenta previa — maternal blood Cervical Labour — cervical dilatation often causes mild bleeding, the show . Always consider labour, because it is managed completely differently. Fetal Vasa previa — fetal blood

entries.t: The Three Placental Causes Side by Side
entries.x: The Three Placental Causes Side by Side Placental abruption Placenta previa Vasa previa What it is Premature separation of the placenta from its maternal (uterine) attachment Placenta implanted over or just beside the internal os Unprotected umbilical vessels crossing the cervix or within 2 cm of the os Whose blood Maternal Maternal Fetal Pain Painful ; contractions that don't let up Painless Painless; often at membrane rupture Uterus Tender , sometimes rigid Soft, non-tender Non-tender Fetus Usually stable at first; distress more likely if concealed or large Usually stable unless the mother becomes unstable Rapid fetal distress , even from a small volume How often ≈ 1 in 200–300 ≈ 1 in 300 at term ≈ 1 in 2500 Diagnosis Diagnosis of exclusion — ultrasound may show nothing Ultrasound , usually the 18–20 wk anatomy scan Ultrasound with Doppler; Apt test on the blood Classic trap Concealed: severe pain, no visible blood Digital cervical exam can cause a massive bleed Mistaken for show while the fetus exsanguinates Sorting bleeding after 20 weeks. Drawn for these notes; the deck teaches the three conditions one at a time and never puts them in sequence. Resuscitation and fetal monitoring happen alongside this, not after it. Placental location comes first because it decides whether the cervix can be examined at all. An abruption can still be present with little pain, which is why it stays a diagnosis of exclusion.

Placental Abruption Also called abruptio placentae : premature separation of the placenta from the uterine lining. About 1 in 200–300 pregnancies, more often in a high-risk centre like London. It is most common in the third trimester (35–38 weeks) but can happen at any gestation. In the first trimester the same process is usually called a subchorionic hemorrhage . Classic presentation Risk factors Painful active vaginal bleeding, mild to profuse “ Unrelenting contractions ” Tender , sometimes rigid uterus Unless severe, mother and fetus are usually stable at first — the fetal heart rate may be normal initially Hypertension Trauma (e.g. car crash, fall) Previous abruption Autoimmune conditions PPROM Smoking, cocaine and other substances Intrauterine infection Revealed vs concealed. Left: most abruptions start at the placental edge . Blood tracks down behind the membranes and out through the cervix, so there is visible bleeding with mild–moderate pain. Right: a concealed abruption starts centrally, and the intact rim traps the blood behind the placenta. There is no visible bleeding and severe pain out of keeping with what you can see. Fetal distress is more common because more of the placental interface is lost. Slide from the deck. What an Abruption Sets Off Blood in the uterine cavity is a potent irritant to the myometrium , so an abruption often turns into active labour (and it is one cause of preterm labour, 6.1 ). A clot behind the placenta stretches and peels the membranes, raising the risk of membrane rupture . Much of the blood drains out through the cervix, so ultrasound is often normal . That is why abruption is diagnosed only once the other causes are ruled out.

Placenta Previa The placenta implants over, or just beside, the internal cervical os . It is usually found at the 18–20 week anatomy scan ( 5.15 ). Up to 10–15% of scans at that stage look like a previa, but most resolve , and only about 1 in 300 pregnancies still have one at term. The Placenta Doesn't Really “Move” Patients are told the placenta has “moved”. What actually happens is that the uterus grows by stretching the muscle between the placental edge and the cervix . A placenta implanted close to the os early in pregnancy ends up further away. Feature Detail Bleeding Painless , mild to severe. The fetus stays stable unless the mother becomes hemodynamically unstable. Sentinel bleed Typically around 26–28 weeks : short, mild–moderate, stops on its own. Many then stay stable to term, but 30–40% bleed again . The main danger Sudden, severe hemorrhage → hypovolemia and shock, and a consumptive coagulopathy that can develop fast. It may need aggressive transfusion and clotting-factor replacement before and after delivery. Delivery Complete previa → caesarean. A marginal previa with the edge > 1 cm from the os may allow a vaginal birth in select cases, with careful counselling. Postpartum Higher risk of needing a hysterectomy to control bleeding Anterior vs posterior Location doesn't change the risk of spontaneous bleeding . But an anterior previa means cutting through the placenta to reach the baby at caesarean, so more surgical bleeding. Why a Previa Bleeds So Badly Any cervical change, even slight thinning or 1 cm of dilatation, can shear the placenta off its attachment. The endometrium is designed to host and later shed a placenta; the cervix is not . There is also almost no myometrium in the cervix , so once the placenta separates there is no muscle to clamp down on the vessels. That is also why the lower segment keeps bleeding after delivery ( 6.5 ). And it is why a digital cervical exam is forbidden until ultrasound has shown the placenta is clear . Marginal vs complete, as the deck defines them. Marginal/partial: the edge is within 2 cm of the os. Complete: the placenta covers the os. Current Canadian terminology (SOGC 2020) has dropped “marginal” and “partial”. It uses placenta previa only when the placenta covers the os, and low-lying placenta when the edge is within 20 mm. You will hear both sets of terms. Slide from the deck. Previous caesarean → the accreta spectrum A previous caesarean or other uterine surgery raises the risk of abnormally in

Vasa Previa Unprotected umbilical (fetal) vessels run through the membranes over the cervix or within 2 cm of it . They rupture when the waters break or labour starts. Unlike abruption and previa, the blood is fetal , so a small volume can cause rapid fetal distress. About 1 in 2500 pregnancies. Type Where the exposed vessels come from Type 1 A velamentous cord insertion The umbilical cord inserts into the membranes rather than the placental disc, so its vessels run unprotected by Wharton's jelly through the membranes before reaching the placenta. : the cord ends in the membranes, and its vessels run unprotected to the placenta Type 2 A succenturiate lobe An accessory lobe of placenta implanted separately from the main disc, connected to it by fetal vessels running through the membranes. or multilobed placenta: fetal vessels cross the membranes between the lobes Fetal vessels in the membranes, over the os. Nothing protects them, neither Wharton's jelly nor placental tissue, so rupture of the membranes can tear them. A previous caesarean is a risk factor for placenta previa, not vasa previa. A velamentous insertion or succenturiate lobe only becomes a vasa previa if the vessels happen to lie low over the cervix. Slide from the deck.

Assessment and Management 1. Degree of bleeding, mother and fetus Mother: ABCs , and O 2 and IV access if unstable Fetus: non-stress test — baseline, accelerations, decelerations ( 6.4 ) 2. History Where is the placenta on the anatomy scan? Earlier bleeding: a sentinel bleed, a subchorionic hemorrhage, an earlier abruption? Hypertension, autoimmune disease, trauma , smoking and cocaine ? 28 weeks, no prenatal care, painless bleeding She has soaked a pad over two hours and has no pain or contractions. Do: a focused history (previous bleeding, trauma, smoking, cocaine), an abdominal exam (tenderness, presentation), and bloodwork. Don't: a cervical exam . With no prenatal care, nobody knows where the placenta is. Examining a previa can cause a significant hemorrhage, so ultrasound comes first. 3. Stat bloodwork Test Why CBC Baseline hemoglobin and platelets INR, PTT, fibrinogen Is a consumptive coagulopathy (DIC) developing? Creatinine Kidney function, especially if the bleed is severe or she is unstable Liver function tests Rule out preeclampsia or acute liver injury — hypertension is a cause of abruption ( 5.16 ) Group and screen In case she needs a transfusion 4. Is it fetal blood? Test Looks for Used when Kleihauer–Betke (fetal–maternal hemorrhage screen) Fetal red cells in the maternal circulation Trauma (car crash, fall down the stairs): these can truly disrupt the fetal–maternal interface. A typical abruption peels the placenta off intact, so fetal blood stays inside it. Apt test Fetal hemoglobin in the vaginal blood Fetal distress with a stable mother , or a known vasa previa or velamentous cord. A positive result means vasa previa . Both work because fetal hemoglobin differs from adult hemoglobin . Fetal bleeding doesn't change the mother's INR or PTT; severe maternal bleeding from a previa or abruption can. 5. Where she goes Situation Plan Active bleeding, preterm Admit to the birthing unit for continuous fetal monitoring. Steroids for the lungs and/or MgSO 4 for neuroprotection as appropriate ( 6.1 ). NICU / tertiary consult if extremely premature (< 28–32 weeks). Bloodwork every 4–6 h if bleeding persists or the first results were abnormal. Term or late preterm (> 35–36 weeks), active bleeding Deliver , even if both are stable. There's little to gain by staying pregnant, and a stable placenta can destabilize. Induction and vaginal birth if mother and fetus are reassuring. Caesarean for a complete previa or if either is not reassuring. Preterm, sta

How Hemorrhage Becomes Coagulopathy Consumptive Coagulopathy The placental bed is a high-flow interface with large exposed vessels . When it bleeds, the body throws platelets and clotting factors at vessels it can't clot over, and uses them up faster than it can make them. The result is a true DIC : the mother now bleeds from everywhere, not just the placenta. That is why fibrinogen is in the stat bloodwork. It is why treatment is aggressive replacement of blood products and clotting factors , and why delivery may be needed if mother and fetus can't be stabilized quickly. The same process drives obstetric shock in 6.6 . Complications of placenta previa Yes Maternal hemorrhagic shock · DIC · preterm birth · caesarean delivery · maternal transfusion · hysterectomy No Fetal hemorrhage (previa blood is maternal) · preeclampsia (not associated)

Learning Objectives Recognize symptoms, signs and initial treatment for a woman presenting in shock. Dr. Laura Sovran, general obstetrics & gynecology. A 7-minute recording, then a 10-minute written case: a ruptured ectopic in a 21-year-old. Elentra lists 17 minutes. The obstetric version of this, postpartum hemorrhage, is in 6.5 ; antepartum causes are in 6.3 .

What Shock Is Shock is a state of cellular and tissue hypoxia from reduced oxygen delivery, increased oxygen consumption, or inadequate oxygen use. Hypovolemic shock is due to reduced intravascular volume . That means reduced preload , and so reduced cardiac output . It is either hemorrhagic or non-hemorrhagic (e.g. fluid losses). This lecture is about hemorrhagic shock. Feature of shock Why it happens Tachycardia The first compensation: keep cardiac output up as stroke volume falls Hypotension Compensation has failed. A late sign. Oliguria The kidneys are underperfused, so a Foley catheter is the running score Abnormal mental status The brain is underperfused: anxious, then confused, then lethargic Tachypnea Breathing off the acid Cool, clammy, cyanotic skin Sympathetic vasoconstriction diverts blood to the core Metabolic acidosis, hyperlactatemia Hypoxic tissues switch to anaerobic metabolism

Stages of Hemorrhagic Shock Four classes of hemorrhage. Read it column by column as blood loss rises: pulse and breathing go up, urine and mental status go down . Blood pressure stays normal through class II , up to 30% of blood volume , and only the narrowing pulse pressure gives it away. The recording says the pulse “decreases” as shock worsens; the table shows it rising , and the table is right. Slide from the deck. Class I Class II Class III Class IV Blood loss ≤ 750 mL (≤ 15%) 750–1500 (15–30%) 1500–2000 (30–40%) > 2000 (> 40%) Pulse < 100 100–120 120–140 > 140 Blood pressure Normal Normal Decreased Decreased Pulse pressure Normal or ↑ Decreased Decreased Decreased Respiratory rate 14–20 20–30 30–40 > 35 Urine (mL/h) > 30 20–30 5–15 Negligible Mental status Slightly anxious Mildly anxious Anxious, confused Confused, lethargic

Why Obstetric Patients Fool You They Look Well Until They Don't Obstetric and gynecologic patients are mostly young and healthy , and they compensate well despite large losses. This is especially true right after delivery . Blood volume expands in pregnancy precisely so she can afford the blood loss of birth. A normal blood pressure does not mean a small bleed. Don't overlook the young, healthy patient : she may have lost far more than she looks. Watch the pulse, the breathing, the urine and her mind.

Management You can't do this alone. Nursing, anesthesia and often the ICU or internal medicine: a team approach, in ABC order . Step Detail ABCs & call for HELP Is she protecting her airway? Breathing adequately? Vitals HR, BP, RR, O 2 saturation; arterial or venous blood gas IV × 2 Two large-bore IVs . Crystalloid (or colloid) to buy volume until blood arrives. Foley to urometer Hourly urine output tells you whether resuscitation is working O 2 By mask, so the hemoglobin she has left carries as much as it can Tests CBC, group & screen (and crossmatch), PTT/INR, fibrinogen (is DIC developing?), creatinine Blood products? Packed red cells, platelets, cryoprecipitate, FFP , guided by hemoglobin and whether bleeding is ongoing or controlled Massive transfusion protocol? Once activated, the blood bank keeps sending red cells, platelets, cryo and FFP until you deactivate it Identify and address the cause Once she is stabilizing: why is she bleeding? The resuscitation only buys time for this. ICU? If she needs inotropes/pressors or central lines . Involve them early.

Prevent the Lethal Triad Arm Why it's lethal What to do 1. Acidosis Clotting enzymes work badly in acid, especially the calcium-dependent complexes. At pH 7.0, recombinant factor VIIa loses about 90% of its activity . Maintain tissue perfusion : oxygen, IV fluids, red cell transfusion 2. Hypothermia Below 35 °C , clotting drops off significantly Warmed IV fluids , a Bair Hugger (forced warm-air blanket), a Level 1 warmer (rapid fluid warmer) 3. Coagulopathy Mostly dilution by IV fluid and transfused red cells. It worsens progressively at 10, 20, 30 units . Limit the blood loss (fix the cause) and give the right products , not just crystalloid and red cells Why It's a Triad Each arm feeds the others. Bleeding causes hypoperfusion, and hypoperfusion causes acidosis. Cold fluids and an open abdomen cause hypothermia. Acidosis and cold both cripple the clotting cascade, and poor clotting means more bleeding. Crystalloid and red cells alone dilute whatever clotting factors are left. So the resuscitation has to warm, perfuse and replace factors at the same time , and the source has to be controlled.

The Case: Jenna The module asks you to commit to an answer before revealing each step . Try it here too: read each box, decide, then read on. In the emergency department Jenna, 21 , brought in by ambulance after a syncopal episode . Right lower quadrant pain all day , getting worse. Conscious but sleepy and pale ; rousable. PMHx healthy · PSHx laparoscopic appendectomy at 18 · Meds levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena) · Social smoker, 2 pack-years; no alcohol or drugs · Gyne menarche at 12; periods irregular since the IUD went in 2 years ago ; one male partner, no condoms. Vitals: HR 110 , BP 90/50 , RR 15, SpO 2 98% RA · Bloods: Hb 90 , WBC 7, platelets 220, β-hCG pending , blood group A negative · Exam: pale, 56 kg; abdomen mildly distended, tender everywhere, worst in the RLQ ; rebound and peritoneal signs ; cervical motion tenderness . Leading diagnosis? Ruptured ectopic pregnancy. A woman of reproductive age with pain, syncope, peritonism and falling hemoglobin has an ectopic until proven otherwise. An IUD with a positive pregnancy test is an ectopic until proven otherwise , and smoking is a risk factor ( 4.9 ). The appendix is already out. What do you order? Abdominal/pelvic ultrasound: blood pooled by the liver and in the pelvis ; normal ovaries with a probable right corpus luteum cyst; a 4 cm right adnexal mass with a fetal heartbeat . Plan: consult gynecology, NPO, IV normal saline . Then her vitals change: BP 70/40 , HR 135 . She can't stand without feeling faint. What do you do? Now Jenna's version A, B Alert, no difficulty breathing, SpO 2 95% on room air, so no oxygen needed yet C Two large-bore IVs ; fluid bolus (NS or Ringer's lactate); Foley for urine output Help Urgent gynecology consult: update them that she is now unstable Bloods CBC, lytes, BUN, creatinine, PTT, INR, fibrinogen , group and screen and crossmatch ; repeat whenever her status changes Resolution Gynecology comes quickly and consents her for a laparoscopic salpingectomy . She is booked as an “A” case and is in the OR within 2 hours . Anesthesia follows her bloodwork. Her hemoglobin falls to 50 and she receives 2 units of packed red cells . About 2 L of blood is evacuated from her abdomen. Reading Jenna Against the Table At arrival (HR 110, BP 90/50, anxious and sleepy) she already looks like class II–III . By HR 135 and BP 70/40 she is class III or worse . The 2 L in her abdomen is roughly half her circulating volume : blood volume is roughly 70 mL/kg in adults (the table's 750 mL ≈

The antenatal care these build on is in Week 5 , especially the anatomy scan ( 5.15 ) and hypertension in pregnancy ( 5.16 ).
