Learning Objectives Define labour. Review and define the stages of labour and birth. Contrast the different methods of fetal monitoring in labour. Define fetal lie and presentation. Describe Leopold's maneuvers. List the changes to the cervix associated with labour and birth. List maneuvers used for intrauterine resuscitation during labour. Define the cardinal movements during labour and birth. Describe the active management of the third stage of labour. Review perineal anatomy and common sites and structures that need repair after birth. Dr. Laura Sovran, general obstetrics & gynecology, LHSC. One 35-minute recording; Elentra lists 36. The slides are adapted from Dr. T. Crumley. This is the normal version; what happens when labour stalls, needs help, or bleeds afterwards is in 6.5 .

Who Shouldn't Labour Before anything else, make sure labour is allowed . The same list rules out induction ( 6.5 ). Contraindication Why Placenta previa, vasa previa, cord presentation Something other than the baby is in the way; labour means hemorrhage or cord compression ( 6.3 ) Abnormal fetal lie (transverse) A transverse baby can't come out vaginally Prior classical caesarean , or uterine surgery entering the cavity High risk of uterine rupture ( 6.5 ) Active genital herpes Transmission to the baby at vaginal birth

How Labour Starts Complex, not fully understood, and not needed in detail . If we understood it we could stop preterm labour ( 6.1 ). Driver What changes at term Oxytocin Myometrial oxytocin receptors, quiet through pregnancy, are activated at term Progesterone withdrawal Progesterone is high all pregnancy; at term its effect falls relative to estrogen Fetal triggers The fetal adrenal and hypothalamic–pituitary axis Prostaglandins Especially PGF Withdrawal of inhibitors Progesterone, relaxin, prostacyclin, PTH-related peptide and nitric oxide (the slide reads “parathyroid hormone” and “nitric acid”) Before labour Braxton Hicks contractions Painless tightenings (sometimes uncomfortable), no cervical change . Start around 28 weeks and become more frequent toward term. Cervical ripening The cervix softens and thins , often without the woman noticing Engagement The head becomes fixed in the pelvis about 2 weeks before labour in a primip . This is the first cardinal movement. In labour, the muscle fibres shorten with each contraction and don't fully relax back . The uterus gets physically smaller and pushes the head down onto the cervix.

The Four Stages Stage From → to Primip Multip First Onset of labour → full dilatation . Latent phase 0–4 cm; active phase 4–10 cm (more predictable change) 6–18 h ; active phase ≈ 1.2 cm/h 2–10 h ; active ≈ 1.5 cm/h Second Full dilatation → birth of the baby . Progress is tracked by station . 30 min – 3 h 5–30 min Third Birth of the baby → delivery of the placenta 2–30 min Fourth The first hour after birth — The whole of labour on one graph. Dilatation creeps through the latent phase , then climbs steeply in the active phase to 10 cm. Descent of the head (right axis) takes over in the second stage . The durations come from Friedman's curves . They are guidelines, not rules, and were drawn from a single-centre, essentially all-white population with no ethnic variation. Slide from the deck.

Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring Intermittent auscultation Continuous electronic monitoring For Low-risk labour High risk (preeclampsia, bleeding, atypical or abnormal FHR) · induction or augmentation with oxytocin · VBAC How Listen every 15 min in stage 1 and every 5 min in stage 2 External monitor, or a fetal scalp electrode (internal) screwed into the scalp when the external trace is poor or may be maternal Note In low-risk women: fewer operative vaginal deliveries, same fetal outcomes Produces a tracing, classified normal, atypical or abnormal The SOGC classification (Fetal Health Surveillance guideline, #197). Read across one row at a time, for example baseline, then variability. Normal (formerly “reassuring”): monitoring can pause for up to 30 min. Atypical : watch closely. Abnormal : act . Review the whole situation, get a scalp pH if appropriate, and prepare for delivery. Slide from the deck. Feature Normal Worth knowing Baseline 110–160 bpm The line of best fit through the trace. > 160 = tachycardia; < 110 = bradycardia Variability 6–25 bpm beat to beat ≤ 5 bpm for < 40 min can be normal (a fetal sleep cycle): keep watching Accelerations Present ≥ 32 weeks: > 15 bpm for > 15 s. < 32 weeks: > 10 bpm for > 10 s. Stroking the fetal scalp should provoke one. Decelerations None, or occasional uncomplicated variables or earlies See the shapes below The three deceleration shapes. Each pair is the fetal heart rate (top) over the contraction (bottom). (A) Early: the lowest point lines up with the peak of the contraction. (B) Variable: abrupt, V-shaped, with or without contractions. (C) Late: the lowest point comes after the peak. Slide from the deck. Deceleration Timing Cause Meaning Early Mirrors the contraction; nadir at its peak Head compression Common and benign, especially once the head is low Variable Abrupt V; any time Cord compression Uncomplicated = shallow and brief. Complicated = deeper, longer, with the features in the abnormal column Late Nadir after the peak Placental insufficiency The worrying one. A single late isn't normal; recurrent lates are a concerning pattern. Normal: baseline around 130, good variability, clear accelerations. On most paper each small box is 10 s and dark line to dark line is 1 min . Atypical: minimal variability (≤ 5 bpm) and no accelerations. Under 40 minutes this can be sleep. Keep monitoring and decide from there. Abnormal: recurrent late decelerations , each starting after its contraction. This probably means placenta

Intrauterine Resuscitation For an atypical or abnormal tracing in labour, work through: Fetal scalp clip — make sure you're tracing the fetus , not the mother Vaginal exam — rule out cord prolapse ; check station, position, dilatation and effacement Reposition — left lateral decubitus (already on the left? roll to the right), to move the baby off its cord Turn off IV oxytocin Oxygen by face mask — more oxygen in her blood means more for the fetus Fluid bolus — normal saline or Ringer's lactate, about 500 mL Plan the delivery if the pattern continues Why Each Step Helps, and Why Dilatation Decides the Exit The placenta gets little or no blood flow during a contraction , so the fetus reoxygenates in the gaps. Stopping oxytocin lengthens those gaps . Oxygen and fluid improve what the placenta has to deliver. Rolling her off her back also takes the uterus off the inferior vena cava , so more blood returns to her heart. That last point is added here; the recording frames the roll as moving the baby off the cord. If the tracing stays abnormal, dilatation decides the route . At 4 cm the only option is a caesarean . At full dilatation , weigh how fast she can push the head down against a safe operative vaginal delivery ( 6.5 ).

Monitoring Progress What How Contractions Palpation every 30 min in early labour · external tocometer for high-risk or slow labours · an intrauterine pressure catheter (IUPC) gives actual pressures (the recording's target is about 200 Montevideo units per 10 minutes) Cervix Every 2–3 h in early labour; sooner for symptoms or the FHR, or before an epidural decision. Each exam raises the risk of chorioamnionitis , so don't over-examine.

entries.t: The Vaginal Exam: Cervix, Station, Position
entries.x: The Vaginal Exam: Cervix, Station, Position Finding Recorded as Dilatation 0–10 cm. It is relative, not ruler-measured. At 10 cm no cervix is felt, only the presenting part. Effacement 0–100% thinning. With a 4 cm cervix, 50% ≈ 2 cm long , 75% ≈ 1 cm, and 100% feels paper-thin. Station The lowermost part of the fetus relative to the ischial spines = 0 . Above is −1 to −3; below is +1 onward (about +4 is at the introitus). Position Where the presenting part's landmark points in the maternal pelvis: the occiput (vertex), sacrum (breech) or chin (face) Dilatation, 0 to 10 cm. The circles give a feel for each centimetre. Effacement : the cervix shortens and thins , from 0% (long) to 100% (paper-thin). Slides from the deck. Station is measured from the ischial spines (0). Depending on the textbook, the reference point is the lowest part of the head or its biparietal diameter . In the second stage, progress is tracked by station rather than dilatation. Slide from the deck. What your fingers feel. Follow the sagittal suture . The posterior fontanelle is small and Y/V-shaped and closes over as the head moulds in labour. It marks the occiput . The anterior fontanelle is a larger diamond you can feel as a divot. Eight positions , named by where the occiput points: OA, LOA, LOT, LOP, OP and so on. LOA is the most common. OP (“sunny side up”) presents a wider head and explains many long second stages. Slides from the deck. Why occiput anterior is best: the deck says OA “presents the smallest BPD”. Strictly, the biparietal diameter (about 9.5 cm) is the side-to-side width and doesn't change with position. What OA gives you is a well-flexed head , which presents its smallest front-to-back diameter, the suboccipitobregmatic (~9.5 cm) . An OP head is usually deflexed and presents a longer one. (That clarification is added here from an obstetric-ultrasound review, not the deck.)

Lie, Presentation and Leopold's Maneuvers Term Definition How common Lie Long axis of the fetus relative to the mother's: longitudinal or transverse/oblique Longitudinal 99% Presentation The part foremost in the birth canal: cephalic (vertex) or breech Cephalic 95% ; breech about 4% Lie is the axis; presentation is what leads. Confirm with a combination of vaginal exam, Leopold's maneuvers and ultrasound . A shoulder can feel like a bottom, especially in a woman with obesity. Slide from the deck. Leopold's Hands on You're asking 1st The fundus What's up here? Consistency, shape, mobility (the round, hard, ballotable head, or the softer breech) 2nd Both sides of the uterus Where is the back , and where are the limbs? Is the lie longitudinal? 3rd Just above the pubic bone Head or breech in the pelvis? 4th Down toward the pelvis Attitude (flexion) and how far the head has descended into the pelvis The four maneuvers , fundus to pelvis. The fourth is done facing the woman's feet. Three breeches. Frank (hips flexed, knees extended) is the most common (~70%). A frank or flexed (complete) breech can deliver vaginally in the right setting. A footling breech can't, except as a second twin by breech extraction. Slides from the deck.

Pain Control Stage Nerve supply to cover First stage (cervix and uterus) T10–L1 visceral afferents (the deck lists T10–12) Descent / second stage (vagina and perineum) S2–S4 , the pudendal nerve Option Notes Epidural The most common and probably the most effective Spinal / combined spinal–epidural Advanced active labour, or a dense block for caesarean Pudendal block Local anesthetic where the pudendal nerve crosses the pelvic floor General anesthesia Caesarean Lamaze breathing and focal points · nitrous oxide · PCA (remifentanil or fentanyl) —

Second Stage: The Cardinal Movements The mechanism of labour, in eight frames. The small insets show the head from below, turning from transverse to occiput anterior and then back (restitution). Frames from four slides in the deck, combined here into one figure. # Movement What happens 1 Engagement The head, floating above the brim, drops into the pelvic inlet 2 Descent Continues throughout labour 3 Flexion The head meets resistance (the sacrum, then the pelvic floor) and tucks its chin 4 Internal rotation The occiput turns anteriorly to pass under the pubic bone 5 Extension Having bottomed out on the pelvic floor, the head extends out under the symphysis 6 External rotation (restitution) The delivered head turns back to line up with the shoulders 7 Expulsion Anterior shoulder first, then the posterior, then the rest The Pelvis Matters, and the Deck Contradicts Itself Narrow or flat pelves can stop the cardinal movements. A trial of labour is the only true test of pelvic adequacy : no X-ray can predict whether the baby will fit. This deck lists the best outcomes as “gynecoid & android” and the problem pelves as platypelloid and anthropoid. That is not the standard teaching, or Dr. Sovran's own dystocia lecture ( 6.5 ). There, as in the literature, the gynecoid pelvis is the most favourable. Anthropoid is acceptable , and android and platypelloid are the unfavourable pair . Checked against Salk et al., Med Princ Pract 2016, which gives the Caldwell–Moloy classification.

Third Stage: The Placenta From the birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta , normally 2–30 minutes . After 30 minutes it is retained , and it is removed manually: leaving it raises the risk of postpartum hemorrhage . Active management of the third stage (WHO / SOGC) 1. A uterotonic Oxytocin (Syntocinon), or ergonovine; misoprostol can be used 2. Gentle traction on the cord Controlled, not a hard pull. Excessive traction can invert the uterus ( 6.5 ) 3. Fundal massage Keeps the uterus contracted Once the placenta is out, the uterus contracts better, and that reduces postpartum hemorrhage . Signs the placenta has separated 1. The uterus becomes firm and globular — the earliest sign 2. A gush of blood 3. The uterus rises in the abdomen, pushed up by the placenta's bulk in the lower segment 4. The cord lengthens at the introitus as the placenta descends Afterward: uterine involution (oxytocin-mediated), then inspect and repair any lacerations .

Perineal Anatomy and Lacerations The superficial layer, which is what tears. Bulbocavernosus slings around the vagina. The transverse perineal muscles are the horizontal support. The external anal sphincter encircles the anus. The deep levator ani (puborectalis) isn't seen and isn't torn in these injuries. Slide from the deck. Degree Injury First Vaginal mucosa only Second Vaginal mucosa and perineal muscles ; the anal sphincter is intact Third Involves the anal sphincter complex : 3a < 50% of external sphincter thickness · 3b > 50% · 3c internal sphincter torn too Fourth External and internal sphincters and the rectal mucosa / anal epithelium — a tear from the vagina into the bowel First to fourth degree , each adding a layer. Real tears are never this neatly delineated. Slide from the deck.

Fourth Stage: The First Hour Who What to watch Mother Autotransfusion : as the uterus contracts, up to ~500 mL of blood returns from the uteroplacental unit to her circulation. That raises cardiac work, which is critical with a cardiomyopathy or valve disease such as aortic valve dysfunction. Watch for postpartum hemorrhage . Baby Transition to breathing air ; starting breast- or bottle-feeding

Learning Objectives Describe the anatomy of the breast as it pertains to lactation. Describe the physiology of breastfeeding. List reasons that milk supply may be less than required. Explain the components and benefits of colostrum. List reasons to supplement with formula. Identify optimal timing of feeding over the first week of life. List resources to assist with breastfeeding. Identify contraceptives that may interfere with breastfeeding. Dr. Laura Sovran, general obstetrics & gynecology. One 27-minute recording and a 50-slide deck. Mastitis also appears in 5.7 ; the postpartum breast timeline is in 6.8 .

Four Words Term Means Mammogenesis Breast preparation: development of the gland. Estrogen → ducts; progesterone → lobules/alveoli. Lactogenesis Synthesis and secretion from the alveoli. Stage I by mid-pregnancy : competent to secrete. Stage II after delivery : copious secretion. Galactokinesis Ejection of milk (let-down) Galactopoiesis Maintenance of lactation

Breast Anatomy Alveoli → lactiferous ducts → sinuses → nipple. Slide from the deck. Each breast has 15–20 lobes , separated by fibrous septa radiating from the centre, with fibrofatty tissue between them. Each lobe divides into lobules , each with 10–100 alveoli . Alveoli are lined by milk-secreting epithelium and wrapped in myoepithelial cells . When these contract (oxytocin), milk is squeezed into the ducts. One lactiferous duct leaves each lobe and widens into a lactiferous sinus , which opens on the nipple.

entries.t: How Milk Is Made and Let Down
entries.x: How Milk Is Made and Let Down Three factors , and removal has to start by day 3 . Slide from the deck. Endocrine → autocrine. Hormones start it; by day 3 milk removal drives supply (supply = demand). Prolactin matters less after about 3 months. Slide from the deck. The reflex arc. Suckling → nipple mechanoreceptors → hypothalamus. Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin squeezes it out. The baby's cry alone can trigger oxytocin. Slide from the deck (Silverthorn, Human Physiology ). Trigger Change Effect Delivery of the placenta ↓ Progesterone (which blocks lactose synthesis and competes at glucocorticoid receptors) Prolactin can act → lactogenesis Nipple stimulation / milk removal ↓ Dopamine from the hypothalamus (dopamine inhibits prolactin) ↑ Prolactin → more milk Nipple stimulation ↑ Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) Myoepithelial contraction → let-down ; also helps the uterus involute

Colostrum and Breast Milk Colostrum : nutritional, immune and growth factors. Slide from the deck. Fact Colostrum alone for 2–4 days : antibodies (IgA and others), cells, vitamins A, D, E, K ; passive immunity and infection prevention Transitional milk (colostrum + mature milk) for ~2 weeks , then mature milk Exclusive breast milk for 6 months (some say 4–6; early food exposure may mean fewer allergies), then complementary foods with breastfeeding to 2 years or beyond (WHO) Breast size doesn't matter. Composition varies by time of day: watery in the morning, fattier in the evening. Who benefits How Infant: gut Faster gastric emptying; in preterms more lactase activity, lower intestinal permeability, less NEC Infant: short term Fewer gastroenteritis, respiratory infections, otitis media, UTI, sepsis while breastfed Infant: long term Possible protection (some evidence controversial): obesity, diabetes, allergy, cancer, adult CVD, cognitive and neurodevelopmental outcomes Mother Faster recovery (oxytocin → involution, which may help prevent delayed PPH) · less stress response · longer anovulation · convenient · less breast and ovarian cancer · less cardiovascular disease Society No water, waste, energy, packaging or transport

entries.t: The First Week: How to Feed
entries.x: The First Week: How to Feed First feed within an hour of birth if possible, with skin-to-skin (bonding, milk supply, less stress for both). On demand : follow infant cues, especially in the first 6 weeks. If the baby is too sleepy to feed (common in the first 24 h), hand-express every 2–3 hours and keep the milk to supplement later. Feed length varies with the baby (one may take 40 minutes, another under 10). Positions: cradle, cross-cradle, football, side-lying . She has a right to feed anywhere . Shaming public breastfeeding undermines it. A good latch is on the areola, not the nipple : mouth wide, lips flanged out, chin on the breast, cheeks full. A nipple-only latch is ineffective and painful, like being pinched rather than gripped. Slide from the deck (UpToDate).

When It Isn't Going Well Latching problems, painful cracked nipples, Candida (oral thrush in the baby, which needs treating), engorgement, blocked ducts. Refer to a lactation consultant early. (The deck's photographs of oral thrush, mastitis and an abscess are left out; the findings are described below.) Mastitis Lactational abscess Looks like A firm, red, tender area that comes on fast; fever > 38.5 °C , chills, myalgia, flu-like; tender axillary nodes. Rarely septic shock. Diagnosis is clinical. A tender, fluctuant area, often after mastitis. Rare unless lactating. Organism S. aureus , including MRSA S. aureus Treatment Antibiotics: the recording gives cephalexin 500 mg PO QID × 10–14 d , or a cloxacillin-type antibiotic. Keep breastfeeding (or pumping). Acetaminophen, ibuprofen, cool compresses. Incision and drainage or needle aspiration , plus antibiotics. Early infection can be reversed with nursing, manual expression and cloxacillin 500 mg PO QID × 7–10 d . Keep emptying the breast; analgesia; a good bra. Risk factors Prior mastitis · blocked ducts · cracked or excoriated nipples · breast pump use · nipple creams (especially antifungals) Other causes of nipple or breast pain: nipple injury from a poor latch · nipple vasoconstriction (Raynaud's: the nipple blanches) · engorgement (interstitial edema) · plugged ducts · infection · oversupply · dermatitis or psoriasis.

Low Milk Supply The most common reason women stop breastfeeding. Diagnose poor intake from the nursing history, fewer wet and dirty diapers , and excess infant weight loss. Assess the latch, augment by pumping, supplement, review drugs, and refer. 1. Inadequate production 2. Poor extraction Insufficient breast development in pregnancy · prior breast surgery or radiation · insulin resistance, high androgens, PCOS , prolactinoma · retained placenta (progesterone stays high) · Sheehan syndrome after a major PPH · drugs: dopamine agonists* , decongestants, estrogen Poor latch · infrequent feeding · cleft lip/palate · sucking or swallowing disorders · neuromotor delay · prematurity · separation of mother and baby. Special needs: cleft palate, NICU babies, neurological impairment, Pierre Robin (small jaw), trisomy 21 *The slide says “dopamine antagonist ”; the recording says agonists , which is right. Dopamine suppresses prolactin, so a dopamine agonist (e.g. cabergoline, the deck's own drug for stopping lactation) reduces supply, and an antagonist would raise prolactin.

Diet, Drugs and Contraindications Exposure Advice Nutrition More fluids, calories, calcium and vitamins Smoking Avoid : more SIDS and infant respiratory illness Alcohol Not contraindicated, but excess blunts the prolactin response and may affect infant motor development. Nurse just before a drink; wait 2 h per standard drink. Street drugs Contraindicated (cocaine and cannabis have long-term effects on the baby). Opioid dependence in a supervised methadone program is compatible. Medications Only what's needed. Goal: milk concentration < 10% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose . Contraindications to breastfeeding HIV in developed countries (WHO says acceptable if both are on ART with a suppressed viral load) · active psychosis · active TB · herpetic breast lesions · antineoplastic drugs · galactosemia in the infant · PKU if the infant's phenylalanine is too high · she declines

Storage, Supplementing and Stopping Topic Laws of 6 Room temperature 6 hours · fridge 6 days · freezer 6 months (longer in a deep freezer; Medela gives stricter guidance) Reasons to supplement with formula Patient choice (respect autonomy; don't guilt her) · inadequate supply with poor growth or failure to thrive · infant dehydration, hypoglycemia, weight loss or poor weight gain Weaning A personal decision. Abrupt weaning isn't recommended : the rapid prolactin drop may worsen depressive symptoms, and it causes engorgement, blocked ducts and infection. Gradual is best, ideally child-led after 6 months, dropping feeds slowly. Stopping lactation Cabergoline 1 mg once (a potent dopaminergic drug) · supportive bra, ice packs, analgesics, cabbage leaves Contraception while breastfeeding Avoid estrogen : it may lower milk quality and quantity. Safe: hormonal or copper IUD · progestin-only pill · condoms and other barriers · Depo-Provera (IM medroxyprogesterone). Timing rules are in 6.8 . Resources: LHSC lactation consultants (mavins.lhsc.on.ca), International Breastfeeding Centre videos, the Canadian Paediatric Society's breastfeeding and human milk banking statements, WHO exclusive breastfeeding guidance.

Learning Objectives Contrast initial resuscitation of a neonate versus an adult. Describe the components of the Apgar score. List the changes that occur in the heart and lungs after birth. Review the components of the newborn exam. List indications why a neonate may need extra evaluation or care. Model bilirubin physiology and investigation in the first week of life. Discuss global perspectives of neonatal care. Dr. Anita Cheng, neonatologist. Elentra lists 99 minutes: a 41-minute recording, a 48-slide deck, a separate video of a full newborn exam, and three knowledge-check cases (worked through below). The first and third objectives aren't taught in the deck or the recording, so the box below covers them from the neonatal resuscitation guideline and says so.

entries.t: Birth: What Changes, and Why a Newborn Isn't a Small Adult
entries.x: Birth: What Changes, and Why a Newborn Isn't a Small Adult Added for these notes — not in the module's deck or recording Heart and lungs at birth. The first breaths clear the fluid-filled lungs: lung fluid is absorbed through epithelial sodium channels. Inflating the lungs and raising the oxygen level make pulmonary vascular resistance fall , so pulmonary blood flow rises. Left atrial pressure then exceeds right, the foramen ovale closes , and the ductus arteriosus constricts. The fetal circulation switches to the adult one in minutes. (Standard physiology.) Resuscitation: ventilation first. A newborn who needs help almost always has a breathing problem, not a primary cardiac one, so inflating the lungs is the priority . A rising heart rate is the best sign it's working. Positive-pressure ventilation starts if the baby is apneic, gasping, or HR < 100 in the first minute. Chest compressions come only if HR stays < 60 after 30 s of good ventilation , at 3 compressions : 1 breath (adult CPR is compressions first, 30 : 2). Keep the baby at 36.5–37.5 °C . Delayed cord clamping (> 30 s) is reasonable if no resuscitation is needed. (2020 AHA/AAP neonatal resuscitation guideline, via its AAFP summary.)

The APGAR Score Developed in 1952 by Dr. Virginia Apgar , an anesthetist. It is scored after the resuscitation, at 1, 5 and 10 minutes , as a record of how the baby transitioned. It doesn't decide what to do. Five signs, 0–2 each, maximum 10. Most babies keep blue hands and feet (acrocyanosis) for a while, so “centrally pink” scores 1 . A heart rate under 100 means bag-mask ventilation. Slide from the deck. Knowledge check: score this baby Centrally pink with blue hands and feet; the nurse counts 12 beats in 6 seconds ; grimaces and cries to stimulation; arms and legs flexed; crying regularly. Appearance 1 · Pulse 2 (12 × 10 = 120/min) · Grimace 2 · Activity 2 · Respiration 2 = 9. A vigorously crying baby usually has HR > 100.

The Newborn Exam Many neonatal problems are failures to adapt from intrauterine to extrauterine life. 3% of neonates have a major malformation , so every one is examined within 24 hours of birth . The module includes a video of a full exam. Look for Why Dysmorphic features Clues to a genetic or congenital anomaly, e.g. Down syndrome: epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots, low-set ears, a smooth philtrum, hand findings A non-patent GI tract A distended abdomen or trouble swallowing. Duodenal atresia is more common in Down syndrome. Cardiac lesions Appearance and pulses as well as auscultation: a cyanotic heart lesion may have no murmur at first Tone Feeding well (breast or bottle) is a good surrogate for normal tone Voided urine and passed meconium Before discharge: shows intake and a patent GI tract Weight, head circumference, length Plotted on a growth chart (preterm-specific charts exist), then followed by the primary care provider for failure to thrive The Ballard score estimates gestational age when the dates are uncertain. It scores neuromuscular maturity (posture, flexibility) and physical maturity (skin, hair, nails, ears, genitalia), and the total converts to weeks. Slide from the deck.

Keeping Them Warm Four ways to lose heat : conduction, convection, evaporation and radiation. Slide from the deck. Why newborns get cold What we do From a warm womb to a cold room, naked, wet , with a large surface area Dry at once (stops evaporation), wrap , hat (the head is a big surface) Little fat: 16% of body weight at 40 wk, only 1% at 27 wk Preterm: a plastic wrap/bag , a hot resuscitation room Can't shiver ; limited metabolic reserve Incubator under 1500 g (servo-controlled); a radiant warmer on the resuscitation bed Very preterm skin is thin Humidity ≥ 80% for the most preterm Cold stress alone can make a baby sick, including respiratory distress. It also spends glucose, which is the next problem.

Keeping Them Sweet: Hypoglycemia Fetus Newborn Glucose is the main fuel, entirely from the mother. Glycogen synthesis in liver and muscle starts in the late 2nd trimester. Fat is the biggest store. Plasma glucose is held up by glycogenolysis : a term baby has glycogen for 8–10 hours (colostrum is only a few mL). Then gluconeogenesis , which isn't fully integrated until 2–4 days . Too little substrate Too much substrate use IUGR / SGA , hypertension in pregnancy, multiple gestation , prematurity : little stored glycogen and fat Infant of a diabetic mother and LGA : the fetus made extra insulin to match maternal glucose; the cord is cut, the insulin isn't. A transient hyperinsulinemic state. Also hypothermia, sepsis, asphyxia . Who to screen (asymptomatic) Signs Infants of diabetic mothers · LGA > 90th · SGA < 10th · preterm < 37 wk . Check 2 h after the first feed. Often none (that's why we screen) · jittery, irritable · lethargic, feeds poorly · can be a sign of sepsis , even in an IDM The numbers. Target 2.6 mmol/L in the first 72 h, 3.3 after . Jitteriness and other neuro signs mean the brain is short of glucose and neurons are being injured. Slide from the deck (CPS position statement). The CPS algorithm. Early, frequent feeding → recheck → IV dextrose. “ Three strikes ”: still low after three checks means an IV. Glucagon if dextrose fails; investigate persistent lows (inborn errors, hormones). Slide from the deck. Knowledge check A 37+0 infant of a diabetic mother, 3989 g, now 12 h old: two glucose readings of 2.3 . Jittery and can't latch or suck ; mother feels she has no milk yet. Next step? Start IV dextrose and recheck in 30 minutes. This is symptomatic hypoglycemia in a baby who can't feed, so feeding-based options (NG formula, dextrose gel, a lactation consult) are too slow.

Bilirubin in the First Week The life of a bilirubin molecule. Each numbered step is a place jaundice can come from. Slide from the deck. Step What happens 1. Production The fetus lives in relative hypoxia, so it has lots of red cells; after birth they break down. Heme → heme oxygenase → biliverdin → biliverdin reductase → bilirubin 2. Transport Bound to albumin to reach the liver 3. Uptake Into the hepatocyte via ligandin 4. Conjugation Glucuronosyltransferase makes it water-soluble. Unconjugated bilirubin can't be excreted. 5. Excretion Into bile and gut; out in stool (and urine as urobilinogen) 6. Enterohepatic circulation Some is deconjugated in the gut and comes back for another pass Universal screening at 24–48 h of life , transcutaneous (a meter on the forehead) or a blood level. The level is plotted by age in hours: first on the risk nomogram (decides follow-up), then on the phototherapy chart (decides treatment). The CPS curves. Separate lines for babies with and without neurotoxicity risk factors : < 38 weeks, albumin < 30, suspected hemolysis, suspected sepsis, significant hemodynamic or respiratory instability. Preterm babies have their own curves. Slide from the deck (Canadian Paediatric Society). Risk factors for hyperbilirubinemia Causes Isoimmune hemolytic disease (ABO, Rh, minor antigens) · G6PD deficiency · asphyxia · respiratory distress · lethargy, temperature instability · bruising, cephalohematoma · sepsis · acidosis · prematurity · a sibling who needed phototherapy · East Asian ethnicity Exaggerated physiological / breastfeeding jaundice (the most common: milk not in, baby dehydrated) · sepsis · hemolysis: isoimmunization (all mothers get ABO and antibody screening), spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, G6PD · cephalohematoma · polycythemia (IUGR, Down syndrome) · drugs that displace bilirubin from albumin ( ceftriaxone, sulfas ) · breast-milk jaundice (rare) · conjugation disorders Red flags Jaundice in the first 24 h is always pathological Cord bilirubin > 68 µmol/L · rise > 85 µmol/L/day · total > 340 µmol/L Direct (conjugated) > 30 µmol/L or > 20% of total : a biliary excretion problem Jaundice > 2 weeks in a term baby · an unwell baby Kernicterus : yellow staining of the basal ganglia. Cropped from the deck; the slide's infant photograph is left out. Why we screen. Bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction ( BIND ): acute bilirubin encephalopathy starts as lethargy, hypotonia and a poor suck , then becomes hypertonia with opisthotonos

Global Perspectives Under-five mortality fell in every WHO region from 1990 to 2017, but Africa is still about 74 per 1000 . Slide from the deck (UNICEF/WHO). 5.4 million children under five die every year; 44% are neonates (first 28 days), about 2.5 million . The big slices: preterm complications, intrapartum events, sepsis. Slide from the deck (Lancet 2015). Where those deaths happen: sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia . Slide from the deck. Helping Babies Survive (AAP, WHO, USAID): simple, picture-based training for anyone who attends births, including community attendants with no medical training. It comes with a low-cost kit (mannequin, self-inflating bag and mask, stethoscope) and culturally matched materials. Course Focus Result shown in the deck Helping Babies Breathe The “ Golden Minute ”: dry, warm, stimulate, bag-mask ventilate within the first minute 47% fewer early neonatal deaths, 24% fewer stillbirths (babies who looked dead were ventilated) Essential Care for Every Baby Kangaroo care, breastfeeding Babies given no breast milk are 7× more likely to die of infection Essential Care for Small Babies Skin-to-skin care for IUGR and preterm babies 36% lower mortality in low-birth-weight babies Improving Care for Mothers and Babies A quality-improvement cycle for the care team —

Take-Home Messages Every newborn: pink (cardiorespiratory transition), warm , sweet (consider glucose screening). Have a systematic approach to respiratory distress , the most common newborn problem. Neonatal sepsis is life-threatening and belongs on the list for any sick baby: hypoglycemia, jaundice, temperature instability, poor feeding. Simple, targeted education measurably cuts neonatal mortality worldwide.

Learning Objectives Describe the timing and changes that occur in the uterus. Describe the changes that occur in the breast. Explain when ovulation and pregnancy may occur. Explain the hormonal state over the first six weeks. List reasons that sleep is altered. List risk factors for postpartum depression (PPD). Identify tools to assess PPD. Identify issues with perineal care and healing after birth. Dr. Laura Sovran, general obstetrics & gynecology. One 36-minute recording and a 36-slide deck; Elentra lists 37 minutes. The breastfeeding physiology itself is in 6.9 .

Going Home Stay Detail Average Vaginal birth 1–2 days · caesarean 2–3 days . Babies have bloodwork at 24 h. Early (2–6 h minimum) Needs close community follow-up, usually by midwives. Without it there is more neonatal morbidity and mortality: deaths from cardiac causes, infection and SIDS, and more feeding problems. The risk is the baby's, which is why early discharge is offered after a stillbirth . Before she goes Check bleeding, bowel, bladder and baby care Discharge < 48 h: maternal criteria Neonatal criteria Knows perineal care · no complication needing treatment or observation · mobile, pain controlled (not pain-free) · bowel and bladder working · RhIg (if Rh− with an Rh+ baby) and MMR (if not rubella-immune) given · can feed the baby · contraception advice · ongoing care provider identified · safe home · knows community resources Term and appropriate for gestational age · no sepsis · stable temperature · feeding well · physical exam within 12 h · has urinated · meds and immunizations given (e.g. hepatitis B vaccine if a family member is positive) · metabolic screen at 24 h · mother able to care for the baby · community provider arranged, first visit within ~72 h Maternal contraindications to discharge (while active): preeclampsia (uncontrolled BP), PPH (still bleeding heavily), fever , an unstable medical condition .

Perineum, Bowels and Breasts Problem Advice Tears / episiotomy Keep clean and dry: sitz baths or soaks in warm or cool (not hot or cold) water; change pads often; a peri-care bottle to rinse after every void and bowel movement for 2–3 weeks. If infected, the repair can open ( dehiscence ) and heal by secondary intention over weeks to months. Constipation, hemorrhoids Fibre, fluids, activity. Laxatives (softeners, stimulants, osmotics, lubricants) are especially useful on narcotics after a caesarean , and when breastfeeding draws fluid into milk. 3rd/4th-degree tear No rectal medications : no suppositories, no enemas Breasts Engorgement in the first days. Colostrum from day 2 to ~day 4 ; lactose rises at 30–40 h ; milk at 3–5 days . Mastitis risk lasts as long as she feeds ( 6.9 ). Life adjustment Exhaustion, relationship change, stress: “with your first you will think you'll break them no matter what you do.”

entries.t: The Puerperium: What Goes Back, and When
entries.x: The Puerperium: What Goes Back, and When System Change Timing Uterus Uterine vessels obliterated by hyaline change — Cervical canal reforms; 50% of HSIL regress 1 week Corpus involutes to non-pregnant size (cells shrink) 4 weeks Endometrium regresses and regenerates 3 weeks Placental site involutes 6 weeks Lochia : rubra (red) → serosa (rust) → alba (white) Up to 56 days Urinary Diuresis Days 2–5 Dilated ureters and renal pelvis back to normal 2–8 weeks Normal micturition . Early atony, incomplete emptying and UTI are common; stress incontinence improves as estrogen returns. 3 months Blood & fluid Leukocytosis settles First few days Blood volume back to pre-pregnancy 1 week Cardiac output stays up (more venous return from the contracting uterus → ↑ stroke volume) 48 h Cardiovascular changes back to baseline 2 weeks Weight Baby + placenta 5–6 kg; diuresis 2–3 kg; most are at pre-pregnancy weight by 6 months 6 months A hypoestrogenic state. Delivering the placenta drops estrogen and progesterone sharply. Estradiol stays basal until cycling resumes, which links to the insomnia, the urinary symptoms and the milk changes. Slide from the deck.

Sex, Ovulation and Contraception Question What the lecture says When can she have sex? No evidence-based minimum. Most wait for the 6-week visit; it's her preference. Very early intercourse may theoretically raise the risk of endometritis . When does ovulation return? Not breastfeeding: ovulation and menses around 6–8 weeks . Breastfeeding: highly variable , from 6–8 weeks to not until weaning. Either way, ovulation comes before the first period . Lactational amenorrhea? Not to be relied on. Encourage at least condoms. When to start contraception By 6 weeks : after that, everyone should consider herself at risk of pregnancy Which method No estrogen before 21 days (VTE risk is far above baseline). Estrogen may reduce milk quantity and quality; the evidence is weak, but offer progestin-only or barrier methods if she's worried. Barrier, combined hormonal (pill, patch, ring, from 3 weeks), POP, Depo-Provera and IUDs (hormonal or copper) are all options, depending on family planning.

Sleep Why sleep is broken Feeds day and night; the longest gap is 3–4 h , and a feed itself can take 30–60 min Stress, adjusting, worry about the baby Light at night during infant care resets the sleep cycle The hypoestrogenic state (as in menopause) The brain shifts to be more alert to the baby What helps Sleep hygiene: no caffeine or alcohol Don't ruminate: write it down for the morning Can't sleep? Leave the room; do something quiet in dim light (a word search) No blue-light screens 1–2 h before sleep ; dim light for night feeds CBT if persistent · rule out a mood disorder

Postpartum Mood “Blues” Postpartum depression Postpartum psychosis How common Up to 85% 10–20% 1–4 per 1000 Timing Onset days 3–10, peak days 2–4 , self-limited, ≤ 2 weeks Major depression within 6 months of delivery. Suspect if the blues last > 2 weeks or are severe in the first 2. Often alongside another mood disorder Features Weepiness, insomnia, poor concentration, anxiety, irritability, labile mood (“crying over spilled milk”) MSIGECAPS. Severe: poor bonding, suicidal or homicidal ideation Can't tell real from unreal ; can endanger the baby Management Support; resolves Antidepressants, psychiatric assessment, support groups, psychotherapy Urgent psychiatric care, often admission Risk factors Life change, hormones See below Young age, primiparity , family psychiatric history, bipolar or schizoaffective disorder MSIGECAPS M ood (depressed, irritable) · S leep · I nterest lost (anhedonia) · G uilt, worthlessness · E nergy · C oncentration · A ppetite · P sychomotor change · S uicidal ideation PPD risk factors Previous depression (perinatal or not): 30% recurrence · high postnatal stress (NICU, stillbirth, conflict, feeding problems) · poor social and financial support · age < 25 · single · family history of PPD or psychiatric illness · intimate partner violence · unintended pregnancy · perinatal anxiety · perinatal sleep disturbance Screening tools, built into the Ontario antenatal record PHQ-2 : two questions, 0–3 each. ≥ 3 → do the EPDS or PHQ-9. Slide from the deck. GAD-2 for anxiety. ≥ 3 → GAD-7. Slide from the deck. EPDS : 10 items about the past 7 days. Any positive answer to item 10 (self-harm) needs immediate assessment. Slide from the deck. The longer tools compared. The EPDS (10 items, < 5 min) is the one built for the perinatal period. Slide from the deck.

Complications After Discharge Problem Definition / features Management Delayed PPH More bleeding > 24 h postpartum : bright red bleeding returns, ± fever, chills, tender uterus. DDx: endometritis, retained products, infected tear/episiotomy . Antibiotics; ultrasound for RPOC; a uterotonic (misoprostol) for a small piece of tissue vs D&C for a larger one. Retained tissue gets infected, hence the antibiotics. Puerperal infection Temp > 38.0 °C on any 2 of the first 10 days, excluding the first 24 h , taken orally at least QID. The most common postpartum complication; 4% of maternal deaths worldwide. By source: endometritis, UTI (catheter, atony), caesarean or perineal wound, mastitis, pyelonephritis, thrombophlebitis, respiratory (atelectasis, aspiration, pneumonia), necrotizing fasciitis (days 3–5) VTE Raised in pregnancy, greatest postpartum . 0.5–3 per 1000 pregnancies. DVT, PE, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. 9% of maternal deaths. LMWH Endometritis Risk factors Caesarean: 30% if non-elective (in labour), 7% if elective; vaginal 3% · prolonged labour or ROM · multiple cervical exams · internal monitoring (scalp clip, IUPC) · manual removal of the placenta Lethal causes Clostridium sordellii (TSS-like) · C. perfringens (necrotizing endomyometritis) · streptococcal or staphylococcal toxic shock Treatment 1. Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg PO BID × 7–10 d (one drug, twice a day: easy with a newborn) · 2. Cephalexin 500 mg QID + metronidazole 500 mg BID × 7–10 d · 3. Clindamycin + gentamicin IV if septic

The 6-Week Visit The Ontario Perinatal Record has a postnatal page. It covers the birth and baby, feeding, medications, a review of systems (bladder, bowel, intercourse, lochia, menses, perineum or incision, smoking, alcohol, mood, relationships), the PPD screen and the exam. Preventive medicine: flu shot in season · MMR if not given before discharge · tetanus · when is the next Pap? Discuss: the transition to parenthood · contraception · pelvic floor physiotherapy · after a caesarean, the next mode of birth and pregnancy spacing · nutrition and activity (often left to family medicine). Pelvic floor physiotherapy for everyone , antepartum and postpartum. Antenatally it means fewer severe tears and shorter pushing; postpartum, less incontinence and better pelvic-floor rehab. It starts after the 6-week check. “We're failing our patients by not discussing it,” but it's expensive (about $120 first visit, $90 after).

Learning Objectives Define preterm labour, preterm birth, and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. Describe the risk factors for and presentation of patients presenting with threatened preterm labour. Provide a general approach to the patient with threatened preterm labour in terms of assessment, including relevant historical features and physical examination findings. Provide a general approach to the management of patients with threatened preterm labour and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, including the management steps to prepare for possible preterm birth. Dr. Harrison Banner, maternal-fetal medicine, Victoria Hospital. Elentra lists 46 minutes; the five recordings run 37. The whole module follows one patient, Jennifer , from triage to the NICU, and the notes below do the same.

The Case: Jennifer Labour & Delivery triage, Victoria Hospital Jennifer, 25, G3P2, at 29+2 weeks , presents with contractions . Before you walk in: what will you ask, what will you examine, and what will you order? Keep her in mind. Each section below ends where the case picks up again.

Four Terms That Sound Alike Term Definition The key word Term 37+0 weeks and later. 36+6 or earlier is preterm. 37 Threatened preterm labour (TPTL) Signs or symptoms of labour before 37 weeks. May or may not have cervical change; may or may not progress. Symptoms Preterm labour (PTL) Regular contractions with cervical change (dilatation) before 37 weeks — active labour. Cervical change Preterm birth (PTB) Delivery before 37 weeks, spontaneous or iatrogenic (induced or by caesarean for a medical reason). Delivery Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) The amniotic membranes rupture before 37 weeks , before labour starts. Waters, early Prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM) Rupture before contractions start, at any gestation. Banner uses it for rupture at term. Waters before labour Every step can stop. Threatened preterm labour becomes preterm labour only if the cervix changes, and preterm labour becomes preterm birth only if it keeps going. Symptoms can settle at any point, and things can sit still for hours, days or weeks. If she is under 37 weeks and mother and baby are well, nothing is done to push labour along . Slide from the deck.

Why It Happens This is a common presentation that is not well understood mechanistically . We still don't know exactly why labour starts at term, let alone early. Five broad categories: Etiology How it triggers labour Examples Premature activation of the HPA axis (maternal or fetal) The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis is thought to help start normal labour; switching it on early can start labour early Maternal stress; certain (uncommon) fetal anomalies Inflammation and infection Inflammation at the chorion and amnion Subclinical or clinical chorioamnionitis Infection of the fetal membranes (chorion and amnion) and amniotic fluid — an intrauterine infection. ; UTI, and especially pyelonephritis Decidual hemorrhage Blood irritates the membranes and myometrium Placental abruption ( 6.3 ) Pathologic uterine distension Stretch of the uterus is itself a labour trigger Twins or triplets, polyhydramnios, Müllerian anomalies Idiopathic — The majority. Most women presenting in preterm labour have none of the above. The five categories on one slide , with a picture for each: the HPA axis, inflamed membranes (chorioamnionitis histology), a placental abruption, and an overdistended uterus. The same list comes back for PPROM below. How the HPA axis fits into normal labour is in 6.4 . Slide from the deck.

Why It Matters Preterm birth causes perinatal death and major morbidity . It is costly for the health-care system and for the family. Every risk below rises the earlier the baby is born. System Complications of prematurity Respiratory — the system most at risk Respiratory distress syndrome ; apnea of prematurity; bronchopulmonary dysplasia; transient tachypnea of the newborn (milder) Brain Intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding into the lateral ventricles); later cerebral palsy , blindness, deafness, learning disability Gut Necrotizing enterocolitis — may need surgery; can leave strictures Metabolic Glucose abnormalities, especially hypoglycemia Eyes Retinopathy of prematurity — can affect sight for life Infection Neonatal sepsis System-level Long NICU stays to feed and grow → very high cost. So preventing preterm birth saves the health-care system money , as well as lives.

Risk Factors They map onto the etiologies above. A saying in obstetrics: if it happened in one pregnancy, it is more likely in the next. A prior preterm birth does not guarantee another one, but the same underlying cause may carry forward. Group Risk factors History Previous spontaneous preterm birth — first on the list, and among the strongest predictors Demographic Age at both extremes (< 20 and > 35). Non-Hispanic Black race — with socioeconomic confounders : much of the data is American and may reflect access to care rather than race itself. This pregnancy Multifetal gestation (spontaneous and iatrogenic preterm birth); assisted reproduction (IVF etc.); lack of prenatal care ; a short cervix on ultrasound (progressively shortening on serial scans) Infection Cervicitis (gonorrhea, chlamydia), bacterial vaginosis , trichomoniasis, Ureaplasma and Mycoplasma . After a previous preterm birth, the latter two are swabbed for early in pregnancy and treated. Cervix and uterus Cervical surgery: cone biopsy > LEEP (more cervix removed = more risk; abnormal Paps alone add a little); Müllerian anomalies and fibroids Maternal disease Chronic disease — diabetes, hypertension, renal and autoimmune disease, especially if poorly controlled. Connective tissue disease (e.g. Ehlers–Danlos) weakens the cervix → cervical insufficiency A cervix that dilates painlessly in the second trimester without contractions, usually causing second-trimester loss. Treated with a cerclage, a stitch around the cervix. Exposures Smoking and substance use Jennifer's history Two previous vaginal births, both preterm — at 36 and at 32 weeks. Cone biopsy at 20 for high-risk Paps. Smokes 1 pack/day , no other substances. Her obstetrician started vaginal progesterone this pregnancy, which lowers the preterm-birth risk after a prior preterm birth. No contractions before today. Cramping this morning , now regular contractions every 5–10 min, lasting 30–40 s over the last hour. No bleeding, no leaking fluid, no infectious symptoms.

Assessment in Triage Step What you are looking for History Contraction frequency and duration; bleeding (abruption?); leaking fluid (PPROM?); infectious symptoms ; prior preterm births; cervical surgery; smoking and substances; what she is already on (progesterone) Abdomen Leopold's maneuvers for presentation ( 6.4 ); fetal heart rate Cervix Dilatation and consistency — then re-examine . A single exam can't tell threatened labour from true labour without a baseline. Investigations Urinalysis and culture (a UTI irritates the uterus); a GBS swab if the status is unknown; speculum tests and ultrasound if membranes may have ruptured (below) Jennifer's exam Leopold's: cephalic . Cervix 2 cm and soft . Fetal heart rate normal . Still contracting every 5–6 minutes. Is this threatened preterm labour or preterm labour? We don't know her cervix before today, so we can't tell yet. She needs reassessment, and meanwhile we prepare for a possible preterm birth.

Management: The Four Tools Tool Why When / how Hydration (and look for a UTI) Dehydration is a common cause of uterine irritability and TPTL symptoms; so is a UTI IV fluids first; urinalysis and culture Tocolysis Drugs that suppress uterine contractions. They temporize; they do not stop true active labour. Can delay birth by up to 48 h — enough to transfer to a tertiary centre and/or give steroids Indomethacin before 32 wk · nifedipine after 32 wk · terbutaline third-line. Only if rehydration fails. Not given for weeks to reach term. Know that they exist; doses are not needed. Antenatal corticosteroids Speed fetal lung maturity: type II pneumocytes make surfactant → less RDS. Also less IVH and NEC , and lower perinatal mortality . Before 34 weeks. Betamethasone 12 mg IM × 2, 24 h apart (dexamethasone takes 4 doses) Magnesium sulfate Fetal neuroprotection — less cerebral palsy (and neonatal seizures) Birth imminent and before 34 weeks . IV bolus then infusion, running at the time of birth . Penicillin (GBS prophylaxis) GBS rarely causes severe neonatal sepsis, and prematurity raises the risk If GBS-positive, or status unknown and preterm . Started when birth is imminent, ideally ≥ 4 h before it. Penicillin is first-line unless allergic. Why Steroids Have a Window Full benefit comes 48 hours after the first dose (dose 1, dose 2 at 24 h, then another 24 h). It is greatest from 48 h to one week . After a week the benefit fades. So steroids are given when birth within the next week is likely . If it isn't, holding them may be better, because a baby born weeks later gets less from them. No one has a crystal ball, so this is decided by obstetrics and neonatology with the family . Why Magnesium Is Given Late, and Steroids Early Steroids take 48 h to work, so they go in as soon as preterm birth looks likely . Magnesium works fast and must be in the circulation at the moment of birth , so it waits until birth is imminent : the cervix is past about 4 cm , or a caesarean is needed under 34 weeks. How it protects the brain is not well understood . The proposed mechanisms: it steadies fetal blood pressure and cerebral blood flow, blocks excitatory glutamate, and has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. What is known is that it works clinically. Jennifer, continued She gets indomethacin and the first dose of betamethasone . Her contractions space out in triage, so she is admitted to the antenatal ward as threatened preterm labour. The next day you are on call again

Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes PPROM = the waters break before 37 weeks . It carries: A high risk of preterm birth Chorioamnionitis — infection inside the uterus Placental abruption — from the sudden decompression when the membranes rupture Cord prolapse — nothing now separates the baby from the outside. If the head isn't plugging the cervix like a cork in a bottle (a breech or transverse baby), the cord can come down: an emergency needing immediate delivery ( 6.5 ) A longer NICU stay than a baby of the same gestation born with intact membranes Confirming it Diagnosis is history plus examination , the same way as for rupture at term: Test A positive result Pooling on speculum exam A collection of amniotic fluid in the vaginal vault Nitrazine A pH paper test. Amniotic fluid is less acidic than the normal vagina, so the paper changes colour. The paper turns blue : amniotic fluid is less acidic than the normal vagina (pH < 4.5, 4.5 ) Ferning Fluid dried on a slide forms a fern-leaf pattern under the microscope Ultrasound Low amniotic fluid — but not zero . Amniotic fluid is fetal urine , and a healthy baby keeps making it. Not a diagnostic test: amniocentesis looking for bacteria. That is not how rupture is confirmed. Why it happens and what happens next Cause: most cases are thought to be subclinical or overt infection . Inflammation, mechanical stress (distension) and bleeding also weaken the membranes at a biochemical level. That is the same list as preterm labour itself. PPROM before 32 weeks, no intervention Proportion delivered Within 48 hours 50% Within 7 days 75% — only 1 in 4 is still pregnant a week later Management Latency antibiotics if there is no reason to deliver. They are not treating an overt infection. They prolong the pregnancy (more pregnancies reach at least another week), and every extra day of gestation improves the baby's outcome. Victoria Hospital uses the Mercer protocol: 2 days IV, then 5 days oral. In the original trial that was IV ampicillin + erythromycin, then oral amoxicillin + erythromycin. Complete the steroid course. Deliver instead if there is overt infection (chorioamnionitis), abruption or fetal distress. PPROM at 28 weeks, not contracting, afebrile, normal FHR — on admission Give Antenatal corticosteroids (lungs) · latency antibiotics (prolong the pregnancy) Not yet Magnesium sulfate — only when birth is imminent · Penicillin G for GBS — only at delivery · Indomethacin — she isn't contracting Wrong tool Cervical

When Birth Is Imminent Now add Because Magnesium sulfate (she is under 34 weeks and past 4 cm) Neuroprotection — less cerebral palsy IV penicillin (her GBS status is unknown, or positive) Preterm birth is itself a risk factor for GBS disease. The routine swab at 35–37 weeks hasn't happened yet. A negative swab on admission would have made it unnecessary. Outcome Jennifer delivers a vigorous baby six hours later , just over 30 weeks. The baby is stabilized and goes to the NICU for several weeks of feeding and growing, and for managing any complications of prematurity. The gestational-age cut-offs in this lecture Cut-off Preterm vs term 37+0 Antenatal corticosteroids before 34 Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection before 34 (and birth imminent) Indomethacin vs nifedipine for tocolysis 32 PPROM counselling numbers (50% in 48 h / 75% in 7 days) before 32 Cerclage for a shortening cervix before 24

Learning Objectives Explain care through pregnancy for a fetus with poor growth. Identify mechanisms of determining when a fetus may be small. Define SGA vs IUGR. List causes of IUGR. Describe the investigation of IUGR. Dr. Jordan Schmidt, obstetrics, 20 minutes, one recording titled “Fetal Growth Restriction”. The deck and module use IUGR (intrauterine growth restriction); FGR (fetal growth restriction) means the same thing. The four ultrasound measurements are shown in 5.15 .

How a Fetus Is Weighed Nomograms give the expected fetal weight at each gestational age. The estimated fetal weight (EFW) comes from a formula built on four ultrasound measurements. The most common is Hadlock , which uses: Measurement Abbreviation Head circumference HC Abdominal circumference AC Biparietal diameter BPD Femur length FL EFW percentile Label Meaning > 90th LGA — large for gestational age — 10th–90th Normal — < 10th SGA — small for gestational age Smaller than expected; usually still healthy < 3rd — Where the risk of adverse outcomes becomes clinically significant . Some sources reserve “true” growth restriction for this. The weight at each percentile changes a great deal across pregnancy , so a percentile always has to be read against the gestational age. (The recording calls the 10th percentile “two standard deviations below” the mean. It is about 1.3 SD below; −2 SD is roughly the 2nd–3rd percentile. That arithmetic is added here; it isn't on the slides.)

Birth-Weight Categories Neonatology also uses absolute weight cut-offs , because below them a baby struggles to take over jobs the placenta used to do. They are purely weight-based and independent of gestational age. Category Birth weight Why it matters Low birth weight < 2500 g Too little body fat and energy reserve to keep warm, breathe and hold blood sugar easily Very low birth weight < 1500 g Usually needs intensive-care monitoring and management Extremely low birth weight < 1000 g Significant breathing and feeding problems — intubation , IV or nasogastric feeding Weight Categories vs Percentiles A baby born at 24 weeks weighing 600 g is extremely low birth weight, yet may be perfectly average, or even LGA, for 24 weeks . Being born at 35 weeks is premature, but that alone doesn't make a baby SGA. SGA is defined only by a birth weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age. No fixed gram count or week defines it.

SGA vs IUGR SGA IUGR What it is Growth below expected norms A pathological process impairing growth potential Usual cause Normal intrinsic factors — constitutionally small (e.g. petite parents) Maternal, fetal or placental disease (below) Percentile < 10th by definition Usually < 10th, but can be above it The baby Usually healthy, following its own curve At risk — needs surveillance IUGR above the 10th percentile Two previous babies were born at term weighing about 9 lb . The third is born at term at 6 lb . That is a normal term weight on the chart, yet it is well short of this family's genetic potential . That baby may have been significantly growth-restricted.

Finding the Small Fetus The earlier poor growth is recognized, the sooner causes can be addressed and the fetus monitored for distress. Tool How it works Symphysis–fundal height (SFH) — the most common screen Tape measure, pubic bone to uterine fundus, in cm. After 20 weeks, cm ≈ weeks. Within 1–2 cm is acceptable; more than 2–3 cm behind suggests poor growth and prompts an ultrasound. It is far from precise. Ultrasound EFW — the only way to confirm Decides whether the fetus is below the 10th or the 3rd percentile Risk-based surveillance — how most IUGR is actually found Known risk factors, in this pregnancy or a previous one, trigger extra growth scans Scans for a pregnancy at risk of IUGR Timing Routine: dating, first-trimester screen (if wanted), anatomy scan First trimester; 18–20 weeks Added growth scans (the minimum) 26–28 weeks and 34–36 weeks Once IUGR is suspected or found More often , for growth and placental function . How often depends on how severe and how early.

Causes of IUGR Category Examples Mechanism Maternal Hypertension , chronic kidney disease, autoimmune disease (lupus), smoking , substance use; a previous IUGR baby Disturb placental implantation and function — microvascular damage at the maternal–placental interface Fetal Trisomy 21, 18, 13 ; single-gene disorders; translocations; intrauterine infection (CMV, toxoplasmosis); multiple gestation Abnormal genetic material impairs cell replication, so organs grow less; infection damages fetal (and placental) tissue; multiples outstrip the supply, especially near term Placental Abruption ; poor implantation; a chromosomal abnormality confined to the placenta Either the microvasculature is abnormal (small clots from lupus, damage from smoking) or the implantation is disrupted (a patch peeled off by an abruption) Intrinsic vs Extrinsic An intrinsic cause is a problem in the fetal tissue itself. The classic example is trisomy 21 , where abnormal cell division means less tissue mass. An extrinsic cause is imposed from outside by limited nutrient delivery . Smoking and hypertension damage placental microvessels. Multiples compete for one mother's supply. An abruption removes placental surface. The categories overlap: hypertension can cause an abruption, and a placental chromosomal abnormality can impair implantation. Placental insufficiency is the common end-point in most cases. Thyroid: hypo thyroidism does not usually affect fetal growth. Hyper thyroidism can, because the raised metabolic demand consumes resources.

Work-up Question How it's answered Who is at risk? Detailed maternal medical history ; detailed obstetric history — previous babies' sizes and growth patterns Is it chromosomal? Review the enhanced first-trimester screen and NIPT ; offer amniocentesis , especially if nothing was done earlier ( 4.16 ) Is it infection? Maternal serology for toxoplasmosis and cytomegalovirus (IgG and IgM for acute infection), and others as the history suggests How is the fetus coping? (EFW < 10th) Umbilical artery Doppler (placental function) · amniotic fluid volume · non-stress test (fetal heart rate pattern) How often these are repeated depends on how severe the growth restriction is, what the NST and Dopplers show, and the gestational age.

Reading the Umbilical Artery Doppler The umbilical artery carries blood from the fetus into the placenta . As the placental microvasculature is damaged, resistance to that flow rises. The fetal heart can push blood in during systole, but in diastole the forward flow falls toward zero . Stage 1: rising resistance. The end-diastolic flow drops closer to the baseline, and the resistive and pulsatility indices rise . The slide calls these abnormal above the 95th percentile for gestation; the recording says 90th, and the slide is followed here. Slide from the deck. Stages 2 and 3: absent, then reversed. Absent EDF (≈ 50% of the microvasculature damaged): flow stops briefly at the end of each beat while the ventricles refill. Reversed EDF (≈ 70%): resistance is so high that blood is pushed back out of the placenta between beats. Here the risk of fetal death rises sharply. Slide from the deck. Waveform Placental microvasculature affected Raised RI / PI (end-diastolic flow falling) Damage beginning Absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) ≈ 50% Reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) ≈ 70% Why the Fluid Falls Too Severe placental insufficiency means less oxygen and nutrient delivery. Fetal renal blood flow falls , so the fetus makes less urine , and amniotic fluid is fetal urine. So a fetus below the 3rd percentile from placental insufficiency is likely to show absent EDF with oligohydramnios . Normal fluid or polyhydramnios would not fit, and vasa previa has no link to IUGR.

Management: When to Deliver Three things decide it: how severe , how early , and whether the cause is reversible . Catch-up growth doesn't happen in utero. Removing a reversible cause (stopping smoking, treating hypertension) can stop things getting worse and keep the baby on a steady percentile. The fetus's demands only grow, and a placenta that is failing can't keep up. When to deliver a growth-restricted fetus. Drawn for these notes; the deck gives these rules as bullets on one slide. The recording splits the middle band. From 32 to 35 weeks , delivery is usually only for severe placental dysfunction (oligohydramnios, worsening Dopplers). From 35 to 37 the threshold is lower. Before 32 weeks, the recording's examples of distress are persistent reversed EDF , abnormal flow in the fetal brain and liver (signs of failing cardiac function), and an abnormal NST. If it has to be a preterm delivery Why Steroids for lung maturation See 6.1 Transfer to a level II or III centre A severely growth-restricted baby needs NICU and paediatric support Mode by the usual obstetric indications Caesarean is more likely with oligohydramnios or abnormal Dopplers. The placenta has so little reserve that the fetus may not tolerate contractions.

> Musculoskeletal The MSK block: anatomy built around clinical problems, region by region. It starts at the spine and the shoulder, then works out to the rest of the limbs and the rheumatologic diseases.
