Learning Objectives Distinguish acute, subacute and chronic pain, and nociceptive from non-nociceptive pain. Outline the roles of health care providers in chronic pain management: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, kinesiology, psychology. Formulate a management plan for chronic non-cancer pain , including non-pharmacological and pharmacological approaches. Dr. Ricardo Viana (Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation), one 77-minute recording with five knowledge checks. The psychological side (assessment, mood, somatic symptom disorders, CBT) is the companion module, 10.8 .

The Pain Pathway Pain is “an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage”. It's subjective , shaped by past pain and the behaviours learned from it. Transduction, conduction, transmission, perception. In the cord the signal also triggers a withdrawal reflex . From the deck. Fibre Myelin, speed Carries Pain feels Aβ (large) Myelinated, 30–70 m/s Touch, pressure, vibration (“non-nociceptor”) Sharp, well localized Aδ (small) Thinly myelinated, 12–30 m/s Pinprick pain, cold Sharp, well localized C (small) Unmyelinated , 0.5–2 m/s Heat, cold, pressure and chemical pain; warmth Dull, poorly localized, persistent In the dorsal horn the first-order fibre releases glutamate, substance P and CGRP onto the second-order neuron. Its NMDA receptor is normally blocked by a magnesium plug . With constant input, the plug is released and the second-order neuron fires harder than the input warrants: wind-up (central sensitization). The signal then crosses the midline and climbs the spinothalamic tract to the brainstem (reticular formation, periaqueductal grey) and thalamus . Ascending system Route Tells you Lateral Thalamus (VPL) → primary sensory cortex Where the pain is (discriminative) Medial Medial thalamus → limbic system The emotional, motivational “suffering” side, coloured by past pain Wind-up : the Mg²⁺ block lifts and the NMDA receptor amplifies the signal. From the deck. Medial (affect) and lateral (location) systems. From the deck.

Turning Pain Up and Down System How it works Gate control C and Aδ input excites the ascending neuron and inhibits the inhibitory interneuron . Aβ (touch) input activates that interneuron, which damps the ascending neuron. That's why rubbing a bruise helps (and the idea behind TENS). Endogenous opioids Enkephalins, endorphins, dynorphins on μ, δ and κ receptors, found at every level (especially the medial system). They hyperpolarize the pre- and postsynaptic neurons, so it takes more to transmit. Descending inhibition Brainstem nuclei send fibres back to the dorsal horn. Norepinephrine and serotonin are the key transmitters; more of them centrally means more inhibition (the reason TCAs and SNRIs work). Gate control. From the deck. Descending modulation by NE and 5-HT. From the deck.

Acute, Subacute and Chronic Timing Features Acute Seconds; at the same time as the cause Proportional to the cause; nociceptive Subacute Hours to days Hyperalgesia (primary or secondary), allodynia (pain from a non-painful stimulus), spontaneous pain; mostly nociceptive, some neuropathic Chronic > 3 months Persistent; may outlast tissue healing ; strong affective component; mostly neuropathic , some nociceptive Neuropathic pain arises from a lesion (e.g. inflammation) or dysfunction (ectopic firing) of the nervous system itself: spontaneous pain or hypersensitivity, often burning, electric, or pins and needles with numbness . Chronic pain Who What's going on Chronic nociceptive Minority Nociceptors kept firing by ongoing disease ( inflammatory arthritis, OA ). Stays where the disease is. Treat the source; investigate these. Chronic neuropathic / centralized Majority Peripheral and central sensitization ( wind-up , more glutamate receptors); reduced descending 5-HT and NE . The injury has healed, but pain is out of proportion and spreads beyond it. Leads to pain avoidance: “fear of harm” .

entries.t: What Chronic Pain Does to People
entries.x: What Chronic Pain Does to People Depression (5–87% in studies; the recording says up to almost 90% have some low mood), often with somatic symptoms (appetite, sleep, energy, weight). Predictors: pain intensity, number of painful areas, frequency of severe pain , other psychosocial factors. Anxiety : one of the most disabling parts; fear of pain leads to avoidance, then deconditioning and isolation . “It hurts when I move” : avoiding activity relieved the acute pain, so the patient generalizes and avoids anything that might hurt ( operant conditioning ). Pain lifting at work, so avoid work, so less pain: this becomes absenteeism instead of modified duties and treatment. Physical, mood, social and societal effects. The knowledge check's answer is “all of the above”: physical function, social isolation, depression and anxiety, lost work. From the deck.

The Team Chronic pain is best managed by a team : drug, non-drug and interventional options, individual and group rehab, and psychology. Refer to a multidisciplinary pain clinic when the patient isn't responding to standard analgesia, when a review of management might open new options, or when activity, mood or social life are slipping because of pain. Who Role Physicians (anaesthesia, neurology, PM&R, internal medicine, psychiatry) Review investigations and management so nothing's missed; trial medications and interventions; screen mood, activity and isolation and refer on; build a long-term plan for the family doctor Nursing Medication management, help with interventions, documentation, triage Psychology Group and individual therapy for depression and anxiety; CBT , pacing , education for families, acceptance Physiotherapy Prescribes and supervises activity programs; mobility, strength, flexibility; modalities as an adjunct; spinal mobilization; sometimes acupuncture Occupational therapy Activity participation, pacing , ergonomic and activity modification for ADLs, IADLs and work: better biomechanics, not avoidance Kinesiologist General exercise prescription and supervision Chiropractor Spinal manipulation and mobilization (more useful early than chronic), plus activity programs

Non-Drug Management Hurt Does Not Equal Harm In most chronic pain the original injury has healed ; the pain comes from faulty signal processing , not ongoing tissue damage. So activity can't do further harm. Returning to activity, stretching and strengthening desensitizes the system and releases endorphins . A little guided discomfort now buys function later. This education is a core part of treatment. Passive modality Evidence TENS (electrodes around the painful area) Slightly better than placebo, only while it's on; an adjunct Therapeutic ultrasound Not better than placebo in chronic pain Low-level laser No evidence it beats placebo, acute or chronic Acupuncture Eastern = Western; moderately better than placebo , with a short-term gain in function Massage Works with exercise and education ; alone, worse than exercise Spinal manipulation (high velocity, low amplitude) and mobilization (low velocity) Maybe in the first 6 weeks ; no evidence long-term Passive modalities are still popular because patients want something done to them , not because of evidence. Active therapy has good evidence : strengthening, flexibility and cardiovascular work; for spinal pain, core strength and flexibility . It works best individualized and supervised . Yoga (associated with less medication use) and tai chi beat general exercise for back pain; aquafit is another option. “Work hardening” (repetitive work-task drills) doesn't work . Any regular activity beats avoidance. Barriers: fluctuating pain, social support, time and money, and readiness to change.

Medications Drug Use and dose Watch for NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, ketoprofen): COX-1 and COX-2 Mild–moderate pain. Limit to a 2–3 week trial . Upper GI bleed and ulcers , renal toxicity , BP , platelets. Monitor renal function and BP if used longer. COX-2 inhibitors : celecoxib 100 mg daily to 200 mg BID; meloxicam 7.5–15 mg daily Mild–moderate pain. COX-1 protects the gut and platelets; COX-2 drives inflammation. Less GI bleeding, but the same kidney and BP effects Acetaminophen Adult 325–1000 mg every 4–6 h, max 4 g/day ; child 10–15 mg/kg every 4–6 h, max 80 mg/kg/day. Often combined (with tramadol; with oxycodone in Percocet). Mechanism unclear (perhaps central prostaglandin inhibition) TCAs : amitriptyline, nortriptyline Pain and sleep 10–50 mg at night ; mood 100–150 mg Sedation SNRIs : duloxetine , venlafaxine Duloxetine 60 mg for pain (up to 120 for mood); venlafaxine 37.5–225 mg for both Help pain and mood: “two birds, one stone” SSRIs Mood No significant effect on pain alone Gabapentin : blocks the α2δ subunit of presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels, so less glutamate, substance P and CGRP Neuropathic and centralized pain. 900–2700 mg/day divided (300 to 900 mg TID) Sedation : start 100 mg/day, add 100 mg every 4–7 days. Each change takes 1–2 weeks to show. Pregabalin : same target, 6× the affinity 75 mg BID to 300 mg BID Sedation: start 25 mg/day, add 25 mg every 4–7 days Cannabinoids Nabilone (synthetic THC) 0.5 mg daily up to 5 mg/day divided; cannabis 0.5–2 g/day , higher CBD:THC strains. Also helps sleep, maybe anxiety. Don't smoke or vape. Inhaled: onset about 15 min, lasts 1–2 h. Oils and edibles: onset 1–1.5 h, last 4–6 h. Rules for every drug: multimodal (combine classes), adjuvants before opioids , start low and go slow , monitor effect and side effects, use short trials . Norepinephrine is the main pain-modulating transmitter; serotonin can both damp and amplify pain, which is why SNRIs and TCAs beat SSRIs for pain.

Opioids: the START Principle The source for all of this is the Canadian opioid guideline at the National Pain Centre (McMaster). START What it means S hould I start? History (pain, medical, psychosocial, psychiatric, meds, personal and family substance use ), exam, screening tool , urine drug screen , stop benzodiazepines , treatment agreement, informed consent T rial Start low, go slow ; no driving until the dose is stable; watchful dose 90 mg MED/day A 's of monitoring Analgesia, ADLs, Adverse effects, Aberrant behaviour R estrict use Pregnancy, adolescents, the elderly, active psychiatric illness (and history of addiction) T erminate Addiction, misuse, poor effect Before starting Opioid Risk Tool (ORT) , the most used screen (most aren't validated). The strongest items: male, age 16–45, personal or family history of substance abuse (alcohol, illicit or prescription drugs), personal psychiatric history . Opioid addiction prevalence is about 3.3% ; aberrant drug-related behaviour about 11.5% . Urine drug screen at baseline (current use, honesty of the history) and at random (adherence; a negative screen on prescribed opioids suggests diversion ). Point-of-care dips detect classes; lab tests can identify specific drugs. Evidence: opioids beat placebo for pain (medium effect) and function (small effect). For fibromyalgia only tramadol works. Many common pains have no good opioid evidence : headache, IBS, pelvic pain, TMJ, whiplash, non-cardiac chest pain. Informed consent covers short-term effects (nausea, vomiting, constipation, dizziness, itch) and long-term ones: low HPA and HPG axis activity (low libido, amenorrhea or irregular menses, galactorrhea, erectile dysfunction), worse sleep apnea , and opioid-induced hyperalgesia (pain spreading and worsening with dose increases; it eases as the opioid is withdrawn). Treatment agreement , signed by both. The patient won't share or sell, won't get opioids elsewhere, stores them safely, keeps appointments and gives urine samples. The doctor won't refill early and may stop if the agreement is broken. One prescriber, one pharmacy. Benzodiazepines plus opioids means sedation, overdose and worse function (especially the elderly). Taper the benzo off first, or start the opioid lower and slower. Opioid Risk Tool : low 0–3, moderate 4–7, high 8+. From the deck. Where opioids have (and haven't) been shown to work , in trials of at most 3 months. From the deck. Special populations Group Recommendation History of addictio

Clinical Pearls Acute phase: investigate fully and treat the injury (fix the fracture). As soon as it's safe, encourage early low-impact activity , walking and normal ADLs and IADLs. Use analgesics in short trials , multimodal. If activity is limited, isolation is growing, or the patient is becoming dependent on medication, refer to a multidisciplinary pain clinic . Educate throughout: why chronic pain develops and why activity matters. A good patient resource: the YouTube video “Understanding Pain: what to do about it in less than five minutes?”

entries.t: Not on the Site: Quick Facts
entries.x: Not on the Site: Quick Facts Topic The short version Sensory terms (case 5) Allodynia : pain from something that shouldn't hurt (light touch, a sling strap). Hyperalgesia : too much pain from something that should hurt a little. Paraesthesia : abnormal sensation, like tingling or pins and needles, that isn't unpleasant ( dysaesthesia is the unpleasant kind). Hypoaesthesia : reduced sensation. Time off work (case 3) Bed rest slows recovery. Stay active and return to modified duties early (days, not weeks); full heavy work as the pain allows. Chiropractor (case 3) Spinal manipulation gives a small short-term benefit, about the same as other conservative care, for acute mechanical back pain without red flags. Serious harm in the lumbar spine is rare. Avoid it with a neurologic deficit, osteoporosis, cancer or infection. It works best alongside staying active and exercise. Radial nerve care (case 5) Wrist cock-up or dynamic extension splint, range of motion so joints don't stiffen, physio and OT. EMG at about 3–4 weeks (after Wallerian degeneration) to grade it, then again at 3–4 months for reinnervation (brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus recover first). No recovery by about 3–6 months: surgical exploration, nerve grafting, or tendon transfers later. Foot drop after hip replacement (case 6) The sciatic nerve's fibular division is the most often injured nerve in a hip replacement (retraction, stretch from lengthening the leg, haematoma). The fibular head (positioning, tight stockings) and L5 are the other two. Help: an ankle-foot orthosis , calf stretching to prevent an equinus contracture, falls prevention, neuropathic pain medication (gabapentinoid or tricyclic), EMG at 3–4 weeks, and urgent imaging if a haematoma is suspected. Root avulsion clues (case 8) Weak rhomboids (dorsal scapular nerve) or serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve), a raised hemidiaphragm (phrenic), or Horner's (T1) point to a root-level injury. Another clue on nerve conduction is that sensory responses are preserved in a numb area, because the sensory cell bodies sit outside the cord. MRI or CT myelogram shows pseudomeningoceles. Avulsions don't recover, so refer early: nerve transfers work best within about 3–6 months . Meanwhile treat the neuropathic pain, keep the shoulder moving, and swap the figure-8 sling for something tolerable. Other differentials (case 2 Part II) Thoracic outlet syndrome (symptoms with the arm overhead; ulnar side of the hand), brachial plexopa

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Learning Objectives Identify the important functional anatomy of the lower extremity and foot, and the bony landmarks on plain radiographs. Trace the arterial supply and venous drainage and the nerves of the foot, and the consequences of lesions at different levels. Describe the clinical presentation and management of common foot and ankle problems: sprain, tendinopathies, plantar fasciitis, bunions, neuroma and diabetic foot ulcer . List and apply the Ottawa Foot and Ankle Rules to decide on imaging after an injury. Dr. Charys Martin (anatomy) and Dr. Caitlin Cassidy (clinical), about 70 minutes over nine recordings. Each anatomy lesson is followed by a clinical one. Foot muscles get less detail than the hand on purpose: they work as a group to support stance and the arches. It's prep for Tuesday's Knee, Leg, Ankle & Foot lab , with 9.6 , 9.7 Anatomy of the Leg and 9.8 .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Bones of the Foot (Review) The tibia's medial malleolus and the fibula's lateral malleolus grip the talus; the lateral malleolus reaches about 2 cm lower . The seven tarsals, metatarsals and phalanges are covered in 9.7 . The ones that matter most here: the talus (it passes weight from the tibia), the calcaneus (heel; its tuberosity takes the Achilles; its sustentaculum tali is a shelf for the talus and a pulley for flexor hallucis longus), the navicular (anchors the spring ligament) and the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal (fibularis brevis; a sudden inversion can avulse it). Knowledge check: label the bones A calcaneus, B sustentaculum tali, C talus, D navicular, E calcaneal tuberosity, F tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal. The blue bone is the cuboid; the purple ones are the cuneiforms. The tarsals, lettered. Slide from the deck (Netter).

entries.t: Soft Tissue of the Dorsum and Sole
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Soft Tissue of the Dorsum and Sole Thickenings of deep fascia called retinacula strap the tendons down as they cross the ankle, so they don't bowstring. The superior extensor retinaculum runs tibia to fibula. The inferior extensor retinaculum is Y-shaped, with its stem on the calcaneus. The flexor retinaculum holds the deep posterior tendons behind the medial malleolus. Tendon Where Key points Tibialis anterior Dorsum, most medial Broad attachment on the medial foot; dorsiflexes and inverts Extensor digitorum longus Dorsum, lateral to it Splits into 4 tendons to the lateral four toes; works with extensor digitorum brevis Extensor hallucis longus Dorsum, to the big toe Dorsiflexes the ankle and extends the big toe; works with extensor hallucis brevis . The dorsalis pedis pulse is just lateral to it. Tibialis posterior ("Tom") 1st tendon behind the medial malleolus Deepest calf muscle; broad attachment on the medial foot (navicular and more); main dynamic support of the medial arch Flexor digitorum longus ("Dick") 2nd tendon behind the medial malleolus Splits into 4 tendons that pass through a split in flexor digitorum brevis to the distal phalanges of toes 2–5. Quadratus plantae helps it by changing its line of pull. Flexor hallucis longus ("Harry") 3rd tendon, deepest and most posterior Runs in a groove under the sustentaculum tali , crosses under flexor digitorum longus, then passes between the two heads of flexor hallucis brevis and the sesamoids to the big toe The two small dorsal muscles, extensor digitorum brevis (toes 2–4) and extensor hallucis brevis (big toe), both arise from the calcaneus and are supplied by the deep fibular nerve . The sole is built like the palm. The plantar fascia has a thick central part, the plantar aponeurosis , which protects the sole, supports the longitudinal arches and holds everything together . Under it are four layers of muscles that mirror the hand. You only need to know they exist and work as a group to support stance and keep up the arches , most of all at toe-off. The dorsum : retinacula and the three anterior tendons. Slide from the deck (Netter). The long tendons in the sole , and flexor hallucis longus under the sustentaculum tali. Slide from the deck (Netter). The plantar aponeurosis and the four muscle layers under it. Slide from the deck (Netter). Knowledge check: the dissected ankle (medial view) Landmark on the medial malleolus and count the tendons behind it: A tibialis posterior (first), B flexor digitor

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Joints and Ligaments Joint Type and bones Movement Support Talocrural (ankle) Hinge synovial: distal tibia and fibula around the trochlea of the talus Dorsiflexion, plantarflexion Capsule thin in front and behind; collateral ligaments on each side Subtalar (talocalcaneal) Plane synovial: under the talus, on top of the calcaneus The bulk of inversion and eversion Interosseous talocalcaneal ligaments Transverse tarsal Two joints in a line: calcaneocuboid (plane) laterally and the talonavicular part of the talocalcaneonavicular joint (ball and socket) medially Helps with inversion and eversion Plantar ligaments (spring, long and short plantar) Why Sprains Happen in Plantarflexion The talus's trochlea is wider in front than behind . In dorsiflexion the wide part wedges between the malleoli, so the joint is most congruent and stable ("digging in your heels"). With the knee and hip extended too, you can stand quietly without muscle effort. In plantarflexion the narrow part sits in the mortise and the joint wobbles (stand on your toes and feel the invertors and evertors working). So most ankle injuries happen stepping down, foot plantarflexed , rolling into inversion. On the inversion side the ligaments are weak; eversion is blocked by the lower lateral malleolus and the strong deltoid ligament . Ankle ligaments Parts Key points Lateral collateral Three separate bands from the fibula: anterior talofibular , posterior talofibular , calcaneofibular Relatively weak : only minor protection against inversion. The anterior talofibular is the most commonly sprained ligament in the body . Medial collateral (deltoid) Four parts from the medial malleolus that act as one thick sheet : anterior and posterior tibiotalar, tibiocalcaneal, tibionavicular Thick and strong ; stabilizes the ankle in eversion The lateral collateral ligament : three thin bands. Slide from the deck (Netter). The deltoid ligament , with the spring ligament just below it. Slide from the deck (Netter). The talocrural joint : the trochlea is wider in front. Slide from the deck. The subtalar joint : inversion and eversion. Slide from the deck (Netter). Plantar ligament Where Key points Plantar aponeurosis The most superficial layer of the sole If you can see the deep central muscles of the sole, it's already gone. Long plantar ligament Deep , at the level of the bones: calcaneus to the cuboid and the bases of the metatarsals Runs the same way as the aponeurosis, so don't confuse them. Its fibres form a tun

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Arches and Weight Bearing The arches spread the load, absorb shock and act as springboards: they flatten under weight and rebound when it's lifted. Arch Bones Character Supported by Medial longitudinal Calcaneus, talus, navicular, the three cuneiforms, the medial three metatarsals Higher; off the ground in stance. The talar head is the keystone . The spring ligament ; tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior (the main one) and fibularis longus Lateral longitudinal Calcaneus, cuboid, the lateral two metatarsals Much flatter; rests on the ground Foot ligaments Transverse Cuboid, cuneiforms, bases of the metatarsals; medial to lateral The longitudinal arches are its pillars Tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior and fibularis longus (the main one: it loops under the foot and pulls the medial side laterally) The medial arch , its keystone, and pes planus. Slide from the deck. The lateral and transverse arches. Slide from the deck. Where the weight goes. Standing on both feet, half your body weight goes down each tibia to the talus. Half of that goes back to the calcaneus and half forward to the metatarsal heads , mostly the first (through its sesamoids) and the fifth , with a little on the middle three. If the transverse arch falls , the middle metatarsal heads take weight they shouldn't and a callus forms in the middle of the ball of the foot. If the medial arch falls , weight spreads along the whole medial foot. High heels shift load onto the metatarsal heads and strain the fibularis longus tendon as it tries to hold up the transverse arch. Dr. Martin: "life is too short for bad shoes." Weight bearing : heel and metatarsal heads; a normal vs a flat footprint; a high heel. Slide from the deck. Pes planus (flat foot). The acquired kind often follows damage to or degeneration of tibialis posterior . Without it, the talar head drops inferiorly and medially, the spring ligament stretches and the medial arch flattens; the footprint shows the medial arch touching the ground. Usually asymptomatic; orthotics (arch support) and foot exercises if it hurts. See tibialis posterior dysfunction .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Arteries, Pulses and Nerves Artery Course Key points Dorsalis pedis The anterior tibial artery renamed as it crosses the ankle between the malleoli. Branches: lateral tarsal, arcuate (gives dorsal metatarsals 2–4), then the deep plantar artery and the 1st dorsal metatarsal. The deep plantar artery dives between the 1st and 2nd metatarsals to the sole, where it completes the deep plantar arch . Posterior tibial Through the tarsal tunnel with "Tom, Dick and Harry", then splits into the medial and lateral plantar arteries , which run between the 1st and 2nd muscle layers The lateral plantar curves across the foot as the deep plantar arch (most of it), which gives plantar metatarsal then plantar digital arteries, as in the hand. The medial plantar supplies the medial sole and big toe and also feeds the arch. The dorsal foot : dorsalis pedis and its branches. Slide from the deck (Netter). The sole : medial and lateral plantar arteries and the deep plantar arch. Slide from the deck (Netter). Pulse Where to feel it Dorsalis pedis Find the extensor hallucis longus tendon and go just lateral to it, compressing the artery against the tarsal bones. It's the pulse farthest from the heart, so it screens for vascular insufficiency : a weak or absent pulse usually means arterial disease . Posterior tibial At or just below the tarsal tunnel , between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon . Invert the foot slightly to relax the flexor retinaculum. Take both sides at the same time and look for symmetry : pulse strength varies between people. Acute arterial occlusion gives the five P's : pain, pallor, paresthesia, paralysis, pulselessness. A puncture wound in the sole that hits the deep plantar arch bleeds heavily from both ends (rich anastomoses) and is hard to tie off. Venous blood drains from the plantar to the dorsal venous network and leaves via the great and small saphenous veins ; lymph follows the veins, deep vessels mostly to the popliteal nodes. Dorsalis pedis , lateral to extensor hallucis longus. Slide from the deck (Clinically Oriented Anatomy). Posterior tibial , behind the medial malleolus; both sides at once. Slide from the deck. Nerve Motor Skin Superficial fibular (lateral compartment) The evertors (in the leg) Lateral leg and ankle and most of the dorsum of the foot Deep fibular (anterior compartment, with dorsalis pedis) The dorsiflexors and the dorsal foot muscles (extensor digitorum and hallucis brevis) Only the first web space Medial plantar (f

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Achilles Tendinopathy and Rupture Achilles tendinopathy Who Common in runners , especially after an increase in training Presentation Pain at the posterior heel , just above or right at the calcaneal insertion; tender ; worse with passive dorsiflexion (stretching it), as in other tendinopathies Education Very important : set expectations for a long, slow improvement that takes consistent effort Non-pharm Activity modification (cut back the extra distance); footwear with no pressure on the insertion ; a heel wedge , cautiously (it takes tension off early on, but long-term use can shorten the tendon ); physio: stretching, eccentric strengthening (realigns the collagen), friction massage, extracorporeal shockwave therapy Pharm NSAIDs (topical or oral), especially when acute; possibly a topical nitroglycerin patch (more blood flow) Surgery Rare Rupture. Most common in active people in their 30s–40s , and increasingly in older people who stay active. Surgical repair and conservative treatment (cast or air-cast boot) are both reasonable. Surgery has a slightly lower re-rupture risk but adds surgical complications: infection, wound problems, scarring, sural nerve injury . Involve the patient : a highly active patient may lean toward surgery; a less active one toward conservative care.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Plantar Fasciitis The plantar fascia protects the sole, supports the arches and holds everything together, which is a lot of work. When it's under too much tension, too often, it develops chronic inflammation at its insertion on the calcaneus. Plantar fasciitis Presentation Pain at the anteromedial calcaneus on the first steps in the morning , and again with ongoing activity. Typically 40–60 years old, F>M . Exam Tender at the medial plantar calcaneus; worse with passive dorsiflexion ; often a tight Achilles (less dorsiflexion range) Education Long, slow improvement; it can become chronic or recurrent Non-pharm Cushioned heel pad; heel lift or wedge (not long term); shoes with good arch support ; weight loss ; physio: plantar fascia and calf stretching , and strengthening the dynamic arch stabilizers (tibialis posterior, the foot's intrinsic muscles) so the fascia does less; night splints or a Strassburg sock to stretch it overnight Pharm Oral NSAIDs if severe; rarely a corticosteroid injection (painful) Surgery Very, very rarely a surgical release Knowledge check A 53-year-old woman with heel pain that's worst first thing in the morning and with activity: which treatment would you not recommend? → two weeks of full-time air-cast boot . That's too much rest for a problem that gets better with active therapy. Achilles stretching, night splints, NSAIDs and weight loss (if appropriate) are all reasonable.

entries.t: Ankle Sprains, Ottawa Rules and Fractures
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Ankle Sprains, Ottawa Rules and Fractures A sprain is a ligament injury; a strain is a muscle or tendon injury. Up to 85% of sprains are lateral : the foot twists into inversion while plantarflexed , for example landing from a jump onto someone's foot or stepping in a hole. The ligaments go in order anterior talofibular > calcaneofibular > posterior talofibular . Each can be anything from stretched to partly or fully torn; when all three are fully torn, the ankle dislocates . Medial (deltoid) sprains are much less common, for example catching the foot on turf during a kick. Exam : swelling, ecchymosis , tenderness over the ligaments; the anterior drawer test (hold the leg, pull the foot forward) checks the anterior talofibular ligament. Do we image? Use the Ottawa rules. The Ottawa Foot and Ankle Rules. Practise palpating A–D in clinical skills. Slide from the deck. X-ray series Pain in Plus any one of Ankle The malleolar zone A bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus (lowest 6 cm); B the same on the medial malleolus ; or inability to bear weight (4 steps) both immediately and in the ED Foot The midfoot zone C tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal ; D at the navicular ; or inability to bear weight (4 steps) both immediately and in the ED Knowledge check A 22-year-old landed awkwardly playing basketball this morning: lateral ankle pain, swelling, early bruising, tender only around the anterior talofibular ligament, and she walks into your office (painfully). X-ray? → No. No malleolar tenderness and she can bear weight, so the Ottawa rules are negative. Start conservative management of a likely lateral sprain. Sprain management Education Most improve on their own, but ligaments heal slowly; discuss how to avoid recurrence Non-pharm RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation), brief immobilization only if needed, early mobilization ; physio for strengthening and proprioception . Bracing and taping help early, but the ankle shouldn't come to rely on them. Pharm Analgesics as needed: acetaminophen, NSAIDs Surgery Rare: ligament reconstruction for ongoing instability despite conservative care When it's not just a sprain What it is Management Unimalleolar One malleolus fractured (here the lateral) May be non-operative (boot or cast), depending on whether the talus is stable Bimalleolar Medial and lateral malleoli; usually forceful eversion (per the slide) Typically surgical Trimalleolar Both malleoli plus the posterior malleolus

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Tibialis Posterior Dysfunction Tibialis posterior holds up the arch, so when it fails, the problems spread from the foot up the leg. Its tendon is hypovascular just distal to the medial malleolus (like the rotator cuff where it rubs over bone): it's prone to injury there and heals poorly, so the damage tends to keep going. Contributing factors: trauma, steroid use, inflammatory arthritis, obesity, diabetes . 1 Medial ankle pain ± swelling A strained, irritated tendon. 2 Mild, then significant weakness It hurts to use, and stops working in a coordinated way. 3 Flexible pes planus The arch drops but can still be popped back up on exam. 4 Rigid flat foot deformity Left too long, the foot stays flat and can't be corrected. "Too many toes" sign : stand behind the patient. Normally only a couple of toes peek out lateral to the heel. On the affected side the hindfoot falls into valgus and the forefoot swings out, so you see too many toes . (The slide's photograph is described rather than shown.) Management Education Address risk factors: weight loss, glucose control Non-pharm RICE in the swollen phase; physio to strengthen tibialis posterior and the other arch stabilizers ; orthoses : a foot orthotic (in the shoe; can prop up a flexible flat foot) or an ankle-foot orthosis (plastic up the back of the calf, a longer lever to control an ankle that has drifted into valgus). Corrective if the deformity is still flexible, accommodative once it's rigid. Pharm NSAIDs if needed (acute, swollen phase) Surgery Various procedures depending on how valgus and how rigid the foot has become

entries.t: Bunions, Morton's Neuroma and the Diabetic Foot
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle
entries.x: Bunions, Morton's Neuroma and the Diabetic Foot Bunion (hallux valgus) Morton's neuroma What The 1st MTP joint points toward the midline while the toe angles away from it ( valgus ) Perineural fibrosis (thickening) of a common digital nerve , usually between the 3rd and 4th metatarsals Why Multifactorial: footwear (partly why it's commoner in women) and anatomy ( metatarsus varus , which the toe compensates for). Can cause secondary toe deformities. Middle age, F>M; worse in high heels with narrow toe boxes , which load and squeeze the metatarsal heads Symptoms Pain at the medial 1st MTP and the tops of the toes in a tight shoe; poor toe-off, so the other toes work harder Burning dysesthesia in the ball of the foot; worse with walking, better with rest Exam Is the deformity flexible or not? Squeezing or palpating reproduces it; maybe sensory loss between or at the tips of the toes; no motor findings (digital nerves are purely sensory) Treatment Educate: treat early and consistently to avoid surgery. Toe spacers or positioning ( only if it's flexible ); a wider toe box . Little pharmacology (maybe a topical NSAID or acetaminophen; it isn't very inflammatory). Surgical realignment if function or pain is significant. Educate and give ownership. Lower heels , a wider, taller toe box , a metatarsal pad in an orthotic (shifts pressure off the metatarsal heads). Neuropathic pain agents, a steroid injection ; surgical excision . Knowledge check Shoe advice for Morton's neuroma or hallux valgus? → a wider toe box . It takes pressure off the medial 1st MTP (bunion) and off the squeezed metatarsals (neuroma). A bigger shoe, looser laces, a more flexible upper or a stiffer sole don't address the problem. The diabetic foot. Microvascular disease starves the skin and extracellular matrix and keeps the healing "soup" of white cells and macrophages from reaching injuries. It also starves the nerves: diabetic neuropathy hits the longest nerves first , so it starts in the feet. Can't feel your feet (sensory): shoes too small, cold without boots, banging the feet without noticing. Dry, cracked skin (autonomic): sweating is lost. Can't move them normally (motor): the intrinsic muscles weaken, the arches and shape change, and new bony prominences take pressure. The joints can break down: a Charcot (neuropathic) arthropathy . From diabetes to a foot ulcer. Slide from the deck (Armstrong 2017). Diabetic foot ulcers are a major complication, in about 15% of people with diabetes.

Learning Objectives Describe the basic principles of fracture management . Describe the unique principles of managing open fractures and their potential complications. Describe significant complications of fractures and fracture care: VTE, compartment syndrome, nonunion and malunion, AVN, heterotopic ossification and post-traumatic arthritis. Three recordings (44 min): management and complications by Dr. Caitlin Cassidy (content from Drs. C. Del Balso and V. Kalia), and fracture healing by Dr. Vishal Kalia, which finishes his 10.4 Fracture Radiology talk. The deck warns of graphic surgical photos; they're left out here.

Goals and the Five Steps Management aims to restore anatomy (length, alignment, rotation, translation), allow early motion (avoiding the complications of immobility), avoid complications of poor healing and improve function . 1 Resuscitate ABCs first. Bones bleed, and sharp bone ends can injure vessels. 2 Reduce Get the bone ends roughly back in line (not needed if non-displaced). Open = in the OR, under anaesthesia, seeing the fracture. Closed = without seeing the fragments, often in the ED. 3 Maintain the reduction Internal fixation (plates, screws, pins, nails; ORIF = open reduction, internal fixation), an external fixator , or a cast or splint . 4 Post-reduction x-rays Check that the reduction is adequate (ortho has criteria you don't need to know) and that it's being held . 5 Rehabilitate As much movement as is safe, as soon as possible. Protect weight bearing as ortho directs. PT and OT for mobility and daily tasks. Prevent contractures . Closed reduction, step by step Why Analgesia and sedation A tense patient splints the fracture with their muscles, and it won't reduce Longitudinal traction , exaggerating the deformity Unlocks overlapping or impacted fragments: “make it worse before you make it better” (finger traps for a wrist) Reverse the deformity while keeping traction Pressure on the right sides pushes the fragments back into line Immobilize in a well-moulded cast Moulding while the cast dries improves and holds the reduction Post-reduction x-rays Confirm the reduction and that it's maintained Open or closed? It depends on the fracture's type and location, how displaced it is, whether it's open, and whether the patient is stable enough for surgery (including other, more life-threatening injuries). An external fixator suits a patient who needs the fracture held but can't have a cast (swelling, skin) or isn't a good surgical candidate. Internal fixation : a plate on a distal radius; an intramedullary (IM) nail in a femur. From the deck. Initial, post-reduction, post-moulding : alignment improves at each step. From the deck.

Open Fractures An open fracture is one where the bone or its hematoma is exposed to the outside through traumatic violation of skin and soft tissue (NIH). Any fracture with a wound, even one some distance away, is open until proven otherwise : even a tiny wound over an ankle fracture can connect to it. Open fractures have more complications ( infection above all, plus nonunion and delayed union ) and more incomplete recovery. Higher-energy injuries mean more tissue damage, contamination and devitalized bone. The goal: turn an unstable, contaminated wound into a stable, clean environment that can heal. In the ED (right away) In the OR (early surgery) Early IV antibiotics Debride : remove all devitalized tissue, including bone fragments Tetanus prophylaxis (update or booster) Irrigate gently with sterile saline Stabilize as well as you can while you wait for ortho (closed reduction and splint) Stabilize definitively with whatever suits the fracture (an external fixator if contamination is heavy) Close the soft-tissue envelope early: direct closure at the ORIF if possible, otherwise a plastic surgery flap , sometimes delayed The module's case: an open tibia A 34-year-old jumps from a moving car; bone shows through a large anterior wound on the leg. Film: open, spiral fracture of the distal third of the tibial diaphysis , mildly displaced: shortened , posterior translation of the distal fragment, apex-lateral angulation (see 10.4 ). ED: cefazolin 2 g IV , tetanus, reduce and splint. OR: debridement, saline irrigation, an intramedullary nail , and, with little contamination and little tissue removed, direct closure at the same operation. The case's films : spiral distal-third tibial fracture. From the deck; the wound photo is left out. After surgery : a locked IM nail. From the deck.

How Fractures Heal Primary (contact) healing Secondary (spontaneous) healing When Bone surfaces held directly apposed : rigid internal fixation Everything else, including casts. Most fractures. On x-ray No callus ; alignment unchanged Callus forms through the stages below Stages of secondary healing , from inflammatory to reparative to remodeling. From the deck. Stage What happens What the x-ray shows Cellular Hematoma draws in macrophages; granulation tissue forms The fracture line Vascular Revascularization and bone resorption at the fracture ends The line widens (10–14 days) . That's healing, not a worse fracture. Primary callus Fibrocartilage bridges the gap Not yet visible (uncalcified) Bony callus Osteoblasts make hard callus : periosteal callus bridges around the outside, endosteal callus across the middle Visible callus from about 2 (2–3) weeks Mature callus Remodeling into compact bone Radiological union : mature bridging callus, cortex and medullary cavity re-established Healing is a clinical diagnosis: no tenderness, no movement at the fracture site, and the patient can bear weight. Region Time to union Slowest Upper limb 3–10 weeks (e.g. a simple fracture 3–6, proximal humerus 4–8) Distal humerus , 8–10 weeks Lower limb 6–12 weeks (weight bearing slows it) Femoral neck and shaft Knowledge check: the wider line at day 7 A closed, casted distal radius fracture looks slightly wider on the 7-day film, with no new angulation or translation and no new pain. That's early fracture healing (resorption at the fracture ends). It's too early to call nonunion, infection is unlikely in a well patient with a closed fracture, and the unchanged alignment means the reduction has held. Primary healing : K-wired phalanx, no callus. From the deck. Secondary healing : a lateral malleolus fracture, then fully remodeled years later. From the deck.

Thromboembolic Disease Most orthopaedic trauma patients have all of Virchow's triad : endothelial injury, stasis, hypercoagulability. Extra risk factors Prevention Multiple injuries; spinal cord or head injury ; lower-limb or pelvic fracture ; older age; prolonged surgery or a long wait for surgery Mechanical: intermittent pneumatic compression; an IVC filter stops emboli reaching the lungs but does not prevent clots . Chemical: ASA or LMWH , the two most used in trauma. Choose for the patient: with an intracranial bleed , lean on mechanical methods.

Compartment Syndrome Pressure inside a closed fascio-osseous space rises past what its contents can tolerate. After a tibial fracture, blood and swelling fill a compartment whose fascia can't stretch far, until blood can't flow in or out. The most metabolically active tissues, muscle and nerve , suffer first: injury begins within about 2 hours of ischemia. Cell death brings inflammation and leaky capillaries, which pour in more fluid and raise the pressure further: a vicious cycle. It's most common in the leg and forearm . The leg's four compartments (see 9.7 ). From the deck. Causes Examples External A cast too tight for the swelling; direct pressure (lying on the limb); circumferential burn eschar , which acts like a cast Internal Hematoma ; fluid leak (extensive burns, after reperfusion of a vascular injury); crush injury Sign When Pain out of proportion to the injury (“POOP”): escalating opioid needs, pain uncontrolled even after fixation Early: the key sign Pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles Early: the key sign Paresthesia Mid Paralysis Very late, often irreversible Pulselessness Not typical. Pulses are usually still there late; if they're gone, “you've 100% missed the boat”. Which Stretch Hurts Passive stretch lengthens the muscles on the other side of the joint. Passive plantarflexion stretches the anterior compartment (the dorsiflexors); passive dorsiflexion stretches the posterior compartments. In the forearm, passive wrist and finger extension stretches the anterior (flexor) compartment. Dr. Cassidy points out that the slide has the leg pair backwards. It's a clinical diagnosis. If the picture fits, no test is needed: urgent call to ortho , because it's limb-threatening. Measure pressures only when the patient can't tell you: uncooperative, obtunded or sedated , or a young child. The lecture's cut-offs: diastolic BP minus compartment pressure < 20 mmHg , or an absolute pressure > 30 mmHg . While you wait: call ortho, remove casts and tight dressings , elevate, cool the limb (lowers its metabolic demand), monitor closely. Definitive: fasciotomy (open the fascia), with delayed closure.

Nonunion and Malunion Term Definition Delayed union Healing takes about twice as long as expected (Dr. Kalia) Nonunion No healing in twice the expected time (Dr. Cassidy), or in 6–9 months (Dr. Kalia). You often need the history (“this was two years ago”) to call it. Malunion Healed, but in an abnormal position or alignment Nonunion type Looks like Points to Atrophic No significant bone formation ; the fracture lines still clear years later Impaired biology : nutrition, metabolic problems, smoking Hypertrophic Lots of bone , but none bridging the gap Not enough stability Infected Infection Managing nonunion: improve stabilization (especially if hypertrophic); biologic activation (fix nutrition and metabolic problems, stop smoking, bone graft to bring in living bone); eradicate infection (irrigation, debridement, antibiotics); then surgical reconstruction . Managing malunion: assess the deformity in every plane (shortened, angulated, rotated, translated?), then the patient : is it hurting comfort or function, now or later? If so, an osteotomy (cut the bone, remove some if needed, realign and fix it). Nonunion (two years on) and malunion . From the deck. Atrophic (no new bone) vs hypertrophic (bone everywhere, no bridge). From the deck.

entries.t: AVN, Post-Traumatic Arthritis and Heterotopic Ossification
entries.x: AVN, Post-Traumatic Arthritis and Heterotopic Ossification Complication Key facts Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) Bone death from lost blood supply, most common where supply is already poor: the femoral head , scaphoid and talus , which all have a retrograde blood supply . Presents with pain ; visible on x-ray once enough bone is lost. Management is surgical . (Talar body AVN follows a talar neck fracture.) Post-traumatic arthritis OA after a peri-articular fracture . Uncommon after hip and knee fractures but very common after ankle fractures (>50%) . Pain, especially weight bearing, and stiffness; the x-ray looks like OA. Manage like OA: analgesia, PT, then surgery if all else fails. Heterotopic ossification Bone forming where it shouldn't (e.g. in muscle). Risk factors: polytrauma (around fracture sites), head injury , burns over 30% TBSA . Joints at risk: hip, knee, elbow . Causes stiffness , up to ankylosis ; early on, redness, swelling and tenderness. X-ray and CT are negative early (not yet calcified); a bone scan picks it up. Control pain and inflammation; excise only once mature , or it grows back. Knowledge check: the 64-year-old's ankle Five years of activity-related ankle pain, relieved by rest, mild end-of-day swelling; the films show arthritis. The answer is post-traumatic arthritis : she had an ankle fracture treated without surgery 40 years ago. Primary OA is common in the hip and knee but uncommon in the ankle , and the films show no heterotopic bone or talar AVN. AVN : femoral head, talus, scaphoid. From the deck. Post-traumatic ankle arthritis : no joint space, sclerosis, osteophytes. From the deck.

Learning Objectives Describe fractures with a systematic approach: the views provided, then location, complexity, pattern, displacement or deformity, joint surface involvement and other findings. List specific views that help identify and characterize fractures or dislocations of particular bones and joints. Define typical timelines for fracture healing and the basic appearance of a healing fracture on x-ray (covered in 10.5 ). Dr. Vishal Kalia's module (58 min): three recorded parts and four knowledge checks. His other Week 10 talk is 10.1 Lower Limb Radiology ; for the upper limb views see 9.1 .

The Approach Three principles guide the read: know the anatomy (which bone, which side), follow the cortex (the bright white outline; a break or step is the fracture) and look for joint extension , usually signalled by a joint effusion . Everything is described with the body in the anatomic position (palms forward), using medial/lateral, proximal/distal and anterior/posterior. OLD ACIDS What to say O pen or closed Does the fracture communicate with the skin? A clinical call, with x-ray clues ( below ) L ocation Which bone, which side, and where in the bone D egree Complete or incomplete A rticular surface Intra- or extra-articular; step or depression; subluxation or dislocation C omminution / type Transverse, oblique, spiral, longitudinal, comminuted (butterfly, segmental) I ntrinsic bone quality Normal bone, osteopenia, or a lesion (pathological fracture) D isplacement Angulation, translation, rotation, distraction, impaction, override S oft tissues Swelling, effusion, air, foreign body Most fractures need more than one descriptor . A worked example from the recording: “AP view of the right hand: complete transverse fracture of the shaft (diaphysis) of the 4th metacarpal” , then add displacement, angulation and joint involvement.

Views The standard set for any bone is AP, oblique and lateral . You need them all: an oblique proximal-phalanx fracture in the module is plain on the oblique view and invisible on the lateral , and a spiral fracture only declares itself across views. Special views vary by body part; three are named: Special view Why Ankle mortise An AP with internal rotation that opens the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis , which the plain AP overlaps. A widened syndesmosis means a significant ankle injury that most likely needs surgical fixation . Y-view (shoulder) The scapular spine, the coracoid and the scapular blade make a Y ; the humeral head should sit centred on the glenoid where the limbs meet. Off-centre anteriorly or posteriorly = a dislocation, including subtle ones. Scaphoid views PA in ulnar deviation and the clenched-fist view, to show the scaphoid (see 8.8 ) Mortise (left) vs AP (right). The mortise opens the tibiofibular joint. From the deck. Y-view : the humeral head should centre on the Y. From the deck.

Location Name the bone , the side and where in the bone . In a child, an immature skeleton is one where you can still see the growth plates; once they fuse (adult), drop the physis and just say epiphysis, metaphysis or diaphysis. Region What it is Epiphysis The end of the bone, carrying the articular surface Physis (growth plate) Makes new bone and lengthens it; a lucent line until it fuses Metaphysis The flared part next to the physis. Fractures where it meets the shaft are often called metadiaphyseal . Diaphysis The shaft Apophysis A non-articular bony prominence where muscles or tendons attach, under big traction forces, e.g. the calcaneal tuberosity (it looks a little sclerotic normally) Small bones also take their anatomic names: a metacarpal has a head, neck, shaft and base . “Shaft” and “diaphysis” are both fine. Immature ankle : epiphysis (blue), physis (black line), metaphysis (red), diaphysis (green). From the deck. Calcaneal apophysis , immature (left) vs mature (right). Radiopaedia, via the deck.

Types Group Type What it looks like Complete (right through the bone) Transverse A straight line across the bone Oblique An angled line across the bone Spiral From a twisting injury; winds round the bone. Looks oblique on one view , so get more views. May have a butterfly fragment . Longitudinal (linear) Runs along the length of the bone; check whether it reaches the joint Comminuted More than two fragments. Two named kinds: butterfly (a triangular wedge broken off between the main fragments) and segmental (a whole length of shaft separated by fractures above and below) Incomplete (children's bones) Bowing The bone bends and stays bent; no fracture line Buckle (torus) The compressed cortex crumples into a bulge Greenstick The convex (tension) cortex breaks; the other side only bends Salter–Harris Fractures involving the growth plate of an immature skeleton Others Avulsion and open fractures ( below ) Fracture patterns on a femur. Hernando Orthopedics, via the deck. Transverse : 4th metacarpal shaft. From the deck. Oblique : seen on the oblique view, not the lateral. From the deck. Spiral : oblique-looking on the AP, spiral on the oblique. From the deck. Longitudinal : 5th metacarpal, into the base. From the deck. Comminuted distal radius, reaching the joint. From the deck. Butterfly fragment (green), humeral shaft. From the deck. Segmental humeral fracture: a whole segment (blue) is detached. From the deck.

Displacement Rule: describe the distal fragment relative to the proximal one. The exception is the clavicle , where the proximal fragment is described relative to the distal, because the neck muscles pull the proximal fragment up. Strictly, “displacement” covers four components (angulation, translation, rotation, distraction), but in everyday reports “displaced” means translated . Descriptor How to describe it Angulation By the direction the apex points (or the way the distal fragment is angled). Varus = apex lateral, distal fragment toward the midline. Valgus = apex medial, distal fragment away from the midline. Also “apex dorsal”, “apex cranial” and so on. Translation (“displacement”) The ends shifted sideways off each other, measured in shaft widths (“half a shaft width medially”). More than one width = off-ended. Rotation The distal fragment turned internally or externally . Hard to see; you need the joints above and below on the film and the anatomic position in your head. Often left out of routine reports. Distraction A gap : the fragments pulled apart along the long axis. Give the maximum gap in mm. Impaction Fragments driven into each other : no gap, bone foreshortened , “telescoped in” Override Foreshortened like impaction, but the fragments overlap side by side (in mm) Varus vs Valgus Without the Panic Look only at the distal fragment. If it points back toward the midline , that's varus (think bow-legged genu varum: the shins come back in). If it points away from the midline , that's valgus (knock-kneed genu valgum, hallux valgus). The apex is always on the opposite side from where the distal fragment points. Varus vs valgus. University of Virginia, via the deck. The slide's “distal fragment” lines are reversed; see the note at the bottom. Translation : distal radius fragment shifted laterally. From the deck. Off-ended : more than one shaft width. From the deck. Impaction vs distraction. From the deck. Distraction : a gap. From the deck. Impaction : telescoped, proximal humerus. From the deck. Override : shortened, with overlapping fragments (about 5 mm here). From the deck.

Joint Involvement Intra-articular Extra-articular Joint surface Involved Spared Reduction Must be anatomic Can be relatively anatomic Healing Slower : synovial fluid bathes the fracture and the joint keeps it moving The bone remodels , especially with weight bearing Long term Risk of secondary OA , faster Lower Step or depression: say how far the articular surface is stepped. For most joints, more than 2 mm matters, because it may need surgical reduction and fixation. Secondary signs: when the line isn't visible, an effusion or a fat-fluid level still tells you the fracture reaches the joint. Marrow fat leaks into the joint with the blood ( lipohemarthrosis ) and floats on top as a straight line. Occult fracture: treat it as a fracture and re-image in 1–2 weeks . Bone resorbs along the fracture line in early healing, so it becomes visible. Subluxation vs dislocation: subluxation = surfaces still partly in contact; dislocation = completely out. Name it by where the distal bone has gone (e.g. a posterior elbow dislocation ). Articular involvement with a small step (radial head). From the deck. Fat-fluid level : an intra-articular fracture you can't see. From the deck. Posterior elbow dislocation : the incongruent joint. From the deck.

Other Findings Finding What to know Open fracture The fracture communicates with the skin, so it's a clinical diagnosis. On the film, suspect it with a skin defect , bone poking through, or air in the soft tissues . Management is in 10.5 . Periprosthetic A fracture around a prosthesis (e.g. along the stem of a hip replacement). Describe it like any other, relative to the hardware. Avulsion A bone fragment pulled off where a tendon or ligament attaches , so you have to know what attaches there. Example: a dorsal triangular fragment at the base of the distal phalanx , where the extensor tendon inserts (mallet finger). Amputation Give the level (e.g. 4th digit at the middle phalanx) Diastasis Widening or incongruence of a joint , with or without a fracture: the pubic symphysis , the AC joint , the scapholunate gap, the ankle syndesmosis Open tibia and fibula fractures. Radiopaedia, via the deck; the wound photograph is left out. Avulsion at the extensor insertion (mallet finger). From the deck. Periprosthetic fractures. From the deck. Diastasis of the pubic symphysis. Wikipedia, via the deck.

Bone Quality Always look at the bone the fracture runs through. A pathological fracture happens in weakened bone : it's usually transverse and comes spontaneously or with trivial trauma (the patient may not remember an injury). Causes: a bone tumour , benign or malignant (see 10.6 ), osteopenia or osteoporosis , metabolic bone disease, or diffuse marrow disease such as lymphoma. In a child, also say whether it reaches the growth plate. Pathological fracture : a transverse fracture through a lucent lesion in a child's distal radius metaphysis. Radiopaedia, via the deck.

Putting It Together The module's practice film: a clavicle Location: midshaft of the left clavicle. Type: complete, oblique. Descriptors: the proximal fragment is displaced cranially by more than a bone width (the clavicle exception), with apex-cranial angulation. What the knowledge checks test That segmental and butterfly fractures are the comminuted ones (spiral, greenstick and oblique are not); that an intra-articular fracture shows both an effusion and a fat-fluid level; and that the clavicle is the one bone where the proximal fragment is described. Healing (the deck's last item): most fractures heal by secondary (callus) healing, and primary healing happens only with rigid internal fixation. Timelines and the x-ray stages are in 10.5 .

entries.x: > Week 10 The lower limb finishes and the clinical topics take over. Monday reads hip, knee and ankle x-rays; grades and localizes nerve injuries (neurapraxia to neurotmesis, root vs nerve, what an EMG can tell you); and works through the ankle and foot: the joints, ligaments, arches and pulses, then sprains and the Ottawa rules, Achilles and plantar fascia problems, tibialis posterior dysfunction, bunions, Morton's neuroma and the diabetic foot. Tuesday describes fractures on x-ray (OLD ACIDS), manages them (reduction, open fractures, healing, compartment syndrome and the other complications) and works up a soft tissue lump without the “whoops” of shelling out a sarcoma. Thursday is chronic pain: wind-up and central sensitization, active vs passive therapy, the drugs and the opioid START principle, then the psychology (fear-avoidance, mood, somatic symptom disorders, CBT). Friday turns to children (growth plate fractures and Salter–Harris, the elbow's ossification centres, apophysitis, DDH, clubfoot, normal leg shapes, the limping child and scoliosis) and then to exercise as medicine: the guidelines, intensity, contraindications and writing a FITT prescription. Monday Nov 2 Lower limb x-rays, nerve injury, then the foot and ankle. 10.1 Lower Limb Radiology The systematic read and TIMS-C; the hip series, Shenton's line and the AP pelvis lines, femoral neck fracture, arthroplasty and OA; the knee's AP, lateral and skyline views, Blumensaat's line, effusions and lipohemarthrosis, bipartite patella, TKA and ACL reconstruction; the ankle mortise, Kager's fat pad, malleolar fractures, spurs and enthesophytes → 10.2 Nerve Injury Nerve layers; neurapraxia, axonotmesis and neurotmesis, Wallerian degeneration and 1 mm a day; radiculopathy vs mononeuropathy, dermatomes and myotomes, the numb thumb (carpal tunnel or C6); what nerve conduction and needle EMG can and can't show; foot drop at the fibular head vs L5; the three practice questions → 10.3 Clinical Approach to the Foot & Ankle Tendons of the dorsum and sole; the talocrural, subtalar and transverse tarsal joints; the lateral and deltoid ligaments and the spring ligament; the arches and weight bearing; arteries, pulses and the foot's nerves; Achilles tendinopathy and rupture, plantar fasciitis, ankle sprains, the Ottawa rules and malleolar fractures, tibialis posterior dysfunction, bunions, Morton's neuroma and the diabetic foot → DSSG Nerve & Soft Tissue Injury: Review Sheet Dr. Cassidy's eight cases (ulnar n

Learning Objectives Identify the important functional anatomy of the lower extremity as it pertains to clinical presentations of leg pathology. Identify the bony landmarks of the lower extremity and relate them to their appearances on plain radiographs . Dr. V. Kalia's interactive module, scheduled for 20 minutes (the title says about 45): general concepts, then the hip, knee and ankle. There are no recordings. It's the lower-limb twin of 9.1 Upper Limb Radiology , which has the full general lesson; the spine version of the same read is 7.5 .

The Systematic Read The general lesson is the same one as in 9.1 : parts of a long bone (epiphysis, physis , metaphysis, diaphysis; cortex and medullary cavity), how the image is made and the order of the read. In a child the physis is a lucent line ; once it fuses it disappears. 1 Skeletal maturity Fused growth plate = mature; visible, unfused growth plate = immature. 2 Bone integrity Cortex and medullary cavity: any break or lesion? Density changes or generalized bone disease? 3 Alignment Malalignment means a fracture, dislocation or other injury. 4 Joints Inflammation, joint-space narrowing, degenerative change. 5 Soft tissues The problem can sit outside the bone: effusions, fat pads, masses. TIMS-C: categories of bone pathology Examples T rauma and T umours Fractures, dislocations; bone tumours I nfection, I nflammatory, I diopathic Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis; idiopathic = cause unknown M etabolic / M alignancy S ystemic / S enile Systemic: leukemia, lymphoma. Senile: osteoarthritis C ongenital Looked for mostly in the immature skeleton

Hip Radiology View What it's for AP hip A focused image of one hip . The beam goes anterior to posterior, centred on the hip joint. AP pelvis Both hips and the whole pelvis , centred on the pubic symphysis. Routinely part of a hip series, so you can compare sides . Cross-table lateral The key lateral projection: opposite leg raised, beam horizontal across the hip. Frog-leg (when indicated) Mostly in children : both femurs abducted and externally rotated, to check that the femoral head epiphyses are symmetrically ossified and in position. Normal anatomy What to find Proximal femur (AP) Femoral head (with the fovea , where the ligamentum teres attaches, often not visible), neck , greater trochanter , lesser trochanter (a curved sclerotic bump) and the intertrochanteric region between them. These landmarks are how you name the fracture for the orthopaedic team. Acetabulum (AP) The acetabular roof (dense sclerotic line), the quadrilateral plate medial to it, the iliopectineal and ilioischial lines, the teardrop and Shenton's line . These describe acetabular fractures. Also the pubic rami, body of the pubis, symphysis and ischial tuberosity. Cross-table lateral Acetabulum (anterior column, quadrilateral plate, posterior column), femoral head, neck, both trochanters, ischial tuberosity. The intertrochanteric region is hard to see here (overlap). AP pelvis Iliac wings and crests, ASIS and AIIS , pubic rami and symphysis, ischium; both proximal femurs (the lesser trochanter is often clearer than on the AP hip); the symphysis, both sacroiliac joints and both hips . Normal AP hip : head (yellow), neck (purple), greater trochanter. From the module. Normal cross-table lateral. From the module. Acetabular landmarks and lines on the AP hip: roof, quadrilateral plate, iliopectineal and ilioischial lines, teardrop, Shenton's line. From the module. AP pelvis line Normal A break suggests Pelvic ring The inner margins of the pelvic bones make one continuous ring A pelvic fracture Obturator rings Each obturator foramen has a complete, unbroken outline An injury to the pubic rami or ischium Shenton's line A smooth curve from the inferior femoral neck along the inferior superior pubic ramus A subtle hip fracture (or other injury) you might otherwise miss Normal AP pelvis with its bones and the three alignment lines. From the module. Hip pathology What you see Femoral neck fracture On the normal side, Shenton's line runs smoothly with no step-off. On the fractured side it's clea

Knee Radiology A routine series is three views: AP (supine, or standing / weight-bearing , which often takes both knees in one exposure for comparison), lateral and skyline (for the patella). View What to find AP Medial and lateral femoral condyles and epicondyles, the intercondylar fossa , the adductor tubercle (medial) and the popliteal groove (lateral, where popliteus arises). The patella overlaps the femur (base and apex). The medial and lateral tibial plateaus (radiologists' term, rather than tibial condyles), the tibial spines with the intercondylar eminence between them, and the fibular head, neck and shaft. The joint spaces are the cartilage , which is invisible because it isn't calcified. Alignment check: a line down the lateral distal femur should pass within 5 mm of the lateral proximal tibia. Lateral Femur, tibia, fibula, patella; the femoral cortices. The condyles overlap. Blumensaat's line is the roof of the intercondylar notch , and the ACL runs parallel to it. The plateaus overlap too: the medial is flatter , the lateral slightly convex . The tibial tuberosity takes the patellar tendon. Skyline Orient first: the soft tissue is thicker on the medial side . Then the medial and lateral patellar facets with the median ridge between them, sitting in the trochlear groove between the medial and lateral trochlea. Normal AP knee. From the module. AP knee, radiology terms. From the module. Normal lateral knee with Blumensaat's line. From the module. Normal skyline : facets in the trochlear groove. From the module. Read the Soft Tissues on the Lateral The quadriceps tendon attaches to the top of the patella and the patellar tendon runs from its lower pole to the tibial tuberosity. Above the patella, two radiolucent fat pads (the anterior suprapatellar , triangular, and the posterior suprapatellar / prefemoral ) sandwich the suprapatellar recess , which is normally collapsed. An effusion distends the recess into a bulbous shape and pushes the fat pads apart. Bleeding into the joint may also show a fat-fluid level . Hoffa's fat pad is the radiolucent pad in front, below the patella. Tendons, fat pads and an effusion (purple, right). From the module. Immature knee : open physes (blue). Check they're uniform, with no epiphyseal displacement or fragmentation. From the module. Knee pathology What you see Proximal tibia fracture with lipohemarthrosis A thin lucent line through the proximal tibia (oblique views help when it's hard to see). If the fracture rea

Ankle Radiology The standard series is the AP (with or without weight bearing), the mortise (ankle rotated slightly inward, which opens up the joint space and the distal tibiofibular joint) and the lateral . The AP and mortise show similar anatomy, so the module teaches the mortise. The ankle series : AP, mortise, lateral. From the module (Radiopaedia). View What to find Mortise The mortise is three structures: the medial malleolus , the tibial plafond (the flat articular surface of the distal tibia) and the lateral malleolus . The talar dome sits in it. Also the malleolar fossa (a curved sclerotic line by the lateral malleolus) and the fibular notch of the tibia, which forms the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis (its ligaments show on MRI, not x-ray). Lateral Distal tibia and fibula with both malleoli; the talus (head, neck, body) and calcaneus (tuberosity, anterior process), which meet at the subtalar joint ; talus to navicular, calcaneus to cuboid. Soft tissues: the Achilles tendon behind, inserting on the calcaneal tuberosity, and Kager's fat pad , a radiolucent triangle in front of it. A soft-tissue bulge by the joint may be an effusion . Immature ankle At 11 years the physes of the distal tibia and fibula are dark lucent lines , and the calcaneal apophysis is visible at the back of the heel. By 17 they've fused; faint sclerotic lines can linger into adulthood. Normal mortise : the talar dome in its socket. From the module. Normal lateral ankle , with the Achilles tendon and Kager's fat pad. From the module. Age 11 vs 17 : open vs fused growth plates. From the module. Ankle pathology What you see Distal tibia and fibula fractures Displaced, oblique fractures of both bones that are extra-articular (they don't reach the joint surface) Medial and lateral malleolus fractures (bimalleolar) A transverse medial malleolus fracture and an oblique lateral malleolus fracture, with a lot of soft-tissue swelling. The mortise looks preserved on this non-weight-bearing film; weight-bearing views may be asked for to stress it. Fracture patterns and management are in 10.3 . Calcaneal spur and Achilles enthesophyte A common reason for heel-pain films. A calcaneal (plantar) spur projects from the plantar calcaneus. New bone at the Achilles insertion is an enthesophyte (chronic stress where a tendon attaches), unlike an osteophyte at a joint margin. A thickened Achilles with a little calcification and encroachment on Kager's fat pad fits Achilles tendinopathy . Osteoarth

Learning Objectives Develop an approach to a patient with a soft tissue mass . Distinguish between tissue types and the characteristics of benign and malignant soft tissue tumours. Identify clinical presentations concerning for MSK malignancy . Develop a management plan for a patient with a soft tissue mass. Three recordings (70 min) from the London sarcoma team: epidemiology and pathology (Dr. B. Wehrli, pathology), then clinical diagnosis and management, and four cases (Dr. D. Logan, medical oncology). The deck also credits Drs. S. Latosinsky (surgical oncology) and D. D'Souza (radiation oncology). Bone sarcomas are “a whole different lecture”; this one is about soft tissue .

What Counts as Soft Tissue Formally: non-epithelial, extraskeletal tissue , excluding the reticuloendothelial system, glia and the supporting tissue of organs. In plain terms, tumours that arise from or resemble connective tissue : skeletal muscle, smooth muscle, fat, fibrous tissue, blood vessels and lymphatics, and peripheral nerve . All come from mesoderm , so these are mesenchymal tumours. The normal tissues soft tissue tumours imitate. From the deck. Epidemiology Benign : malignant About 100 : 1 (benign about 300 per 100,000; malignant about 2 per 100,000). Many benign lumps never come to attention. Sarcoma A malignant soft tissue tumour (“malignant sarcoma” is redundant). Two big groups: bone and soft tissue . Age Rises with age; most are in adults. Childhood ones: rhabdomyosarcoma , Ewing sarcoma , osteosarcoma (and the deck lists neuroblastoma). Where Anywhere there's connective tissue, most often the lower limb, especially the thigh , then the retroperitoneum and abdomen How rare Canada (2013): about 1,255 soft tissue and 405 bone sarcomas, against about 27,000 each of lung, colorectal and breast cancer. So they're referred to tertiary sarcoma centres .

Causes About 99% have no known cause. Trauma doesn't cause sarcomas; it just draws attention to a lump that was already there (the exception is myositis ossificans , a benign reactive lesion after trauma). Category Exposure or condition Tumour Environmental Asbestos Mesothelioma Vinyl chloride Angiosarcoma Herbicides (dioxin), prior radiation therapy , foreign material Undifferentiated sarcoma (post-radiation sarcoma: uncommon, but you'll see it) Virus HHV-8 Kaposi sarcoma (all forms; the lab can test for it) Immune / lymphatic Chronic lymphedema , e.g. after axillary dissection for breast cancer ( Stewart–Treves ) Angiosarcoma Genetic Li–Fraumeni p53 mutation Hereditary retinoblastoma RB mutation Neurofibromatosis type 1 (autosomal dominant) NF1 (neurofibromin) mutation; malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour

Classification and Names Soft tissue tumours are classified by the adult tissue they most resemble (their phenotype): fibrous, fatty, smooth muscle, skeletal muscle, nerve, vascular, or unknown (many tumours have no normal counterpart). Behaviour category What it means Benign Limited growth; may recur if not fully removed; no metastasis Intermediate, locally aggressive Invades neighbouring structures but doesn't metastasize; can still kill (e.g. intra-abdominal fibromatosis compressing vessels, kidneys or bowel) Intermediate, rarely metastasizing Looks benign, yet 5–10% metastasize unpredictably Malignant (sarcoma) Locally aggressive and frequently metastasizes , mainly to the lungs . About 25% already have metastases at diagnosis. Adult tissue Benign Malignant Fat Lip oma Lipo sarcoma Skeletal muscle Rhabdo myoma Rhabdo myosarcoma Smooth muscle Leio myoma Leio myosarcoma Fibrous tissue Fibr oma Fibro sarcoma Peripheral nerve Neurofibr oma Neurofibrosarcoma, usually called malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST) Normal muscle, rhabdomyoma, rhabdomyosarcoma. The benign tumour resembles muscle; the sarcoma has a few muscle-like pink cells among sheets of primitive blue ones. From the deck.

How the Diagnosis Is Made Clinical findings and imaging usually can't tell benign from malignant , so you need tissue, usually a core biopsy (a hollow cutting needle, guided by ultrasound or CT if deep). It's only a partial sample , hoped to represent the whole tumour. 1 Routine histology (H&E) Builds the differential and decides which extra tests to run. Sometimes it's diagnostic on its own, e.g. myxoid liposarcoma : uniform oval cells, a myxoid stroma, branching capillaries and lipoblasts (vacuoles scalloping the nucleus). 2 Histochemistry Special stains (reticulin, PAS-D) that show patterns or inclusions 3 Immunohistochemistry Antibodies that turn a target protein brown (e.g. MDM2 , CD34 , TFE3) 4 Cytogenetics and molecular tests FISH and sequencing for characteristic translocations and mutations; increasingly used 5 Electron microscopy Rarely used now Because several tests are often needed, a sarcoma diagnosis can take days to weeks . A malignant result goes to the multidisciplinary meeting . Myxoid liposarcoma on a core biopsy: lipoblast, uniform oval cells, branching capillaries, myxoid stroma. From the deck.

History and Exam Two presentations: “Doctor, I have this lump” , and the one to avoid, “Whoops, it's a sarcoma!” : a lump assumed benign is excised with little or no margin, and the pathology comes back as sarcoma. History Why When first noticed, how big then, how big now Be persistent. Anchor to life events (“last Christmas?”) and use fruit and nuts for size (blueberry, kiwi, grapefruit). Confirm: “so it's about twice the size?” Trauma Often noticed after an injury; ask anyway Symptoms Sarcomas are usually painless. Significant pain or numbness makes you think of a metastasis from a commoner cancer. Document before you do anything. Recurrence Removed before? What was it called? Other lumps Multiple lipomas are common Family history Lipomas and sarcomas can run in families Exam What to note Look Location, size, skin changes (redness, warmth, dilated veins, ulceration) Feel Consistency (soft like fat, rubbery, rock hard); superficial (subcutaneous) or deep (in muscle: have the patient tense the muscle underneath); mobile, tethered or fixed Regional nodes Uncommonly involved ; nodes argue against a sarcoma

The Suspicious-Mass Guideline From the Cancer Care Ontario sarcoma diagnostic pathway. This is the key piece to remember , and all four cases run through it. When to excise and when to image and biopsy. From the deck. Mass Do < 5 cm, no suspicious features (limited growth, minimal symptoms, superficial) Excise > 5 cm (even if it looks like a lipoma) Imaging ( MRI preferred , or CT, rarely US) or a surgical expert , then biopsy . Do not excise. < 5 cm with suspicious features : rapid growth, pain, recurrence, deep, fixed , difficult location MRI : a superficial lesion with a dark fat plane between it and the muscle, so it hasn't invaded deeper. From the deck.

Biopsy Image before you biopsy , and have the biopsy done by someone experienced in sarcoma . A badly placed biopsy disrupts the tumour, enlarges the resection and can cost the patient cure or the limb. Method Pros Cons Fine needle aspiration Cheap, easy, fast, atraumatic, in the office Discouraged if sarcoma is possible : few cells, can't type the tumour or see its architecture, little left for extra tests Excisional Removes the whole lesion Minimal surrounding tissue: not ideal if sarcoma (this is the “whoops”) Incisional More tissue; shows how the cells are organized More invasive Core The best compromise : less invasive, adequate tissue, good diagnosis, doesn't disturb the lesion. Often CT-guided by radiology. A partial sample Incisional vs excisional. From the deck.

Staging and Treatment Staging sets the goals of care. Sarcomas spread to the lung , so stage with a CT chest (a chest x-ray at the first visit too). Every possible sarcoma goes to a multidisciplinary team (surgery, radiation and medical oncology, pathology, radiology) at a tumour board , before any surgery. Cure with surgery and radiation: e.g. leiomyosarcoma, liposarcoma . Cure with chemotherapy plus radiation and/or surgery: osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma (chemo before surgery), especially in young adults.
