Adjuvant (post-op) chemotherapy is not standard for soft tissue sarcoma: no clear survival benefit, because current drugs work poorly. It's used for select subtypes or in trials. Not curable: palliative measures can greatly improve quality of life. Prognosis can be estimated with the Memorial Sloan Kettering nomogram (histology, grade, depth, site, size). Resection What it is Marginal Through the tumour's pseudocapsule: the “whoops” operation Wide (preferred) A cuff of normal tissue around the tumour, ideally 1–2 cm (rarely achieved; anatomy often leaves a close or positive margin ) Radical The whole compartment removed Radical, wide, marginal. boneandspine.com, via the deck. Ideal vs usual margins , which is why radiation is added. From the deck. Why Radiation, and Why Before Surgery Adding radiation to surgery cuts local recurrence from about 30% to 10% , mostly by treating the close margins anatomy forces on the surgeon. Pre-op (the norm in Canada and Europe; post-op is commoner in the US) uses a lower dose , targets only the tumour , and the surgeon then removes most of the irradiated tissue , so long-term function is better . Post-op radiation has to treat a larger, scarred bed. Pre-op vs post-op radiation. From the deck.

Cases Case 1: 33-year-old man, back/flank mass History: noticed 6 years ago, “big”, not quite doubled, uncomfortable; multiple other lumps; an uncle with lumps. Exam: big, subcutaneous, easily mobile , normal skin; other obvious lipomas. Guideline: no suspicious features, but > 5 cm , so image or refer, don't just excise . Ultrasound: 17 × 16 × 5 cm, subcutaneous, homogeneous, not involving the deep fascia; “probable lipoma, can't rule out sarcoma”. A sarcoma surgeon removed it. Pathology: fat with spindle and multinucleated cells . The differential is a benign spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma (observe) vs well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumour). MDM2 negative, CD34 positive → lipoma. Case 2: 18-year-old man, right hip mass History: noticed about 18 months ago, no change, no trauma, no symptoms, no other lumps, no family history. Exam: plum-sized, subcutaneous, tethered , nodes clear. Guideline: < 5 cm but suspicious (tethered), so image first . CT: in the subcutaneous fat, not attached to muscle, odd shape. Biopsy and tumour board ; he's young, so they try to avoid radiation : wide excision, with post-op radiation only if margins were positive. Chest x-ray clear. Pathology: an unusual spindle cell sarcoma ; margins adequate (closest peripheral 4 mm; the surgeon's orienting sutures let the pathologist check each margin). Follow-up every 6 months with an annual chest x-ray; no recurrence at 5 years, discharged. Case 1 : MDM2 negative, CD34 positive = lipoma. From the deck. Case 2 : subcutaneous, separate from muscle. From the deck. Case 3: 55-year-old man with neurofibromatosis, left thigh mass History: noticed a year ago, now football-sized (more than doubled), a dull ache for 2–3 months, still working; NF1 . Exam: cantaloupe-sized, in the quadriceps, tethered , no inguinal nodes. Guideline: > 5 cm plus suspicious features (rapid growth, pain, deep, fixed). MRI: in one muscle group, compartmentalized. Core biopsy: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour arising in NF1. Management: CT chest (clear), tumour board, pre-op radiation for 6 weeks, surgery 6–8 weeks later ; no adjuvant chemo (poor prognosis, chemo-resistant). Back to work, CT chest every 6 months. At 1 year: multiple lung metastases , unresectable, incurable (with only a few, a metastasectomy might be offered). Medical oncology (no standard chemo, goals of care, molecular profiling for a targeted-therapy trial ) and, most importantly, palliative care . Case 3 : an intramuscul

Learning Objectives Prognosticate recovery from a peripheral nerve injury. Differentiate between neurapraxia, axonotmesis and neurotmesis and describe the expected timeline of recovery for each. Describe an approach to localizing peripheral nerve pathology (how you'd tell a terminal branch lesion from a root lesion ). List the tests used to diagnose nerve injuries and what each one tells you. Dr. Michael Payne (Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation), about 45 minutes over three recordings, plus three practice questions. It builds on the somatic nerve in 7.1 , the brachial plexus in 8.1 and the fibular nerves in 9.7 . Monday afternoon's small group is on nerve and soft-tissue injury.

entries.t: The Somatic PNS and Nerve Structure
entries.x: The Somatic PNS and Nerve Structure The peripheral nervous system is somatic plus autonomic . The somatic part does two jobs: it carries afferent signals from skin, muscle and joints (pain, proprioception) up to the CNS, and it carries efferent signals down to skeletal muscle. A "nerve" in the anatomy lab is many axons , wrapped in layers. That redundancy explains why a partial injury causes some weakness but not complete paralysis. Layer Wraps Endoneurium Each axon (with its Schwann cell): a protective tube Perineurium Each fascicle (a bundle of axons) Epineurium The whole nerve : a bundle of fascicles, with blood supply and other connective tissue. It's the layer a nerve surgeon works at under the microscope. Endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium. Slide from the deck.

entries.t: How Bad Is It? The Seddon Classification
entries.x: How Bad Is It? The Seddon Classification Grade What's damaged Typical cause Recovery Neurapraxia The myelin sheath only; the axon is intact Compression Good. Remyelination usually takes weeks (6–12) once the cause is addressed. Axonotmesis The axon , with varying damage to the endoneurial tube and perineurium; epineurium intact Crush, stretch Can recover on its own, slowly : about 1 inch a month (1 mm a day) , guided by the intact tube Neurotmesis The epineurium : the nerve is in discontinuity Cut None on its own : with no tube to follow, regrowing fibres wander off course. Needs surgical repair. Seddon's three grades and their mechanisms. Slide from the deck. Dr. Payne's road analogy. Neurapraxia: a traffic jam ; the road and the cars are fine. Axonotmesis: the road is intact but the traffic is blocked; once the block clears, it flows again. Neurotmesis: the road is washed out , with nowhere for traffic to go. Slide from the deck. Myelin Injury: Saturday Night Palsy Myelin lets the signal jump from node to node (saltatory conduction) and keeps it insulated. Damaged myelin slows conduction or blocks it entirely. Classic example: someone drunk falls asleep with an arm over a chair, compressing the radial nerve , and wakes with a wrist drop that can last weeks. If only the myelin is hurt, the prognosis is excellent . Neurapraxia and Saturday night palsy. Slide from the deck. Wallerian degeneration, then regeneration. Slide from the deck (Gaudet 2011). Axon injury. The axon beyond the injury disintegrates: the cytoskeleton breaks down, the membrane fails and macrophages clear the debris ( Wallerian degeneration ). The muscles it supplied are left denervated . Then Schwann cells proliferate and release growth factors, the cell body releases trophic factors, and the axon starts to regrow . It does this much better with an endoneurial tube to follow, and very poorly with no epineurium to guide it. Do the maths: a lesion at the elbow has to regrow about 30 cm to reach the small hand muscles, so it takes 10–12 months to know whether it will.

entries.t: Where Is It? Localizing the Lesion
entries.x: Where Is It? Localizing the Lesion Level Name Anterior horn cell Motor neuronopathy Spinal nerve root Radiculopathy Brachial or lumbosacral plexus Plexopathy One named nerve , anywhere along it Mononeuropathy Peripheral nerves diffusely Polyneuropathy Radiculopathy Mononeuropathy Lesion A spinal nerve root , typically compressed in the intervertebral foramen ("pinched nerve") A named peripheral nerve , typically compressed at a common site (carpal tunnel, ulnar nerve at the elbow) Pain Neck or back pain radiating down the arm or leg Numbness, tingling, possibly burning or electric pain Sensory loss A dermatome , with fuzzy borders (dermatomes overlap) A well-defined area Weakness A myotome : muscles of several nerves that share the root; reflex loss Only that nerve's muscles, not other muscles from the same root supplied by a different nerve Think in terms of Dermatomes and myotomes The peripheral nerve map (median vs ulnar vs radial) A dermatome is the skin supplied by one spinal root (C6: lateral arm, forearm and thumb). A myotome is the group of muscles supplied by one root, whatever peripheral nerve carries the fibres . C6, for example, reaches deltoid (axillary nerve), biceps (musculocutaneous) and pronator teres (median). Case: the numb thumb A patient has frequent tingling, and the exam shows diminished sensation over the thumb. The differential has to include carpal tunnel syndrome and a C6 radiculopathy : the thumb sits in both the median nerve territory and the C6 dermatome . Look outside the overlap: Abductor pollicis brevis is weak (thenar eminence, median nerve): its root supply is C8 , not C6, so a C6 lesion can't explain it → median nerve (carpal tunnel). Sensory loss also over the lateral forearm (lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm) plus a weak biceps : both are musculocutaneous nerve, C6, outside the median territory → C6 root . Median territory vs C6 dermatome : they overlap at the thumb. Slide from the deck. Tracing the fibres. C6 reaches the thumb via the median nerve, and the lateral forearm and biceps via the musculocutaneous nerve. C8 supplies abductor pollicis brevis via the median nerve. Slide from the deck. Why roots and nerves don't line up. The radial nerve leaves the plexus carrying all five roots (C5–T1) , but each branch takes only some of them. On the slide, triceps is C7–C8 , brachioradialis is C5–C6 and extensor indicis is C8–T1 , all carried by the same nerve. (In the surgical EMG series, almost every C7 lesion affect

entries.t: Is It a Nerve Injury? The Clinical Picture
entries.x: Is It a Nerve Injury? The Clinical Picture Negative phenomena Positive phenomena Loss of sensation, weakness, loss of reflexes Pain, spontaneous sensations ( paresthesia ): the "numbness and tingling" Pin down what "numb" means : true loss of sensation, or tingling? Other things cause the same symptoms. A torn tendon causes weakness. Cardiac pain radiates down the left arm; don't hunt for a nerve lesion in someone with a cardiac story. Pain and weakness are hard to separate. If contracting a muscle hurts, the patient won't push hard. (Try pushing up under a desk with a palmful of thumbtacks.) True sensory loss is neurogenic , but it could still be central (stroke, spinal cord) or peripheral. Radiculopathy Mononeuropathy Onset Sudden or insidious; usually a fairly clear time of onset Depends on mechanism: chronic compression = insidious (more common); a cut = acute Location Neck or back pain plus pain down the limb in a dermatome; fuzzy borders A well-circumscribed area Duration Months (an injured axon recovers slowly) Variable Character Aching or sharp in the neck or back, with electric, burning, zinging pain along the dermatome Numbness, tingling, possibly burning or electric pain Aggravating / relieving Worse in some positions (neck extension); better when nerve tension is relieved (hanging the arm overhead) Worse with things that irritate the nerve (leaning on the elbow, driving, typing); better with position and rest Radiation Down the limb May radiate beyond the territory as symptoms, but not as objective signs Associated Myotomal weakness, myotomal reflex loss Weakness of that nerve's muscles only Spurling's manoeuvre narrows the cervical foramen to reproduce radicular arm pain: the neck goes into extension, rotation and lateral bending (toward the painful side). Weakness: Walk the Whole Chain Dr. Payne's differential for weakness runs from top to bottom: brain (stroke) → brainstem → spinal cord → anterior horn cell → root → plexus → peripheral nerve → neuromuscular junction (acetylcholine) → muscle → tendon → joint . A break anywhere looks like weakness. A strength exam also needs effort and compliance .

Electrodiagnostic Studies (EDX) Ordered as an " EMG ", but it's two tests, plus a consultation with a physiatrist or neurologist: Test How What it tells you Nerve conduction studies (NCS) Stimulate the nerve electrically and record the response further along, over a muscle or a sensory nerve Size of the response = how many axons conduct (half the axons, about half the response; repeat studies show recovery or decline). Timing / speed = the myelin , which is useful in focal entrapments such as carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar neuropathy at the elbow. Needle electromyography (EMG) A recording needle in a specific muscle; listen and watch at rest, then during voluntary contraction At rest : a denervated muscle fires abnormally. On contraction : the firing pattern and the shape of the motor units. It can isolate muscles the exam can't, such as the ulnar half vs the median half of flexor digitorum profundus , or pronator quadratus . The foot drop case : findings and the fibular vs tibial nerve map. Slide from the deck. Dermatome and myotome , with the C6 examples. Slide from the deck. EDX can tell you EDX can't tell you Whether a nerve problem explains the symptoms Where along the PNS it is (for example, suprascapular nerve at the suprascapular notch , which hits supraspinatus and infraspinatus, vs the spinoglenoid notch , which hits infraspinatus only) How severe it is and whether it will recover: is the myelin involved? The axon (you can see and hear denervation)? Is the nerve in continuity ? What's the timeline (may need repeat studies)? If it's not a nerve, whether it's a primary muscle problem (myopathy) The cause of all musculoskeletal pain (for example, a rotator cuff tear ) Central nervous system disease (for example, a stroke ) A normal study still helps: it points you to those other causes.

Case: Foot Drop The horseback rider Yesterday a rider hit a fence with the right knee, was thrown over and landed on the low back. The knee hurts, and an x-ray shows a fibular head fracture . They can't dorsiflex, extend the toes or evert ; plantarflexion and knee flexion are weak but painful. Foot drop = dorsiflexion weakness (can't lift the foot against gravity). Sensory : reduced pinprick over the dorsum of the foot , with clear borders. Motor : hip flexion, knee extension, hip adduction and abduction, plantarflexion and tibialis posterior 4+/5 (pain-limited). Dorsiflexion, extensor hallucis longus and eversion 0/5 . Reflexes : patellar and plantar intact. Only the common fibular territory is affected; the tibial muscles (gastrocnemius, tibialis posterior) work. Where along the nerve? The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common fibular division in the thigh . If it's spared, the lesion is below that branch, at the fibular head . When the exam is too painful to tell, send for EDX. Ending 1 : only the common fibular muscles below the knee are abnormal (red), and the short head of biceps femoris is spared → common fibular neuropathy at the fibular head . Slide from the deck. Ending 2 : gluteus medius (superior gluteal), semimembranosus and tibialis posterior (tibial) and the L5 paraspinals are also abnormal: several nerves, one root → L5 radiculopathy (from the fall onto the back). Slide from the deck. What kind of injury? In ending 1, nerve conduction gets no response from the superficial fibular sensory or fibular motor studies. EMG shows lots of abnormal spontaneous activity (denervation) and no voluntary motor units in the fibular muscles. That's an axonal injury : "common fibular axonopathy at the fibular head". A few weeks out you can't yet tell axonotmesis from neurotmesis ; recovery a year later would prove the nerve was in continuity. The skill is knowing when to intervene while it can still help, rather than waiting two or five years to find out it was neurotmesis.

Practice Questions 1. The knife wound A knife wound to the medial arm at the elbow . Two weeks later: no sensation along the medial hand , and no contraction of abductor digiti minimi or the first dorsal interosseous (ulnar). Best management? → Refer to a peripheral nerve injury clinic (via PM&R/EMG or plastics). A laceration probably means neurotmesis of the ulnar nerve, which has a poor prognosis. Not "follow 12 weeks for remyelination": this isn't a compression injury. Not ultrasound or MRI: they can miss a small but significant lesion, and the axons can be injured with the epineurium intact . 2. Hip adduction plus knee extension Sudden unilateral weakness of hip adduction and knee extension ; hip flexion and dorsiflexion are normal . Most likely lesion? → the L3 nerve root . It supplies muscles of both the obturator (adductors) and the femoral (quadriceps) nerves. An obturator lesion alone wouldn't weaken knee extension, and a femoral lesion alone wouldn't weaken adduction. Two separate nerve lesions are possible, but one lesion is more likely. 3. The tourniquet A tourniquet at the proximal humerus , then a dense wrist drop and sensory loss in the superficial radial territory; everything else is normal. At one month , needle EMG of extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor digitorum and extensor indicis shows no denervation , but the muscles can't be activated voluntarily. Two months later the arm is fully back, as predicted. How did we know? → The EMG fits neurapraxia : a conduction block across the injury that resolves quickly with remyelination. Not conversion or factitious disorder (be careful: the same EMG fits poor effort, but this mechanism and pattern would be hard to fake). Not "12 inches at 1 inch a week": regrowth is 1 inch a month , and an axonal injury would show denervation. A compressive mechanism makes neurotmesis unlikely, but the axons could still be injured, and that would take longer.

Learning Objectives Develop an approach to pediatric musculoskeletal pathology . Describe the unique fracture types and overuse injuries that occur in children. Explain the Salter–Harris classification of fractures involving the physis and their complications. Define developmental dysplasia of the hip , list its risk factors, explain the exam manoeuvres and outline management. Define clubfoot and outline a timeline for its management. Describe a basic approach to rotational and angular variation of the legs, and the child with a limp . Define scoliosis and describe its assessment, investigation and treatment. Dr. Caitlin Cassidy (Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation), five recordings (about 55 minutes) with four knowledge checks. The words for the parts of a bone are also in 10.4 , and closed reduction and casting in 10.5 .

Kids Are Different Feature In children Bone More porous and pliable ; adult bone is more brittle Periosteum Thick, strong and very active : it builds width and drives a robust healing and remodelling response Physis (growth plate) Cartilage at the ends of long bones and a site of relative weakness . Injure it and you risk uneven growth or growth arrest . Ligaments Relatively strong , so the bone or physis fails first: fewer sprains and dislocations Epiphysis (the end), physis , metaphysis (the flare), diaphysis (the shaft). From the deck. Apophyses : secondary ossification centres where tendons attach (calcaneus, pelvis). From the deck. How long bones grow. A hyaline cartilage model forms in utero. Bone replaces it at the primary ossification centre (diaphysis) and the secondary centres (epiphyses): endochondral ossification . The physis is the last cartilage left, and it closes at a different age in each bone, so what's normal on a child's x-ray depends on age.

Fractures and How They Heal Most pediatric trauma is one limb and minor : falls from low heights and sport, then pedestrians struck by vehicles and vehicle operators (ATVs). In infants and toddlers , think of non-accidental injury . Buckle (the cortex fails in compression and bulges), greenstick (fails in tension on one side, bends on the other) and plastic deformation (micro-fractures leave the bone bowed; it remodels). Avulsions and growth plate fractures are the other two pediatric patterns. From the deck. Healing is rarely the problem : “as long as the two bone ends are in the same room, they will heal together.” It's still easier to get the alignment right early than to fix it later, and what's acceptable depends on age. Remodelling is the growing skeleton restoring its pre-injury alignment in response to load. Remodels well Remodels poorly Growth left At least 2 years of growth remaining Little growth left Site Metaphyseal fracture Mid-shaft fracture with significant angulation or rotation ; a displaced intra-articular fracture Plane Deformity in the plane of the joint's motion Deformity out of plane A 3-year-old : displaced distal fibula, no reduction, realigned on its own by 6 months . From the deck. A 4-year-old : proximal humerus 100% displaced , treated with a sling only; remodelled by 7 months . From the deck. Closed reduction when the deformity is more than that bone can remodel: have everything ready first, then a haematoma block or conscious sedation (the most control), a splint or cast (how long depends on the site and fracture), always post-reduction films , and timely follow-up. Casting is an active treatment that takes skill. Why reductions fail Not planned from the x-rays and the deformed limb Details missed: the direction and size of the force (reverse it), translation as well as angulation , where the hands mould the cast Too much padding , or a cast that's too short A distal radius and ulna fracture with 90° of dorsal angulation , then held after closed reduction in a well-moulded cast. From the deck.

The Pediatric Elbow An often confusing area: six ossification centres that appear at different ages (none at all in a baby) can look like fracture fragments, and a hurt child won't let you examine much. Know what should be there for the child's age; a fragment where no centre should be yet raises your suspicion . Each small island is an ossification centre , not a fracture. From the elbow deck. CRITOE , on the AP and lateral. From the elbow deck. CRITOE Centre Seen by about C Capitellum 1 year R Radial head 3 years I Internal (medial) epicondyle 5 years T Trochlea 7 years O Olecranon 9 years E External (lateral) epicondyle 11 years Rule of thumb: one every 2 years from 1 to 11 ; the capitellum is the most predictable. A swollen elbow means a high index of suspicion for a bony injury. Call pediatric ortho for a significantly swollen elbow (especially one that isn't ossified yet), any concern about instability , a displaced fracture , or a dislocation that didn't reduce congruently.

Growth Plate Fractures: Salter–Harris Types I–V. From the deck. Type Line runs through Key points Treatment I The physis only (x-ray may look normal) Often misdiagnosed as a sprain (e.g. a swollen lateral ankle = distal fibula SH I); excellent prognosis Stable with closed reduction II Physis, then out through the metaphysis Most common ; most common at the distal radius ; usually good prognosis Usually stable with closed reduction III Physis, then out through the epiphysis Intra-articular ; prognosis usually good Anatomic reduction , usually surgery (screws) IV Metaphysis, physis and epiphysis Intra-articular; a bony bridge can form across the physis and arrest growth. Most common at the lateral condyle of the humerus and the distal tibia Anatomic reduction V Compression (crush) of the physis Often missed ; diagnosed late, when growth arrest shows. Highest risk of growth arrest Refer to ortho for follow-up SH I , distal fibula: the “sprain”. From the deck. SH II , distal tibia: a metaphyseal corner comes with it. From the deck. SH III , distal tibia: into the joint through the epiphysis. From the deck. SH IV , distal tibia: straight across all three. From the deck. SH V : a crushed, narrowed physis that's easy to miss. From the deck. Growth arrest : one side of the physis stopped, the other kept growing, and the ankle angulated. From the deck. About 10% of physeal injuries cause a growth disturbance . Risk rises with the child's age (growth left), severity , type (IV and V worst), the method of reduction , the physis's blood supply , and an open injury. The problem is asymmetric growth : angulation and a length discrepancy , treated according to how much growth is left. Three Messages 1. Any growth plate injury is serious , whatever the type or site, and needs orthopedic follow-up . 2. Follow it for at least 1 year, preferably 2 . 3. Warn the family about growth complications, so they don't get lost to follow-up.

The Apophysis: Avulsions and Apophysitis Case: the sprinter A 14-year-old boy has sudden right anterior hip pain in a 100 m dash , with an antalgic limp. → An avulsion of the anterior inferior iliac spine (rectus femoris). In a growth spurt the bones lengthen faster than the muscles and tendons, so the apophysis is under tension, and a burst of contraction pulls it off. The sprinter's x-rays: a fragment pulled off the anterior inferior iliac spine . From the deck. Pelvic avulsion sites and the muscles that cause them. From the deck. Avulsions can happen at any apophysis ; common ones are the pelvis , the 5th metatarsal base and the medial epicondyle . Treatment is often non-surgical : relative rest and sometimes immobilization. Overuse apophysitis : repeated traction causes micro-avulsions at the same sites. Apophysitis Where Who and what Osgood–Schlatter Tibial tubercle (patellar tendon) Running and jumping adolescents: girls 8–14 , boys 10–15 . Gradual localized pain, swelling and tenderness, a bump on the tubercle. Diagnosed clinically Sinding-Larsen(–Johansson) Lower pole of the patella The same process at the other end of the patellar tendon Sever's Calcaneal apophysis (Achilles) Heel pain in active children Osgood–Schlatter : the patellar tendon tugs on the tubercle. From the deck. The lateral x-ray: a fragmented, teardrop tubercle. From the deck. Management of apophysitis : educate (benign and self-limiting; it settles, though it can take up to 2 years ; excellent prognosis), RICE when acute, activity as tolerated (often modified, which young athletes find hard), and NSAIDs as needed . Other adolescent overuse injuries: stress fractures and osteochondritis dissecans (OCD). In OCD, repetitive loading (and other factors) cut the blood supply to the bone under the cartilage, which softens and can come loose as a loose body . Without mechanical symptoms it's usually managed conservatively.

Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip A spectrum from a shallow (dysplastic) acetabulum to a hip that subluxes or dislocates . 1–6 per 1000 live births, the left more often than the right. Every newborn is screened, because the picture and the treatment depend on the age at diagnosis and the severity. Risk factors The “4 Fs”: firstborn , female , family history , frank breech Oligohydramnios (a crowded uterus) Ancestry: more common in white and North American Indigenous populations, less in Black and Asian populations Other packaging problems : torticollis, calcaneovalgus foot, clubfoot, scoliosis Exam How Positive Barlow (“sign of exit”) Supine, hips and knees at 90°; adduct the thigh and push backward The femoral head slips out : a reduced but dislocatable hip. Reduce it afterwards Ortolani (“sign of entry”) Same position, long finger on the greater trochanter; lift and abduct the thigh The head clunks back in : a dislocated hip that reduces Galeazzi Hips and knees flexed, feet level One knee lower : the short side (subluxed or dislocated) Range of motion Abduct the flexed hips Limited abduction Walking child Watch the gait A painless limp or waddle Barlow and Ortolani are unreliable after 3–6 months , when muscle tone resists them. Also do a general exam for other musculoskeletal problems and dysmorphism. Barlow : adduct and push back. From the deck. Ortolani : lift and abduct, and it clunks in. From the deck. Galeazzi : the low knee is the bad hip. From the deck. A 15-month-old brought in for a leg length difference : the right hip is dislocated (missed or not screened at birth). From the deck. Pavlik harness and spica cast . From the deck. Age Treatment Up to 6 months Pavlik harness : hips flexed and abducted, pointing the head into the acetabulum so both develop normally Older, or the harness fails Closed reduction and a spica cast Later still Open reduction ± osteotomies Diagnose early : treatment is simpler and long-term disability is prevented.

Clubfoot (Congenital Talipes Equinovarus) The ankle is plantarflexed (equinus) and the heel and forefoot are in varus . There's a genetic component , and associations with spina bifida and other syndromes. Untreated , it's a progressive, stiffening deformity that badly limits walking and activity and makes footwear a problem. 1 Weekly manipulation and casting, 4–6 weeks Started early, while the foot is small and malleable; each cast holds the latest correction. 2 Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy Under local anaesthetic, to bring the foot to about 15° of dorsiflexion . 3 Cast for 3 weeks 4 Abduction brace: “boots and bars” Full time for 3 months , then at night for 2–3 years , feet turned out with the legs slightly apart. The skeleton of a clubfoot : pointed down and turned in. From the deck. Ponseti manipulation and serial casts. From the deck. Boots and bars. From the deck. For a foot that resists Ponseti or recurs: a posteromedial (comprehensive) release , surgically lengthening the contracted structures and realigning the foot. It's a much bigger dissection of joints, tendons and ligaments.

Rotational and Angular Variation In-toeing, out-toeing, knock knees, bowlegs and flat feet are very common referrals , and nearly all are normal development that rarely affects function or appearance. Know the normal pattern so you don't overtreat . Shape What it is Normal Genu varum (bowlegs) Knees point away from the midline Birth to 2 years : reassure Genu valgum (knock knees) Knees point toward the midline 3 to 7 years : reassure In-toeing / out-toeing The foot progression angle : how far the foot points off the line of walking Wide normal range; within about 10–15° either way is likely fine Foot progression angle by age, with the normal range. From the deck. Warning signs (angular) Excessive variation Short stature Progressive genu varum (it should be gone by 2) Asymmetry Varum or valgum persisting past 7–8 years A known or suspected cause: nutritional deficiency , metabolic bone disease , skeletal dysplasia, previous trauma

The Child with a Limp Many causes, and the child's age reorders the differential . Child Health small groups go deeper; the hip conditions are their topic. Cause Typical age Note DDH (missed in infancy) Toddler A painless limp; not a teenager's first presentation Clubfoot Seen at birth Rarely a mystery later Transient synovitis Any, most often young children Inflammation of the hip's synovial lining Legg–Calvé–Perthes About 4–8 Avascular necrosis of the femoral head Slipped capital femoral epiphysis Adolescents with an open proximal femoral physis The femoral head epiphysis slips off the neck through the physis Other Any Overuse injuries; trauma, accidental or not ; neuromuscular disorders; inflammatory arthritis Gait warning signs : asymmetry , progression , a leg length difference , pain , deformity , or a suspected underlying condition.

Scoliosis A structural lateral curvature with rotation of the spine, of at least 10° . The rotation matters as much as the curve. A normal spine and one with scoliosis . From the deck. Type Cause Idiopathic Most common ; typically adolescent onset; F > M ; runs in families Neuromuscular Cerebral palsy, spina bifida, neurofibromatosis, spinal muscular atrophy Congenital A vertebral anomaly (e.g. a hemivertebra ) Other secondary Post-traumatic, etc. Step What to do History Rarely painful ; often found incidentally; the complaint is usually a rib hump . A neurological review of systems matters: rule out a neuromuscular or congenital cause. Family and past medical history Exam Properly undressed (back and a full neuro exam). Gait, general exam. Look for spinal dysraphism : a sacral dimple, hairy patch, lipoma or haemangioma . Palpate the spinous processes. Assess the curve's severity and flexibility . Thorough neuro exam Adams forward bend Bend to touch the toes: the rotation shows as a rib prominence on the side of the convexity . A purely postural curve has no hump X-ray The first and often only test: location, levels, direction, magnitude (the Cobb angle ), and any congenital anomaly, trauma or tumour. MRI only if a neurological cause is suspected Describe it: right, thoracic, T7–T12, 45° . The Cobb angle uses lines along the end plates of the most tilted vertebrae (you won't have to measure one). From the deck. A TLSO (“Boston”) brace , worn at least 16 hours a day . From the deck. Pedicle screw instrumentation and fusion. From the deck. Risk of progression is higher with Management Girls > boys; younger physiological age , especially pre-menarchal ; bigger curves; double > single; thoracic > lumbar Educate (natural history, risk of progression, monitoring plan). Orthosis for the right curve, size and age. No drugs. Surgery depending on the curve and its risk of progression: the goal is to stop progression by fusing the curve, with instrumentation holding the correction while the fusion takes. Modern pedicle screws give more correction and stability, at more cost and longer surgery than the old single rods.

Knowledge Checks What the module asks A physeal injury in a long bone raises the risk of? → Growth arrest (not infection, nonunion or nerve injury). Which physeal injury carries the highest risk of growth arrest? → Compression of the growth plate (SH V) ; the others, properly stabilized, leave the physis largely intact. Which child doesn't need ortho? → A 5-year-old with genu valgum (normal at 3–7); a 6-month-old with a leg length difference needs a DDH work-up, and a clubfoot needs treatment. Scoliosis often presents with back pain? → False.

Learning Objectives Summarize the health benefits of regular physical activity: physiological effects and effects on morbidity and mortality. Outline the Canadian Physical Activity Guidelines , distinguish light, moderate and vigorous activity, and give ways to hit the right intensity. List and categorize the relative and absolute contraindications to exercise. Construct a safe, specific exercise prescription using the FITT principle, taking the patient's medical and socioeconomic situation into account. Dr. Jane Thornton (Sport and Exercise Medicine, Fowler Kennedy), three recordings (about 40 minutes) and five practice questions. Exercise as treatment also runs through 10.7 chronic pain (active vs passive therapy).

The Case: Nancy 68-year-old woman Recently widowed and now sedentary ; she used to love walking her dog on the trails. She's worried about falling . New, untreated hypertension (140/85). Her father died after an MI at 70 ; her mother broke a hip at 73 . How would you write her a physical activity prescription? Think benefits, side effects, risks and dose, as for any drug.

Health Benefits Risk reductions with regular activity. From the deck. Low fitness predicts death as strongly as smoking, hypertension or high cholesterol (Blair 1996). From the deck. System What activity does Musculoskeletal 55% fewer hip fractures , mostly through fewer falls (strength, proprioception, coordination, gait, reaction time). Bone density rises only 1–3% with high-impact training, but the bone's architecture strengthens. Heart Contractility ↑ , coronary blood flow ↑ , oxygen demand ↓ , stroke volume ↑ , resting heart rate ↓ Blood and vessels Oxygen uptake and utilisation ↑ , endothelial function ↑ , plasma volume ↑ , blood viscosity ↓ , resting blood pressure ↓ (it rises transiently during exercise) Cardiovascular disease Getting a patient active is as important as helping them quit smoking or lowering their blood pressure and cholesterol The cardiovascular effects. From the deck. As good as medication? In coronary disease, stroke and heart failure, exercise's mortality benefit stacks up with the drugs (Naci & Ioannidis, BMJ 2013). From the deck. A 2018 network meta-analysis (391 trials) found exercise lowers systolic blood pressure about as much as antihypertensive drugs , with no head-to-head trial yet. Many patients would rather not start a pill but don't know where to begin with lifestyle, so offering exercise is patient-centred. There's evidence for activity as treatment in dozens of conditions, from depression and dementia to COPD, osteoarthritis and type 2 diabetes.

The Guidelines and Intensity Physical activity is any movement; exercise is planned, structured activity to build fitness. They're used interchangeably here. Canadian guidelines, adults Detail Aerobic At least 150 minutes a week of moderate-to-vigorous activity. Bouts no longer need to be 10 minutes; even 5 minutes counts. Strength Muscle and bone strengthening with the major muscle groups at least 2 days a week . The part people forget. More More activity gives more benefit; also “build strength, sit less, improve balance”. The WHO and US guidelines say the same. Intensity How it feels Talk test Examples Light Barely raises breathing Can sing Gardening, walking to the printer Moderate Breathing and heart rate up ; warmer, may sweat if hot or humid Can talk Brisk walking, stair climbing, cycling, dancing, swimming Vigorous Breathing and heart rate well up Can't keep a conversation going Sport, running, aerobics, cardio machines Muscle strengthening A weight heavy enough that no more than 10–15 repetitions are possible — Sit-to-stand, stairs, heavy gardening, carrying shopping, weights, bands, push-ups, soup-can curls The same brisk walk can be light for one person and vigorous for another, so judge intensity by the person, not the activity. Ways to track it: the talk test (simplest for beginners), rate of perceived exertion , METs , or heart rate , which a beta-blocker blunts. Some is good, more is better. Risk keeps falling even at 10× the guideline, but the steepest drop is from sedentary to a little : that's where to focus. Start low, go slow. From the deck.

Taking an Exercise History 1 Current activity? 2 Intention to be active? 3 Past activity and preferences? What they enjoyed (school, work, leisure, active commuting); solo or group , indoors or outdoors; barriers ; goals (playing with grandchildren, not getting breathless on stairs, cutting risk after an MI or cancer, or just looking good: meet them where they are). 4 Is it safe? Current symptoms and past medical history. Often the most important question.

entries.t: Is It Safe? Risk and Contraindications
entries.x: Is It Safe? Risk and Contraindications Vigorous exercise is relatively safe : 47 deaths per 100,000 a year vs 190 for motorcycle accidents. Most exercise deaths are in people without baseline fitness . From the deck. Cardiovascular risk Advice Asymptomatic, low risk Self-directed activity Asymptomatic, low risk but significant risk factors (e.g. high BP) Start at low-to-moderate intensity Asymptomatic, high risk Consider cardiac investigations first (ECG) Symptomatic cardiovascular disease Supervised initial exercise, or refer to an exercise specialist (stress testing) ACSM pre-participation screening : regular exerciser? signs or symptoms? known disease? → whether clearance is needed and what intensity. Stop and get assessed for chest, neck, jaw or arm pain, breathlessness at rest or on mild exertion, dizziness or syncope, orthopnoea or PND, ankle oedema, palpitations, claudication, a known murmur, or unusual fatigue. Tell patients this. From the deck. Absolute contraindications to exercise (cardiovascular disease) 1. New or uncontrolled arrhythmia 2. Resting or uncontrolled tachycardia 3. Resting SBP > 180 mmHg or DBP > 100 mmHg 4. Symptomatic hypotension 5. Unstable or crescendo angina 6. Acute or unstable heart failure 7. Unstable diabetes 8. Acute febrile illness The rule behind the list: anyone with unstable or uncontrolled symptoms is reviewed before starting. Side effects of exercise are real but outweighed by the benefits: delayed-onset muscle soreness, aches and pains, and acute or overuse injuries.

Writing the Prescription The 3 As What to do Ask About current activity, and whether they know the benefits of moving more Advise On the benefits, especially for their own conditions Act Signpost to help and support: handouts, community programs, free classes, online resources FITT Example for 150 minutes F requency 5 times a week (aerobic) I ntensity Sing (low), talk (moderate) , conversation impossible (high) T ime 30 minutes T ype What they'll enjoy: walking, cycling, dancing, swimming, jogging Patients want something tangible and personal : write it down like a prescription. Hypertension: do Hypertension: don't Control BP > 180/100 with medication before exercising Very strenuous resistance training (left ventricular pressure can pass 300 mmHg) A long warm-up (15 min) and cool-down (10 min) Vigorous exercise with known left ventricular hypertrophy Keep the feet moving afterwards (blood pools if you stop dead) Lying-down exercises (postural hypotension) Protect the joints if obese or inactive Isometric exercises (e.g. wall sits; they push BP up more) One rest day a week Overhead exercises Antihypertensives and exercise. From the deck. Drug With exercise ACE inhibitor / ARB Minimal problems: recommended ; first line in athletes Calcium channel blocker Small risk of postural hypotension : extend the cool-down. Recommended Beta-blocker ↓ max heart rate and performance: bad for high intensity (avoid in athletes; banned in some sports), but limits the hypertensive response Diuretic Dehydration ; needs a toilet nearby Antihypertensives are not a contraindication to exercise. Back off if exercise brings severe pain , pain that doesn't settle to the usual level afterwards, more night pain , or more joint swelling . Follow up at about 6 weeks . Nancy's Prescription At 140/85 and asymptomatic she can be self-directed , starting at low-to-moderate intensity and building slowly. Benefits to share: fewer falls and hip fractures , lower blood pressure, lower cardiovascular risk. F : most days, I : moderate by the talk test, T : working up to 30 minutes, T : walking her dog (her preference), plus strength and balance 2 days a week (sit-to-stands, stairs). Warm up and cool down, and stop and call if she gets chest pain, breathlessness or dizziness.

The Doctor's Role Why it's worth 30 seconds A physician's prescription is cost-effective Only about 25% of physicians counsel on activity, but 92% of patients say they'd follow their doctor's advice A prescription raises a patient's activity by about 10% ; across Canada that could save about $2 billion a year In hospital , patients lose function lying in bed: get them dressed and moving (#EndPJparalysis), and track activity (one hospital used about 1000 steps a day as a discharge marker) Most effective approach : know why it works and why it matters in your specialty; ask about history and preferences; focus on behaviour change ; use shared decision-making ; signpost to evidence-based resources, remembering the social determinants of health (a gym or trainer may be unaffordable, and walking outside gets most of the benefit); and follow up .

Practice Questions What the module asks Not an absolute contraindication? → A resting SBP of 160 (the cut-off is > 180/100); new arrhythmia, symptomatic hypotension, crescendo angina and acute heart failure all are. Least useful way to track moderate intensity on a beta-blocker? → Heart rate as a percentage of maximum . Physical inactivity is the WHO's ___ greatest risk factor for death? → 4th . The Canadian adult guideline? → 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a week and 2 sessions of resistance or muscle and bone strengthening . Two cardiovascular effects? → the key is oxygen uptake ↑ and endothelial function ↑ . The distractors get blood viscosity (it falls), coronary flow (it rises) and blood pressure (it falls at rest and rises during exercise) backwards. “Stroke volume ↑ and heart rate ↓” also matches the slide, but it isn't the keyed answer.

Learning Objectives Assess the interaction between psychological factors and chronic non-cancer pain . Assess the impact of affective disorders on pain , and vice versa. Identify presentations that may indicate somatic symptom and related disorders . Dr. Jarmain (psychiatry): four recordings (75 min) built around one patient, Fred, plus a short review. The pain physiology, the drugs and opioids are in 10.7 .

Meet Fred The module's patient Fred , 47, divorced, a sanitation worker, lives alone; his 12-year-old son visits every other weekend. A year ago his right lower leg was crushed between a garbage truck and a car: tibia and fibula fractures, external fixation , “good healing”. He's off work on WSIB , with no legal case. Now: constant aching plus burning in the right leg and foot after too much use; waxing and waning muscle aches. Avoids narcotics; occasional acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Mood “okay”, but excessive worry : will he be disabled for life, keep up with his son, is a flare making the injury worse? The worry tenses his muscles and keeps him awake. No PTSD symptoms, no suicidal thoughts. He's cut back activity, gained about 20 lb and is smoking more .

Assessment Ask about Why Duration and nature of the pain Its sensory character and pattern Associated symptoms , physical and psychological, including suicidal ideation Mood, anxiety, sleep, substance use Past care : contacts, treatments, alternative therapies, medications, home remedies What has and hasn't worked Function What the pain stops them doing Investigations: review everything done; fill gaps only as clinically indicated. Pain charting: descriptive words, 0–10 numerical scores , faces scales (children), visual analogue scales, and multidimensional tools such as the McGill Pain Questionnaire . A pain assessment form lets the patient map the pain on a body outline and rate past treatments. Pain diary: records the situation, the sensation (1–10) and the distress (1–10) separately, plus what they did. Separating them teaches the patient that distress isn't only about pain intensity: thoughts, feelings and context drive it too. Pain diary : sensation and distress rated separately. From the deck.

entries.t: Pain Is More Than the Signal
entries.x: Pain Is More Than the Signal Descartes saw pain as hard-wired: a stimulus passively carried to the brain. Now we know it's shaped bottom up (sensitization) and top down (prior experience, attention and expectation , mood ; depression and anxiety make pain worse). Then and now. Bingel and Tracey, Physiology 2008, via the deck. The six dimensions of pain. From the deck. Dimension Examples Physiological Location, onset, duration, cause Sensory Intensity, quality, pattern Affective Mood: anxiety, depression, well-being Cognitive What the pain means (childbirth vs a car crash), view of self, coping, beliefs Behavioural How pain is communicated, a spouse who rewards pain behaviour , pushing through vs avoiding, medications, help-seeking, sleep Sociocultural Family support or dismissal, work and home roles, leisure, environment; work is often key Pair the subjective story with objective indicators : pain behaviours (and whether they're out of proportion ), physiological changes (pulse, BP, sweating) and, above all, change in function . How psychology feeds pain: attention has to be on the stimulus for pain to be felt; fear can make that attention hypervigilant . Interpretation and beliefs (“hurt means harm”, “pain means stop”) drive avoidance, deconditioning and withdrawal. At work, individual factors (skills, meaning, support) and workplace factors (physical load, organization) combine to raise stress, fatigue and the risk of further injury. The fear-avoidance model. Fear leads to avoidance, then disuse, depression and disability; no fear means confrontation and recovery. Vlaeyen and Linton, via the deck.

Psychological Symptoms and the Differential Emotional, behavioural and cognitive symptoms can just be part of the pain experience. When they cause significant distress , last, and impair function , work through the differential: Diagnosis Key features Adjustment disorder (DSM-5) Emotional or behavioural symptoms within 3 months of an identifiable stressor (here, the pain or disability), with distress out of proportion and/or impaired function . Not another mental disorder or normal bereavement. Resolves within 6 months of the stressor (or its consequences) ending. Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions Psychological factors that change the course of the illness (timing), interfere with treatment (poor adherence) or add health risks ; e.g. anxiety in COPD, depression in coronary disease Comorbid depression 8–50% of chronic pain patients have current major depression. It goes with more disability, more negative thoughts, higher pain intensity , less sense of control, more passive-avoidant coping, and predicts persistent pain . Comorbid anxiety 50% have anxiety symptoms; 19–30% an anxiety disorder (panic, GAD). After an accident, consider acute stress disorder or PTSD . Substance use disorders Higher than the general population (13.2% vs 7% in one study); more opioid dependence after injury Somatic symptom and related disorders Below About 20% of Canadians live with chronic pain, half of them for over 10 years. It's more common and more severe in groups facing social inequity : people in poverty, Indigenous Peoples, some ethnic communities and women (Canadian Pain Task Force, 2019). So assess the whole person .

Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders Medically unexplained symptoms (MUS) are persistent bodily complaints with no adequate structural explanation after proper examination. They come as pain in different places , functional disturbance of organ systems , or fatigue , and may reflect physiological disturbance, emotional problems or a condition not yet diagnosed. They're common: 15–25% in primary care , 39–52% in specialist clinics, over 60% in neurology . Functional somatic syndromes ( IBS, chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia ) are similar: more common in women, with heavy overlap with anxiety and depression, and their cause is still unclear. DSM-5 regrouped these to improve diagnostic accuracy (the DSM-IV somatoform categories overlapped), make them usable outside psychiatry, move away from mind-body dualism and the idea that symptoms “aren't real”, and focus on the distress and the abnormal thoughts, feelings and behaviours , not on whether the symptom is explained. Disorder Criteria / key points Somatic symptom disorder A. One or more distressing or disruptive somatic symptoms. B. Excessive thoughts, feelings and/or behaviours about them. C. Symptomatic state > 6 months (any one symptom needn't be constant). About 5–7% of the population; 20–25% of primary care patients with acute somatic symptoms go on to develop it. Linked to hypervigilance to body sensations, childhood neglect or sexual abuse, chaotic lifestyle, substance misuse, personality disorders. Risk: repeated care-seeking and unnecessary tests . Illness anxiety disorder Part of the same group Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) One or more symptoms of altered voluntary motor or sensory function (weakness, abnormal movements, swallowing or speech symptoms, attacks or seizures, sensory loss). Findings are incompatible with recognized neurological or medical disease (e.g. a deficit that doesn't follow anatomy). Not better explained by another disorder; causes distress or impairment. Specify acute (< 6 months) or persistent, and with or without a stressor. A diagnosis of exclusion : some patients later turn out to have a neurological disease. Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions See above Factitious disorder (Munchausen) Moved into this chapter in DSM-5. Imposed on self or on another (formerly “by proxy”). Presents self or another as ill or injured, with deception even without obvious external reward (e.g. injecting insulin to cause hypoglycemia).

Management 1 Multimodal No single intervention is enough. 2 Multidisciplinary The pain-clinic team (see 10.7 ). 3 Start with the patient Collaborative, realistic measurable (SMART) goals , management not cure . By now they're often frustrated by many doctors and tests: start where they are, using motivational interviewing . Domain Options Biological: physical TENS, heat and cold, acupuncture and acupressure, massage, physiotherapy, injections and blocks. Modest benefit, but it matters to some patients. Biological: drugs Stepwise ( WHO pain ladder ): non-opioid ± adjuvant (NSAID, acetaminophen); then weak opioid + non-opioid (e.g. Tylenol #3 ); then strong opioid + non-opioid (morphine + acetaminophen). Adjuvants: analgesic antidepressants, anticonvulsants. Avoid opioids where possible. Psychological: CBT Links thoughts, feelings and behaviours to pain; aims at managing, not curing . Individual or (especially) group ; limited RCTs but effective (e.g. 53% of chronic headache patients improved). Other psychological Psychodynamic therapy as a second-line option for lifelong patterns. Relaxation and meditation : slow breathing switches on the parasympathetic system. Avoid progressive muscle relaxation in muscular pain (they can tense, not release); use breathing, mindfulness, visualization. Rehabilitative Education and adaptation (ergonomics, new ways to do old things: a foot on the lower cupboard while doing dishes); pacing (no boom-and-bust); exercise (aerobic, stretching and strengthening, meditative), starting gradually; vocational planning and work modification CBT pieces What they are Cognitive distortions (“stinking thinking”) Mental filter (only noticing evidence that pain means harm), catastrophizing (something terrible will happen), emotional reasoning (it feels harmful, so it is) Common components Patient and family education; contingency management (ABCs: antecedents, behaviours, consequences); relaxation; problem-solving; communication; distraction; behavioural activation (meaningful activities); cognitive restructuring The relaxation response : awareness plus deep breathing lets the patient choose a different response to the pain spike. © 2012 Authentic Leadership Global, via the deck. Fred: diagnosis and plan Fred's pain is real; his worry (catastrophizing, all-or-nothing thinking about never working again) tenses him, disturbs sleep and drives avoidance , weight gain and smoking. No PTSD, no depression, no suicidality. The module's three key int

Secondary Prevention and General Strategies Secondary prevention How Early Time is vital: act before lifestyle is disrupted (before 12 weeks) . A return to work, even modified, prevents later disability. Active Focus on health and behaviour , not medical problems: daily activity, training, return to work , daily structure and sleep Patient as partner It can't be cured and needs behaviour change, so engage the patient Communication Liaise (with permission) with the workplace , family, insurer and other caregivers Follow-up Reassess and adjust regularly; visits about goals , not pain complaints One physician, regular visits : build trust. Goal-directed : celebrate steps forward. Understand the communication : distress is often expressed through physical symptoms. Limit investigations and operations , but remember these patients still get new acute illnesses . Motivational interviewing. Monitor yourself : watch your countertransference; if you can't stay objective and empathic, refer on.

Learning Objectives Define and distinguish mono-, oligo- and polyarthritis . Determine a differential diagnosis for acute and chronic monoarthritis. List the common pathogens for septic arthritis and outline a management plan. Distinguish the two commonest non-infectious acute monoarthritides, gout and pseudogout : presentation, risk factors, investigations and treatment. Three short recordings (28 min) by Dr. G. Rohekar (rheumatology), one patient each: Mr. Williams' ankle (septic arthritis), Mike's toe (gout), Mary's knee (pseudogout). Septic arthritis is covered in depth in 11.1 . Mono = 1 joint, oligo = 2–3, poly = 4 or more (Dr. Jiang's definitions in 11.3 ; JIA counts differently).

entries.t: The Approach to a Hot Joint
entries.x: The Approach to a Hot Joint Acute hot, red monoarthritis 1. Infection 2. Infection 3. Infection 4. Gout 5. Pseudogout 6. “Oh, did I mention… infection ?” Rarer: reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis. “If the joint is red, aspirate it!” (“To inject is human, to aspirate divine.”) The 3 C's Turnaround Cell count A couple of hours Culture and sensitivity (and Gram stain , which is quick) 24–48 hours Crystals (polarized microscopy) A couple of hours The three cases Cell count (×10 9 /L) Culture Crystals Diagnosis Mr. Williams, 62, ankle 59 Gram-positive cocci in clusters None Septic arthritis Mike, 48, big toe 15 No growth at 24 h Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent Gout Mary, 78, knee 18 No growth at 24 h Rhomboid, intracellular, positively birefringent Pseudogout All three counts are inflammatory ; only the septic joint is in the very high range, and the counts overlap, which is why you need the culture and the crystals.

Septic Arthritis Acute bacterial arthritis is a medical emergency : without fast detection and treatment it causes fulminant joint damage . Risk factors Systemic Immunosuppression : diabetes, cancer, drugs ( methotrexate, leflunomide, prednisone, anti-TNF and other biologics ); age (very young or old); alcohol excess, IV drugs ; a recent infection Local Prosthetic joint ; recent joint surgery ; an abnormal joint (e.g. arthritis); penetrating trauma; skin infection Route: hematogenous spread from a remote site is #1 ; then direct inoculation (penetrating trauma, surgery) and spread from a contiguous site (infected bone). Organisms. From the deck. Why it's an emergency. From the 11.1 deck. Organism Share Gram-positive cocci 80% : staphylococci 60%+, streptococci 20% Gram-negatives 15% : the immunocompromised, elderly, neonates, IV drug users Anaerobes The rest 1 Urgently to the ED; consult orthopedics Aspirate: 59 × 10 9 /L, no crystals, Gram-positive cocci in clusters. 2 Admit; OR that evening for incision and drainage An infected joint is an infection in a closed space , like an abscess: it needs drainage . Repeat I&D until the surgeon is confident the joint is clean. 3 Empiric IV antibiotics, analgesia, rest The deck uses cefotaxime (Dr. Devlin's choice in 11.1 is cefazolin). IV antibiotics for 4–6 weeks.

entries.t: Gout: Who, Why and How It Looks
entries.x: Gout: Who, Why and How It Looks Acute inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid (monosodium urate) crystal deposition in the joint; “the disease of kings” (rich food and drink). Aspirating a first MTP is hard (tiny joint, and the patient won't let a needle near it), but try. Acute gout of the first MTP (podagra). From the deck. Urate crystals : needle-shaped, negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis, blue when perpendicular). From the deck. The sink: uric acid comes in through the tap (cell turnover and dietary purines : meat, shellfish, alcohol) and leaves through the drain (the kidneys ). Steady state: production = excretion. Under-excretion (a clogged drain) is the commonest cause of hyperuricemia . A full sink is fine; gout is when it overflows . Under-excretion : the clogged drain. From the deck. Acute gout : the sink overflows. From the deck. Gout Who First attack in men aged 35–50 ; in women after menopause (estrogen promotes urate excretion) Risk factors Impaired renal function ; diuretics (furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide); excess alcohol (beer especially); family history; male sex Associations (“a disease of plenty”) Obesity, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia Triggers: SMARTS S urgery, M echanical injury (micro-trauma may be why the big toe), A lcohol, R ecent illness, T ravel/dehydration, S tarting or stopping allopurinol The attack Over a few hours , very intense; swollen, warm, red; can't bear the bedsheet ; may be unwell with fever : looks just like an infected joint Joints Usually one lower-limb joint ; first MTP in 50% Duration Untreated: 7–10 days Recurrence 60% within 1 year, 80% within 2, 90% within 5 Uric acid and age : women stay flat until menopause, then climb like men. From the deck.

Confirming It, and the Bloodwork The only proof is the aspirate: urate crystals, needle-shaped, negatively birefringent in polarized light. Order Why CBC May show a high WBC and reactive thrombocytosis Creatinine Renal function (the drain) Serum uric acid Helpful if high, but can be normal during an attack : if it's normal and you still suspect gout, recheck after the attack Fasting glucose, fasting lipids The comorbidities A Word About Uric Acid Lots of people walk around with hyperuricemia and never get gout. So hyperuricemia can't make the diagnosis , and isolated hyperuricemia isn't treated , however high, if they've never had an attack.

entries.t: Treating Gout: Mop the Floor, Then Unclog the Sink
entries.x: Treating Gout: Mop the Floor, Then Unclog the Sink First treat the attack (mop up the water); then decide whether to lower the level in the sink (treat the hyperuricemia). Acute attack Details Non-drug Rest, ice, elevate ; diet : meat and seafood (shellfish, crustaceans) bad, vegetables and low-fat dairy good; less alcohol (beer is high in purines); hydration Intra-articular corticosteroid Fast, effective, no systemic side effects ; patients may refuse a needle in a very painful joint Oral NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor E.g. indomethacin 50 mg PO TID Oral colchicine 0.6 mg , up to q8h on the slide; diarrhea means most only tolerate it once or twice a day Oral prednisone When you can't inject: 30 mg daily × 2 days, then down 5 mg every 2 days (30, 30, 25, 25 … 5, 5, stop); the taper can be adjusted to the flare Consider allopurinol when 1. Recurrent attacks affecting their life (not one every couple of years) 2. The patient is at risk from the drugs needed for acute attacks 3. The patient accepts lifelong treatment 4. Tophi (almost always start) Allopurinol turns off the tap by inhibiting xanthine oxidase . From the deck. Tophi : urate deposits in skin and bone after years of hyperuricemia; urate-lowering therapy is indicated and can shrink them. From the deck. Why Allopurinol Causes Flares Any change in urate level, up or down, can trigger an attack. So don't start it during an acute attack (unless pain is well controlled), warn the patient , and give prophylaxis with an NSAID or colchicine . A flare after starting isn't a side effect, it's a known effect. Target: the lower limit of the lab reference range , < 360 µmol/L in Canada.

Pseudogout (Acute CPP Crystal Arthritis) Acute inflammatory arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals. Proof is the aspirate: intracellular, rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals. Mary's swollen right knee. From the deck. CPP crystal : rhomboid, inside a cell. From the deck. Gout Pseudogout Crystal Monosodium urate Calcium pyrophosphate Shape Needle Rhomboid , intracellular Birefringence Negative Positive Who Men 35–50; women after menopause Older people , often with OA Joint First MTP (50%) Knee (commonest) Onset Over hours, very intense Fast, but less intense and slower to peak Untreated attack 7–10 days Several days to a few weeks Treatment Steroid injection, NSAID, colchicine, prednisone; allopurinol long term Rest, ice, elevation, hydration; intra-articular steroid (the knee is easy to tap and inject), NSAID, prednisone taper Pseudogout vs Chondrocalcinosis Pseudogout is the acute arthritis from CPP crystals in the joint. Chondrocalcinosis is a radiographic finding : CPP calcification in the cartilage. You can have chondrocalcinosis on x-ray without ever having an attack, so the x-ray doesn't diagnose pseudogout. Normal knee (left) and chondrocalcinosis (right, blue arrow) : a fine line of calcium in the cartilage. From the deck.

Learning Objectives Identify patients whose symptoms suggest a connective tissue disease , and describe the distinguishing features of lupus, scleroderma and Sjögren's , and of myositis . Describe common rheumatologic blood tests (RF, ANA, ESR, CRP) and the expected results in SLE; when ordering them is inappropriate. Outline treatment with DMARDs and biologics, and their role. Five recordings (73 min) by Dr. Janet Pope (rheumatology, St. Joseph's): CTDs and a lupus case, SLE criteria, SLE epidemiology and treatment with antiphospholipid syndrome, Sjögren's and myositis, and systemic sclerosis. ANA, ENA and complement are in 11.3 . Face photographs (malar rash, heliotrope, parotid swelling) are described rather than shown.

The CTDs Disease Prevalence Systemic lupus erythematosus 1 in 1,000 (the commonest) Primary Sjögren's About 2 in 10,000 (secondary Sjögren's with RA is commoner) Systemic sclerosis 1 in 10,000 Polymyositis / dermatomyositis 1 in 100,000 Mixed and undifferentiated CTD — All are commoner in women , usually have autoantibodies (almost always a positive ANA), often Raynaud's , and affect multiple organs . Knowledge check: Ehlers–Danlos (a collagen synthesis defect) and Crohn's (autoimmune, not a CTD) aren't autoimmune CTDs.

A Lupus Case 22-year-old student New malar rash , a rash in the sun ( photosensitivity ), fatigue, Raynaud's , weight loss, hair loss , morning hand stiffness with knuckle swelling; a cousin with JIA. Tests (for diagnosis, prognosis and treatment safety): CBC with differential , ESR, creatinine and urinalysis (kidneys), ANA , a pregnancy test; then ENA, anti-dsDNA and complement. Results: WBC 2.8, Hb 111, platelets 43 , normal creatinine and urine, ANA 1:320 speckled , anti-Smith positive , anti-dsDNA negative, low C3 and C4 → SLE . The malar (butterfly) rash crosses the cheeks and nose but spares the nasolabial folds ; rosacea runs into the folds (and has dilated vessels). Lupus = wolf.

Classification Criteria Criteria are for research populations and are applied only if you already suspect lupus . Features count if ever present and not better explained. 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria : entry ANA ≥ 1:80; ≥ 10 points with ≥ 1 clinical domain; only the highest item in each domain counts. Aringer, Ann Rheum Dis 2019, via the deck. EULAR SLE treatment : hydroxychloroquine for all, escalating by severity. Fanouriakis, Ann Rheum Dis 2019, via the deck. ACR 1982 criteria (4 of 11; still widely used) 1–3. Skin Malar rash ; discoid rash (raised, scaly, follicular plugging, scars ); photosensitivity 4. Oral or nasal ulcers Often multiple, witnessed, sometimes painless 5. Arthritis Inflammatory, non-erosive (deformities can be reduced: Jaccoud's) 6. Serositis Pleuritis (pain on inspiration, effusion), pericarditis (pain lying down, effusion, ECG changes) 7. Renal Glomerulonephritis: protein and blood, red cell casts ; nephrotic syndrome 8. Neurologic Seizures or psychosis not from drugs or metabolic causes 9. Hematologic Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia , leukopenia, lymphopenia , thrombocytopenia 10. ANA > 95% of SLE; a negative ANA makes SLE highly unlikely; healthy people often have a positive one 11. Immunologic Anti-dsDNA , anti-Smith (very specific), antiphospholipid antibodies Common but not criteria (1982): Raynaud's (25% of SLE) and alopecia (alopecia is in the 2019 criteria).

Lupus Rashes and Organs “Lupus loves rashes”: malar, discoid (deep, scarring), photosensitive (on sun-exposed skin; on the fingers it spares the knuckles , the opposite of dermatomyositis), livedo reticularis, vasculitis. Cutaneous lupus can be skin-only: discoid lupus is often skin-only; subacute cutaneous lupus (widespread, photosensitive, usually anti-Ro ) is systemic in about half. Photosensitive lupus rash : chest V and fingers (sparing the knuckles). From the deck. Oral ulcers : often multiple, sometimes painless. From the deck. Non-erosive lupus arthritis : RA-like deformity, no erosions on x-ray. From the deck. Serositis : a pericardial effusion (“a pumpkin in the chest”). From the deck. Livedo reticularis : lacy purple mottling; in SLE and especially antiphospholipid syndrome (nonspecific if transient). From the deck. Vasculitis in CTD : digital arteries (fingertip loss) and leukocytoclastic purpura. From the deck.

entries.t: Lupus: Who Gets It, Why, and Treatment
entries.x: Lupus: Who Gets It, Why, and Treatment Women 9:1 , young (any age possible), 1 in 1,000 (vs RA 1 in 100, middle-aged). Rarely drug-induced (milder: joints, skin, serositis). Polygenic + environment (UV light, smoking, infection, silica, hormones, drugs); HLA-DR2/DR3, complement deficiencies, the X chromosome. More apoptosis and slow clearance of nuclear debris give the immune system time to lose tolerance. Families cluster with other autoimmune diseases (RA, JIA, thyroid, MS, Crohn's, type 1 diabetes, psoriasis, celiac). Knowledge check: SLE is multifactorial (not a single gene), clusters in families , and is commoner in women and girls. Treatment Non-drug Education, rest; sun avoidance and SPF 30+ (sun can flare skin and systemic disease); PT/OT; rheumatology follow-up; cardiovascular risk (more smoking, hypertension, lipids, diabetes, clots; ~50× cardiovascular events) Hydroxychloroquine Every patient unless contraindicated: the anchor drug , protects against major flares, helps skin and joints. (Knowledge check: hydroxychloroquine anchors SLE, methotrexate anchors RA .) NSAIDs, corticosteroids NSAIDs for joints; steroids topical (skin), low-dose oral (arthritis), high-dose (major organs) Immunosuppressants Azathioprine, methotrexate; severe: mycophenolate , cyclophosphamide , belimumab, rituximab Prognosis: worse with major organ involvement. Deaths from infection (immunosuppression), later accelerated atherosclerosis , and steroid harms (AVN, osteoporosis). So limit immunosuppression and treat cardiovascular risk.

Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome Antibodies against cell-membrane phospholipids → clotting. Antibodies (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant [falsely prolongs the PTT], anti-β2-glycoprotein I) plus recurrent venous or arterial thrombosis and/or recurrent pregnancy loss . Half is primary (knowledge check: it can be), half secondary , mostly with SLE . Rarely catastrophic APS , a “thrombotic storm” with high mortality. Often livedo reticularis and low platelets. Situation Treatment Antibodies, no events Nothing, or aspirin 81 mg ; aspirin if pregnant or planning (“baby aspirin for a baby”) Venous clot (DVT/PE) Warfarin (DOACs work less well) Arterial event (stroke, TIA) Antiplatelet Recurrent events Both

Sjögren's Syndrome Lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands (lacrimal, parotid, salivary) → sicca . Feature Dry eyes (xerophthalmia) Gritty, painful, worse through the day; artificial tears; corneal lesions Dry mouth (xerostomia) Hard to swallow dry food, altered taste, trouble speaking, bad breath, dental caries (frequent dentist visits) Gland swelling Parotid (looks like mumps), submandibular Extraglandular Raynaud's, leukocytoclastic vasculitis (purpura on the legs), inflammatory arthritis, peripheral neuropathy, rarely ILD Lymphoma Higher risk (chronic gland inflammation) Labs Anemia of chronic disease, leukopenia, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia , very high ESR , ANA 80–90% , RF often , anti-Ro and anti-La Leukocytoclastic vasculitis on the shins in Sjögren's. From the deck. Knowledge check: severe dry eyes and mouth 3 years of dry eyes (now a corneal ulcer), repeated cavities, swollen wrists and MCPs → Sjögren's . Order CBC, ANA, creatinine and urinalysis (± RF). If ANA positive, an ENA for anti-Ro/La , or just refer. Sjögren's carries a higher lymphoma risk and can occur with RA, SLE and systemic sclerosis .

Inflammatory Myositis Inflamed muscle causing proximal weakness (shoulders, hips, neck; trouble getting out of bed). Pain that makes a muscle give way isn't weakness. Two types: polymyositis and dermatomyositis . Causes of proximal weakness (rule these out) Drugs Steroids (myopathy without inflammation), statins , colchicine, hydroxychloroquine, cyclosporine Toxins Alcohol Endocrine Thyroid (hypo and hyper), parathyroid, adrenal Electrolytes High or low K, low PO 4 , low Mg Other Sarcoidosis, infection (influenza), inflammatory, malignancy Dermatomyositis Polymyositis Age Peaks in children and older adults Any age Skin Rash, photosensitivity None Cancer Paraneoplastic in the elderly (not in children); think of it with an ulcerating rash Usually not Gottron's papules over the knuckles (raised; flat = Gottron's sign). From the deck. Mechanic's hands : cracked, hyperkeratotic radial fingers. From the deck. V-neck rash (a shawl on the back). © ACR, via the deck. Periungual erythema with dilated capillaries. From the deck. Other dermatomyositis signs: the heliotrope rash (purple-pink eyelids), livedo, calcinosis . Antisynthetase syndrome = myositis + specific antibodies (e.g. anti-Jo-1 ) + rash + ILD. Labs Concerning features Raised CK ; ESR up in about half; ANA in about 80%; anti-Jo-1 → interstitial lung disease (bad prognosis); PM/Scl in scleroderma overlap Esophagus (dysphagia, aspiration), heart (arrhythmia, failure), lungs (ILD, diaphragm weakness), cancer (adenocarcinomas: ovary, prostate, colon, stomach, lung, breast) Treatment: high-dose prednisone + a steroid-sparing drug (azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, IVIg, rituximab); prevent steroid osteoporosis, watch glucose and lipids; lung disease needs aggressive specialist care. A classic dermatomyositis picture (weakness, Raynaud's, knuckle rash, high CK) is a clinical diagnosis , no biopsy or EMG needed.

Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma) A rare CTD (1 in 10,000) with a triad: fibrosis (collagen in skin and organs), vasculopathy (intimal proliferation, Raynaud's, obliterated vessels) and autoimmunity (knowledge check). Unlike other CTDs, there's no vasculitis. Not the same as skin-only morphea or linear scleroderma . Sclerodactyly : tight finger skin, fingers that can't straighten or make a fist. From the deck. The two killers : basal ILD and pulmonary arterial hypertension. From the deck. 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria (Dr. Pope is the senior author) Sufficient on its own: skin thickening of the fingers of both hands extending proximal to the MCPs Otherwise add points for: puffy fingers or sclerodactyly; fingertip ulcers or pitting scars; telangiectasia; abnormal nailfold capillaries ; pulmonary arterial hypertension and/or ILD ; Raynaud's ; SSc antibodies ( anti-centromere , anti-Scl-70 [topoisomerase I], anti-RNA polymerase III ) Limited cutaneous (lcSSc) Diffuse cutaneous (dcSSc) Skin Distal to elbows and knees (+ face) Also proximal: upper arms, thighs, trunk Antibodies > 95% ANA; ~50% anti-centromere > 95% ANA (often nucleolar); anti-Scl-70 (~30%, with pulmonary fibrosis); anti-RNA pol III (renal crisis) Organs Renal and heart rare, less lung; PAH in long-standing disease More of everything (skin, heart, kidney, ILD); PAH about equal; higher mortality “ CREST ” (calcinosis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) is an older name for limited disease; it's dropped because both subsets can have all five. The “15% rule” Nearly all Raynaud's , GERD (severe: a lax lower esophageal sphincter and a “lead pipe” esophagus); many have dysphagia; half ever have digital ulcers About 15% each A digital ulcer at any time (15% of those complicated: gangrene, osteomyelitis, amputation); significant ILD ; PAH ; inflammatory arthritis; Sjögren's; myopathy/myositis; renal crisis (in diffuse disease) The Most Lethal CTD About half of patients die of the disease: pulmonary fibrosis (ILD) and pulmonary arterial hypertension are the main causes, then heart involvement. Scleroderma renal crisis (sudden severe hypertension, intravascular hemolysis in half, renal failure in half) was a big killer: 80% mortality unrecognized, < 20% with an ACE inhibitor . Treatment is by organ: methotrexate for early diffuse skin; immunosuppression for lung disease; autologous stem cell transplant prolongs survival in severe early diffuse disease (not a cure).

Raynaud's Phenomenon Reversible colour change of the digits on cold: pallor (white), then cyanosis (blue) and/or rubor (red) on rewarming. In 3% of people, 25% of SLE, ~98–99% of systemic sclerosis (where it's most severe). Raynaud's : well-demarcated pallor. From the deck. Dilated nailfold capillaries : the sign that makes Raynaud's worrying. From the deck. Primary (Raynaud's disease) Secondary What Vasospasm alone With a disease, mostly a CTD Clues Young, otherwise well Late onset (a red flag), dilated nailfold capillaries , digital ulcers, positive ANA Raynaud's + dilated nailfold capillaries + anti-centromere (centromere-pattern ANA): 1 in 3 develop scleroderma within 5 years . Knowledge check: the least likely to develop SSc is the medical student with Raynaud's and reflux relieved by antacids; late-onset Raynaud's with puffy fingers or anticentromere is high risk. Treating Raynaud's Avoid cold (hat, mitts not gloves, hand warmers, warm feet), stop smoking Calcium channel blocker (nifedipine) : the main drug Severe: PDE5 inhibitors , topical nitrates, IV prostacyclin (iloprost), other vasodilators

Match the CTD Presentation Diagnosis Rash in the sun, mouth and nose sores, ANA and anti-dsDNA positive, blood and protein in the urine SLE Dry eyes and mouth, new cavities, parotid swelling, ANA, Ro and La positive, leukocytoclastic vasculitis on the shins Sjögren's Retrosternal dysphagia, tight skin of hands, arms and face, basal crackles, nucleolar ANA, anti-Scl-70 Systemic sclerosis Proximal weakness, new Raynaud's, rash over the knuckles, high CK Dermatomyositis Proximal weakness, high CK, no rash Polymyositis Repeated clots, livedo reticularis Antiphospholipid syndrome Interstitial lung disease Any, but commonest in SSc (and myositis)

entries.t: Week 11 · Infections, Arthritis and Connective Tissue Disease
entries.p: Week 11 · Infections, Arthritis and Connective Tissue Disease
entries.x: > Week 11 Rheumatology begins. Monday is the hot joint: hand infections (cellulitis vs a deep infection, bites, paronychia, felon, Kanavel's signs), septic arthritis (the aspirate, the organisms, cefazolin and a washout), osteomyelitis (sequestrum, MRI, vertebral OM) and the diabetic foot, then the rheumatologist's acute monoarthritis: infection first, then gout and pseudogout, their crystals and their treatment. Tuesday widens to many joints: classifying polyarthritis by time, count and pattern, the extra-articular clues, RF, anti-CCP and ANA (and when not to order them), synovial fluid and x-rays; then the same questions in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis: its seven subtypes, silent uveitis, growth and treatment. Thursday covers the spine and the commonest arthritis: ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic and reactive arthritis, then osteoarthritis (a clinical diagnosis, staged on x-ray, treated with exercise first). Friday is systemic disease: vasculitis (giant cell arteritis and ANCA vasculitis) and the connective tissue diseases (lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome, Sjögren's, myositis, systemic sclerosis and Raynaud's).
