Monday Nov 9 MSK infections, then acute monoarthritis. 11.1 MSK Infections Cellulitis vs deep hand infections, cat and fight bites, paronychia, felon and Kanavel's four signs; septic arthritis (history and exam, the monoarthritis differential, the aspirate, hematogenous seeding, S. aureus and strep, washout and cefazolin; gonococcal, Lyme, TB, viral, reactive and prosthetic joints); osteomyelitis (biofilm, sequestrum, who gets it, MRI, OVIVA, the vertebral OM case); the diabetic foot (why, assessment, probe to bone, swabs, imaging, antibiotics by severity) → 11.2 Acute Monoarthritis “Infection, infection, infection, gout, pseudogout”; aspirate the red joint for the 3 C's; septic arthritis risk factors, organisms and I&D; gout (the sink, who, SMARTS triggers, needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals, normal urate in an attack, steroid/NSAID/colchicine/prednisone, allopurinol and tophi); pseudogout (rhomboid positive crystals, the knee, chondrocalcinosis) → Tuesday Nov 10 Polyarthritis in adults, then in children. 11.3 Approach to Polyarthritis Inflammatory vs degenerative, acute vs chronic, mono/oligo/poly; onset and course (episodic, migratory, additive); the four distribution patterns and which joints each disease favours; risk factors and viral arthritis; extra-articular features of RA, psoriatic and reactive arthritis, go

Learning Objectives Describe the diagnostic criteria and classification of JIA . Identify the extra-articular manifestations of juvenile inflammatory arthritis. Describe the expected test results in JIA (CBC, ESR/CRP, ANA, RF, HLA-B27) and when to order them. Compare treatment in children vs adults , and know when DMARDs and biologics are considered. Two recordings (41 min) by Dr. R. Berard (pediatric rheumatology, Children's Hospital, LHSC): diagnosis, subtypes and complications, then pGALS, the workup and treatment; plus six practice questions. The adult approach is in 11.3 ; the limping child in 10.9 . Photographs of children are left out.

entries.t: What JIA Is and How It Presents
entries.x: What JIA Is and How It Presents JIA criteria 1. Onset before age 16 2. Arthritis in one or more joints 3. Lasting more than 6 weeks (rules out the common short-lived childhood arthritides) 4. Other causes excluded (a diagnosis of exclusion) Epidemiology: JIA 0.1% ( 1/1,000 , about 25,000 Canadian children) vs RA 1%. Most subtypes are commoner in girls . Rare before 6 months . Presentation: joint aches with inflammatory features : morning stiffness , better with movement, responds to NSAIDs. Usually subacute or chronic . Children keep functioning but change how : a toddler who'd started walking goes back to crawling or bum-scooting, or stops pulling up in the crib. Red Flags: Think of Something Else Constitutional symptoms , acute onset , severe pain , can't walk , night pain that wakes them, or a joint that's very tender or red . These point to infection, malignancy (leukemia, bone tumours) or an orthopedic problem rather than JIA (systemic JIA is the exception for fever).

The Seven Subtypes Subtypes, frequency, age and sex. Oligoarthritis is commonest (35–50% depending on the cohort); only ~5% are RF positive , unlike adult RA. From the deck. Subtype Who Features Oligoarticular (≤ 4 joints in the first 6 months) Girls 1–3 (under 6); F:M 4:1 1–2 large joints (knee, ankle; wrist, elbow), warm and swollen but not very painful : a “painless limp” . Extremely uncommon in the hip. Highest uveitis risk. Polyarticular, RF negative (≥ 5 joints in the first 6 months) Girls (3:1); two peaks: 2–5 and 10–14 Insidious; morning/post-inactivity stiffness ≥ 60 min ; fatigue . Younger children: fewer joints, can be asymmetric. Polyarticular, RF positive Teenage girls ; only 3–5% of JIA Many joints (20–30), symmetric: like adult RA Systemic (Still's disease) 10%; all ages ; M = F Fever, rash, arthritis ; the only one that can be life-threatening (below) Enthesitis-related 10%; the only one commoner in boys , usually > 10 “The baby brother of ankylosing spondylitis”: enthesitis (Achilles), sacroiliitis (spine itself rarely), dactylitis, lower-limb large joints. HLA-B27 in ~50% (vs 80–90% in adult AS); 30% go on to AS . Symptomatic (painful red) uveitis. Family history of AS, IBD, psoriasis, uveitis, reactive arthritis. Good prognosis unless axial. Psoriatic 10%; biphasic (young and preteen) Most don't have psoriasis yet , so look for a first-degree relative with psoriasis , nail pitting , onycholysis , dactylitis (and check the umbilicus for plaques) Undifferentiated 15% Fits none , or 2 or more categories (e.g. an 8-year-old girl with oligoarthritis, a family history of psoriasis and HLA-B27) Oligoarticular course: 1/3 never involve another joint (may remit for good); 1/3 add a joint or two but stay at ≤ 4; 1/3 go on to many joints, “extended oligoarthritis” , which behaves like polyarthritis. Enthesitis-related arthritis : complete ankylosis of the sacroiliac joints. From the deck.

Systemic JIA (Still's Disease) Named after Sir George Frederic Still (1897); the adult version is adult-onset Still's disease . It may eventually be reclassified as an autoinflammatory disease. These children are often admitted first for presumed infection or leukemia . Feature What it looks like Fever Dramatic, ≥ 39°C , once daily (quotidian) or twice daily, peaking late afternoon/early evening , often dipping below normal after. Looks very unwell with fever, rallies between. Rash Evanescent, salmon-coloured , often only with the fever; lasts hours Arthritis Often only joint pain without swelling early; effusions come later, which makes the diagnosis harder Other Organomegaly (hepato-/splenomegaly), lymphadenopathy , serositis (pericardial, pleural, peritoneal), lethargy, weight loss, growth disturbance Blood Markedly abnormal: high WBC (neutrophils), high platelets, anemia ; ESR/CRP always raised Macrophage Activation Syndrome The serious complication of systemic JIA: a cytokine storm . Persistent fever, lymphadenopathy, a very sick child, raised transaminases and a very high ferritin . Serositis can also cause pericardial tamponade . Needs prompt recognition and treatment.

Musculoskeletal and Growth Complications Untreated synovitis: muscle atrophy , joint contracture ; joint damage (narrowing, erosion) and deformity only after years untreated (unlike adults). Leg length discrepancy: an inflamed knee is hyperemic , which the growth plate reads as a growth spurt, so the leg first grows longer ; untreated, the physis closes early and the leg ends up shorter . (Inflammation in adolescence can instead delay closure, giving a long limb.) General growth: slows during active disease; severe refractory disease can stunt height. The jaw: the TMJ is very often involved, and its growth centre sits just below the condyle. Bilateral = micrognathia ; unilateral = asymmetry and deviation on opening .

Uveitis Anterior uveitis (the iris and ciliary body; inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber) is the most common extra-articular manifestation of JIA. The uveal tract : choroid, ciliary body, iris. From the deck. An irregular pupil from synechiae (scar tissue tethering the iris). From the deck. Uveitis in JIA Symptoms None (no red eye, no photophobia), except in enthesitis-related arthritis , where it's painful, red, photophobic, often recurrent, so the child seeks care Risk factors ANA positive , female , young at onset, early in the disease; oligoarticular most of all (up to 20%) Timing Usually within the first 4 years ; doesn't parallel the joints (the eye can drive treatment when the joints are quiet) Screening Regular slit-lamp exams , interval set by subtype, age at onset, disease duration and ANA: e.g. every 3 months for young, ANA-positive oligo or poly JIA in the first years; systemic JIA every 12 months. Toddlers need a pediatric ophthalmologist . Complications Synechiae (irregular pupil), glaucoma (disease or steroids), cataract , band keratopathy, macular edema , blindness Screening intervals : not for memorizing; the point is how often the youngest, ANA-positive children are examined. From the deck. Long-term morbidity: uveitis and blindness, functional disability, rarely joint replacement, growth disturbance, and still lower rates of finishing school and reaching vocational goals .

pGALS: the Screening Exam Paediatric Gait, Arms, Legs and Spine : a 2-minute, validated MSK screen designed in the UK (Dr. Helen Foster) for non-specialists. Watch the four videos (gait, arms, legs, spine) on YouTube. Do a pGALS when a child has… Muscle, joint or bone pain Is unwell with fever (+ constitutional symptoms, rash) A limp Delayed or regressing motor milestones (also picks up neurologic disease) A chronic disease with known MSK involvement (e.g. IBD) What it covers: look at the spine and watch them walk (and on heels and toes); arms out straight, fists, finger opposition; MCP squeeze ; wrist extension and flexion; arms up and neck movements; open the mouth (TMJ); knee and hip range; Adams forward bend (scoliosis).

Investigations The history and exam make the diagnosis; tests support it and rule out other things. Test In JIA CBC Systemic JIA : high WBC (neutrophils), thrombocytosis , anemia. Other subtypes: mostly normal, ± anemia of chronic disease ESR, CRP Normal or raised (always raised in systemic). Don't track joint count : 20 swollen joints with normal markers, or one knee with high ones. ANA Used to predict uveitis risk , not to diagnose JIA (and not a screening test) RF Positive in only 3–5% ; for classifying and prognosis in polyarticular JIA HLA-B27 Enthesitis-related arthritis (positive in 30–50%; also reactive and IBD arthritis) Liver enzymes, creatinine Baseline before NSAIDs and other drugs Radiographs : effusions (here a knee and an elbow “sail sign” from fluid, not a fracture). From the deck. Oligoarticular course. From the deck. X-ray finding Why it matters Soft tissue swelling, effusion , periarticular osteopenia Active arthritis Joint damage (space loss, erosions) Uncommon at diagnosis Advanced maturation on the affected side Unique to children: e.g. the patella ossifies around age 3 , so after months of knee arthritis it may appear on that side only. Always image both sides ; it hints at chronicity. Later: ankylosis of the C-spine (posterior elements) and wrist; short limb or small mandible from early physeal closure Long-standing disease Rule out other causes (e.g. tumour) Especially with a single joint

Treatment Aims: short term, relieve discomfort, preserve function, prevent deformity, control inflammation; long term, minimize disease and drug side effects, normal growth and development , rehabilitation, psychosocial and school support. It takes a team : pediatric rheumatologist, nurse, physio, OT, ophthalmology/optometry, family doctor or pediatrician, social worker, psychologist, the school. Non-drug: education, physio (range and fitness; these children are less active than peers), OT (splints, devices), nutrition. Course Treatment Oligoarticular (1–4 joints) NSAIDs and/or intra-articular steroid (about equivalent; NSAIDs may have more side effects). Young children are injected under nitrous or general anesthesia ; awake in clinic only from about age 10. Not improving or extended: treat as polyarticular. Polyarticular NSAIDs for symptoms; steroid injections in target joints; oral steroids as a bridge ; then methotrexate (first-line second-line agent; takes ~2 months; leflunomide an alternative). 20–25% fail and need a biologic (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab [anti-TNF], tocilizumab, abatacept), chosen with the family. Systemic NSAIDs and, for most, systemic steroids at diagnosis. Fever and systemic features: IL-1 blocker (anakinra) or IL-6 blocker (tocilizumab) first line; these transformed a disease once marked by steroid toxicity and growth failure. Arthritis left without fever: treat as oligo/poly. Uveitis With ophthalmology: steroid drops → (limited) oral steroids → methotrexate → infliximab or adalimumab Enthesitis-related Exercise and stretching; NSAIDs (may be enough if mild); DMARDs for peripheral disease ; anti-TNF especially for axial disease (sacroiliitis); topical steroids for uveitis Polyarticular course. From the deck. Systemic course. From the deck. Children vs Adults Naproxen is the commonest NSAID (twice daily and comes as a liquid ; indomethacin is the other liquid). All doses are weight-based . Joint injections need sedation in young children. There are fewer trials and fewer approved biologics , with slower access, than in adults. And treatment watches what adults don't have: growth and the eye .

entries.t: The Two Cases and the Practice Questions
entries.x: The Two Cases and the Practice Questions Case 1: 5-year-old girl, 3 months of knee swelling and a morning limp Systemically well; both knees, the left wrist and many small hand joints active. If JIA: polyarticular, RF-negative (≥ 5 joints). Primary care next steps: baseline blood work , refer to rheumatology and an optometrist/ophthalmologist , and consider starting naproxen while waiting. Case 2: 3-year-old boy, 3 months of intermittent fevers 2 months of pain and swelling in both knees and ankles, a faint rash lasting hours ; fatigued, pale, splenomegaly , effusions. First rule out infection and malignancy (ask about long-bone pain and night symptoms). If JIA: systemic JIA ; the serious complication is macrophage activation syndrome . Next steps: he's sick: send him to the emergency department (or call the rheumatologist if the diagnosis is clear, which it usually isn't). Practice question (Sarah, 3, right knee and left ankle for 3 months) Answer Most likely subtype Oligoarticular JIA (current nomenclature; the typical age and large-joint pattern) Most important step besides an ANA Refer to ophthalmology : silent uveitis in up to 20% of oligo patients needs regular slit-lamp screening First-line drug Naproxen : twice daily, liquid Two years later: both knees, ankles and wrists. Second-line agent? Methotrexate (first DMARD in extended oligo or poly JIA) Known complications All three : leg length discrepancy (knee hyperemia), micrognathia (TMJ), vision loss (uveitis) “Will she outgrow it?” Even in oligoarthritis, at least 50% still need care for arthritis as adults

Learning Objectives Determine a differential diagnosis for an acutely swollen joint or soft tissue. List the common pathogens for septic arthritis and outline a management plan (investigations and treatment). Describe the pathology, presentation and management of osteomyelitis and discitis . Describe the pathology, presentation and management of superficial and deep space hand infections . Describe the pathology, presentation and management of diabetic foot infections . Four recordings (80 min): hand infections (Dr. K. Faber, hand surgery, 12 min), then septic arthritis, osteomyelitis and diabetic foot infection (Dr. M. Devlin, infectious diseases, 25, 21 and 22 min). Monoarthritis from the rheumatology side (gout and pseudogout) is in 11.2 .

Cellulitis vs Deep Infection Cellulitis Deep infection (abscess) Depth Superficial skin infection Deep tissue : a collection of pus Where Dorsum , from the wrist to the MCPs ; rarely onto the fingers Fingertip , around joints , palmar surface Edges Irregular margins of redness Localized swelling and pus Treatment Antibiotics , rest, elevation, gentle movement; settles quickly Incision and drainage, wound care, antibiotics (broad first, then narrowed to the culture) Cellulitis : dorsal, wrist to MCPs, irregular edge. From the deck (photo: NHS). The fight bite : a tooth goes through skin and extensor tendon into the MCP joint of a clenched fist. From the deck.

The Deep Hand Infections Infection Where and who Organisms Cat bite (septic joint) Teeth enter the PIP or DIP joint Mixed; Pasteurella multocida Human “bite” (fight bite) Young men, fights ; the MCP joint Mixed mouth flora; Eikenella corrodens Paronychia Nail fold . F > M ; common in health care workers (wet hands) S. aureus ; mixed in diabetes; fungal if immunocompromised Felon Pulp space of the fingertip, often after a small puncture (a thorn) Cultured at drainage Suppurative (flexor) tenosynovitis Pus in the flexor tendon sheath , often days after a small palmar puncture Cultured at drainage All of them: incision and drainage, wound care, antibiotics (start broad, then narrow to the culture). Bites need broad-spectrum cover. Left alone they progress fast: the cat bite below went from septic joint to bone erosion (osteomyelitis) in 10 days. Cat bite, day 0 and day 10 : septic MCP joint now eroding bone. From the deck. Paronychia : nail fold. Drained with a small slit along the nail edge. From the deck. Felon : tense, swollen pulp space. From the deck. Kanavel's four cardinal signs. From the deck. Why the Finger Sits Flexed The tendon sheath holds the most volume when the finger is slightly bent , so the finger rests flexed to make room for the pus. Straightening it squeezes the sheath, which is why passive extension hurts most . Tenderness runs along the sheath and stops beyond it (at the pulp). Flexor tenosynovitis of the long finger , a week after a splinter: fuller and more flexed than the index and ring fingers. From the deck.

History, Exam and the Differential History Why Onset (OPQRST) and pattern : how many joints, symmetric? One joint, acute = acute monoarthritis Associated features : fever, rash Pustules point to disseminated gonococcal infection Exposures : injection drug use, sexual contact, travel Tell you which organism , and so which antibiotic Risk factors : immune compromise, diabetes , alcohol, age > 80, injection drug use, RA (or other joint disease); surgery, trauma, injections Why this patient, why now Exam What to note General Vital signs : is this sepsis? Inspection Effusion (loss of the parapatellar gutters), erythema, an old scar, a rash Palpation Warmth compared with the other side (a > 2°C difference is significant); a subtler effusion Range of motion and function Severely limited by pain , active and passive Red, hot, swollen knee : erythema, lost parapatellar gutters, an effusion. From the deck. Why it's an emergency : purulent effusion → enzymes destroy the cartilage → ankylosis. From the deck (textbook figure). Acute monoarthritis: differential Infection Bacterial (by far the commonest, especially a knee); viral, mycobacterial, fungal Crystal Gout (think of it first for a hot big toe), CPPD (pseudogout); see 11.2 Inflammatory Reactive arthritis, RA, sarcoid Trauma / blood Injury; hemarthrosis (coagulopathy) Malignancy Rare, more subacute Red flags for infection: fever, pain, and a big drop in range of motion.

Investigations and the Joint Aspirate Bloodwork: CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, CRP . Microbiology: blood cultures and a joint aspirate . ± Imaging (point-of-care ultrasound for the effusion). Think about coagulopathy, HIV and travel too. Aspirate goes to For Reading it Hematology Cell count > 50,000 WBC: very likely bacterial. > 20,000 : inflammatory. Cut-offs vary in the literature; septic joints can be lower and gout can be higher. The cells are mostly neutrophils . Microscopy Crystals Gout or CPPD Microbiology Gram stain and culture Gram-positive cocci in clusters = staphylococci; in chains = streptococci Test yourself: left, needle-shaped crystals among neutrophils (urate: gout); right, purple (Gram-positive) cocci beside a neutrophil. From the deck. Back to the 28-year-old Aspirate: 21,500 cells (this shows on the chart as “21.5”), mostly neutrophils, no crystals : inflammatory, but lower than you'd expect for a bacterial joint. Then you notice pustules on his skin. Young and sexually active: think disseminated gonococcal infection .

entries.t: How It Happens and What Grows
entries.x: How It Happens and What Grows “Why is there bacteria in this knee?” Most people assume trauma, but the vast majority are hematogenous : a small break in the skin, bacteremia, then seeding of the joint. Direct inoculation (trauma, surgery) is the minority. Synovial fluid is a “petri dish” ; it's the inflammatory response (neutrophils, cytokines, enzymes) that destroys the joint. Petri dish → inflammation → joint damage. From the deck. The organisms : S. aureus and beta-hemolytic strep. From the deck. Who Organisms Adults S. aureus (MSSA and MRSA); streptococci : group A ( S. pyogenes ), also groups B, C and G; rarely Gram-negative bacilli Children S. aureus , streptococci (see 10.9 for the limping child)

Treatment 1 Call orthopedics: urgent surgical washout Decompress the joint, irrigate out the organisms and the proteolytic and lysosomal enzymes, debride necrotic tissue. The goal is to save the synovium as an immune barrier. They may need to go back more than once. 2 Empiric IV antibiotics Cefazolin (Ancef) 2 g IV q8h covers S. aureus and the beta-hemolytic streptococci. Vancomycin 15 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h if MRSA risk (injection drug use, known colonization); many use it reflexively, which isn't necessary. A Gram-negative on culture gets targeted therapy. 3 Duration References say 2–4 weeks ; in practice S. aureus gets 4–6 weeks . The OVIVA trial (below) supports switching to oral. Culture negative? Usually because antibiotics were given before the tap (streptococci die quickly with a beta-lactam). Then think of the organisms that don't grow on routine culture.

Other Infectious Causes Gonococcal, Lyme and TB arthritis. From the deck; the same content is in the table below. Cause Clue Tests Treatment Gonococcal arthritis Young, multiple partners , MSM, F > M ; large-joint mono- or oligoarthritis (knee, wrist, ankle) Blood cultures; NAAT/culture of urine, rectum, throat ; joint fluid (positive in only ~50%) Ceftriaxone × 10–14 days Disseminated gonococcal infection Triad: tenosynovitis, dermatitis (pustular rash), polyarthralgia Same Same Lyme arthritis Hiking in an endemic area ; large-joint monoarthritis Lyme serology ; joint-fluid PCR (lower yield) IV ceftriaxone × 28 days Tuberculosis From an endemic country ; subacute large-joint monoarthritis Joint fluid for AFB RIPE × 9 months–1 year Infectious poly arthritis Bacterial Think infective endocarditis! Viral Parvovirus B19 (with anemia); chikungunya, Zika, dengue (travel); hepatitis B and C, HIV Older patient: septic joint or gout? Septic arthritis Gout Fever ± ± (gout can cause fever) Blood Leukocytosis Joint fluid Positive Gram stain or culture 20,000–50,000 cells; monosodium urate crystals on microscopy Reactive arthritis: a mono- or oligoarthritis days to weeks after a GI ( Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia , C. difficile ) or GU ( Chlamydia trachomatis ) infection, ± dactylitis and enthesitis ; HLA-B27 . Only a small subset has the full Reiter triad : urethritis, conjunctivitis, arthritis (“can't pee, can't see, can't climb a tree”). Reactive arthritis and its GI and GU triggers. From the deck. Prosthetic Joint Infection Don't put a needle into a prosthetic joint in the ED or the office. It's managed by the orthopedic surgeon (the one who did it, or a tertiary centre) with ID . It may not look like a red hot knee: less virulent organisms (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium [formerly Propionibacterium ] acnes ) give indolent pain or a draining sinus , so keep a high index of suspicion . Early vs late infections are handled differently.

How Bone Gets Infected Route Typical settings Hematogenous seeding Vertebral osteomyelitis , pediatric OM (most cases) Non-hematogenous (commoner overall): contiguous spread or direct inoculation Diabetic foot infection , next to a cellulitis; trauma; post-surgical (e.g. after a lumbar decompression) S. aureus dominates (septic joints have more streptococci). It's “sticky” : fibrinogen-binding adhesins , biofilm , and it can hide inside osteoblasts from the immune system. Hematogenous vs contiguous. From the deck. Biofilm : attach, multiply, signal (quorum sensing), mature, disperse. From the deck. Why Biofilms Beat Antibiotics Biofilms are everywhere (dental plaque, Pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis lungs) and grow on foreign bodies : prosthetic joints, heart valves, pacemakers. Bacteria deep in the film are metabolically inactive , and most antibiotics only kill replicating bacteria; the matrix also blocks penetration .

Acute vs Chronic Osteomyelitis Bacteria on or in bone → inflammation (edema, vascular congestion, small-vessel thrombosis ) → impaired blood supply → bone dies. Cancellous (spongy) bone is usually replaced; cortical bone may not be, leaving pockets of dead bone, the sequestrum . No blood supply means no antibiotic reaches it , so it seeds relapse after relapse. Inflammation → impaired blood supply → sequestrum. From the deck. A sequestrum (E, the dead central bone) with a draining sinus (D). From the deck.

Who Gets It, and Imaging Population Notes Diabetic foot The commonest you'll see (contiguous or hematogenous); Part 4 Vertebral (native vertebral OM) People who inject drugs , middle-aged men; TB ( Pott's disease ) Traumatic / surgical Open fractures, surgical-site infections Sacral wound Pressure ulcers in quadriplegia, spina bifida, the bedbound: constant soiling with feces makes cure by antibiotics alone very hard Children Hematogenous , usually < 12 years , in the vascular metaphysis . Easier to treat (good blood supply). S. aureus always ; Salmonella in sickle cell disease ; Kingella (a Gram-negative bacillus, rising) and other Gram-negatives. Why Salmonella in Sickle Cell Disease Dr. Devlin leaves this one for you to look up. The usual explanation: repeated splenic infarction (functional asplenia) weakens clearance of encapsulated bacteria such as Salmonella ; sickling causes bowel microinfarcts that let gut organisms into the blood; and infarcted bone is a good place for them to settle. (Added from outside the lecture: a PMC case review of Salmonella osteomyelitis in sickle cell anemia; the mechanism is mostly inferred from observational data.) Imaging Use X-ray, CT Not sensitive enough to exclude OM; a good place to start (x-ray), and positive findings count MRI Most sensitive ; the test for vertebral OM . Findings persist after cure , so don't routinely repeat imaging in someone improving on treatment (Choosing Wisely). Nuclear medicine tagged WBC scan (with a bone scan) Shows acute infection, including acute-on-chronic relapse; takes 2 days

Treating Osteomyelitis “What is my chance of curing this?” It depends on the blood supply , chronicity , whether it needs debridement , and patient engagement . Antibiotics alone will not save you ; chronic OM usually needs a surgeon. Dose high (e.g. ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h ): bone has a poor blood supply, so you need high drug levels. Oral can be enough: the OVIVA trial ( NEJM 2019) found that switching to oral antibiotics within the first week was non-inferior to 6 weeks of IV for bone and joint infections. Caveats: mostly hips, knees and feet (vertebral only ~2.5%), endocarditis and S. aureus bacteremia excluded, and the oral drug must be highly bioavailable (quinolones were used most; oral beta-lactams like cephalexin are less bioavailable). Dr. Devlin still prefers IV for vertebral OM . Treatment by site. From the deck.

Vertebral Osteomyelitis 55-year-old man, 5 days of 9/10 low back pain Afebrile, HR 92, BP 140/70. Normal neuro exam : 5/5 strength, normal reflexes and sensation, normal anal tone, no saddle anesthesia . No classic red flags, but he is high risk (injects drugs) . If it “smells a little iffy”, get the MRI. Next steps: CBC, creatinine, CRP , blood cultures , and go straight to an MRI spine (not CT). Guidelines suggest a spinal biopsy; in practice it's often not done. MRI: marrow edema and enhancement of L3 and L4 with irregular endplates = spondylodiscitis and osteomyelitis . The module's knowledge check (a 45-year-old who injects drugs, new back pain, fever yesterday): order CBC, CRP and blood cultures to find the infection and the organism, and repeat CBC and CRP to follow treatment. CK and urine culture don't help (no urinary symptoms); a urine tox screen doesn't explain the pain. Read the report for “epidural abscess” : it can compress the cord. A paravertebral one sits beside the spine. From the deck. Spondylodiscitis on MRI. From the deck. Microbiology hint S. aureus The vast majority Gram-negatives Older men with BPH and recurrent UTIs TB ( Pott's disease ) Epidemiology (endemic country). Favours the thoracic spine; bacterial disease favours the lumbar. Brucella Epidemiology (e.g. the Middle East) M. bovis After BCG therapy for bladder cancer Treatment: 6 weeks of antibiotics, IV preferred here. The deck's empiric choice is IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone (vancomycin for possible MRSA, especially in people who inject drugs); target the organism once blood cultures are back. Any neurologic compromise or cord compression: call neurosurgery emergently. Longer courses are for specialists (not examined).

Why Diabetic Feet Get Infected Vascular: macro- and microvascular disease → poor blood supply → poor healing. Neuropathy: sensory (no warning pain), autonomic (dry, atrophic, cracked skin) and motor (claw and hammer toes, Charcot foot ) → repeated pressure on one spot → ulcer. Immunity: diabetics are more infection-prone (e.g. weaker neutrophil function). Angiopathy + neuropathy + trauma + abnormal immunity. Ramírez-Acuña et al., Antibiotics 2019, via the deck.

Assessment Ask Why Is it truly infected? A wound isn't an infection How long has it been there? Years-old ulcers change the plan and the bugs Systemic symptoms? Fever, chills: be more aggressive Why did this happen? Soft tissue injury (new shoes or sandals, a scrape); mechanical (new job on their feet, not wearing the prescribed boot or orthotic); diabetic control (can they afford the meds?); known vascular disease, Charcot foot, prior ulcers Exam: the full diabetic foot exam: gait and footwear ; skin ( tinea , onychomycosis , calluses, cracks); bony deformity; monofilament (Canadian guidelines: 3 sites per foot; some sources use 10) and vibration; pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial). Then: where is it and why (how do they walk onto it)? Is blood supply the problem (vascular surgery)? How bad ? The diabetic foot exam. Shrestha et al. 2019, via the deck. IDSA severity grades (2012). From the deck. Severity What it looks like Likely bugs Mild A cellulitis around the wound Staph and strep Moderate Deeper than the skin, or erythema > 2 cm ± polymicrobial Severe Moderate + systemic features (SIRS) : admission, ortho Polymicrobial Smelly = anaerobes (not Pseudomonas , as many assume). Probe to bone = high likelihood of osteomyelitis . Dead tissue: you can probe firmly.

Investigations: Swabs and Imaging Bloodwork (CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, CRP ) if they look unwell; CRP is very useful here. Dr. Devlin's Two Rules on Swabs 1. Just because there is a wound doesn't mean it's infected. 2. If you swab any wound, you WILL find bacteria. Only swab a wound you think is infected, and get a good deep specimen (clean the surface first, e.g. with alcohol), not the skin colonizers on top. Imaging Use X-ray A place to start: doesn't rule OM in or out (if you see it, it's probably there); shows deformity for ortho MRI Most sensitive, but changes lag behind clinical cure : never repeat it in a patient who's getting better Tagged WBC scan Relapsed or chronic OM: is there acute-on-chronic infection?

Treatment Multidisciplinary, and number one is the patient : their engagement and ability to offload . Then: blood supply (revascularization? there's no point to antibiotics in a gangrenous foot), chronicity (dead bone needs debridement ), and offloading (a fitted boot at a diabetic foot clinic). Picture Antibiotic Mild, monomicrobial (cellulitis around a wound) Oral : cephalexin, doxycycline, or amoxicillin-clavulanate; IV cefazolin if needed Polymicrobial (chronic ulcer, colonized with Gram-negatives; smelly = anaerobes) Amoxicillin-clavulanate ; severe: IV ceftriaxone + metronidazole Pseudomonas on a good swab, or very severe Piperacillin-tazobactam MRSA history or risk Add vancomycin The summary table. From the deck. Case 1 : callus and oozing, no surrounding erythema. From the deck. Case 1: callused plantar ulcer Dry skin, no surrounding erythema , no deformity, but lots of callus and oozing. Infected? Hard to say. Ask: how long , what footwear keeps building the callus (which damages the tissue under it), and does it need debridement ? Debriding the callus down to healthy tissue may mean no antibiotics at all ; antibiotics alone would do nothing. Case 2: ulcer with a discoloured toe Diffuse ulceration and a dusky fourth toe : worry about blood supply (palpable pulses don't exclude microvascular disease). Involve vascular surgery ; systemic therapy such as ceftriaxone + metronidazole or piperacillin-tazobactam . Any severe infection: exclude necrotizing fasciitis ; blood cultures ; a deep swab if you can; call ortho or vascular ; start piperacillin-tazobactam (+ vancomycin if MRSA history or risk). Case 2. From the deck. The module's prevention question (Moishe, 62, A1c 9.2%, new cashier job on his feet, tight running shoes): his helpful steps are foot orthotics , inspecting his feet daily and seeing a podiatrist (regular checks, fast response). Merely having a metformin prescription doesn't help; taking it does. The new job on his feet is a risk, not a protection.

Learning Objectives Define and describe osteoarthritis : basic pathophysiology, epidemiology, risk factors and radiographic features. Propose an approach to the diagnosis and treatment of OA: non-pharmacologic, pharmacologic and surgical. Three recordings (41 min) by Dr. Tom Appleton (rheumatology, St. Joseph's): diagnosis and staging, OA as a disease, and treatment, each built on a case. Acute monoarthritis is 11.2 ; the hand nodes and OA x-ray features are also in 11.3 .

Chronic Monoarthritis: the Differential OA also causes polyarthritis (hand DIPs and PIPs), but this module is about OA as a monoarthritis , classically the knee. OA as polyarthritis : bony nodes at the DIPs and PIPs. From the deck. OA as monoarthritis : a suprapatellar effusion in one knee. From the deck. Chronic monoarthritis 1–3. Osteoarthritis By far the commonest 4. Chronic crystal arthritis CPPD (pseudogout) ; chronic gout (late, with damage); basic calcium phosphate (e.g. Milwaukee shoulder) First separate it from mechanical/sports causes of knee pain without arthritis (e.g. tendinopathy) Less common Inflammatory: RA, seronegative, JIA ( 11.5 ) Charcot (neuropathic) joint : diabetes, syphilis Chronic infection : atypical mycobacteria, with immunosuppression Neoplasm : pigmented villonodular synovitis, synovial chondromatosis AVN / spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee

entries.t: How OA Presents and How It's Diagnosed
entries.x: How OA Presents and How It's Diagnosed Typical OA monoarthritis Joint One joint: knee >> hip ; ankle; shoulder >> first MTP; thumb CMC or a DIP (usually with hand polyarthritis) Symptoms Pain, aching or stiffness brought on by activity ; not chronic widespread pain (think fibromyalgia) Morning stiffness < 30 min , usually < 5 Exam Joint tenderness, cool (never warm or hot) ± effusion, joint thickening, crepitus No red flags Infection, autoimmune disease (RA, SpA), malignancy, fracture, AVN Knowledge check: the typical chronic knee OA symptom is knee pain going down stairs (not a red, warm knee, psoriasis, night sweats or light-touch hypersensitivity). OA is a clinical diagnosis : must have the symptoms, must not have another cause. From the deck. Imaging in OA X-ray stages the disease (and is used for research criteria). X-ray changes without symptoms aren't OA , and you don't need an x-ray to diagnose it. MRI and bone scans: almost never , only to rule out a competing diagnosis (the knowledge-check answer). They're expensive and change nothing when the picture is clearly OA.

Staging on X-ray The space between femur and tibia represents cartilage and meniscus; losing it means tissue loss. Stage X-ray Early (Kellgren–Lawrence 1–2) Joint space normal; small osteophytes may start Late (KL 3) Joint space narrowing , some cartilage left; bigger osteophytes End stage (KL 4) Bone on bone : joint space gone, sclerosis , flattening and deformity Kellgren–Lawrence grades 1–4. From the deck. Late-stage OA (Mr. Liebowitz): medial narrowing and osteophytes. From the deck.

Epidemiology and Burden 14% of Canadian adults over 20 (1 in 7; just behind hypertension). The knowledge-check answer is 14%. The most common joint disease in the world; $27.5 billion in Canadian direct and indirect costs (2010), much of it lost work. Hip and knee OA rank 11th of 291 causes of years lived with disability (WHO), above TB and heart disease. Symptomatic knee OA mostly starts at 35–55 , then plateaus, so people live with it for decades. OA: 14% of Canadian adults , second only to hypertension. Public Health Agency of Canada, 2019, via the deck.

entries.t: Primary vs Secondary OA and Risk Factors
entries.x: Primary vs Secondary OA and Risk Factors What it is Primary (most) Risk factors, no single cause Secondary Post-traumatic (ACL or meniscus tear → OA in 5–10 years); metabolic/endocrine arthropathy that looks like OA ( acromegaly, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis ); rare monogenic dysplasias (Stickler); joints damaged by inflammatory arthritis (e.g. RA) Risk factors for primary OA. From the deck. Young, old and OA cartilage : ageing thins it (raises risk); OA loses proteoglycan and fissures. From the deck. Risk factor Note Obesity / metabolic syndrome Load and metabolic inflammation (it raises hand OA risk too) Age A risk factor, not the cause Mechanical Joint trauma , malalignment, occupation (heavy labour, kneeling) Genetics Polygenic : family history Female sex 1.4× Muscle weakness Common, and a target for treatment Knowledge check: neutral joint alignment is not a risk factor (ageing, an ACL tear, type 2 diabetes and inactivity are).

Pathophysiology: the “Sick Joint” OA affects every tissue of the joint : cartilage loses proteoglycan and fissures; released cytokines and chemokines inflame the synovium ; bone thickens, turns over and grows osteophytes . Chronic metabolic and mechanical stress leads to inflammation, pain and breakdown: joint failure , like heart failure, the joint failing to heal. It is not simply wear and tear , so treatment aims to remove what impairs healing (obesity, inactivity). OA is a disease of the whole joint organ. Nefla et al., Nat Rev Rheumatol 2016, via the deck. Ms. Markus has post-traumatic knee OA ; her risk of needing a knee replacement by 55 is probably > 50% , higher without good management.

entries.t: The Four Questions (“the Only Slide You Really Need”)
entries.x: The Four Questions (“the Only Slide You Really Need”) 1 What stage? Early, late or end stage 2 Which biomechanical factors can be treated? Alignment, overuse, weakness, gait 3 Is there a role for medical treatment? To improve pain, function and quality of life 4 Do they need surgery (joint replacement)? Only for end-stage disease with unacceptable symptoms and impact on quality of life No treatment yet preserves or extends the life of the joint ; the goals are less pain, better function, less disability and better quality of life.

Evidence-Based Management The Canadian OA Tool (Arthritis Alliance of Canada, CFPC, Centre for Effective Practice, 2017), via the deck. Non-drug Detail Exercise Active physio with neuromuscular exercise (balance, strength: Tai Chi, GLA:D): best evidence (knowledge check). 150 min/week of activity Weight Even 5% loss helps Assistive devices Walking aids, insoles, shoes, unloader brace (small effect) Joint protection, education OT; avoid aggravating movements Self-management, heat CBT (limited evidence), topical heat Not recommended Passive therapies: ultrasound, TENS, laser, acupuncture Drugs Detail Topical NSAIDs Diclofenac two to three times a day: effective and safe , the choice in chronic kidney disease Acetaminophen Small, questionable effect Oral NSAIDs If no contraindication (not in renal failure) Duloxetine (SNRI) Trial of 2–3 months when others fail Intra-articular corticosteroid Short-term relief Opioids Generally avoid (tramadol debated) Not recommended / inconclusive Hyaluronic acid injection, PRP, stem cells, glucosamine , chondroitin, capsaicin, neuropathic pain drugs Mr. Liebowitz's plan Physio (neuromuscular strength and stability) for at least 3 months and OT ; topical NSAID , no oral NSAIDs (renal failure); a steroid injection if refractory; then a 2–3 month duloxetine trial. Two years later: worse pain, a cane, bone-on-bone on x-ray despite all of the above → refer to orthopedics for knee arthroplasty . Surgery Evidence Joint replacement Recommended for end-stage disease: strong level 1 evidence over non-surgical care (Skou, NEJM 2015). A salvage procedure, not for earlier stages. Knee arthroscopy (± meniscectomy or repair) Not recommended : strong level 1 evidence of no meaningful benefit (Kirkley, NEJM 2008, done at Western). Knowledge check: not indicated in a 49-year-old with knee OA and a degenerative meniscal tear.

Learning Objectives Determine a differential for oligo- and polyarthritis , including seronegative and seropositive inflammatory arthropathies; distinguish acute from chronic polyarthritis. Compare the epidemiology, clinical features and joint distributions of RA and the seronegative spondyloarthropathies ; identify their extra-articular manifestations . Describe RF, ANA, ANCA, ESR, CRP and HLA-B27 : when to order them, when not to, and the expected results in RA, SLE, the seronegative arthropathies, JIA and GCA/PMR. Outline DMARD and biologic treatment, and compare adult and pediatric strategies. (You won't be asked to choose between specific biologics, only when they're considered.) Three recordings (61 min) by Dr. J. Jiang (rheumatology, St. Joseph's): classification, then the history and extra-articular features, then investigations and a brief look at management. Several objectives are shared with later modules (seronegative arthritides, connective tissue disease, rheumatology investigations and treatment). Children: 11.4 .

Three Ways to Classify Arthritis Type, duration, number of joints. From the deck. Inflammatory Non-inflammatory What Synovitis : inflamed synovium makes more fluid ( swelling ), with warmth, pain, stiffness ; redness mostly in infection or crystals (not usually RA) Degenerative : cartilage breakdown from repeated structural trauma (bone, menisci, ligaments), ending bone on bone Causes The immune system attacks itself (autoimmune: autoantibodies, immune-complex deposition, molecular mimicry), or attacks something foreign : infection (bacteria, viruses, fungi, mycobacteria) or crystals (urate = gout, calcium pyrophosphate = pseudogout) Primary OA ; secondary : trauma, avascular necrosis, neuropathic (Charcot) joints, recurrent hemarthrosis , hemochromatosis. Untreated inflammatory arthritis is itself a secondary cause of OA. Joints Depends on the disease (below) Any number; weight-bearing joints, spine, hands and feet Acute vs chronic inflammatory polyarthritis. Many acute ones become chronic if the basis is autoimmune. From the deck. Acute (< 6 weeks) Chronic (> 6 weeks) Polyarticular gout (severe gout with very high urate can mimic RA) Infectious and post-infectious , including viral Rheumatic fever (after strep, in children) Drug reactions (serum sickness) Early RA, CTD, vasculitis or seronegative arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Connective tissue disease : SLE, myositis, Sjögren's, scleroderma, MCTD Reactive arthritis ; seronegative spondyloarthropathies (psoriatic, enteropathic) Palindromic rheumatism ; systemic vasculitis; polyarticular JIA into adulthood; adult-onset Still's; sarcoidosis; drug reactions

Temporal Pattern Pattern Think of Onset Acute : peaks in hours to days Crystals, bacterial infection Insidious : builds over weeks to months RA, CTDs, OA Course Episodic : comes and goes, attacks lasting days Crystal arthropathy Migratory : 1–2 joints for a few days, settle, then new joints Palindromic rheumatism, rheumatic fever, early gonococcal arthritis Additive / progressive : more and more joints over time RA , CTDs, OA The module's knowledge check: right wrist for 3 weeks, then the right 2nd–5th MCPs, then 6 weeks later the left knee and wrist = chronic (≥ 9 weeks), additive : the common RA pattern.

Distribution: Which Joints, and How Small joints: MCP, PIP, DIP, MTP, IP. Medium/large : shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles. Axial : spine, sacroiliac. The four patterns. From the deck. Joint Favoured by Axial (spine, SI joints) Ankylosing spondylitis ; prominent SI joints = think spondyloarthropathy 1st CMC (base of thumb) OA (inflammatory arthritis usually spares it) 1st MTP Gout , OA DIPs OA, psoriatic arthritis ; spared in RA and other CTDs MCPs RA , CPPD (pseudogout) Wrists, shoulders, elbows, ankles RA, CPPD, psoriatic arthritis Type of involvement What it is Synovitis Joint swelling Tenosynovitis Inflammation of a tendon and its synovial sheath Dactylitis A sausage digit (the whole finger or toe swells): seronegative, especially psoriatic Enthesitis Inflammation where tendon inserts into bone (e.g. Achilles): seronegative Bursitis Anyone, but more with arthritis Deformities Nodules, Heberden's (DIP) and Bouchard's (PIP) nodes, swan-neck, boutonnière, ulnar deviation, MCP subluxation

Risk Factors and Triggers Age of onset : OA is rare young; RA and CTDs peak around 40, with a second, elderly-onset RA wave. From the deck. Arthrocentesis : fluid from clear to cloudy to pus to blood. From the deck. Factor Examples Demographics Age, sex, ethnicity. Symptomatic OA is rare under ~50 (unless an inflammatory disease set it up); RA and most CTDs peak around 40 (can start in the 20s); elderly-onset RA at 60–80 Family history Autoimmune disease, psoriasis, IBD : these cluster Triggers Infection ; medications (serum-sickness-like reactions); injury (OA); diet (gout) Comorbidities Psoriasis, IBD (spondyloarthropathies); CKD and hyperuricemia (gout) Viral Arthritis Seen much more since COVID. Polyarthritis during the infection or weeks after it (post-viral). Common culprits: hepatitis A, B, C ; HIV, CMV, EBV ; parvovirus ; chikungunya ; influenza; COVID-19 . Usually self-limited : supportive care (rest, ice, NSAIDs), and a short course of prednisone if severe. The module's knowledge check: COVID, parvovirus, hepatitis B, HIV and influenza can all cause it.

Extra-articular Manifestations System Manifestations Eye Uveitis , scleritis, episcleritis, sicca Mouth Aphthous ulcers Skin (the most common and useful) Malar rash , photosensitive rash, Gottron's , vasculitic rash, erythema nodosum, livedo reticularis, Raynaud's , tophi , nodules, keratoderma blennorrhagicum, skin thickening, sclerodactyly , calcinosis, digital ulcers Nails Psoriasis, pitting , psoriatic nail dystrophy Lungs ILD , pleural effusions, nodules Heart, kidney Pericarditis, myocarditis; glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis GI, GU Esophageal dysmotility, IBD; urethritis, genital ulcers Blood, constitutional Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia; lymphadenopathy, fevers Disease Look for Rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid nodules (extensor surfaces), ulnar deviation and MCP subluxation , episcleritis /scleritis, pulmonary nodules Psoriatic arthritis Skin psoriasis, nail pitting and dystrophy (onycholysis, yellowing), dactylitis , enthesitis (Achilles), uveitis Reactive arthritis Conjunctivitis, urethritis, arthritis (“can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree”; not everyone has all three); vesicopustular skin lesions Gout Tophi (ear, fingers, toes, elbows), podagra , olecranon bursitis Osteoarthritis Heberden's (DIP) and Bouchard's (PIP) nodes SLE Malar (butterfly) rash , discoid lupus (scarring), oral ulcers , subacute cutaneous rash on sun-exposed chest and arms Dermatomyositis Heliotrope (eyelids), shawl sign (upper back) and V sign (anterior chest), Gottron's papules (over the knuckles), mechanic's hands (cracked radial fingers), holster sign (lateral thighs) Scleroderma Sclerodactyly (thick skin, contracted fingers), dilated nail-fold capillary loops, Raynaud's (demarcated pallor on cold), calcinosis RA : nodules, ulnar deviation, episcleritis, lung nodules. © ACR, via the deck. Psoriatic arthritis : plaques, pitting, enthesitis, uveitis, dactylitis. © ACR/ASAS, via the deck. Gout : tophi, podagra, olecranon bursitis. © ACR, via the deck. OA : Heberden's (DIP) and Bouchard's (PIP). © ACR, via the deck. Dermatomyositis : Gottron's, mechanic's hands, holster sign. From the deck (the face photos are left out). Scleroderma : sclerodactyly, nail-fold capillaries, Raynaud's, calcinosis. © ACR, via the deck. Reactive arthritis. © ACR, via the deck. The knowledge check: of nail psoriasis, Achilles enthesitis, dactylitis, uveitis and malar rash , only the malar rash (SLE) isn't a psoriatic arthritis feature.

Routine and Special Labs Test What it tells you CBC + differential ↓ Hb: anemia of chronic disease (normocytic); ↑ platelets: inflammation ; ↓ platelets or WBC: autoimmune cytopenia (e.g. lupus) Creatinine AKI from glomerulonephritis or vasculitis; drug clearance (NSAIDs, some DMARDs) AST, ALT Drug clearance; autoimmune hepatitis with some CTDs CRP The marker used; is this truly inflammatory, is it flaring? ESR Not routinely ordered : nonspecific, raised by many things Uric acid Gout Viral serology Parvovirus, EBV, Lyme, hepatitis B and C, HIV, COVID-19 HLA-B27 Ankylosing spondylitis (less useful for other spondyloarthropathies) CPPD workup Underlying causes: hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism The knowledge check: active inflammation = thrombocytosis, normocytic anemia, raised CRP and ESR. Thrombocytopenia is not a marker of inflammation (it's an autoimmune cytopenia, e.g. lupus).

RF, Anti-CCP, ANA and ENA RF : an IgM that binds the Fc of IgG. From the deck. ANA patterns → ENA antibodies → disease. From the deck. Test Key facts Rheumatoid factor Positive in 70–80% of RA . Also in 5–20% of healthy people (more with age); rheumatic (Sjögren's, SLE, myositis, MCTD); infection (hep B, hep C , TB, syphilis, endocarditis ); chronic lung disease (IPF, silicosis, sarcoidosis); lymphoma . Neither sensitive nor specific : order only in the right context. Anti-CCP Antibodies to citrullinated proteins (arginine converted to citrulline after translation). ~95% specific for RA ; separates RA from other causes of a positive RF; often present years before the arthritis. ANA Antibodies to nuclear contents; used for SLE and other CTDs . Positive in up to 30% of normal people , plus RA, ILD, autoimmune thyroid and liver disease, PBC, IBD, MS, infections (TB, viral hepatitis, HIV, EBV, CMV, parvovirus), lymphoma and leukemia, after vaccines. Positive doesn't rule CTD in; negative typically rules it out. ENA Ordered after a positive ANA to name the antigen (figure above) When to Order RF and Anti-CCP, and When Not To Order once, for diagnosis , when you suspect RA: truly swollen joints with raised inflammatory markers . Don't repeat them to monitor : titres don't predict flares or treatment response. They do carry prognosis : seropositive patients tend to have more aggressive disease (more joints, erosions, extra-articular features). Don't order ANA and RF reflexively for joint pain; build the differential first. Lupus activity: in a flare, anti-dsDNA rises and C3 and C4 fall (complement is consumed in the cascade). Seroconcordant = the markers move as expected in a flare; serodiscordant = they don't. The knowledge checks: a positive ANA alone doesn't diagnose SLE (it's clinical: compatible symptoms, exam and a positive ANA). RF can be raised in a healthy older person, hepatitis C and CTDs, but not acute rheumatic fever (a transient post-strep illness that doesn't lead to RA).

Synovial Fluid Arthrocentesis (usually the knee, at the bedside, 5–10 minutes) tells inflammatory from non-inflammatory, rules out infection and crystals, and can be therapeutic (draining a tense effusion relieves pain). The WBC count is the key number . Normal Non-inflammatory Inflammatory Infectious Colour Clear Yellow Yellow Yellow-green Clarity Transparent Transparent Cloudy Cloudy Viscosity High High Moderate Low WBC (/mm 3 ) < 200 < 2,000 > 2,000 > 2,000 % PMNs < 25% < 25% > 50% > 75% Crystals None None Possible None Gram stain, culture Negative Negative Negative Positive The > 2,000 line separates inflammatory from not; septic joints usually run far higher (> 20,000–50,000; see 11.1 ). Dr. Jiang's own clinic example: a cloudy, slightly amber knee tap with ~5,800 WBC , which turned out to be gout . The synovial fluid table. From the deck. Urate (needles, negative, yellow) vs CPPD (rhomboid, positive, blue). From the deck.

X-rays Not very helpful in acute polyarthritis : damage takes time (sometimes years). And not all inflammatory arthritis erodes : yes in RA, psoriatic arthritis and other spondyloarthropathies, gout, septic arthritis; no in SLE and Sjögren's , even after months untreated. When x-rays help: a baseline before treating an autoimmune arthritis; telling inflammatory from degenerative in long-standing symptoms; telling one inflammatory arthritis from another ; checking for progressive damage despite treatment (time to escalate?). Inflammatory Degenerative Periarticular osteopenia Osteophytes Soft tissue swelling: periarticular, fusiform Subchondral sclerosis Joint space narrowing: symmetric (the whole joint is inflamed) Subchondral cysts Erosions (marginal) Joint space narrowing: asymmetric Periostitis (new bone, e.g. psoriatic) Erosions only in erosive OA (a particular look) Deformities: subluxation, deviation Deformities: deviation from extra bone growth The knowledge check: periarticular erosions separate inflammatory from degenerative; osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and asymmetric narrowing are OA. Joint distribution matters too. Normal (left), gout (middle), RA (right). Gout's erosions are well defined, “rat-bite”, with overhanging edges (arrows); RA has obliterated joint spaces, subluxation and erosions everywhere. The osteoarthritis hand Dr. Jiang describes (carpal sclerosis, narrowing and osteophytes at the finger joints) sits hidden behind the gout image on the slide. From the deck. Knee OA : medial joint space lost (asymmetric), subchondral sclerosis. From the deck.

Management, Briefly Non-drug Drugs Gentle physiotherapy , stretching and strengthening ; cool or warm compresses; rest Analgesia : acetaminophen, NSAIDs Corticosteroids : prednisone, IM methylprednisolone (Depo-Medrol), joint injections (large joints: shoulders, wrists, knees, ankles) DMARDs if RA or lupus is suspected (below) Gout : colchicine, NSAIDs, steroids; long term allopurinol or febuxostat Pseudogout : colchicine, NSAIDs, steroids (weak evidence for prophylaxis) DMARD class Examples Conventional synthetic (csDMARDs) Methotrexate , hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide Targeted synthetic (tsDMARDs) Tofacitinib (a JAK inhibitor) Biologics (bDMARDs) Adalimumab (anti-TNF), tocilizumab (anti-IL-6) Disease-specific treatment comes in the later modules.

Rheumatoid arthritis has its own section near the end, because it runs through the polyarthritis lecture and its treatment comes in Week 12. entries.t: From “My Joints Hurt” to a Diagnosis
entries.x: From “My Joints Hurt” to a Diagnosis Joint or muscle pain One hot, swollen, painful joint? Fever or not: septic arthritis, gout and pseudogout can look identical Yes Aspirate it now 3 C's: cell count, culture + Gram stain, crystals; blood cultures Septic: orthopedics for washout + cefazolin 2 g IV q8h (vancomycin if MRSA risk) Needles, negative = gout ; rhomboids, positive = pseudogout . Crystals don't exclude infection. 11.2 · 11.1 No Over 50 with a new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or vision change? Or new shoulder and hip girdle stiffness (PMR) Yes Giant cell arteritis Draw ESR and CRP , then prednisone 1 mg/kg (max 60 mg) the same day . Biopsy or ultrasound (halo sign) within 1–2 weeks; steroids don't spoil it. Vision loss is painless and permanent. 11.7 No Systemically unwell with purpura, hemoptysis, blood in the urine or a new organ problem? Yes Vasculitis or lupus Urinalysis, creatinine, chest x-ray , CBC, liver enzymes, ESR/CRP Rule out infection first (hepatitis B/C, HIV, endocarditis), plus drugs, cocaine and cancer ANCA, ANA, complement; pulmonary-renal = admit , active sediment = urgent nephrology 11.7 · 11.8 No Is it really the joint? Swelling, or pain on passive movement through the whole range No Around the joint, or everywhere One tender spot, pain on resisted movement: tendinitis, bursitis, enthesitis Widespread pain, tender points, normal exam and labs: fibromyalgia Over 50, shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, high ESR: PMR (ask the GCA questions) Proximal weakness rather than pain, high CK: myositis Yes Inflammatory? Morning stiffness > 60 min, gelling after rest, better with use; warm, boggy swelling; fatigue No Mechanical: osteoarthritis Stiffness < 30 min, worse with use, cool bony joint, crepitus; knees, hips, DIPs, 1st CMC. A clinical diagnosis : x-ray stages it, MRI almost never. Exercise and weight loss first. 11.6 Yes How many joints, and for how long? Mono 1 · oligo 2–3 · poly ≥ 4 · acute ≤ 6 weeks Mono (1 joint) Acute: septic, gout, pseudogout, trauma/hemarthrosis Chronic: OA, chronic crystal disease, TB or fungal, Charcot, synovial tumour, AVN A child: septic, transient synovitis, oligo JIA (never a lone hip) Oligo (2–3), often legs ± back Spondyloarthritis: AS, psoriatic, reactive, IBD Gout or pseudogout, gonococcal, Lyme A child: oligoarticular JIA (girl, 1–3, painless limp) Poly (≥ 4) Acute: viral (parvovirus, hepatitis B/C, HIV), polyarticular gout, rheumatic fever, early autoimmune Chronic: RA , SLE and the

The Pattern Names the Disease Four patterns. From 11.3's deck. Pattern Think The tell Symmetric small joints (MCP, PIP, wrist, MTP) ± large, DIPs spared , additive Rheumatoid arthritis ; SLE and the CTDs (non-erosive) Stiffness > 1 hour, RF/anti-CCP; lupus has skin, kidney and blood clues Asymmetric oligo, legs, + DIPs , dactylitis, enthesitis Psoriatic (or reactive) Psoriasis, nail pitting , sausage digit, pencil-in-cup Spine and SI joints ± large leg joints Ankylosing spondylitis and the SpA family Young, inflammatory back pain, HLA-B27, uveitis, Achilles Knees, hips, DIPs, PIPs, 1st CMC Osteoarthritis Heberden's (DIP) and Bouchard's (PIP) nodes, cool and bony 1st MTP, episodic , then ankle/knee Gout Hours to peak, tophi, diuretics/alcohol/kidneys Knee or wrist in an older person Pseudogout (CPPD) Chondrocalcinosis; MCPs 2–3 + hemochromatosis Migratory (one joint settles, the next flares) Gonococcal, rheumatic fever, palindromic RA Gonococcal: tenosynovitis + pustules + sexually active A child, > 6 weeks, < 16 years JIA (diagnosis of exclusion) Oligo: painless knee, ANA → uveitis; systemic: quotidian fever, salmon rash Time course: additive = RA and the CTDs; episodic = crystals; migratory = rheumatic fever, early gonococcal, palindromic. 11.3

Look Outside the Joint The skin is the most useful place to look. One clue often names the disease before any test. Where Clue Points to Skin Plaques, nail pitting Psoriatic arthritis Malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, discoid lesions SLE Heliotrope, Gottron's papules, shawl/V sign, mechanic's hands Dermatomyositis Sclerodactyly, calcinosis, digital ulcers, dilated nailfold capillaries Systemic sclerosis Palpable purpura Small-vessel vasculitis (rule out infection, hepatitis C) Nodules on extensor surfaces RA (tophi in gout) Keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis Reactive arthritis Evanescent salmon-pink rash with fever spikes Systemic JIA (Still's) Eye Red painful eye, anterior uveitis Spondyloarthritis (HLA-B27) Silent uveitis on slit lamp Oligo JIA (ANA positive) Scleritis, episcleritis, dry eyes RA, Sjögren's Painless sudden vision loss over 50 GCA Mouth Painless oral ulcers SLE Dry mouth, cavities, parotid swelling Sjögren's Lungs ILD Myositis (anti-Jo-1), systemic sclerosis, RA Nodules, hemorrhage, sinus disease GPA (c-ANCA) Asthma + eosinophilia EGPA Kidney Red cell casts, proteinuria Lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis New hypertension + rising creatinine Scleroderma renal crisis (ACE inhibitor) Gut, GU Diarrhea or urethritis 1–3 weeks before Reactive arthritis Crohn's or ulcerative colitis IBD-associated SpA Severe reflux, dysphagia Systemic sclerosis Hands, cold White → blue → red fingers Raynaud's: all the CTDs, ~100% of SSc Blood, pregnancy Clots, miscarriages, low platelets Antiphospholipid syndrome 11.3 · 11.8 · 11.5

Twins to Tell Apart Twins The one feature that splits them Septic arthritis vs gout Only the aspirate. Fever, redness and a high WBC happen in both; urate can be normal in an attack. Gout vs pseudogout Needles, negative, 1st MTP, hours to peak vs rhomboids, positive, knee, older, slower but lasts longer. RA vs OA hands RA: MCPs/PIPs/wrists, DIPs spared , soft swelling, > 1 h stiffness. OA: DIPs/PIPs/1st CMC, bony nodes, < 30 min. RA vs psoriatic Symmetric, DIPs spared, RF/anti-CCP vs asymmetric, DIPs, dactylitis, enthesitis, nails, seronegative. RA vs lupus arthritis Both symmetric small joints; lupus is non-erosive (deformities reducible) with skin, kidney, blood and ANA/dsDNA. Inflammatory vs mechanical back pain < 40, insidious, > 3 months, night pain, > 60 min stiffness, better with exercise vs any age, acute, worse with activity. GCA vs PMR Both over 50 with a high ESR. Headache, jaw, scalp or vision = GCA (60 mg); girdle stiffness alone = PMR (low-dose prednisone). GPA vs MPA Sinuses, nose, lung nodules, c-ANCA/PR3 vs no ENT, p-ANCA/MPO. EGPA = asthma + eosinophils. Limited vs diffuse SSc Skin distal to elbows/knees, anticentromere, pulmonary hypertension late vs proximal/trunk, anti-Scl-70, ILD and renal crisis early. Transient synovitis vs septic hip (child) Well, afebrile, after a cold, can bear weight vs febrile, unwell, won't bear weight, high CRP: aspirate.

entries.t: What to Order, and What It Means
entries.x: What to Order, and What It Means Test Order it when Reading it Joint aspirate Any hot joint; any new effusion you can't explain WBC < 2,000 non-inflammatory; > 2,000 inflammatory; very high with > 75% PMNs + Gram stain/culture = septic. Crystals under polarized light. CBC, creatinine, liver enzymes, urinalysis Baseline for any inflammatory arthritis; always in suspected vasculitis/CTD Cytopenias (lupus), active sediment (nephritis, vasculitis); also needed before DMARDs ESR, CRP Inflammation suspected; GCA/PMR Non-specific. Both normal essentially rules out GCA. RF Suspected RA, once 70–80% of RA; also 5–20% of healthy people, hepatitis C, endocarditis, TB, Sjögren's. Never to monitor. Anti-CCP With RF in suspected RA ~95% specific ; positive = more erosive disease ANA A CTD is suspected from clinical features Positive in up to 30% of normal people. Negative rules lupus out ; positive needs the specific antibodies. Specific antibodies ANA positive and the picture fits dsDNA (lupus, flares, kidney), Smith (lupus, very specific), Ro/La (Sjögren's, neonatal lupus), Jo-1 (myositis + ILD), centromere (limited SSc), Scl-70 (diffuse SSc) C3, C4 Lupus activity Low in a flare with dsDNA rising Antiphospholipid antibodies Clots, pregnancy loss, lupus Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I; repeat at 12 weeks ANCA Suspected small-vessel vasculitis c-ANCA/PR3 = GPA; p-ANCA/MPO = MPA, EGPA. Biopsy confirms. HLA-B27 Inflammatory back pain, with SI imaging > 90% of AS but 8% of everyone: supports, never diagnoses Serum urate Gout, ideally 2 weeks after the attack; to titrate allopurinol Can be normal in an attack; high urate alone is not gout. Target < 360 µmol/L. CK Proximal weakness High in myositis (check statins, hypothyroidism) 11.3 serology · synovial fluid

Imaging in One Table Inflammatory (RA) Degenerative (OA) Other tells Joint space Symmetric (uniform) narrowing Asymmetric, worst where it bears weight Gout: space kept until late Bone Periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions Osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts Gout: punched-out erosions with overhanging edges; PsA: pencil-in-cup Spine C1–C2 instability Disc space loss, facet OA AS: sacroiliitis, thin syndesmophytes, bamboo spine; PsA: bulky asymmetric ones When MRI Osteomyelitis (most sensitive); early sacroiliitis (non-radiographic axial SpA). Almost never for OA.

arterial: antiplatelet; pregnancy: aspirin 81 mg Sjögren's Dry eyes and mouth, parotids Anti-Ro/La Symptoms; watch for lymphoma Dermatomyositis Proximal weakness + rash CK, anti-Jo-1, biopsy Steroids; Rheumatoid Arthritis 1 Suspect it Swollen, tender MCPs, PIPs, wrists or MTPs , symmetric , > 6 weeks, morning stiffness > 1 hour, fatigue. Squeeze tenderness across the MCPs or MTPs. DIPs spared. Women 2–3:1, peak 30–50; smoking is the big modifiable risk. 2 Test it RF and anti-CCP (once), CRP/ESR, CBC, creatinine, liver enzymes, hand and foot x-rays (erosions = established damage). Hepatitis B/C and TB screening before treatment. 3 Exclude the mimics Viral arthritis (parvovirus, hepatitis), lupus, psoriatic arthritis, polyarticular gout or CPPD, hand OA, PMR in older adults. 4 Treat early Refer to rheumatology. Methotrexate is the anchor DMARD (with folic acid; not in pregnancy), often with a short steroid bridge; add or switch to biologics or a JAK inhibitor if targets aren't met. Week 12 covers the drugs. The 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria For a patient with at least one swollen joint not better explained by another disease. ≥ 6 of 10 points = RA. Domain Finding Points Joints 1 large joint 0 2–10 large joints 1 1–3 small joints 2 4–10 small joints 3 > 10 joints, at least 1 small 5 Serology RF and anti-CCP negative 0 Low positive RF or anti-CCP 2 High positive (> 3× upper limit) 3 Acute phase Abnormal CRP or ESR 1 Duration ≥ 6 weeks 1 Outside the joint: nodules, ulnar deviation, episcleritis, lung nodules. From 11.3's deck. Beyond the joints What to know Hands Ulnar deviation, MCP subluxation, swan-neck and boutonnière deformities Neck C1–C2 (atlantoaxial) instability : x-ray the neck before an anesthetic Skin, eyes, mouth Nodules (seropositive); episcleritis, scleritis; secondary Sjögren's Lungs, heart ILD, nodules, effusions; pericarditis; higher cardiovascular risk Blood Anemia of chronic disease; Felty's (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia)

Six Patients 1. A 68-year-old on hydrochlorothiazide, hot swollen knee overnight, 38.2°C Path and answer One hot joint → aspirate before anything else. Gout is likely (diuretic), but septic arthritis has to be excluded by Gram stain and culture, and both can coexist. Rhomboid crystals with chondrocalcinosis would make it pseudogout. 2. A 74-year-old, 3 weeks of headache and pain chewing, ESR 88 Path and answer Over 50 + new headache + jaw claudication = GCA . Prednisone 60 mg today, bone protection, biopsy or ultrasound within 1–2 weeks. Don't wait for the biopsy. 3. A 41-year-old woman, 4 months of swollen MCPs and wrists on both sides, 2 hours of stiffness Path and answer Joint, inflammatory, poly, chronic, symmetric small joints, DIPs spared = RA . RF + anti-CCP, CRP, hand/foot x-rays, refer for early methotrexate. 4. A 24-year-old man, 8 months of low back pain that wakes him at night and eases at the gym; a red painful eye last year Path and answer Inflammatory back pain + anterior uveitis = axial spondyloarthritis . SI x-ray (MRI if normal) and HLA-B27; exercise and NSAIDs first. 5. A 29-year-old woman, painful small joints, a rash on her cheeks after the beach, mouth ulcers; urine shows protein Path and answer Multi-system + organ involvement → SLE with possible nephritis. ANA, dsDNA, Smith, C3/C4, CBC, urinalysis with microscopy and creatinine; urgent rheumatology; hydroxychloroquine. 6. A 63-year-old, knee pain worse at the end of the day, 10 minutes of stiffness, crepitus Path and answer Joint, mechanical → osteoarthritis . No bloods or MRI; x-ray only to stage. Exercise, weight loss, topical NSAID.

Learning Objectives Determine a differential for oligo- and polyarthritis , including seronegative and seropositive inflammatory arthropathies. Compare the epidemiology, clinical features and joint distributions of rheumatoid arthritis and the seronegative spondyloarthropathies; identify their extra-articular manifestations . Describe HLA-B27 and the inflammatory tests: when to order them and what to expect. Outline DMARDs vs biologics and when biologics are considered (you won't be asked to choose a specific biologic). Three recordings (40 min) by Dr. Sherry Rohekar (rheumatology): spondyloarthritis and AS, psoriatic and reactive arthritis, then exam and treatment. The patterns and serology are in 11.3 ; enthesitis-related JIA in 11.4 .

The Spondyloarthritis Family “Seronegative” because rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are negative . The diseases overlap; ankylosing spondylitis is the prototype. The SpA family , AS at the centre. From the deck. Clues to SpA : symptoms, imaging, inflammatory markers, NSAID response; plus HLA-B27, family history and associated diseases (infection, psoriasis, Crohn's/colitis). From the deck.

Inflammatory vs Mechanical Back Pain Inflammatory Mechanical Age of onset < 40 (late teens, 20s) Any age Onset Insidious Acute Duration > 3 months < 4 weeks Morning stiffness > 60 min < 30 min Night pain Yes, especially the second half of the night No Activity Improves Worsens Exam SI joint tenderness, loss of mobility in all planes, reduced chest expansion No SI tenderness, abnormal flexion, normal chest expansion Neuro deficits Unlikely Possible (sciatica) The module's knowledge check: of the options, only morning stiffness > 60 minutes marks inflammatory pain (worse with activity, onset > 45 and neuro deficits point the other way). Mechanical back pain is in Week 7 .

Ankylosing Spondylitis Greek ankylos (bent) + spondylos (vertebra). An autoimmune attack on the spinal joints that starts in the SI joints and ascends ; the inflammation triggers new bone , which fuses the spine into a rigid column ( bamboo spine ) and, untreated, the “question-mark” posture. Epidemiology HLA-B27 In > 90% of white AS patients, 50–80% of non-white; but also 8% of the general Caucasian population , so the gene alone isn't AS. HLA-B27 positive = 50–100× relative risk. Twins 60% concordance in identical twins, 20–25% in HLA-B27-positive non-identical twins Prevalence Up to about 1–1.4% Untreated AS over 25 years : the progressive “question-mark” posture. From the deck. Normal, early (inflammation), advanced (fusion). From the deck. Classification Criteria Modified New York (1984) (older; still comes up) Radiographic sacroiliitis (grade ≥ 2 bilateral or 3–4 unilateral) + ≥ 1 clinical criterion : back pain > 3 months better with exercise not rest; limited lumbar motion; limited chest expansion ASAS axial SpA (current) Entry: back pain ≥ 3 months, onset < 45 . Then sacroiliitis on imaging + ≥ 1 SpA feature , or HLA-B27 + ≥ 2 SpA features SpA features: inflammatory back pain, arthritis, enthesitis (heel) , uveitis , dactylitis , psoriasis , Crohn's/colitis , good NSAID response , family history, HLA-B27, raised CRP. ASAS axial SpA criteria (Rudwaleit 2009). From the deck.

entries.t: Sacroiliitis and the Spine on Imaging
entries.x: Sacroiliitis and the Spine on Imaging Sacroiliitis is usually bilateral and symmetric , in the synovial lower two-thirds of the joint. Earliest change: erosion on the iliac side (thinner cartilage) → “pseudowidening” → sclerosis → complete fusion (ankylosis) . Spine: thin, marginal syndesmophytes bridge the vertebrae → bamboo spine . Non-radiographic axial SpA: no diagnostic SI changes on x-ray but diagnostic MRI (bone marrow edema). “X-ray negative, MRI positive.” Bilateral sacroiliitis going on to fusion (arrows). Rheumtext, via the deck. Bamboo spine : thin, elegant syndesmophytes. From the deck. Active sacroiliitis on MRI : bone marrow edema (dark on T1, bright on STIR). This is how non-radiographic axial SpA is found. ASAS handbook, via the deck.

Enthesitis and Extra-articular Disease An enthesis is where ligament, tendon or capsule inserts into bone; enthesitis inflames it, ending in new bone or fibrosis. Sites: SI joints, discs, manubriosternal joint, pubic symphysis, iliac crests, trochanters, patellae, clavicles, and the calcaneus (Achilles insertion and plantar fascia) . Achilles enthesitis : swollen, tender insertion. Rheumtext, via the deck. AS is more than back pain (the deck's “ANKSPOND”) A ortic Aortic insufficiency, ascending aortitis, conduction abnormalities, pericarditis (long-standing disease) N eurologic Atlantoaxial subluxation, cauda equina syndrome K idney Amyloidosis; chronic prostatitis S pine Cervical fracture (the new bone is disorganized and brittle), spinal stenosis, osteoporosis P ulmonary Upper lobe fibrosis; restrictive defect (rigid chest) O cular Anterior uveitis in 25–30% N ephropathy IgA nephropathy D iscitis Spondylodiscitis Also Microscopic colitis (terminal ileum, colon) in 30–60% Peripheral arthritis in AS is usually a lower-limb oligoarthritis (a knee, an ankle), and can come before the back pain. Knowledge check: nasal ulcers are not a SpA feature (uveitis and IBD are).

Psoriatic Arthritis Psoriasis : thick, red, silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces, scalp, genitals, gluteal cleft; nail changes. Look for hidden psoriasis: umbilicus, scalp, behind the ears, perianal, nails . Psoriasis comes first in 67% ; arthritis first or at the same time in 33%. Psoriasis in 1.2% of people; PsA in 5–7% of those with psoriasis ; axial in 2%. First-degree relatives 50× more likely. HLA-B38, B39, DR4, B27 . Where to look for psoriasis. From the deck. DIP-predominant PsA with nail changes on the same fingers. Rheumtext, via the deck. Pattern Share Notes Asymmetric oligoarthritis > 50% Usually lower limbs Axial 20–40% Like AS but often asymmetric (one SI joint) Rheumatoid-like polyarthritis 15–25% MCPs, PIPs, ulnar deviation DIP-predominant 5–10% Goes with nail psoriasis (the nail bed and DIP form one enthesis complex) Arthritis mutilans 5% Rapid destruction, telescoping digits , pencil-in-cup Arthritis mutilans : pencil-in-cup (the pencil sits in an upside-down cup). Rheumtext, via the deck. Jug-handle syndesmophytes : large, non-marginal, skipping levels (vs AS's thin, even bamboo spine). Rheumtext, via the deck. Nails in 80% of PsA (30% of psoriasis alone); conjunctivitis 20%, uveitis 7%. From the deck. Dactylitis (“sausage digit”). From the deck. Psoriatic arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Sex M = F Women about 2:1 Rheumatoid factor < 10% About 80% DIP joints 30–50% Uncommon Pattern Asymmetric, “ray” (a whole digit) Symmetric, “row” (across the hand) SI joints / spine About 35%, any level Only the cervical spine, late Other MSK Enthesitis, dactylitis, periarticular redness — Extra-articular Skin, nail dystrophy Nodules, sicca, vasculitis X-ray DIP erosions, fluffy periostitis / bony proliferation Periarticular osteopenia, wrist erosions

Reactive Arthritis An inflammatory arthritis in response to a bacterial infection elsewhere (not an infected joint). Formerly “Reiter's syndrome”; the eponym is dropped because Reiter was a Nazi. Can't see Can't pee Can't climb a tree Conjunctivitis or uveitis Urethritis or cervicitis Large-joint oligoarthritis, sacroiliitis, enthesitis Triggers: GI Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter (also Yersinia ); GU Chlamydia trachomatis and other STIs. Young men 20–40 , 1–3 weeks after the infection. RF negative, HLA-B27-linked . Psoriasis-like skin: circinate balanitis (glans) and keratoderma blennorrhagicum (soles, sometimes palms). Most settle within 12 weeks; chronic arthritis or sacroiliitis in 15–30% . Treat symptoms; treat chronic disease like chronic arthritis. Keratoderma blennorrhagicum : the knowledge-check answer for reactive arthritis's classic skin finding. From the deck (the genital photo is left out).

Spinal Mobility Exam Test How Normal Modified Schober (lumbar) Standing: mark the line between the PSISs (the dimples of Venus) and a point 10 cm above ; bend forward maximally; measure 10 cm opens to about 15 cm Chest expansion (thoracic) Hands on/behind the head; tape at the 4th intercostal space (now often the xiphisternum); maximal in- minus expiration About 5 cm Occiput-to-wall (cervical) Heels and shoulders on the wall, chin level; try to touch the head to the wall (or measure tragus-to-wall) 0 cm Best of two tries for each. Modified Schober. ASAS handbook, via the deck. Chest expansion. ASAS handbook, via the deck.

Treatment Axial SpA Physiotherapy For everyone : posture, chest expansion, fewer deformities NSAIDs Mild–moderate symptoms; possibly disease-modifying; indomethacin works best. Watch GI effects, and NSAIDs can flare IBD (check with GI) Conventional DMARDs Don't work for spinal disease : only for predominantly peripheral arthritis TNF inhibitors Very effective (symptoms, range of motion, fatigue); likely disease-modifying early IL-17 inhibitors Very effective; disease modification not yet known Psoriatic arthritis Conventional DMARDs Methotrexate (treats skin and joints), sulfasalazine, leflunomide; limited evidence against x-ray progression. Hydroxychloroquine is often avoided (case reports of severe psoriasis flares) Apremilast PDE4 inhibitor : skin and joints, slows x-ray progression, weaker than biologics TNF inhibitors Axial and peripheral; skin, joints, enthesitis, dactylitis, nails; slow x-ray damage IL-12/23 inhibitors Great for skin, good for peripheral joints, not axial disease IL-17 inhibitors Excellent for skin; axial and peripheral; maybe best for enthesitis and dactylitis JAK and IL-23 inhibitors Peripheral joints (and skin); axial effect uncertain

Learning Objectives Identify patients whose symptoms may be consistent with vasculitis . Describe the pathophysiology and presentation of giant cell arteritis . Categorize the other vasculitides and the clinical features that should put vasculitis at the top of the differential . Three recordings (69 min) by Dr. Lillian Barra (rheumatology): introduction (with a purpura case), giant cell arteritis, and a primer on ANCA vasculitis; plus three interactive cases. Kawasaki disease and IgA vasculitis (HSP) are covered in pediatrics.

What Vasculitis Is Immune cells infiltrate the vessel wall, which thickens and narrows the lumen → turbulent flow, thrombosis , occlusion → ischemia . Or the damaged wall weakens → aneurysm → rupture and bleeding . Most vasculitis is systemic : fever, weight loss, fatigue, tachycardia, diffuse aches. It can hit any organ , and some types are uniformly fatal if untreated . Narrowing, occlusion, aneurysm. NIH, via the deck. Immune cells in the wall, thrombus in the lumen. PLoS ONE 2016, via the deck.

entries.t: Secondary vs Primary, and Vessel Size
entries.x: Secondary vs Primary, and Vessel Size Secondary (a cause you can find) Examples Infection (rule out first) Hepatitis B and C , HIV , other viruses (maybe COVID-19); meningococcus, mycobacteria, S. aureus ; fungi (can also mimic vasculitis) Drugs and toxins Hypersensitivity to antibiotics, some antihypertensives, antithyroid drugs; cocaine and its cutting agent levamisole Cancer Hematologic malignancy, paraneoplastic Connective tissue disease Lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's Primary vasculitis (cause unknown, autoimmune): over 20 types, classified by the size of vessel involved, which decides the symptoms. Classification by vessel size. From the deck.
