Size Types to know Large Giant cell arteritis (the most common adult vasculitis), Takayasu Medium Polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki (children), Behçet's Small ANCA vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA), cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (case 1's purpura; alone or part of others), IgA vasculitis / HSP (children)

entries.t: When to Suspect It and How to Work It Up
entries.x: When to Suspect It and How to Work It Up It's hard: rare (ANCA vasculitis about 20 per million), variable between patients, can grumble for years with only fatigue and pain, mimics common diseases, and has secondary causes. Suspect primary vasculitis when… Chronically unwell with fevers, chills, weight loss Symptoms in multiple organ systems ; purpura Very sick with multi-organ failure, especially pulmonary hemorrhage + renal dysfunction And no underlying infection or malignancy found 1 Head-to-toe history and exam There's no single test; the clinical picture drives which investigations you order. 2 Basic labs CBC (normocytic anemia, thrombocytosis), ESR/CRP , albumin (low = chronic), creatinine , liver enzymes . Inflammatory markers are nonspecific. 3 Look for silent organs Urinalysis (blood and protein = glomerulonephritis) and chest x-ray (nodules) in everyone . 4 Rule out infection and cancer WBC; blood and urine cultures (sputum for fungi and AFB if lungs involved); hepatitis B and C, HIV, syphilis ; cryoglobulins and complement with hepatitis C; age-appropriate cancer screening + SPEP (myeloma). 5 Biopsy and refer A biopsy of involved tissue clinches it (secondary causes still need excluding). Urgent rheumatology referral , plus other services by organ (nephrology for the kidney). Case 1: purpura, ankle arthritis 45-year-old man, 6 weeks of painful non-blanching purpura below the knees, ankle arthritis with 2 hours of morning stiffness; past IV drug use, tattoos ; ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily. Initial tests: CBC, creatinine, ALT and albumin, INR and PTT (coagulopathy causes purpura), ESR or CRP, urinalysis, blood cultures, hepatitis B and C, HIV , a urine tox screen with consent (cocaine), chest x-ray, ankle x-rays. Not yet: urine culture (unless the urinalysis suggests infection), RF/ANCA, CT, and skin biopsy (not needed first, and not for non-ulcerating purpura of < 4–6 weeks, which often resolves). Result: ALT 70, CRP 50, anti-HCV positive → HCV viral load and cryoglobulins . Hepatitis C causes vasculitis and arthritis directly or via cryoglobulins; first-line treatment is antivirals . Symptom relief meanwhile: topical steroid (first line for non-severe cutaneous vasculitis), another NSAID (he got naproxen 500 mg twice daily + a PPI), colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily; oral steroids work but avoid if possible. Not acetaminophen (barely helps), cannabinoids (no evidence) or methotrexate (slow, and immunosuppressive and hepatotoxic in a hepatitis

What GCA Is A large-vessel vasculitis with a predilection for the cranial arteries , especially the temporal artery (“temporal arteritis” undersells it: it's systemic). Only over 50 (most over 70). The most common vasculitis in adults . Lifetime risk about 1% in women, 0.5% in men ; commoner with northern European descent. The arteries GCA likes : cranial branches, then the aorta and its branches. From the deck. A swollen, rope-like temporal artery. From the deck. Artery Symptom Temporal New headache , temporal and scalp tenderness Facial Jaw claudication Lingual Tongue claudication Ophthalmic Vision loss , diplopia Intracranial (rare) Stroke Aorta and branches (subclavian, carotid) Limb claudication, Raynaud's, digital ischemia, chest pain, aneurysm Systemic Fatigue, fever, weight loss; polymyalgia rheumatica (shoulder and hip girdle pain and morning stiffness) is the commonest extra-arterial feature; some get arthritis Exam: tender temples, swollen rope-like temporal artery with a weak pulse (bad atherosclerosis can mimic it), optic disc swelling, absent or unequal radial pulses, bruits (subclavian, carotid), a blood pressure difference between arms . Vision Loss In 15–20% . Often transient first (amaurosis fugax: “a curtain” for seconds to minutes). Untreated, it goes on to total loss in that eye and then the other within days to months. It's painless (patients may not mention it) and permanent , which is why you treat on suspicion. Differential of a GCA-like headache. Ask: is this a new headache? Infections matter most, since high-dose steroids would worsen them. From the deck.

Diagnosing GCA Test What to know ESR and CRP, immediately < 2% of GCA have both normal, so both normal essentially rules it out (if not on steroids) Temporal artery biopsy (within 1–2 weeks) Transmural inflammation + giant cells + fragmented internal elastic lamina = 100% specific . But 50–70% are negative ( skip lesions ), so a negative biopsy doesn't rule out GCA . Steroids raise false negatives over time. Temporal artery Doppler ultrasound Halo sign (wall edema): specificity > 85%, absent in ~30%; unreliable outside specialty centres Temporal arteritis : giant cells (arrows) and transmural inflammation. Pathpedia, via the deck. The halo sign. From the deck. Knowledge check: when to consider GCA Yes: an 80-year-old with new headache, jaw claudication, weight loss, CRP 50 and a diagnostic biopsy; a 72-year-old with painless vision loss , bitemporal headache and CRP 65, even with a normal biopsy . No: a 20-year-old ( never under 50 ); burning temporal pain with vesicles (shingles); a 78-year-old with occipital headache, mechanical joint pains and normal ESR and CRP (degenerative).

Treating GCA 1 Draw ESR and CRP, then start prednisone immediately 1 mg/kg/day, max 60 mg . Don't wait for results or the biopsy; if blood can't be drawn now, start anyway. Delay risks blindness and stroke . 2 Protect against the steroid PPI (gastritis, ulcers), calcium and vitamin D (fractures). The slides add a bisphosphonate; the knowledge check says it can wait until the diagnosis is confirmed. 3 Vision loss or stroke symptoms → emergency department Urgent ophthalmology or neurology. 4 Confirm and refer Temporal artery biopsy (or ultrasound at a specialty centre) within 1–2 weeks; refer to rheumatology . Expect 80–100% improvement in 2–3 days ; if not, rethink the diagnosis. The module's case (65-year-old, 70 kg, new right headache, PMR symptoms): urgent labs at this visit (CBC, creatinine, ALT, ESR, CRP, urinalysis), urgent biopsy referral , prednisone 50 mg now (not 15 mg, not after results), calcium, vitamin D and a PPI , urgent rheumatology referral .

entries.t: The Three Types and the ANCA Test
entries.x: The Three Types and the ANCA Test Type Old name ANCA Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) (commonest in Canada) Wegener's c-ANCA → anti-PR3 Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) — p-ANCA → anti-MPO Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) Churg–Strauss p-ANCA → anti-MPO ANCA = antibodies against granule proteins in neutrophils . Immunofluorescence shows the pattern (c = cytoplasmic, p = perinuclear) and detects a mix of antibodies; ELISA detects one antigen (PR3 or MPO) and is more specific for vasculitis. c-ANCA : the whole cytoplasm lights up (GPA). From the deck. p-ANCA : a ring around the nucleus (MPA, EGPA). From the deck. Interpreting ANCA False positives (5–10%) Infection, especially infective endocarditis (can look just like GPA), cancer (lymphoproliferative), medications, cocaine False negatives Up to 30% of GPA and 50–60% of MPA/EGPA are ANCA negative: a negative test doesn't rule out vasculitis Who orders it Only if small-vessel vasculitis is suspected; usually the specialist (it isn't covered by OHIP). Reasonable for primary care if a specialist can't be seen quickly.

Clinical Features Described in every organ . The common ones: Site Presentation Sinonasal (commonest) Bloody, crusty nasal discharge , sinus pain; can be erosive and destructive Orbit Retro-orbital mass: diplopia, vision loss Lungs Dyspnea; nodules (may cavitate) ; adult-onset severe asthma (EGPA); PE more common; pulmonary hemorrhage (a hallmark, high mortality) Kidneys Rising creatinine, hematuria and proteinuria ; a cause of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis Joints, nerves Inflammatory arthritis; mononeuritis multiplex (weakness, paresthesias) Skin Palpable purpura (commonest); urticarial vasculitis (lasts longer than hives, scars, non-blanching rim); ulcers (scarring, can lead to amputation) Purpura and urticarial vasculitis. From the deck. Lung nodules in GPA : kidney and lung disease can be silent. From the deck.

Workup, Biopsy and First Steps Everyone: head-to-toe history and exam; CBC, creatinine, liver enzymes, ESR/CRP, urinalysis ; chest x-ray ; rule out infection (blood cultures, hepatitis, HIV); then organ-specific tests. Biopsy for single-organ disease: purpura or urticarial vasculitis → punch biopsy in primary care (histology, immunofluorescence, culture); ulcers → deep excisional biopsy by a surgeon (fungal infection, cancer); refer for orbital pseudotumour, sinonasal mass, lung nodule, lymph node, renal biopsy for an active sediment, sural nerve biopsy for neuropathy. If… Then Unstable vitals, pulmonary hemorrhage , significant dyspnea, or renal failure Admit to hospital Stable, active urine sediment, normal creatinine Urgent nephrology (RPGN risk) and close monitoring Otherwise Urgent rheumatology + specialists for the organs involved Case: sinusitis that won't resolve 55-year-old woman (a PSW; travel to the Philippines): 2 months of sinusitis despite 2 antibiotic courses, crusting, epistaxis , ear fullness and hearing loss; new inflammatory polyarthritis ; 10 kg weight loss . Hb 100, platelets 520, WBC 13, CRP 80. Next tests: blood cultures, TB skin test (travel), HIV, urinalysis and chest x-ray , RF/anti-CCP and ANA, and a sinonasal biopsy (exclude fungal and TB infection before immunosuppression). Not sputum cultures (low yield) or an MRI head; CT chest and PFTs only if the x-ray is normal; ENA and complement only if ANA positive; ANCA once infection is excluded. Results: ANA, RF and anti-CCP negative; chest x-ray with multiple cavitary lesions ; urine with blood and protein . Differential: GPA , TB, disseminated fungal infection, lymphoma or other cancer (lupus and rheumatoid vasculitis unlikely when ANA and RF are negative). Next step: she's stable with a normal creatinine, so no admission, but call nephrology urgently , call ENT to expedite, and refer urgently to rheumatology and respirology . Don't start high-dose prednisone yet : infection is still possible.

Learning Objectives Create a plan to evaluate and treat non-arthritic body pain. Describe the clinical features of polymyalgia rheumatica and an approach to its management. Describe the clinical features of fibromyalgia and an approach to its management. A 40-minute module by Dr. Sabeen Anwar (rheumatology): two recordings (Fibromyalgia 17 min, PMR 9 min) with five knowledge-check cases. Central pain also appeared in Week 10's chronic pain lectures.

Three Kinds of Pain Nociceptive Neuropathic Central Cause Inflammation or mechanical damage in the tissue Damage to peripheral nerves Disturbance of pain processing → hyperalgesia Sounds like “My left knee is sore all the time” (focal) “My arms and legs feel numb, burning” “I hurt everywhere; it hurts to be hugged; light pressure, lights, noise and smells bother me” Responds to NSAIDs, opioids, local steroid injection Local and central drugs Drugs that change pain neurotransmitters (NE, 5-HT); not opioids Examples RA, knee OA, acute injury Diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia Fibromyalgia, IBS, TMJ dysfunction, tension headache Any combination can coexist in one person (Dr. Daniel Clauw's model), and nociceptive pain lasting long enough can centralize . Clues that pain is “centralizing” Diffuse or multifocal ; waxes and wanes; often migratory Sounds neuropathic; touch and tight clothing hurt Pain in other body regions earlier in life CNS comorbidities: fatigue, sleep, memory, mood Global sensory hyper-responsiveness (light, noise, odour); a pan-positive review of systems

Diagnosing Fibromyalgia: the Criteria ACR 1990 (“be aware of it, then forget it”) ACR 2010/2016 (“know it”) Pain ≥ 3 regions of chronic pain (> 3 months): above and below the waist, both sides, and axial Widespread Pain Index (WPI) : painful regions in the past week (0–19). Generalized pain in ≥ 4 of 5 regions (jaw, chest and abdomen excluded) Exam / symptoms Tender in 11 of 18 points at 4 kg pressure (until the fingernail blanches); pain, not just tenderness Symptom Severity (SS) : fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive symptoms + somatic symptoms (0–12) Cut-off WPI ≥ 7 and SS ≥ 5 , or WPI 4–6 and SS ≥ 9 Duration > 3 months Similar level for ≥ 3 months Other diagnoses Valid irrespective of other diagnoses (2016) The 18 tender points (ACR 1990). From the deck. 2016 revision (Wolfe et al.). From the deck. The 2010 questionnaire : tick the painful regions (WPI) and score the symptoms (SS). From the deck (Clauw, JAMA 2014).

entries.t: What It Sounds Like in Clinic
entries.x: What It Sounds Like in Clinic Domain What the patient says Fatigue “I'm so tired I've cut back work and family duties.” Cognitive “I forget things; I'm in a fog.” Unrefreshed sleep “Even after 8 hours I wake feeling I didn't sleep.” Boom and bust “When I feel well I do a lot, then for days I can't do anything. I'm a yo-yo.” Somatic Headaches; TMJ dysfunction ; irritable bowel ; irritable bladder (feels like a UTI); non-cardiac chest pain ; morning stiffness and hand pain but “the rheumatologist said my joints aren't swollen” More common with: any rheumatologic disease, IBD, any psychiatric disease, MS, war or natural disasters, weeks of acute nociceptive pain (MVA, trauma), hepatitis B/C, HIV, Lyme, EBV.

entries.t: Not a Diagnosis of Exclusion, but Rule Out Mimics
entries.x: Not a Diagnosis of Exclusion, but Rule Out Mimics Fibromyalgia + Something Else It's common to diagnose FM plus another disease . Treating an RA/SLE/Sjögren's patient's fibromyalgia “features” with immunosuppression does not help those symptoms . Complaint Rule out with Muscle pain CK (myositis) Neuropathic symptoms Metabolic workup (e.g., diabetes) Joint symptoms Exam for swelling Fatigue CBC, ferritin, TSH, CRP, ALT, creatinine, albumin , sleep study Other somatic complaints Targeted tests, with common sense Don't order an ANA for fatigue and widespread pain alone ( 12.2 ).

The Science: Two Pain Pathways Turned up and not turned down. From the deck. Pathway Normally In fibromyalgia Ascending facilitatory (substance P, glutamate via NMDA ) Relays pain up to the brain Up-regulated : temporal summation (repeated stimuli leave persistent pain after they stop); ↑ CSF substance P and glutamate Descending inhibitory ( NE, 5-HT , opioids) Dials pain down. Diffuse noxious inhibitory control : 2–5 min of intense pain produces whole-body analgesia Attenuated : DNIC absent (also in OA and IBS); ↓ NE and 5-HT metabolites in CSF; any drug that raises NE and 5-HT helps

Treating Fibromyalgia Who? The family doctor : the Canadian guidelines (fmguidelines.ca) say to establish the diagnosis as early as possible without specialist confirmation . 1 Education Family doctor, group programs, Arthritis Society, Rheuminfo.com. 2 Exercise (crucial) Weight bearing and non-weight bearing, tai chi, yoga , warm pool (if available). 3 CBT Sleep hygiene, pacing (“don't overdo it”), mindfulness for chronic pain. 4 Treat the nociceptive inputs Mechanical back pain → physio; OA → injections; comorbid RA, IBD, endometriosis. 5 Treat sleep apnea and psychiatric illness 6 Drugs that target the brain One drug, lowest dose, titrate slowly, see the patient regularly, set expectations, consider combinations. Drug class Examples Key point SNRI Duloxetine (best evidence), venlafaxine Works with or without depression ; doesn't help sleep Gabapentinoids Pregabalin , gabapentin Help sleep ; act on the calcium channel in the ascending pathway Tricyclics (low dose) Amitriptyline , nortriptyline, cyclobenzaprine Improve pain, fatigue and sleep ; no effect on mood at low dose Opioids Including Tylenol #3 No role; avoid. In 1,700 patients, opioid users did worse on sleep, disability and pain interference, with no better pain scores. Set Expectations With any of duloxetine, TCAs, pregabalin, exercise, CBT or education: 50% of patients get a 30% improvement . Pregabalin 300 mg/day: NNT 9 for 30% relief, NNT 14 for 50%, NNH 17 to stop for side effects (somnolence, dizziness, weight gain, nausea).

Who and What The girdles : neck, shoulders, upper arms, hips and thighs. From the deck. The mimics. From the deck. Feature PMR Age Over 50 (defining); incidence 15–115/100,000 Who Women; Northern European descent Symptoms Insidious pain and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles ; profound morning stiffness (> 1 h; “a Tin Man who needs oil”, looser by mid-afternoon), fatigue; trouble dressing and getting out of bed Systemic Weight loss, low-grade fever; ↑ ESR and CRP , anemia , thrombocytosis (reactive; never thrombocytopenia ) Exam Normal apart from pain ; no weakness Pathology Cause unknown. The name misleads: muscles are histologically normal ; imaging shows inflammation of the joints, bursae and tendons of the shoulders and hips Mimic How it differs Fibromyalgia Normal markers ; stiffness everywhere, proximal and distal Myositis Weakness , usually painless; CK /aldolase high Inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA) Distal joints (wrists, MCPs, PIPs, DIPs); ↓ active and passive range OA Minimal stiffness; worse with activity Cancer Asymmetric, localized, other symptoms Infection Asymmetric, warmth and swelling (e.g., one septic joint) The Steroid Test None of the mimics improves as fast and as dramatically with prednisone as PMR. Avery took 20 mg and felt almost normal in 12 hours . Mr. Jones (64, back and thigh pain, fevers, ESR 54) was only 10% better after a week → the diagnosis is probably wrong: investigate other causes (don't increase the dose or wait longer).

Treating PMR Phase Dr. Anwar's regimen Start Prednisone 15–20 mg/day (by patient size). Expect ~90% better in 48 h . Hold Until the patient feels well and the markers normalize (usually 1–2 months ) Wean 15 mg × 1 month → 12.5 mg × 1 month → 10 mg × 1 month → then −1 mg per month Total 16–18 months for most; average ~ 2 years ; some need low dose long term; relapses are common Don't forget Reassess for other causes; never treat raised markers alone . Keep cancer screening (colonoscopy, mammogram) up to date. Steroid side effects : GI upset, reflux, insomnia, weight gain, mood change, bone loss (but not joint swelling ; steroids can cause generalized edema). Osteoprotection for anyone expected on > 7.5 mg for > 3 months : calcium 1,500 mg elemental/day, vitamin D 1,000–2,000 IU /day, an antiresorptive (e.g., denosumab, risedronate); update the bone density. GCA occurs with PMR in ~15%: headache, jaw claudication or visual symptoms → high-dose prednisone ( 11.7 ).

Practice Patients 1. Mrs. Peterson has rheumatologist-diagnosed fibromyalgia. Which is NOT acceptable: gabapentin, duloxetine 60 mg, Tylenol #3 PRN, amitriptyline 10 mg qhs, tai chi? Answer Tylenol with codeine : opioids have no role in fibromyalgia. 2. Jeannette, 34: 6 months of generalized aches, “swollen” hands, dry eyes and mouth, profound fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, IBS and headaches. ANA 1:2560, RF 300, anti-Ro positive. WPI 8, SS 6. Answer She has an autoimmune disease that needs workup (Sjögren's, RA or another CTD) and fibromyalgia (WPI ≥ 7 + SS ≥ 5, > 3 months). FM is not a diagnosis of exclusion. 3. Maria, 53: since an MVA 5 years ago, worsening whole-body pain; flinches at light touch; normal sensation, no swelling; Percocet helps a little. Answer Central pain = a disturbance of pain processing . It responds poorly to opioids and isn't peripheral nerve damage. 4. Mrs. Abbey, 74: neck, shoulder and back stiffness for 3 months, 5 lb weight loss, Hb 112, platelets 79, ESR 103, CRP 78. Which is NOT a PMR feature? Answer Thrombocytopenia. PMR causes a reactive thrombocytosis ; a low platelet count should send you looking elsewhere.

entries.t: Week 12 · Rheumatology Treatment, Neuroanatomy and Body Pain
entries.p: Week 12 · Rheumatology Treatment, Neuroanatomy and Body Pain
entries.x: > Week 12 Rheumatology wraps up and neurology begins. Monday is two review modules: how rheumatologists treat (prednisone doses and side effects, joint aspiration and injection, NSAIDs, the four DMARDs and their toxicities, biologics and when not to use a TNF inhibitor) and which blood tests to order and when not to (RF, anti-CCP, ANA, anti-DNA, ENA, complement, ANCA). Tuesday starts the neuro block with neuroanatomy (lobes, deep grey matter, the brainstem and the rule of 4, cranial nerves, tracts, ventricles, vessels) and the neurologist's approach (UMN vs LMN, patterns of weakness, time course and VITAMINS C&D), and closes rheumatology with non-arthritic body pain: fibromyalgia and polymyalgia rheumatica. Tuesday’s neuro modules live in the new Neurology unit. Monday Nov 16 Two rheumatology review modules. 12.1 Rheumatology Treatment Prednisone by dose (the high-dose four, PMR, gout, RA flares), routes and the 15 side effects; aspiration and injection (consent, C3G, contraindications); NSAIDs, COX-2 and their heart/gut/kidney risks, acetaminophen, opioids; treating RA early and to target; methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and leflunomide side by side (GHMI); biologics and TNF inhibitor contraindications → 12.2 Rheumatology Investigations No diagnosis by blood test alone; RF and anti-CCP; ANA (1 in 3 women, when to order, never repeat), anti-dsDNA, ENA (Ro, La, Sm, Scl-70, Jo-1) and complement; ANCA (c vs p, levamisole); expected labs in RA, SLE, SpA, JIA, GCA, PMR and fibromyalgia → Tuesday Nov 17 Neuro begins; rheumatology ends with body pain. 12.3 Introduction to Neuroanatomy CNS vs PNS, grey and white matter; directions, planes and CT/MRI (T1, T2, FLAIR); lobes and their jobs, limbic lobe, basal ganglia, diencephalon; midbrain, pons and medulla with their landmarks; the rule of 4 and where each cranial nerve leaves; spinal cord horns and tracts; ventricles and CSF flow, the blood–brain barrier, the middle meningeal artery, the arterial circle and dural sinuses → 12.4 Introduction to Neurology The vocabulary (plegia, paresis, aphasia, ataxia); neuron to cord; the motor pathway and UMN vs LMN signs; the homunculus and MCA vs ACA; sensory and visual pathways; the four-step approach, how to localize, patterns of weakness, time course and VITAMINS C&D; four practice cases (migraine aura, chronic subdural, cervical myelopathy, Parkinson’s) → 12.5 Body Pain: Fibromyalgia and PMR Nociceptive vs neuropathic vs central pain; fibromyalgia criteria

Learning Objectives Develop a plan for appropriate investigations of a possible rheumatologic condition. Describe RF, ANA, ANCA, ESR, CRP and HLA-B27 : when to order them and when ordering is inappropriate . Describe the expected results in RA, SLE, seronegative arthropathies, JIA and GCA/PMR. A 26-minute module by Dr. Janet Pope (rheumatology): text sections on RA, CTD and vasculitis tests plus one 8-minute recording, “Lab tests for Connective Tissue Diseases.” The “expected results” table at the end pulls ESR/CRP, HLA-B27 and the Week 11 diseases together from 11.3 – 11.8 .

RF and Anti-CCP Rheumatoid factor (RF) Anti-CCP (an ACPA) What it is An autoantibody (often IgM ) against the Fc portion of IgG : an antibody against an antibody Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide : the commonest test for antibodies against citrullinated proteins Seen in RA, connective tissue diseases , hepatitis C , healthy older people RA (common) Specificity Not specific for RA Fairly specific for RA (not totally) Prognosis More severe RA: erosions , extra-articular disease, interstitial lung disease , nodules More severe RA: erosions Order it? When you suspect RA Not unless you suspect RA ; not reimbursed in Ontario Refer With a Sentence, Not a Test Better than ordering anti-CCP: a referral that says “ I suspect early RA: swelling in the wrists, MCPs and PIPs, and stiffness across the MTPs. ” Inflammatory conditions also show ↑ ESR, ↑ CRP and anemia of chronic disease .

ANA: The Most Over-Ordered Test Antinuclear antibodies bind antigens in the nucleus : a loss of self-recognition. The numbers So… ~ 1 in 3 women (a bit fewer men) have a positive ANA SLE , the commonest CTD, is 1 in 1,000 women ; RA is 1 in 100 ANA is ordered 10× more than RF → ~100× too often Most positives are false positives . A positive ANA causes angst, unnecessary referrals and more tests. ANA pearls Don't order it unless you suspect an autoimmune CTD A positive ANA does NOT make a diagnosis A negative ANA helps rule out SLE (sensitive, not specific) Once positive, repeating it is a waste ; a positive at any time counts toward the SLE criteria. Don't follow the titre. If negative, don't repeat unless there are new symptoms or signs of a CTD Titre: the higher the denominator, the stronger (doubling dilutions: 1:40 cut-off, 1:80 slightly positive … 1:1280 strong ). A strong positive matters more than a borderline one. Pattern: speckled and homogeneous are common and unhelpful; peripheral (rim), nucleolar, centromere are less common and possibly more helpful. The pattern can change with dilution.

Should I Order an ANA? Patient ANA? 88-year-old man, low WBC from myelodysplastic syndrome, no lupus features No 32-year-old woman, fatigue and widespread pain (fibromyalgia) No 54-year-old woman, weight loss, new rash in the sun, high CK, new weakness Yes (dermatomyositis) 17-year-old, recurrent oral ulcers, hair loss, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia Yes (SLE) 44-year-old, new glomerulonephritis (RBC casts, proteinuria), cause unknown Yes / maybe Negative ANA a year ago, no new symptoms: repeat? No 22-year-old woman, low WBC, lymphopenia, low platelets, malar rash, hair loss: order anti-DNA? No: ANA first , and anti-DNA only if it's positive

Anti-dsDNA Anti-DNA is one kind of ANA (left); ANA immunofluorescence patterns (right). From the deck. Double-stranded DNA is only in the nucleus , so anti-DNA can't be positive without a positive ANA . Feature Anti-dsDNA Order when ANA positive and you expect SLE Specificity Highly specific for SLE (but modern kits also pick up single-stranded DNA and noise, so less specific than the old labour-intensive assay) Sensitivity Insensitive : positive in only ~50% of SLE , so a negative doesn't rule SLE out (a negative ANA does) Correlates with Disease activity and lupus nephritis ; often high in active disease and may turn negative after treatment

ENA (Extractable Nuclear Antigens) The lab screens positive or negative; if positive, it identifies which antibody. If the ANA is negative, don't order an ENA , and unless you're a specialist you may struggle to interpret it. Many kit antibodies are irrelevant noise. Antibody Goes with Anti-Ro (SSA) ← learn this one SLE with rash and photosensitivity ; Ro + La together = Sjögren's ; pregnant Ro-positive mothers are followed for congenital heart block (rare); babies may get neonatal lupus (very rare) Anti-La (SSB) Usually with Ro: Sjögren's Anti-Sm (Smith) Fairly specific for SLE (not in everyone) Anti-RNP Mixed connective tissue disease and SLE Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase 1) Scleroderma with interstitial lung disease Anti-Jo-1 Myositis with ILD (“a bad antibody to have”) Anti-PM-Scl Dermatomyositis–scleroderma overlap Anti-RNA polymerase III Scleroderma renal crisis

Complement (C3, C4) Low in active lupus , especially nephritis , and may track activity. Why low: autoantibodies bind tissue, activate complement , and it gets consumed (named because it “complemented” antibodies in killing bacteria). Can also be low from an inherited deficiency . A waste of money if you're not a specialist.

ANCA (Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody) Pearl Order only if you really suspect vasculitis ; not reimbursed in Ontario c-ANCA (cytoplasmic; antigen PR3 , proteinase 3) is more likely to mean real vasculitis (GPA) p-ANCA (perinuclear; antigen MPO , myeloperoxidase) has more false positives (MPA, EGPA) p-ANCA and c-ANCA both positive → suspect cocaine-induced vasculitis : a reaction to the levamisole cut into nearly all cocaine ANCA titres may vary with activity, but concordance is poor Full vasculitis workup in 11.7 : rule out infection first, then urinalysis and chest x-ray in everyone.

Expected Results by Disease Disease ESR / CRP Antibodies and markers Don't RA ↑; anemia of chronic disease RF ± anti-CCP (both = worse erosive disease); a seronegative RA exists Order anti-CCP without suspecting RA SLE ESR ↑, CRP often normal (CRP ↑ suggests infection or serositis) ANA + (negative essentially rules out); then anti-dsDNA , anti-Sm ; low C3/C4 when active; cytopenias Anti-DNA or ENA before a positive ANA Seronegative SpA (AS, PsA, reactive) Normal or ↑ RF and anti-CCP negative ; HLA-B27 supports AS (~90% of white patients with AS) but 8% of the population carries it Use HLA-B27 as a screening test for back pain JIA ↑ in systemic and polyarticular; can be normal in oligo ANA + = higher uveitis risk (not diagnostic); RF+ poly behaves like adult RA; HLA-B27 in enthesitis-related Use the ANA to diagnose JIA GCA ESR and CRP high ; both normal essentially rules it out (< 2%) No antibody; anemia, thrombocytosis; temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound Wait for results before prednisone PMR High No antibody; anemia, thrombocytosis (not thrombocytopenia); CK normal Treat raised markers alone Fibromyalgia Normal None; ANA not indicated Order an ANA ( 12.5 )

Practice Patients 1. A family doctor orders an ANA on a tired 30-year-old woman with no other findings. It comes back 1:80 speckled. Answer Almost certainly a false positive (1 in 3 women). Don't repeat it, don't chase anti-DNA/ENA, don't refer for a weak positive ANA alone. It should not have been ordered. 2. An SLE patient's anti-dsDNA rises and C3/C4 fall; urinalysis shows protein and blood. Answer Active lupus, likely nephritis : anti-DNA and low complement track activity and renal disease. Urgent rheumatology / nephrology; high-dose steroid territory ( 12.1 ). 3. A 34-year-old with purpura, sinusitis and hematuria is both p-ANCA and c-ANCA positive. Answer Ask about cocaine : double positivity suggests levamisole-induced vasculitis . 4. A pregnant woman with Sjögren's is anti-Ro positive. What does the obstetric team watch for? Answer Congenital heart block in the fetus (rare) and neonatal lupus in the baby (very rare).

Learning Objectives Propose a treatment plan for inflammatory and rheumatologic conditions. Describe the role of steroids (systemic and intra-articular) and list the side effects of chronic steroid use. List the contraindications for MSK injections and what informed consent needs. Explain the use and side effects of acetaminophen and NSAIDs , and the limited role of opioids. Outline treatment with DMARDs and their important toxicities. Distinguish biologics from DMARDs and explain their role. A 90-minute self-study module by Dr. Tristan Boyd (rheumatology): five slide decks with knowledge-check questions and no recordings . Slides marked “Remember this slide” in the decks are flagged ★ below. The objectives also list adult vs children's treatment, which the decks don't cover; see 11.4 JIA for the children's ladder.

How Prednisone Works and When Anti-inflammatory actions (all non-specific) Clinical effect Binds transcription factors → blocks pro-inflammatory proteins ↓ neutrophil migration Directly inhibits cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) ↓ prostaglandins and leukotrienes ↓ pain, ↓ swelling, ↓ stiffness, ↓ disability. Most useful in the ACUTE setting because it works rapidly. The adrenals make the equivalent of ~7 mg prednisone a day .

★ Dose Depends on the Condition Dose Conditions Regimen High (~1 mg/kg) organ- or life-threatening 1. ANCA-associated vasculitis 2. Lupus nephritis 3. Inflammatory myositis (polymyositis, dermatomyositis) 4. Giant cell arteritis ~1 mg/kg ideal body weight. In an emergency, pulse IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily × 3 days to jumpstart, then high-dose oral. Medium flares without major organ involvement RA flare 20–40 mg daily, taper as the DMARD (steroid-sparing therapy) starts Polymyalgia rheumatica 15–20 mg daily, taper to 10 mg, then −1 mg every 4 weeks until off (details in 12.5 ) Acute gout 25–30 mg daily × 3 days , then taper by 5 mg every 3 days until off. Self-limited; doesn't need high dose. Low (≤ 5 mg) Chronic disease where steroids can't be stopped or steroid-sparers aren't tolerated Long term The High-Dose Four The module's question: which is not treated with high-dose steroid? GPA with hemoptysis and hematuria (yes), dermatomyositis with dysphagia (yes: the upper two-thirds of the esophagus is skeletal muscle), class III lupus nephritis (yes; milder lupus doesn't always need it), GCA with amaurosis fugax (yes, often pulsed) → PMR gets medium dose (e.g., 20 mg). But PMR with GCA (~15%) needs high dose to prevent blindness.

Which Route? Route Use Oral (PO) Easy to taper or stop because the dose can change Intramuscular (IM) Lasts 3–4 weeks ; consider with non-adherence Intravenous (IV) Rapid effect before switching to high-dose oral (e.g., GCA with vision involvement ) Intra-articular (“cortisone injection”) Few joints swollen or a weight-bearing joint. Fewer systemic effects because the steroid stays in the joint. Inflammatory arthritis, OA, rotator cuff tendinitis. Module Case 75-year-old, hot first MTP, intracellular urate crystals, culture negative. End-stage renal disease, heart failure on diuretics, poorly controlled diabetes. Best: intra-articular steroid (minimal absorption). Oral prednisone worsens CHF and diabetes; NSAIDs are out with ESRD .

★ Side Effects of Chronic Prednisone “Good short term, not long term!” From the deck. System Side effects Metabolic ↑ appetite, weight gain , Cushing's syndrome , hyperglycemia , hypertension Bone and muscle Osteoporosis , avascular necrosis , proximal myopathy Eye Cataracts and glaucoma Skin Acne, thinning skin, delayed wound healing Other GI upset (gastritis), mood and behaviour change (psychosis) , ↑ infection Relative contraindications (choose a steroid-sparer instead): diabetes, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, recurrent infections, glaucoma/cataracts . Steroid-sparing drugs = the DMARDs (Part 4).

★ Informed Consent: the Complications Every procedure needs consent: benefits, complications, and a competent patient (or substitute decision-maker). Complication From Infection (septic joint): very low risk The needle Small risk of bleeding (intra- or periarticular) The needle Very small risk of tendon rupture (why landmarking matters) The needle Fat atrophy or skin depigmentation (usually if injected too superficially) The steroid Minimal systemic absorption (worse diabetic control, hypertension) The steroid Post-injection flare : uncommon, resolves on its own The steroid Aspiration vs Injection Consent for a plain aspiration : infection, bleeding, tendon rupture. Post-injection flare and steroid absorption belong to steroid injection , not to aspiration (the module's question).

Diagnostic Arthrocentesis: C3G C3G and the two containers. From the deck. Cloudier fluid = more cells. From the deck. Container Test Answers Lavender top C ell count (with differential) > 2,000 = inflammatory; < 2,000 = non-inflammatory (OA). > 50,000 with mostly neutrophils → suspect septic joint , consult orthopedics. C rystals (light/polarized microscopy) Urate (gout) or calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout) Sterile container C ulture and G ram stain Septic arthritis Always aspirate the first presentation of acute monoarthritis to rule out infection. Send only these three things ; synovial glucose has no diagnostic use .

Therapeutic Arthrocentesis and ★ Injection Contraindications Therapeutic: remove fluid to ease pain and swelling; inject steroid (e.g., triamcinolone : local control of synovitis, OA pain) or hyaluronic acid (OA pain). Relative contraindications to a steroid injection. From the deck. Relative contraindication Why 1. Septic joint (or high suspicion) Steroid makes infection worse: tap, then wait until the culture is negative before injecting 2. Overlying cellulitis or skin infection The needle carries bacteria into the joint (psoriatic plaques are full of skin flora) 3. Skin covered by psoriatic plaques 4. Prosthetic joint Infection risk 5. Severe thrombocytopenia or bleeding disorder Bleeding 6. Allergy to the topical anesthetic

NSAIDs Why coxibs spare the stomach : they leave the COX-1 prostaglandins that protect the mucosa. From the deck. Type Drug and usual dose Non-selective : reversibly inhibit COX-1 and COX-2 Ibuprofen 600–800 mg TID Naproxen 500 mg BID Meloxicam 15 mg daily Diclofenac 75 mg BID Indomethacin 50 mg TID COX-2 selective Celecoxib 200 mg daily Efficacy is similar across NSAIDs ; some patients respond better to one, so try another. Indications: OA, RA, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, CPPD. ★ NSAIDs Are Not Disease-Modifying in RA They help pain and swelling in new RA or a flare, but they don't prevent disease activity and don't delay erosions .

★ NSAID Side Effects Heart, gut, kidney. From the deck. Organ Risk Heart / vessels Hypertension, MI, stroke Gut Gastritis, peptic ulcer ( less with celecoxib , but still possible: add a PPI if risky) Kidney Renal insufficiency (avoid in ESRD) Interactions / pregnancy Other anticoagulants; 3rd trimester : premature closure of the ductus arteriosus Risk is similar for all NSAIDs except less GI toxicity with celecoxib. Screening bloods: CBC, ALT, creatinine.

Acetaminophen and Opioids Acetaminophen Opioids Action Analgesic, not anti-inflammatory Analgesic Use OA, mechanical back pain, regional pain syndromes Hardly ever in rheumatology: the goal is to treat inflammation, which relieves pain. Maybe chronic pain, but other options are preferred (opioid crisis, misuse). Dose Up to 3 g/day divided (2 Extra Strength TID); max 2 g/day in cirrhosis Side effects Minimal : no gastritis, constipation, blood pressure or cognitive effects Impaired cognition, constipation, dependence and withdrawal Module Case 65-year-old with gastritis and hand OA, failed OT, topical NSAID, acetaminophen and glucosamine. NSAID with the least GI toxicity? Celecoxib (COX-2 selective), still with caution ± a PPI.

★ The Approach to Treating RA Damage comes early. Erosions (top) and ulnar deviation with subluxation (bottom). From the deck. Why hurry How 90% of the joints affected are involved within the first year Erosions in > 90% within 2 years ; progression fastest in the first 2 years 50% work-disabled at 10 years Severe disease raises mortality “Window of opportunity” : treat before any erosions. 1. Treat early : DMARDs/biologics within 3 months of symptom onset 2. Treat aggressively : triple therapy beats one agent in early RA 3. Treat appropriately : treat to target , goal = remission (no swollen or tender joints); adjust every 3–6 months if not there 1 Start triple therapy for 3–6 months Methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine; optimize dose and route. Prednisone bridges while they kick in. 2 Incomplete response Switch methotrexate PO → SC (better bioavailability); add leflunomide . 3 Still active Add a biologic (Part 5). Starting any DMARD: discuss common and severe side effects; check interactions and contraindications; baseline bloods (incl. hepatitis B and C ); give a blood-work form , because most need monthly bloods . Other DMARDs: gold, azathioprine, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide.

entries.t: The Four DMARDs Side by Side
entries.x: The Four DMARDs Side by Side Mnemonic for the shared toxicities: GHMI = G I upset, H epatotoxicity, M yelosuppression, I nfection. You don't need the mechanisms. Methotrexate Hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) Sulfasalazine Leflunomide (Arava) Dose 20–25 mg PO or SC once WEEKLY 200–400 mg PO daily (6.5 mg/kg/day ideal body weight) 500–1,000 mg/day, ↑ weekly to 2 g/day divided (max 3 g) 10–20 mg PO daily (load 100 mg × 3 days, optional) Onset 6–8 weeks 6–12 weeks 6–8 weeks 6–8 weeks GHMI All four GI only; no myelosuppression All four ( aplastic anemia ) All four (leukopenia) Signature toxicity Oral ulcers , acute pneumonitis (dry cough, SOB, fever), fatigue, alopecia Retinal toxicity (~1/5,000; bull's eye maculopathy ), ↓ accommodation, rash, photosensitivity, headache Headache (33%) , rash/photosensitivity, reversible oligospermia (33%) Hypertension , peripheral neuropathy , alopecia (10–15%), weight loss, pneumonitis (less than MTX) Pregnancy Teratogenic Safe Safe Teratogenic (cholestyramine washout 8 g TID × 11 days) Monitoring Baseline incl. hep B/C ± CXR; monthly CBC-diff, ALT, creatinine, ESR/CRP No bloods ; baseline + yearly eye exam (acuity, colour vision, fields) Baseline incl. hep B/C; monthly CBC-diff, ALT, creatinine, ESR/CRP Baseline CBC, transaminases, hep B/C, BP ; monthly bloods as MTX Notes Folic acid 5 mg weekly cuts side effects; avoid alcohol; avoid sulfa antibiotics (cytopenias; sulfasalazine is fine); dose by eGFR Also the anchor drug in lupus ( 11.8 ) Screen G6PD ; don't use with sulfa allergy Avoid alcohol Methotrexate and its pneumonitis. From the deck. Hydroxychloroquine : bull's eye maculopathy. From the deck. Sulfasalazine : drug rash. From the deck. Leflunomide : hypertension and pneumonitis. From the deck. Quick quiz from the deck Answer Which DMARD needs a yearly eye exam ? Hydroxychloroquine Which DMARD causes hypertension ? Leflunomide Which DMARDs cause lung toxicity ? Methotrexate and leflunomide Which biologic can worsen CHF ? Any TNF inhibitor (not with class III/IV heart failure) Psoriatic arthritis on sulfasalazine, itchy urticarial rash: which is not a sulfasalazine side effect? Acute pneumonitis (methotrexate, less often leflunomide). The rash is a drug rash: avoid sulfa drugs in future.

★ What Makes a Biologic Different DMARDs Biologics Goal Suppress inflammation and prevent joint damage (both disease-modifying) Mechanism Non-specific Specific molecule or cell: TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, T cells, B cells Cost Cheap ~$10,000–20,000/year : need drug coverage, so usually after failed DMARDs Newer: small molecules (JAK-STAT inhibitors, e.g., tofacitinib ) and biosimilars (copies made after a biologic's patent expires). Where each biologic acts (Chen et al., Nat Rev Rheumatol 2019). From the deck. Why block TNF-α : it drives IL-1, IL-6 and IL-8, which erode cartilage and bone. From the deck. Class (RA) Examples (names not needed) How given TNF inhibitors Monoclonal antibodies (“-mab”): infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, certolizumab; decoy receptor : etanercept Infliximab IV ; the other four SC . Onset 2 weeks–3 months. IL-6 inhibitor Tocilizumab T-cell co-stimulation blockade Abatacept B-cell depletion Rituximab

entries.t: ★ TNF Inhibitors: Adverse Effects and Contraindications
entries.x: ★ TNF Inhibitors: Adverse Effects and Contraindications Adverse effects Contraindications (don't use) 1. Injection-site (or infliximab infusion) reactions 2. ↑ infection , incl. TB and opportunistic 3. Demyelinating disease (MS) 4. Worsens CHF 5. Slight ↑ malignancy : skin cancer (< 1%), possibly lymphoma 6. Drug-induced lupus (malar rash) 1. Active infection (e.g., sepsis) 2. Recent or recurrent infection (recurrent UTI, pneumonia) 3. CHF class III/IV 4. Active malignancy 5. Multiple sclerosis (or a family history) Hold the TNF inhibitor with a fever , an infection , a course of antibiotics , and before surgery (delays wound healing). Module Cases Coronary artery disease is not a contraindication (only advanced CHF is). A 24-year-old with RA, failed sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine, wants pregnancy soon (so no methotrexate or leflunomide), family history of MS → avoid TNF inhibitors . Other classes don't cause demyelination; pregnancy data on newer biologics are limited.

Practice Patients 1. A 32-year-old with new lupus: malar rash, oral ulcers, pleurisy, synovitis, anti-dsDNA, low complement. Starting prednisone and hydroxychloroquine. Which is NOT a prednisone side effect: weight gain, psychosis, ↓ infection risk, AVN, cataracts? Answer ↓ risk of infection : prednisone raises infection risk. Every other option is real. 2. A resident sends ankle fluid for cell count, crystals, culture, Gram stain and glucose. Which is unhelpful? Answer Glucose. C3G only. Cell count > 2,000 = inflammatory; > 50,000 neutrophil-rich = think septic. 3. A 45-year-old on hydroxychloroquine 400 mg for 20 years, no recent eye exam. What retinal finding worries you? Answer Bull's eye maculopathy. Warn at the start; yearly eye exams . 4. A man with RA on methotrexate develops dry cough, shortness of breath and fever. He was also started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI last week and his counts are falling. Answer Think methotrexate pneumonitis (stop it, assess urgently), and the sulfa antibiotic worsens methotrexate cytopenias. Methotrexate + sulfa antibiotics = avoid; methotrexate + sulfasalazine is fine. 5. A patient on adalimumab calls with a fever of 38.5°C and a cough. Answer Hold the TNF inhibitor and assess for infection (including TB and opportunistic organisms). Restart once the infection has been treated.

Learning Objectives Determine a differential diagnosis and management plan for patients with axial pain: recognize normal spinal anatomy on plain x-rays and identify common spinal anomalies on plain x-rays ( fracture, spondylolysis, scoliosis ). Dr. Vishal Kalia, radiology. A text-and-image Rise module with no recordings (the module estimates about an hour). It covers the x-ray objective that 7.2 also lists, and pairs with the clinical side in 7.3 . Every image below is from the module's own PDF. Most come in pairs: the plain film, and a colour-coded copy with the anatomy highlighted.

The Systematic Approach: ABCS Step What to check A — Alignment The overall curves: cervical mild lordosis , thoracic kyphosis (curving posteriorly), lumbar lordosis . Then how each vertebra lines up with its neighbours, using the alignment lines (below). B — Bones Follow the cortices , the dense white outer layer. Check vertebral body height , pedicles, transverse processes, and every other bone you can see. C — Cartilage and joints Cartilage isn't radiopaque, so you see the disc space instead. A disc may show up if it calcifies or ossifies, and you may see bony bridging (ankylosis) across it. Check the facet joints too. S — Soft tissues The prevertebral tissues (in front of the vertebrae) and the paraspinal tissues (alongside) Then: the whole image C-spine films catch part of the lungs, T-spine films the lungs and mediastinum, and L-spine films the abdominal soft tissues. Compare with prior imaging whenever you can, because subtle changes are easier to see side by side.

Cervical Spine View Purpose AP Count the vertebrae, spinous process alignment, facets, uncinate and transverse processes Lateral The single most important view : bones, the four alignment lines, ADI, prevertebral soft tissue, airway Right and left oblique The neural foramina Open-mouth (odontoid or dens) C1–C2 alignment Flexion and extension Not routine. Only if subluxation or instability is suspected. Acute Trauma Changes the Plan With a patient in a cervical collar , the obliques are skipped because you don't want to move the neck; AP and lateral views give an overview if possible. In fact most acute trauma patients get a CT instead . Plain films miss subtle fractures, because soft tissue overlaps and the image is only two-dimensional. AP view The AP C-spine. Count from T1 : find the first rib and follow it to its vertebra, which is T1; C7 is just above. The mandible may hide C1–C2, which get their own view, though a well-exposed AP may show the dens (outlined in red). The spinous processes are round densities over the midline that should form a straight line . The facet joints should appear as parallel lines . The uncinate processes (pink) project from the posterolateral body edges and can hypertrophy in osteoarthritis . Cervical transverse processes are small, though C7's are a little more prominent. A C7 transverse process longer than about 2–2.5 cm suggests a cervical rib . From the module. Lateral view The lateral C-spine , colour-coded: the dens (light green) rising from C2, the anterior and posterior arches of C1, the prevertebral soft tissues (beige), disc spaces and facet joints. Count from the top (C1, C2), using the C7 spinous process (vertebra prominens) as a landmark. A good film shows C1 to T1 . Behind each articular pillar , formed by the superior and inferior articular processes, comes the lamina, then the spinous process. From the module. The four lines to trace on every lateral C-spine: anterior vertebral (red), posterior vertebral (brown), spinolaminar (green, where the laminae meet the spinous processes) and spinous process (blue, the tips). Each should be a smooth curve, and a step in any of them suggests fracture, injury or malalignment. The left panel adds the ADI and the prevertebral measurements . From the module. Measurement Normal Why it matters Atlantodental interval (ADI) : back of the anterior arch of C1 to the front of the dens < 3 mm adults , < 5 mm children C1–C2 instability . Flexion and extension views can test it. Prev

Thoracic Spine The standard views are AP, lateral and the swimmer's view . AP thoracic. Count by the ribs : the first rib gives T1 and the 12th gives T12. Spinous processes look like teardrops over the bodies (pink). The endplates are the sclerotic margins against the discs. Pedicles are corticated ovals on each side (green rings). Then the transverse processes and ribs. A mild positional scoliosis can appear when the patient is in pain. From the module. Lateral thoracic. Check the kyphosis . The pedicles look elongated here and bound the oval neural foramina (yellow). The facet joints are easiest to see in the mid-to-lower thoracic spine, and the curved lines behind are the ribs. From the module. Swimmer's view , a lateral film taken with one arm raised and the beam centred higher, over the cervicothoracic junction. It's for the upper thoracic spine , which overlapping soft tissue hides on the standard views. Find T1 just below C7 (the prominent spinous process) or by its rib. From the module.

Lumbar Spine and Sacrum The standard views are AP and lateral . Obliques are added for the pars, and dedicated sacrum or SI views only when requested. AP lumbar. L1 is the vertebra just below the 12th rib ; count down to L5. Some people have four or six lumbar-type vertebrae ( transitional vertebrae ). The bodies are bigger and the processes more horizontal than thoracic ones. The pedicles are round with sclerotic margins . Inferiorly, check the sacral ala , the sacral foramina and arcuate lines (for symmetry) and the SI joints (purple). From the module. Lateral lumbar. Bodies, endplates and disc spaces; pedicles (green) and the foramina between them (yellow); the facets at L4–5. Then the pars interarticularis (orange). A defect there can progress to spondylolisthesis and can cause low back pain. From the module. On the AP Lumbar Film, Look Off the Spine Too Check both renal areas for stones , the right upper quadrant for gallstones , the colon for fecal loading , the bowel for abnormally dilated loops , and look for free air . That's on top of the paraspinal soft tissues. The pars interarticularis is the bone between the superior and inferior articular processes . From the module. The Scotty dog on the oblique view. Nose = transverse process, eye = pedicle, ear = superior articular facet, front leg = inferior articular facet, neck = pars interarticularis . A defect shows as a lucent line through the neck: a collar . From the module. Sacrum and SI joints. The sacral ala (grey) sits lateral to the first sacral foramina, and the S2–S4 foramina (pink rings) have the lateral masses (purple) beside them. The coccyx (green) has 4 or 5 segments. The SI joint runs obliquely , from medial to lateral going back to front, so on an AP film its margins overlap and only parts of the joint are seen in profile. From the module.

entries.t: A Mnemonic for Any Bone Film: TIMS-C
entries.x: A Mnemonic for Any Bone Film: TIMS-C Letter Category Examples T Trauma, tumours Hyperflexion and hyperextension injuries, compression and burst fractures, distraction injuries; bone tumours. Trauma is one of the commonest spine pathologies you'll meet. I Infection, inflammatory, idiopathic RA, ankylosing spondylitis ; idiopathic means cause unknown M Metabolic, malignancy — S Systemic, senile Leukemia, lymphoma; osteoarthritis C Congenital Looked for mostly in the immature skeleton

Cervical Spine Trauma The common injury patterns , often from motor vehicle collisions. Slide from the module. Injury What it is Jefferson fracture C1 : fractures through the anterior and posterior arches at several sites Hangman's fracture C2 : bilateral fractures through the pars interarticularis , giving a traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2. Unstable. Extension teardrop A fragment off the anteroinferior corner of the body (a hyperextension injury); rotational stress can injure the cord Hyperextension with spondylosis Can widen a disc space without any visible fracture . In the right setting that means a ligamentous injury, so get an MRI . Hyperflexion injuries An interspinous ligament injury widens the gap between spinous processes . A simple wedge (anterosuperior corner) is stable; an unstable wedge also involves the posterior structures. Facet dislocation The facets lose their congruence and “perch” , making a step. Unilateral causes less slip and bilateral more. Can come with a cord injury. Flexion teardrop The anterior body, with injury to the cord, posterior column and interspinous ligaments Dens fractures Type I tip; type II mid-portion or base ; type III into the C2 body. You don't need these in detail. The One Stability Rule You Need Classification systems vary, but for this module: fractures confined to the front of the vertebral body are more likely stable. Once a fracture reaches the posterior elements, it is unstable. That's why radiologists always comment on posterior-element involvement. Ligament injuries can be invisible on plain film, so think MRI . Extension teardrop of C2 : the anteroinferior corner fragment, highlighted. From the module. Type II dens fracture across the base, seen on x-ray and confirmed on CT. From the module. Fractures at C5 and C7. A comminuted fracture at the front of C5 and a compression fracture of C7 (lost central height). The C5–6 disc space is widened , and both the anterior (green) and posterior (orange) lines step, with C6–7 alignment lost. The middle column is involved. The facets stay congruent. From the module. An unstable C4 fracture. C4 has lost height, the adjacent discs are mildly widened, and a fragment is pushed back toward the canal , breaking the posterior vertebral line (yellow). Because it extends past the back of the body, it's unstable. The film labels a second fracture lower down, at the front of C6–7. From the module. Perched facets. C5 has slipped forward on C6, so the facets lose their para

Degeneration and Soft-Tissue Disease Cervical spondylosis , the most common non-traumatic C-spine pathology . The lordosis is straightened (perhaps from muscle spasm), the discs are narrowed , there are anterior marginal osteophytes , and the endplates are sclerotic (brighter than normal C2–3). These are the same signs as OA in other joints, such as the shoulder and knee. From the module. Retropharyngeal abscess. The prevertebral tissue is wider than the vertebral body at C5–6 and pushes the airway forward. Look for small air locules , which can mean an anaerobic infection or an airway problem. The reason you always check the soft tissues. From the module. Isthmic spondylolisthesis. L4 has slipped about 4–5 mm forward on L5, the disc is narrowed, and there is a pars defect (pink, blue arrow). The red arrow marks the narrowed disc. Without a pars defect, a slip is usually degenerative , in older adults. Slips are measured in mm and graded. From the module. The Scottie dog collar sign at L5 (red circle): a lucent line through the neck means a pars defect . The neck above, outlined in purple, is intact. The oblique view helps when the lateral is equivocal. From the module.

Inflammatory Disease and Tumour Late ankylosing spondylitis. The ALL and PLL are ossified , with ossification across the discs (transdiscal ankylosis) and fused facets , especially in the neck. A rigid spine fractures easily , particularly next to the segments that still move. From the module. Sacroiliitis. Erosions on both the iliac and sacral sides make the joints look wider ( pseudo-widening ), with mild sclerosis on the iliac side. Ankylosis comes late. Active inflammation (marrow edema) needs an MRI , because plain film isn't sensitive or specific for it. From the module. Aneurysmal bone cyst (confirmed by MRI and biopsy). On the AP, the right pedicle is gone , replaced by an expansile lytic lesion; compare the normal left pedicle (ringed). On the lateral there is only a subtle, nonspecific lucency. This is why you always read both views . From the module.

Spinal Hardware Transpedicular screws through the pedicles of L2–L4, joined by rods on both sides. They stabilize the spine after correction or decompression, e.g. for scoliosis or spondylolisthesis. From the module. Vertebroplasty : bright cement injected into compressed vertebral bodies . The bone around it is diffusely less dense than normal. It is done for severe pain from compression fractures and to prevent progression. It does not restore height . From the module.

Scoliosis and the Cobb Angle Scoliosis is an abnormal curve of the spine to the right or left. It may also rotate , which shows as a change in the shape and position of the pedicles. Cobb angle Meaning < 10° Within normal: a normal variant > 10° Scoliosis > 50° Usually means considering surgical correction Measuring the Cobb angle. Find the most tilted vertebrae at each end of the curve. Draw a line along the superior endplate of the top one and the inferior endplate of the bottom one , then perpendiculars to each. The angle where the perpendiculars cross is the Cobb angle. This one measures 49°, just under the 50° surgical threshold. From the module. Marked scoliosis. A right thoracic primary curve and a left lumbar compensatory curve that keeps the spine balanced, with rotation. Cobb lines are drawn on the AP. From the module. After correction : longitudinal Harrington rods and transpedicular screws across many levels, here from the upper thoracic spine to the thoracolumbar junction. They hold the correction and reduce progression. From the module.

Normal Variants Variant What it is Why it matters Cervical rib An extra rib from C7 , osseous (visible) or fibrous (invisible on x-ray). It may pseudoarticulate with the first rib . A source of neck pain . It can compress the neurovascular bundle , giving pain referred into the arm and neck. Transitional vertebrae Lumbarization or sacralization at the lumbosacral junction (4 or 6 lumbar-type vertebrae) Affects how you count the levels Schmorl's nodes Focal depressions in the vertebral endplates ; the cause is debated Usually incidental . Whether they cause pain is debated. Limbus vertebra A triangular bone fragment, usually at the anterosuperior corner : the ring apophysis (the vertebral-edge growth plate) failed to fuse . Seen in adolescents, often at L4 . Not a fracture. Usually asymptomatic. Mild curve Scoliotic curvature < 10° Normal Bilateral osseous cervical ribs (arrows). The right one pseudoarticulates with the first rib. From the module. Two variants on one film. Limbus vertebrae (white arrows): triangular corner fragments, not fractures. Schmorl's nodes (yellow arrows): endplate dimples. From the module (LearningRadiology.com).

Summary 1 Know the normal The number of vertebrae, their alignment, their parts, and the anterior and posterior columns. 2 Alignment first A break in alignment tells you where to look. 3 Then the vertebrae, discs and soft tissues, systematically The finding may be in the soft tissue rather than the spine, as with an abscess or an airway foreign body. 4 Compare with prior imaging Subtle abnormalities are much easier to see side by side.

entries.t: Week 7 · The Spine, Back & Neck Pain, and the Shoulder
entries.p: Week 7 · The Spine, Back & Neck Pain, and the Shoulder
entries.x: > Week 7 The first MSK week. Thursday lays the foundation, then takes on back and neck pain. First the vocabulary used for the rest of the block: position and movement, the spinal nerve, dermatomes, contractions and joints. Then mechanical pain (worse with movement: discs, facets, muscles, whiplash) and non-mechanical pain (radiculopathy, stenosis, cauda equina, myelopathy and the red-flag conditions). Friday is the bones and joints of the shoulder, and reading spine x-rays. Thursday's 7.2 and 7.3 are also the preparation for Friday's neck and back anatomy lab. Thursday Oct 15 The MSK vocabulary, then back and neck pain, mechanical and not. 7.1 Introduction to MSK Anatomy The concept reference for the whole block: anatomical position, planes and directional terms; the terms of movement; the generic spinal nerve, dorsal and ventral rami, and the reflex arc; dermatomes and myotomes; isometric, concentric and eccentric contractions; open and closed kinetic chains; synovial joints, Hilton's law and what makes a joint stable; the skeleton and bony terminology → 7.2 Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain Mechanical pain (worse with movement, better with rest) versus the red flags; the vertebral column, a typical vertebra and its joints, and how cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebrae differ; the ligaments; degenerative disease; discogenic versus facetogenic pain and disc herniation; the back muscles and myofascial pain; whiplash; and who needs imaging → 7.3 Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain The spinal cord, nerve roots and meninges; radiculopathy, which root a disc hits, and the dermatome, myotome and reflex for C5–C8 and L3–S1; lumbar stenosis with neurogenic claudication, and cauda equina; cervical myelopathy; inflammatory back pain; spondylosis versus spondylolysis versus spondylolisthesis; visceral pain, infection and tumour → Friday Oct 16 The shoulder's bones and joints, and how to read a spine x-ray. 7.4 Osteology & Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity The pectoral girdle and its four joints, and scapulohumeral rhythm; the clavicle, scapula and humerus; the AC and glenohumeral joints; AC osteoarthritis versus AC separation (types I–V); shoulder arthritis, read from active and passive motion; instability, traumatic (a torn labrum, Hill–Sachs) versus AMBRI; and frozen shoulder → 7.5 Axial Spine Radiology The ABCS approach; the normal C-, T- and L-spine and sacrum view by view, with the four lines, ADI and prevertebral soft-tis

Learning Objectives Review these to prepare for the MSK block: Foundations in anatomy: anatomical terminology for MSK; terms of movement. Somatic nervous system: the somatic nerve pathway; the reflex arc; dermatomes and myotomes. Types of muscle contraction: isotonic (eccentric, concentric) and isometric. Kinetic chain: open and closed. Joints: characteristics of synovial joints; the laws of joints. The skeleton: axial and appendicular; bony terminology. Dr. Charys Martin, anatomy. A concept reference for the whole block: twelve short recordings (about an hour in total, though Elentra lists 97 minutes) with knowledge checks in between. Most of it is review from Foundations of Medicine, but Dr. Martin warns that the terms here “will be referred to throughout the course”.

Anatomical Terminology Every description of the body assumes it is in anatomical position , so everyone pictures the same thing. Term Meaning Anatomical position Standing erect, feet flat with the toes forward, arms at the sides with the palms forward, face forward Supine Anatomical position lying on the back Prone Anatomical position lying on the stomach Axilla (axillary fossa) The armpit. The anterior axillary fold is pectoralis major; there is a posterior fold too. The folds give the axillary lines used as landmarks. Arm vs forearm Arm = shoulder to elbow only . Forearm = elbow to wrist. Cubital fossa The front of the elbow, where many procedures and assessments happen Inguinal ligament The groin fold between abdomen and thigh, running from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle Thigh vs leg Thigh = hip to knee. Leg = knee to ankle only , not the whole lower limb. Popliteal fossa The hollow at the back of the knee Anatomical position , shown with the body planes. Left: sagittal planes, splitting left from right. Middle: coronal , front from back. Right: transverse , top from bottom. The planes aren't discussed in the recording, but every MSK description assumes this starting position. Slide from the deck.

Terms of Movement These describe movement away from anatomical position. Movement Definition Example Flexion / extension Decreasing / increasing the angle at a joint Lifting / lowering a biceps curl Abduction / adduction Moving away from / toward the midline Jumping jack, out / in Circumduction Flexion, abduction, extension and adduction combined Arm circles Retraction / protraction Scapulae brought together / spread apart Squeezing the shoulder blades back / reaching forward Elevation / depression Scapulae raised toward the head / lowered A shrug Plantarflexion / dorsiflexion Pointing the toes / bringing the toes toward the shin Up on tiptoes to reach a shelf / heel walking Supination / pronation Rotating the palm to face forward or up / back or down Supinated hand “holds a bowl of soup ”; hands flat on a keyboard are pronated Movements at the elbow and shoulder. Flexion and extension at the elbow, abduction and adduction at the shoulder, and circumduction, which combines all four. Slide from the deck. The tricky ones at the scapula, ankle and forearm. Retraction pulls the scapulae together, elevation shrugs them up, plantarflexion points the toes, and supination turns the palm up. Slide from the deck. Watch Out: the Module's Own Quiz Gets This Backwards In the “Anatomical Movements” review quiz, the answer feedback for the biceps-curl question says protraction brings the scapulae together and retraction moves them apart . That is reversed. The slide, the recording and the later quiz feedback all agree: retraction = together, protraction = apart .

The Generic Spinal Nerve All 31 spinal nerves , and some cranial nerves, carry somatic fibres to the body wall : the skin and its connective tissue, skeletal muscle and joints. Fibre Direction Carries General sensory (afferent) Toward the CNS, in through the dorsal root Pain, temperature, pressure, touch and proprioception (knowing where your body is in space, from tendons, ligaments and joints) General motor (efferent) Away from the CNS, out through the ventral root Impulses to skeletal muscle Part What it is Dorsal root The doorway into the CNS for sensory afferents Dorsal root ganglion The swelling on the dorsal root that holds the cell bodies of the sensory afferents Ventral root The doorway out of the CNS for motor efferents Spinal nerve Just the short segment after the roots join and before the rami split Dorsal ramus Mixed. Supplies only the deep muscles of the back and the skin over the back . Ventral ramus Mixed. Supplies everything else : back of the head, neck, upper limb, trunk wall, perineum and lower limb. Grey horns Dorsal (posterior, sensory), ventral (anterior, motor) and the small intermediolateral horn on the side The generic spinal nerve, posterior at the top. The slide is a labelling quiz, so here are the answers. A dorsal grey horn, B intermediolateral horn, C ventral grey horn, D dorsal root, E ventral root, F dorsal root ganglion, G spinal nerve, H ventral ramus, I dorsal ramus. Slide from the deck; key from the recording and the module's knowledge check.

entries.t: The Somatic Nerve Pathway and the Reflex Arc
entries.x: The Somatic Nerve Pathway and the Reflex Arc Dr. Martin's example: a mosquito lands on your arm and you swat it away. 1 Receptor → general sensory afferent It travels in the ventral ramus (the arm is not the back), then the spinal nerve, then the dorsal root . Its cell body sits in the DRG. 2 Spinal cord → brain It synapses with a second-order sensory neuron that ascends to the brain, and the brain decides to swat. 3 Upper motor neuron → lower motor neuron The UMN descends to the right spinal level and synapses with the lower motor neuron (the general motor efferent) in the ventral horn. 4 Out to the muscle Ventral root → spinal nerve → ventral ramus → arm muscles. Only fibres to the deep back muscles leave through the dorsal ramus. The full pathway. The afferent (blue) goes from the receptor through the DRG into the dorsal horn and up to the brain. The decision comes back down to the ventral horn, and the efferent (red) runs out to the muscle. Slide from the deck. The reflex arc short-circuits it inside the cord. Grabbing a hot marshmallow off the stick, the afferent synapses on an interneuron in the dorsal grey horn , which fires the efferent in the ventral horn . No upper motor neuron, and no thinking. Slide from the deck.

Dermatomes and Myotomes Step What happens Somites Paired blocks of paraxial mesoderm , each supplied by a single spinal nerve Dermomyotome Splits into a dermatome , which forms the skin and subcutaneous tissue of the body wall, and a myotome , which forms the muscles of the axial skeleton, body wall and limbs Myotomes fuse Several myotomes elongate and fuse into one muscle, so a muscle gets more than one spinal segment (e.g. C5 and C6). The nerves also merge and split again in the plexuses. Dermatomes fuse On the limbs the neat embryonic stripes become blocks, and neighbouring dermatomes overlap Why one muscle has several roots. Each somite brings its own spinal nerve, and myotomes fuse to make muscles. Slide from the deck. Embryology vs the clinic. The left maps are the neat segmental stripes. The right is Foerster's map , built from anatomy plus clinical experience, and is the one used for testing. Slide from the deck. How to Test a Dermatome A dermatome is a specific zone of skin that, developmentally, was supplied by a single spinal nerve . Near its edges the neighbouring nerves overlap. So never test on a border : on the mid-thigh you can't tell whether you're testing L2 or L3. Test in the middle of the territory. The course will show you the exact test sites as it goes. The one place with no overlap is along the dark axial lines on the map, where non-adjacent segments meet (e.g. L3 next to S2 down the back of the leg). Overlap only happens between consecutive spinal segments.

Types of Muscle Contraction Muscles can only shorten , so they only ever pull bones together. Different contraction types are what control a joint through a whole movement. Type Length Example Isometric No change. Sarcomeres shorten to a point and hold. Wall sit (quadriceps), plank Isotonic: concentric Shortens. The “typical” contraction. Up phase of a biceps curl; up phase of a push-up (triceps) Isotonic: eccentric Lengthens while contracting. Some sarcomeres let go, others hold, giving controlled lowering. Down phase of a curl; down phase of a squat (quadriceps); setting something heavy down instead of dropping it Isometric vs isotonic. A plank holds a fixed length; a push-up changes length, eccentric on the way down and concentric on the way up. Muscles are never fully relaxed: there's always some tonic contraction . Slide from the deck.

Open and Closed Kinetic Chain Open kinetic chain Closed kinetic chain The limb Free to move in space Fixed , e.g. to the floor Examples Biceps curl, bench press, lifting a drink, raising your hand, swinging your legs while sitting, arms out to the side Push-up, squat, standing up from a chair, pushing down on the chair to stand What it demands The rest of the body can be stabilized while one segment moves Every joint in the chain must be held stable. Rotation at one link causes rotation at the next , all the way up. “The leg bone's connected to the thigh bone.” In a closed chain, poor biomechanics at a distal joint twist every joint above it. A runner whose upper body twists usually has twisting in the lower body too. Closed-chain exercise is more functional because it uses the stabilizers. Slide from the deck.

Synovial Joints Most joints in MSK are synovial : the common, freely movable kind. Feature Role Hyaline (articular) cartilage Covers the bone ends with a smooth, nearly frictionless surface Fibrous joint capsule Surrounds the joint and gives structural support . Intrinsic ligaments are thickenings of the capsule where it needs reinforcing. Synovial membrane Lines every inner surface not covered by cartilage and secretes synovial fluid (hyaluronic acid, egg-yolk consistency: “syn-ovia”) Synovial fluid Reduces friction, nourishes the cartilage , and absorbs some shock Where joint pain comes from. Cartilage and synovium are poorly innervated . Pain comes from the well-innervated capsule, ligaments and bone , including bone rubbing on bone once the cartilage has worn through. Slide from the deck. Type Axes Example Movement Hinge Uniaxial Elbow Flexion and extension only Pivot Uniaxial C1 on C2 ; proximal and distal radioulnar joints Rotation (pronation and supination) Saddle Biaxial Thumb CMC Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction: the opposable thumb Condyloid Biaxial MCP Convex in concave: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction Plane Uniaxial AC joint Gliding and sliding of two flat surfaces Ball-and-socket Multiaxial Glenohumeral, hip All of the above plus rotation Hinge, pivot, saddle, condyloid , each beside a mechanical model of how it moves. Slide from the deck (ECA T1.3). Plane (the AC joint) and ball-and-socket (glenohumeral; the hip is the other). Slide from the deck (ECA T1.3). The laws of joints Law Meaning Crossing = acting Any muscle that crosses a joint acts on it, even if that isn't its main job. Biceps mainly flexes the elbow but also helps flex the shoulder. Hilton's law The sensory supply to a joint comes from the nerves supplying the muscles that act on that joint . Stability 1. Shape of the articulating surfaces (the primary factor) → 2. ligaments → 3. muscles (dynamic stability from tonic contraction) Why the Shoulder Dislocates and the Hip Doesn't The femoral head sits deep in the acetabulum , like a ball in a bowl, so the bone shape alone makes the hip stable. The humeral head sits on the shallow glenoid fossa , “a plate with a small lip”. The knee is two bones stacked on top of each other, with a lot of mobility and little bony stability. Joints that can't rely on their bones lean on ligaments and muscles, and the stability of a joint decides how easily it is injured.

The Skeleton A supportive framework that supports soft tissue , protects organs (the thoracic cage around the heart and lungs) and gives levers for muscles : the bones are the levers and the muscles pull on them. It is mostly bone, plus some cartilage (the costal cartilages and the pubic symphysis ). Part Bones Key points Axial skeleton Skull Many bones joined by sutures Sutures barely move. The only freely movable joint is the TMJ . Vertebral column Five regions Vertebrae get bigger going down as they carry more weight. The sacrum passes the load to the pelvis at the sacroiliac joints . The coccyx bears no weight and is tiny. Sternum, ribs 12 pairs of ribs The upper ribs join the sternum through costal cartilage. Ribs 11 and 12 are floating . The clavicles also attach to the sternum. Upper extremity Pectoral girdle Clavicle, scapula The whole upper limb hangs off the axial skeleton by one small joint: the sternoclavicular . Arm Humerus Proximally the glenohumeral joint ; distally it meets the ulna and radius at the elbow Forearm Ulna (medial), radius (lateral) The ulna is the elbow's hinge and plays only a minor role at the wrist. The radius, with its disc-shaped head, does the rotation at the radioulnar joints and forms most of the wrist. Hand 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, phalanges Three phalanges per digit, two in the thumb Lower extremity Pelvic girdle Two pelvic bones Joined to the sacrum by the SI joints , which barely move and are held by strong ligaments. Movement there (common in pregnancy) hurts. The two bones meet in front at the fibrocartilaginous pubic symphysis ; each has an acetabulum for the hip. Thigh Femur Much bigger than the humerus. The head joins the shaft by an angled neck , the usual site of a “broken hip” . Patella Sesamoid bone Forms within the quadriceps tendon and acts as an extra pulley for more quad force Leg Tibia, fibula The tibia bears the weight and forms most of the ankle. The slender fibula isn't part of the knee but completes the ankle. No movement between them, unlike the forearm. Foot 7 tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges Three phalanges per toe, two in the big toe Axial skeleton : skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs. Slide from the deck. Upper extremity , from the pectoral girdle to the phalanges. Slide from the deck. Lower extremity , with the patella (a sesamoid bone), the SI joint and the pubic symphysis. Slide from the deck.

Bony Terminology Group the names and they make sense. Most bumps on a bone are made by something pulling on it : a ligament or tendon tugs, and the bone ossifies there. Group Term Definition · example Projections that form joints Articular Head Expanded, rounded end that tapers to a neck Facet Small, smooth, nearly flat surface another bone sits on (vertebrae, ribs) Condyle Rounded projection on the distal end of a bone (distal humerus) Projections for ligaments and tendons Attachment Process Any bony prominence Protuberance A smaller projection from the surface Trochanter Very large, blunt, irregular; only on the femur (greater and lesser) Tuberosity Large rounded projection, often roughened (smaller than a trochanter) Tubercle Small rounded projection (smaller than a tuberosity) Epicondyle Raised area around a condyle. The medial epicondyle of the humerus is the bump on the inside of your elbow. Crest Narrow, prominent ridge, often a long attachment Line Small, narrow ridge, less prominent than a crest Spine A slender, pointed ridge (the spine of the scapula ) Depressions Depressions Groove A furrow often occupied by a structure Sulcus A narrow crevice that holds a structure. The intertubercular sulcus (bicipital groove) carries the long head of biceps. Notch An indentation at the edge (the suprascapular notch ) Fossa A basin-like depression that often forms a joint. The olecranon fossa receives the olecranon of the ulna. Openings and other Openings Foramen Round or oval hole through bone Fissure Narrow, slit-like opening Meatus A canal through thick bone (mostly in the skull) Other Ramus Where the bone changes angle (the ramus of the mandible) Neck The narrowing where the shaft meets a head Sinus An air-filled cavity in bone lined by mucous membrane

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Learning Objectives The objectives are shared with 7.3 , 7.5 , the anatomy lab and Clinical Skills. Each module covers part of them.
