Functional anatomy of the neck and back: the distinguishing features of vertebrae at different levels and why they differ; the innervation and function of the neck and back muscles and their role in causing or preventing back pain; how ligaments and discs keep the spine stable; dermatomes and myotomes, with the root deficits at C5–C8 and L3–S1. Axial pain: red flags and what they suggest; the anatomical basis of common spine disorders; recognizing myofascial pain, SI joint pathology, mechanical back pain, spinal stenosis, cauda equina, radiculopathy and cervical myelopathy from the history and exam. Inflammatory vs non-inflammatory back pain; spondylosis vs spondylolysis vs spondylolisthesis. Normal spinal anatomy and common anomalies on plain x-ray (fracture, spondylolysis, scoliosis). Management, including investigations and treatment, of these common painful spinal conditions. Dr. Caitlin Cassidy (clinical) and Dr. Charys Martin (anatomy). Seven recordings, about 75 minutes, in two halves, each an anatomy break followed by the clinical side. This page follows that order. The module offers a “detailed” version of the slides that adds every muscle's origin and insertion. Dr. Martin: you only need origins and insertions where they're printed on the slide , and greyed-out boxes are nice-to-know.

entries.t: Why It Matters, and How to Sort It Out
entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Why It Matters, and How to Sort It Out Back and neck pain are among the most common complaints in primary care. A specific anatomical diagnosis is often hard to make, and in uncomplicated (“mechanical”) back pain it often doesn't change treatment. What you can't miss is the patient whose pain is not uncomplicated. Many structures can hurt: paraspinal muscles and soft tissue, the disc , the facet (zygapophyseal) joint , the nerves leaving the intervertebral foramen, and the SI joint . The arrows pointing off the page (“over here”, “down here somewhere”) are a reminder that the source may not be in the spine at all. Slide from the deck. Start with the history: OLDCARS (onset, location, duration, character, alleviating and aggravating factors, radiation, severity), plus red flags . Red flag group Ask and look for Neurologic Progressive weakness or sensory change, saddle anaesthesia , loss of hand dexterity , ataxic gait, incontinence , erectile dysfunction, abnormal reflexes Inflammatory Morning stiffness , pain in the second half of the night , family history, rashes, eye symptoms, pain that improves with exercise (the opposite of mechanical pain) Neoplastic Young age , severe night pain or no relief with rest, unintentional weight loss , night sweats, history of cancer , associated signs (e.g. hematuria). The cancer may be in a nearby organ and only presenting as back pain. Infectious Fevers, sweats, IV drug use , immunosuppression Fracture (subacute or chronic) A fall or trauma, osteoporosis , a previous fragility fracture Vascular Neck: vertebral artery insufficiency , with dizziness on neck movement, cranial nerve signs or drop attacks. Limbs: distal claudication , pain in the extremities with activity, with or without back or neck pain. Then examine for axial abnormalities and contributing limb problems, neurologic abnormalities , and signs of the red-flag conditions . For example, if a young patient has night pain and morning stiffness, look for the rash that supports an inflammatory cause. The exam itself is taught in Clinical Skills. What you can feel: the C7 prominens (your landmark for counting up and down), the acromion, the spine and medial border of the scapula, ribs 6–12, the iliac crest and the sacrum. Slide from the deck. Investigations Test Good for X-ray ($) A quick screen of alignment and fractures . Says little about soft tissue or nerves. CT ($$) Bony detail, trauma . Not much help for nerves or canal patency. MRI ($$$) The best view of

entries.t: What Mechanical Spine Pain Looks Like
entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: What Mechanical Spine Pain Looks Like By definition, axial pain that is worse with movement. “Worse with movement” is the defining feature, and the opposite of inflammatory back pain, which improves with movement. OLDCARS Mechanical pattern Onset Anywhere from acute to chronic. Usually changes that have accumulated over time (degenerative), often “tweaked” by something acute, like bending wrong or going down stairs, on a background that has been grumbling for a while. Location Midline or just beside the midline of the neck or back Duration Variable Character Dull and aching, or sharp and stabbing Aggravating / alleviating Aggravated by movement, relieved by rest Radiation Variable, but it usually doesn't reach the tips of the limbs , as nerve pain would Severity Variable Red flags None From the module's knowledge checks A 28-year-old construction worker has had left > right low back pain for 4 weeks since lifting something heavy. It's worst at night, and he's had a low-grade fever for a few days. → Arrange imaging. Young age, fever and night-dominant pain are red flags, so this is not a case for reassurance or physio. A 72-year-old with 5 weeks of severe mechanical pain, no red flags, who hasn't tried anything yet. → Physical therapy , the mainstay. A facet injection comes only after therapy fails, codeine and other opioids are to be avoided (and he hasn't even tried acetaminophen), and surgery is for axial pain with neurologic features. Surgery for purely axial mechanical pain has poor outcomes.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: The Vertebral Column It runs from the base of the skull to the coccyx. It protects the spinal cord and nerves , bears and transmits body weight , absorbs shock , maintains posture, and gives a mobile framework. Small movements at each level add up to large ones overall: flexion, extension, lateral flexion and rotation. Region Vertebrae Curve Cervical 7 (C1–C7) Secondary , concave posteriorly (lordosis) Thoracic 12 (T1–T12) Primary , concave anteriorly (kyphosis) Lumbar 5 (L1–L5) Secondary , concave posteriorly (lordosis) Sacrum 5, fused Primary , concave anteriorly Coccyx 4, fused — 33 vertebrae and four curves. The primary curves, thoracic and sacral, are left over from the flexed fetal position; the newborn's spine is one C-shape. The secondary curves come from extension: the cervical curve appears when an infant lifts its head lying prone and then holds it up sitting, and the lumbar curve when a toddler stands and walks. The lumbar curve is more pronounced in females, and the sacral curve is less pronounced, keeping the coccyx out of the birth canal. Slide from the deck. Abnormal curve What it is Usual causes Kyphosis An exaggerated thoracic curve Erosion or fracture of the anterior vertebrae , which wedge the bodies forward: osteoporosis and aging Lordosis An exaggerated lumbar curve with an anterior pelvic tilt Weak trunk (abdominal) muscles ; pregnancy Scoliosis Increased lateral curvature with rotation of the vertebrae Weak back muscles, poor posture, congenital defects, unequal leg length. Through the kinetic chain, the rotation passes down to the pelvis and lower limbs.

entries.t: Anatomy of a Vertebra and Its Joints
entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Anatomy of a Vertebra and Its Joints Part Description Body The large anterior part that carries weight, getting bigger going down Vertebral arch Pedicles , short stout processes joining the arch to the body, plus laminae , flat plates closing the arch behind Transverse processes Project posterolaterally from where pedicle meets lamina; muscle and ligament attachments Spinous process Projects posteriorly where the laminae meet; muscle and ligament attachments Articular processes Four, two superior and two inferior, that form the zygapophysial (facet) joints with the vertebrae above and below Vertebral foramen Body plus arch: the opening for the spinal cord Intervertebral foramen The inferior vertebral notch of the vertebra above plus the superior notch of the one below: the exit for the spinal nerve The parts of a vertebra. The two notches stack into the intervertebral foramen , the spinal nerve's exit. Slide from the deck (Netter). Two connections at every level: the disc in front and the paired facet joints behind. Slide from the deck. Joint Key facts Intervertebral disc Anulus fibrosus (outer concentric rings of fibrocartilage) around the nucleus pulposus (gelatinous, high water content). It meets the body at the vertebral endplate , a cartilage layer fused to the disc over a thin layer of porous bone. It attaches the vertebrae, permits movement and absorbs shock. Discs are thickest in the cervical and lumbar regions and make up about 25% of column height . There is no disc between C1 and C2 . Zygapophysial (facet) joints Plane synovial joints between the inferior articular facets of the vertebra above and the superior facets of the one below. They glide and hold the column together at the back. Atlanto-occipital (skull on C1) Flexion and extension: nodding “yes” Atlanto-axial (C1 on C2) C1 pivots around the dens : shaking “no” Costovertebral The rib's head meets the costal facets of its own vertebra, the vertebra above, and the disc between them. Its tubercle meets the transverse process of its own vertebra (costotransverse joint).

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Regional Differences Feature Cervical Thoracic Lumbar Body Small Heart-shaped, with costal facets Large , with heavy pedicles Vertebral foramen Large (the cervical enlargement supplies the arms) Small , circular Large, triangular Transverse processes Short, with transverse foramina Long, with facets for the rib tubercles No costal facets Spinous processes Short and bifid , except C7 (vertebra prominens) Long, sloping down over the next vertebra Short, stout, broad Movement Free: flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation Some flexion, little extension (the sloping spines block it), rotation, some lateral flexion Flexion, extension, some lateral bending, limited rotation Tell them apart by body size, foramen shape, and what's on the transverse process : a hole (cervical), a rib facet (thoracic) or neither (lumbar). The CTs underneath show the same shapes as they look on imaging. Slide from the deck. The Vertebral Artery and C7 Every cervical vertebra has transverse foramina, but the vertebral artery only runs through C6 to C1 on its way to the brain, protected inside bone the whole way. C7's foramina carry only the vertebral vein. C7 is also the odd one out for its long, single (not bifid) spinous process : flex your neck and it's the bump at the bottom. C1 (atlas) is a ring with no body : anterior and posterior arches joined by lateral masses, which carry the skull's occipital condyles (“yes”). C2 (axis) has the dens sticking up where C1's body would be (anatomists used to call it C1's body), and C1 rotates around it (“no”). Slide from the deck. Note: the recording calls the lumbar transverse processes “short and wide”. The module's own mini-text calls them “long and slender”, and the table follows the mini-text, which matches standard anatomy texts. Everyone agrees the lumbar spinous processes are short and broad.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: The Ligaments Ligament Where Job Anterior longitudinal (ALL) Strong, broad band down the front of the bodies and discs, occiput to sacrum Resists hyperextension Posterior longitudinal (PLL) Narrow, inside the canal on the back of the bodies and discs Resists hyperflexion Ligamentum flavum Pale yellow tissue joining lamina to lamina Seen from inside the canal at laminectomy Supraspinous Tips of the spinous processes, C7 to the sacrum . The most posterior ligament. Ligamentum nuchae Continues the supraspinous ligament above C7, from the external occipital protuberance, and fills the cervical curve Attachment for the neck and upper back muscles Interspinous, intertransverse Between neighbouring spinous processes, and between transverse processes A common mistake: the PLL is not on the back of the spinous processes . It lies inside the canal, on the back of the vertebral bodies. The ligament on the spinous process tips is the supraspinous . The MRI arrows show where each one lies. Slide from the deck. Clinical Note: Laminectomy Cutting through the laminae on both sides lets the surgeon lift off the spinous processes and see into the canal (the ligamentum flavum is on the inside). It is done to relieve pressure on the cord or roots from a tumour, a herniated disc or bony overgrowth. Lateral C-spine, with the answers from the feedback video. A vertebral body (C5), B C7 prominens (the long spinous process at the bottom), C facet joints, D spinous process (C5), E intervertebral disc. Count down from C1 to find your level. Slide from the deck. Lateral L-spine. A spinous process, B vertebral body, D facet joints (these overlap more than in the neck because lumbar facets face medially and laterally), F intervertebral foramen, G disc space, H sacrum (L5 sits on the sacral promontory). C and E are the vertebral notches: E, the cup open upward, is the superior notch, and C, open downward, is the inferior notch. The recording names both without assigning the letters, so that pairing comes from the shapes. Slide from the deck.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Degenerative Spine Disease The degenerative cascade. Repetitive axial loading damages the endplates, then microtears form in the anulus, the nucleus herniates inside the disc (internal disc disruption), and the disc loses height. The disc doesn't sit alone: the angles change, the facets take repetitive microtrauma, and they go through synovial hypertrophy, cartilage loss, osteophytes , capsular laxity ± subluxation, and enlarged articular processes. The cervical image shows a neck that has become kyphotic instead of lordotic , with anterior osteophytes. Slide from the deck. Term Meaning Spondylosis “Spondy” = vertebra, “-osis” = a state of disease. The whole degenerative picture : degenerative disc disease plus facet arthropathy, with periarticular changes (loss of disc height, ligament hypertrophy). In short, arthritis of the spine , made more complicated than other joints by the discs. Spondylolisthesis “Listhesis” = slipping: one vertebra slips on the next, usually forward (see the bridge, below)

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Discogenic Pain and Disc Herniation The disc itself hurts , rather than pressing on something else. Slide from the deck (CFEP Back Tool, 2016). From bulge to sequestration. A diffuse bulge, a broad-based protrusion (25–50% of the circumference), a focal protrusion (< 25%), an extrusion (the bulge is wider than its neck, b > a), and a sequestration , where a fragment has lost contact with its parent disc. Slide from the deck (Braddom 2011). Discogenic pain (internal disc disruption) Acute disc herniation What's happening The anulus is intact ; the nucleus pushes out through radial or concentric tears and irritates the disc itself Disc material herniates out, causing both discogenic pain and possibly compression of nerves Who 20–40% of back pain patients Younger people (40s–50s), often while lifting something Pattern Axial-predominant (back > leg), mechanical, worse with forward flexion , which squeezes the disc between the bodies Sudden axial pain, worse with coughing or sneezing (the Valsalva effect raises disc pressure), ± leg pain if a root is compressed Treatment Conservative: therapy and exercise, NSAIDs acutely, acetaminophen The same for the mechanical part. The nerve side is in 7.3 . Why Discs Herniate Posterolaterally The PLL is strong down the midline at the back of the disc, so herniations usually squeeze out to the side of it. That is good for the cord , which stays clear of the central canal, but bad for the nerve roots , which leave laterally. That's why herniations cause radiculopathy. (The slide says the disc moves away from the “ligamentum flavum”, but that ligament joins the laminae. The recording's PLL explanation is the anatomically correct one and is the one used here.)

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Facetogenic Pain The facets are synovial joints , so they get arthritis like any other. But facet degeneration on imaging doesn't track with symptoms (almost every adult's x-ray, CT or MRI shows some), which is why imaging helps so little here. Feature Facetogenic pain Where Localized axial pain, often off to one side , ± some radiation, but not to the fingers or toes Neck Commonly headache , or shoulder and neck pain Low back Buttock, hip, thigh or low back pain; it is uncommon to go past the knee Mechanics Classically worse with extension, relieved by flexion , because extension jams the facets together and flexion opens them Treatment Flexion-based therapy; NSAIDs acutely; acetaminophen; image-guided facet injection , medial branch block or ablation Facet joints in motion (inset): bending forward opens the facets and bending back compresses them, which is why extension hurts. Slide from the deck. Where facets refer pain. The upper cervical facets go to the head, the lower ones to the neck and shoulder. The lumbar facets go to the low back, buttock, groin and thigh. Dr. Cassidy warns that these maps vary between sources. Slide from the deck (Gellhorn et al. 2013). The Take-Home Disc and facet pain are treated almost identically, with physio first plus NSAIDs and acetaminophen. That is exactly why a precise anatomical diagnosis isn't critical in mechanical pain. The one practical difference: facet pain gets flexion-based exercises.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Muscles of the Back Three layers. Superficial (extrinsic): trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae. They move and stabilize the upper limb and are supplied by ventral rami (brachial plexus branches, plus CN XI for trapezius). Intermediate : serratus posterior superior and inferior, which are mainly proprioceptive and not covered. Deep (intrinsic): splenius, erector spinae and transversospinalis. They support and move the spine and are supplied by dorsal rami . Slide from the deck. Superficial muscle Action Nerve Trapezius : a diamond shape covering the upper back, from the skull and the cervical and thoracic spinous processes to the point of the shoulder Elevates, depresses and retracts the scapula; rotates the glenoid superiorly Spinal accessory (CN XI) : need to know. C3–C4 carry its pain and proprioception (the familiar trapezius ache). Latissimus dorsi : large, flat and fan-shaped, from the thoracolumbar fascia , iliac crest, lower ribs and spines; wraps forward to the intertubercular groove of the humerus Extends, adducts and medially rotates the humerus Thoracodorsal (nice-to-know) Rhomboids (major and minor, often fused): deep to trapezius, from the upper thoracic spines to the medial border of the scapula Retract the scapula, rotate to depress the glenoid , hold the scapula to the chest wall Dorsal scapular (nice-to-know) Levator scapulae : a thin strap from the upper cervical transverse processes to the superior medial border of the scapula Elevates the scapula, rotates to depress the glenoid Dorsal scapular plus C3–C4 Trapezius , CN XI. Slide from the deck. Latissimus dorsi. The greyed box (thoracodorsal nerve) is nice-to-know. Slide from the deck. Rhomboids. Slide from the deck. Levator scapulae. Slide from the deck. Deep muscle group Action Nerve Erector spinae : I liocostalis (lateral, to the ribs), L ongissimus (intermediate), S pinalis (medial, to the spinous processes), all from a broad tendon off the sacrum, iliac crests and lumbar spines. “ I Like Standing ”, lateral to medial. You won't be asked to identify the three individually. Bilateral: extend the column and head, and eccentrically control trunk flexion so you don't fall forward (think deadlifts). Unilateral: lateral flexion. Part of the core. Dorsal rami : need to know. These deep muscles are the only motor targets of the dorsal rami. entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Muscle Problems Problem What it is Acute strain or spasm — Repetitive strain injury WSIB definition: from repetitive tasks, forceful exertion, vibration, mechanical compression, or sustained or awkward positions Myofascial pain syndrome Trigger points: “hyperirritable areas of tissue that are tender when compressed and can give rise to referred pain” Managing Muscle Pain There is no test for it. Investigate only to rule something else out. Management is conservative: rule out red flags, then educate and reassure . Movement may hurt, but it won't cause damage , and patients can become fearful of moving. Explain the excellent prognosis . Use relative rest, ice or heat, topicals, a short course of oral NSAIDs if needed, and physio to strengthen postural support . Tight and weak muscles are often asymmetric: for example, strengthen the hip extensors and abdominals and stretch the hip flexors to support the normal lumbar lordosis.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Whiplash-Associated Disorder Question Answer What Neck symptoms after an acceleration–deceleration injury, e.g. an MVC Tissue Most often muscle (strains or partial tears of the paraspinals). Less often, in decreasing order: facets > ALL > bone (fracture) > cord (SCI) . Prognosis Most improve with conservative care. < 5% have severe symptoms at 2 years. Image? If there's more than subjective pain, stiffness and tenderness, with a real loss of range: x-ray if you suspect a fracture , ± MRI if there's any neurologic abnormality Straightforward WAD Keep moving and avoid C-collars ; heat and ice; acetaminophen or NSAIDs (oral or topical); “modest” physio , because aggressive early programs may make it worse

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Who to Image The Mechanical Pain Conundrum Mechanical pain comes from irritated structures, but imaging is often normal , and abnormal imaging is common in people with no pain at all . In one review of MRIs in adults without back pain, disc degeneration was reported in 0–76% (Endean et al. 2011). Degeneration comes with aging, so a finding may be contributing, or may be incidental. Patients often want a scan, and the scan often won't answer the question. Situation Imaging (Canadian Association of Radiologists) No red flags, mechanical, < 6 weeks None. Red flags : suspected cancer, infection, cauda equina , severe or progressive neurologic deficit, suspected compression fracture MRI is the best modality. Image urgently if you suspect an epidural abscess or hematoma , which can present with acute pain before any neurologic signs. Suspected uncomplicated disc herniation or stenosis Only after an unsuccessful 4–6 week trial of conservative care CT Only when you'd order an MRI but can't (contraindication, availability), or for trauma and fine bony detail X-ray For red-flag conditions (fracture, malignancy), or as a quick first step if symptoms persist past 6 weeks despite good conservative care . It's fast and catches gross malalignment or an old fracture. The CAR referral guideline (C06, lower back pain) the slide quotes: MRI “indicated in special circumstances”, with the red-flag list and the 4–6-week rule for herniated discs and stenosis. Slide from the deck (car.ca). Knowledge check: which of these gets a CT? A 35-year-old after an MVC this morning, normal C-spine x-rays, still with severe neck pain despite analgesia → CT , to look for an occult fracture. The others: a 50-year-old with 6 weeks of buttock-radiating mechanical pain and minimal benefit from weekly PT hasn't really done adequate PT, which should be done at home. If she has, the test is an MRI for stenosis, or an x-ray first. A 27-year-old with morning stiffness that eases with activity and lumbar pain worse overnight is inflammatory, so MRI . A 69-year-old with 3 months of leg pain to the toes, weakness and a numb patch on the lateral leg despite PT is root compression, so MRI (CT only if MRI is contraindicated).

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: The Bridge to Non-Mechanical Pain 1 Spondylosis Degenerative change in the disc and/or the facets. 2 Things start taking up space Subluxation, joint enlargement (osteophytes, ligament hypertrophy ), disc bulge or herniation, and degenerative spondylolisthesis , where one vertebra slips, usually forward, on the next. 3 Stenosis Lateral stenosis is encroachment on the root in the neural foramen. Central canal stenosis narrows the canal where the roots or the cord run. Both are now non-mechanical problems ( 7.3 ). Degenerative spondylolisthesis in a drawing, a lateral x-ray and an MRI: one body has shifted forward on the one below, narrowing the space for the nerves. Slide from the deck. Dr. Cassidy stresses that degeneration is only one route to this. Anything space-occupying in the canal or foramina, such as an infection or a tumour, compresses nerves the same way.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Learning Objectives These objectives are shared with 7.2 and 7.5 . This module carries the neurologic and “everything else” half. Define dermatome and myotome, and outline the sensory and motor deficits expected with root pathology at C5–C8 and L3–S1 . Define red flags for back and neck pain and what they suggest; describe the anatomical basis of common spine disorders. Recognize myofascial pain, SI joint pathology, mechanical back pain, spinal stenosis, cauda equina, radiculopathy and cervical myelopathy from the history and exam. Distinguish inflammatory from non-inflammatory back pain, and spondylosis vs spondylolysis vs spondylolisthesis . Develop an approach to management, investigations and treatment, of these conditions. Dr. Charys Martin (spinal cord anatomy) and Dr. Caitlin Cassidy (clinical). Four recordings, about 42 minutes. With 7.2 , this is the preparation for Friday's Clinical Anatomy of the Neck & Back lab .

entries.t: The Spinal Cord and Spinal Nerves
entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: The Spinal Cord and Spinal Nerves Feature Fact Extent From the brainstem (foramen magnum) to about L1/L2 in adults Cervical enlargement Cord levels C4–T1 , for the brachial plexus (the whole upper limb) Lumbosacral enlargement Cord levels L1–S3 , for the lumbosacral plexus (the whole lower limb) Spinal nerves 31 pairs : 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal Exit rule C1–C7 exit above their vertebra and C8 exits below C7 (8 nerves, 7 vertebrae). From T1 down, every nerve exits below its vertebra. Cord vs column The cord stops growing before the column does, so it ends up in only the upper two-thirds of the canal. Lower roots travel further and further down before exiting. Conus medullaris The tapered end of the cord, just below the lumbosacral enlargement Cauda equina “Horse's tail”: the roots continuing below the end of the cord Filum terminale A slender continuation of pia from the conus to the coccyx. It anchors the cord so it can't move and pull on the roots. It is the vestigial remnant of the embryo's tail-like caudal cord. The cord ends at L1/2 , but its 31 nerve pairs still exit at their own levels. The two enlargements feed the two limb plexuses. Slide from the deck (Netter). Conus, filum, cauda. The cord tapers into the conus medullaris, the filum terminale runs on to the coccyx, and the roots of the cauda equina hang around it. Slide from the deck (Netter). Structure Carries Cell bodies Ventral rootlets → ventral root Motor (efferent) fibres plus presynaptic autonomic fibres Ventral (anterior) grey horn Dorsal rootlets → dorsal root Sensory (afferent) fibres Dorsal root ganglion Spinal nerve Mixed. The two roots join inside the intervertebral foramen . — Dorsal ramus (smaller) Mixed. Skin of the back and the deep back muscles only. — Ventral ramus Mixed. Everything else : both plexuses and the intercostal nerves. — Roots are not rami. The roots are single-purpose doors: the dorsal root brings sensation in and the ventral root sends motor out . The rami , after the spinal nerve splits, are both mixed . The module's feedback video stresses this, because students mix them up. Slide from the deck (Netter). Clinical Note: Why L5 Gets Squeezed Going down the lumbar spine, the spinal nerves get bigger while the intervertebral foramina get smaller . The L5 nerve is the largest and its foramen the smallest , so the lower nerves are the most vulnerable to compression. (From the module's mini-text.)

entries.t: The Meninges and the Spaces Between
entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: The Meninges and the Spaces Between Layer or space Key facts Dura mater (“tough mother”) The tough outer covering, continuous with the cranial dura. It forms the dural sac down to S2 , is pierced by the spinal nerves, and is anchored to the coccyx. Arachnoid mater (“web-like”) Delicate and avascular. It encloses the subarachnoid space and is held against the dura by CSF pressure rather than attached to it. Pia mater Directly on the cord, roots and vessels. Its tooth-like denticulate ligaments anchor the cord in the dural sac, and it continues as the filum terminale . Epidural space Real , outside the dura: fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus Subdural space Only a potential space, between dura and arachnoid Subarachnoid space Real : CSF plus the cord's vessels Three layers. The dura (outer, to S2), the arachnoid (pushed against it by CSF) and the pia (on the cord, with denticulate ligaments). Slide from the deck (Netter). Epidural vs lumbar puncture. Both go in at L3/4 or L4/5 , below the end of the cord. The epidural stops outside the dura; the LP enters the lumbar cistern. Slide from the deck. Procedure Where the needle goes Why it's safe there Epidural block Anesthetic into the epidural space , around the dura. It bathes the cauda equina roots after they leave the dural sac, so sensation is lost below the block . Used often in labour. It's done below the cord , and the needle isn't meant to enter the dura at all. Lumbar puncture Into the lumbar cistern , the enlarged subarachnoid space between the end of the cord (L2) and the end of the dural sac (S2) . The patient lies on their side with the trunk flexed. The cistern holds only the cauda equina, and its floating roots move out of the way of the needle. Lab knowledge check (the cadaver photo isn't reproduced here): A conus medullaris, B dorsal ramus (piercing iliocostalis on its way to the skin), C filum terminale, D cauda equina, E dura mater, pinned open.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Radiculopathy “Radix” = root, “pathos” = suffering or disease. It is compression or malfunction of a nerve root in or around the neural foramen, from any cause . “A problem to the side.” Nucleus pulposus breaks through the anulus posterolaterally and presses on the root as it leaves through the neural foramen. Slide from the deck. Causes Degenerative : by far the most common Disc herniation, spondylosis, ligament hypertrophy. In the lumbar spine, < 1% are anything else . Everything else Neoplasm (primary, metastases, carcinomatous meningitis), infection (abscess, TB), sarcoidosis, trauma, AVM, and diabetic neuropathy affecting the root, which is malfunction without compression OLDCARS Radiculopathy Onset Acute or insidious, depending on the cause Location Arm or leg > neck or back. Patients find the limb more bothersome, the reverse of mechanical pain. The pain and sensory change are in a dermatome . Character Neuropathic : burning, tingling, electric shocks Alleviating Positions that take tension off the nerve : the arm resting overhead, the legs curled up Associated Weakness and hyporeflexia in a myotomal pattern Radiation Along the dermatome Commonest levels Lumbar L5 and S1 . Cervical C7 and C6 , mostly from cervical spondylosis.

entries.t: Which Root Does the Disc Hit?
entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Which Root Does the Disc Hit? Neck: nerves exit above their vertebra (except C8), so the bulge hits the root of the lower vertebra. C4/5 → C5. Slide from the deck. Low back: nerves exit below their vertebra, yet the answer is still the lower number. At L4/5, L4 has already left through its foramen above the disc, so a typical bulge catches L5 traversing down past it. Slide from the deck. The one twist: lumbar far-lateral discs. A paracentral L4/5 disc , by far the commonest, hits the traversing L5 . A far-lateral L4/5 disc hits the exiting L4 . In the neck there is only one root per level, so a C6/7 disc means C7 whether it's foraminal or central. Slide from the deck (Orthobullets). Knowledge check A right paracentral L5/S1 herniation affects S1 . The L5 root has “already left” above the disc. Only a far-lateral L5/S1 disc, which is less common, would catch L5.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Root Levels: Dermatome, Myotome, Reflex Root Dermatome Myotome Reflex C5 Lateral shoulder to lateral elbow Shoulder abduction , elbow flexion Biceps (C5/6), brachioradialis (C5/6) C6 Lateral forearm, digits I and II Elbow flexion, wrist extension Biceps (C5/6), brachioradialis (C5/6) C7 Digit III Elbow extension Triceps (C7) C8 Beyond the deck Little-finger (ulnar) side of the hand and forearm Finger flexion — L3 Beyond the deck Anterior thigh down to the medial knee Knee extension — L4 Medial lower leg, medial malleolus Dorsiflexion Patellar (L4) L5 Dorsum of the foot (1st–3rd web spaces) Great toe extension Hamstrings (L5). Often absent normally, so compare with the other side. S1 Lateral foot, lateral heel Plantar flexion Achilles (S1) The deck's table covers C5–C7 and L4–S1. The objectives ask for C5–C8 and L3–S1 , so C8 and L3 are added . Their dermatomes are read off the clinical dermatome map in 7.1 , and their key muscles (finger flexors for C8, knee extensors for L3) are from the international spinal cord injury exam standard (ISNCSCI worksheet, ASIA/ISCOS). Dermatomes and myotomes overlap by design , so a single-root lesion often gives no clean patch of sensory loss , because the roots above and below still cover it.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Managing Radiculopathy 1 Rule out red flags, and decide on imaging Image if there are red flags, if the neurologic impact is severe or progressing (intractable pain, progressive weakness ), or if the history suggests a non-degenerative cause (e.g. infection → MRI). A mild radiculopathy improving with physio may need no imaging at all . Consider an EMG to test root function if symptoms are ongoing or severe. 2 Conservative care, which is “shockingly” like the mechanical plan Educate and reassure : even severe radicular pain usually resolves on its own over months . Use relative rest, ice or heat, topicals, oral anti-inflammatories if needed, and a short course of opioids if the pain is severe . Physio for postural support speeds recovery and prevents recurrence. 3 Still not better: escalate Image-guided epidural steroid injection , or surgical decompression for refractory symptoms after an adequate conservative trial, a progressive or severe deficit, or certain red-flag conditions (tumour, large abscess, trauma). CAR guideline C04: neck pain, brachialgia, degenerative change. These apply once you've looked for red flags and found none. MRI only with neurologic signs or symptoms , or pain persisting more than 4 weeks despite conservative care. CT only if MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. X-ray is not indicated : degenerative change appears from early middle age and usually has nothing to do with the symptoms. Slide from the deck (car.ca).

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Why the Level Changes Everything A broad-based central bulge. Herniations usually go to the side, but not always: central ones press straight back into the canal. Slide from the deck. Lumbar central stenosis Cervical central stenosis What's compressed Roots (the cord ends around L1) The cord , which there is no way to avoid up here Name Lumbar stenosis, with cauda equina syndrome at the severe end Cervical myelopathy Picture Bilateral leg symptoms, worse with walking (neurogenic claudication) Like an atraumatic spinal cord injury Imaging Mild–moderate: none, or a non-urgent MRI. Cauda equina: urgent MRI . MRI Treatment Flexion-based activity and physio. Cauda equina: emergency decompression . Urgent neurosurgery or spine consult for decompression

entries.t: Lumbar Central Stenosis and Cauda Equina
entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Lumbar Central Stenosis and Cauda Equina OLDCARS Lumbar central stenosis Onset Typically insidious Location Legs > back (though patients often describe both), usually bilateral Character Burning, tingling, electric Aggravating Walking a predictable distance Radiation Non-specific, often distal > proximal , because the blood supply to the nerves is compressed Bowel and bladder Normal in simple stenosis Neurogenic vs Vascular Claudication Both cause leg pain after walking a certain distance. Neurogenic claudication is relieved by forward flexion , which takes pressure off the front of the canal. Patients say it's better leaning on a grocery cart or walking uphill . Sitting helps too, but slowly . With vascular claudication , relief comes quickly, within minutes of stopping. Cauda equina syndrome is the same process as stenosis, further along the severity spectrum, with the lower roots badly compromised. Slide from the deck. Red flags: ask every back pain patient Weakness , especially severe or progressive Saddle anaesthesia : numbness in the groin and perineum Bladder changes : urinary retention is the most common Bowel changes : fecal incontinence Erectile dysfunction Cauda equina is a neurosurgical emergency. Send the patient to the ED for an urgent MRI . Outcomes are significantly better if decompression is done within 48 hours of symptom onset.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Cervical Myelopathy Feature Why Loss of hand dexterity , wasting of the hand intrinsics Cord compression at the cervical enlargement Upper limb paresthesias , distal > proximal — Urinary incontinence Often retention with overflow Gait change , ataxia, balance problems Long tracts to the legs Radiculopathy at the level plus UMN signs below it It is hard to squeeze the cord centrally without also catching a root on its way out Knowledge check A 73-year-old with chronic neck and back pain has, over 3 months, pain radiating into the thumb and index finger . She's been dropping things and breaking dishes, and has new urinary incontinence , with a UTI ruled out. → MRI of the cervical spine. Neck pain, arm radiation, loss of dexterity and incontinence together suggest cervical myelopathy . Acetaminophen, a repeat urinalysis, or plain films would each miss it.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Inflammatory Spine Pain Feature Mechanical Inflammatory Movement Worse with movement Better with movement and exercise Rest and night Better with rest Worse with rest. Night pain in the second half of the night. Morning stiffness — Significant Where Midline or paramidline Often the SI joints Review of systems — Eye symptoms (redness, pain), rashes, family history, enthesopathy (tendinopathy right at the tendon's insertion), other inflammatory joint pain Think of Disc, facet, muscle The seronegative spondyloarthropathies : ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, IBD-associated arthritis, reactive arthritis. More in rheumatology. Knowledge check Which is not a feature of inflammatory back pain? → “Worsens with movement” , which is mechanical. Morning stiffness, improvement with exercise, SI joint pain and overnight pain are all inflammatory.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Fractures, and the Three “Spondy” Words Osteoporotic compression fracture (arrow on the wedged body). It happens in older adults and patients on chronic steroids , after minor or no trauma . Axial pain may radiate, but not into the limbs unless there's neurologic compromise. Treat the pain and treat the osteoporosis. Slide from the deck. Spondylolysis : a fracture of the pars interarticularis , where the lamina meets the pedicle. It happens in young athletes who repeatedly extend the back (gymnasts, football players, weightlifters) and can lead to spondylolisthesis. Slide from the deck. Word Means Typical patient Spondyl osis “A state of disease”: degeneration , i.e. degenerative disc disease plus facet arthropathy An aging spine ( 7.2 ) Spondyl olysis A fracture of the pars interarticularis A young athlete who does a lot of back extension Spondyl olisthesis “Listhesis” = slipping : one vertebra slides on the next, usually forward Degenerative (older, from facet laxity) or after a pars fracture (spondylolysis)

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Visceral Pain, Infection and Tumour Group Causes Clues Cardiovascular AAA ; vertebral insufficiency; atypical cardiac pain A pulsatile mass; dizziness and cranial nerve signs GI Peptic ulcer disease, pancreatitis, others — GU and gynecologic Pyelonephritis, nephrolithiasis, endometriosis — Infection Osteomyelitis, discitis, epidural abscess Fevers, sweats, IV drug use , immunosuppression Neoplasm Bone tumour; epidural or intradural mass; drop metastases ; referred pain (e.g. renal carcinoma ) Young age , severe night pain, weight loss, night sweats, cancer history, associated signs (e.g. hematuria ) These are only found if you ask about red flags in every patient with back pain .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
entries.x: Putting It Together Red flag found First investigation Possible fracture Plain films , then CT if you're still worried and the x-ray is normal Significant neurologic compromise, infection, neoplasm MRI (an x-ray may come first) None Mechanical or nonspecific pain and non-emergent neurologic pain (radiculopathy, lumbar stenosis) all start with the same conservative plan Triage for the adult with low back pain. First exclude non-spinal causes : hip, visceral, vascular (AAA, claudication), systemic (endocarditis), viral. Then sort: serious spinal disease < 1% , radicular pain or neurogenic claudication 5–10% , non-specific LBP 90–95% . Everyone not in the serious group gets advice and reassurance , with no immediate imaging. Acute non-specific pain: stay active, no bed rest , PT, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants or weak opioids. Persistent pain: exercise, psychological and multidisciplinary therapy, cautious NSAIDs. Radicular pain: exercise, PT, neuropathic agents, opioids only for rescue. Slide from the deck (adapted from Traeger et al., CMAJ 2017; the Centre for Effective Practice back tool).

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Osteology & Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Learning Objectives Identify the functional anatomy of the upper extremity as it relates to arm pathology: the features of its bones and joints, and how they look on plain radiographs. Create a differential and management plan for upper extremity complaints: numbness, weakness, pain and loss of range of motion. Describe the anatomical basis of common shoulder pathology: AC separation, rotator cuff disease, biceps tendinopathy, arthritis, instability and adhesive capsulitis . Outline an approach to diagnosis and management, including non-pharmacologic, pharmacologic and surgical options, for these conditions. Dr. Charys Martin (anatomy) and Dr. Ken Faber (orthopaedic surgery, Roth McFarlane Hand & Upper Limb Centre). Eleven recordings, about 75 minutes. Rotator cuff disease and biceps tendinopathy are listed in the objectives but not covered here. The module says these objectives are spread across other modules, labs and Clinical Skills, and it tells you to do “Brachial Plexus” and “Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder” before the Proximal Upper Extremity Part I lab.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Osteology & Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: The Pectoral Girdle The clavicle and scapula attach the upper limb to the axial skeleton, through a series of four joints , not one. Joint Between Key point Sternoclavicular (SC) Medial clavicle and the manubrium The only articulation joining the upper limb to the axial skeleton. It is very strong, so the clavicle fractures before the SC joint dislocates . Acromioclavicular (AC) Lateral clavicle and the acromion A plane synovial joint, with a weak capsule and strong ligaments Glenohumeral (GH) Glenoid fossa and the humeral head The “true” shoulder joint: ball-and-socket Scapulothoracic The deep scapula on the chest wall A conceptual joint: the scapula gliding over the ribs The girdle and its four joints , circled on the skeleton and the radiograph. Slide from the deck. Scapulohumeral Rhythm The shoulder has the widest range of motion of any joint : flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction, and medial and lateral rotation. Raising the arm overhead takes movement at all the girdle joints. About two-thirds happens at the glenohumeral joint and one-third at the scapulothoracic (2:1), with some at the SC joint too. The scapula has to move the glenoid into position, and the muscles need a stable origin to work from. Note: the module's knowledge-check feedback says the pectoral girdle is “the clavicle and humerus”. It is the clavicle and scapula , as the next line of the same feedback and the mini-text both say.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Osteology & Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Clavicle, Scapula, Humerus Bone and feature What to know Clavicle Shape An S-bend: the medial half is convex forward and the lateral half concave forward Ends Sternal end enlarged and triangular (“like a trumpet”); acromial end flattened where it meets the acromion Scapula: a triangular flat bone on the posterolateral thorax Acromion Meets the clavicle at the AC joint Coracoid process “Duck's beak”: a large anterior projection for attachments Glenoid fossa A shallow, concave oval socket for the humeral head. The supraglenoid tubercle above it is the origin of the long head of biceps ; the infraglenoid tubercle below is the origin of the long head of triceps . Spine Divides the back of the scapula into the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae , which hold those muscles. The front is the subscapular fossa . Angles, notch Superior and inferior angles (where the border changes direction). The suprascapular notch becomes a foramen under the transverse scapular ligament, a passage for neurovascular structures. Humerus Head ; greater (lateral) and lesser (anterior) tubercles The tubercles are soft-tissue attachments, with the intertubercular (bicipital) groove between them for the tendon of the long head of biceps Anatomical neck vs surgical neck The anatomical neck separates the head from the tubercles. The surgical neck is the narrowing below the tubercles and is the common fracture site . Radial (spiral) groove On the back of the shaft, carrying the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery Distal humerus Trochlea (medial, with the ulna) and capitulum (lateral, with the radial head). The medial epicondyle is the big palpable bump and the origin of the forearm flexors; the ulnar nerve runs behind it. The smaller lateral epicondyle is the origin of the extensors. The coronoid fossa takes the coronoid process in full flexion; the olecranon fossa takes the olecranon in extension. Proximal forearm Ulna medial, radius lateral. The radial tuberosity is the insertion of biceps. The olecranon (triceps) is the point of the elbow; the coronoid (brachialis) is in front. The scapula from the front (subscapular fossa, coracoid) and back (the spine splitting the supra- and infraspinous fossae). Slide from the deck (Netter). Proximal humerus , on bone and on x-ray: head, tubercles, bicipital groove, and the radial groove behind. Slide from the deck (Netter). The distal humerus and proximal forearm , needed because several arm muscles cross the elbow too. Slide from the deck (N

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Osteology & Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: The Acromioclavicular Joint Feature Detail Type Plane synovial , uniaxial: two flat surfaces, with a wedge-shaped articular disc in the joint space. Little bony stability , so it depends on the capsule, ligaments and muscles. Capsule Weak Acromioclavicular ligament A thickening of the capsule, strongest superiorly Coracoclavicular ligament Coracoid to clavicle, in two parts, conoid and trapezoid . It gives the joint most of its strength and lets the scapula and arm hang from the strut-like clavicle. Movement The acromion glides and rotates on the clavicle, letting the scapula move on the thorax for scapulohumeral rhythm Two ligament systems hold the AC joint: the AC ligament (capsule, blue) and the coracoclavicular ligament (pink). Slide from the deck (Netter). Where is the AC ligament? B. A sternoclavicular joint, B AC joint (the ligament is its capsule), C coracoclavicular ligament, D coracohumeral ligament, E coracoacromial ligament. Slide from the deck.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Osteology & Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: The Glenohumeral Joint A true ball-and-socket synovial joint that sacrifices stability for mobility . Remember the three stability factors from 7.1 : here the bones contribute little (a ball on a plate) and the capsule is deliberately lax, so the shoulder relies on the soft tissues, above all the rotator cuff . Structure Role Capsule Strong but lax . The axillary recess hangs down into the axilla to allow overhead reach. Glenohumeral ligaments (superior, middle, inferior) Thickenings of the anterior capsule, from the glenoid rim to the lesser tubercle. You can't separate them in the lab, but the front of the capsule is thicker than the back. Coracohumeral ligament Base of the coracoid to the greater tubercle: strengthens the capsule superiorly Coracoacromial ligament Coracoid to acromion, forming the coracoacromial arch , a roof that prevents upward displacement of the head. The arch is so strong that a huge upward force fractures the humerus or clavicle first. (It doesn't stabilize the AC joint.) Transverse humeral ligament Bridges the bicipital groove over the biceps tendon Labrum A fibrocartilage rim around the glenoid that deepens the socket a little , from a plate to “a pasta dish” Articular cartilage Covers far more of the humeral head than of the glenoid, because the head rotates Bursae Subacromial (often continuous with the subdeltoid), between the acromion, cuff tendons and deltoid. It reduces friction in a tight space that gets tighter overhead. Also the subscapular bursa, deep to subscapularis. Long head of biceps Runs inside the joint from the supraglenoid tubercle down the bicipital groove From the front: the capsule with its superior, middle and inferior glenohumeral ligaments (S, M, I), under the coracoacromial ligament roof. Slide from the deck (Netter). Coronal section and the view into the glenoid: the labrum, cartilage, synovium, subacromial bursa, and the rotator cuff tendons wrapped all round . They are the joint's real stabilizers. Slide from the deck (Netter). Clinical Notes from the Mini-Text Dislocation is usually anteroinferior. The coracoacromial arch blocks the top and the capsule is weakest anteroinferiorly. The axillary nerve is at risk. Impingement: the supraspinatus tendon gets pinched in the subacromial space, causing tendonitis. Chronic overuse can stretch the static stabilizers, causing mild instability and more load on the cuff. The cuff weakens, the head rides up, and secondary impingement follows.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Osteology & Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: AC Osteoarthritis vs AC Separation Only two common things happen here, and the history usually sorts them. AC osteoarthritis AC instability (“separation”) Onset Gradual , from wear and tear Acute injury : a fall onto the point of the shoulder (over the handlebars, into the boards). The acromion is driven down and the clavicle up. Symptoms Localized pain at the tip of the shoulder , activity-related, worst reaching across the chest Pain over the AC joint after the injury Exam A small bump, tenderness over the joint . Motion is usually normal (most motion is glenohumeral and scapulothoracic), but there may be pain-related weakness. A prominence where the clavicle sits high relative to the acromion X-ray Asymmetric joint-space loss progressing to obliteration, osteophytes , subchondral cysts , sclerosis The clavicle displaced from the acromion. More displacement means a higher type. Treatment Education; activity modification ; ice and heat; a steroid plus local anaesthetic injection ; NSAIDs. Last resort: resect the distal clavicle , opening a gap that fills with scar as a new cushion, which is predictably effective. Types I–III: education, sling, analgesics, ice, early range of motion . Types IV–V: surgery . The classification is just a ladder of displacement. A blow to the acromion drives it down, and the force tears the ligaments in sequence, first the AC ligaments and then the coracoclavicular . The more ligament torn, the higher the type (I–V) and the further the clavicle rides up. Most are types I–III. Slide from the deck. A widely displaced separation , the kind Dr. Faber calls an “ear tickler” because the clavicle sticks up so high. This is the IV–V end, treated with surgery. Slide from the deck. The fix: a small screw in the coracoid , with threads passed up through the clavicle and tied over a plate. In effect it rebuilds the coracoclavicular ligament. Slide from the deck. Knowledge check A 24-year-old was checked into the boards and has pain right over the AC joint. Her x-ray shows an essentially congruent AC joint, perhaps with mild upward migration. → Conservative: sling, ice, analgesia, early exercises. You won't be asked to type separations on x-ray, but you should know the features that point to surgery: marked displacement or compromise. Dr. Faber's own example is a 47-year-old competitive rower treated with education, a sling and early motion. Six months later he was rowing at a high level, still with a visible bump.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Osteology & Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Shoulder Arthritis A progressive disorder of pain, reduced motion and loss of function . It comes in two patterns, and the range of motion tells them apart . Non-inflammatory: OA, post-traumatic Inflammatory: RA, psoriatic, crystal (e.g. pseudogout) Pain Deep, aching Deep, aching Motion Active AND passive reduced : osteophytes physically block it, so it won't go even when you push Active reduced, passive often better : no marginal osteophytes, so the patient can reach higher helping with the good arm Rotator cuff Usually intact Usually poor : the disease damages the cuff as well as the cartilage X-ray Asymmetric joint-space narrowing (best seen on the axillary view), osteophytes , cysts, subchondral sclerosis Symmetric (concentric) narrowing, bone deformity , periarticular erosions , osteopenia Replacement Anatomic total shoulder Reverse total shoulder OA. On the axillary view, the back of the joint is worn to nothing while the front still has cartilage ( asymmetric wear). There is a big inferior osteophyte , cysts, and dense subchondral sclerosis where the load lands. Slide from the deck. Inflammatory. The joint space is narrowed evenly all the way round. The bone is deformed and eroded (the glenoid rubbing on the humeral neck) and washed out , with thin cortices. Slide from the deck. Treatment Details Non-operative, first for everyone Education and natural history; activity modification; medications (the new inflammatory-arthritis drugs have “revolutionized” treatment; ibuprofen and acetaminophen for OA); physio for strength and mobility Debridement For young patients. Not curative : it clears out mechanical “catching”. Anatomic total shoulder (OA) The humeral head is cut and replaced with an uncemented, textured stem that bone grows onto, plus a metal head, and a cemented plastic glenoid Reverse total shoulder (inflammatory) The ball goes on the glenoid and the cup on the humerus . It's used when the cuff is poor and the joint is structurally deformed, and it's cemented because the bone quality won't grip an implant. Outcomes 85% good to excellent; 90% still working at 10 years. Failures come from complications: infection, loosening (“like tires, it wears out”), instability, periprosthetic fracture at the stem tip, and progressive cuff disease. Anatomic replacement for OA. The plastic glenoid isn't visible on x-ray except for a small metal marker in one peg. Slide from the deck. Reverse replacement for inflammatory arthritis : a ball on the glenoid and

entries.p: Clinical Approach to Osteology & Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Shoulder Instability The inability to keep the humeral head centred on the glenoid. It runs on a continuum from reduced to subluxated (off-centre but still touching) to dislocated (no normal contact). Reduced, subluxated, dislocated. Slide from the deck. Stability factor In the shoulder Ligaments (most important) Can be torn (traumatic) or stretched or lax (multidirectional instability, possibly a connective tissue disorder or poor motor control) Labrum (most important) Increases surface area and depth, and acts as a bumper Bones Relatively flat against each other, like a golf ball on a tee, so the head can slide. Compare the elbow, whose bone shape prevents side-to-side sliding. Rotator cuff and muscle forces Stabilize, but misfiring muscles can cause instability Nerves Proprioceptive fibres in the capsule. Unstable shoulders usually have poor proprioception. Ligaments torn, or ligaments stretched : the two routes to instability. Slide from the deck (TeachMeAnatomy). The labrum is a bumper. In a dislocation, the head can tear it off the glenoid rim. Slide from the deck. Bone anatomy: a golf ball on a tee. There is very little bony constraint. Slide from the deck. Three questions to name the problem: what was the onset (traumatic or atraumatic)? Which direction (anterior, posterior, inferior, a combination)? What degree (subluxation or dislocation)? Traumatic Atraumatic (AMBRI) Onset An injury that forced the head out A traumatic: it can just “pop out” in the wrong position Direction Unidirectional , almost always anterior (anterior >> posterior) M ultidirectional, often B ilateral Problem “Torn loose” : the labrum and capsule are torn “Born loose” : lax tissue, poor motor control Treatment Surgery often , especially in the young and in recurrent dislocators: arthroscopic capsule-labral repair (85% success). At arthroscopy the torn labrum sits off the front of the glenoid, and there is often a dent in the back of the humeral head (a Hill–Sachs lesion ). The labrum is freshened so it bleeds and heals, then reattached with suture anchors. R ehab: physio for motor control and proprioception , for at least a year. Only then an I nferior capsular shift, open or arthroscopic (70% success open). Surgery is uncommon. Age Decides What a Traumatic Dislocation Means In the teens and twenties , recurrence after a first dislocation is very likely , so the threshold to repair is lower. In the 50s and beyond , recurrent instability is less likely, and what follows a disl

entries.x: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder) Feature Fact Who 2% of adults , but up to 20% of people with diabetes , often in both shoulders one after the other. Onset in the 40s–50s . Cause Pathophysiology unknown; most often idiopathic . Associated with diabetes (strongly), cervical disc disease, thyroid disease and cardiac disease, and with trigger finger and Dupuytren's contracture. Definition (ASES) “A condition of uncertain etiology characterized by a restriction of active and passive motion that occurs in the absence of a known intrinsic shoulder disorder” Exam Global restriction: elevation, external and internal rotation, abduction. Active = passive , both markedly reduced. X-ray Normal : no arthritis, no post-traumatic deformity, no heterotopic bone Pathology The capsule thickens from about 1–1.5 mm to almost 1 cm , leathery and contracted Sorting Out a Stiff Shoulder Think intra-articular (arthritis or post-traumatic deformity, a mechanical block), extra-articular ( capsular , i.e. adhesive capsulitis; muscular spasticity, e.g. after a stroke; heterotopic bone , bone forming where it shouldn't, such as in muscle), or combined . The x-ray separates them. If the x-ray is normal and there's no trauma, a stiff shoulder with equal loss of active and passive motion is the capsule. Stage (Uhthoff) What's happening 1. Freezing Inflammatory : a red, angry synovium. This is the painful phase. 2. Frozen The synovium becomes thick, leathery capsule. Very stiff. 3. Thawing The capsule regains some elastic recoil and motion returns Through the arthroscope: the red, inflamed synovium of the freezing stage, and the pale, leathery capsule of the frozen stage. Slide from the deck. Treatment What the evidence says Education (the most important) Patients are very distressed: it hurts, then it's disabling (they can't wash their hair). Knowing it's self-limited puts them at ease. Pain control Acetaminophen plus ibuprofen, especially early Physiotherapy Controversial. No quality studies show a significant effect. Early on it may be “gas on the fire”; it has more of a role later. Physiotherapists are great at the education. Intra-articular steroid Given in the inflammatory stage, it probably shortens the course and is superior to PT early, but there's no difference at 1 year Hydrodistension (“brisement”, from the French briser , to break) Saline injected under pressure to burst the capsule Surgery : arthroscopic capsulectomy ± manipulation under anaesthesia Faster return of mo

Learning Objectives Identify the important functional anatomy of the upper extremity, as it pertains to clinical presentations of arm pathology. Identify the components of the brachial plexus and its anatomic relationships to surrounding structures. Determine the sensory and motor loss anticipated with injuries to specific sites of the plexus (the roots and the terminal branches ). Dr. Charys Martin's 50-minute module: one recording plus a knowledge check. It builds on the neck and back modules. Dr. Martin's advice: work through it, then practise drawing the plexus a few times before the lab (Tuesday's Clinical Anatomy of the Proximal Upper Extremity Part I). Lesion localization is applied in the modules that follow.

What the Plexus Is Brachial = arm, plexus = braid. The ventral rami of the cervical enlargement (C5–T1) merge and re-split, so most upper-limb muscles end up supplied by more than one root . Everything above the cords sits in the neck; the cords and terminal branches are what you see in the axilla. From the neck to the axilla. Slide from the deck (Netter plate). The five sections, medial (right) to lateral (left) on this right-side plexus. “Really Thirsty? Drink Cold Beer.” Slide from the deck. The Colour Code On every diagram C5 and C6 are red (they almost always travel and innervate together), C7 is blue (it does its own thing), and C8 and T1 are green (they usually travel together). Follow the colours down and you can read each nerve's root contributions off the picture.

Roots, Trunks and Divisions Level Made of Branches you need Roots (5) Ventral rami C5, C6, C7, C8, T1. Mixed: motor + sensory Dorsal scapular (C5): pierces middle scalene → rhomboids (and levator scapulae) Long thoracic (C5, 6, 7): runs down the lateral thoracic wall on the superficial surface of serratus anterior Trunks (3) Superior = C5 + C6 Middle = C7 alone Inferior = C8 + T1 Suprascapular (C5, 6), off the superior trunk → supraspinatus and infraspinatus Divisions (6) Each trunk splits into an anterior and a posterior division None. Anterior divisions → nerves of the flexor (anterior) compartments; posterior divisions → nerves of the extensor (posterior) compartments Root branches: dorsal scapular (C5) and long thoracic (C5, 6, 7). Slide from the deck. Trunk branch: the suprascapular nerve (C5, 6) leaves the superior trunk. Slide from the deck. Divisions: three anterior, three posterior, and no branches. Slide from the deck. Don't let the nerve to subclavius (C5, 6) confuse you on diagrams. Dr. Martin points it out only so you don't think you've missed something: the muscle and the nerve aren't taught.

Cords and Their Branches The cords are named for their relationship to the axillary artery : the lateral cord lies lateral to it, the medial cord medial, and the posterior cord behind it. Cord Formed by Branches (roots) → supply Lateral Anterior divisions of the superior + middle trunks Lateral pectoral (C5, 6, 7) → pectoralis major and minor (runs superomedial to pec minor) Then the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve Medial Anterior division of the inferior trunk (it just changes name) Medial pectoral (C8, T1) → pierces pec minor, then pectoralis major Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm → skin of the medial arm Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm (C8, T1) → skin of the medial forearm Then the medial root of the median nerve and the ulnar nerve Posterior All three posterior divisions Upper subscapular (C5, 6) → subscapularis Thoracodorsal (C6, 7, 8; aka middle subscapular) → latissimus dorsi Lower subscapular (C5, 6) → subscapularis and teres major Then the axillary and radial nerves The cord branches with their roots. Note that the branches of the posterior cord don't all carry all five roots: the subscapulars are C5–6 and the thoracodorsal C6–8. Slide from the deck. The Pectoral Nerve Trap In the cadaver the medial pectoral nerve often lies lateral to the lateral pectoral nerve . They aren't named for where you find them; they're named for the cord they come off .

Terminal Branches: Find the “M” The lateral and medial cords join in an M : musculocutaneous is the lateral leg, the two roots of the median nerve are the middle, and the ulnar nerve is the medial leg. The posterior cord gives off the axillary nerve, then continues as the radial . Nerve (roots) From Motor Sensory Course in the arm Musculocutaneous (C5, 6, 7) Lateral cord All the anterior arm muscles Ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm Pierces coracobrachialis , then runs between brachialis and biceps Median (C5–T1) Lateral + medial roots Most forearm flexors and five hand muscles Part of the hand Lateral to the brachial artery, crosses medial to it mid-arm; in the cubital fossa, deep to the bicipital aponeurosis and the median cubital vein Ulnar (C8, T1) Medial cord 1½ anterior forearm muscles and most hand muscles Medial side of the hand Medial in the anterior compartment, then pierces the medial intermuscular septum at mid-arm into the posterior compartment Axillary (C5, 6) Posterior cord Deltoid and teres minor Skin of the shoulder — Radial (C5–T1) Posterior cord (its continuation) Triceps and the extensors of the posterior arm and forearm Posterior upper limb Behind the brachial artery, then with the profunda brachii in the radial groove ; pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to run between brachialis and brachioradialis The M. Find the axillary artery first: the lateral and medial cords flank it and point you straight to the M. Slide from the deck. Root contributions on your fingers (thumb = C5): 3 M usketeers (musculocutaneous C5–7), A ssassinate (axillary, C5–6: the “gun”), 5 M ice (median), 5 R ats (radial), 2 U nicorns (ulnar, C8–T1). Slide from the deck. Knowledge check (cadaver photo described, not shown) A dissection with the clavicle removed, labelled A–H. Start with the axillary artery (it becomes the subclavian at the first rib, and the subclavian passes deep to anterior scalene). The ventral rami emerge between anterior and middle scalene . Answers: A C7 root · B superior trunk · C axillary artery · D lateral cord · E posterior cord · F musculocutaneous (it dives straight into coracobrachialis, an easy landmark) · G median · H ulnar.

Draw It You need to be able to draw the plexus from memory, then move past drawing to lesions : if this nerve or this root were cut, what would the patient lose, and how would they present? 1 “3 Wise (Y) Men (M)” Draw three Ys, head to toe: two open at the roots end, one at the branches end. Add the M for the terminal branches. 2 “…go bowling. One got a strike (X); the other got a spare (\)” The X and the \ are the crossing divisions. 3 Label it Roots C5–T1 top to bottom; superior, middle, inferior trunks; every trunk sends a posterior division to the posterior cord; lateral, posterior and medial cords; then axillary and radial (posterior cord) and musculocutaneous, median and ulnar (the M). The finished drawing. Slide from the deck.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm
entries.x: Learning Objectives Identify the important functional anatomy of the upper extremity, as it pertains to clinical presentations of arm pathology. Identify the major muscles of the upper extremity (shoulder girdle, brachium, the forearm muscles from the medial and lateral epicondyles, the hand). Create a differential diagnosis and management plan for upper extremity complaints: numbness, weakness, pain and loss of range of motion. Describe the anatomic basis of common shoulder pathology: AC separation, rotator cuff disease, biceps tendinopathy , arthritis, instability and adhesive capsulitis. Dr. Charys Martin (anatomy) and Dr. Caitlin Cassidy (proximal biceps tendinopathy), 33 minutes. The objectives are shared with the other upper-limb modules, the labs and Clinical Skills. This module and Neurovascular Supply are the prep for the Proximal Upper Extremity Part II lab . It builds on Muscles of the Shoulder , Brachial Plexus and the joints of the proximal upper extremity .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm
entries.x: Arm Organization: Two Compartments The arm runs from the shoulder to the elbow. Under the skin and subcutaneous tissue is its deep fascia, the brachial fascia . Two septa run from the fascia to the humerus and split the arm into two compartments. Each compartment has one job and one nerve, so learn the compartment and you know every muscle in it. Compartment Muscles Function Nerve Anterior Biceps brachii, coracobrachialis, brachialis Flex the shoulder and elbow; supinate the forearm Musculocutaneous (terminal branch of the lateral cord) Posterior Triceps brachii (three heads) Extend the shoulder and elbow Radial (supplies the whole posterior upper limb) The septa run from the brachial fascia to the humerus (H). Slide from the deck (Netter plate).

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm
entries.x: The Anterior Compartment Muscle Origin Insertion Crosses Action Biceps brachii Long head: supraglenoid tubercle Short head: coracoid process Radial tuberosity + forearm fascia via the bicipital aponeurosis Shoulder + elbow Strong supinator ; flexes the forearm (mainly when supinated); weak shoulder flexor; resists dislocation Coracobrachialis Coracoid process Middle ⅓ of the medial humerus Shoulder only Flexes and adducts the arm; resists dislocation Brachialis Distal ½ of the anterior humerus Coronoid process of the ulna Elbow only Primary flexor of the forearm Biceps brachii. Slide from the deck. Coracobrachialis (biceps removed). Slide from the deck. Brachialis. Slide from the deck. Biceps Gets the Credit, Brachialis Does the Work Put two fingers on your biceps tendon and turn the forearm palm-up, palm-down: the tendon tightens with every supination , with no elbow movement at all. Biceps only helps flex the elbow when the forearm is supinated (a classic curl). In a hammer curl or a reverse curl the work is brachialis. Brachialis flexes in any position, and as it bulks up it pushes the biceps forward, so the biceps looks bigger and gets the credit. A crossed joint is an acted-on joint. Biceps crosses the shoulder, so it's a weak shoulder flexor and helps hold the head in the glenoid. Brachialis crosses only the elbow; coracobrachialis only the shoulder. The long head is the longer head , even if it looks shorter in the picture: it runs through the intertubercular groove and over the top of the humeral head to reach the supraglenoid tubercle. The musculocutaneous nerve leaves the lateral cord and immediately pierces coracobrachialis , supplies it, then carries on to the rest of the compartment. Dr. Martin's advice on attachments: you don't need them in fine detail, but know roughly where each muscle starts and ends; that gives you its action and lets you find it in the lab. Note the attachment points that keep coming up, such as the coracoid (pec minor, the short head of biceps and coracobrachialis all attach there).

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm
entries.x: The Posterior Compartment: Triceps Head Origin Crosses the shoulder? Long (medial side, superficial) Infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula Yes : extends the shoulder and resists dislocation Lateral Proximal ⅓ of the posterior humerus No Medial (deep to the lateral head) Distal ⅓ of the posterior humerus No All three join one common tendon on the olecranon process of the ulna, the bony point of the elbow. Together they are the primary elbow extensor , supplied by the radial nerve . Posterior compartment. Slide from the deck. Triceps brachii , lateral head reflected to show the medial head. Slide from the deck. Two Long Heads, Two Tubercles The long head of biceps starts above the glenoid (supraglenoid tubercle); the long head of triceps starts below it (infraglenoid tubercle). Both cross the shoulder, so both act on it and both help keep the humeral head in the glenoid fossa. Knowledge checks Nerve to each compartment (on the brachial plexus diagram): the anterior compartment is the musculocutaneous nerve (D on the diagram) and the posterior compartment is the radial nerve (H). The cadaver exercise (subscapularis A, brachialis B, biceps brachii C, deltoid D) is a photograph, so it's left out.

entries.t: What It Is and Why It Happens
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm
entries.x: What It Is and Why It Happens A common cause of shoulder pain , nearly always in the long head . The word “tendinopathy” is deliberate. “Tendinitis” means inflammation only, but most proximal biceps problems are chronic overuse and degeneration (tendinosis) . Tendinopathy covers the whole spectrum: tendinosis, acute inflammation, and partial or complete tears. Who Why Younger Athletes, especially overhead throwing ; inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis Older (much more common) Overuse and degeneration over time, often alongside rotator cuff disease “Location, location, location”: the anatomy explains the disease. Slide from the deck. Anatomy of the long head So… Lies right beside the rotator cuff insertions Cuff breakdown drags it into the same process Runs through the tight intertubercular groove Friction and irritation Passes under the acromion to the supraglenoid tubercle Impingement, as with the cuff Also arises from the superior glenoid labrum Labral problems = biceps problems The proximal tendon is relatively hypovascular Degenerates and heals poorly

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm
entries.x: Presentation and Diagnosis Finding History Acute (tear or inflammation) or, more often, chronic (degeneration, overuse) onset. Deep anterior shoulder pain : achy, or sharp after a flare. Palpation Tender over the tendon in the intertubercular groove , the most useful exam step. Can't find it? Rotate the arm in and out, and the rope-like tendon rolls under your thumb. Provocation Worse with shoulder flexion and elbow flexion , particularly with the forearm supinated ( Speed's and Yergason's tests, taught in Clinical Skills) Frank tear Weakness (supination especially; other muscles cover flexion, so motion is rarely lost outright). The muscle retracts down the arm , leaving a bunched-up distal bulge: the Popeye deformity . The examination slide is photographs of a model and an examiner, so it's described rather than shown. Differential: other causes of anterior shoulder pain Diagnosis Why it's on the list Rotator cuff tendinopathy Often coexists and can be hard to separate Subacromial bursitis Same neighbourhood Labral tear (SLAP lesion) The long head arises from the superior labrum, so the pain is similar Glenohumeral or AC joint arthritis Can present this way Cervical radiculopathy An upper root (C4 or C5) can put the pain at the shoulder; look for neuropathic pain, numbness or tingling, and weakness Referred pain Facetogenic (cervical facet joints refer to the top of the shoulder) or visceral : don't forget organs can present as shoulder pain Investigations Test Use Clinical exam Often the most helpful step, and the mainstay of decisions X-ray Doesn't show tendon tears or tendinopathy; consider it if you suspect impingement or arthritis Ultrasound If the diagnosis is unclear: sees the biceps, the cuff tendons and the subacromial bursa at the same time MR arthrogram (dye injected into the joint) If you suspect a SLAP lesion Knowledge check A patient has anterior shoulder pain. Which is low on the differential: AC separation, glenohumeral arthritis, rotator cuff pathology, proximal biceps tendinopathy or C8 radiculopathy ? → C8 radiculopathy . All the others can cause anterior shoulder pain. A high cervical root (C4 or C5) can give shoulder symptoms, but C8 pain and paraesthesiae go to the hand .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm
entries.x: Management 1 Education Prognosis depends on the injury. An athlete with an acute rupture is a different conversation. Most cases are chronic degeneration in older patients, and they improve with conservative care . 2 Physiotherapy: the mainstay Modalities (ultrasound, heat, cold) can help acute pain, but active therapy that strengthens the muscle and its supporting muscles is what resolves it. Add relative rest from overhead activity . 3 Analgesia as needed Acetaminophen, or topical or oral NSAIDs. Steroid injection is possible, ideally with a specialist. 4 Surgery for refractory cases A degenerate or chronically torn tendon usually can't be stitched back together. Instead the tendon is released proximally and reattached lower down (a tenodesis), keeping its length and tension without the painful pull.
