entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Forearm Organization The forearm runs from the elbow to the wrist. Its deep fascia, the antebrachial fascia (antebrachium = forearm), continues from the brachial fascia and attaches to the ulna, which you can feel all the way down the medial forearm. The radius , the ulna , the interosseous membrane and one anterior intermuscular septum (radius to fascia) make two compartments. In cross-section they look more medial and lateral than anterior and posterior. They're named for where their tendons end up: the front or the back of the wrist and hand. Compartment Common origin Function Nerve Anterior (3 layers: 4 + 1 + 3) Medial epicondyle (except the deep layer) Flex the wrist and fingers; pronate the forearm Median , except 1½ muscles (ulnar) Posterior (2 layers: 6 + 5) Lateral epicondyle (except the deep layer) Extend the wrist and fingers; supinate the forearm Radial (and its branches), no exceptions Two compartments in cross-section. Slide from the deck (Netter). Palmar carpal ligament vs the deeper flexor retinaculum . Slide from the deck (Netter). Why the Muscle Is in the Forearm Most forearm muscles work the hand. If all that bulk sat in the hand, the hand would be too fat to be dexterous. So the bellies stay in the forearm and send long tendons across the wrist. Those tendons need holding down or they'd bowstring when they contract. The palmar carpal ligament (a thickening of the antebrachial fascia) does it at the front and continues round as the extensor retinaculum at the back. The flexor retinaculum is a different structure, deeper and more distal , and is often confused with the palmar carpal ligament.

entries.x: The Thumb, the Snuffbox and Wrist Movements The three “outcropping” muscles (APL, EPL, EPB) emerge from under the superficial extensors to reach the thumb. Their tendons frame the anatomical snuffbox : EPL on one side, EPB and APL on the other. Extend your thumb to see it. The snuffbox , its tendons and its floor. Slide from the deck. Thumb movements. Slide from the deck. Thumb movement What it is Flexion / extension Across the palm, staying in the plane of the hand / back out again Abduction / adduction Away from the plane of the palm (forward) / back into it Opposition / reposition Thumb to the little finger, which sets us apart from other animals / back to anatomical position Why the Snuffbox Matters Its floor is the scaphoid (with the trapezium), so snuffbox tenderness is where you palpate for a scaphoid fracture . The radial artery crosses it: press it against the scaphoid and you feel a pulse. It's named for people who put snuff (tobacco) there to sniff. Wrist movements. Slide from the deck. Sheaths, tunnels and connections. Slide from the deck (Netter). Wrist movement Done by Flexion Anterior compartment Extension Posterior compartment Abduction (radial deviation) Both compartments: FCR + ECRL + ECRB Adduction (ulnar deviation) Both compartments: FCU + ECU Extensor feature Point Synovial sheaths Every extensor tendon crossing the wrist has one, to cut friction under the tight retinaculum 6 osseofibrous tunnels Under the extensor retinaculum, formed by its attachments to the radius and ulna. You don't need which tendon goes where. Intertendinous connections Link adjacent extensor digitorum tendons near the knuckles, so the middle and ring fingers can't extend independently . The index and little fingers can: they have their own extensors. Extensor expansion A triangular aponeurosis over the back and sides of each finger. Extensor digitorum, EDM, extensor indicis and the lumbricals and interossei all insert through it.

entries.x: Ganglion Cyst and Mallet Finger Synovial (ganglion) cyst Mallet (baseball) finger What A cyst of clear, mucinous fluid, most often on the dorsum of the wrist . It is connected to the synovial sheaths of the extensor tendons. Grape-sized, sometimes plum-sized; cause unknown. A “ganglion” here isn't a nerve ganglion. A jammed fingertip (sudden hyperflexion) tears or avulses the extensor tendon from the base of the distal phalanx : the DIP swells and can't be actively extended Treatment Usually nothing ; drain or excise if painful or a problem (drainage risks infection). The old “ Bible bump ” treatment was bursting it with a heavy book. RICE and a splint holding the DIP in extension , so the tendon heals short enough to extend. A complete avulsion fracture (bone pulled off with it) needs surgery to pin the fragment. Mallet finger: the mechanism. Drawing from the deck; the patient photographs on these slides are left out. Bony mallet: an avulsion fragment (circled) means surgery. X-ray from the deck. Knowledge check: the posterior forearm specimen A photograph, so not shown. A anconeus (small triangle), B extensor digitorum (four tendons), C extensor carpi ulnaris , D extensor digiti minimi , E extensor indicis , F brachioradialis (high origin, wraps forward), G ECRL (small belly, long tendon), H ECRB (broader belly in the same fascia, so separate them yourself in the lab), I abductor pollicis longus , J extensor pollicis brevis .

entries.x: Tendinitis vs Tendinosis Tendinitis Tendinosis How common Less common than we think More common than we think What True inflammation : rheumatologic disease, acute overload (too much, too suddenly), infection (e.g. infectious tenosynovitis) Collagen degeneration from chronic overuse with too little recovery, not the inflammatory cascade. Under the microscope: immature, disorganized collagen and abnormal vascularity. Treatment Reduce inflammation: RICE for acute injury, anti-inflammatories, treat the cause (antibiotics, rheumatology) Little inflammation to reduce: therapy to encourage collagen recovery ; analgesics (anti-inflammatories only for their pain relief) Recovery Faster, once the cause is fixed Slow and stuttering: “100+ days” to make new collagen

entries.x: Lateral and Medial Epicondylosis Lateral epicondylosis (“tennis elbow”) Medial epicondylosis (“golfer's elbow”) Structure Common extensor origin, mostly extensor carpi radialis brevis Common flexor origin Who 1–3% of people a year; 30s and 40s ; occupational more often than recreational Repeated forceful wrist flexion (the golf swing) Symptoms Pain just distal to the lateral epicondyle ; classic “pain and weakness”, especially gripping + supination (it hurts to use, so it looks weak) Pain just distal to the medial epicondyle Exam Tender over the common extensor origin; pain with resisted middle-finger extension ± wrist extension ± supination; pain on passive stretch (wrist pulled into flexion) Tender over the common flexor origin; pain with resisted wrist flexion and pronation ; pain on passive stretch (into extension) The examination slides are photographs of an examiner and a patient, so they're described rather than shown. Knowledge check A left-handed woman's elbow hurts after tightening a lot of screws on a weekend project, and you diagnose golfer's elbow. What's injured? → the common flexor origin at the medial epicondyle (medial epicondylitis/osis).

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Biceps Tendinopathy and Rupture Tendinitis / tendinosis Rupture Clinical points Insidious onset; pain on resisted movement and on stretch; usual treatments Trauma or “end-overuse”; a pop heard or felt; pain (or, once it has let go, little); bruising ; weakness ; a change in muscle contour Proximal (long or short head) Anterior shoulder pain ( 8.3 ) Not uncommon , especially in the elderly; often degenerative. Usually still functional (brachialis, brachioradialis and the other head still flex), so typically non-operative . The belly bunches low: the Popeye bulge. Distal Anterior elbow pain Rare but consequential : both heads let go, so poor supination and weak flexion; usually younger and acute ; the belly retracts up the arm. Call ortho early : once the tendon has retracted it's hard to pull back down and reattach.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Managing Tendinitis and Tendinosis 1 Educate Name it, and set expectations: many improve quickly, some become chronic. Find and address the offending movements . 2 Modify the activity Ice/RICE. Relative rest by time or by task : less time at it, more breaks, or change how it's done. Adjust ergonomics and biomechanics to cut excess force. 3 Orthoses and taping A counterforce strap worn during the offending activity, pressing just distal to the point of maximal tenderness , spreads the force away from the tendon origin. 4 Physiotherapy: the mainstay Eccentric strengthening twice a day for 12 weeks to stimulate collagen. For tennis elbow: lift the hand into extension with the other hand, then lower the weight (a water bottle) slowly into flexion. Massage may stimulate fibroblasts too. 5 Medication Anti-inflammatories can be tried but help less in chronic tendin osis . Prefer topical : upper-limb tendons are shallow enough for it to work, with fewer systemic effects. 6 Intervention Regenerative options such as platelet-rich plasma (evidence unclear, sometimes useful). Surgical referral if refractory ; surgery is avoided where possible. Practice Pointer Don't ask “have you tried physio?” (the answer is always yes). Ask “ show me what you've been doing in physio ”. If they can't, they're probably only doing the exercises in the gym every two weeks, and that explains why they aren't better.

Winged Scapula Injure the long thoracic nerve (it runs down the lateral chest wall on serratus anterior) and serratus can no longer hold the scapula's medial border flat. Push along the long axis of the arm, against a wall, and the medial border lifts off the chest: a winged scapula . It points to the long thoracic nerve or the muscle itself. (The slide's photograph of a winged scapula is described, not shown.) Pectoral nerves: some textbooks give pec minor the medial pectoral nerve only. For this course, both pecs get both nerves: a communicating branch joins the two after they leave the plexus.

Supraspinatus Is the One That Tears It's the most commonly torn cuff tendon, usually from repetitive overhead sport or work: there is little room between its tendon and the acromion, and the subacromial/subdeltoid bursa (one continuous bursa) sits on top and can inflame too. Rotator cuff tendinitis is the most common cause of shoulder pain , and like subacromial bursitis it hurts in mid-abduction (Dr. Martin: about 40–120°), the painful arc . The suprascapular nerve's route explains why one nerve supplies two fossae: superior trunk → suprascapular notch → supraspinous fossa (supraspinatus) → round the spinoglenoid notch , between the scapular spine and the glenoid → infraspinous fossa (infraspinatus). entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder
entries.x: Function and Pathophysiology Rotator cuff disease is the most common shoulder disorder in practice. It starts in the 40s , becomes more common with age, and is considered progressive . Function: the cuff's primary job is to stabilize the shoulder, keeping the humeral head centred in the glenoid against the pull of the big movers (deltoid, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi). Moving the arm is its secondary job. Intrinsic (the tendon itself) Extrinsic (something outside the tendon) What Vascularity: capillaries in the tendon thin out with age, starting on the articular side, so it heals poorly Tension overload: repetitive reaching work, strain after strain Degeneration: more collagen cross-linking and less water make it brittle Acromion morphology and a small subacromial space: the undersurface of the acromion abrades the cuff How common The usual cause Once thought the main cause; now probably exceptional Intrinsic causes. Slide from the deck. Extrinsic: acromion shape and subacromial space. Slide from the deck. Why the Acromion Lost the Argument If the acromion were grinding the cuff from outside, tears would start on the bursal side and work inward. They don't: cuff disease usually starts on the articular side (against the humerus) and propagates outward. That fits an intrinsic, tendon-level process.

entries.x: Symptoms and Examination Symptoms: restricted motion (because it hurts), pain, and weakness (from pain, or because the tendon is no longer attached to bone). Exam What you do → what it means Move Active < passive motion: contracting the cuff hurts, but the examiner can lift the arm further Neer sign The examiner lifts the arm, driving the cuff against the anterior acromion → pain Hawkins test The arm is forced into internal rotation , bumping a different part of the cuff against the acromion → pain Painful arc Raising the arm out to the side (“snow angel”) hurts through mid-range; the patient hikes the shoulder to get through it, and higher up the pain goes away Strength tests Supraspinatus and infraspinatus tested side to side; subscapularis : hand on the small of the back, can they lift it off ? entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Arteries of the Forearm At the distal cubital fossa the brachial artery splits into the radial and ulnar arteries, named for the side they run down. Artery Course Branches Radial Deep to brachioradialis ; the radial pulse is taken against the distal radius, between the FCR and APL tendons. It then wraps laterally round the wrist to the back, through the anatomical snuffbox on the scaphoid. Recurrent radial (joins the radial collateral round the elbow) Ulnar Deep to pronator teres , then down the ulnar side; enters the wrist lateral to the pisiform Anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent (join the inferior and superior ulnar collaterals) Common interosseous , which splits at once into the anterior interosseous (with the anterior interosseous nerve, on the front of the interosseous membrane) and the posterior interosseous (over the membrane into the posterior compartment) Anterior forearm arteries and the elbow collaterals. Slide from the deck (Netter). Posterior forearm: posterior interosseous artery. Slide from the deck (Netter). Collateral circulation at the elbow. Slide from the deck. Why the Elbow Collaterals Matter The collateral arteries coming down from above (radial collateral, superior and inferior ulnar collateral) meet the recurrent arteries coming up from below. If the brachial artery is occluded or clamped in surgery distal to the profunda brachii , this network still gets enough blood to the forearm and hand.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Veins and the Cubital Fossa The dorsal venous network on the back of the hand drains into the cephalic (lateral) and basilic (medial) veins, joined across the cubital fossa by the median cubital vein . The textbook arch is often just a network, and the connections vary a lot. Perforating veins shunt blood from the superficial veins into the paired deep veins (radial, ulnar, brachial) that run with the arteries. Forearm veins. Slide from the deck (Netter). Cubital fossa: borders and “TAN”. Slide from the deck (Netter); the photographs of an IV, a BP cuff and a blood draw are left out. Cubital fossa Shape A shallow triangular depression on the front of the elbow Borders Brachioradialis (lateral), pronator teres (medial), a line through the medial and lateral epicondyles (top) Contents, lateral → medial Biceps T endon (easy to palpate) → brachial A rtery (and veins) → median N erve: “TAN” . Also the radial nerve and its branches, laterally. Superficial Median cubital, cephalic and basilic veins; the medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm Why it matters The median cubital vein is used for blood draws and IVs. The brachial artery is used for blood pressure: its pulse is felt against the biceps border higher up, or against the biceps tendon in the fossa. All three TAN structures are fairly superficial here. Knowledge check: the angiogram Label the arteries on an arm angiogram: A brachial , B ulnar , C radial .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
entries.x: The Median Nerve Musculocutaneous has already ended (as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm), and the radial nerve ducks into the posterior forearm, so the median and ulnar nerves supply the anterior forearm. Median nerve (C5–T1) Course Through the cubital fossa deep to the bicipital aponeurosis and the median cubital vein, medial to the brachial artery → between the two heads of pronator teres → between FDS and FDP → under the flexor retinaculum (carpal tunnel) Supplies directly Pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus, FDS Anterior interosseous branch Leaves just below the cubital fossa and runs on the interosseous membrane with its artery: lateral half of FDP, FPL, pronator quadratus Sites at risk 1. Cubital fossa : unprotected and superficial (it can be severed there) 2. Between the heads of pronator teres : pronator syndrome 3. Deep to the flexor retinaculum : carpal tunnel syndrome (in the wrist and hand modules) The three nerves entering the forearm. Slide from the deck (Netter). Median nerve and its anterior interosseous branch. Slide from the deck (Netter). Median nerve: three sites at risk. Slide from the deck (Netter). Pronator Syndrome Any nerve that passes through a muscle can be squeezed when that muscle hypertrophies. In pronator syndrome the median nerve is compressed between the two heads of pronator teres, usually from muscle hypertrophy with elbow overuse . It causes pain and tenderness over the proximal anterior forearm and altered sensation over the palmar lateral 3½ digits and the adjacent palm.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
entries.x: The Ulnar Nerve Ulnar nerve Course Down the medial arm → behind the medial epicondyle → forward between the two heads of FCU → down between FCU and FDP → through Guyon's (ulnar) canal at the wrist Supplies in the forearm FCU and the medial half of FDP (digits 4, 5): the “1½”. Location, location, location: it runs right between them. Sites at risk 1. Behind the medial epicondyle : on bone and just under the skin, so at risk from external trauma, posterior elbow dislocation and supracondylar fractures 2. Between the two heads of FCU : compression from hypertrophy 3. Guyon's canal at the wrist Ulnar nerve: FCU and medial FDP. Slide from the deck (Netter). Ulnar nerve: three sites at risk. Slide from the deck (Netter). Guyon's canal and handlebar neuropathy. Slide from the deck. The Funny Bone Isn't a Bone Find your medial epicondyle and dig a fingernail in just behind it: the cord that rolls under it is the ulnar nerve . That's what you hit when you “hit your funny bone”, with tingling down into the forearm and hand. Guyon's canal is formed by the pisiform , the hook of the hamate and the overlying (pisohamate) ligament, and carries the ulnar artery and nerve . Compression there ( ulnar canal syndrome ) gives hypoesthesia of the medial 1½ digits and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles . Cyclists get it from leaning on extended wrists with pressure over the hook of the hamate: handlebar neuropathy .

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
entries.x: The Radial Nerve Radial nerve (C5–T1) In the arm Runs in the radial (spiral) groove and gives off the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm (skin of the posterior forearm) At the elbow Appears in the lateral cubital fossa between brachialis and brachioradialis , then splits into two terminal branches Deep branch Pierces supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve between the superficial and deep extensors. Motor to most of the posterior forearm . Superficial (dorsal sensory) branch Runs under brachioradialis and emerges just above the wrist, crossing the roof of the anatomical snuffbox . Sensory to the dorsum of the hand lateral to the 4th digit . Sites at risk 1. Where it pierces supinator (hypertrophy compresses it) 2. The superficial branch in the snuffbox Posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm. Slide from the deck (Netter). Deep vs superficial branch. Slide from the deck (Netter). Which branch supplies which muscle. Slide from the deck (Netter). For the Exam, “Radial” Is Right The radial nerve supplies the entire posterior arm and forearm . The slides split it into radial (brachioradialis, ECRL), deep branch and posterior interosseous nerve, because clinicians often name the branch. Dr. Martin: for the anatomy, answering “radial nerve” is correct. A snuffbox story: an elastic sheet strap flicked into Dr. Martin's snuffbox and injured her superficial radial nerve, numbing the lateral thumb. Sensation came back over 4–5 months as the nerve regrew.

Slide from the deck (Netter). Testing spinal levels. Slide from the deck. Testing spinal levels (from the slide; a peripheral nerve's territory spans several levels). Movements: C5 deltoid abduction + biceps; C6 biceps + wrist extension; C7 triceps, wrist flexion and finger extension; C8 finger flexion; T1 finger abduction/adduction. Sensory test sites: C5 lateral elbow, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial elbow. If biceps is weak with a normal deltoid and weak wrist extension, think C6 rather than C5. The matching knowledge check pairs C5 arm abduction, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension, C8 finger flexion and T1 finger abduction/adduction. Knowledge checks A 26-year-old's arm “feels funny” after six weeks on crutches, and the radial nerve is damaged. What can't he do? → extend the elbow , extend the wrist and supinate the forearm : the radial nerve runs the whole posterior arm and forearm. He can still abduct the arm, flex the elbow and wrist, and pronate. A 31-year-old's hand goes numb after a rugby game; EMG shows the nerve behind the medial epicondyle is injured. Sensory loss? → the medial 1½ digits and the palm (ulnar).

entries.t: Ulnar Neuropathy at the Elbow (Cubital Tunnel Syndrome)
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Ulnar Neuropathy at the Elbow (Cubital Tunnel Syndrome) The ulnar nerve can also be compressed at the wrist, but that's less common. Here the problem is where it runs through the cubital tunnel , behind the medial epicondyle, its most common site of compression. Causes of irritation How Direct trauma Hitting the funny bone Repeated pressure Leaning on a desk Sustained elbow flexion Stretches the nerve round the corner, e.g. sleeping with the arm bent under the head Subluxation The nerve slips partly in and out of its groove as the elbow bends Ligament hypertrophy? Medial epicondylosis (bulk)? Pressure from neighbouring tissue The cubital tunnel. Slide from the deck. Ulnar, not MCNFA, not C8. Slide from the deck. Feature Detail Symptoms Medial elbow pain ; numbness and tingling down the medial forearm into the ring and small fingers , which “fall asleep” Tinel's sign Tapping lightly over the nerve at the entrapment site reproduces tingling in its distribution (here, digits 4 and 5) Objective sensory loss In the ulnar territory of the hand (palmar and dorsal medial hand, digits 4 and 5). The medial forearm is spared : patients feel tingling there, but it belongs to the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm. A C8 radiculopathy would affect both areas. Motor May or may not be weak; if weak, it's the small muscles of the hand Keep perspective Tingling can come from nerve, muscle, tendon, ligament, joint, or referred pain (think cardiac) . True sensory loss is neurogenic. 1 Rule out red flags Significant or progressive weakness is the red flag and may need earlier, more aggressive treatment. Subjective symptoms alone aren't. 2 EMG / nerve conduction studies Confirm the diagnosis and grade its severity, especially if the diagnosis is unclear or the hand is weak. 3 Educate: critical here Irritation ( neuritis ) and damage ( neuropathy ) can be told apart on EMG/NCS. Neuritis is fully reversible , and so is mild neuropathy . Recovery depends on the patient changing habits. 4 Non-pharmacologic Avoid external pressure (don't lean on it; fix the workstation). Avoid elbow hyperflexion overnight with a towel splint (a towel taped round the arm) or an elbow pad. 5 Medication Not much: nerves recover when they're put in a happy position. 6 Surgery If refractory or severe: ulnar neurolysis (free it from scar and surrounding tissue) or anterior transposition (move it in front of the medial epicondyle, out of the way of pressure and stretch). entries.x: Learning Objectives Identify the important functional anatomy of the upper extremity, as it pertains to clinical presentations of arm pathology. Determine the sensory and motor loss anticipated with injuries to specific sites of the plexus (the roots and the terminal branches ). Identify the major arteries and veins of the upper extremity and their relationships to surrounding structures. Create a differential diagnosis and management plan for upper extremity complaints: numbness, weakness, pain and loss of range of motion. Describe the anatomic basis of common elbow and arm complaints (medial and lateral epicondylitis, distal biceps rupture, olecranon bursitis, ulnar neuropathy, arthritis, subluxation/dislocation, UCL injury) and outline their diagnosis and management. Dr. Charys Martin, 80 minutes: vascular supply (11 min), nerve supply (18 min), then a 10-question clinical quiz on the shoulder . The elbow objectives are taught in 8.5 , 8.6 and 8.7 . This module and Muscles of the Arm are the prep for the Proximal Upper Extremity Part II lab .

entries.x: The Arterial Tree The whole limb runs off one artery, which changes its name at each landmark. The subclavian comes off the brachiocephalic trunk on the right and straight off the aortic arch on the left . Slide from the deck. Subclavian branches to the shoulder. Slide from the deck. entries.t: The Axillary Artery and the Scapular Anastomosis
entries.p: Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: The Axillary Artery and the Scapular Anastomosis Pectoralis minor lies in front of the axillary artery and divides it into three parts. Part 1 is above pec minor, part 2 behind it and part 3 below it. Part 1 has one branch, part 2 two and part 3 three. Part Extent Branches 1st 1st rib → superior border of pec minor Superior thoracic (upper thoracic wall; for interest only ) 2nd Deep to pec minor Thoracoacromial : acromial, clavicular, deltoid and pectoral branches Lateral thoracic (runs with the long thoracic nerve; for interest only ) 3rd Inferior border of pec minor → inferior border of teres major Subscapular , a short trunk splitting into the circumflex scapular (round the lateral border of the scapula) and the thoracodorsal (with the thoracodorsal nerve) Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral , encircling the surgical neck; the posterior runs with the axillary nerve Three parts around pec minor. Slide from the deck. 2nd part. Slide from the deck. 3rd part. Slide from the deck. The scapular anastomosis , from behind: subclavian branches (suprascapular, dorsal scapular) meet axillary branches (circumflex scapular, posterior circumflex humeral, thoracoacromial). Slide from the deck. Why Every Joint Has Collateral Circulation Some positions temporarily kink a vessel. Sleep for hours with your arm above your head and the vessels on the upper side can be occluded, but the collateral network keeps the whole joint supplied. Dr. Martin: you don't need the names of all these branches, just that they exist and what they do. The same goes for the collateral network round the elbow. The cords of the brachial plexus are named for where they sit around the axillary artery: lateral, medial and posterior. In the lab this is around its 2nd part , behind pec minor.

entries.p: Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: The Brachial Artery It continues from the axillary artery below teres major and runs down the arm medial to biceps and in front of coracobrachialis and brachialis, ending in the cubital fossa as the radial and ulnar arteries. Branch Where it goes Profunda brachii (deep artery of the arm) Behind the humerus in the radial groove, with the radial nerve , deep to a head of triceps, to supply the posterior compartment . Near the elbow it becomes the radial collateral artery . Superior and inferior ulnar collateral The collateral network round the elbow Brachial artery: BP and the two fracture sites. Slide from the deck. Profunda brachii to the posterior compartment. Slide from the deck. An Artery on Bone Is an Artery at Risk Blood pressure: the cuff around the arm compresses the brachial artery, and the stethoscope listens over it in the cubital fossa. Fractures: the brachial artery lies against the medial humeral shaft, so a mid-shaft or supracondylar fracture can injure it. The profunda brachii is stuck to the humerus in the radial groove, so a mid-shaft fracture threatens it too.

entries.p: Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: Venous Return Blood starts in the dorsal venous network of the hand and climbs the limb in superficial veins. Communicating veins shunt it into the deep veins, away from the skin. Vein Course Note Cephalic Lateral forearm and arm → deltopectoral triangle (between deltoid and pec major) → pierces the clavipectoral fascia → axillary vein The triangle is where you'll first find it in the lab; preserve it down the arm Basilic Medial forearm and lower arm; dives deep about halfway up the arm to join the brachial veins, forming the axillary vein Median cubital Crosses the cubital fossa obliquely, joining cephalic and basilic Blood draws and IV access : superficial, under thin skin Deep veins Paired , running with the major arteries (the brachial artery's are the venae comitantes ) Removed from the field in the lab once identified Cephalic, basilic and median cubital veins. Slide from the deck (Netter, with a stock photo of a blood draw). Knowledge checks Which part of the brachial plexus is named for its position around the axillary artery? → the cords . A film character cuts her arm near the elbow on a toxic bush, and the infection tracks up the lateral arm along the large cutaneous vein. Which vein? → the cephalic (basilic is medial; brachial is deep; median cubital stays in the cubital fossa).

entries.t: The Pectoral Girdle: Nerves Travel With Arteries
entries.p: Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity
entries.x: The Pectoral Girdle: Nerves Travel With Arteries Nerve Travels with Supplies Suprascapular Suprascapular artery Supraspinatus, infraspinatus Dorsal scapular Dorsal scapular artery Rhomboids Long thoracic Lateral thoracic artery Serratus anterior Thoracodorsal (middle subscapular) Thoracodorsal artery Latissimus dorsi Axillary Posterior circumflex humeral artery Deltoid, teres minor; skin over the deltoid Upper and lower subscapular Subscapularis (both); teres major (lower) Medial and lateral pectoral Pectoralis major and minor The pectoral girdle: nerve–artery pairs. Slide from the deck (Netter). The “M” and the two small medial cutaneous nerves. Slide from the deck (Netter). Finding Your Way in the Axilla (Lab) Find the “M” first. Lateral leg = musculocutaneous (short, dives straight into coracobrachialis). Middle = median (from both cords; stays midline). Medial leg = ulnar (dives behind the basilic vein). Don't mistake the cutaneous nerves for the ulnar. The medial cutaneous nerves of the forearm and the arm run right beside it and leave the medial cord higher up (the arm's highest). They're smaller and go into the skin, so they come away when the skin is reflected. You need their territories and their cord, but won't have to identify them in the lab. The posterior cord is hidden behind the axillary artery. On the lab exam the whole M and the artery will be pulled aside and pinned, showing the posterior cord splitting into axillary and radial .

entries.x: Nerves of the Arm Nerve (roots) From Course in the arm Supplies in the arm Musculocutaneous (C5, 6, 7) Lateral cord Pierces coracobrachialis , runs between biceps and brachialis, reappears lateral to biceps as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm All three anterior muscles Median (C5–T1) Lateral + medial cords With the brachial artery: lateral to it, then crossing to its medial side mid-arm; in the cubital fossa, deep to the bicipital aponeurosis and the median cubital vein Nothing Ulnar (C8, T1) Medial cord Medial arm; about mid-shaft it pierces the medial intermuscular septum into the posterior compartment, then passes behind the medial epicondyle Nothing Radial (C5–T1) Posterior cord Enters behind the brachial artery, medial to the humerus, in front of the long head of triceps; runs in the radial (spiral) groove with the profunda brachii , under the lateral head; pierces the lateral intermuscular septum and comes forward between brachialis and brachioradialis All of the posterior compartment (triceps), no exceptions Anterior compartment nerves. Slide from the deck. Posterior compartment: the radial nerve in its groove. Slide from the deck. Clinical Points Biceps reflex: tap the biceps tendon and it should give an involuntary contraction. A normal response confirms the C5 and C6 segments. Excessive, diminished or prolonged responses suggest central or peripheral nervous system disease and need more testing. Mid-shaft humeral fracture: the radial nerve and profunda brachii lie on the bone in the radial groove. First concern: bleeding . Second: radial nerve damage.

entries.x: The Quiz, Worked Two patients, two sets of questions. It pulls together Week 7's shoulder joints , rotator cuff disease and the axillary nerve. The x-rays are described rather than shown. # Question Answer Why A 26-year-old falls off his bicycle onto his shoulder 1 The x-ray: which structures are injured? Acromioclavicular ligaments A grade 3 AC separation : the AC and coracoclavicular ligaments are torn. No GH dislocation, and cuff pathology is uncommon at 26. 2 Initial treatment? Sling with early range of motion Trials show a sling works as well as surgical stabilization, without the risks of surgery. Surgery is for AC separations with greater displacement . A 47-year-old woman with one month of shoulder pain 3 Can't sleep on it; hurts to elevate; active forward elevation 90°, external rotation 10°, internal rotation to the buttock; passive ≈ active ; cuff testing too painful. Differential? Osteoarthritis and adhesive capsulitis Only these two restrict both active and passive motion. OA builds over months to years; adhesive capsulitis over weeks to months. Calcific tendinitis and cuff syndrome reduce active motion only. Septic arthritis restricts both but comes on in hours to days. 4 Best imaging? X-rays They show calcific tendinitis and OA cheaply, and adhesive capsulitis has a normal x-ray . A bone scan is non-specific; a WBC scan looks for infection; MRI and CT add cost without adding much. 5 Her x-rays are normal. Which disorder commonly goes with her condition? Diabetes mellitus A normal x-ray supports adhesive capsulitis. Diabetes is its most common association, and diabetics recover less completely. A 64-year-old falls from a ladder cleaning eavestroughs 6 Shoulder pain, can't move the arm; ABCs fine. X-rays? Anterior shoulder dislocation The most common direction of traumatic instability. The axillary view shows the direction. There's also a large Hill-Sachs lesion . 7 After closed reduction: numb lateral upper arm , can't elevate, deltoid absent , biceps and infraspinatus present. Axillary nerve injury Musculocutaneous would weaken biceps and numb the lateral forearm . A C5 root lesion would also weaken biceps and infraspinatus. C6 numbs the lateral forearm. A cuff tear causes no sensory change. 8 6 months on: sensation back, pain less, but poor overhead function; active ≈ half of passive . entries.p: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity & Clinical Approach to the Elbow
entries.x: The Elbow Joint A synovial hinge joint, uniaxial : flexion and extension only. Of its two articulations, the humeroulnar does the hinging; the humeroradial articulates but the radius's real job is the separate proximal radioulnar joint . With the trochlea in its notch it's more stable than the glenohumeral joint, but it still won't hold together without its soft tissues. Hinge with two articulations. Slide from the deck (Netter). Capsule and ligaments. Slide from the deck (Netter). Structure Attachments Key point Capsule Weak anteriorly and posteriorly (lax, to allow the hinge); reinforced medially and laterally by the collateral ligaments. Muscles strengthen the front and back. Ulnar (medial) collateral ligament Medial epicondyle → coronoid process and olecranon Three bands: anterior (cord-like, strongest ), posterior (fan-like, weakest ), oblique (deepens the socket for the trochlea) Radial (lateral) collateral ligament Lateral epicondyle → blends with the anular ligament Anular ligament From the ulna, round the radial head, back to the ulna Part of the proximal radioulnar joint: it lets the head rotate Subcutaneous olecranon bursa Between the olecranon and the skin Stops the skin rubbing over the olecranon all day Say Which Bone Use ulnar and radial collateral ligament rather than medial and lateral: every hinge joint has “medial and lateral collateral ligaments”, and said alone those usually mean the knee . Carrying angle: over 15° is valgus, under 5° varus. Slide from the deck. The carrying angle is the normal outward angle of the forearm from the arm in extension. It's larger in women (one theory: wider hips; another: it makes cradling a baby easier). What matters clinically is symmetry with the other side: an abnormal angle, increased ( cubitus valgus , over 15°) or decreased ( cubitus varus , under 5°), is usually from soft-tissue problems at the elbow.

entries.x: The Radioulnar Joints Joint Type Detail Proximal Synovial pivot Radial head in the radial notch of the ulna, held by the anular ligament . It sits inside the elbow's capsule and shares its synovial membrane and fluid. Intermediate Syndesmosis The interosseous membrane . It moves with the radius but its job is to hold the bones together. Distal Synovial pivot The ulnar head in a notch on the radius Three radioulnar joints. Slide from the deck (Netter). Supination holds the bowl of soup; in pronation the radius crosses the ulna. Slide from the deck. Proximal radioulnar joint and the anular ligament. Slide from the deck (Netter). Why FOOSH Breaks Wrists Put a finger on your distal radius and pronate: it moves from the lateral side to the medial side as the radius crosses the ulna. People usually fall onto a pronated outstretched hand, with the bones crossed, which loads the distal radius and the carpals . Dr. Martin's counter-intuitive advice is to land on the ulnar border of the forearm , the strong ridge you can feel down its medial side: bruises and road rash, but fewer fractures.

Location Differential Anterior Arthritis (degenerative, post-traumatic, inflammatory); distal biceps tendinopathy Medial Medial epicondylosis (golfer's elbow); ulnar neuritis/neuropathy; UCL sprain/tear Lateral Lateral epicondylosis (tennis elbow) Posterior Olecranon bursitis ; arthritis; triceps tendinopathy Anywhere Fracture Joint and ligament problems show up as trouble with range of motion , stability or pain .

entries.x: Arthritis of the Elbow Category Examples Degenerative Osteoarthritis: wear and tear Inflammatory Rheumatoid arthritis, gout, psoriatic arthritis, and infection (septic arthritis), which can happen anywhere Post-traumatic OA that starts earlier , possibly in a different pattern, because old damage changed how the joint is loaded Elbow OA , with osteophytes arrowed on the x-ray. Slide from the deck. OA of the elbow History Gradual onset; somatic pain (achy, sore, with flares); mechanical symptoms : stiffness, loss of ROM, locking (stuck at one angle). Bony lumps may show from outside. X-ray Loss of joint space ; osteophytes (extra bone that blocks the hinge); subchondral sclerosis (whiter) and cysts (darker) just under the articular surface Educate Name it; expect a long, grumbling course (no cure for OA) Non-pharm Ice; PT to keep ROM ; OT to keep function by modifying tasks Pharm Topical anti-inflammatories; oral acetaminophen or NSAIDs (mind the side effects); corticosteroid injection Surgery (intolerable, end-stage) Debridement (clear out what's in the way, e.g. osteophytes) or arthroplasty

entries.p: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity & Clinical Approach to the Elbow
entries.x: Subluxation and Dislocation The elbow has two joints that can come apart, and they present very differently: the humeroulnar joint (an elbow dislocation) and the proximal radioulnar joint (nursemaid's elbow). Elbow dislocation Radial head subluxation (nursemaid's / pulled elbow) Who Anyone; FOOSH is probably the most common mechanism Almost only children ( rare after 5 ); more common in girls and the left arm Mechanism Usually posterior (ulna displaced backwards) Longitudinal traction on the arm (being pulled or swung by the hands). The anular ligament is thinner and weaker distally in children, so the radial head slips out and the ligament is pinched between the head and the capitulum. Picture Major trauma: capsule and ligament ruptures , skin tears, the ulnar nerve (right behind the joint) and compartment syndrome Acute pain, then refuses to use the arm , holding it flexed (semi-pronated) against the body Imaging Only to rule out something else , e.g. a fracture Treatment Red flag , not the usual algorithm. Closed reduction (traction, then reduce) and splint at 90° . If soft tissue is interposed or it won't stay reduced → ORIF . Closed reduction by pronation + extension ; no cast or orthosis Compartment syndrome , in one line: too much bleeding and swelling inside a fixed fascial compartment cuts off flow, and the tissues inside die. More in the orthopaedic modules. Nursemaid's elbow. Slide from the deck. Knowledge check: the toddler who won't colour A parent holds a 2-year-old's hands while she “walks up” into their arms. Right afterwards she says her arm hurts, cradles it against her body in a semi-prone position, and won't use it to eat or colour. → Nursemaid's elbow (radial head subluxation), treated by closed reduction . Lessons from the story behind it. A supination–flexion attempt did nothing: no pop and little change. The next morning the paediatric ED used pronation–extension (a little traction while extending and pronating). It works about 80% of the time and is tried first, with supination–flexion as the fallback. Within seconds there was an audible pop , a brief cry, and full use of the arm. They don't discharge until the child reaches with the affected arm (a popsicle). It recurred several times through toddlerhood, the family were taught to reduce it at home, and she grew out of it.

entries.p: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity & Clinical Approach to the Elbow
entries.x: Ulnar Collateral Ligament Injury UCL injury Role of the UCL Stabilizes the medial elbow Who Chronic, repetitive overuse : the baseball pitcher , but recreational athletes too Presentation Anywhere from sprain to complete tear. A sudden tear may pop over the medial elbow; tender medial elbow ; on valgus stress (elbow toward the midline, forearm away) there's no end point , just excessive, spongy motion instead of the hard end-feel of an intact ligament. Diagnosis Probably needs an exam by sports medicine or orthopaedics ; MRI may help Educate Ligaments heal very slowly , if at all, depending on the tear Non-pharm Ice; PT to strengthen the dynamic stabilizers (the muscles) and retrain proprioception , much of which came from the ligament; orthoses (braces) for external stability Pharm Pain control only: topical anti-inflammatories, acetaminophen, NSAIDs Surgery Reconstruction (Tommy John surgery) , only if needed for functional goals (e.g. a throwing athlete). A tendon graft ( palmaris longus , semitendinosus , others, or a synthetic) replaces the UCL, followed by 1–2 years of PT . The pitcher and the Tommy John photographs on these slides are left out.

entries.p: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity & Clinical Approach to the Elbow
entries.x: Olecranon Bursitis Bursae (over 150 of them) are thin fluid-filled sacs between bone and soft tissue, the skin included, that cushion and let tissues glide. A normal bursa is flat; irritated or inflamed, it fills with fluid and causes pain, focal tenderness, restricted ROM and, if superficial, visible swelling. The olecranon bursa is the most common superficial bursitis . Causes of olecranon bursitis, with a drawing of the bursa. Slide from the deck. Cause Story Single hard trauma A fall onto the point of the elbow Sustained or repetitive trauma Regularly leaning on the elbow , building over months : construction, plumbers, HVAC technicians in tight spaces, office desks, some athletes Infection (red flag) Through an identifiable skin break (bite, scrape) or none you can find. The usual bursitis symptoms plus erythema , heat and possibly systemic signs such as fever. A traumatic bursitis with a skin break can become infected. “Not scary” bursitis “Bad” (septic) bursitis Looks like A big, soft lump on the back of the elbow Much more swollen, red , warm , indurated (skin harder than around it) Work-up Often none . X-ray if there was trauma; US or MRI if it doesn't behave normally. Aspirate the bursa Treatment Benign, often self-limited once the offending factor is removed . RICE; modify the activity; pad the elbow ; topical anti-inflammatories ± NSAIDs. Bursectomy if it becomes chronic (a thickened bursa). Antibiotics chosen appropriately, ± irrigation and debridement if severe or not settling. Bursectomy is also considered if infected. Is It the Bursa or the Whole Elbow? A bursitis is a lump on the point of the elbow. If the whole elbow is swollen, think gout or an inflammatory arthropathy instead, which need their own treatment. Rule out fracture with an x-ray if there's real concern. The two bursitis photographs on the slides are described here rather than shown.

entries.x: Joints of the Hand All are synovial , each supported by a capsule and ligaments, like small elbows. The distal radioulnar and intercarpal joints also exist, wrapped in strong ligaments, but aren't detailed. entries.t: Reading the X-ray: Crooked, Short, Smooth
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 1
entries.x: Reading the X-ray: Crooked, Short, Smooth A very common injury from a fall on an outstretched hand , with localized pain . If the anatomy isn't restored, function is poor , particularly in young, active people. Ask three questions of every film. Question How to read it If it's abnormal 1. Is it crooked (bent)? On the lateral , draw the long axis of the radius and a tangent across its joint surface. Normally the surface tilts toward the palm, about 12° of palmar tilt . Tilted back past neutral = too crooked. The distal radioulnar joint is thrown out of line (asymmetric on CT), so forearm rotation becomes restricted 2. Is it short? At the DRUJ the radius normally sits a little longer than the ulna . Some people are born with a short radius, so compare with the other side . Ulnar impaction syndrome : the ulna jams into the carpus (the triquetrum), and the cartilage frays into arthritis 3. Is the joint surface smooth? Trace the joint outline: it should be uninterrupted. A gap is okay; a step isn't . A step over 1 mm (2 mm or more) leads to post-traumatic radiocarpal arthritis (pain, stiffness). In the young the only good fix is a fusion . Normal: 12° palmar tilt. Slide from the deck. Too crooked: the DRUJ is thrown out. Slide from the deck. CT: DRUJ asymmetry, injured vs uninjured. Slide from the deck. Length: compare to the other side. Slide from the deck. Too short: ulnar impaction. Slide from the deck. Smooth? Over 1 mm of step means arthrosis. Slide from the deck. Not smooth: arthritis, then fusion. Slide from the deck.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 1
entries.x: Treating a Distal Radius Fracture Why Age Changes Everything Treatment is forgiving at the extremes of age . In the very young , fast-growing bone remodels itself straight. The elderly put lower demands on the wrist and have laxer ligaments, so a crooked result bothers them less. Active middle-aged people are the ones who suffer if the alignment isn't restored. 1 Adequate analgesia A hematoma block (local anaesthetic injected straight into the fracture hematoma), regional anaesthesia (block the nerves higher up), or conscious sedation (IV drugs in the other arm). 2 Closed reduction (1) Traction against countertraction on the arm (by hand, or finger traps with a weight on the humerus) to restore length. (2) Increase the deformity to unlock the fragments. (3) Correct the deformity and lock the piece in place. 3 Cast with a 3-point mold Padding first. Press on the distal forearm and the hand, and gently up at the fracture site. Well molded doesn't mean tight. Follow with weekly x-rays in clinic. 4 Surgery if the reduction is inadequate External fixation (pins through the skin joined by carbon-fibre rods, ± fine wires) or open reduction and internal fixation with a volar plate . 5 Rehabilitate Get the motion and strength back once the fracture has healed. 20° dorsal tilt (normal is 12° palmar): reduce it. Slide from the deck. Hematoma block. Slide from the deck. Closed reduction in three moves. Slide from the deck. 3-point mold. Slide from the deck. A good cast frees the thumb, the knuckles and the elbow. Slide from the deck. A successful closed reduction. Slide from the deck. Still not smooth after reduction: surgery. Slide from the deck. External fixation. X-ray from the deck; the photo of the frame on an arm is left out. Casting choice Pros Cons Plaster of Paris Cheaper; easily molded Poor resistance to water; heavy (low strength-to-weight ratio) Fiberglass Light yet strong ; waterproof options; more radiolucent Expensive; harder to mold Padding Cotton: cheap, used under either. Synthetic: waterproof. A good cast isn't too tight, leaves room at the base of the thumb so it can move, stops short of the MCP joints so the fingers can bend, and is short enough to bend the elbow . The volar plate, in words (from the surgical video): an incision over the volar distal forearm, along the flexor carpi radialis tendon, which is pulled aside. FPL is retracted toward the ulna, and pronator quadratus is lifted off the radius, since the fracture is almost always underneat

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 1
entries.x: Why the Scaphoid Is Different The most common carpal fracture , usually in young people , typically from a FOOSH. Most heal uneventfully, but they're sometimes hard to diagnose . A patient who writes it off as a sprain may come back in midlife with the complications. Delayed diagnosis is associated with complications. Retrograde blood supply. Slide from the deck. Push–pull test on the thumb. Drawing from the deck; the photo of a swollen wrist is left out. Retrograde Blood Supply Branches of the radial artery enter the scaphoid distally (the dorsal ridge and the palmar tubercle) and run backwards to the proximal pole. A fracture through the waist (the most common site) or the proximal pole cuts the proximal fragment off from its blood. That risks nonunion (it never heals) and osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis: the bone dies and crumbles), and later arthritis . A distal fracture keeps its blood supply. Exam finding How Swelling The anatomical snuffbox fills in with blood and loses its hollow Localized tenderness In the snuffbox (the waist), over the scaphoid tubercle (the distal pole) and dorsally Push–pull test Pull the thumb, then push it in: loading the scaphoid through the thumb metacarpal hurts at the base of the thumb

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 1
entries.x: Imaging and Treatment Be Suspicious Plain x-rays are usually enough. But if the mechanism fits (a fall off a bike or a skateboard) and the scaphoid is swollen and tender, a normal x-ray doesn't rule it out. Treat it as fractured (cast) and get additional imaging, CT or MRI , or re-evaluate 10–14 days later. Fracture Treatment Why Undisplaced , or distal (e.g. the tubercle) Cast until union , about 6–8 weeks (a short arm cast; CT confirms healing, since it's hard to see on x-ray) A distal piece keeps its blood supply Displaced , or proximal pole Surgery : reduce it and fix it with a screw (e.g. through a volar approach, moving the FCR tendon aside) Poor blood supply: high risk of nonunion and osteonecrosis Be suspicious of a normal x-ray. Slide from the deck. CT and MRI show the waist fracture. Slide from the deck. Cast vs screw. Slide from the deck. Case Findings Plan 1. Scaphoid tubercle fracture Distal, good blood supply Cast 2. 25-year-old, fell off a skateboard X-rays look nearly normal; CT shows an undisplaced waist fracture Cast ; healed on CT at 8 weeks 3. Football player Displaced proximal pole fracture Surgery : a screw whose coarser trailing threads grip more bone, compressing the fracture to stimulate healing Case 1: tubercle fracture. Slide from the deck. Case 2: the x-ray misses it, the CT doesn't. Slide from the deck. Case 3: displaced proximal pole. Slide from the deck. Complications Complication The story Osteonecrosis An old fracture treated as a sprain: the proximal fragment's blood supply failed and the bone is crumbling Nonunion A “sprain” splinted 5–6 years earlier but never x-rayed. With no arthritis yet: operate, fix with a screw. With arthritis: an arthritis operation. Late arthrosis The end point of untreated nonunion or necrosis; treated with a fusion (the wrist still rotates but no longer flexes or extends) Osteonecrosis. Slide from the deck. Nonunion. Slide from the deck. Late arthrosis ends in fusion. Slide from the deck.

entries.t: Fascia, the Carpal Tunnel and the Compartments
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 1
entries.x: Fascia, the Carpal Tunnel and the Compartments Structure What it is Palmar carpal ligament A thickening of the antebrachial fascia, continuous with the extensor retinaculum; superficial and proximal to the flexor retinaculum Flexor retinaculum Deeper and more distal: the roof of the carpal tunnel , from the scaphoid and trapezium to the pisiform and hook of the hamate Palmar aponeurosis Thick longitudinal fibres from the retinaculum to the medial four digits , blending into their fibrous sheaths. Palmaris longus inserts into it. Its septa divide the hand into compartments. Through the carpal tunnel (deep to the retinaculum) Over it (superficial) FDS (4 tendons), FDP (4 tendons), FPL , and the median nerve Ulnar nerve and artery (in Guyon's canal), the palmar branch of the median nerve, the palmaris longus tendon Fascial layers of the palm. Slide from the deck (Netter). Four compartments. Slide from the deck (Netter). Intrinsic hand muscles start and end in the hand; extrinsic ones are the forearm muscles whose bellies sit outside it. The thenar eminence is the fleshy base of the thumb; the hypothenar eminence the medial side of the palm. Dupuytren's Contracture From the anatomy notes: an unexplained, progressive shortening, thickening and fibrosis of the palmar aponeurosis (nodules and cords) that draws the fingers into permanent flexion . The diseased fascia must be surgically excised for the patient to open the palm.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 1

Slide from the deck (Netter). Abductor pollicis brevis. Slide from the deck. Flexor pollicis brevis. Slide from the deck. Opponens pollicis. Slide from the deck. Adductor pollicis. Slide from the deck. Hypothenar compartment. Slide from the deck (Netter). Abductor digiti minimi. Slide from the deck. Flexor digiti minimi brevis. Slide from the deck. Opponens digiti minimi. Slide from the deck. Flexor pollicis brevis note: the notes and slide split it into a superficial head (recurrent median: flexes) and a deep head (deep ulnar: adducts), which is the slide's “1 exception”. Dr. Martin: for this course, treat FPB as fully thenar, supplied by the recurrent median . There's no flexor digiti minimi longus in a typical human; it's a rare variant, common in other mammals, which is why the hand's one is “brevis”.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 1
entries.x: Lumbricals and Interossei The central compartment , under the palmar aponeurosis, carries the long flexor tendons (FDS splitting so FDP can pass to the distal phalanx) and the lumbricals. The deepest adductor-interosseous compartment holds adductor pollicis and the interossei (“between the bones”). Muscle From → to Nerve Action Lumbricals (4, “worm-like”) Arise from the FDP tendons → lateral side of the extensor expansions, digits 2–5 Lateral two: median ; medial two: deep ulnar (they follow their FDP tendons) Flex the MCP and extend the IP joints (the “Z” movement: fingers straight, knuckles bent) Palmar interossei (3) Side of MC 2, 4, 5 facing the midline → the same side of the proximal phalanx / expansion Deep ulnar PAD : adduct digits 2, 4, 5 toward the middle finger Dorsal interossei (4) Adjacent sides of two metacarpals → the outer side of digits 2–4 Deep ulnar DAB : abduct digits 2–4 from the midline. The middle finger gets two : it can abduct either way. Lumbricals. Slide from the deck. PAD and DAB. Slide from the deck. The Hand Has Its Own Midline In the hand, abduction and adduction are measured from the middle finger , not the body's midline. Both palmar and dorsal interossei lie between the metacarpals; the palmar ones are just more anterior. The 1st dorsal interosseous and adductor pollicis make up the web between thumb and index finger. Bedside tests (from the notes): dorsal interossei , spread the fingers against resistance; palmar interossei , hold a sheet of paper between adjacent fingers while you tug; adductor pollicis , grip paper between thumb and index finger.

entries.t: Digital Sheaths and the Palmar Arches
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 1
entries.x: Digital Sheaths and the Palmar Arches Sheath What Function Fibrous digital sheaths Osseofibrous canals binding the long tendons to the phalanges A pulley system for the long tendons' force; without them the tendons bowstring Synovial sheaths Bursae of synovial fluid round the tendons in the fibrous canals Lubricate the tendons and cut friction (they can also form synovial cysts) From the notes: an injury can infect a digital sheath, giving tenosynovitis , a swollen finger that's painful to move. Each digit has its own sheath, so infection usually stays in that finger, but it can spread through connections to the common flexor sheath and into the anterior forearm. Fibrous and synovial sheaths. Slide from the deck (Netter); the photo of a bowstringing finger is left out. Arch Main contributor Completed by Where / branches Superficial palmar arch Ulnar artery (entering via Guyon's canal, superficial to the flexor retinaculum) Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery Just deep to the palmar aponeurosis , superficial to the tendons; gives the common palmar digital → proper palmar digital arteries Deep palmar arch Radial artery (after the snuffbox it dives between the heads of the 1st dorsal interosseous) Deep branch of the ulnar artery Across the metacarpals just distal to their bases, deeper than the tendons; gives the palmar metacarpal arteries. The radial artery also gives the princeps pollicis (thumb) and radialis indicis (index). Superficial arch: mainly ulnar. Slide from the deck (Netter). Deep arch: mainly radial. Slide from the deck (Netter). Knowledge checks An 18-year-old slices her palm and cuts only the recurrent branch of the median nerve. Which thumb movement does she lose? → opposition (opponens pollicis). Adduction is ulnar, and flexing the distal phalanx is FPL (anterior interosseous). A dissection with an arrow on the arch in the palm (a photograph, so not shown): its main blood supply? → the ulnar artery . It's the superficial palmar arch.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
entries.x: Learning Objectives Identify the muscles of the gluteal region and the three thigh compartments , their actions and their nerves. Describe the passage of structures through the greater and lesser sciatic foramina , and the femoral triangle, adductor canal and popliteal fossa . Relate the anatomy to Trendelenburg gait, safe gluteal injections, sciatic nerve injury, hamstring and adductor strains, popliteal aneurysm and femoral hernia . Dr. Charys Martin, 112 minutes over nine short recordings and their knowledge-check feedback videos. Dr. Martin warns it's a large module, built as separate lessons so it works as a reference. It builds on the Hip Joint , and with it and Thursday's Hip Pain module it's the prep for Friday's Hip & Thigh lab. Attachments are left out of the tables below except where they matter clinically; the slides show them.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
entries.x: Ligaments and Spaces Two ligaments turn the sciatic notches into foramina. The sacrotuberous ligament runs from the sacrum to the ischial tuberosity ; the sacrospinous ligament , deep to it, from the sacrum to the ischial spine . Greater sciatic foramen: pelvis → gluteal region Lesser sciatic foramen: gluteal region → perineum Piriformis ; the superior and inferior gluteal vessels and nerves; the sciatic nerve ; the posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh ; the nerve to quadratus femoris; and (passing through both) the pudendal nerve , nerve to obturator internus and internal pudendal vessels The pudendal nerve , nerve to obturator internus and internal pudendal vessels (they leave the pelvis, then go straight back in to reach the perineum); the obturator internus tendon Surface landmarks : the iliac crests at L4, the greater trochanter, the ischial tuberosity, the gluteal fold. Slide from the deck. Knowledge check Which structures pass from the pelvis to the gluteal region or thigh through the greater sciatic foramen? → the superior and inferior gluteal neurovascular bundles , piriformis , the sciatic nerve and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh . The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels pass through it too, but they're heading to the perineum, not the buttock or thigh.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
entries.x: Gluteal Muscles As a group they abduct, laterally rotate and extend the hip. Muscle Action Nerve Point Gluteus maximus Extends the hip; helps you stand up from sitting Inferior gluteal Ends partly in the IT band , which matters for hip and knee pain Gluteus medius and minimus Abduct and medially rotate the hip; stabilize the pelvis in gait Superior gluteal Weakness = Trendelenburg Tensor fasciae latae Flexes the hip; tenses the IT band Superior gluteal Arises from the ASIS (avulsed in teens, below) Deep lateral rotators: laterally rotate (and abduct) the thigh; hold the femoral head in the acetabulum Piriformis Lateral rotation; abduction Nerve to piriformis Pear-shaped; leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen: the key landmark Superior gemellus, obturator internus Lateral rotation Nerve to obturator internus Obturator internus's tendon leaves through the lesser sciatic foramen Inferior gemellus, quadratus femoris Lateral rotation Nerve to quadratus femoris Gluteus maximus. Slide from the deck (Netter). Gluteus medius and minimus. Slide from the deck (Netter). The deep lateral rotators. Slide from the deck (Netter). Piriformis, the landmark. Slide from the deck (Netter). Trendelenburg: Which Side Is Weak? When one foot leaves the floor, the gluteus medius and minimus of the standing leg contract to stop the pelvis tipping toward the unsupported side. If they're weak or the superior gluteal nerve is injured (e.g. in hip replacement surgery), the pelvis drops on the side of the swinging leg : a positive Trendelenburg test (standing on one leg) and a Trendelenburg gait . The dropped side's leg is now too long to clear the floor, so the patient leans away from it (a gluteus medius gait). Always think of both the muscle and its nerve. Knowledge check A 72-year-old is limping two weeks after a total hip replacement; her right hip drops every time the right leg swings. → the left gluteus medius (with minimus) isn't working: the stance side. Its nerve is the superior gluteal . In the video it's far less dramatic than you'd expect.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
entries.x: Gluteal Neurovasculature Structure Exits the greater sciatic foramen Supplies Superior gluteal artery and nerve (L4–S1) Above piriformis ; the nerve runs between medius and minimus Gluteus medius, minimus and TFL Inferior gluteal artery and nerve (L5–S2) Below piriformis Gluteus maximus Nerves to obturator internus and quadratus femoris Below piriformis The lateral rotators (with the gemelli) Pudendal nerve (S2–S4) and internal pudendal artery Below piriformis, then back through the lesser sciatic foramen The perineum Sciatic nerve (L4–S3) Below piriformis, into the posterior thigh The largest nerve in the body: really two nerves in one sheath , the tibial and the common peroneal (fibular) Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh (S1–S3) Below piriformis, deep to gluteus maximus Skin of the lower buttock, posterior thigh and popliteal fossa Gluteal arteries above and below piriformis. Slide from the deck (Netter). Gluteal nerves. Slide from the deck (Netter). The sciatic nerve and what injures it. Slide from the deck. Where to inject? The upper outer (here upper right) quadrant. Slide from the deck. Clinical point Detail Sciatica (sciatic nerve injury) Pain, tingling or numbness from the buttock to the foot . Causes: a herniated disc, hip surgery, piriformis syndrome , an intragluteal injection. Piriformis syndrome The nerve usually exits below piriformis, but may pass partly or wholly through it and get squeezed. Common in athletes who overuse the glutes. NSAIDs, rest, stretching. Intragluteal injections Thick muscle with a large area for absorption. Inject the superolateral quadrant : index finger on the ASIS , spread the fingers back along the iliac crest, inject between index and middle finger. That's away from the sciatic nerve and the structures leaving the greater sciatic foramen; low and lateral is the bony greater trochanter, without thick muscle.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
entries.x: Thigh Organization The deep fascia, the fascia lata , sends medial, lateral and posterior intermuscular septa in to the femur, making three compartments. Compartment Function Nerve Anterior Flex the hip, extend the knee Femoral Medial Adduct the hip Obturator , with two exceptions: the hamstring part of adductor magnus (tibial) and pectineus (femoral) Posterior Extend the hip, flex the knee Branches of the sciatic Three compartments, three jobs, three nerves. Slide from the deck (Netter).

entries.p: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
entries.x: Posterior Compartment: the Hamstrings Muscle Action Nerve Point Biceps femoris Extends the hip (long head), flexes the knee Long head: tibial division; short head: common peroneal division The lateral hamstring, to the head of the fibula; the short head is the one that doesn't start at the ischial tuberosity Semitendinosus Extends the hip, flexes the knee Tibial division A long tendon ; part of the pes anserinus Semimembranosus Extends the hip, flexes the knee Tibial division Deep to semitendinosus, muscular lower down The pes anserinus ("goose's foot") is the joint tendon of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the anteromedial proximal tibia, superficial to the MCL ("SGT", one muscle from each compartment). The hamstrings. Slide from the deck (Netter). Sciatic divisions and the perforating arteries. Slide from the deck (Netter). Structure Detail Sciatic nerve Its tibial and common peroneal divisions run in one sheath deep to the long head of biceps femoris . Tibial supplies every posterior muscle except the short head of biceps. Perforating arteries (from the profunda femoris) Pierce adductor magnus to reach the back of the thigh. The compartment has no artery of its own: it's fed by the inferior gluteal, medial circumflex femoral, perforating and popliteal arteries. Popliteal artery and vein The femoral vessels, renamed after passing through the adductor hiatus (a gap between adductor magnus and the femur) Hamstring Strains and Avulsions A muscle tears when it's actively contracting while passively stretched : the hurdler's lead leg. Expect extreme pain and a big hematoma (torn fibres rupture their vessels). Forcible hip flexion with the knee extended can avulse the common hamstring origin off the ischial tuberosity . The muscle keeps pulling the bony piece away, so a displaced avulsion needs surgical reattachment . Knowledge check A 26-year-old hurdler feels a pop in the back of his lead thigh; three days later there's extensive bruising and an x-ray shows an avulsion fracture at the ischial tuberosity. Which muscles? → biceps femoris (long head), semimembranosus and semitendinosus , from the common origin. Mechanism: active contraction plus passive stretch. Symptoms: a massive hematoma and pain. Treatment: surgical reattachment . entries.x: The Popliteal Fossa Boundaries Contents Superolateral: biceps femoris . Superomedial: semimembranosus and semitendinosus . Inferior: the medial and lateral heads of gastrocnemius . The tibial and common peroneal nerves , the popliteal artery and vein (with genicular branches), the end of the small saphenous vein , popliteal lymph nodes and fat. Deep to superficial: artery, vein, nerve . The popliteal fossa. Slide from the deck (Netter). The genicular anastomosis. Slide from the deck (Netter). Why the Knee Has Backup Plumbing The genicular anastomosis (the genicular arteries, plus the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral and the descending genicular from above) keeps the leg supplied during full knee flexion , which can briefly kink the popliteal artery, or if the popliteal or femoral artery is blocked. Knowledge check An 85-year-old has 6 weeks of painless right leg swelling and a pulsatile mass high in the right popliteal fossa. → a popliteal aneurysm : pulsatile means arterial. It's the most common peripheral aneurysm , at risk of embolization, thrombosis and rupture ; 80% are asymptomatic . High-risk ones get surgery (the stretched segment is replaced or stented). Half are bilateral , so check the other leg. (Rupture is a hemorrhage that can cost the foot or leg.)

entries.x: Anterior Compartment Muscle Action Nerve Point Iliopsoas (psoas + iliacus) Flexes the hip Femoral (+ L1–L3 rami for psoas) Comes from high on the posterior abdominal wall; tight from long sitting, so stretch it and strengthen its opponents Sartorius Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip; flexes the knee Femoral The "tailor's" muscle (cross-legged sitting); in the pes anserinus Pectineus Adducts and flexes the hip Femoral Sits with the medial group but takes the femoral nerve Quadriceps femoris: one common tendon over the patella to the tibial tuberosity Rectus femoris Extends the knee (less so with the hip flexed); helps flex the hip Femoral The only quad that crosses the hip Vastus lateralis, medialis, intermedius Extend the knee Femoral Intermedius lies deep to the others The anterior compartment. Slide from the deck (Netter). The quadriceps and the patellar reflex. Slide from the deck (Netter). Iliopsoas. Slide from the deck (Netter). Femoral, saphenous and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves. Slide from the deck (Netter). Nerve Course and supply Femoral nerve (L2–L4) From the lumbar plexus, passes deep to the inguinal ligament into the femoral triangle, lateral to the femoral vessels ; muscular branches to the anterior thigh, cutaneous branches to the front of the thigh Saphenous nerve The femoral nerve's terminal cutaneous branch, down the femoral triangle and adductor canal: skin of the anteromedial knee, leg and foot Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2–L3) Under the inguinal ligament next to the ASIS : skin of the lateral thigh The Patellar Reflex Strike the patellar ligament with the patient sitting, legs dangling: the quadriceps contract and the knee extends. It tests the femoral nerve and L3–L4 . A weak or absent reflex points to a lesion interrupting the nerve supply of the quadriceps. (The central part of the quadriceps tendon from patella to tibial tuberosity is also called the patellar ligament; Dr. Martin accepts either name.) Knowledge check A dissection of the anterior thigh (a photograph, so not shown): tensor fasciae latae (small, from the ASIS into the IT band), sartorius (wrapping medially), rectus femoris (central), vastus lateralis and medialis on either side (intermedius is hidden deep), and the quadriceps tendon with the patella in it.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
entries.x: Medial Compartment Muscle Action Nerve Point Adductor longus Adducts the thigh Obturator Borders the femoral triangle and adductor canal Adductor brevis Adducts the thigh Obturator Deep to longus; the obturator nerve's divisions straddle it Adductor magnus Adductor part: adducts and flexes ; hamstring part: adducts and extends Adductor part: obturator; hamstring part: tibial The gap between its two parts is the adductor hiatus Gracilis Adducts the thigh, flexes the knee, helps rotate the leg medially Obturator The most medial; a weak adductor that can be transplanted (with its nerve and vessels) to replace a damaged muscle Obturator externus Laterally rotates the thigh Obturator The medial compartment. Slide from the deck (Netter). Adductor magnus : two parts, two nerves. Slide from the deck (Netter). The obturator nerve (L2–L4) runs down the medial side of psoas and through the obturator foramen with the obturator vessels, supplies the medial muscles (not the hamstring part of adductor magnus) and some medial thigh skin. Slide from the deck (Netter). Clinical point Detail Groin pull Tearing or stretching of the adductors near their origin : active contraction plus passive stretch, in sports with quick starts or extreme stretching (soccer, sprinting, gymnastics). Bruising and pain; conservative care ( RICE, NSAIDs ). Avulsion in teenagers The cartilaginous growth plate is weaker than the muscle–tendon unit on its apophysis, so a powerful movement can break bone. Strong hip flexion can avulse the ASIS (the origin of sartorius and TFL). Knowledge check A dissection of the medial thigh (a photograph, so not shown): iliopsoas very deep and proximal, adductor longus (brevis and magnus hidden deep to it) and gracilis on the most medial side. Separate the fascial planes to see the deep ones.

entries.p: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
entries.x: Vasculature of the Anteromedial Thigh Vessel Detail Femoral artery The external iliac renamed as it passes under the inguinal ligament (the internal iliac stays in the pelvis); the femoral pulse is felt there. Superficial in the femoral triangle, so vulnerable to injury. Profunda femoris (deep femoral) Its big branch, deep in the femoral triangle, giving: the perforating branches (3–4, to the back of the thigh; they supply all three compartments), the lateral circumflex femoral (lateral thigh muscles; ascending, transverse and descending branches, the last to the knee anastomosis) and the medial circumflex femoral (between iliopsoas and pectineus to the back: most of the blood to the femoral head and neck ) Femoral vein The popliteal vein continued above the adductor hiatus; up the adductor canal, out in the femoral sheath to become the external iliac vein (has valves) Great saphenous vein Superficial: from the dorsal venous arch of the foot up the medial leg and thigh with the saphenous nerve, through the saphenous opening into the femoral vein (has valves). The usual coronary bypass graft (accessible, muscular and elastic wall); the saphenous nerve is at risk when it's harvested. Arteries of the thigh. Slide from the deck (Netter). Collaterals: cruciate at the hip, genicular at the knee. Slide from the deck (Netter). Why You Can Tie Off the Femoral Artery The cruciate anastomosis (medial and lateral circumflex femoral, inferior gluteal and first perforating arteries) joins the internal iliac's branches to the femoral system. So if the femoral artery has to be ligated , blood still reaches the limb. The hip and the knee both have extensive collateral circulation.

entries.t: The Femoral Triangle and Its Neighbours
entries.p: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
entries.x: The Femoral Triangle and Its Neighbours Space Boundaries Contents and notes Femoral triangle Inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle), sartorius , adductor longus : it really is a triangle Lateral to medial: NAVEL : femoral N erve, A rtery, V ein, E mpty space (the femoral canal), L ymphatics (in the canal). Also the end of the great saphenous vein. Femoral sheath Continuation of the iliac and transversalis fascia Wraps the femoral artery, vein and canal , but not the femoral nerve Femoral ring The small abdominal opening of the femoral canal Normally lymphatics and fat; bowel can push through it: a femoral hernia Adductor canal Sartorius, vastus medialis, adductor longus Carries the femoral artery and vein (and saphenous nerve) down to the adductor hiatus Adductor hiatus Between the adductor and hamstring parts of adductor magnus The femoral vessels pass to the popliteal fossa and become the popliteal artery and vein NAVEL , lateral to medial; the nerve sits outside the femoral sheath. Slide from the deck (Netter). Knowledge checks A 52-year-old woman has a groin bulge that grows when she does crunches; it's below her inguinal ligament. → a femoral hernia : abdominal contents through a weak femoral ring , below the inguinal ligament. More common in women (a wider pelvis means a wider ring). Rule out an incisional hernia by asking about surgery; direct and indirect inguinal hernias (more common in men) can't be ruled out on sex alone. Small asymptomatic ones may be watched; large ones can strangulate and are repaired with mesh . ("Groin" isn't an anatomical term; it can mean anything in the inguinal or medial region.) An angiogram of the thigh: the femoral artery dividing, the profunda femoris , its two circumflex branches wrapping the femur, and the perforating branches to the back. Telling the medial from the lateral circumflex here "would never be a question on the exam". A dissection of the femoral triangle (a photograph, so not shown): its boundaries sartorius, the inguinal ligament and adductor longus , and its contents, lateral to medial, the femoral nerve, artery and vein .

Nodes Drain Then to Superficial inguinal (top of the femoral triangle) The abdominal wall below the umbilicus , the perineum , the thigh and the medial leg Mostly the external iliac nodes; some to the deep inguinal Deep inguinal (medial to the femoral vein) Deep lymph of the limb External iliac nodes Superficial veins and lymphatics run superficial to the fascia lata .
