entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
entries.x: Learning Objectives Identify the bones and landmarks of the proximal lower extremity and the features of the hip joint that make it stable. Describe the blood supply of the femoral head and why fractures and dislocations threaten it. Outline an approach to a suspected hip fracture : presentation, imaging, fracture types, management and post-operative care. Dr. Charys Martin (osteology and joint features of the hip, 30 minutes) and Dr. Caitlin Cassidy (hip fractures, 26 minutes); the deck also credits Dr. Jordan Vanderende. About 56 minutes in all. It's the foundation for the Gluteal Region & Thigh and Thursday's Clinical Approach to Hip Pain, and prep for Friday's Hip & Thigh lab.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
entries.x: The Hip Bone Three bones, ilium, ischium and pubis , fuse into the hip bone, and all three meet in the acetabulum , which articulates with the femoral head. Bone Landmark Why it matters Ilium: the largest part; top of the acetabulum Iliac crest Its top sits at L4 : the landmark for a lumbar puncture ASIS, AIIS, PSIS, PIIS The anterior and posterior, superior and inferior iliac spines; the PIIS forms the top of the greater sciatic notch Greater sciatic notch Turned into the greater sciatic foramen by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments: the doorway from pelvis to gluteal region Ischium: posteroinferior; back of the acetabulum Ischial spine Anchors the sacrospinous ligament Ischial tuberosity What you sit on ; the hamstrings arise here Lesser sciatic notch Becomes the lesser sciatic foramen, from the gluteal region into the perineum Pubis: anteromedial; front of the acetabulum Pubic tubercle Anchors the inguinal ligament Superior and inferior rami With the ischium, they ring the obturator foramen (covered by the obturator membrane; the obturator nerve and vessels pass through) The hip bone. Slide from the deck (Netter). The femur. Slide from the deck (Netter). The tibia and fibula. Slide from the deck (Netter). The femur is the largest bone in the body and carries weight from the hip to the tibia. The tibia is the leg's weight-bearing bone (its two condyles form the tibial plateau ; the patellar ligament ends on the tibial tuberosity ). The fibula bears no weight.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
entries.x: The Hip Joint A ball-and-socket synovial joint , multiaxial. It's the most stable joint in the body because of (1) its congruent fit (more than 50% of the femoral head sits in the acetabulum), (2) stout ligaments , including the strongest in the body, and (3) a thick cuff of muscle for dynamic support. It sacrifices some mobility for that stability; the glenohumeral joint does the reverse. Structure Role Acetabular labrum Fibrocartilage rim that deepens the socket Transverse acetabular ligament Bridges the gap in the labrum at the acetabular notch Ligament of the head of the femur Carries the artery of the ligament of the head ; gives no real strength Joint capsule Attaches to the intertrochanteric line in front but not to the femur behind; its inferior fibres wind round the back of the neck. Its thickenings are the three ligaments below. Ligament Where Job Iliofemoral ("Y ligament of Bigelow") Anterior and superior Strongest ligament in the body ; limits extension Pubofemoral Anterior and inferior Limits abduction Ischiofemoral Posterior Strengthens the back of the joint Inside the hip joint. Slide from the deck (Netter). The three spiral ligaments. Slide from the deck (Netter). Why You Can Stand Without Effort The ligaments run in a spiral . Moving into extension (and medial rotation) twists them tight, which screws the femoral head into the acetabulum , like wringing out a towel. That locks the joint for "quiet" standing with little muscle work.

entries.t: Blood Supply of the Femoral Head
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
entries.x: Blood Supply of the Femoral Head Artery Contribution Medial circumflex femoral (from the profunda femoris) The most significant supply to the head and neck, via retinacular arteries running up the neck Lateral circumflex femoral (from the profunda femoris) The rest of the circumflex supply Artery of the ligament of the head (from the obturator artery) The main supply in children , while the growth plate between head and neck is open; only minor in adults Inferior gluteal artery Anastomoses with the circumflex arteries: collateral circulation if the proximal femoral artery is blocked The head is fed from below , up the neck, mostly by the medial circumflex femoral artery. Slide from the deck (Netter). Why a Neck Fracture Kills the Head A femoral neck fracture cuts the circumflex supply running up the neck, leaving only the artery of the ligament of the head, which is usually inadequate in adults . The head can die ( avascular necrosis ) and collapse, often needing a total hip replacement. These fractures are especially common in women over 60 with osteoporosis . Hip problem Key points Congenital dislocation A malformed acetabulum and/or femur at birth: less congruent, less stable Acquired (traumatic) dislocation Uncommon, because the joint is so strong. About 90% are posterior : the " dashboard injury " in a car crash, force driven up the long axis of the femur. The limb looks shorter and medially rotated . Watch the sciatic nerve (stretched or compressed), bleeding from the circumflex arteries, and avascular necrosis . Osteoarthritis Common with age: cartilage, subchondral bone, synovium and soft tissues change (a thick subchondral plate, osteophytes, deformed bone). Conservative care rarely lasts; severe OA gets a hip replacement . Knowledge checks Bo Jackson's hip dislocated posteriorly in a 1990 NFL playoff tackle; after surgery and rehab he had avascular necrosis and needed a hip replacement. Which artery was disrupted? → the medial circumflex femoral artery . The injury ended his football career; he went on to Major League Baseball. A disarticulated cadaveric hip (a photograph, so not shown): the femoral head, the lesser trochanter (a small bump on the back), the acetabular labrum (the fibrocartilage rim) and the cut ligament of the head of the femur.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
entries.x: Why Hip Fractures Matter "Hip fracture" really means a proximal femur fracture ; you can't fracture a joint. They're a big deal because they're common , especially with age, and carry huge morbidity , much of it from immobility. 147 per 100,000 Canadians over 40; women 2× as likely to fracture; 25% die within a year (men 1.3× more likely to). Source: Canadian Chronic Disease Surveillance System 2020. Slide from the deck. Risk = things that make you fall… …plus things that make bone break (osteoporosis) Intrinsic: previous falls; comorbidities (peripheral vascular disease, COPD, stroke, other weakness); polypharmacy (sedatives, diuretics, psychotropics, antiarrhythmics); poor nutrition; poor eyesight. Extrinsic: clutter, rugs and carpets at home. The slide's indications for a BMD test (as in Endocrinology): a fragility fracture, long-term glucocorticoids, hypogonadism or early menopause, malabsorption, primary hyperparathyroidism, a parental hip fracture, smoking, heavy alcohol, low weight, rheumatoid arthritis, and everyone 65+

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
entries.x: Is It a Hip Fracture? History (OLDCARS) Physical exam Onset sudden, after a fall or trauma. Location : the groin or lateral upper thigh (true hip-joint pain is groin pain). Character sharp or a deep ache. Aggravated by movement and weight bearing, alleviated by staying still (sometimes it barely hurts at rest). May radiate to the knee. Severity varies hugely. Look: the leg is shortened, externally rotated and slightly abducted (a position of comfort, with the hip muscles pulling it there); unable to bear weight. Feel: tenderness over the hip (or not). Move: painful range of motion, painful log roll and straight leg raise. Keep Your Suspicion High In the elderly , think hip fracture even if the pain or the trauma was minimal : these fractures can hide. Image with an AP pelvis and hip x-ray (follow the cortex around the head, neck, trochanters and shaft on both sides for any break or loss of the smooth curves). If it's negative but suspicion stays high, get a CT , which is more sensitive. A normal AP pelvis. Slide from the deck. Three zones: neck (subcapital), intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric. Slide from the deck. Femoral neck fractures: a collapsed neck, a sharp step in the head–neck curve, a tilted head. Slide from the deck. Intertrochanteric fractures , one with the lesser trochanter broken off. Slide from the deck. Subtrochanteric , clearly displaced. Slide from the deck.

entries.t: The Approach to a Suspected Hip Fracture
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
entries.x: The Approach to a Suspected Hip Fracture 1 Is this a hip fracture? The history, exam and imaging above. 2 Is the patient stable? Other injuries? Especially in the young , whose hip fractures come from high-velocity trauma: ABCs , then look for a pelvic fracture, vascular injury or nerve injury. Check distal pulses and sciatic nerve function (tibial and peroneal: can the foot dorsiflex and plantarflex?). 3 Why did they have a hip fracture? Why did they fall? Recent illness, poor eating or drinking, syncope or presyncope, cardiac history; consider a CBC (anemia), electrolytes , troponin , an ECG (atrial fibrillation) and a chest x-ray (pneumonia). Why did they break? A fall from standing shouldn't break a healthy femur: look for a pathologic fracture (primary bone tumour or metastasis), and treat a low-trauma break as a fragility fracture , which automatically qualifies as osteoporosis; start the workup. 4 What's the plan for the fracture? See the table below. 5 After surgery Prevent complications and regain function.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
entries.x: Managing the Fracture The vast majority get surgery , within 24–48 hours (the standard of care), because it gets people back to weight bearing sooner and cuts the complications of lying still. You can't cast a proximal femur, so non-operative care means weeks off their feet. For displaced femoral neck fractures surgery is also needed to protect the femoral head's blood supply. Fracture Treatment Femoral neck, non-displaced Rarely non-operative (only a very non-displaced fracture, perhaps through one cortex, in a poor surgical candidate); maybe screws across the fracture (internal fixation); often arthroplasty Femoral neck, displaced Arthroplasty , always: a hemiarthroplasty (new femoral head on a stem, press-fit or cemented) is the smaller surgery with a quick recovery; a total arthroplasty (head + acetabulum) if the joint was already arthritic. The choice is the surgeon's. Intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric Essentially all surgical (they're unstable), with the same operation: an intramedullary nail down the femoral canal, locked with screws. That's an ORIF : open, reduce the fragments, fix them internally. Hemiarthroplasty, total arthroplasty, screws. Slide from the deck. An intramedullary nail for inter- and subtrochanteric fractures. Slide from the deck. After surgery: complications (all tied to immobility) Plan VTE : common after hip fracture Prophylaxis: LMWH for 14–30 days (Thrombosis Canada) Pneumonia : a common cause of death after hip fracture (anaesthesia, immobility, or the reason they fell) Watch for it Muscle atrophy : shockingly fast in bed Bed exercises; get moving Infection : the wound, and UTI rises with immobility Watch for it Delirium : a high-risk time in older patients Reduce the risk; treat it Pressure sores Keep them moving; nursing checks Don't Let It Happen Again Early mobilization with interdisciplinary rehab (inpatient or outpatient, PT and OT) is the best strategy against complications. Falls prevention: optimize comorbidities, fix the home environment, strength and balance work, and a gait aid (a walker at first). Fracture prevention: check vitamin D and calcium, work up secondary osteoporosis, and consider antiresorptive therapy . Knowledge checks An 86-year-old falls at home, can't get up and can't bear weight on the left. How do you expect the left leg to lie? → abducted and externally rotated , and it looks shortened . Treatment for a displaced femoral neck fracture? → arthroplasty (hemi or total). Left alone it's at hig

Learning Objectives Localize hip pain to the anterior, lateral or posterior hip and build a differential from the structures there. Describe the presentation, examination, investigations and treatment of hip osteoarthritis, labral tears, avascular necrosis, greater trochanteric bursitis and pain syndrome, and piriformis syndrome . Tell greater trochanteric pain syndrome from hip osteoarthritis . The module is by Dr. Jordan VanderEnde (physical medicine and rehabilitation). It has two recordings: anterior hip pain (11 minutes) and lateral and posterior hip pain (14 minutes). There are no notes; the knowledge checks are on the slides. It builds on the Hip Joint and the Gluteal Region & Thigh . With those two, it's the prep for Friday's Hip & Thigh lab.

Where Does It Hurt? Patients point to very different places when they say "my hip hurts." Find out where, picture the anatomy under the patient's hand, and the differential follows. They point to Think of Differential Anterior hip or groin "True" hip pain: intra-articular Arthritis (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, septic; the specifics come in the rheumatology weeks), a labral tear , avascular necrosis . Also iliopsoas tendinopathy , treated like any muscle problem from MSK basics. Lateral buttock or thigh Tensor fasciae latae, gluteus medius and maximus, the greater trochanteric bursa Greater trochanteric bursitis , greater trochanteric pain syndrome (gluteal tendinopathy) Posterior buttock Piriformis , the sacroiliac joint, the lumbar spine Piriformis syndrome , sacroiliac joint problems, radiculopathy (later weeks) The overlap catches people out: arthritic pain sits deep in the joint, so it can wrap around the hip and be felt laterally too (see GTPS or hip OA ).

Osteoarthritis of the Hip Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease, the age-related "wear and tear" (there's a fuller introduction in the rheumatology weeks). There are two types: primary , which is idiopathic and seen in the elderly, and secondary , which is post-traumatic and seen in younger people. History Physical exam Anterior groin pain , often with a "C sign" : the patient cups a hand around the side of the hip, because the deep pain wraps around. Onset can be gradual or sudden. It's worse with prolonged activity , and there may be night pain. Morning stiffness lasts under about 30 minutes ; stiffness also comes on after prolonged sitting (long drives, desk jobs). Crepitus , locking or sticking. Lost range : trouble getting in and out of a car, bending, rotating. An antalgic gait , with a shorter stance phase on the sore side. Look: a leg length discrepancy, either caused by the arthritis or predisposing to it. Feel: the joint is too deep to palpate. Palpation helps more for neighbours like iliopsoas tendinopathy , which is tender, and more so on resisted flexion. Move: internal rotation is lost first ; abduction and external rotation go later. Special tests: FABER, Stinchfield, FADIR (below). Test How Positive FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation) The figure-four position. Press down on the opposite ASIS and on the bent knee. Pain in the anterior groin . Always ask where it hurts: pain at the knee or the ASIS doesn't count. Stinchfield Supine, the patient lifts the straight leg, heel about a foot off the bed, against your hand: resisted hip flexion Groin pain FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) Flex the hip and knee, then adduct and internally rotate Groin pain Hip osteoarthritis on x-ray. Slide from the deck. The FADIR test. Slide from the deck. Stinchfield and FABER. Slide from the deck. The X-ray Isn't the Patient Hip OA is a clinical diagnosis . An x-ray confirms it and can track progression, though that isn't always needed. Radiographic changes don't correlate with symptoms : some people with severe OA on film have few symptoms, and some with marked symptoms have little OA on film. CT and MRI aren't needed for the diagnosis. Order them to look for secondary causes, to rule other diagnoses in or out, or for surgical planning. Step Treatment Non-drug (always first) Education about OA, its prognosis and progression. Exercise , above all strengthening the muscles around the hip , with a physiotherapist or trainer. Short of

Labral Tear Who Any age, but commonly active females Pain Often a vague groin pain at first, with clicking, catching, snapping and occasionally locking Exam FABER and FADIR are often positive, as in most intra-articular hip problems Imaging An x-ray , usually normal, to exclude other pathology; an MR arthrogram is the study of choice Treatment Start with the general hip pain approach: physio and strengthening. If that fails, arthroscopic labral debridement or repair . A torn acetabular labrum. Slide from the deck.

Avascular Necrosis (Osteonecrosis) The bone dies when its blood flow is disrupted . The hip, specifically the femoral head , is the most common site because its supply is so tenuous: it comes up the neck from the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries (see the Hip Joint ). It usually presents as anterior groin pain . Common causes Less common Trauma : a femoral neck injury tears the circumflex arteries. Steroids , whether oral, intramuscular or intra-articular. Alcohol . Lupus , sickle cell disease , radiation to the area Steroids Plus New Hip Pain: X-ray Now A patient on oral steroids who develops significant hip pain, or anyone who gets new hip pain after an intramuscular or intra-articular steroid injection , needs an x-ray right away to look for avascular necrosis. If they're on oral steroids, also ask whether the drug is still the right one for them.

Greater Trochanteric Bursitis A very common cause of lateral hip pain . Chronic friction of the IT band over the greater trochanter irritates the trochanteric bursa that sits on it. It's much more common in females , probably because wider hips change the biomechanics through the hip and femur. Diagnosis Clinical. Point tenderness over the greater trochanter is highly sensitive: if pressing on it doesn't hurt, bursitis is very unlikely. Weight bearing Makes it worse . Gluteus medius and minimus, the big hip abductors, work hard in stance phase to keep the pelvis level, right over the irritated bursa. Sleep Can't lie on that side ; side sleepers wake in pain Radiation Up into the buttock along gluteus medius, and/or down the thigh toward the knee along the IT band Skin No visible swelling, redness or skin changes: the bursa is too deep Story Often an inciting event or a recent increase in activity ; imaging is rarely needed Exam Positive Ober's test and point tenderness over the greater trochanter Treatment Physio: stretch the IT band, strengthen the hip abductors . PRICE, NSAIDs, a corticosteroid injection into the bursa. The trochanteric bursa sits between the IT band and the greater trochanter. Slide from the deck.

Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome Bursitis is only half the story. -itis means active, acute inflammation; -osis means chronic degeneration. Very often there's an overuse, chronic tendinopathy (tendinosis) of gluteus medius and minimus , which insert on the greater trochanter, and it sets off acute flares of bursitis and tendinitis . That combination is greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) . It matters because the chronic tendinopathy needs treating, not just the flare. Presentation Like trochanteric bursitis, but more chronic or recalcitrant . It hasn't settled with IT band stretches and a bursa injection, because the tendinopathy was never addressed. Single-leg stance test The patient stands on the affected leg for at least 30 seconds . Positive if it brings on pain over the greater trochanter, perhaps into the buttock or down to the knee. It's sensitive for both GTPS and trochanteric bursitis. Onset Insidious and worsening over time, or a sudden flare after unaccustomed exercise, a fall, prolonged weight bearing or sporting overuse (especially long-distance running ) Imaging Often an x-ray , because it's recalcitrant: are we missing something? Ultrasound or MRI to look for a complete tear or a different diagnosis Treatment Stretch the IT band, but focus on strengthening the hip abductors and load management : pacing, so the muscles aren't overused again. Weight management if appropriate. Short courses of NSAIDs. Injections aren't curative : they settle the pain long enough to do the strengthening, which is often too painful otherwise. Shockwave therapy (ESWT) and therapeutic ultrasound have only weak evidence. Surgery is an option for complete tears, unless the tear is very chronic with marked fatty atrophy.

GTPS or Hip OA? Arthritic pain can wrap around the hip and be felt laterally, so these two get confused. One question helps: "Can you put your socks on?" GTPS Hip OA History Pain on activity over the lateral buttock; pain lying on that side that disrupts sleep Morning stiffness; associated groin pain; a progressive course Exam Tender greater trochanter ; pain on single-leg stance at 30 seconds Trouble putting on socks ; reduced range of motion; pain on internal and external rotation Sorting lateral hip pain. Slide from the deck. Why Socks Separate Them Putting on socks sitting down takes hip flexion and external rotation , which is basically a FABER test. That hurts an arthritic hip. In GTPS the hip joint itself moves freely, and sitting puts no weight on the trochanter, so socks are easy. Ask them to stand on that leg instead: single-leg stance loads the tendinopathic hip abductors and hurts in GTPS. Knowledge check A 71-year-old woman has lateral hip pain, and the history could fit either GTPS or hip OA. She says she has absolutely no difficulty getting her socks on in the morning when she's sitting down. Which is more likely? → GTPS .

Piriformis Syndrome This can be a typical muscle strain or tendinopathy with pain in the buttock , treated like any MSK problem. Piriformis can also impinge the sciatic nerve , giving radicular symptoms down the leg . The nerve normally exits below the muscle, but variants are common: a divided nerve can pass through or above piriformis, or the nerve can split the muscle. You don't need to know the types. Details Causes Trauma to the buttock (a swollen piriformis presses on the nerve); prolonged sitting (cab drivers, office workers); anatomic anomalies; perhaps piriformis hypertrophy Symptoms Pain in the buttock, worse getting out of bed, with prolonged sitting and with hip movements Palpation Tender over piriformis. Start at the greater trochanter and move toward the sacrum, around the 10 to 11 o'clock line. If pressing there reproduces the radicular symptoms, think of sciatic irritation. Investigations Usually none. Ultrasound or MRI if other conditions are in the differential. An EMG if you suspect sciatic nerve involvement. Treatment Physio ( stretch piriformis , range of motion, deep massage), a short course of NSAIDs, an ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection into piriformis, and surgery if all of that fails Test How Positive PACE Seated; resisted abduction and external rotation of the thigh Buttock pain Beatty Side-lying, knee flexed; lift the knee off the table and hold it in abduction Buttock pain FAIR Flexion, adduction, internal rotation Buttock pain Freiberg Forceful internal rotation of the extended thigh Buttock pain When there are many tests for one condition, none of them is very good. Do several: the more that are positive, the more likely the diagnosis. Piriformis and the sciatic nerve , with the nerve's variants. Slide from the deck. Finding piriformis : from the greater trochanter toward 10 or 11 o'clock. Slide from the deck.

Snapping Hip Syndrome A snapping sensation around the hip is super common : lots of muscles, tendons and ligaments slide over lots of bony prominences. Two rules. First, if it isn't painful, don't worry about it . Second, if it is painful, ask where they feel the snap and what structures are there. Dr. VanderEnde says not to memorize which snap comes from where; the table is just for understanding. Where it snaps Likely structure Deep (intra-articular) OA with loose bodies; a labral tear Anterior Iliopsoas over a bony prominence Lateral The IT band or gluteus maximus over the greater trochanter Posterior The hamstrings over the ischial tuberosity For a muscle problem, stretch and strengthen the muscle. A bony problem can't be changed without surgery, and there's little we can do to a ligament , so in both cases start by stretching and strengthening the muscles. After that, consider an injection, then surgery if it still isn't working.

Explain what each ligament prevents , how it's injured and how it's tested . Describe the presentation, evaluation, treatment and return to play of ACL, PCL, MCL, LCL and meniscal injuries , and the unhappy triad . entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: Bones of the Knee The femur, tibia and fibula meet here, along with the patella , a sesamoid bone that sits inside the quadriceps tendon. There are three articulations : lateral femoral condyle with lateral tibial condyle, medial with medial, and patella with femur. Most people guess the fibula is the third, but the fibula plays no part in the knee joint . Landmark Why it matters Femoral condyles (medial, lateral) The articulating surfaces. They're larger at the back, where they roll on the tibia in flexion. Femoral epicondyles Where the collateral ligaments attach Intercondylar fossa (notch) The gap between the femoral condyles, where the cruciate ligaments sit Tibial condyles and the intercondylar eminence The eminence is the bumpy ridge between the tibial condyles, where ligaments attach. Together they form the tibial plateau , the top of the tibia. Tibial tuberosity Where the patellar tendon ends Patellar surface of the femur Covered in articular (hyaline) cartilage, which makes the patellofemoral joint space seen on x-ray Knee x-ray view What it's good for AP and lateral The standard views: condyles, eminence, tibial tuberosity, patella Skyline (axial) The patellofemoral joint and patellar fractures Tunnel Loose bodies or bone fragments in the joint Because x-ray images are superimposed, you can see the patella's inferior pole through the femur even on a posterior view. Anterior view and AP x-ray. Slide from the deck. The skyline view of the patellofemoral joint. Slide from the deck. Posterior view and the tunnel radiograph. Slide from the deck.

entries.t: The Capsule and What Holds the Knee Together
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: The Capsule and What Holds the Knee Together Recall the three sources of joint stability from MSK basics: the bony fit , the passive stabilizers (ligaments) and the dynamic stabilizers (muscles). At the knee the surfaces are incongruent, so compared with the hip the bony fit is very unstable . The knee relies on its ligaments and, most of all, on the muscles around it, especially the quadriceps . It's the largest joint in the body, with the largest capsule and synovial membrane. Side Reinforced by Anterior The quadriceps tendon , which actually replaces the capsule here, with the patella inside it. Aponeurotic extensions of vastus medialis and lateralis form the medial and lateral patellar retinacula . The IT band blends in laterally. Medial The medial (tibial) collateral ligament : strong, long, broad and flat, femoral epicondyle to tibia, with deep fibres firmly attached to the medial meniscus . Muscles add support: the pes anserinus (sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus: "SGT"), semimembranosus and the medial head of gastrocnemius. Lateral The lateral (fibular) collateral ligament : a strong, rounded, cord-like ligament from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the head of the fibula . It's a distinct structure, attached to nothing else ; the popliteus tendon passes deep to it. Biceps femoris and the IT band add support. Posterior A true fibrous capsule, without the tendon extensions seen in front. The oblique popliteal ligament is an expansion of the semimembranosus tendon. The arcuate popliteal ligament runs from the fibular head over popliteus. Popliteus and the gastrocnemius tendons give dynamic support. The front : the quadriceps tendon and retinacula form the capsule. Slide from the deck. The back : a true fibrous capsule. Slide from the deck (the cadaveric photo beside it is cropped off). Patellar Tendon or Patellar Ligament? Some call the part from the patella to the tibial tuberosity the patellar ligament . Dr. Martin disagrees: a sesamoid bone forms inside a tendon , so the whole thing is the patellar tendon . She won't mark "patellar ligament" wrong, but thinking of it as one tendon makes the anatomy make sense. Supply Detail (from the notes) Nerves Hilton's law : a joint is supplied by the nerves to the muscles that act on it. For the knee that's the femoral and sciatic nerves, plus articular branches of the obturator and saphenous nerves. Arteries The genicular anastomosis : four genicular branches of the popliteal artery (superior and inferior

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: The Collateral and Cruciate Ligaments The cruciates are named for where they attach on the tibial plateau . The ACL rises from the front of the plateau and runs back and laterally to the inner side of the lateral femoral condyle. The PCL rises from the back of the plateau and runs forward and medially to the inner side of the medial femoral condyle. They cross, hence "cruciate". Both are inside the joint capsule but outside the synovial membrane , which wraps around in front of them; synovial fluid would break down their tissue. Ligaments from the front , knee flexed. Slide from the deck (cadaveric photo cropped off). Ligaments from behind . Note how separate the LCL is and how big the PCL is. Slide from the deck (cadaveric photo cropped off). ACL PCL Strength Thinner and weaker ; torn more often Broader and stronger ; torn less often Tight in Extension (lax in flexion) Flexion (lax in extension) Foot planted (tibia fixed) Stops the femur moving posteriorly on the tibia Stops the femur moving anteriorly on the tibia, which is why it's busy when you walk or run downhill Foot free (femur fixed) Stops the tibia moving anteriorly under the femur Stops the tibia moving posteriorly under the femur Also (notes) Resists hyperextension and excessive medial rotation of the tibia — Tests Lachman (knee at about 30°, draw the tibia forward): the gold standard. Anterior drawer (hip at 45°, knee at 90°, check the hamstrings are relaxed, draw the tibia forward). Pivot shift . Posterior drawer (push the tibia back), sag sign , reverse Lachman Which Bone Is Moving? A cruciate only "does" something to one bone when the other bone is fixed, so always describe it that way. Dr. Martin pictures a planted foot , as in a sports injury: the tibia is fixed while the femur keeps going or gets hit. Do the same in clinical skills. In the Lachman and drawer tests, ask yourself which bone you're fixing and which you're moving. You hold the femur and pull the tibia forward to test the ACL, or push it back to test the PCL. What each cruciate stops. Slide from the deck. The cruciates are outside the synovial membrane. Slide from the deck (Netter). Because the PCL is so strong, it's injured less often. When it goes, it's usually a dashboard injury . A seated driver has the knee flexed; the dashboard hits the front of the tibia just below the tuberosity and drives the tibia backward under the femur. That can rupture the PCL. The force is big enough to injure the patellar tendon or avulse the

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: ACL Injury Knee case 1: a pivoting injury A 27-year-old football player plants his left foot and pivots to change direction to the right. He feels his knee "move" as it gives way, collapses, and can't bear weight because of significant pain and swelling. The video shows a player injured exactly this way while celebrating. → an ACL tear . ACL injury Risk factors Female (4.5:1); pivoting sports (football, rugby, soccer; much less in running or cycling); anatomic and biomechanical factors Mechanism Non-contact in 60–80% : cutting or pivoting while decelerating. The pivot adds rotation, with the femur turning externally and the tibia internally, which loads the ACL until it snaps. Contact in about 30% : a direct blow causing hyperextension or valgus, often injuring the MCL too. Presentation A "pop" : it isn't the ligament snapping but the lateral femoral condyle slamming back onto the tibial plateau . That bone contusion is also the main source of pain, so the pain is often lateral . Immediate swelling (hemarthrosis). A sense of instability or "giving out". Evaluation The history often makes the diagnosis. Lachman has the best sensitivity and specificity; the anterior drawer is clinically not as good; the pivot shift is done mostly in the operating room. X-rays rule out fractures and are usually normal. MRI if you can't tell on exam, or for surgical planning. Treatment PRICE (protected rest, ice, compression, elevation), weight bearing as tolerated, crutches as needed (often a couple of weeks before they trust the knee). Physio is crucial : it keeps range of motion and prevents quadriceps disuse atrophy , which makes recovery much harder. Refer to orthopedics for reconstruction . The graft can be patellar tendon, semitendinosus or gracilis tendon, or donor (cadaveric) or bovine tissue, depending on the surgeon and the patient. Return to play 9–12 months after surgery , closer to 12 for most people (some pros go back sooner); a 3–6% reinjury rate

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: PCL Injury PCL injury Mechanism A direct blow to the anterior tibia with the knee flexed (the dashboard injury), or hyperextension Presentation Poorly defined pain , sometimes posterior; minimal swelling . Much less common than ACL tears, and often associated with meniscal and chondral injuries . Evaluation History (a flexed knee hit on the tibia) and exam: posterior drawer , sag sign , reverse Lachman . X-rays and stress x-rays show the sag and help grade it. MRI looks for the associated injuries, especially a posterolateral corner injury. Treatment Physio is generally sufficient , plus PCL bracing. Surgical reconstruction if conservative care fails, if there's rotatory instability, or with posterolateral corner injuries. Return to play About 50% return to the same or a higher level of activity

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: MCL and LCL Injuries MCL (medial) LCL (lateral) How common Very common Uncommon, especially in isolation Cause Almost always a collision ; a valgus force (a blow to the outside of the knee) stretches the medial side Almost always a collision; a varus force (high energy). Blows to the inside of the knee are rarer, which is why LCL injuries are rarer. Swelling Minimal to none None in isolation Associations Sometimes medial meniscal tears , since its fibres attach to the meniscus. A complete tear often comes with an ACL tear . PCL injuries (it isn't attached to the lateral meniscus, so meniscal tears are less linked) Severity Like any ligament injury, from a sprain (the ligament is still intact) to a complete tear Exam (notes) Valgus stress on the flexed knee Varus stress on the flexed knee Treatment Early range of motion and bracing , plus strengthening for stability Bracing ; surgical repair if there are other injuries or instability Valgus force: the MCL tears. Slide from the deck. Varus force: the LCL tears. Slide from the deck. Knowledge check A basketball player comes down from a jump shot and an opponent lands on the outside of her knee, forcing her lower leg away from her body. She has immediate medial knee pain with minimal swelling. → MCL : a valgus force sprains it. The ACL can tear as part of the unhappy triad, but that usually means significant swelling and a higher-energy mechanism. The PCL goes with hyperextension or dashboard injuries, the LCL with varus force.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: Meniscus Anatomy and Function Knee case 2: a twisting injury A 23-year-old hockey player falls awkwardly on the ice with his skate caught under another player. His knee rotates and he has immediate medial pain. There's no obvious swelling at first, but a moderate amount develops later that night. → a meniscal tear . The menisci are fibrocartilage . They're thick at the margins and thin toward the centre , which makes the femoral and tibial surfaces fit better. Dr. Martin's image: they turn the tibial plateau from a dinner plate into a pasta bowl . They deepen and stabilize the joint and act as shock absorbers for this heavily loaded joint. They're firmly attached in the middle (the intercondylar area) and movable at their outer margins. A transverse ligament links them in front so they move together as the femur rolls; you don't need its name. Medial meniscus Lateral meniscus Shape C-shaped , broader posteriorly Nearly circular , smaller Attachment Firmly adhered to the MCL , so less mobile Freely movable , separate from the LCL; the popliteus tendon passes nearby Injury Torn more often , usually along with the MCL Less susceptible to injury The menisci from above. Slide from the deck (Netter). Vascular rim, avascular centre. Slide from the deck (Netter). Where It Tears Decides Whether It Heals Fibrocartilage has no blood supply of its own. The peripheral meniscus is richly supplied from the surrounding soft tissue, so a tear there can heal and can be repaired . The central meniscus is avascular and is nourished only by synovial fluid, so a tear there won't heal on its own. Between the two is a watershed zone: the red–red, red–white and white–white zones.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: Locking and Unlocking the Knee In the last 15–20° of extension , the shapes of the condyles and menisci make the femur rotate medially on the tibia . If the foot is free, the tibia rotates laterally instead; you can see it if you watch your shin as you straighten your knee sitting down. This screw-home mechanism tightens the ligaments, especially the ACL, MCL and LCL, and locks the knee for quiet standing with little muscle work, like the hip screwing into the acetabulum in extension. To unlock it, popliteus contracts and rotates the femur laterally about 5° before flexion can start. It also pulls the lateral meniscus back during flexion. Screw home, then popliteus unlocks. Slide from the deck. So Why "Don't Lock Your Knees"? Locking out for a short spell of quiet standing is perfectly fine. Over long periods of standing , though, active muscles keep the blood circulating so it doesn't pool in the legs. In sport , a locked knee that gets bumped is more likely to be injured than one held by contracting muscles. Knowledge check Label the dissected knee (a cadaveric photo, so it isn't shown here). It's a right knee seen from behind, with the fibula on the lateral side. A is the lateral collateral ligament and B the medial collateral ligament. C is the lateral meniscus, the disc shape, clearly separate from A. D is the medial meniscus, which flows straight into the MCL. E and F are the ACL and PCL, identified by where they attach on the tibial plateau: front and back.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: Meniscal Tears Meniscal injury Mechanism It depends on age and degeneration . A young knee with no degenerative change needs a bigger, higher-velocity injury. A degenerative knee is inherently less stable, so something as small as planting a foot and twisting while getting out of a car can tear it. Usually it's rotation or twisting with the foot planted . Presentation Medial or lateral joint line pain , right after the injury or delayed (in degenerative tears often by a day or two). Delayed or intermittent swelling : a little discomfort, then they wake the next day with a swollen, painful knee. Mechanical symptoms (locking, catching) aren't always present but are worth asking about, along with any loss of end range . Exam The two biggest findings are a joint effusion and joint line tenderness . McMurray and Thessaly tests exist, but they're not very sensitive or specific; as usual, many tests means none is great. So lean on the mechanism, the effusion and the tenderness. Imaging X-rays are usually normal, especially in the young, but they show how much OA a degenerative knee has. MRI if conservative treatment is failing or a large tear is suspected; consider it earlier in a young patient with a significant injury. Vascular zones and tear types. The types don't need to be known, only that there are several. Slide from the deck (Brukner and Khan). Treatment Degenerative tear Traumatic tear (the young) Physio The mainstay. Active physio : keep or improve range of motion and strengthen the quadriceps and hamstrings , which stabilizes the knee and makes future tears less likely. Always start here. If they're much better within weeks, no further workup is needed. Medication Oral over-the-counter drugs are all that's needed; a short NSAID course if there's swelling. An intra-articular corticosteroid can calm the pain enough to allow active physio. Over-the-counter drugs. An intra-articular steroid isn't a bad idea, depending on age and comorbidities (the slide queries it). Bracing, activity changes Accommodative , not corrective: they don't fix the tear, but they're reasonable here Avoid early accommodations in the young, who'd live with them for decades (the slide queries it) Surgery Depends on the OA . With moderate to severe OA, arthroscopic repair or debridement doesn't help ; persistent flares mean a knee arthroplasty , the last resort. With minimal or no OA, arthroscopy is possible, but only after a proper conservative trial, and outcomes aren't great. Earl

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 1
entries.x: The Unhappy Triad (1) A forced valgus stretches the MCL , which tears from the joint. (2) The medial meniscus is attached to the MCL, so the force carries into it, giving a bucket-handle tear . (3) With the medial side opened, abduction, external rotation and slight flexion load the ACL , which tears. The result, MCL + medial meniscus + ACL , is an extremely significant injury. MCL, then medial meniscus, then ACL. Slide from the deck. Knowledge check Which structures are injured in a classic unhappy triad? → the ACL, MCL and medial meniscus . Not the LCL, PCL, lateral meniscus or fibular head.
