entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 2
entries.x: Keeping the Patella on Track The knee has little bony stability, so it leans heavily on dynamic support from the surrounding muscles. The most important is the quadriceps , which forms the anterior capsule and carries the patella in its tendon. Several forces act on the patella. The patellar tendon pulls it down toward the tibial tuberosity. The quadriceps tendon pulls it up, but along the line of the femur, which slants, not straight up and down. The angle between those two lines of pull is the Q-angle , and their resultant pulls the patella laterally , so it tends to sublux laterally. The IT band and the rest of the quadriceps all pull laterally too; only vastus medialis pulls medially . Q-angle The angle between a line from the ASIS to the middle of the patella and a line from the patella to the tibial tuberosity . It's greater in females : wider hips set the femur, and so the quadriceps' line of pull, further out. Genu valgum (knock-knees; notes) The femur sits at a sharper angle: a bigger Q-angle and more weight through the lateral condyles Genu varum (bow legs; notes) The femur is more vertical: a smaller Q-angle and more weight through the medial condyles Two Defences Against Lateral Subluxation (1) The pull of vastus medialis , which keeps the patella centred in the groove between the femoral condyles. (2) An extra buttress of bone : the lateral side of the femur's patellar surface (the lateral femoral condyle) stands higher than the medial. If the lateral pull is strong enough to override them, the patella keeps rubbing against that buttress . That extra contact is patellofemoral pain syndrome , with wear on the lateral patellar facet and the lateral patellar surface of the femur. Q, P and the lateral resultant R. Slide from the deck. Vastus medialis and the lateral buttress. Slide from the deck. A wider pelvis, a bigger Q-angle. Slide from the deck.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 2
entries.x: Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome (PFPS) Knee case 3: anterior knee pain An 18-year-old woman has 3 months of worsening anterior knee pain in both knees. There was no injury, but she recently started running. At first it hurt only with exercise; now it hurts with prolonged sitting and on stairs . There's no swelling , and she describes a deep anterior aching pain. → a fairly classic PFPS . PFPS What A clinical syndrome of anterior knee pain during or after repetitive loading of the extensor mechanism . The lateral pull drags the patellar facets against the lateral femoral condyle, which irritates it. Risk factors Females, adolescents ; an increased tibiofemoral angle and Q-angle . Less common in males, whose shallower Q-angle pulls less laterally. Presentation Very common (a 30% lifetime prevalence). Usually a gradual onset from biomechanical overload: a new hobby, or more running or anything else that loads knee flexion and extension. It can also follow trauma (a patellar contusion). The pain is anterior and aching , worse after activity and with prolonged sitting . There's no joint swelling and no radicular component: the pain stays around the knee. Evaluation A clinical diagnosis from the history and exam; no imaging is needed . X-rays or an MRI are sometimes ordered to rule out other problems if it isn't responding to treatment. Treatment Activity modification : dial back whatever provokes it. Physio , mainly strengthening vastus medialis (terminal extension exercises) to balance vastus lateralis and correct the dynamic misalignment. Bracing or taping can help the pain but is accommodative: it corrects nothing. Then a graduated return to play once the pain has settled. Knowledge check Which treatments could be offered for PFPS? (Select all.) → knee bracing, activity modification and strengthening vastus medialis . Not "taping the patella to prevent medial translation in flexion": the problem is lateral translation, and tape that prevents lateral translation would help. Not arthroscopy or arthroplasty: knee surgery hasn't been shown to improve PFPS.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 2
entries.x: Knee Bursitis Bursae protect the tendons crossing the knee from rubbing on bone, and the knee has many of them. Bursitis is irritation or swelling of a bursa, usually from chronic friction . It's a clinical diagnosis : mild swelling and tenderness over the bursa, developing slowly. Treat with PRICE and perhaps a short course of NSAIDs . Bursa Where (notes) Bursitis Prepatellar Superficial to the patella; lets the skin move freely over it Housemaid's knee : friction between the skin and the patella, in people who move around and work on their knees Infrapatellar (superficial and deep) Superficial and deep to the patellar ligament Clergyman's knee (the superficial one): friction between the skin and the tibial tuberosity, in people who kneel upright on hard surfaces for long periods Suprapatellar Deep to the quadriceps tendon; attached to the synovial membrane and to a small muscle, articularis genu , which pulls it tight in extension so the tendon and patella glide over the femur One of the three that most often swell The suprapatellar, prepatellar and infrapatellar bursae. Slide from the deck (Netter). Don't Confuse It With Septic bursitis : significant redness and heat, or systemic symptoms that suggest infection. Trauma : if there was an injury, look for the associated injuries. A slow, gradual onset of mild swelling and tenderness over the bursa points to plain bursitis.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 2
entries.x: Popliteal (Baker's) Cyst A cystic extension of the synovial cavity (or the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa) into the popliteal fossa through a defect in the posterior capsule . It's a pouch of fluid connected to the knee joint. It rarely arises on its own: another knee problem raises the synovial fluid, and the swelling escapes backward through the defect. Baker's cyst Presentation (adults) An uncomfortable swelling in the popliteal fossa . It may limit flexion , since it takes up space, and it can grow large enough to reach the mid-calf . Investigations Ultrasound confirms the cyst and helps rule out the differential. An x-ray looks for other orthopedic injuries. MRI if it isn't improving, because ultrasound is imperfect at excluding a soft-tissue tumour and can't see inside the joint. Differential Popliteal artery aneurysm , a soft-tissue tumour , DVT , a meniscal cyst Treatment Conservative for the first 6 weeks , unless there's vascular or neural compromise : the popliteal artery and the tibial and common fibular nerves run right there. Compromise means investigating and managing sooner, possibly surgically. Conservative care is PRICE and NSAIDs , which is usually enough. If the knee is painful and swollen, an intra-articular corticosteroid injection helps: settle the joint and you settle the cyst. Not settling at 6 weeks MRI and surgical referral . The surgeon treats the intra-articular cause . Simply removing the cyst rarely works: the posterior capsule is hard to repair perfectly, so the cyst comes back with the next swelling. A Baker's cyst in a drawing and on MRI. Slide from the deck.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 2
entries.x: IT Band Friction Syndrome It's covered with the hip, but it presents as knee pain because the IT band inserts on the lateral knee. The IT band rubs over the lateral femoral epicondyle during stance phase; the friction happens below 30° of knee flexion. Mechanism Running , especially excessive downhill running; friction is less likely with sprinting Presentation An aching lateral knee pain during running , gradually getting worse Treatment Stretch the IT band , PRICE and a graduated return to exercise Where the IT band rubs. Slide from the deck (Brukner and Khan). Knowledge check Which findings fit IT band friction syndrome? (Select all.) → pain at the insertion of the IT band, a positive Ober's test, and lateral knee pain that gets worse with running . It's worse running downhill , not with sprinting or running uphill. A positive McMurray's sign is a meniscal finding. The IT band is extra-articular, so there's no effusion. Pain on valgus stress points to the MCL, not the IT band. Also on the medial side, just below the knee: pes anserine bursitis , under the insertions of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus. It's covered in the approach below.

entries.t: Corticosteroid, Hyaluronic Acid, PRP, Stem Cells
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 2
entries.x: Corticosteroid, Hyaluronic Acid, PRP, Stem Cells Injection What it is Benefits Limitations Corticosteroid ("steroid", "cortisone") Local delivery of a potent anti-inflammatory, for joint, bursa and tendon disorders Rapid onset ; inexpensive (under $20) Short-acting (4–12 weeks). There's weak evidence of chondrotoxicity and OA progression when injected into the joint (a 2017 JAMA trial of triamcinolone vs saline). It probably builds up with repeated injections, and no one knows how many is too many. So not every 3 months for a 20-year-old, but much less worry at 85. Hyaluronic acid Found naturally in synovial fluid; FDA-approved for intra-articular use in 2001. Replacing it theoretically restores viscoelasticity , so better shock absorption and lubrication. Lasts longer: more than 26 weeks . A good safety profile , without the chondrotoxicity concern. Expensive ($300–500); heterogeneous studies. Overall, no better than corticosteroid for pain or function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP; not testable) The patient's own blood (20–60 mL), centrifuged or filtered down to 3–10 mL with supraphysiologic platelets and growth factors, then injected into a joint, tendon, ligament or muscle Might improve repair or regeneration of tissue; this hasn't been seen Very expensive ($500–1,500), paid by the patient, since it isn't OHIP-covered. Studies carry a high risk of bias (it's a money-maker) and preparation isn't standardized . A 2014 Cochrane review of 19 RCTs (1,088 patients) in soft-tissue injuries and as a surgical adjunct found no clinically significant improvement over placebo. The 2010 IOC consensus said firm recommendations can't be given. Mesenchymal stem cells (not testable) Claimed to regenerate articular cartilage, which hasn't been shown Not shown to be better than other injections Very limited human studies; $3,000–10,000 . In May 2019 Health Canada said stem cell therapies are drugs that need formal approval after rigorous review. Dr. VanderEnde actively counsels patients against them. What Injections Are Actually For Dr. VanderEnde starts with corticosteroid , because it's covered and inexpensive, and he talks through the possible toxicity with patients. In meta-analyses the pain and function outcomes are about the same for corticosteroid, hyaluronic acid and PRP. No injection is the whole treatment, and none of them removes the arthritis. Take knee OA: the aim is to optimize conservative care to delay surgery as long as possible, and the mainstay is physio

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 2
entries.x: History Ask about Details Symptoms Pain and its quality (aching, burning, throbbing, stabbing). Inflammatory signs (swelling, stiffness, redness, warmth). Always ask about neurologic symptoms (tingling, shooting pain, numbness, heaviness of the leg when walking or standing). Function Structural : instability, catching, giving way, locking . Does it lock in one position, or have they lost range because it locks out? Pain or neurologic : weakness, limping, trouble walking. Provoking factors Weight bearing (walking, standing, running), uphill or downhill, stairs (up or down), sitting , inactivity

entries.t: Traumatic Knee Pain: When Did It Swell?
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 2
entries.x: Traumatic Knee Pain: When Did It Swell? After trauma Think of Swelling within 6 hours ACL tear (especially with the plant, pivot, pop and immediate swelling), fractures (any trauma big enough: don't miss them), patellar dislocation , large chondral injuries Swelling after 6 hours An OA flare , meniscal injuries , a PCL injury , an MCL sprain (high grade). MCL injuries rarely swell much, so an MCL injury that swells is usually a higher grade, toward a complete tear. No swelling: anterior A PFPS flare; prepatellar or infrapatellar bursitis No swelling: posterior A PCL injury; a gastrocnemius or hamstring strain; a popliteus strain No swelling: medial An MCL sprain; an OA flare; a hamstring strain No swelling: lateral IT band bursitis; an OA flare; a biceps femoris injury; a superior tibiofibular joint injury No swelling: diffuse Pain that can't be pinned to one region

entries.t: Non-Traumatic Knee Pain: Where Is It?
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Knee, Part 2
entries.x: Non-Traumatic Knee Pain: Where Is It? Location Differential Anterior PFPS ; patellar tendinopathy , focal over the patellar tendon; quadriceps tendinopathy, a bit more proximal; infrapatellar and prepatellar bursitis; apophysitis , in children, at the growth plates; a stress fracture of the patella; referred pain from the hip ; neoplasm Posterior A PCL injury; popliteus tendinopathy; gastrocnemius tendinopathy; a Baker's cyst ; biceps femoris tendinopathy; DVT ; neoplasm; referred pain from the hip; radiculopathy Medial A medial meniscal injury; medial knee OA; pes anserine bursitis ; MCL injuries; referred pain from the hip; radiculopathy Lateral IT band friction syndrome ; biceps femoris tendinopathy; a lateral meniscal injury; a peroneal nerve injury ; lateral knee OA; referred pain from the hip; radiculopathy; neoplasm; superior tibiofibular joint pathology Pes Anserine Bursitis: Inject the Bursa, Not the Knee Sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus attach to the tibia just below the knee (see Dr. Martin's anatomy lectures). Bursitis under that insertion isn't knee joint pain and is managed differently. Physio should strengthen the pes anserinus muscles . If an injection is needed, it goes into the bursa : a knee joint injection won't help. So on exam, check whether the tenderness is over the pes anserinus or over the joint line . Think Structures, and Look Above and Below Localize the pain, then list the anatomic structures in that region (Dr. Martin's lectures). Any muscle there can give a tendinopathy, which you treat with the MSK basics. Referred pain from the hip can turn up anywhere in the knee, so examine the joint above and below. Look for radicular symptoms (pain, numbness, tingling), which will make more sense after the neurology unit. Watch for neoplasm red flags : deep night bone pain , unintentional weight loss, unexplained fevers, chills, night sweats, or a history of cancer. When knee pain doesn't respond to conservative care as expected, get advanced imaging so you don't miss one. Knowledge check: the emergency department A 23-year-old soccer player pivots to avoid a defender, feels a "pop" and his left knee gives way. He came off and didn't return to play. It swelled, but he isn't sure when, and he can't bear weight. He's otherwise healthy. Which diagnoses are possible? (Select all.) Diagnosis In the list? The module's feedback Acute meniscal tear Yes Twisting injuries: a flexed knee rotated on a planted foot. Chronic degenerative tears

Learning Objectives Identify the bones and landmarks of the leg and foot , on drawings and on x-rays. Describe the four compartments of the leg : their muscles, actions and nerves. The lab guide says exact origins and insertions won't be tested. Trace the arteries, veins and nerves of the leg, and relate them to compartment syndrome, varicose veins, foot drop and nerve entrapments. Dr. Charys Martin, about an hour over seven recordings. They cover the introduction and osteology, the anterior, lateral and posterior compartments, and the neurovasculature, plus two knowledge-check feedback videos. Dr. Martin asks you to connect this to the regions above (the thigh and knee) and below (the foot and ankle). It's prep for next week's Knee, Leg, Ankle & Foot lab, with the Knee, Parts 1 and 2 . Attachments are left out of the tables below except where they matter clinically; the slides show them.

entries.t: Bones of the Leg and Foot
entries.x: Bones of the Leg and Foot Bone Key points Tibia The leg's weight-bearing bone . It lies just under the skin anteromedially (the "shin bone"), so its periosteum bruises easily . Its condyles form the tibial plateau; the tibial tuberosity takes the patellar tendon; the soleal line on its back is where soleus arises; the medial malleolus passes weight to the talus. Fibula Posterolateral to the tibia. Its head articulates with the tibia above; its lateral malleolus grips the talus below, along with the medial malleolus. It bears no weight , which makes it the bone of choice for grafts ; you can walk, run and jump without part of it. Where Leg Bones Break (Notes) The tibia breaks most often at its narrowest point, between the middle and distal thirds , which is also where its blood supply is poorest. The fibula breaks most often just above the lateral malleolus , when extreme inversion drives the talus against it. The interosseous membrane is strong, so when the tibia breaks the fibula sometimes goes with it. The foot is built like the hand: it has seven tarsal bones in place of the eight carpals, then metatarsals and phalanges. Bone Key points Talus The link between the leg and the foot: it sits between the medial and lateral malleoli , on the calcaneus and behind the navicular. It's the only bone in the body with no muscle or tendon attachments . It passes weight from the tibia to the calcaneus and the forefoot. Calcaneus The heel and the largest foot bone ; it passes weight to the ground. The calcaneal tuberosity at the back takes the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon . The sustentaculum tali , on its medial side, is a shelf for the talus and a pulley for the flexor hallucis longus tendon . Navicular Boat-shaped, in front of the talus. A key ligament attachment : its tuberosity anchors the spring (calcaneonavicular) ligament , which holds up the medial longitudinal arch. Cuboid, cuneiforms "Nice to know, not need to know." The cuboid is the most lateral tarsal. The medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms sit in front of the navicular, and their wedge shape builds the transverse arch . Metatarsals, phalanges The tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal is where fibularis brevis inserts. A sudden inversion can make brevis pull it off: an avulsion fracture . Metatarsals also break when a heavy object lands on the foot, and in the "dancer's fracture" , when a ballet dancer loses balance and comes down with all their weight on the metatarsals. Sesamoid bones Two under the

Fascia and Compartments As everywhere else in the limbs, group the leg muscles by compartment, each with a common function and a common innervation . A thick deep fascia, the crural fascia , wraps the whole leg. The tibia, fibula, interosseous membrane and the anterior and posterior intermuscular septa divide it into anterior, lateral and posterior compartments. The transverse intermuscular septum then splits the posterior compartment into superficial and deep parts. Compartment Where Main job Nerve Artery Anterior Just lateral to the tibia: the meaty part beside your shin Dorsiflexion Deep fibular Anterior tibial Lateral Lateral to the fibula Eversion Superficial fibular Branches of the fibular Superficial posterior The calf Plantarflexion Tibial Posterior tibial Deep posterior Between the interosseous membrane and the transverse septum Plantarflexion, inversion, toe flexion Tibial Posterior tibial and fibular "Fibular" and "peroneal" are both acceptable; clinicians tend to say peroneal. Thickenings of fascia called retinacula hold the tendons against the ankle so they don't bowstring. The superior and inferior extensor retinacula bind the anterior tendons; the inferior one is Y-shaped. The superior and inferior fibular retinacula bind the lateral tendons. The flexor retinaculum runs from the medial malleolus to the calcaneus and roofs the tarsal tunnel . Four compartments in cross-section. Slide from the deck (Netter). Sealed Compartments (Notes) The fascia seals the anterior, lateral and posterior compartments at the joints. Neither swelling nor infection can spread from one compartment to the next. When pus, or inflammation from strenuous or unaccustomed exercise, raises the pressure inside a compartment, the nerves get pinched and the arteries compressed. That's compartment syndrome : painful, with too little oxygen reaching the muscle and bone. A fasciotomy relieves the pressure and lets any infection be debrided. Shin splints are a mild form of anterior compartment syndrome: microtrauma to the tibial periosteum where the anterior compartment muscles attach, especially tibialis anterior. They hit inactive people who suddenly walk or run long distances, and runners who skip their warm-up or cool-down. Movements: dorsiflexion brings the toes toward the shin and plantarflexion points them. Inversion turns the sole inward; it's the classic rolled ankle. Eversion turns the sole outward. You can invert much further than you can evert, because the lateral m

Anterior Compartment: Dorsiflexors Four muscles, all supplied by the deep fibular nerve , all dorsiflexing the ankle . Muscle Action Point Tibialis anterior Dorsiflexes the ankle; inverts the foot The most anterior and medial muscle: the one you feel beside the shin. It ends on the medial side of the foot, which is why it inverts. Shin splints start where it attaches to the tibia. Extensor digitorum longus Dorsiflexes; extends the lateral four toes Lateral to and partly deep to tibialis anterior; splits into four tendons Extensor hallucis longus Dorsiflexes; extends the big toe The deepest of the three, lying on the interosseous membrane. "Hallux" means the big toe. Fibularis (peroneus) tertius Weakly helps dorsiflexion and eversion; may help proprioception A grey-box muscle you don't need to know. It usually shares a belly with extensor digitorum longus and inserts on the dorsum of the 5th metatarsal base. About 20% of people don't have it. Dorsum of the foot (also the deep fibular nerve) Extensor digitorum brevis Helps extend toes 2–4 Works with extensor digitorum longus Extensor hallucis brevis Helps extend the big toe Works with extensor hallucis longus Anterior compartment. Slide from the deck (Netter). Knowledge check Label the dissected anterior compartment (cadaveric photos, so not shown). Tibialis anterior is the meaty muscle beside the tibia. Extensor digitorum longus is the tendon that splits into four. Extensor hallucis longus has its belly deep against the interosseous membrane and its tendon running to the big toe. The extra little tendon running with extensor digitorum longus to the 5th metatarsal is fibularis tertius: you don't need to know it, but that's what it looks like if you find it.

Lateral Compartment: Evertors Two muscles, one superficial and one deep, both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve , both evert the foot . Their tendons are held behind the lateral malleolus by the fibular retinacula. Muscle Action Point Fibularis (peroneus) longus Everts the foot; weakly plantarflexes; supports the transverse arch The superficial one. Its long tendon loops behind the lateral malleolus and then under the foot to the medial plantar foot (the base of the 1st metatarsal and the medial cuneiform). Fibularis (peroneus) brevis The same three actions Deep to longus, arising lower on the fibula. It ends on the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal , the site of the inversion avulsion fracture. Lateral compartment. Slide from the deck (Netter).

Superficial Posterior Compartment: the Calf This is the largest compartment, split by the transverse intermuscular septum. The superficial part holds three muscles, all supplied by the tibial nerve , and they're the strong plantarflexors . All three end on the back of the calcaneus via the calcaneal tendon . Dr. Martin's take: "Achilles tendon" (named after the myth of the arrow) is correct, but "calcaneal tendon" is more correct. Muscle Action Point Gastrocnemius Plantarflexes the ankle when the knee is extended ; raises the heel in walking; flexes the knee The "glory muscle", like biceps: it takes the credit but doesn't do most of the work. Its two heads, from the medial and lateral femoral condyles, form the lower border of the popliteal fossa and give dynamic support behind the knee. It has fast-twitch fibres, for power . Soleus Plantarflexes the ankle, always It does the work. It's the big belly deep to gastrocnemius, with a wide origin from the tibia (the soleal line) and fibula. It has slow-twitch fibres, for endurance , and carries you around all day. Plantaris Weak plantarflexion, if anything (perhaps proprioception) Tiny, with a "dental-floss" tendon running beside the calcaneal tendon. All you need to know is that it exists and is used for tendon grafts ; losing it costs no function. Superficial posterior compartment. Slide from the deck (Netter). Standing or Seated Calf Raise? In a standing calf raise the knee is straight, so gastrocnemius , which crosses the knee, has the mechanical advantage and is the prime mover . In a seated calf raise the knee is bent, which takes gastrocnemius out of the picture: it can't plantarflex at all with the knee flexed. Soleus becomes the prime mover. Soleus still works in the standing raise, and the weaker plantarflexors of the deep compartment help in both. A prime mover isn't the only muscle working. Clinical note Detail Calcaneal tendinitis Microscopic tears in the tendon, usually a little above its attachment; common in runners . Long-term tendinitis can lead to rupture. Calcaneal tendon rupture Usually in poorly conditioned people, during a forceful plantarflexion: an audible snap , then sudden calf pain. A complete rupture leaves a palpable gap , and the patient can't plantarflex against resistance . Surgery is usually advised for the young and active; non-surgical care may be enough for older, non-athletic patients.

entries.t: Deep Posterior Compartment and the Tarsal Tunnel
entries.x: Deep Posterior Compartment and the Tarsal Tunnel Four muscles, again all supplied by the tibial nerve , so the whole posterior compartment, superficial and deep, is tibial. The three long ones pass under the flexor retinaculum , behind the medial malleolus, through the tarsal tunnel , the leg's version of the carpal tunnel. Muscle Action Point Popliteus Unlocks the knee : rotates the femur laterally about 5° on a fixed tibia (or the tibia medially when the foot is free); weakly flexes the knee It sits so high that it isn't in the leg cross-section. Its tendon arises from the lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus. The hamstrings are the strong knee flexors. Flexor digitorum longus ("Dick") Flexes the lateral four toes ; plantarflexes; supports the longitudinal arches In the calf it's the most medial, right against the tibia; it splits into four tendons. Toe flexion is curling the toes under, exactly as in the fingers. Tibialis posterior ("Tom") Plantarflexes (assisting gastrocnemius and soleus); inverts the foot ; supports the longitudinal arch The deepest , lying on the interosseous membrane. In the lab you may need to pull the two flexors aside to find it. It has a wide insertion on the medial plantar foot, mainly the navicular tuberosity. Flexor hallucis longus ("Harry") Flexes the big toe ; weakly plantarflexes; supports the medial longitudinal arch The most lateral , from the fibula. Its tendon loops under the sustentaculum tali , which acts as a pulley for a powerful toe-off : the big toe is the last thing to leave the ground in every step. Tom, Dick and Harry Behind the medial malleolus, from anterior to posterior , the tarsal tunnel holds T ibialis posterior, flexor D igitorum longus, the posterior tibial A rtery, the tibial N erve and flexor H allucis longus: " Tom, Dick, And Not Harry ". The other version, " Tom, Dick, A Very Nervous Harry ", adds the posterior tibial V eins: an artery always has 2–3 veins with it. The tendon order isn't the muscle order. In the calf, from medial to lateral, it's Dick, Tom, Harry , because the tibialis posterior tendon crosses deep to flexor digitorum longus on its way to the ankle. Harry stays the most lateral throughout and goes off on his own under the sustentaculum tali. Deep posterior compartment and the tarsal tunnel. Slide from the deck (Netter). The order in the calf vs the tunnel. Slide from the deck. Tarsal tunnel syndrome (notes): swelling of the tendon sheaths in the tunnel compresses the tibial

Arteries The femoral artery gives the profunda femoris , whose perforating branches supply the posterior thigh. It then passes through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal artery behind the knee. At the lower border of the popliteal fossa, the popliteal artery splits into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries. Artery Course and territory Anterior tibial Passes forward through a gap at the top of the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment. There it runs with the deep fibular nerve , deep to tibialis anterior. Between the malleoli it becomes the dorsalis pedis on the dorsum of the foot, where you can feel a pulse by pressing it against the bones beneath. Dorsalis pedis gives the lateral tarsal and arcuate arteries (the arcuate gives the 2nd–4th dorsal metatarsals), then ends as the deep plantar and 1st dorsal metatarsal arteries. Posterior tibial Stays posterior , in the deep posterior compartment with the tibial nerve , between flexor digitorum longus and tibialis posterior. It supplies the posterior compartment and reaches the foot behind the medial malleolus, through the tarsal tunnel . Fibular (peroneal) The largest branch of the posterior tibial , given off near its origin. It runs down beside the fibula (within flexor hallucis longus) and sends branches to the posterior and lateral compartments. Anterior tibial to dorsalis pedis. Slide from the deck (Netter). Posterior tibial and fibular arteries. Slide from the deck (Netter).

Veins and Venous Return The deep veins lie deep to the deep fascia, accompanying every major artery, usually in pairs or threes. The superficial veins , in the subcutaneous tissue, travel alone. Both have valves, more of them in the deep veins. Perforating veins pierce the deep fascia, and their valves let blood flow only from superficial to deep , away from the skin. Superficial vein Course Great saphenous Starts where the dorsal venous arch meets the dorsal vein of the big toe. It passes in front of the medial malleolus , up the medial leg and behind the medial condyle of the knee. At the top of the thigh it goes through the saphenous opening in the fascia lata into the femoral vein . Small saphenous Starts at the arch and the dorsal vein of the little toe and runs lateral to the calcaneal tendon. It pierces the deep fascia, travels between the two heads of gastrocnemius and drains into the popliteal vein . Getting blood back uphill How Valves Their cusps let blood through toward the heart. When it starts to fall back, the cusps fill and close, opening and closing with every beat like the aortic and pulmonary valves. Arteriovenous pump The paired deep veins share a tight connective-tissue sheath with their artery. Each time the artery expands with a pulse, it flattens the veins and pushes their blood up. The arrangement also works as a countercurrent heat exchanger. Musculovenous pump Contracting muscle bellies expand against the unyielding deep fascia (the crural fascia, the fascia lata) and squeeze the deep veins, "milking" the blood toward the heart . The valves keep it from going back down. Superficial veins : great and small saphenous. Slide from the deck (Netter). Three ways back to the heart. Slide from the deck (Clinically Oriented Anatomy). Varicose Veins The great saphenous vein and its tributaries dilate until the valve cusps no longer meet . Blood then flows down the veins instead of up, and they become varicose. They're common in the posteromedial leg and can be uncomfortable. They can affect any vein but are most visible in the superficial ones. In laser treatment , the heat damages the vein, scar tissue closes it off, and the closed vein loses its blood supply and dies; after a year or two it's likely to disappear. Working valves (B, C) and an incompetent one (D). Slide from the deck; the photos of varicose legs beside it are left out.

Nerves The sciatic nerve (L4–S3) is really two nerves in one sheath, the tibial and common fibular . They separate at the top of the popliteal fossa, though they can divide anywhere higher up. Nerve Course Supplies Tibial Down the back of the leg with the posterior tibial artery, then through the tarsal tunnel ; in the foot it divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves The whole posterior compartment , superficial and deep, then the sole. Gives off the medial sural cutaneous nerve. Common fibular (peroneal) Through the lateral popliteal fossa, then wraps around the neck of the fibula , just under the skin, and splits in two Its superficial and deep branches; gives off the lateral sural cutaneous nerve Superficial fibular Runs in the lateral compartment between fibularis longus and brevis, then pierces the crural fascia to become cutaneous Fibularis longus and brevis ; skin of the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot Deep fibular Arises between fibularis longus and the fibular neck, enters the anterior compartment with the anterior tibial artery, deep to tibialis anterior, then dives into the foot All anterior compartment muscles and the muscles on the dorsum of the foot; only the skin of the first web space Why is the "deep" one anterior and the "superficial" one lateral? Both come from behind. The deep branch travels further, into the anterior compartment, and stays deep all the way into the foot. The superficial branch surfaces to supply the skin of the foot. Tibial nerve and the sural contributions. Slide from the deck (Netter). Common fibular, deep and superficial. Slide from the deck (Netter). Skin nerve From Territory Saphenous Femoral Medial leg and foot Lateral sural cutaneous Common fibular Lateral (posterolateral) leg Medial sural cutaneous Tibial Posterior leg Sural Joined by both sural cutaneous nerves Lateral ankle and foot Superficial fibular Common fibular Anterolateral leg and the dorsum of the foot , except the first web space Deep fibular Common fibular The first web space only Medial and lateral plantar Tibial The sole Cutaneous territories. Slide from the deck (Clinically Oriented Anatomy). Use Sensation to Find the Lesion The common fibular nerve is easily hurt where it wraps around the fibular head and neck, just under the skin. If the dorsum of the foot and the first web space are both numb , the common fibular nerve is damaged. If there's a deficit but the first web space still has feeling , the lesion is below the split

Learning Objectives Identify the distinguishing features of the bones and joints of the upper extremity and relate them to their appearance on plain radiographs . Dr. V. Kalia's interactive module, about 20 minutes: general concepts, then the shoulder, elbow and wrist. The general lesson is repeated in all three P2 radiology modules. For the spine version of the same systematic read (ABCS), see 7.5 .

Basic Concepts for Image Interpretation Everything is described with the body in anatomic position (medial = toward the midline, lateral = away; proximal = closer to the body, distal = farther). Part of a long bone What it is On x-ray Epiphysis The end of the bone; contains a growth centre Physis (growth plate) Where new bone is made during growth A lucent line between epiphysis and metaphysis in children; invisible once fused in the mature skeleton Metaphysis The transition zone between epiphysis and diaphysis Diaphysis The shaft, most of the length Cortex / medullary cavity The dense outer layer / the inner cavity Check both for abnormalities, density changes or generalized bone disease Parts of a long bone. From the module. The same parts on an AP shoulder. From the module. How an x-ray is made: the patient is positioned between the x-ray tube and the image receptor (detector); x-rays are attenuated by the tissues (bone most) on the way through; the computer stores the image in PACS ; a radiologist reads it and sends a report to the ordering physician. 1 Skeletal maturity Fused growth plate = mature; visible, unfused growth plate = immature. 2 Bone integrity Cortex and medullary cavity: any break or lesion? Density changes or generalized bone disease that weakens bone? 3 Alignment Essential for joint function; misalignment means a fracture, dislocation or other injury. 4 Joints Inflammation, joint-space narrowing, degenerative change. 5 Soft tissues Muscle and soft tissue can be abnormal when the bones look normal. TIMS-C: the categories of bone pathology (any body part) Examples T rauma and T umours Fractures, dislocations; bone tumours I nfection, I nflammatory, I diopathic Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis; idiopathic = cause unknown M etabolic / M alignancy S ystemic / S enile Systemic: leukemia, lymphoma. Senile: osteoarthritis C ongenital Looked for mostly in the immature skeleton

Shoulder Radiology Standard views are for general indications such as trauma or osteoarthritis; special views (instability, confirming a dislocation) aren't covered. The module shows the AP, axillary and Y views . View What to find AP The glenoid, humeral head and tuberosities, clavicle, acromion and coracoid. The glenoid's labrum is fibrocartilage, so it isn't visible . Two reference lines (not visible structures) used to describe fractures: the anatomical neck (where head meets neck) and the surgical neck (a transverse line just below the articular surface). Axillary (arm out from the body, beam through the axilla) Harder to read. Find the distal clavicle, acromion (together the AC joint ), glenoid and humerus; some overlap is normal but the joint space shouldn't look widened. The coracoid and the lesser tuberosity both point anteriorly , which orients the film. Watch for an os acromiale (an unfused ossification centre: a lucent line or separate bit of acromion), not a fracture . The anatomical and surgical necks aren't distinguishable here. Y-view The "Y": coracoid = anterior limb, scapular spine = posterior limb, scapular body = vertical limb, with the glenoid at the centre . The humeral head should be centred over (overlapping) the glenoid . Head in front = anterior subluxation or dislocation; behind = posterior. Normal AP shoulder. From the module. Normal axillary view : coracoid and lesser tuberosity are anterior. From the module. Normal Y-view : the head sits on the centre of the Y. From the module. The AC (green) and glenohumeral (pink) joints on the axillary view. From the module. Shoulder pathology What you see Osteoarthritis (age-related degenerative joint disease) (1) Joint-space narrowing from cartilage loss (cartilage is radiolucent, so the space is the cartilage), (2) subchondral sclerosis (denser bone under the surface from stress, not necessarily stronger), (3) marginal osteophytes (new bone at the joint edges as the body tries to stabilize it). Graded mild, moderate or severe on the combination. Surgical neck fracture A fracture line along the surgical neck with mild displacement Dislocation Anterior : the head lies in front of the glenoid, usually subcoracoid (under the coracoid). Posterior : it lies behind, farther from the coracoid. The Y-view tells them apart. A subluxation keeps partial contact with the glenoid; a dislocation is complete loss of contact. Severe shoulder OA : osteophytes (green), a nearly gone joint space, sclerosis.

Elbow Radiology The standard views are the AP (elbow extended on the plate) and the lateral . Radiographs are two-dimensional, so you need the three-dimensional anatomy in your head. View What to find AP Find the medial side first : the medial epicondyle is larger than the lateral, and the ulna is medial . Medial to lateral across the distal humerus: medial epicondyle, trochlea, capitellum, lateral epicondyle ; the coronoid and olecranon fossae. On the ulna, the sublime tubercle : the UCL attaches there, so check it after trauma. The AP is the best view for telling capitellum from trochlea. Lateral (1) The humeral shaft ; the capitellum and trochlea overlap (the capitellum is the one next to the radius, slightly magnified). (2) The proximal ulna : olecranon, trochlear notch, coronoid process, all fracture-prone. (3) The radius : head, neck, radial tuberosity (where biceps attaches), shaft. (4) The fat pads , then the olecranon bursa and soft tissues. Normal AP elbow. From the module. Normal lateral elbow. From the module. Fat pads and the olecranon bursa. From the module. Posterior fat pad sign (right): always abnormal. From the module. The Fat Pad Rule The anterior fat pad is normally seen as a small radiolucent triangle in front of the distal humerus. The posterior fat pad is normally hidden in the olecranon fossa; when a joint effusion lifts it into view, the posterior fat pad sign is always abnormal , usually trauma. Then look hard for a fracture matched to skeletal maturity: a supracondylar fracture in a child (visible epiphysis, physis and metaphysis), a radial head or neck fracture in an adult . Alignment line Normal Abnormal means Anterior humeral line (lateral view, along the anterior humeral cortex) Passes through the centre of the capitellum (slight variation is fine) Through the anterior capitellum, with an elevated posterior fat pad, in an immature skeleton: supracondylar fracture (in an adult, think radial head or neck) Radiocapitellar line (along the radial shaft's axis) Passes through the centre of the capitellum on every view (AP, oblique, lateral) Misses the capitellum: radial head dislocation or another alignment problem (also seen with displaced supracondylar fractures) Anterior humeral line : normal (left pair) and anterior to the capitellum's centre (right pair). From the module. Radiocapitellar line : normal and abnormal. From the module. Elbow pathology What you see Osteoarthritis The same three features (narrowing, subchondral scle

Wrist Radiology The standard views are the AP (hand flat, palm down) and a true lateral (hand on its side). View What to find AP The distal radius and ulna meeting at the DRUJ ; the beak-like ulnar styloid and the broader radial styloid ; the radiocarpal joint ; the two carpal rows; metacarpals 1–5. The circled TFCC region: fibrocartilage, so invisible, but calcification there may mean TFCC pathology . Lateral Trace the dorsal radius to Lister's tubercle (a dorsal bump separating extensor tendon compartments; check it for fractures). The distal radial joint surface, the overlapping ulna and its styloid. Proximal row: scaphoid (anterior), lunate, triquetrum (posterior), pisiform (anterior); distal row: trapezium, capitate, hamate (the trapezoid hides behind the trapezium). So many bones overlap that the AP is essential for spotting fractures . Normal AP wrist and the TFCC area. From the module. The eight carpal bones. From the module. Lateral wrist with Lister's tubercle. From the module. Always radial to ulnar : scaphoid and trapezium on the thumb side, pisiform and hamate on the little-finger side. From the module. Gilula arc Follows 1st The proximal surfaces of the proximal carpal row 2nd The distal surfaces of the proximal row 3rd The proximal surfaces of the distal row All three should be smooth and continuous . A break, step-off, widened joint space or loss of congruity suggests a carpal fracture, subluxation or instability. The three Gilula arcs. From the module. Wrist pathology What you see Scaphoid and triquetrum fractures A thin lucent line through the proximal pole of the scaphoid and another through the triquetrum. Inspect every cortex: any disruption or lucent line is a fracture in the right setting. The Gilula arcs are preserved , so carpal alignment is intact. Distal radius and ulnar styloid fractures A transverse distal radius fracture (displacement and impaction are for the fracture module) and a fracture at the base of the ulnar styloid; carpal alignment maintained. Giant cell tumour (not shown) An expanded distal radius with a large lytic lesion , a markedly thinned cortex, reaching the subarticular surface Scaphoid and triquetrum fractures , arcs preserved. From the module. Distal radius and ulnar styloid fractures. From the module.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 2
entries.x: Learning Objectives Identify the important functional anatomy of the upper extremity as it pertains to clinical presentations: the nerve supply of the hand and the carpal tunnel and its contents. Create a differential diagnosis and management plan for upper extremity numbness, weakness and pain . Describe the anatomic basis, presentation and management of carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar neuropathy at the wrist . Dr. Charys Martin (nerve supply of the hand, 33 minutes) and the wrist and hand neuropathies recording (8 minutes), plus the 10-minute Clinical Approach to the Upper Extremity quiz. This is Part 2; Part 1 covered distal radius and scaphoid fractures and the hand muscles. With it, the whole upper limb is done, so nerve lesion cases can be followed from the brachial plexus to the fingertips. This module is prep for the Distal Upper Extremity lab .

entries.t: The Median Nerve in the Hand
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 2
entries.x: The Median Nerve in the Hand It enters the hand through the carpal tunnel, deep to the flexor retinaculum . Branch Where it goes Why it matters Palmar cutaneous branch Leaves proximal to the carpal tunnel to the skin of the central palm Doesn't pass through the tunnel, so its patch of mid-palm is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome Recurrent branch Runs a superficial course just distal to the tunnel to the thenar muscles : abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head) At risk with a superficial cut to the lateral palm . It must be repaired, or the thenar muscles atrophy and opposition is lost. Dr. Martin calls the median nerve the most important nerve in the hand. Common and proper palmar digital nerves Motor to lumbricals 1 and 2 ; sensory to the lateral palm and the palmar lateral 3½ digits , plus their distal dorsal halves and nail beds Sets the median sensory map you test on exam The median nerve's branches in the hand. Slide from the deck (Netter).

entries.t: The Ulnar Nerve in the Hand
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 2
entries.x: The Ulnar Nerve in the Hand Two cutaneous branches leave proximal to the wrist : the palmar cutaneous branch (over the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis to the medial palm) and the dorsal cutaneous branch (medial half of the back of the hand and the proximal dorsal medial 1½ digits). The nerve itself passes through the ulnar (Guyon's) canal , a fibro-osseous arch between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate , enters the hand lateral to the pisiform, and splits in two. Branch Supplies Superficial branch Skin of the palm and the palmar (and dorsal tip) skin of the medial 1½ digits , via common and proper palmar digital nerves Deep branch The hypothenar muscles (ODM, ADM, FDM), lumbricals 3 and 4 , adductor pollicis , all the interossei and the deep head of FPB ; sensation to the metacarpals and proprioception from the joints The ulnar nerve's branches. Slide from the deck (Netter). Cutaneous territories: median, ulnar, radial. Slide from the deck. Nerve Skin of the hand (the knowledge-check answer key) Median The lateral 3½ palmar digits and the dorsal distal 3½ digits Ulnar The medial 1½ digits , palmar and dorsal Radial (superficial branch) The lateral dorsum of the hand , not including the distal digits Knowledge checks Which of these doesn't pass through the carpal tunnel: median nerve, FDS tendons, FDP tendons, FPL, ulnar artery? → the ulnar artery . It runs with the ulnar nerve through Guyon's canal, superficial to the flexor retinaculum. Match each compartment to its main nerve. → intrinsic hand muscles: ulnar ; anterior arm: musculocutaneous ; anterior forearm: median ; posterior forearm: radial . Feedback points: thumb and finger movements use the midline of the hand as the reference, and different hand presentations point to lesions at different places along a nerve.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 2
entries.x: Nerve Lesions in the Hand Lesion What you see Median nerve: usually forearm or wrist, most often the carpal tunnel At the wrist (carpal tunnel, or a wrist laceration, since the nerve lies close to the surface) Paralysis and wasting of the thenar muscles and lumbricals 1–2. Opposition is impossible, fine control of digits 2–3 is impaired, and sensation is lost over the thumb and adjacent 2½ fingers . Recurrent branch only (a minor cut over the thenar eminence) Thenar paralysis, loss of opposition At the elbow (cubital fossa, or between the two heads of pronator teres) Loss of PIP and DIP flexion (FDS, FDP) and MCP flexion (lumbricals) of digits 2–3: the "hand of benediction" when trying to make a fist Ulnar nerve: behind the medial epicondyle (most common), between the heads of FCU, at the wrist, in the hand Proximal (e.g. at the elbow) Extensive motor and sensory loss in the hand. Wrist flexion is weak and the hand is pulled radially by FCR (no FCU). Digits 4–5 can't flex at the DIP, the MCPs hyperextend and the IPs can't straighten: the ulnar "claw hand" , from the unopposed extensors and FDP once the interossei waste. At the wrist (Guyon's canal: ulnar canal syndrome ) Reduced sensation in the medial 1½ fingers and weak intrinsic hand muscles . Digits 4–5 may claw, but unlike a proximal lesion their flexion is intact and there's no radial deviation . Median nerve at risk: the carpal tunnel. Slide from the deck (Netter); a photo of a patient's hands with thenar wasting is left out. Median nerve at the elbow and the hand of benediction. Slide from the deck (Netter); photos of patients' hands are left out. Ulnar nerve sites at risk and the claw hand. Slide from the deck (Netter); a photo of a patient's hand is left out. Guyon's canal and handlebar neuropathy. Slide from the deck. Brachial plexus injury Roots Mechanism Result Upper: Erb–Duchenne palsy C5–C6 (superior trunk or roots) An excessive increase in the neck–shoulder angle : thrown from a motorcycle, a newborn's neck over-stretched in delivery "Waiter's tip" : shoulder adducted, arm medially rotated, elbow extended; numb lateral upper limb Lower: Klumpke paralysis (less common) C8–T1 (inferior trunk or roots) The upper limb suddenly pulled upward : a baby's arm pulled in delivery, grabbing something to break a fall Affects the ulnar nerve: weak intrinsic hand muscles, a claw hand

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 2
entries.x: The Carpal Tunnel An osseofibrous tunnel . Its floor is the carpal bones (hamate, capitate, trapezoid, trapezium) and its roof the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament), which runs from the scaphoid and trapezium to the pisiform and hook of the hamate. Within the tunnel Superficial to the tunnel Median nerve , flexor pollicis longus , the 4 FDS tendons and the 4 FDP tendons , in their synovial sheaths Flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, the ulnar artery and nerve , flexor carpi ulnaris The carpal tunnel is deep to the flexor retinaculum. FDS tendons are stacked (3 and 4 over 2 and 5), which is why you can't find all four at once in the lab. Slide from the deck (Netter). Why the Median Nerve Suffers Anything that shrinks the tunnel squeezes it, and the median nerve is the most sensitive structure inside . The commonest cause is inflammation of the synovial sheaths (these line tendons running through osseofibrous tunnels to cut friction); fluid retention, infection and overuse can swell them too. Compression numbs the lateral palm and lateral 3½ digits and weakens the thumb's intrinsic muscles, but not the mid-palm patch of the palmar cutaneous branch.

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 2
entries.x: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Compression of the median nerve at the wrist . By far the most common nerve problem seen anywhere in the body: "the bread and butter peripheral nerve diagnosis". Causes Examples Extrinsic (less space) Fracture; flexor tenosynovitis (the finger flexor tendons share the space; probably part of "repetitive use" CTS, e.g. typing); ganglia; inflammation (e.g. RA); pregnancy (edema, quite common); acromegaly Intrinsic (a more susceptible nerve) Diabetes , amyloidosis, alcohol Idiopathic Very common; perhaps an anatomically smaller tunnel Clinical presentation Detail Numbness and tingling in median territory The main symptom. Often worse at night (hands tucked under the head) and with a flexed or extended wrist (driving, holding a phone), because tunnel pressure rises in those positions. Thumb weakness (APB) Only once it's advanced enough to disrupt the motor fibres Median function above the tunnel is normal All the median-supplied forearm muscles work, since the nerve is fine until the compression point Tinel's sign Tapping over the median nerve at the base of the hand sends tingling into median territory Phalen's sign Holding both wrists hyperflexed, backs of the hands together, brings on numbness and tingling in the fingers Differential: Is It the Wrist or the Neck? The main item is C6 radiculopathy : C6 and the median nerve both cover the thumb, so a numb thumb could come from the neck (with symptoms down the lateral arm) rather than the tunnel. Also consider tendinopathy around the thumb (tingling isn't always neurologic) and CMC osteoarthritis at the base of the thumb. EMG/NCS objectively test the sensory and motor nerve, the neuromuscular junction and the muscle: they separate nerve from muscle or bone, tell CTS from C6, and grade how damaged the nerve is (for prognosis and planning). You don't need the details of how they work yet. 1 Education A common problem. Explain which hand positions provoke it, and that caught early it's quite reversible with simple non-invasive care. 2 Non-pharmacologic: the mainstay, especially when mild A rigid wrist–hand orthosis worn overnight only : it holds the wrist near neutral, widening the tunnel and lowering its pressure for the hours you sleep. It can reverse mild and sometimes moderate CTS. Avoid aggravating positions and vibratory tools . 3 Pharmacologic Not oral or topical drugs, but a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel to shrink the swelling. Often not long term if the swelling r

entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 2
entries.x: Ulnar Neuropathy at the Wrist The elbow is by far the commonest place for the ulnar nerve to get into trouble (see 8.7 ), but Guyon's canal is a second entrapment point, a tight space it shares with the ulnar artery. Ulnar neuropathy at the wrist Causes Mostly extrinsic (intrinsic nerve problems like diabetes rarely cause it here): fracture of the carpal bones, ganglia, inflammation, and most commonly direct compression : handlebar neuropathy in cyclists, or pressure from crutches and canes Presentation Hypoesthesia of the medial 1½ digits (4 and 5) and intrinsic hand muscle weakness ; when advanced, a scooped-out look between the thumb and index finger and along the hand Differential Main item: C8 radiculopathy (also numbs digits 4–5); also ulnar neuropathy at the elbow and tendinopathy. EMG/NCS tell nerve from muscle or bone, elbow from wrist from C8, and grade severity. Management Education about hand position and pressure (reversible if caught early). Relieve the pressure: padded gloves, new handlebars, adjusted gait-aid handles . Few drugs or injections (it's mechanical). Guyon's (canal) release if needed. Knowledge check Numbness and tingling in the index finger and thumb: which would NOT be high on your differential? → C8 radiculopathy , ulnar neuropathy at the elbow and ulnar neuropathy at the wrist . The index finger sits in the C6 dermatome and median territory , so carpal tunnel syndrome and C6 radiculopathy both fit; ulnar and C8 problems numb digits 4 and 5.

entries.t: Clinical Approach to the Upper Extremity Quiz
entries.p: Clinical Approach to the Wrist & Hand, Part 2
entries.x: Clinical Approach to the Upper Extremity Quiz The module's 10-minute quiz, mostly on Part 1's fractures. The radiographs and clinical photos aren't shown; the answers and the feedback are below. A 26-year-old falls off a mountain bike onto her wrist Best x-ray description? → intra-articular, shortened radius, dorsally tilted radius . Initial treatment? → closed reduction and immobilization : displaced fractures are reduced and immobilized first. After closed reduction and casting under a hematoma block, is the reduction satisfactory? → no: neither the length nor the articular tilt is corrected . She has ORIF. Three months later she suddenly can't flex the thumb's IP joint; sensation is normal. → flexor pollicis longus rupture . No sensory symptoms, so not carpal tunnel syndrome; an anterior interosseous nerve injury would also weaken FDP to the index and middle fingers, and nerve injuries show up right after the injury or surgery; the first dorsal interosseous doesn't flex the thumb IP; adhesions appear soon after surgery, not at three months. An 81-year-old trips on a rug (type 2 diabetes, COPD) Displaced distal radius fracture, closed reduction and cast; the post-reduction film still shows a short, dorsally tilted radius. Plan? → cast until it heals, then range-of-motion and strengthening exercises . The injury is forgiving in older people, and surgery doesn't beat closed treatment. Three days later: more pain, numb thumb, index and middle fingers, pain on passive finger movement. → split the whole length of the cast and padding down to skin, and elevate the arm . The cast is too tight, causing acute carpal tunnel syndrome and possibly early compartment syndrome . Reassess every 15–20 minutes. Don't give steroids or stronger painkillers, which can mask compartment syndrome. His symptoms settled within 60 minutes; he went home in a split (bivalved) cast. A 63-year-old with 24 hours of index finger pain after gardening Increasing pain on the palmar side of the finger and less movement; redness along the palmar finger. Two most likely? → the key gives flexor tenosynovitis and septic arthritis . The feedback: the redness sits over the flexor tendon sheath , so cellulitis (usually worse dorsally) is less likely; septic arthritis hurts with joint movement but isn't tender along the sheath; the skin injury makes gout and psoriasis unlikely. It was flexor tenosynovitis with all the cardinal signs, treated with irrigation and debridement . A 19-year-old motocross
