Learning Objectives Define and use fundamental neuroanatomical terms ; separate structural from functional organization. Identify the major regions of the brain, spinal cord and PNS , and the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain. Identify the lobes and the functions of the motor, somatosensory and visual cortices. Describe the basal ganglia and cerebellum in motor control and movement disorders. Describe CT and MRI and what each shows. A 100-minute module by Dr. Andrew Deweyert (anatomy and cell biology): six recordings (organizing principles; cortex and basal ganglia; brainstem, spinal cord, ventricles and vessels; and an optional lab demonstration with cranial nerves and the arterial circle on specimens). Why it matters: knowing what lives where lets you localize a lesion from the symptoms ( 12.4 ), and the meninges explain epidural, subdural and subarachnoid bleeds.

Divisions of the Nervous System CNS and PNS. From the deck. Anatomical Functional CNS : brain and spinal cord, in the skull and vertebral canal, protected by meninges and CSF . Role: integration and coordination . PNS : spinal nerves, cranial nerves, ganglia, sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves Sensory input (afferent, from inside and outside the body) → integration (process, interpret, decide) → motor output (efferent, to muscles and glands) Simple vs complex: stepping on a sharp object fires a reflex that never needs the brain (fast, for survival); planning universal health care needs the whole cortex. Part of the brain Made of Brainstem Medulla + pons + midbrain Cerebellum Grows embryologically out of the pons but is its own region Diencephalon Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus (subthalamus on the slide) Cerebrum Two hemispheres = 80% of brain mass Grey matter inside, white matter around it, hollow ventricles in the middle; the cerebrum and cerebellum add an outer sheet of grey matter, a cortex . All other brain grey matter sits in clusters called nuclei .

Directions and Planes Rostral/caudal and dorsal/ventral bend with the neuraxis at the midbrain–diencephalon junction. From the deck. Plane Cut Coronal Dorsal to ventral (like a slice of bread facing you) Horizontal (axial) Parallel to the horizon: how CT and most MRI are viewed Sagittal Front to back, splitting left from right

Neuroimaging T1, T2, FLAIR. From the deck. Modality Shows Use X-ray Bone only ; nervous tissue invisible Bony abnormalities CT Sections at ~ 2 mm resolution; brightness by density; lesions differ in density from brain Fast (acute bleed, trauma) MRI T1 CNS tissue vs fluid; some grey–white contrast; CSF dark Anatomy MRI T2 CSF bright ; less grey–white contrast Fluid, edema FLAIR No CSF signal White matter abnormalities (e.g., MS plaques)

Fissures, Sulci and Gyri Term Meaning Longitudinal fissure Separates the right and left hemispheres Transverse cerebral fissure Separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum Sulcus A shallow groove Gyrus A ridge between sulci Corpus callosum The big white-matter bridge between the hemispheres

The Lobes Lobes and their jobs. From the deck. Lobe Functions Boundary / site Frontal Voluntary movement , planning movement, eye movement , speech production ; executive function In front of the central sulcus ; anterior cranial fossa Parietal Sensory processing , spatial awareness , understanding speech Behind the central sulcus, in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus Temporal Auditory and olfactory cortex; recognizing objects, words, faces ; memory Below the lateral sulcus ; middle cranial fossa Occipital Visual cortex Behind the parieto-occipital sulcus Insula Taste (gustatory) , general visceral sensation Hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by frontal, parietal and temporal lobes Limbic Emotion and memory (with the limbic system) Medial surface: cingulate and parahippocampal gyri The limbic lobe on the medial surface. From the deck.

Basal Ganglia Caudate + putamen = striatum ; substantia nigra in the midbrain. From the deck. A set of deep forebrain nuclei that integrate cortical activity into one motor output : they set the intensity and speed of movement, initiate it, run rhythmic repetitive tasks and help learn habits. Lesions don't cause weakness ; they cause slowness and rigidity (parkinsonism) or extra movements (chorea, dystonia, hemiballismus). The basal forebrain nuclei make acetylcholine (arousal, learning, memory); their degeneration is linked to Alzheimer's disease .

Diencephalon The relay hub. From the deck. Part Function Thalamus Sensory nuclei for every conscious sense except smell ; everything going to the cortex relays through a thalamic nucleus . Links to the limbic system (memory, emotion), basal ganglia (motor coordination) and primary sensory areas. Hypothalamus The visceral control centre : autonomic nervous system (HR, BP, digestion, glands), emotion and motivation, temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep , the endocrine system . The mammillary bodies (memory; Papez circuit) are hypothalamic. Epithalamus Most dorsal; the pineal gland makes melatonin (sleep at night)

entries.t: The Three Parts of the Brainstem
entries.x: The Three Parts of the Brainstem Part (rostral → caudal) Function Anterior landmarks Posterior landmarks CN nuclei Midbrain Motor control, visual and auditory reflexes Cerebral peduncles (with the interpeduncular fossa between), mammillary bodies just above Tectum : superior colliculi (visual reflexes) and inferior colliculi (auditory reflexes) III, IV Pons Relay station (cerebrum ↔ cerebellum via pontine nuclei); movement coordination; facial expression The bulging pons (the giveaway for the anterior surface) Superior, middle, inferior cerebellar peduncles ; floor of the 4th ventricle V, VI, VII, VIII Medulla Vital autonomic centres : breathing, heart rate, blood pressure (vasomotor), digestion; cough, sneeze, swallow, hiccup Pyramids (motor tracts; most fibres cross at the decussation of the pyramids ) and olives lateral to them Fasciculus gracilis (leg) and cuneatus (arm) bumps; obex IX, X, XI*, XII * CN XI nuclei sit in the rostral cervical cord . The decussation of the pyramids is why each hemisphere moves the opposite side of the body. Anterior brainstem. From the deck. Posterior brainstem (cerebellum removed). From the deck.

entries.t: Cranial Nerves and the Rule of 4
entries.x: Cranial Nerves and the Rule of 4 The 12 nerves on the inferior surface. From the deck. Level Nerve Where it leaves Forebrain I Olfactory Olfactory tract and bulb on the cribriform plate, directly off the cortex II Optic Off the forebrain; the optic chiasm sits in the midline Midbrain III Oculomotor The interpeduncular fossa , between the cerebral peduncles IV Trochlear The only nerve off the posterior brainstem , just below the inferior colliculi; thin, long course wrapping around (often torn in dissection); one muscle Pons V Trigeminal Big and chunky, lateral mid-pons VI Abducens Pontomedullary junction, in the midline VII Facial Pontomedullary junction, laterally, one after the other; travel together through the internal acoustic meatus VIII Vestibulocochlear Medulla IX Glossopharyngeal Wisps behind the olive (hard to tell apart) X Vagus XI Spinal accessory Rootlets from the upper cervical cord (and medulla); climbs up through the foramen magnum , exits the jugular foramen XII Hypoglossal Between the pyramid and the olive (the only one there); in line with the cervical roots; tongue Why the Rule of 4 Matters Four nerves at or above the midbrain, four in the pons, four in the medulla and below. A brainstem lesion with a CN VI or VII palsy is in the pons ; with XII , the medulla ; with III , the midbrain . (Rule 1 of the “four rules of four”; the rest come in the brainstem lectures.) Nuclei by level. From the deck.

Spinal Cord and Its Tracts Horns, roots and rami. From the deck (adapted from Dr. Charys Martin). Ascending (left) and descending (right) tracts. From the deck. Structure Carries Dorsal grey horn / dorsal root (with the dorsal root ganglion) Sensory in Ventral grey horn / ventral root Motor out Ventral ramus All the limbs and the front of the body Dorsal ramus Only the deep (intrinsic) back muscles and the skin over them The five key tracts Direction Carries Dorsal columns : fasciculus gracilis (medial, lower limb) and cuneatus (lateral, upper limb) Ascending Fine touch, vibration, proprioception Spinothalamic (lateral + ventral) Ascending Pain and temperature Spinocerebellar (dorsal + ventral) Ascending Proprioception to the cerebellum Lateral corticospinal Descending Primary motor to the limbs Corticobulbar Descending Ends in the brainstem : motor to cranial nerve nuclei (facial expression)

The Ventricular System and CSF The ventricles. From the deck. Choroid plexus and CSF flow. From the deck. Ventricle Where Lateral × 2 (formerly 1st and 2nd) C-shaped, one per hemisphere: anterior horn (frontal), posterior horn (occipital), inferior horn (temporal) Third Midline slit between the two thalami (diencephalon); joined to each lateral ventricle by an interventricular foramen Cerebral aqueduct Through the midbrain , 3rd → 4th Fourth Between the pons/medulla and the cerebellum ; continues as the central canal; lateral and medial apertures open to the subarachnoid space 1 Made By ependymal cells of the choroid plexus (in every ventricle). 2 Flows Lateral ventricle → interventricular foramen → 3rd → aqueduct → 4th → apertures → subarachnoid space around the brain and cord. 3 Absorbed At the top of the brain through arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses . CSF floats and cleans the brain. Block the flow or make too much and you get hydrocephalus (obstructive or communicating): expanded ventricles with mass effect.

Blood–Brain Barrier Four layers between blood and brain. From the deck. Keeps circulating substances out of the CSF/CNS (the brain is a privileged site , like the testes). Four components: tight junctions , basement membrane , astrocyte foot processes (the astrocytes maintain the barrier and do the active transport), pericytes . Everything crosses by active transport except non-polar, lipid-soluble substances, which diffuse rapidly. That's why many drugs (chemotherapy, antiepileptics) struggle to reach the brain.

Arteries and Venous Sinuses Middle meningeal artery : rupture = epidural hematoma . From the deck. The cerebral arterial circle (circle of Willis). From the deck. Vessel Key point Middle meningeal artery Branch of the external carotid , enters via the foramen spinosum , supplies the dura . Rupture (often a temporal skull fracture) → arterial bleed into the epidural space : dangerous. Vertebral → basilar Up through the foramen magnum; the basilar supplies brainstem and cerebellum (AICA, PICA) and ends as the posterior cerebrals Internal carotid Enters the skull through the carotid canal ; gives the MCA and ACA MCA Runs laterally : lateral frontal and parietal, temporal lobes, the motor and sensory cortex for the face and hand/arm ACA Runs along the midline (longitudinal fissure): medial surface, the cortex for the leg, foot and genitals PCA Posteriorly: occipital lobe Anterior / posterior communicating Close the circle: ACom joins the two ACAs; PCom joins the PCA to the internal carotid. Important for occlusions, aneurysms and watershed zones. Dural venous sinuses. From the deck. Venous drainage: superior sagittal sinus (receives CSF via the arachnoid granulations) and inferior sagittal → straight sinus meet at the confluence of the sinuses → transverse → S-shaped sigmoid → jugular foramen → internal jugular vein.

Practice Questions (from the lecture notes) 1. The central sulcus separates which lobes? Answer Frontal and parietal. 2. Which cell maintains the blood–brain barrier: neurons, microglia, ependymal cells, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes? Answer Astrocytes (ependymal cells make CSF). 3. Which imaging best detects white matter abnormalities? Answer FLAIR MRI. 4. The insular cortex: spatial awareness, visual cortex, gustatory cortex, object recognition or speech? Answer Gustatory (taste) cortex. 5. The midbrain is associated with which cranial nerves? Answer III and IV. 6. The dorsal grey horn transmits sensory or motor information? Answer Sensory. 7. After a blow to the temple, a man is lucid for an hour, then deteriorates. Which vessel, which space? Answer Middle meningeal artery → epidural hematoma (arterial, between skull and dura).

Learning Objectives Outline the Neuroscience, Eye and Ear block. Define common terms used in neurology. Discuss why localizing the lesion and the differential diagnosis matter in focal neurological symptoms. Describe the organization of the nervous system, microscopic to macroscopic. Dr. Christen Shoesmith (neurology): a 20-minute introduction (recorded) plus optional review chapters from her Foundations of Medicine lecture (75 min of text: organization, motor and sensory/visual pathways, localization, lesion differential and four practice cases). The block: weeks 1–1.5 neuroanatomy and neurophysiology; 1.5–4 clinical neurology and neurosurgery; week 4 eye and ear. ~10% of family-practice visits are for a neurological symptom.

The Vocabulary Term Meaning -plegia Paralysis : essentially no voluntary movement -paresis Weakness Hemiplegia Can't move one arm and the same-side leg Paraparesis Weakness of both legs Quadriparesis / quadriplegia Weakness of / inability to move all four limbs Dysarthria Trouble with articulation (the mechanics of speech) Aphasia Trouble producing or understanding language Dysphagia Trouble swallowing Ataxia Trouble with coordination Dysmetria Trouble reaching a target (overshoot, undershoot) Obtunded Reduced awareness; can't be fully roused Dominant hemisphere Where language lives: the left in nearly all right-handers and most left-handers (27% of left-handers are right-dominant)

From Neuron to Brain The neuron : impulses run dendrite → cell body → myelinated axon → synapse. From the module (NICHD). Main cortical regions. From the module. Level Components Microscopic Neurons generate, modify and transmit impulses; supporting cells include myelin-makers that insulate axons CNS Brain (cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem) and spinal cord. Grey matter : cortex (folded into gyri), basal ganglia, thalamus, nuclei. White matter : myelinated axon tracts joining one area to another. PNS Cranial nerves, nerve roots (axons entering/leaving the cord), nerves, neuromuscular junction , muscle, sensory receptors Deep grey matter. From the module. Structure Does Lesion gives Meninges Connective tissue covering the brain Meningitis = infection of them Ventricles Hold CSF, which is made constantly and absorbed into the veins Blocked flow → hydrocephalus (↑ volume and pressure) Basal ganglia Execution of movement: initiation, speed, motor learning Parkinsonism or extra movements Thalamus Integrates sensory and motor information; relays sensation to the cortex Cerebellum Coordination : fine-tunes speech, swallowing, limbs, gait Incoordination, not weakness Brainstem Midbrain, pons, medulla: all cranial nerve nuclei ; tracts in and out Spinal cord Cervical (C1–C8), thoracic (T1–T12), lumbosacral (L1–S4) segments; ends at ~L1 vertebra ; below it the roots float as the cauda equina

entries.t: The Motor Pathway, UMN and LMN
entries.x: The Motor Pathway, UMN and LMN Central motor pathway : one neuron from cortex to anterior horn (up to 60 cm long). From the module. Peripheral motor pathway : 1 anterior horn cell, 2 nerve, 3 NMJ, 4 muscle. From the module. 1 Motor cortex (frontal lobe) Plans the movement, on the opposite side to the moving limb. 2 Internal capsule → brainstem Axons descend through white matter; cross in the medulla (pyramids). 3 Spinal cord → anterior horn cell Synapse at the level of the intended movement. Everything to here = UMN . 4 Root → nerve → NMJ → muscle Acetylcholine at the NMJ triggers contraction. From the anterior horn cell on = LMN . Upper motor neuron (UMN) Lower motor neuron (LMN) Localizations Brain, brainstem, spinal cord Anterior horn cell, root, plexus, nerve, NMJ, muscle Reflexes Hyperactive Reduced or absent Plantar Extensor (Babinski) Flexor or absent Tone Spasticity Normal (or low) Atrophy No Yes Fasciculations No May be present LMN sign: atrophy of the right first dorsal interosseous. Compare sides, and know normal bulk. From the module. Weak or Just Clumsy? Cerebellum and basal ganglia loop back to the motor cortex to refine movement (cerebellum = accuracy; basal ganglia = control and timing). Their lesions don't cause weakness . Cerebellum: incoordination; picture someone drunk (slurred speech, clumsy limbs, unsteady gait). Basal ganglia: hard to start, slow, rigid ( parkinsonism ), or too much movement ( chorea, dystonia, athetosis, hemiballismus ).

The Homunculus Leg medial, face lateral, hand next to face. From the notes (UCSF). Medial → lateral Artery So… Leg, foot (medial surface) ACA ACA stroke: contralateral leg > arm Shoulder → hand → face, mouth, tongue (lateral) MCA MCA stroke: contralateral face and arm > leg The hand sits next to the face : an expanding lesion in the face area weakens the hand and thumb before the elbow or shoulder .

Sensory and Visual Pathways Sensory route: receptor → peripheral nerve → root → spinal cord → brainstem → thalamus → subcortical white matter → primary sensory cortex → association cortex. Nice to know Dorsal column Spinothalamic Carries Vibration, proprioception Pain, temperature In the cord Dorsal; same side as the input Lateral; opposite side Crosses In the medulla At entry to the cord The visual pathway. From the module (Geeky Medics). Colour key : left eye sees green (left field) and yellow (right field); right eye sees blue and red. From the module. Where Carries Lesion Retina / optic nerve (before the chiasm) Everything one eye sees Monocular loss Optic chiasm (“crossing”) The left hemifield of each eye goes to the right tract, and vice versa Optic tract → visual cortex (behind the chiasm) The opposite visual field from both eyes : left cortex = whole right field Same-side field loss in both eyes (homonymous) The retina receives the image flipped and inverted (a camera obscura); the occipital pole processes it.

The Neurological Approach 1 What is the problem? History and exam: summarize the symptoms and signs. 2 Where is the lesion? Use logic on the signs to localize. 3 What is the differential? From the rate of onset and progression , demographics, other symptoms and the localization. Most likely? What must I not miss (treatable, serious)? 4 Investigations and treatment Chosen by the localization and differential. Why Localize? It narrows the diagnosis and picks the test: don't order a CT head for a spinal cord problem , or a spine MRI for a muscle problem . Nerve and muscle problems need EMG and nerve conduction studies , not imaging.

How to Localize Step Ask 1. CNS or PNS? UMN features (brisk reflexes, spasticity, Babinski) → CNS . LMN features (↓ reflexes, atrophy, fasciculations) → PNS . 2. Narrow it down Cortical signs? Language impairment or neglect = cortex Sensation spared? Anterior horn cell, NMJ and muscle disorders spare sensation Painful? Root problems usually hurt Distribution? Does it fit a root, nerve or pattern? Bladder? Suggests spinal cord or cauda equina Pattern of weakness Localization Hemibody with face or cranial nerves Brain Hemibody, no face or cranial nerves (Cervical) spinal cord Quadriparesis Cervical cord Paraparesis Thoracic cord or lumbar roots One myotome A root One nerve's territory / several nerves Mononeuropathy / multiple Eyes and swallowing Neuromuscular junction Generalized proximal Muscle Cord vs roots: the cord ends at about L1 . Lesions at L1 and above give a UMN pattern; below L1 (cauda equina) an LMN pattern. Cord segments and what they run. From the module.

entries.t: The Differential: Time Course and VITAMINS C&D
entries.x: The Differential: Time Course and VITAMINS C&D Onset Think Hyperacute (seconds–minutes) Stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic), migraine aura (resolves over minutes), trauma Acute (hours–a couple of days) Inflammation, infection Subacute (days–weeks) Inflammation, infection, tumour , toxic (and slowly growing bleeds) Chronic (months–years) Degenerative , hereditary VITAMINS C&D V ascular · I nfectious · T rauma · A utoimmune · M etabolic · I nflammatory/iatrogenic · N eoplastic · S eizure/p S ychogenic · C ongenital · D egenerative Sudden aphasia: the differential Ischemic stroke · intracranial hemorrhage · migraine · post-ictal Todd's paresis · metabolic upset on top of an old structural lesion (e.g., hypoglycemia ) · psychogenic Language: expressive (motor) language is in the inferior frontal lobe , receptive in the posterior temporal lobe , both in the dominant hemisphere.

The Four Practice Cases 1. A 44-year-old physician sees flashing lights on her right; covering either eye, both right half-fields are distorted. It lasts 20 minutes, then a throbbing left headache. Localization and diagnosis The right field of both eyes = behind the chiasm ; vision only, no other deficits → left occipital (visual) cortex (the left optic tract is possible but sits beside too many other structures). Hyperacute but gone in 20 minutes and followed by headache → migraine aura . If it had persisted: occipital stroke. 2. A 75-year-old: 2 months ago trouble naming objects, 1 month ago wrong words, this week sentences make no sense. Slight right facial droop, poor naming and repetition, follows commands, normal reflexes. Localization and diagnosis Aphasia + right face → left cerebral cortex (dominant). Subacute progression over 2 months fits infection, tumour, inflammation or a slowly growing bleed ; strokes are sudden and then improve, and Alzheimer's progresses over years. CT: a chronic subdural hematoma over the left hemisphere with midline shift. Elderly people get them after even minor trauma ; acute blood is white on CT, chronic blood turns dark . 3. A 68-year-old woman: 3 weeks of worsening gait with falls, clumsy hands, urinary frequency and urgency. Mild bilateral hip flexor weakness, very brisk reflexes in arms and legs, both toes up, poor vibration at both great toes, wide unsteady gait. Localization and diagnosis UMN (brisk reflexes, Babinski). Bilateral and symmetric (one brain lesion would be one-sided), with bladder symptoms → spinal cord ; hands involved → cervical (a thoracic lesion spares the hands). MRI: cervical spondylotic myelopathy , cord compressed at C4/C5 by degenerative discs and vertebrae, with bright signal (injury) in the cord. 4. A 59-year-old woman: 6 months of low energy, feeling stiff and slowed down; no sensory or bladder symptoms. Reduced blinking, soft voice, normal power and reflexes, mild rigidity in both arms, slow finger taps, reduced arm swing. Localization and diagnosis Slow movement with normal strength and reflexes = basal ganglia . Slowly progressive → Parkinson's disease .
